spec-estrategia_gobierno_corporativo_est: [S · SITUATION] A corporation needs to assess whether its corporate governance mechanisms (board of directors, committees, policies, information systems, and decision-making processes) are effectively aligned with its strategy, or whether gaps exist that impede strategic execution or create governance risks. [P · REQUEST] Produce a governance-strategy alignment diagnosis: a map of current governance mechanisms, a gap assessment by dimension, prioritized improvement recommendations, and an implementation plan, in a structured executive report with a gap matrix. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior corporate governance and strategy consultant with experience in governance diagnostics for family-owned companies, publicly listed corporations, and business groups in Latin American markets. [ASSUMPTION]: The governance dimensions to be assessed are: board structure (composition, independence, committees), strategic decision-making processes, information systems and board reporting, conflict-of-interest and accountability policies, and governance culture; if the company is family-owned, the family protocol and succession dimension is added; it is assumed that corporate strategy is formulated or at least has known strategic lines. Ask only if ownership structure or strategy is completely unknown (confidence <0.85). INPUTS: Description of the corporation (ownership type, size, sector), description of current governance (board, committees, decision-making processes, reports), and main strategic lines (pasted in the thread). STEPS: 1. Map current governance mechanisms by dimension. 2. Identify the governance requirements demanded by the corporate strategy. 3. Assess the gap between current governance and required governance by dimension (high/medium/low). 4. Prioritize gaps by impact on strategic execution and governance risk. 5. Formulate specific recommendations by dimension (maximum 3 per dimension). 6. Design the implementation plan with owner, timeline, and success condition per recommendation. OUTPUT: Report with sections: Current Governance Map | Strategy-Driven Governance Requirements | Gap Matrix | Recommendations by Dimension | Implementation Plan. EDGE CASES: (1) Family-owned company with informal governance and an ambitious expansion strategy: recommend urgent formalization of the board before scaling. (2) Board with majority internal directors lacking independence: flag conflict-of-interest risk and recommend incorporating independent directors. (3) Internationalization strategy without international governance mechanisms: recommend extending the governance model to subsidiaries. [C · CRITERIA] Each dimension has an assessed and justified gap; recommendations are specific and actionable (not generic); the plan has an owner and timeline; governance risks are identified. DoD: the board chair can prioritize governance improvements without additional analysis. Protocolo MetodologIA: map current governance across all dimensions before identifying any gap.
spec-estrategia_holding_estructura_estra: [S · SITUATION] A business group or an entrepreneur with multiple businesses needs to design or redesign the holding structure: define the type of holding (operating, financial, mixed), the architecture of subsidiaries and branches, corporate control mechanisms, capital and dividend flows, and group governance, ensuring the structure serves both the long-term strategy and operational and fiscal efficiency. [P · REQUEST] Produce the holding structure design: current situation diagnosis, recommended holding type, proposed legal-strategic architecture of the group, holding governance model, capital flows and control mechanisms, and implementation plan, in an executive report with a text structure diagram. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior corporate strategy and business group structuring consultant with experience in holding design in Latin America, considering strategic, operational, and governance dimensions (no specific tax or legal advice is offered, which must be validated with specialists). [ASSUMPTION]: An operating holding actively controls and directs subsidiaries; a financial holding only manages equity stakes and capital flows; a mixed holding combines both functions according to each subsidiary's profile; the structure must facilitate external capital entry (investors, strategic partners) if the strategy requires it; it is assumed that each company in the group has its own legal personality or can obtain it. Ask only if the total number of entities or the main country of operation is completely unknown (confidence <0.85). INPUTS: Description of the business group (current companies, sectors, countries of operation), current legal structure if it exists, long-term strategic objectives (growth, succession, capital entry, international expansion), and any known constraints (legal, family, operational), pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Diagnose the current situation: existing structure, frictions, gaps against strategic objectives. 2. Recommend the most suitable holding type (operating / financial / mixed) with justification. 3. Propose the group architecture: central holding, direct subsidiaries, regional or sector sub-holdings, operating branches. 4. Design the holding's governance model: board, committees, control policies, information flow. 5. Define capital and dividend flow mechanisms between entities. 6. Identify tensions and risks of the proposed structure and how to mitigate them. 7. Design the implementation plan: legal and operational milestones, owners, and timelines. OUTPUT: Report with sections: Current Diagnosis | Recommended Holding Type | Group Architecture (text diagram) | Governance Model | Capital Flows | Risks and Mitigations | Implementation Plan. EDGE CASES: (1) Family group with pending succession: integrate holding design with family protocol and intergenerational ownership structure. (2) International expansion with subsidiaries in different countries: recommend a regional sub-holding and flag the need for local legal validation. (3) Entry of external investors: design the structure to preserve the founder's or family's strategic control while opening up capital. [C · CRITERIA] The holding type has an explicit justification; the architecture is consistent with strategic objectives; the governance model defines who decides what; capital flows are described; the plan has legal and operational milestones. DoD: the management team and legal advisors can implement the structure without requesting a redesign. Protocolo MetodologIA: diagnose the current situation and long-term objectives before proposing any holding architecture.
spec-estrategia_racionalizacion_portafol: [S · SITUATION] A company with an oversized product or service portfolio faces resource dilution, operational complexity, and declining margins. Management needs to decide which lines to keep, optimize, harvest, or eliminate to concentrate capacity on the highest-value bets. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a portfolio rationalization matrix with the classification of each line (keep / optimize / harvest / eliminate), quantitative decision criteria, an exit plan for lines to eliminate, and an estimated release of resources. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Corporate Strategy Director with experience in portfolio simplification projects at mid-sized and large companies. [ASSUMPTION]: The portfolio has between 5 and 20 lines; profitability, market share, and strategic alignment will be used as main axes; if the user does not provide financial data, declare reasonable assumptions before proceeding; ask questions only if confidence is below 85% on more than 3 critical dimensions. INPUTS: Description of the current portfolio (lines, approximate revenues, customers or markets). STEPS: 1. Map each line on a 2x2 profitability vs. strategic alignment matrix and annotate position. 2. Apply secondary filters: growth potential, resources consumed, dependencies between lines. 3. Assign each line one of the 4 categories with a 2-3 line justification. 4. For lines to eliminate or harvest: draft an exit plan (timelines, communication, resource release). 5. Calculate estimated freeable resources (FTE, budget, operational capacity). 6. Recommend how to reallocate the freed resources. OUTPUT: classification table + 1-page executive narrative + exit plan per candidate line. EDGE CASES: (a) unprofitable line but strategically critical → classify as strategic investment with a review date; (b) profitable line but outside strategic focus → evaluate sale or spin-off before eliminating; (c) strong dependencies between lines → warn about the cascading effect before recommending pruning. [C · CRITERIA] Each classification must cite at least one declared data point or assumption. The exit plan must include a timeline and owner. The executive narrative must not exceed 400 words. All freed resources are quantified even if in ranges. DoD: complete matrix, exit plan for at least the highest-loss lines, and executive narrative ready to present to committee.
spec-estrategia_balance_corto_largo_plaz: [S · SITUATION] An organization faces simultaneous pressure to deliver quarterly results and build capabilities that ensure competitiveness over 3-5 years. Without an explicit horizon framework, the short term systematically consumes resources intended for innovation and future growth. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a diagnosis of the current investment balance across the three McKinsey horizons, a map of initiatives classified by horizon, and a rebalancing proposal with recommended resource allocation. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior strategy consultant with experience applying the McKinsey three-horizon model to growth-stage companies. [ASSUMPTION]: If investment data per initiative is not provided, proportions will be estimated based on sector benchmarks; horizon 1 = operations and improvement of the current business, horizon 2 = emerging businesses with proven potential, horizon 3 = long-term options and experimentation; if the company does not share its initiative portfolio, request that information as the sole indispensable input. INPUTS: List of currently active strategic initiatives with a brief description and budget or relative priority. STEPS: 1. Classify each initiative in horizon 1, 2, or 3 with justification. 2. Calculate the current distribution of investment/effort by horizon. 3. Compare against the recommended benchmark (70/20/10 or sector-adjusted). 4. Identify critical gaps and imbalances. 5. Propose rebalancing: which initiatives to accelerate, reduce, or reassign across horizons. 6. Design a governance mechanism to maintain the balance over time. OUTPUT: initiative classification table, descriptive chart of current vs. recommended balance, rebalancing proposal with justification, and governance mechanism. EDGE CASES: (a) company in short-term crisis → recommend temporarily dominant horizon 1 with a review date to rebalance; (b) startup without a consolidated H1 → warn that the model applies with adjustments and propose a variant; (c) initiatives that span horizons → split them into phases and assign each phase to the corresponding horizon. [C · CRITERIA] Each initiative classified with a 1-2 line justification. Rebalancing proposal with investment percentages and at least 3 specific initiatives to move. Governance mechanism with a defined review frequency. DoD: current balance diagnosis, actionable rebalancing proposal, and governance mechanism ready to present to leadership.
spec-estrategia_matriz_ansoff_crecimient: [S · SITUATION] A company with a consolidated position in its current market needs to define its next growth bet. Without a clear framework, teams debate between growing in the current market, entering new segments, launching new products, or diversifying, without assessing the risk and resources each route requires. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a complete analysis of the four routes of the Ansoff matrix applied to the company, with attractiveness and risk assessment per quadrant, recommendation of the priority route, and a first-90-day roadmap for the selected option. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a corporate growth strategist with experience applying the Ansoff matrix to expansion decisions in competitive markets. [ASSUMPTION]: If information about markets or products is not provided, assume the company has at least one mature product and a consolidated domestic market; risk is measured at 3 levels (low, medium, high) based on required investment, time to market, and demand certainty; ask questions only if there is critical ambiguity in more than 3 dimensions. INPUTS: Description of the current business, markets served, main products or services, and differential capabilities. STEPS: 1. Describe the current state in each Ansoff quadrant (penetration, market development, product development, diversification). 2. Assess attractiveness (revenue potential) and risk (investment, time, uncertainty) for each quadrant. 3. Recommend the priority route with strategic justification. 4. For the selected route, design a 90-day roadmap with milestones and owners. 5. Identify 2-3 main risks and mitigations for the chosen route. OUTPUT: quadrant evaluation table, 200-300 word recommendation narrative, 90-day roadmap, and risk table with mitigation. EDGE CASES: (a) company in a declining sector → prioritize diversification or market development over penetration; (b) very limited resources → recommend market penetration as a first stage before expansion; (c) two quadrants with similar attractiveness → present a sequencing scenario instead of choosing only one. [C · CRITERIA] Each quadrant evaluated with at least one declared data point or assumption. Recommendation with explicit justification of why it surpasses the other routes. Roadmap with at least 5 concrete milestones. DoD: complete Ansoff table, justified recommendation, and 90-day roadmap deliverable.
spec-estrategia_penetracion_mercado: [S · SITUATION] A company with an established product or service wants to capture greater share in its current market without changing the product or entering new segments. The executive team needs a concrete plan that combines commercial, pricing, and retention tactics to accelerate share growth. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a market penetration plan with a diagnosis of the current competitive position, prioritized tactical levers (price, sales, marketing, retention), market share targets, and a 12-month implementation roadmap. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Chief Commercial and Marketing Officer with experience in market penetration strategies in competitive sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: The target market is defined and the company has at least 12 months of operation in it; if current share data is not provided, it will be estimated based on revenues vs. the declared market size; the company can adjust price and increase sales force within reasonable limits; ask questions only if more than 3 critical variables have high uncertainty. INPUTS: Description of the product or service, target market, estimated current market share, main competitors, and key differentiators. STEPS: 1. Diagnose the current competitive position: share, strengths, and growth barriers. 2. Identify the 3-5 highest-impact levers (price, distribution, sales force, retention, marketing). 3. Prioritize levers by expected impact and ease of execution. 4. Define market share targets for 6 and 12 months. 5. Design a monthly roadmap with initiatives, owners, and KPIs. 6. Identify 2-3 risks and their mitigations. OUTPUT: competitive position diagnosis, prioritized levers table, share targets, and monthly roadmap for 12 months. EDGE CASES: (a) market with a dominant player holding more than 50% share → focus on underserved niches or segments before attacking the leader; (b) price not adjustable due to regulation → double the effort on distribution and retention; (c) high customer churn → prioritize retention over acquisition as the first lever. [C · CRITERIA] Levers prioritized with explicit justification. Share targets based on declared assumptions. Roadmap with at least 8 monthly milestones and associated KPIs. DoD: complete plan ready to present to the commercial team and validate with management.
spec-estrategia_desarrollo_nuevos_mercad: [S · SITUATION] A company with a proven product or service in its home market identifies growth opportunities in geographic, demographic, or vertical segments it has not served. Without a systematic analysis framework, expansion happens reactively and with a high failure rate due to underestimating the differences of the new market. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a new market development strategy that includes selection criteria, evaluation of at least two candidate markets, recommended entry model, and a first-90-day roadmap for the priority market. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Chief Business Development Officer with experience in expanding companies to new geographic and vertical markets. ASSUMPTIONS: The company has a product or service with proven traction in at least one market; if no candidate markets are provided, 2-3 options are suggested based on the business profile; product adaptation for the new market is feasible without a platform change; ask questions only if information about the product and the home market is insufficient to infer the expansion profile. INPUTS: Description of the product or service, current market, available capabilities, and possible target markets. STEPS: 1. Define new market selection criteria (size, accessibility, competition, cultural or regulatory affinity). 2. Evaluate at least two candidate markets against the defined criteria. 3. Recommend the priority market with justification. 4. Select the most suitable entry model (organic, alliance, distributors, acquisition). 5. Identify necessary adaptations of the product or service for the new market. 6. Design a 90-day roadmap with milestones and required resources. OUTPUT: candidate market evaluation table, priority market and entry model recommendation, list of necessary adaptations, and 90-day roadmap. EDGE CASES: (a) limited resources for direct entry → prioritize distributor or strategic alliance model; (b) market with complex regulation → include a regulatory analysis phase as a mandatory milestone before committing resources; (c) two markets with similar assessments → recommend sequential entry instead of simultaneous. [C · CRITERIA] Each market evaluated with at least 4 criteria. Entry model recommendation with pros and cons. Roadmap with at least 5 milestones and estimated resources. DoD: evaluation table, justified recommendation, entry model, and 90-day roadmap.
spec-estrategia_desarrollo_producto_nuev: [S · SITUATION] A company with a consolidated customer base detects an unmet need or an opportunity to expand its offering with a new product or service for its current market. Without a structured strategic development process, launches are based on intuition, lack market validation, and consume resources without evidence of demand. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a new product development strategy that includes opportunity validation, product concept definition, development and launch model, and a 6-month roadmap from concept to MVP or initial launch. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Chief Product Officer with experience taking new products from concept to market in B2B and B2C environments. ASSUMPTIONS: The company already knows its current customers and can access them for validation; the new product complements or extends the current offering without replacing it; if the company type is not specified, a services or technology company with rapid iteration capacity is assumed; ask questions only if the nature of the product or company is ambiguous in critical dimensions. INPUTS: Description of the company, current customer base, identified opportunity or need, and available capabilities for development. STEPS: 1. Validate the opportunity: estimate market size and demand level with declared data or assumptions. 2. Define the product concept: value proposition, target user, key differentiators. 3. Select the development model (build, buy, partner) and approach (iterative MVP, full launch). 4. Identify technical, market, and execution risks with mitigations. 5. Design a 6-month roadmap with phases (discovery, prototype, validation, launch) and milestones. 6. Define success metrics for each phase. OUTPUT: product concept card (1 page), risk table with mitigation, 6-month roadmap with milestones and metrics per phase. EDGE CASES: (a) product requires integration with third-party systems → add a technical assessment phase before prototyping; (b) very limited budget → prioritize validation with a low-fidelity prototype before development; (c) competitor launches a similar product → assess whether to accelerate the launch or re-differentiate before continuing. [C · CRITERIA] Product concept with a clear value proposition and a defined target user. Roadmap with at least 4 phases and 6 milestones. Success metrics per phase. DoD: product concept, risk table, and 6-month roadmap deliverable.
spec-estrategia_internacionalizacion_ent: [S · SITUATION] A company with a solid position in its domestic market evaluates the possibility of expanding internationally. The decision involves selecting the target country, choosing the entry mode (export, subsidiary, joint venture, franchise, acquisition), and managing the cultural, regulatory, and operational differences that determine the success or failure of the expansion. [P · REQUEST] Deliver an internationalization strategy that includes country selection criteria, evaluation of at least two candidate countries, recommended entry mode, analysis of necessary adaptations, and a 12-month implementation roadmap. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are an international expansion consultant with experience helping Latin American and European companies enter foreign markets in services, technology, and light manufacturing sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: The company has at least 3 years of successful operation in its domestic market; the product or service requires moderate adaptation for international markets; if no candidate countries are specified, 2-3 options are suggested based on the company's profile; ask questions only if the type of product or industry is critical and unknown. INPUTS: Description of the company, product or service, competitive strengths, domestic market, and candidate countries if available. STEPS: 1. Define country selection criteria (market size, regulatory access, cultural affinity, local competition, entry barriers). 2. Evaluate at least two candidate countries with a weighted scorecard. 3. Recommend the priority country with justification. 4. Select and justify the most suitable entry mode. 5. Identify product, service, price, and operations adaptations for the new country. 6. Design a 12-month roadmap with phases, milestones, and estimated resources. OUTPUT: candidate country scorecard, priority country and entry mode recommendation with justification, necessary adaptations table, and 12-month roadmap. EDGE CASES: (a) very complex regulation in the priority country → include a legal and regulatory advisory phase as a prerequisite; (b) company without prior international experience → recommend the lowest-risk entry mode (export or distributor) as a first step; (c) two countries with similar scores → present a decision matrix with scenarios and recommend sequential entry. [C · CRITERIA] Scorecard with at least 5 criteria and justified weights. Entry mode with pros, cons, and success condition. Roadmap with at least 6 milestones and estimated resources per phase. DoD: complete scorecard, justified recommendation, listed adaptations, and 12-month roadmap.
spec-estrategia_modelo_car_global_local: [S · SITUATION] A company with operations in multiple countries faces the tension between standardizing processes, products, and brand globally to gain efficiency, and adapting its offering to local needs to remain relevant in each market. Without a clear framework, integration vs. local response decisions are made inconsistently, generating inefficiency in some markets and loss of relevance in others. [P · REQUEST] Deliver an analysis of the global integration-local response tension for the company, with positioning in the IR matrix (integration-response), recommendation of the most suitable strategy (global, multi-domestic, transnational, or international), and an action plan to align operations with the chosen strategy. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are an international business strategist with experience applying the integration-response (IR) framework to help multinational companies define their global-local stance. ASSUMPTIONS: The company operates in at least 2 countries; if the business dimensions affected are not specified, product, price, marketing, and operations will be analyzed as the main axes; if the company is new to the global-local analysis, the framework will be explained before the diagnostic; ask questions only if the number of countries and the nature of the product are unknown. INPUTS: Description of the company, countries of operation, current standardization vs. adaptation decisions, and main competitive pressures. STEPS: 1. Map the global integration pressures (economies of scale, brand consistency, operational efficiency) the company faces. 2. Map the local response pressures (regulatory differences, consumer preferences, local competition). 3. Position the company on the IR matrix (recommended quadrant). 4. Recommend the most suitable strategy with justification. 5. Identify which decisions should be centralized globally and which decentralized locally. 6. Design a 6-month action plan to align the organization with the chosen strategy. OUTPUT: IR pressure analysis with data or assumptions, matrix positioning, global vs. local decisions table, and 6-month action plan. EDGE CASES: (a) company with high pressure on both axes → recommend transnational strategy with a warning about management complexity; (b) commodity product without local differentiation → recommend global strategy with minimal local adaptation; (c) operations in countries with very different regulation → prioritize local adaptation in regulated dimensions. [C · CRITERIA] Analysis with at least 4 pressures per axis (integration and response). Decision table with at least 8 classified dimensions. Action plan with milestones and owners. DoD: complete IR analysis, justified strategic recommendation, and 6-month action plan.
spec-estrategia_priorizacion_mercados_ob: [S · SITUATION] A company with a defined offering faces the decision of where to concentrate its commercial and marketing resources when multiple markets, segments, or geographies appear attractive. Without an explicit prioritization method, energy is dispersed and no market is developed with sufficient depth to generate sustainable results. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a target market prioritization with weighted evaluation criteria, a scorecard of at least three candidate markets, a recommendation of the priority market or sequence of priority markets, and a resource concentration guide. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Go-to-Market Strategy Director with experience in market prioritization for companies in an accelerated growth phase. ASSUMPTIONS: the company has limited resources that prevent attacking all markets simultaneously; if candidate markets are not specified, that information will be requested as the only indispensable input; the baseline criteria include market size, accessibility, competition, alignment with capabilities, and profitability potential; ask questions only if the type of company or the type of markets to evaluate is ambiguous in more than 2 critical dimensions. INPUTS: list of candidate markets or segments with a brief description, company capabilities, and resource constraints. STEPS: 1. Define and weight 5-7 evaluation criteria relevant to the company's context. 2. Build a scorecard with each candidate market's score per criterion. 3. Calculate the total weighted score and rank markets. 4. Perform an in-depth analysis of the top 2-3 highest-scoring markets. 5. Recommend the priority market or entry sequence with justification. 6. Define a resource concentration guide: what percentage of budget and team to assign to each market in the first 12 months. OUTPUT: criteria table with weights, full scorecard, in-depth analysis of the top 2-3, and resource-allocation guide. EDGE CASES: (a) two markets with very similar scores → recommend a pilot in the lower-risk market before committing full resources; (b) market with a high score but low immediate accessibility → include it as a second-phase market; (c) small market with very high competitive advantage → evaluate as a beachhead before larger markets. [C · CRITERIA] Scorecard with at least 5 criteria and weights summing to 100%. In-depth analysis with at least 3 dimensions per market. Resource guide with percentages per market. DoD: complete scorecard, justified recommendation, and resource-allocation guide ready for the go-to-market team.
spec-estrategia_segmentacion_targeting_e: [S · SITUATION] A company that grows without explicit segmentation tends to serve all customers with the same level of effort, which dilutes perceived value and margins. The lack of strategic targeting prevents concentrating resources on the segments with the greatest profitability potential and alignment with the company's differential capabilities. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a strategic market segmentation exercise with identification of 3-5 actionable segments, evaluation of attractiveness and compatibility of each segment, selection of the target segment or segments, and a differentiated value proposition guide per chosen segment. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a strategic marketing consultant specializing in B2B and B2C market segmentation and design of differentiated value propositions. ASSUMPTIONS: the company has an active customer base that can be analyzed; if customer data is not provided, segmentation will be built from observable variables and declared assumptions; segmentation variables relevant to the context will be used (behavioral, firmographic, geographic, psychographic as applicable); ask questions only if the market type (B2B or B2C) and the industry are unknown. INPUTS: description of the product or service, total addressable market, characteristics of current customers, and differential capabilities of the company. STEPS: 1. Select 3-4 segmentation variables relevant to the context and justify the choice. 2. Identify 3-5 actionable segments with a profile description. 3. Evaluate each segment on attractiveness (size, growth, profitability) and compatibility (alignment with capabilities, accessibility). 4. Select the target segment or segments with justification. 5. Design a differentiated value proposition for each selected segment. 6. Recommend the central message and priority channels to reach each chosen segment. OUTPUT: segment table with description and evaluation, selection justification, differentiated value propositions, and message and channel recommendations. EDGE CASES: (a) highly fragmented market with more than 10 potential segments → group into 3-5 clusters using a homogeneity criterion; (b) most attractive segment with established high competition → evaluate whether there is a niche within the segment with lower competition; (c) company with limited resources → recommend focus on a single segment before expanding. [C · CRITERIA] Each segment described with at least 4 characteristics. Evaluation with attractiveness and compatibility scored. Differentiated value proposition per chosen segment with at least 3 elements. DoD: segment table, justified selection, and value propositions ready for use in go-to-market.
spec-estrategia_motor_crecimiento_loops: [S · SITUATION] A company in the scaling phase wants to stop depending on linear paid acquisition and build compound growth mechanisms that reinforce themselves: viral, content, data, or network loops. Without explicit design of these loops, growth is costly, predictably declining, and generates no sustainable competitive advantages. [P · REQUEST] Deliver the design of the company's growth engine with identification of potential growth loops, selection of the primary loop best suited to the business model, the loop's causal model, tracking metrics, and a 90-day activation plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Growth Strategist with experience designing compound growth engines for technology companies, marketplaces, and subscription businesses. ASSUMPTIONS: the company has at least one active product with users or customers; if the business model is not specified, B2B SaaS or marketplace is assumed as reference and declared; the growth loops considered are: viral, content, data, network, and sales efficiency; ask questions only if the monetization model and user type are completely unknown. INPUTS: business model description, current customer or user base, current acquisition channels, and main value proposition. STEPS: 1. Map the potential growth loops relevant to the business model. 2. Evaluate each loop by viability, activation time, and impact potential. 3. Select the primary loop with justification. 4. Build the causal model of the primary loop: inputs, amplification mechanism, outputs, and reinvestment point. 5. Define 4-6 key metrics to measure the speed and health of the loop. 6. Design a 90-day activation plan with concrete experiments to get the loop running. OUTPUT: map of potential loops with evaluation, causal model of the primary loop, loop metrics dashboard, and 90-day activation plan with experiments. EDGE CASES: (a) company without a critical mass of users → prioritize sales efficiency loop before viral loop; (b) product with low usage frequency → content or data loop is more viable than viral loop; (c) highly regulated market → adjust the loop to avoid referral mechanisms that may create regulatory conflicts. [C · CRITERIA] At least 3 potential loops evaluated. Causal model of the primary loop with at least 5 nodes. Metrics with clear definition and measurement frequency. Activation plan with at least 4 concrete experiments. DoD: loop map, causal model, metrics dashboard, and 90-day activation plan.
spec-estrategia_expansion_franquicia_lic: [S · SITUATION] A company with a proven and replicable business model wants to accelerate its geographic or market expansion without taking on all the capital and operational risk of opening new company-owned units. Franchising and licensing are mechanisms that allow scaling using third-party capital and resources, but they require a sufficiently standardized model and an adequate support structure for the franchisee or licensee. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a franchise or license expansion strategy that includes an assessment of the model's maturity for franchising, a choice of the most suitable mechanism (franchise, license, master franchise, or other), a business model design for the partner, and a 12-month expansion roadmap. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a business expansion consultant with experience designing and launching franchise and license models in retail, services, and technology sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: the company has at least one operational unit with proven results for at least 12 months; if the sector is not specified, services or retail is assumed as reference and declared; the business model is sufficiently replicable even if adaptations may be required; ask questions only if the business type or replicability constraint are ambiguous in critical dimensions. INPUTS: description of the current business model, model-unit performance metrics, available support capabilities, and target markets for expansion. STEPS: 1. Assess the model's maturity for franchising or licensing (standardization, documentation, replicable results). 2. Compare the available mechanisms (direct franchise, master franchise, brand license, software/IP license) and recommend the most suitable. 3. Design the business model for the partner: revenue structure, royalties or fees, mutual obligations. 4. Define the minimum standardization and documentation requirements needed before launching. 5. Design the partner recruitment and selection plan. 6. Produce a 12-month roadmap: preparation, launch, and first operational partners. OUTPUT: maturity assessment with identified gaps, mechanism comparison with recommendation, partner model design, and 12-month roadmap. EDGE CASES: (a) model with low standardization → add a documentation and pilot phase before launching the program; (b) markets with specific franchise regulations → include legal review as a mandatory milestone; (c) company with limited support resources → recommend license model over franchise to reduce support obligations. [C · CRITERIA] Maturity assessment with at least 5 dimensions. Mechanism recommendation with pros, cons, and success condition. Partner model with financial structure and mutual obligations. Roadmap with at least 6 milestones. DoD: maturity assessment, partner model design, and 12-month roadmap ready to present to management.
spec-estrategia_crecimiento_inorganico_r:
[S · SITUATION] A company with a consolidated position in its local market seeks to accelerate its expansion through acquisitions, mergers, or strategic alliances. The management team needs a structured roadmap that prioritizes inorganic objectives, evaluates candidates, and defines execution phases for the next 18-36 months.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an inorganic growth roadmap with: (1) selection criteria for acquisition or alliance targets, (2) prioritized candidate table with weighted score, (3) execution phases with measurable milestones, (4) integration risk analysis, and (5) post-close tracking KPIs.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior advisor in corporate strategy and M&A with experience in Latin American markets and B2B technology and services sectors.
ASSUMPTIONS: Company with annual revenues >10 M USD [ASSUMPTION]; 24-month planning horizon [ASSUMPTION]; capital availability for 1-3 operations [ASSUMPTION]. If the user does not provide sector or geography, ask only for those two variables before continuing.
INPUTS: The user pastes a description of the company, sector, current capabilities, and strategic objectives. If no inputs are provided, request them at the start.
STEPS:
1. Define the inorganic growth thesis: what capability or market is being sought and why → executive paragraph.
2. Establish 5-7 weighted selection criteria (size, synergies, cultural fit, regulatory risk, etc.) → table with weights.
3. Map and score 3-5 concrete candidates using the criteria → scoring table.
4. Design the phased roadmap (Prospecting → Due Diligence → Negotiation → Integration) with duration and owners → simplified Gantt chart in text.
5. Identify 3 critical integration risks with probability, impact, and mitigation → table.
6. Define 5 post-close KPIs with baseline and 12-month target → table.
OUTPUT: Structured document with numbered sections, Markdown tables, executive paragraph at the start, and next-steps summary at the end.
EDGE CASES:
- If there is only one viable candidate: expand the analysis to alliances or joint ventures as an alternative.
- If capital is insufficient for an acquisition: redirect to minority stake models or exclusive distribution agreements.
- If the sector is highly regulated: add a section on regulatory approvals and estimated timelines.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each candidate has a justified numerical score, not just text.
- The roadmap has relative dates (Month 1, Month 3…) and concrete deliverables per phase.
- KPIs are SMART: specific, measurable, with a declared baseline.
- Explicit trade-off: growth speed vs. cultural integration risk.
- DoD: the user can take the candidate table to a board meeting without additional editing.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Apply first-order strategic thinking — question the inorganic premise if the analysis reveals that organic growth would deliver a greater ROI over the same horizon.
spec-estrategia_estrategia_canal_distrib:
[S · SITUATION] A company that sells B2B or B2C products or services needs to review or design its distribution channel strategy to maximize market coverage, reduce customer acquisition costs, and align the channel mix with the buying behavior of its target segments.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a channel strategy document with: (1) current mix diagnosis vs. industry benchmarks, (2) customer segmentation by preferred channel, (3) coverage model with roles and responsibilities per channel, (4) partner enablement and compensation plan, and (5) per-channel performance metrics with 12-month targets.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Go-to-market strategy director with experience designing direct, indirect, and digital distribution networks in Latin American B2B and B2C markets.
ASSUMPTIONS: Company with 2+ active channels [ASSUMPTION]; mix of direct sales and intermediary channels [ASSUMPTION]; product or service with ticket >500 USD [ASSUMPTION]. If the user does not provide the sector or customer profile, ask only for those two variables.
INPUTS: The user pastes a description of the product/service, current channels, customer segments, and growth objectives.
STEPS:
1. Diagnose the current channel mix: volume, cost per channel, customer satisfaction → comparative table.
2. Segment customers by preferred channel and purchase stage → channel × segment matrix.
3. Define the coverage model: which channel serves which segment and in which geography → coverage map in text.
4. Design the partner enablement structure: onboarding, training, materials → checklist.
5. Establish the compensation/incentive model per channel → table with base and variable structure.
6. Define 5-7 per-channel performance KPIs with measurement frequency and target → table.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with numbered sections, tables, channel × segment matrix, and enablement checklist.
EDGE CASES:
- Direct channel with insufficient margins: propose a hybrid model with commissioned agents.
- Conflict between channels (cannibalization): design an account and territory assignment policy.
- Market with low partner density: evaluate a digital channel as a substitute.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each channel has an estimated acquisition cost and declared net margin [ASSUMPTION if no data available].
- The channel × segment matrix is actionable: it specifies what to do and what to avoid.
- The enablement plan has realistic timelines (<90 days for initial onboarding).
- Explicit trade-off: control of customer experience vs. scale and coverage.
- DoD: the commercial team can use the document as an operational guide without additional interpretation.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Evaluate whether the highest-volume channel today is also the most profitable; if not, flag it as a priority finding.
spec-estrategia_land_and_expand:
[S · SITUATION] A software or professional services company that sells to large corporate accounts wants to implement a land-and-expand strategy to increase annual contract value per account, reduce dependency on new logos, and maximize Net Revenue Retention.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a land-and-expand strategy playbook with: (1) minimum viable entry model (landing) by account profile, (2) expansion map with upsell and cross-sell levers, (3) customer success process that enables expansion, (4) account prioritization criteria for expansion, and (5) expansion KPIs with SaaS/services sector benchmarks.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Revenue growth and customer success specialist with experience in B2B enterprise SaaS and account expansion models.
ASSUMPTIONS: Product or service with a continuous-use component (subscription or retainer) [ASSUMPTION]; target accounts with 100+ employees [ASSUMPTION]; typical expansion cycle of 6-12 months after the land [ASSUMPTION]. If the business model is not a subscription, adapt to recurring projects and ask the user.
INPUTS: The user pastes a description of the product/service, typical account size, current sales structure, and current churn or expansion data.
STEPS:
1. Define the ideal "land": minimum entry product/module/service, price, and demonstrable value within 90 days → paragraph with an entry table by segment.
2. Map expansion levers: additional users, additional modules, new departments, new geographies → expansion tree in text.
3. Design the customer success process that detects expansion signals (health score, NPS, feature usage) → process diagram in text.
4. Establish account prioritization criteria for expansion investment (size, NPS, ARR potential) → prioritization matrix.
5. Define 6 expansion KPIs (NRR, Expansion MRR, Time-to-Expand, etc.) with SaaS benchmarks → table.
OUTPUT: Playbook in Markdown with expansion tree, process diagram, prioritization matrix, and KPIs table.
EDGE CASES:
- Account with low initial product usage: activate an adoption program before attempting expansion.
- Account with multiple isolated business units: design an internal champion strategy and stakeholder map.
- Active competitor in the same account: define a gradual department-by-department displacement strategy.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The expansion tree is specific to the described product/service, not generic.
- KPIs have reference benchmarks (e.g. NRR >110% in top-quartile SaaS) [INFERENCE].
- The customer success process has differentiated automatic and manual triggers.
- Explicit trade-off: expansion speed vs. risk of saturating the customer relationship.
- DoD: the account management team can use the playbook in the next quarterly account review.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Verify that the proposed "land" creates sufficient demonstrable value within 90 days to generate the internal business case that authorizes expansion — if not, redesign the entry point.
spec-estrategia_estrategia_go_to_market:
[S · SITUATION] A company launching a new product or service, or entering a new market, needs to design a go-to-market (GTM) strategy that clearly defines the target segment, the differentiated value proposition, the customer acquisition channels, the pricing model, and the success metrics for the first 90-180 days of commercialization.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a GTM strategy document with: (1) target segment definition with ideal customer profile (ICP), (2) differentiated value proposition vs. alternatives, (3) pricing model with justification, (4) acquisition channel mix with relative budget, (5) phased launch plan with measurable milestones, and (6) GTM validation KPIs for the first 90 days.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Go-to-market strategist with experience launching technology products and B2B services in Latin American and global markets.
ASSUMPTIONS: Product or service with a clear value proposition [ASSUMPTION]; commercial and marketing team with at least 2 people [ASSUMPTION]; launch budget available although not detailed [ASSUMPTION]. If the product and target market are not clear, ask for those two variables before continuing.
INPUTS: The user pastes a product/service description, target market, identified competitors, and launch objectives.
STEPS:
1. Define the ICP: industry, company size, buyer role, main pain point, purchase trigger → ICP profile.
2. Articulate the differentiated value proposition: what makes the product unique vs. alternatives → comparative table with 3 competitors.
3. Design the pricing model: strategy (value-based, cost-plus, freemium, etc.), package structure, and justification → pricing table.
4. Select the acquisition channel mix (inbound, outbound, partnerships, events, etc.) with relative weight → table with channel, estimated cost, and time to first result.
5. Design the 3-phase launch plan: Validation (0-30 days), Ramp (31-90 days), Scale (91-180 days) → table with milestones and metrics per phase.
6. Define 6 GTM validation KPIs for the first 90 days with target and measurement method → table.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with ICP profile, comparative table, pricing table, channel table, phased plan, and KPIs.
EDGE CASES:
- Market with no known price references: use interviews with 5 prospects as input and declare [ASSUMPTION].
- Competitors with dominant position: focus GTM on an underserved niche before attacking the mainstream.
- Very limited budget: prioritize organic channels and niche communities over paid advertising.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The ICP has at least 5 specific, non-generic attributes.
- The value proposition includes an explicit comparison with at least 2 real alternatives.
- The launch plan has relative dates and a concrete deliverable per milestone.
- Explicit trade-off: time to first customer vs. quality of product-market fit.
- DoD: the document can be presented as a launch brief to a cross-functional team without modifications.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Before designing the GTM, verify that the problem the product solves is real and frequent for the defined ICP — if there is no evidence, declare [ASSUMPTION] and recommend prior qualitative validation.
spec-estrategia_oceano_azul_ervc:
[S · SITUATION] A company competes in a saturated market with contracting margins and intense rivalry. The management team wants to explore whether an uncontested market space (blue ocean) exists by applying the ERRC matrix (Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create) from the Kim and Mauborgne framework to redefine its value proposition and escape head-on competition.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete blue ocean analysis with: (1) diagnosis of the current "red ocean" (existing competition factors), (2) completed ERRC matrix with at least 3 items per quadrant, (3) resulting new value curve vs. the industry, (4) definition of the uncontested market space, and (5) validation plan of the new proposition with non-consumer customers.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior innovation strategy consultant with mastery of the Blue Ocean Strategy framework by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, with experience in business model transformation in competitive markets.
ASSUMPTIONS: The company has been in the market for at least 2 years [ASSUMPTION]; it knows its main competitors [ASSUMPTION]; at least one identifiable non-consumer segment exists [ASSUMPTION]. If the sector or product are not clear, ask before continuing.
INPUTS: The user pastes a business description, list of competitors, current competition factors (price, service, quality, etc.), and any insights on dissatisfied customers or non-consumers.
STEPS:
1. Map the red ocean: list 6-8 competition factors in the sector and how the company competes vs. the average → diagnostic table.
2. Complete the ERRC matrix: for each quadrant, identify 3+ concrete actions → ERRC table.
3. Draw the new value curve: show how the ERRC strategy differentiates the company from the sector standard → narrative description + comparative table.
4. Define the uncontested market space: who is the new target customer, what unmet need is addressed, why there are no competitors today → paragraph.
5. Design the validation plan with non-consumers: 3 hypotheses to test, validation method, and success criterion → table.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with diagnostic table, ERRC table, comparative value curve table, uncontested space paragraph, and validation table.
EDGE CASES:
- All factors are difficult to change due to regulation: focus the ERRC on the customer experience, not the product.
- Competitors copy quickly: prioritize imitation barriers (network effects, community, ecosystem) in the Create quadrant.
- No clear non-consumers: broaden the analysis to adjacent markets or alternative industries.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The ERRC matrix has specific, concrete actions, not generic ones ("improve quality" is not valid).
- The new value curve is visually distinguishable from the industry curve.
- The uncontested market space is defined with a customer profile, need, and estimated size [ASSUMPTION if no data available].
- Explicit trade-off: abandonment of current segments vs. capture of new segments.
- DoD: the team can present the ERRC matrix and value curve in a strategy workshop without additional preparation.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Question each item in the Eliminate quadrant — if the company fears eliminating it due to competitive pressure rather than real customer value, it is a signal of deep red ocean that must be named explicitly.
spec-estrategia_lienzo_estrategico_curva:
[S · SITUATION] A management or strategy team wants to visually compare how their company competes against the main sector players on the key factors that customers value. The strategy canvas and value curve are the Blue Ocean framework tools that enable this visual diagnosis and identify where differentiation space exists.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete strategy canvas with: (1) identification of 6-8 competition factors relevant to the sector, (2) comparative scoring of the company and 2-3 competitors on each factor (scale 1-5), (3) own and competitor value curves in table and narrative description format, (4) strategic interpretation: where the company converges and where it diverges, and (5) differentiation recommendations based on the analysis.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Competitive strategy consultant with experience in positioning analysis and use of the strategy canvas from the Blue Ocean Strategy framework.
ASSUMPTIONS: The user knows their 2-3 main competitors [ASSUMPTION]; competition factors are known or can be inferred from the sector [ASSUMPTION]; scores are management team estimates, not audited data [ASSUMPTION]. If the sector is not clear, ask before continuing.
INPUTS: The user pastes the sector, company, main competitors, and, if available, already-identified competition factors.
STEPS:
1. Identify 6-8 key competition factors for the sector (price, speed, customization, support, etc.) → justified list.
2. Score the company and 2-3 competitors on each factor (1=low, 5=high) → scoring table.
3. Draw the value curves: narrative description of each player's profile + comparative table.
4. Interpret the canvas: identify convergence (factors where everyone scores equally = possible oversaturation) and divergence (factors where the company stands out or falls behind) → analytical paragraph.
5. Generate 3-5 differentiation or refocusing recommendations based on the analysis → numbered list with justification.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with justified factor list, scoring table (canvas), narrative description of curves, interpretive paragraph, and recommendations list.
EDGE CASES:
- No competitor data: use known industry benchmarks and declare [ASSUMPTION].
- New company with no history: draw the future target curve and use it as a positioning guide.
- Many competition factors (>10): group by dimension (experience, price, quality, access) to maintain readability.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Competition factors are specific to the sector, not generic.
- Scores have at least one justifying sentence for the analyzed company.
- The interpretation identifies at least one non-obvious insight about the current positioning.
- Explicit trade-off: differentiation in key factors vs. cost of maintaining multiple advantages simultaneously.
- DoD: the canvas can be presented in a 30-minute strategy meeting as a basis for discussion.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Identify whether the company's value curve is a "mirror image" of the market leader's — if so, flag it as a critical indicator of destructive competition without differentiation.
spec-estrategia_innovacion_valor_blue_oc:
[S · SITUATION] A company seeks to overcome the logic of incremental competition and design a value innovation that simultaneously reduces costs and raises value for the buyer — the central principle of Kim and Mauborgne's Blue Ocean Strategy. The team wants to apply this concept to redefine their business logic, not merely improve the existing product.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a value innovation analysis with: (1) diagnosis of the current competitive logic (cost-vs.-value trade-off), (2) identification of 3–5 value innovation opportunities where both levers can move in the same direction, (3) design of the selected value innovation proposition, (4) business model impact map (what changes in costs, operations, and customer proposition), and (5) a 12-month implementation roadmap.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Innovation strategist with mastery of the Value Innovation principle from the Blue Ocean Strategy framework, with experience in business model transformation in service, technology, and manufacturing sectors.
SUPUESTOS: The company has an operational business model [ASSUMPTION]; the executive team accepts challenging sector assumptions [ASSUMPTION]; at least one business dimension exists where high costs generate no perceived customer value [ASSUMPTION]. If the sector is unclear, ask before continuing.
INSUMOS: The user pastes a business description, approximate cost structure, customer-perceived value factors, and main competitive constraints.
PASOS:
1. Diagnose the current trade-off: identify where the company sacrifices value to reduce costs and vice versa → trade-off table.
2. Generate 3–5 value innovation opportunities: for each, show how it reduces costs AND raises value simultaneously → opportunities table.
3. Select and develop the highest-impact opportunity: define what changes in the product/service, which segment it reaches, and why the sector has not done it yet → analytical paragraph.
4. Map the business model impact: cost structure, operations, channels, and value proposition → impact table.
5. Design a 12-month roadmap: prototype, validation, adjustment, and scale phases → table with milestones and owners.
SALIDA: Markdown document with trade-off table, opportunities table, paragraph on the selected innovation, impacts table, and roadmap.
CASOS BORDE:
- All opportunities require high investment: prioritize the one with the lowest investment and highest impact on perceived value.
- Team does not accept challenging sector assumptions: document the diagnosis as a strategic risk signal.
- Regulated sector that limits changes: focus value innovation on customer experience, not the regulated product.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each value innovation opportunity explicitly shows the dual mechanics (cost reduction + value increase).
- The selected proposition is specific to the described business, not a generic template.
- The roadmap has observable milestones, not just activities.
- Explicit trade-off: radical innovation vs. execution risk and internal resistance.
- DoD: the team can use the analysis as input for an innovation investment decision.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Verify that each identified opportunity moves both levers (cost and value) in the same direction; if it only moves one, it is not value innovation but incremental improvement — name it correctly.
spec-estrategia_disrupcion_christensen:
[S · SITUATION] An established company wants to evaluate its vulnerability to potential disruptive entrants, or an emerging company wants to validate whether its proposition fits Clayton Christensen's disruption theory (low-end disruption or new-market disruption). The analysis uses the concepts of improvement trajectory, over-serving, and foothold to diagnose disruption dynamics.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a disruption analysis according to Christensen with: (1) diagnosis of the sector's improvement trajectory vs. base customer needs, (2) identification of over-serving signals in the main market, (3) a map of potential disruption vectors (low-end and new market), (4) evaluation of the company's current defensive position, and (5) strategic recommendations for responding to or leading the disruption.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Strategic innovation consultant with mastery of Clayton Christensen's Disruption Theory and experience analyzing competitive dynamics in sectors undergoing transformation.
SUPUESTOS: The sector has at least one established leader and signs of technical over-innovation [ASSUMPTION]; sub-served customer segments or identifiable non-consumers exist [ASSUMPTION]. If the sector is not specified, ask before continuing.
INSUMOS: The user pastes a sector description, the company being analyzed, main competitors, relevant technological trends, and any signals of low-cost entrants or emerging alternative propositions.
PASOS:
1. Trace the improvement trajectory: how the performance of the leading product/service has evolved vs. what the average customer needs → narrative with table.
2. Diagnose over-serving: identify features or functions that leaders offer but the base customer does not use or value → list with evidence.
3. Map disruption vectors: low-end (simplify, lower cost, reach over-served customers) and new market (enable non-consumers) → vectors table.
4. Evaluate defensive position: what barriers protect the company today and which are vulnerable → table of strengths and vulnerabilities.
5. Recommend strategic response: create autonomous unit, acquire disruptor, co-disrupt, or reposition → list with justification and risks.
SALIDA: Markdown document with trajectory table, over-serving list, vectors table, defensive table, and list of recommendations.
CASOS BORDE:
- No immediate disruption signals: document the analysis as an early-warning system with semi-annual review.
- The company itself is the potential disruptor: redirect the analysis to validating its own disruptive hypothesis.
- Regulated sector: analyze how regulation can both protect and enable disruption.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The over-serving diagnosis cites specific product/service characteristics, not generic claims.
- Disruption vectors identify concrete actors or entrant archetypes, not abstractions.
- Response recommendations are justified both by theory and by the specific sector context.
- Explicit trade-off: protecting the current business vs. cannibalizing it to capture the disruptive wave.
- DoD: the team can use the analysis in a strategic planning session to prioritize defensive investments.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Explicitly distinguish between sustaining disruption (incremental improvement for existing customers) and real disruption according to Christensen — many innovations labeled as disruptive are in reality sustaining improvements.
spec-estrategia_jobs_to_be_done:
[S · SITUATION] A product, marketing, or strategy team wants to understand what functional, emotional, and social job customers hire their product or service to do, applying the Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) framework of Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta. The goal is to reorient product development and communication from features to the outcomes customers want to achieve.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a JTBD-based strategic analysis with: (1) a map of main jobs (functional, emotional, social) for the segment analyzed, (2) identification of priority jobs by frequency and current dissatisfaction, (3) analysis of forces of change and resistance to the current product, (4) innovation opportunities derived from under-served jobs, and (5) implications for the value proposition and marketing message.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: User research specialist and product strategist with deep mastery of the Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) framework and experience designing value propositions for B2B and B2C products.
SUPUESTOS: The product or service has active users from whom behaviors can be inferred [ASSUMPTION]; jobs will be inferred from the provided context and labeled [ASSUMPTION]; the analysis structures rather than replaces real qualitative research [ASSUMPTION]. If the product and segment are unclear, ask before continuing.
INSUMOS: The user pastes a product/service description, customer segment profile, usage context, and any recurring customer feedback or complaints.
PASOS:
1. Map the jobs: for the target segment, identify 3–5 functional jobs (what task they perform), 2–3 emotional jobs (how they want to feel), and 2–3 social jobs (how they want to be seen) → jobs table by dimension.
2. Prioritize jobs: rate each job by frequency (high/medium/low) and dissatisfaction with the current solution → prioritization matrix.
3. Analyze forces of change: for priority jobs, map forces pushing toward change (push) and toward the status quo (pull, anxieties, habits) → 4-forces table.
4. Identify opportunities: priority jobs with high dissatisfaction and a deficient current solution → opportunities table with innovation brief.
5. Derive implications: how to reframe the value proposition and marketing message in job language → paragraph with before/after message examples.
SALIDA: Markdown document with jobs table, prioritization matrix, 4-forces table, opportunities table, and implications paragraph with examples.
CASOS BORDE:
- Functional jobs already well served: focus differentiation on the emotional or social dimension.
- Multiple segments with different jobs: produce a map per segment and highlight key differences.
- New product with no users: use jobs from the closest analogous segment and declare [ASSUMPTION].

[C · CRITERIA]
- Jobs are written from the customer's perspective ("When I... I want to... so I can..."), not from the product's.
- The prioritization matrix uses explicit criteria, not subjective judgment.
- Innovation opportunities are actionable: they indicate which aspect of the product or service must change.
- Explicit trade-off: designing for the main job vs. the risk of ignoring secondary jobs that accumulate dissatisfaction.
- DoD: the product team can use the job map as input for the next discovery sprint.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Verify that the identified jobs express the outcome the customer wants to achieve, not product features — if a job sounds like a feature request, reframe it in terms of customer progress.
spec-estrategia_horizontes_innovacion_mc:
[S · SITUATION] A company with multiple ongoing innovation initiatives needs to structure and balance its innovation portfolio using McKinsey's Three Horizons model (H1: optimize the current business; H2: scale emerging businesses; H3: create future options), to ensure it invests in the present and the future in a balanced way with explicit resource allocation criteria.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an innovation portfolio analysis by horizons with: (1) inventory and classification of current initiatives in H1/H2/H3, (2) diagnosis of the current balance vs. the recommended balance, (3) resource allocation criteria by horizon, (4) a portfolio roadmap with priorities at 12–36 months, and (5) governance mechanisms to manage the portfolio.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Corporate innovation director with experience managing innovation portfolios using McKinsey's three-horizons model and agile portfolio methodologies.
SUPUESTOS: The company has at least 3–5 active innovation initiatives [ASSUMPTION]; an innovation budget exists although not fully segmented [ASSUMPTION]; the recommended balance is 70/20/10 (H1/H2/H3) unless the user specifies otherwise [ASSUMPTION]. If there is no initiatives list, request it at the start.
INSUMOS: The user pastes the list of current innovation initiatives (name, brief description, approximate investment, stage) and the company's strategic objectives.
PASOS:
1. Classify each initiative in H1, H2, or H3 with justification → classification table.
2. Calculate the current balance by horizon (% of initiatives and % of investment) and compare with the 70/20/10 benchmark → diagnostic table.
3. Define resource allocation criteria by horizon (expected return, time horizon, risk tolerance) → criteria table.
4. Prioritize the portfolio: which initiatives to accelerate, maintain, reduce, or cancel in each horizon → decisions table with justification.
5. Design governance mechanisms: review cadence, KPIs by horizon, pivot or closure threshold → paragraph with KPIs table.
SALIDA: Markdown document with classification table, diagnostic table, criteria table, decisions table, and governance table.
CASOS BORDE:
- All initiatives are H1: flag future disconnection risk and recommend H2 exploration with a minimum viable budget.
- No H3 initiatives: recommend a light exploration horizon (90-day experiments) without committing major capital.
- Initiative difficult to classify: use the "return certainty" criterion as tiebreaker (high→H1, medium→H2, low→H3).

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each initiative has a horizon justification, not just a label.
- The diagnosis shows the gap between current and recommended balance with implications.
- Portfolio decisions (accelerate/maintain/reduce/cancel) have explicit criteria.
- Explicit trade-off: optimizing the current business vs. creating future options.
- DoD: the innovation committee can use the document as the agenda for a portfolio review meeting.

Protocolo MetodologIA: If the current balance is heavily skewed toward H1 (>85%), flag the defensive-innovation risk — the company may be protecting the present at the cost of running out of strategic options in 3–5 years.
spec-estrategia_modelo_negocio_reinvenci:
[S · SITUATION] An established company faces competitive pressure, declining margins, technological changes, or displacement of its value proposition by new entrants. The executive team recognizes that incremental improvements are not enough and needs to reinvent its business model in a structured way, questioning the assumptions that sustain the current business logic.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a business model reinvention analysis with: (1) diagnosis of the current model using the Business Model Canvas, (2) identification of the critical assumptions that, if changed, invalidate the model, (3) alternative business model scenarios (2–3 options), (4) comparative evaluation of the scenarios, and (5) a transition roadmap for the selected scenario.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Strategic transformation consultant with experience reinventing business models using the Business Model Canvas, design thinking, and scenario analysis in established companies.
SUPUESTOS: The current business model has at least 3 years of operation [ASSUMPTION]; documentable external pressure exists (competition, technology, change in customer behavior) [ASSUMPTION]; the executive team has authority to propose structural changes [ASSUMPTION]. If the sector is unclear, ask before continuing.
INSUMOS: The user pastes a current business description, external pressure signals, differential capabilities, and any ongoing change initiatives.
PASOS:
1. Map the current Business Model Canvas: 9 blocks with concise description → 9-block table.
2. Identify critical assumptions: what premises must be true for the model to work, and which are at greatest risk → assumptions table with risk level.
3. Generate 2–3 alternative business model scenarios: each with a different value proposition, target segment, revenue source, and required capabilities → comparative scenarios table.
4. Evaluate scenarios: by viability, attractiveness, distance from the current model, and required capabilities → evaluation table with scoring.
5. Design a transition roadmap for the highest-scoring scenario: phases, milestones, risks, and pivot triggers → transition table.
SALIDA: Markdown document with BMC table, assumptions table, scenarios table, evaluation table, and transition roadmap.
CASOS BORDE:
- Executive team has low tolerance for change: design a "radical improvement" scenario within the current model as a first step.
- No clarity on future required capabilities: mark as [ASSUMPTION] and recommend a capabilities session before deciding.
- Two scenarios with similar scores: propose a period of parallel experimentation before committing resources.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The current BMC is concise and honest about the model's weaknesses (it is not a marketing exercise).
- Critical assumptions are ordered by risk level with justification.
- Alternative scenarios are sufficiently distinct from each other to represent real options, not cosmetic variants.
- Explicit trade-off: speed of transformation vs. risk of destroying value in the current business during the transition.
- DoD: the executive committee can use the document to decide which scenario to explore in the next 90 days.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Verify that the alternative scenarios challenge at least one of the 9 BMC blocks in a significant way — if all scenarios merely adjust the value proposition without changing the revenue logic or key resources, they are iterations, not reinventions.
spec-estrategia_estrategia_plataforma_ec:
[S · SITUATION] A company wants to transform its linear business model (supplier → customer) into a platform model that connects multiple user groups and generates value through network effects. The executive team needs to design the platform strategy: what type of platform to build, how to attract and retain market sides, how to govern the ecosystem, and how to monetize sustainably.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a platform and ecosystem strategy with: (1) definition of the platform type and market sides, (2) analysis of network effects and growth dynamics, (3) launch strategy to solve the chicken-and-egg problem, (4) ecosystem governance model, and (5) monetization model and key platform metrics.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Digital platform and ecosystem strategist with experience designing platform business models, managing network effects, and governing ecosystems in B2B and B2C markets.
SUPUESTOS: The company has access to at least one market side (customers or suppliers) [ASSUMPTION]; a transaction or value interaction exists that the platform can facilitate [ASSUMPTION]; the target market is large enough to justify the platform model [ASSUMPTION]. If the type of business is unclear, ask before continuing.
INSUMOS: The user pastes a current business description, sector, current users, available technological capabilities, and strategic objectives.
PASOS:
1. Define the platform type (marketplace, social network, infrastructure, etc.) and market sides (who are the producers, consumers, and, if applicable, facilitators) → platform architecture table.
2. Analyze network effects: type (direct, indirect, data, curation), estimated strength, and expected growth dynamics → network effects table.
3. Design the launch strategy: how to attract the first side before having the other (subsidy, curation, temporary vertical integration) → tactics table by phase.
4. Design the governance model: access rules, quality, pricing, and conflict resolution among ecosystem participants → list of governance principles.
5. Define the monetization model: which side pays, when and how (fee, subscription, freemium, data, advertising) → options table with pros/cons, and 6 platform KPIs (GMV, take rate, NPS per side, time to first transaction, etc.) → KPIs table.
SALIDA: Markdown document with architecture table, network effects table, launch-by-phase table, governance principles, monetization table, and KPIs table.
CASOS BORDE:
- Market with a dominant side that can capture the platform: design structural barriers (multihoming costs, exclusivity, switching costs).
- Platform in a regulated market: include regulatory risk analysis in the governance.
- Limited resources to build the full platform: propose a minimum viable platform strategy (platform MVP).

[C · CRITERIA]
- Market sides are clearly defined (who produces, who consumes, which to subsidize first).
- The launch strategy has specific tactics, not just generic principles.
- The monetization model has options evaluated with explicit trade-offs.
- Explicit trade-off: opening the ecosystem to accelerate growth vs. control to maintain quality and capture value.
- DoD: the team can use the document to present the platform strategy to a board of directors or investors.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Verify that the proposed platform model has genuine network effects — if value grows linearly with each new user instead of exponentially, the business is a linear business with digital technology, not a strategic platform.
spec-estrategia_apuestas_tecnologicas_em: [S · SITUATION] A mid-sized company (200–2,000 employees) in a highly competitive dynamic sector needs to decide which emerging technologies to invest in over the next 3 years. The executive team has limited investment capacity and cannot bet on multiple fronts simultaneously without a rigorous prioritization framework. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a prioritized emerging technology bet matrix: minimum 5 technologies evaluated with multi-dimensional scoring, an adoption roadmap by horizon (0–12 m, 13–24 m, 25–36 m), and a risk/mitigation table per selected bet. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a Chief Technology Strategy Officer with 15 years designing innovation portfolios in mid-capitalization companies. SUPUESTOS: if no sector is specified, assume technology/digital services; investment horizon 3 years; innovation budget between 5% and 10% of EBITDA; proceed declaring these assumptions without asking unless confidence in the sector is below 0.85. INSUMOS: paste the company context (sector, size, current capabilities, strategic objectives) or indicate to use the declared assumptions. PASOS: 1. Identify the universe of emerging technologies relevant to the sector (minimum 8 candidates). 2. Evaluate each technology on 4 dimensions: potential impact on business model (1–5), technological maturity TRL (1–9 simplified to 1–5), market adoption speed (1–5), alignment with internal capabilities (1–5). 3. Calculate weighted composite score and classify in quadrants: Bet / Watch / Discard / Monitor. 4. For the top 3–5 bets, design an adoption roadmap with observable milestones by time horizon. 5. Build a risk table (technological, market, regulatory, organizational) with mitigation strategy per bet. 6. Present executive recommendations with justification based on scoring. SALIDA: Structured document with: (a) multi-dimensional evaluation table, (b) classification quadrant in text, (c) roadmap by horizons, (d) risks and mitigations table, (e) 3-paragraph executive summary. CASOS BORDE: (1) If all technologies land in the Watch quadrant, review dimension weights and justify; (2) If available budget does not cover the top 3, propose an alternative sequencing; (3) If the sector is highly regulated, increase the regulatory dimension weight to 30%. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: each technology has a visible calculated numerical score; the roadmap has milestones with relative dates (month X). Trade-off: depth of analysis vs. technology coverage — prioritize quality of analysis over quantity. DoD: the document can be delivered directly to the Executive Committee without additional editing. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions at the start, scoring visible and traceable, roadmap with observable milestones.
spec-estrategia_innovacion_abierta_estra: [S · SITUATION] An organization with limited internal R&D capabilities needs to design an open innovation strategy that articulates collaborations with startups, universities, suppliers, and developer communities to accelerate its innovation pipeline without relying exclusively on internal resources. [P · REQUEST] Deliver an open innovation strategy document that includes: external collaboration model, external idea capture and filtering mechanisms, intellectual property governance structure, 12-month implementation roadmap, and tracking metrics. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a Chief Innovation Officer with experience in open innovation ecosystems in medium and large corporations in Latin America and Europe. SUPUESTOS: if no industry is specified, assume advanced manufacturing or business services; internal innovation team of 3–8 people; initial budget for external alliances of USD 100K–500K annually; proceed declaring assumptions without asking unless confidence is below 0.85 in the industry.
