EDGE CASES: (a) monolithic system without clear layers — propose the recommended logical decomposition marking with [PROPOSAL] and explain the benefit; (b) system with more than ten subsystems — group into three to five first-level logical domains and decompose each at the second level; (c) input describes existing microservices — the logical view groups services into business capabilities, not listing them one by one. [C · CRITERIA] The diagram compiles in PlantUML; each subsystem has a single main responsibility stated in one sentence; traceability toward scenarios is explicit; design decisions include the justification; trade-off: model completeness vs. documentation time — document critical subsystems 100% and the rest 70%. DoD: diagram delivered, subsystems table complete, traceability toward two scenarios present, minimum three design decisions documented. Protocolo MetodologIA: an architecture that cannot be explained in a diagram is not designed, it is improvised.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_api_first_openapi: [S · SITUATION] A development team is going to build or redesign a REST API and wants to adopt the API-First approach: define the OpenAPI 3.x contract before writing any implementation code, ensuring that consumers and producers agree on the interface from the start and that the contract is the single source of truth. [P · REQUEST] Generate a complete and valid OpenAPI 3.x YAML contract for the described API, including the info and servers definition, the endpoints with their correct HTTP methods, the request and response schemas using reusable components, the appropriate status codes, the authentication strategy, and at least three request/response examples, ready to use with tools like Swagger UI or Stoplight. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior API engineer with experience designing OpenAPI contracts for platforms with more than one hundred consumers and deep knowledge of REST constraints, versioning, and API lifecycle management. Design the request and response schemas in components/schemas with precise types and descriptions. 4. Define the paths with operations, parameters, requestBody, and responses with complete status codes (200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 422, 500). 5. EDGE CASES: (a) API with more than twenty endpoints — model the ten most critical ones 100% and list the remaining as paths with operation summary only; (b) operations with non-CRUD semantics (business actions) — use POST with a descriptive action path and document the business effect in the description; (c) API that requires webhooks or a return event — add the webhooks section of OpenAPI 3.1 and declare [ASSUMPTION] if upgrading the version. [C · CRITERIA] The YAML validates without errors in the official OpenAPI validator; all schemas have type and description; error codes include a reusable standard error schema; the endpoints table is readable by a product manager without technical knowledge; trade-off: contract completeness vs. design speed — complete the main-path endpoints 100% and auxiliary ones 70%. Protocolo MetodologIA: the contract is the promise between teams — a field without a description is a communication debt.
spec-desarrollo_mapa_de_capacidades_nego: [S · SITUATION] An enterprise or microservices architecture team needs to build an explicit map relating the organization's business capabilities to the software services that support them, in order to identify coverage gaps, duplications, cross-domain dependencies, and opportunities for modernization or decomposition into microservices. INPUTS: business description, functional org chart, list of current systems, existing architecture, or process documentation pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the main business domains (five to eight) that group the level-1 capabilities. 2. Decompose each domain into three to six level-2 capabilities with a business noun name. 3. Produce the map in hierarchical table format and as a PlantUML block map diagram. OUTPUT: (a) hierarchical table with columns domain / level-2 capability / current systems / coverage status / microservice candidate, (b) PlantUML block diagram grouped by domain, (c) prioritized list of three to five action recommendations based on the identified gaps. EDGE CASES: (a) organization with more than twelve domains — consolidate into eight first-level domains grouping by strategic affinity; (b) no current system known — produce the target capability map and mark all systems as [TO BE DEFINED]; (c) capabilities with a technology name in the input (e.g., ERP inventory module) — rename to business capability (e.g., Inventory management) and add a trace note. [C · CRITERIA] Each capability is named with a business noun without technology references; the table covers at least eighty percent of the described business functions; recommendations are actionable with a specific action verb; the PlantUML diagram compiles without errors; trade-off: map exhaustiveness vs. delivery speed — cover all domains at level 1 100% and level 2 80%. DoD: complete hierarchical table, PlantUML diagram delivered, minimum three prioritized action recommendations. Protocolo MetodologIA: the capability map is the strategic software inventory — what does not appear on the map does not exist for the architecture.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_idempotencia_serv:
[S · SITUATION] A backend team works on distributed services that process payments, reservations, or critical state updates. Operations can be duplicated by client retries, network failures, or repeated messages in queues. Without guaranteed idempotency, each retry can create double charges, duplicate records, or inconsistent states.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a technical idempotency design and retry policy for the pasted endpoints or message consumers, including: idempotency key schema, result store, TTL, concurrency handling, and retry policy with exponential backoff with jitter.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior distributed systems architect with experience in resilience patterns (idempotent receiver, exactly-once semantics) and design of REST/gRPC APIs and message brokers.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no technology stack is specified, assume a REST service over HTTP with PostgreSQL as the store; if no TTL is indicated, use 24 hours; if no broker is mentioned, assume direct processing. Ask only if the type of operation (payment, reservation, other) is not inferrable from the pasted context.
INPUTS: Endpoint or consumer contract (route, payload, operation semantics) pasted directly.
STEPS:
1. Identify non-idempotent entry points in the pasted code or contract → list of at-risk operations.
2. Design idempotency key schema (who generates it, format, header or field) → documented decision with justification.
3. Design idempotent result table/cache (fields: key, status, result, expiration, payload hash) → DDL or data structure.
4. Define concurrency handling (optimistic vs pessimistic locking, unique index, SELECT FOR UPDATE) → pseudocode or SQL snippet.
5. Specify client retry policy: maximum attempts, base exponential backoff + jitter, HTTP/error codes that trigger retry → policy table.
6. Define expiration, key collision, and payload change cases → edge-case matrix with expected response.
OUTPUT: Technical markdown document with sections: Identified risks, Key schema, Store model, Concurrency logic, Retry policy, Edge cases. Include code or pseudocode snippets in steps 3-5.
EDGE CASES: (a) Same idempotency-key with different payload → reject with 422 and explicit message; (b) Expired key received again → treat as new operation and process; (c) Two concurrent requests with same key → only one processes, the other waits and returns the cached result.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the design allows 100 identical retries to produce exactly one business effect. Trade-off: implementation simplicity vs strict consistency — prioritize consistency in monetary operations, document explicitly. DoD: the document has all artifacts from the OUTPUT step and passes peer review with no open concurrency questions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Declare assumptions used, cite the inferred stack, and mark each section with [CÓDIGO], [CONFIG] or [INFERENCIA] as appropriate.
spec-desarrollo_estrategia_versionado_ap:
[S · SITUATION] A platform team needs to define — or review — how its API will evolve over time without breaking existing consumers. Today changes are deployed without a formal policy, causing silent breaking changes, lack of communicated deprecation, and accumulation of legacy endpoints.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an API versioning strategy document covering: versioning mechanism (URI, header, query param), lifecycle policy (introduction, deprecation, retirement), compatible vs breaking changes, changelog structure, and migration guide for consumers.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior API architect with experience in evolutionary design, backward compatibility, and communicating changes to consuming teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the API type is not specified, assume REST/JSON over HTTPS. If no preferred versioning mechanism is indicated, recommend URI path versioning (v1, v2) as the most explicit option, documenting trade-offs. If there is no deprecation SLA data, assume 6 months of coexistence. Ask only if there is a gateway or proxy restriction that prevents any mechanism.
INPUTS: Description of the current API or OpenAPI specification fragment pasted by the user.
STEPS:
1. Classify possible changes into: additive compatible (new fields, new endpoints), incompatible modifications (renaming fields, changing types), and eliminations → change taxonomy table.
2. Recommend versioning mechanism with advantages and disadvantages of URI, Accept header, and query param → comparison table with justified recommendation.
3. Define version lifecycle: phases (current, deprecated, sunset), entry criteria for each phase, minimum deprecation period → state diagram in text or mermaid.
4. Design semantic changelog structure per version (format, mandatory fields, examples) → template filled with a fictional example.
5. Write consumer migration guide: how to detect active version, how to negotiate version, how to receive deprecation notices (Sunset, Deprecation headers) → migration checklist.
6. Define backward compatibility policy for optional fields, enum values, and extensions → rules section with compliance and non-compliance examples.
OUTPUT: Structured markdown document: Change taxonomy, Versioning mechanism (comparison table + decision), Lifecycle (diagram), Changelog (template), Migration guide (checklist), Compatibility policy.
EDGE CASES: (a) Consumer ignores Sunset header and keeps calling retired version → 410 Gone response with explanatory body; (b) Two teams request incompatible evolutions in the same version → minor version branching policy vs new major version; (c) Internal API without external clients → simplified policy without formal deprecation period.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: any team engineer can classify a proposed change and know whether it requires a major version bump. Trade-off: versioning granularity vs maintenance burden — document explicitly. DoD: document reviewed and approved by at least one representative consumer team.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each section with [DOC], [CONFIG] or [INFERENCIA] and list the declared assumptions at the beginning.
spec-desarrollo_modelado_amenazas_stride:
[S · SITUATION] A development team is about to begin or has finished the design of a software component (microservice, module, system integration) and needs to identify security threats before it reaches production. No prior formal security analysis or documented threat model exists.

[P · REQUEST] Apply the STRIDE framework to the described component to produce a complete threat model: textual data flow diagram (DFD), asset and trust boundary inventory, threat table by STRIDE category with prioritized mitigations, and actionable security backlog.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior threat modeling and application security specialist, with command of STRIDE, level 0 and 1 DFDs, and threat elicitation techniques in agile teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the stack is not specified, assume a web service with relational database and external access. If criticality level is not indicated, assume personal or financial data (high impact). If the architecture diagram is not provided, build a textual DFD from the description. Ask only if trust boundaries between components are completely ambiguous.
INPUTS: Component description or architecture diagram pasted by the user (text, list of components and integrations).
STEPS:
1. Build textual DFD levels 0 and 1: actors, processes, data stores, flows, and trust boundaries → DFD in structured text or mermaid flowchart format.
2. Inventory critical assets and classify by impact (data, processes, channels) → asset table.
3. Apply STRIDE element by element in the DFD: for each flow, process, and store enumerate possible threats → table with columns: Element | STRIDE Category | Specific Threat | Probability (H/M/L) | Impact (H/M/L).
4. Propose concrete mitigations for each threat (technical control, not just policy) → additional column in the table.
5. Prioritize with simplified DREAD (Damage + Reproducibility + Exploitability + Affected + Discoverability) the 5 highest-risk threats → top 5 ranking with score.
6. Generate security backlog: user story + security acceptance criterion for each top-5 mitigation → list of actionable items.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: DFD (mermaid or text), Asset table, Complete STRIDE table, Top 5 ranking with DREAD scores, Security backlog with user stories.
EDGE CASES: (a) Component without authentication because it is internal → model the lateral movement threat and suggest minimal authentication; (b) Integration with undocumented legacy system → mark as [SUPUESTO] and propose a validation workshop; (c) Multiple actors with different trust levels → separate into explicit trust boundaries before applying STRIDE.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the STRIDE table covers all DFD elements without omissions. Trade-off: analysis thoroughness vs time — prioritize coverage of external flows and stores with sensitive data. DoD: the backlog has at least 5 items with verifiable acceptance criteria and has been reviewed by the tech lead.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each threat with [CÓDIGO], [INFERENCIA] or [SUPUESTO] according to the evidence source, and declare stack assumptions at the beginning.
spec-desarrollo_revision_owasp_top_ten:
[S · SITUATION] A development team needs to review source code fragments to detect vulnerabilities corresponding to the OWASP Top Ten categories (2021 edition). The review may be part of a security code review, a pre-deployment audit, or a security-focused pair programming session.

[P · REQUEST] Analyze the pasted code, identify each vulnerability present aligned to OWASP Top Ten 2021, classify it by category and severity, explain the exploitation vector, and provide the corrected snippet with technical justification.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior application security engineer (AppSec) with experience in secure code review, conceptual SAST, and vulnerability remediation in web applications and APIs.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the language is not explicit, infer it from the pasted code. If the framework is not specified, declare the one assumed. If there is no authentication context, assume the code can be reached by unauthenticated users (worst case). Ask only if the code depends on a critical external context not inferrable (e.g., database schema with sensitive logic).
INPUTS: Source code fragment(s) pasted directly by the user.
STEPS:
1. Read the code and build an internal data flow map (inputs, transformations, outputs, external calls) → brief flow description.
2. For each finding, complete: OWASP ID (A01-A10:2021) | Vulnerability name | Affected line(s) | Severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) | Attack vector explained in one sentence → findings table.
3. For each finding, show: vulnerable code (original block) → corrected code (remediated block) with explanatory comment → remediation section.
4. Verify absence of false negatives in all 10 OWASP categories: for categories with no finding, explicitly confirm they were reviewed and do not apply or are not evident in the fragment → coverage table.
5. Generate executive summary: number of findings by severity, most frequent category, estimated overall risk → 3-5 line paragraph.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Data flow map, OWASP findings table, Remediation section (original vs corrected code), Coverage table for all 10 categories, Executive summary.
EDGE CASES: (a) Code with no visible error handling → flag absence as potential A09 (Security Logging and Monitoring Failures) and recommend pattern; (b) Use of third-party library → annotate as possible A06 (Vulnerable Components) with recommendation to check version; (c) Business logic that depends on roles not present in the fragment → mark as [SUPUESTO] and document the worst-case hypothesis.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each finding has an OWASP ID, severity, line, and remediation with code. Trade-off: analysis thoroughness vs superficial coverage — prioritize critical and high findings with complete remediation, medium/low with description and reference. DoD: coverage table for all 10 categories complete, at least one finding or non-applicability confirmation per category.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each finding with [CÓDIGO] if it is in the fragment, [INFERENCIA] if derived from the flow, or [SUPUESTO] if it requires external context.
spec-desarrollo_analisis_owasp_api_secur:
[S · SITUATION] A team has an API (REST, GraphQL, or gRPC) in production or in design and needs to evaluate its security risks against the OWASP API Security Top 10 reference framework (2023 edition). No prior formal analysis exists and incidents or concerns about data exposure and access control have been reported.

[P · REQUEST] Analyze the pasted API specification or description to produce a structured risk report against the 10 OWASP API Security 2023 categories, with findings, severities, exploitation vectors specific to the API context, and prioritized technical remediation recommendations.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior API security specialist with experience in OWASP API Security Top 10, API pentesting, access control design, and data protection in REST and GraphQL interfaces.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the API type is not specified, assume REST/JSON with JWT authentication. If no OpenAPI specification is provided, work with the endpoint and behavior description the user pastes. If the authorization context is not indicated, assume multi-tenancy with users of different privilege levels. Ask only if the authorization structure is critical for the analysis and cannot be inferred.
INPUTS: OpenAPI specification, list of endpoints with methods, description of authentication and authorization flows, or a combination of these, pasted by the user.
STEPS:
1. Map endpoints and flows to the 10 OWASP API Security 2023 risks: API1 (BOLA), API2 (Broken Authentication), API3 (Broken Object Property Level Authorization), API4 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption), API5 (BFLA), API6 (Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows), API7 (SSRF), API8 (Security Misconfiguration), API9 (Improper Inventory Management), API10 (Unsafe Consumption of APIs) → mapping table.
2. For each category with findings: describe the affected endpoint/flow, the specific exploitation vector (not generic), probability and impact → findings table.
3. For any of the 10 categories with no finding: explicitly confirm the review and the reason for non-applicability → coverage table.
4. Order findings by risk (Probability × Impact) → prioritized ranking.
5. For the top 5 risks: propose concrete technical controls (e.g., object ownership validation, per-user rate limiting quota, disabling GraphQL introspection in production) → remediation section.
6. Generate executive summary with overall risk and the 3 most urgent actions → 4-6 line paragraph.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Endpoint-risk mapping table, Findings table with specific vector and severity, Coverage table for all 10 categories, Prioritized ranking, Top 5 remediation section, Executive summary.
EDGE CASES: (a) API without declared authentication → report as critical API2 regardless of context; (b) GraphQL without depth limiting → report as API4 with introspection abuse vector; (c) Read-only API → reduce BOLA severity but maintain data exposure analysis.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each of the 10 categories has an explicit status (finding with severity or does not apply with justification). Trade-off: analysis depth vs coverage — prioritize depth on API1, API2, and API5 as the most exploited. DoD: report reviewed by the security team before the next remediation sprint.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each finding with [DOC] if it comes from the pasted specification, [INFERENCIA] if deduced from the design, or [SUPUESTO] if it requires additional validation.
spec-desarrollo_gestion_secretos_codigo:
[S · SITUATION] A development team needs to audit its source code, configuration files, and scripts to detect embedded secrets (passwords, API tokens, private keys, connection strings, cloud credentials) and assess whether secrets management practices are secure. Git history with already-committed secrets may exist.

[P · REQUEST] Audit the pasted code or configuration to identify all exposed secrets or insecure secrets management practices, classify them by risk, estimate the blast radius if compromised, and provide an immediate remediation plan with secure alternatives.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior DevSecOps security specialist with experience in secrets detection, credential management, secret managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault), and CI/CD pipeline hardening.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the cloud environment is not specified, assume multi-cloud or agnostic and propose a portable solution (e.g., Vault or CI/CD-injected environment variables). If it is not indicated whether there is compromised git history, assume there may be and include urgent rotation instructions. Ask only if the type of secret requires a specific rotation process not inferrable (e.g., code-signing certificates).
INPUTS: Code fragment, configuration file (.env, config.yaml, application.properties, Dockerfile, script), or scan tool output pasted by the user.
STEPS:
1. Scan the pasted content looking for: literal credentials (passwords, API keys, tokens, connection strings), secret patterns (JWT format, base64-encoded keys, PEM patterns), comments with credentials, committed .env or configuration files → list of findings with line and type.
2. For each finding: secret type | line | affected service/system | blast radius if compromised (access to which systems/data) | rotation urgency (immediate / high / medium) → findings table.
3. Evaluate management practices: are environment variables used?, is there an adequate .gitignore?, is a secret manager integrated?, are secrets accidentally logged? → list of evaluated practices with status (secure / insecure / absent).
4. Propose remediation per finding: concrete secure alternative (environment variable + CI/CD injection, secret manager reference, credential rotation + revocation) → actions table.
5. Generate emergency rotation plan for immediate-urgency findings: ordered steps, who does what, estimated time → prioritized checklist.
6. Recommend preventive controls: pre-commit hooks (detect-secrets, gitleaks), CI/CD scanning, secret manager access policy → controls section.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Findings table (type, line, blast radius, urgency), Evaluation of current practices, Remediation actions table, Emergency rotation checklist, Recommended preventive controls.
EDGE CASES: (a) Secret in environment variable but with insecure hardcoded default value as fallback → report as high-severity finding; (b) Secret mock or placeholder in test → mark as [SUPUESTO] with recommendation to confirm it does not reach production; (c) Secret in git history already removed from current code → note that rotation is equally urgent.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: all literal secrets in the fragment are identified with line and rotation urgency. Trade-off: rotation speed vs availability impact — document the rotation order that minimizes downtime. DoD: rotation checklist has concrete executable steps without additional knowledge required.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each finding with [CÓDIGO] if explicitly in the fragment, [INFERENCIA] if a deduced pattern, or [SUPUESTO] if it requires confirmation.
spec-desarrollo_hardening_dependencias_s:
[S · SITUATION] A development team needs to evaluate and strengthen the security posture of third-party dependencies in their software project. Outdated or vulnerable dependencies represent one of the most frequent attack vectors (OWASP A06:2021). The team lacks a formal Software Composition Analysis (SCA) process or wants to review an existing one.

[P · REQUEST] Based on the pasted dependency manifest (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, go.mod, or other), produce a dependency hardening report: known vulnerability inventory, classification by CVE severity, prioritized update plan, and SCA tool configuration for the CI/CD pipeline.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior DevSecOps and Supply Chain Security engineer with experience in SCA, CVE management, SBOM (Software Bill of Materials), and configuration of tools such as Dependabot, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, and Trivy.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the ecosystem is not explicit, infer it from the manifest format. If no SCA tool output is provided, analyze the manifest based on knowledge of known vulnerabilities up to the knowledge cutoff date, marking each finding as [SUPUESTO] and recommending verification with an updated tool. If no CI/CD environment is indicated, assume GitHub Actions. Ask only if dependency licensing is an additional requirement that cannot be inferred.
INPUTS: Dependency manifest file or SCA tool output (npm audit, pip-audit, mvn dependency:tree) pasted by the user.
STEPS:
1. Parse the manifest and inventory direct and relevant transitive dependencies → table with name, current version, type (direct/transitive).
2. Identify dependencies with known vulnerabilities: CVE ID, CVSS severity, affected version, available fixed version → CVE table.
3. Identify dependencies without active maintenance (deprecated, abandoned, no releases in more than 12 months) → list of supply chain risk dependencies.
4. Prioritize actions: urgent (CVSS ≥ 9.0), high (CVSS 7.0-8.9), medium (CVSS 4.0-6.9), low (CVSS < 4.0) → priority table with recommended update version.
5. Generate update plan: update order (most critical dependencies first, considering compatibility), update command for the detected ecosystem, recommended minimum testing → ordered checklist.
6. Propose SCA tool configuration in CI/CD: configuration file (.github/workflows or equivalent) with automatic scanning, failure threshold, and notifications → YAML configuration snippet.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Dependency inventory, CVE table, Unmaintained dependency list, Priority table, Update plan (checklist), SCA configuration snippet for CI/CD.
EDGE CASES: (a) CVE fix version not yet available → document temporary mitigation (virtual patching, WAF rule, disable feature) and estimated upstream fix date; (b) Dependency update introduces breaking change → flag and recommend major version update with regression testing note; (c) Vulnerable transitive dependency not directly updatable → recommend forced version resolution (overrides/resolutions in manifest).

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: all CVEs with CVSS ≥ 7.0 have an explicit action plan. Trade-off: update speed vs stability — document feature freeze strategy during the hardening window. DoD: CI/CD pipeline has SCA scanning configured with a failure threshold that blocks merges with CVSS ≥ 9.0.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label CVEs with [CÓDIGO] if they come from the pasted SCA output, [INFERENCIA] if derived from the analyzed manifest, or [SUPUESTO] if they require verification with an updated tool.
spec-desarrollo_revision_autenticacion_a:
[S · SITUATION] A development team needs to review the authentication and authorization mechanism implemented in their application or service. There are doubts about whether the access controls correctly prevent unauthorized access, privilege escalation, horizontal access between users, and brute force attacks or session hijacking.

[P · REQUEST] Review the pasted authentication and authorization code to identify security deficiencies, map them to concrete attack vectors, and produce technical remediation recommendations with corrected code or pseudocode, prioritized by severity.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior application security engineer specialized in design and review of authentication systems (sessions, JWT, OAuth2), access control (RBAC, ABAC, PBAC), and secure authorization patterns.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the authentication mechanism is not explicit, infer it from the code (JWT, session cookie, API key). If the authorization model is not specified, assume RBAC with user roles. If the framework is not mentioned, infer it from the code or declare the assumed one. Ask only if the role/permission data model is critical for the analysis and cannot be inferred.
INPUTS: Authentication middleware code, authorization handlers, user/role models, or relevant fragments pasted by the user.
STEPS:
1. Map the authentication flow: how identity is verified, how the session or token is created/validated, how logout is handled → textual flow diagram.
2. Review authentication against checklist: secure credential validation, password hashing (algorithm and parameters), session management (TTL, invalidation, rotation), brute force protection (rate limiting, lockout), JWT token security (algorithm, expiration, revocation) → table of items with status (secure / insecure / absent).
3. Review authorization against checklist: resource ownership verification (IDOR prevention), privilege separation by role, authorization on each endpoint (not only in UI), prevention of horizontal and vertical escalation → table of items with status.
4. For each deficiency: attack vector description | severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) | vulnerable code fragment | corrected fragment with comment → findings section with code.
5. Identify absent or incorrect design patterns: principle of least privilege, deny-by-default, separation of authentication and authorization → architecture recommendations.
6. Generate AuthN/AuthZ security verification checklist for team use in future reviews → checklist of 15-20 items.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Authentication flow diagram, AuthN checklist table, AuthZ checklist table, Findings section with code (vulnerable vs corrected), Architecture recommendations, Reusable checklist.
EDGE CASES: (a) JWT without server-side signature verification → report as Critical with token forgery vector; (b) Authorization only on the client side (frontend) → report as Critical; (c) Admin endpoint without server-side role verification → report as Critical with attack vector proof of concept.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each finding has vulnerable code, corrected code, and attack vector explained. Trade-off: speed of control implementation vs user experience — document UX impact of each security control. DoD: reusable checklist has 15+ items verifiable in code review.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each finding with [CÓDIGO] if it is in the pasted fragment, [INFERENCIA] if deduced from the design, or [SUPUESTO] if it requires additional context.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_oauth2_oidc:
[S · SITUATION] A development team needs to implement or review an authentication and authorization delegation flow based on OAuth2 and OpenID Connect (OIDC). This may involve a new identity provider integration, a flow for a mobile application, web SPA, backend-to-backend, or the exposure of their own Authorization Server. There is uncertainty about which flow (grant type) to use, how to handle tokens securely, and how to protect against common OAuth2 attacks.

[P · REQUEST] Design the appropriate OAuth2/OIDC flow for the described use case, producing: justified grant type selection, detailed sequence diagram, scopes and claims specification, token configuration (TTL, rotation, revocation), and list of mandatory security controls against the most frequent OAuth2 attacks.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior identity and access architect (IAM) with command of OAuth2 RFC 6749/6750, OIDC Core 1.0, PKCE (RFC 7636), token introspection, and OAuth2 security patterns (RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice).
ASSUMPTIONS: If the client type is not specified, ask (it is critical for selecting the grant type). If the identity provider is not specified, assume a standard OIDC-compatible provider. If the access token type is not indicated, assume structured JWT by default for own APIs. Ask only if the client type (public/confidential, SPA, mobile, server) is not inferrable.
INPUTS: Use case description: client type (web app, SPA, mobile, M2M service), protected resources to access, identity provider if it exists, session requirements.
STEPS:
1. Select optimal grant type based on the use case: Authorization Code + PKCE (for public clients), Client Credentials (M2M), Device Authorization Grant (browserless devices), Implicit (deprecated, document why not to use) → decision with justification and discarded alternatives.
2. Design detailed sequence diagram of the selected flow: actors (user, client, AS, RS), messages with key parameters (response_type, code_challenge, state, nonce, scope) → diagram in mermaid sequenceDiagram format.
3. Specify scopes and claims: OAuth2 scopes (resource access), OIDC claims (user identity), mapping to permissions in the Resource Server → scopes/claims table.
4. Configure token parameters: access_token (TTL, JWT vs opaque format), refresh_token (TTL, rotation, revocation), id_token (mandatory claims, validation) → configuration table.
5. List mandatory security controls: PKCE, state/nonce validation, exact redirect_uri, token binding, token revocation, CORS on AS endpoints, open redirect protection, CSRF → controls checklist with implementation description.
6. Describe token renewal and revocation flow on logout: refresh steps, revocation at AS (RFC 7009), client-side token cleanup → lifecycle management section.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Grant type selection (decision + justification), Mermaid sequence diagram, Scopes/claims table, Token configuration table, Security controls checklist, Token lifecycle section.
EDGE CASES: (a) SPA with refresh token → apply Refresh Token Rotation with sender-constrained tokens and document token leakage risk; (b) Multiple Resource Servers → design audience claim and per-RS validation; (c) External identity provider that does not support PKCE → document risk and mitigation alternative.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the sequence diagram covers all flow steps including error handling. Trade-off: token security vs validation latency (local JWT vs remote introspection) — document the decision. DoD: the design complies with the recommendations of OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700) without undocumented deviations.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each design decision with [CONFIG], [DOC] (reference to RFC/spec), or [INFERENCIA], and list the declared assumptions at the beginning.
spec-desarrollo_validacion_entrada_sanea:
[S · SITUATION] A development team needs to review or implement input validation and data sanitization controls in an application. The lack of these controls exposes the application to injections (SQL, NoSQL, command, LDAP, XSS, SSRF) and to processing of malformed data that can cause errors, data loss, or unexpected behavior.

[P · REQUEST] Review the pasted code to identify entry points without adequate validation or sanitization, map each finding to the corresponding injection vector, and provide the corrected code with the appropriate validation and sanitization strategy for each data use context.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior application security engineer with experience in injection defense, validation layer design, contextual encoders, and sanitization strategies in web applications, APIs, and data processing services.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the language is not explicit, infer it from the code. If the data use context is not clear (does it go to SQL? to HTML? to the file system?), infer it from the code and declare the assumption. If no validation framework is specified, recommend a standard one for the detected ecosystem. Ask only if there is a completely ambiguous data use context with high impact on the sanitization strategy.
INPUTS: Code fragment that processes user inputs: endpoints, forms, queries, calls to external systems, file processing.
STEPS:
1. Identify all external data entry points: HTTP parameters, headers, JSON/XML body, uploaded files, environment variables read from request → entry point inventory.
2. For each entry point: trace the data flow to its final use (is it used in a SQL query? in an HTML template? in a system command? in an HTTP call?) → data flow table with use context.
3. Classify deficiencies: absent validation, incorrect validation (allowlist vs blacklist), insufficient sanitization for the context, incorrect trust in third-party data → findings table with vulnerability type and severity.
4. For each finding: vulnerable code | exploitable injection vector | corrected code with strategy appropriate to the context (parameterized queries for SQL, contextual encoding for HTML, schema validation for JSON, canonicalized path for files) → remediation section with code.
5. Propose validation layer architecture: boundary input validation (schema validation), context-specific output sanitization (output encoding), defense in depth principle → layer diagram in text.
6. Generate validation checklist for the detected application type: data types to validate, controls per use context → reusable checklist.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Entry point inventory, Flow table with use context, Findings table (type, vector, severity), Remediation section with code, Validation layer architecture, Reusable checklist.
EDGE CASES: (a) Blacklist validation → always replace with allowlist with justification; (b) Data validated on the frontend but not on the backend → report as Critical; (c) Uploaded file with validated extension but unverified content → recommend magic bytes validation and processing sandbox.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each entry point has a validation and sanitization strategy specific to its data use context. Trade-off: validation strictness vs usability — document when strict validation may reject legitimate input and propose informative error handling. DoD: no entry points remain without documented validation, and no data flows with risky context use without sanitization.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each finding with [CÓDIGO] if it is in the fragment, [INFERENCIA] if deduced from the data flow, or [SUPUESTO] if the use context requires confirmation.
spec-desarrollo_threat_dread_priorizacio:
[S · SITUATION] A security or development team has a set of identified threats (possibly from a STRIDE exercise, pentesting, or bug bounty) and needs to prioritize them to allocate limited remediation resources. Without a consistent scoring method, prioritization decisions are subjective and not reproducible.

[P · REQUEST] Apply the DREAD scoring model (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected Users, Discoverability) to the pasted threat list, produce a prioritized ranking with justified scores, and generate a remediation plan by risk tier.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior security risk analyst with experience in threat scoring models (DREAD, CVSS, FAIR), security backlog prioritization, and risk communication to technical and business stakeholders.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the DREAD scoring system is not specified, use a 1-10 scale per dimension with total score = average of the 5 dimensions. If system context is not provided, request minimum context to estimate Affected Users accurately; if not provided, use relative estimation and mark as [SUPUESTO]. Ask only if a threat description is so ambiguous that no dimension can be estimated.
INPUTS: List of threats with at least one description of the attack vector per threat, pasted by the user.
STEPS:
1. Confirm understanding of each threat: for each threat in the list, formulate a standardized description sentence (Actor + Action + Affected Object + Consequence) → table of normalized threats.
2. Apply DREAD scoring to each threat: for each dimension (D, R, E, A, Di) assign a 1-10 score with a one-line justification → scoring table with columns per dimension + total.
3. Calculate total score (average) and sort from highest to lowest → prioritized ranking.
4. Classify into risk tiers: Critical (score ≥ 8.0), High (6.0-7.9), Medium (4.0-5.9), Low (< 4.0) → table with risk color and count per tier.
5. For Critical and High tiers: propose an immediate remediation action, suggested owner (team/role), and recommended time window → remediation plan table.
6. Identify threats with high Discoverability and low Exploitability → quick wins section (easy for attackers to find, easy to mitigate).
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Normalized threats table, Full DREAD scoring table, Prioritized ranking, Risk tier classification table, Remediation plan for Critical and High, Quick wins section.
EDGE CASES: (a) Two threats with the same total score → tiebreak by Damage dimension (higher impact first); (b) Threat dependent on another → document the dependency in the remediation plan; (c) Threat with Reproducibility=1 (requires very specific conditions) but Damage=10 → keep in High tier and document residual risk.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each threat has a DREAD score with per-dimension justification and is placed in a risk tier. Trade-off: scoring objectivity vs. contextual knowledge — document when an estimate is relative due to missing data. DoD: the ranking is reviewable and reproducible by any team member with the same inputs.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label scores with [INFERENCIA] if derived from the described vector, or [SUPUESTO] if the estimate requires unavailable data; declare assumptions at the start.
spec-desarrollo_revision_criptografia_ap:
[S · SITUATION] A development team uses cryptography in its application to protect data in transit and at rest, sign tokens, store passwords, or manage keys. Without a specialized review, it is common to find obsolete algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4), incorrect implementations (ECB mode, fixed IV, reused nonce), or use of low-level cryptographic primitives where a high-level library should be used instead.

[P · REQUEST] Review the pasted code to identify every cryptography use, evaluate whether the algorithms, modes of operation, parameters, and key management are secure according to current standards (NIST, OWASP), and provide concrete remediations with corrected code.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior applied cryptography engineer with experience reviewing cryptographic implementations, NIST SP 800 series, OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet, and secure cryptographic libraries by ecosystem (libsodium, Bouncy Castle, Web Crypto API, cryptography.io).
ASSUMPTIONS: If the language is not explicit, infer it from the code. If the cryptographic library is not specified, evaluate the one imported in the code. If the purpose of the cryptographic use is not clear, infer it from code context (password storage, data encryption, signing, key exchange) and declare the assumption. Ask only if the threat context (who is the adversary?) is critical for the recommendation and cannot be inferred.
INPUTS: Code snippet that uses cryptography: hashing, symmetric/asymmetric encryption, digital signing, key derivation, random number generation, certificate management.
STEPS:
1. Inventory all cryptographic uses in the code: function/method | algorithm used | detected purpose | library → cryptographic inventory table.
2. Evaluate each use against current security criteria: is the algorithm approved by NIST/OWASP? is the mode of operation correct (e.g. AES-GCM vs AES-ECB)? is the key length sufficient (≥128 bits symmetric, ≥2048 RSA, ≥256 ECC)? is the IV/nonce random and unique? is a key derivation function used for passwords (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2)? is a CSPRNG used for randomness? → evaluation table with status (secure / insecure / discouraged).
3. For each insecure use: description of the specific weakness | known attack that exploits the weakness (e.g. Padding Oracle, Birthday Attack, Related-Key Attack) | severity → findings table.
4. For each finding: vulnerable code | corrected code with secure algorithm/mode/parameter + technical comment explaining the reason for the change → remediations section.
5. Evaluate key management: where keys are stored, how they are derived, whether they are rotated, whether environment separation exists → key management evaluation section with recommendations.
6. Recommend high-level library alternatives that eliminate the need to manually configure primitives → recommendations section by ecosystem.
OUTPUT: Markdown document: Cryptographic inventory, Evaluation table (algorithms/modes/parameters), Findings table (weakness + attack + severity), Remediations section with code, Key management evaluation, Library recommendations.
EDGE CASES: (a) MD5 used for integrity checksum (not security) → evaluate the context; if there is no adversary, document as low risk but recommend migration to SHA-256; (b) Custom cryptography implemented from scratch → report as Critical without needing to review details; (c) Correct algorithm with hardcoded static IV → report as Critical (equivalent to ECB in practice).

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: every cryptographic use in the code has an evaluated status and insecure uses have a remediation with code. Trade-off: immediate migration vs. compatibility with existing data — document a gradual migration strategy when applicable. DoD: no obsolete algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4, 3DES) or insecure modes (ECB, CBC without MAC) remain without a documented finding.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Label each finding with [CÓDIGO] if it is in the snippet, [INFERENCIA] if deduced from the use, or [SUPUESTO] if it requires adversary context; cite the relevant standard (NIST/OWASP) for each recommendation.
spec-desarrollo_checklist_secure_coding: [S · SITUATION] A development team ships code to production without a systematic review of common vulnerabilities; the languages in use are Java, Python, or JavaScript (Node.js). The technical lead needs a checklist applicable before each merge to reduce the attack surface. [P · REQUEST] Produce a secure coding checklist specific to the indicated language: at least 20 items grouped by category (input validation, authentication/authorization, secrets handling, dependency management, secure logging, error handling, cryptography), with an observable compliance criterion and severity level (Critical / High / Medium) per item. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Application security expert (AppSec) with CSSLP certification and 10 years reviewing production code in financial systems. ASSUMPTIONS: language = Java if not specified; environment = backend REST API; standard ecosystem framework (Spring Boot / FastAPI / Express); if confidence in context < 0.85, declare the assumption before continuing without asking. INPUTS: code snippet pasted by the user or description of the module to review. STEPS: 1. Identify the language and framework from the provided code. 2. Select the risk categories applicable to the module type. 3. Draft each item as a verifiable audit question. 4. Assign severity based on OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25. 5. Present a Markdown table with columns: #, Category, Item, Compliance criterion, Severity. 6. Include a 'References' section with CWE/OWASP ID per item. OUTPUT: Exportable Markdown table + numbered references section. EDGE CASES: (a) unsupported language → map to the closest language and note differences; (b) module with no authentication logic → omit that section and explain it; (c) legacy code without tests → add specific minimum coverage items. [C · CRITERIA] Each item must be verifiable with a tool or manual inspection in < 5 minutes. Trade-off: depth vs. adoption speed — prefer actionable items over theoretical exhaustiveness. DoD: checklist reviewed by the technical lead and approved for use in the CI pipeline within one sprint.
spec-desarrollo_code_review_estructurada: [S · SITUATION] An agile team performs ad hoc code reviews without homogeneous criteria; reviewers focus on surface-level style and miss design, performance, or security issues. The tech lead wants to standardize the process with a structured checklist that guides consistent reviews on medium-sized pull requests (< 400 changed lines). [P · REQUEST] Execute a structured code review of the provided snippet or diff, producing: (a) findings table by category with severity and reference line, (b) 5-line executive summary, (c) prioritized list of required vs. suggested actions. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior software engineer with 12 years of code reviews in distributed teams, specializing in design quality and technical debt. ASSUMPTIONS: language = as detected in the diff; team standards = Google Style Guide for the corresponding language if none other is indicated; Pull Request = feature branch to main; if confidence < 0.85 declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: diff or code snippet pasted directly. STEPS: 1. Read the full diff and identify the purpose of the change. 2. Review by category: logical correctness, security, performance, readability, error handling, test coverage, design/architecture. 3. Record each finding with: category, description, affected line(s), severity (Blocker/Major/Minor/Nit), required action. 4. Draft executive summary. 5. List actions in priority order: required first. OUTPUT: Markdown findings table + executive summary + action list. EDGE CASES: (a) diff without sufficient context → request complete relevant files before continuing; (b) purely cosmetic change → indicate this and confirm whether an in-depth review is desired; (c) auto-generated code → review only the business logic and document it. [C · CRITERIA] Each finding must cite a specific line or block. Trade-off: thoroughness vs. reviewer time — prioritize Blockers and Majors. DoD: findings table approved by the tech lead before merge.
spec-desarrollo_revision_pull_request_di: [S · SITUATION] A developer opens a pull request with a diff that mixes new business logic, refactoring, and configuration adjustments. Reviewers have difficulty separating intentional changes from accidental ones and evaluating the real impact of the PR on the system. [P · REQUEST] Analyze the provided pull request diff and produce: (a) change map by type (new logic, refactor, config, tests, dependencies), (b) impact assessment by area (functional, performance, security, compatibility), (c) list of questions to the author to clarify intent, (d) approval verdict with conditions. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior technical reviewer with experience in systems design and continuous delivery, accustomed to evaluating 200–600 line PRs in critical systems. ASSUMPTIONS: base branch = main/master; the PR is ready for review (not WIP); system context = REST microservice if not specified; if confidence < 0.85 declare and continue. INPUTS: complete PR diff pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Classify each modified file by type of change. 2. Identify high-impact changes (critical logic, error paths, database queries, security configuration). 3. Detect inconsistencies between the PR title/description and the actual diff content. 4. Formulate numbered clarification questions for the author. 5. Issue verdict: Approve / Approve with minor changes / Requires changes / Reject + justification. OUTPUT: change map (table), impact assessment (table), questions to author (numbered list), verdict with justification (paragraph). EDGE CASES: (a) diff too large > 600 lines → request splitting into smaller PRs; (b) no PR description → work only with the diff and note the limitation; (c) infrastructure-as-code PR → apply additional idempotency and reversibility criteria. [C · CRITERIA] The change map must cover 100% of the modified files. Trade-off: review speed vs. depth — prioritize high-impact changes. DoD: verdict documented with traceable criteria before PR approval.
spec-desarrollo_redaccion_comentarios_pr: [S · SITUATION] Reviewers on an engineering team write vague or unconstructive PR comments ('this is wrong', 'refactor this'), which generates friction, defensive rejections, and unnecessary review cycles. The tech lead wants to raise the communicative quality of reviews so that each comment is understood and implemented correctly on the first attempt. [P · REQUEST] Given a technical finding in a PR (problem description, code snippet, and context), draft 3 versions of a review comment with different tones: (a) technical-direct, (b) collaborative-explanatory, (c) learning-oriented. Each version must include: problem identification, reasoning, concrete suggestion with alternative code if applicable, and urgency level. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior engineer with experience in technical leadership of remote teams and a psychologically safe feedback culture. ASSUMPTIONS: the reviewer knows the PR context; the author is a mid-level developer; the team values autonomy; if confidence < 0.85 declare assumption. INPUTS: description of the finding + problematic code snippet pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify the type of problem (bug, design, readability, security, performance, test). 2. Formulate the technical reasoning behind the problem. 3. Draft the 3 comment versions according to the indicated tone. 4. Include suggested code in a Markdown code block if the change is concrete. 5. Assign an urgency label: [BLOCKER] [SUGGESTION] [NIT]. OUTPUT: 3 comments in Markdown, each with a tone header + urgency label + alternative code if applicable. EDGE CASES: (a) subjective style issue → use only collaborative tone and note it; (b) critical security bug → always mark as [BLOCKER] without softening; (c) AI-generated code → address with pedagogical tone about review responsibility. [C · CRITERIA] Each comment must be actionable in < 30 minutes by the author. Trade-off: firmness vs. receptivity — calibrate according to urgency. DoD: the 3 comments reviewed by the tech lead and directly usable in GitHub/GitLab.
spec-desarrollo_revision_legibilidad_nom: [S · SITUATION] An engineering team maintains a multi-year codebase with inconsistent naming conventions: single-letter variables, functions with ambiguous names, generic classes like 'Manager' or 'Helper', and comments that contradict the code. Onboarding of new developers takes twice as long as expected due to low code readability. [P · REQUEST] Review the provided code snippet and produce: (a) table of identifiers with readability problems (current name → suggested name + justification), (b) overall readability evaluation with a 1–10 score and criteria, (c) recommended naming rules for the detected language in a one-page style guide format. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Software engineer specializing in clean code and team onboarding, author of internal style guides at technology companies. ASSUMPTIONS: language = as detected in the snippet; naming convention = camelCase for methods/variables, PascalCase for classes (adjust if the language uses a different convention); if confidence < 0.85 declare and continue. INPUTS: code snippet pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify all identifiers: variables, functions, classes, parameters, constants. 2. Evaluate each name against criteria: intentionality, pronounceability, searchability, avoid non-standard abbreviations, avoid generic prefixes/suffixes. 3. Propose an alternative name with brief justification. 4. Calculate a readability score of 1–10 with an explicit rubric. 5. Draft a one-page naming guide for the language. OUTPUT: identifier table + score + naming guide in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (a) code in a language other than English → respect the team's language and note it; (b) names that are framework reserved words → annotate the conflict; (c) minified or generated code → note that naming review does not apply. [C · CRITERIA] At least 80% of the reviewed identifiers must have a suggested name with justification. Trade-off: expressiveness vs. brevity — prefer expressiveness for business domain code. DoD: naming guide approved by the tech lead and published in the repository.
spec-desarrollo_revision_clean_code: [S · SITUATION] A development team applies Clean Code principles inconsistently: long functions with multiple responsibilities, unnecessary comments that explain the 'how' instead of the 'why', logic duplication across modules, and mixed abstraction levels within the same function. The team wants to adopt Clean Code systematically using guided reviews. [P · REQUEST] Review the provided code snippet against Clean Code principles (Uncle Bob) and produce: (a) diagnosis by principle with concrete findings and reference lines, (b) suggested refactoring of the most problematic snippet, (c) cleanliness score 1–10 with rubric, (d) 3-step prioritized improvement plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Software architect and technical trainer with deep mastery of Clean Code, SOLID, and refactoring patterns, with experience guiding development teams on technical debt. ASSUMPTIONS: language = as detected; applicable principles = those from Robert C. Martin's Clean Code (small functions, one level of abstraction per function, do not repeat yourself, intentional names, comments only for the why); if confidence < 0.85 declare and continue. INPUTS: code snippet pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify the language and purpose of the snippet. 2. Evaluate against each applicable Clean Code principle. 3. Record findings with violated principle, description, line(s), and severity. 4. Select the most problematic snippet and offer a refactoring with explanation. 5. Calculate score 1–10. 6. Propose a 3-step improvement plan ordered by impact vs. effort. OUTPUT: findings table + refactored code block + score + improvement plan in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (a) snippet too short (< 10 lines) → apply applicable principles and declare limitation; (b) infrastructure/config code → omit domain naming principles; (c) already very clean code → confirm high score and point out the single improvement opportunity. [C · CRITERIA] The suggested refactoring must pass the same tests (or be equivalently testable) as the original. Trade-off: Clean Code purity vs. pragmatism — do not break public APIs for aesthetic preference. DoD: improvement plan with effort estimate and assigned sprint.
spec-desarrollo_revision_solid: [S · SITUATION] An object-oriented development team notices that their classes grow in responsibilities over time, their inheritance hierarchies become fragile, and their modules are difficult to extend without modifying existing code. The tech lead wants a systematic design review oriented around the five SOLID principles to identify concrete violations and plan refactorings. [P · REQUEST] Review the provided code snippet or class diagram against the five SOLID principles (SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP) and produce: (a) evaluation by principle with a 1–5 score and concrete findings, (b) refactored class diagram in text (simplified UML notation or Mermaid), (c) refactoring plan with suggested design pattern and estimated effort in days. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Object-oriented software architect with 15 years designing scalable systems and training teams in SOLID and design patterns. ASSUMPTIONS: language = object-oriented (Java/C#/Python/TypeScript); the code represents a domain module, not infrastructure; if confidence < 0.85 declare and continue. INPUTS: code snippet or class description pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify the classes, interfaces, and dependencies present. 2. Evaluate each SOLID principle with evidence from the code. 3. Assign a 1–5 score per principle with rubric. 4. Draw the refactored diagram in Mermaid or pseudo-UML notation. 5. Propose a design pattern for each main violation. 6. Estimate refactoring effort in developer-days. OUTPUT: SOLID evaluation table + refactored diagram + plan with patterns and effort. EDGE CASES: (a) procedural code → apply only SRP and DIP and note it; (b) multiple interconnected violations → address in the order SRP → DIP → OCP → ISP → LSP to progressively undo dependencies; (c) ORM/framework-generated code → exclude from analysis and note it. [C · CRITERIA] Each violation must have a suggested design pattern (Strategy, Factory, Decorator, etc.) with justification. Trade-off: SOLID adherence vs. added complexity — do not over-abstract simple modules. DoD: refactoring plan approved by the tech lead with priorities assigned to the backlog.
spec-desarrollo_definicion_definition_of: [S · SITUATION] An agile development team has a vague Definition of Done (DoD) that only includes 'code review approved' and 'deployed to staging'. Without precise technical criteria, user stories are considered done with insufficient test coverage, without updated API documentation, and with accumulated technical debt. The Scrum Master and tech lead want to redefine the DoD with measurable and verifiable technical criteria. [P · REQUEST] Design a complete technical Definition of Done for the provided team context, including: (a) list of criteria ordered by category (code, tests, security, performance, documentation, deployment, review), (b) observable verification criterion per item (automatable vs. manual), (c) responsibility table by role (developer, QA, tech lead, DevOps), (d) documented exception process. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Technical Scrum Master and engineering team coach with experience defining quality agreements in organizations migrating from waterfall to agile. ASSUMPTIONS: team of 4–8 people; 2-week sprints; stack = microservices if not specified; active CI/CD with a basic pipeline; if confidence < 0.85 declare and continue. INPUTS: description of the team context and the product type (API, frontend, data service, etc.) pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Gather the team context and product type. 2. Identify the applicable criteria categories. 3. Draft each criterion as a verifiable condition: 'The code has X% unit test coverage, verified with [tool]'. 4. Classify each criterion as automatic (CI) or manual (human review). 5. Assign responsibilities by role in a simplified RACI table. 6. Document the exception process with conditional acceptance criteria. OUTPUT: Complete DoD in Markdown with criteria table, simplified RACI, and exception process. EDGE CASES: (a) team without formal QA → redistribute responsibilities among developers; (b) infrastructure product → add idempotency and reversibility criteria; (c) excessively long DoD (> 25 items) → prioritize top 15 and move the rest to 'good practices'. [C · CRITERIA] At least 70% of the criteria must be automatable in the CI/CD pipeline. Trade-off: rigor vs. delivery speed — calibrate based on team maturity. DoD of the DoD: approved by the entire team in a retrospective and signed by the tech lead.
spec-desarrollo_revision_manejo_errores: [S · SITUATION] A production system generates unhandled exceptions that cause silent crashes, error messages that expose stack traces to the end client, and logs without enough context to diagnose problems. The team needs a systematic review of error handling in their codebase to implement a robust and consistent strategy. [P · REQUEST] Review the provided code snippet and produce: (a) an inventory of error-handling issues with severity and reference line, (b) classification of identified errors (expected/recoverable vs. unexpected/fatal), (c) error-handling refactoring with a suggested strategy (fail-fast, circuit breaker, retry, fallback), (d) a standard error template for the detected layer (API, service, repository). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) with experience in fault-tolerant system design and production observability. ASSUMPTIONS: environment = production microservice; error handling must include structured logging with trace correlation; the client is a REST API unless otherwise specified; if confidence < 0.85, declare and continue. INPUTS: code snippet pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify all error-handling points: try/catch, validations, error responses. 2. Classify each error: expected (business validation) vs. unexpected (infrastructure failure). 3. Evaluate: is the error logged with sufficient context? Does it expose sensitive information to the client? Is it propagated correctly? Is there recovery or fallback? 4. Propose a refactoring with the appropriate strategy. 5. Draft a standard error template for the detected layer. OUTPUT: problem table + error classification + refactored code block + error template in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (a) code with no error handling at all → flag the risk and propose a structure from scratch; (b) excessive error handling with generic catch → identify error swallowing as Blocker; (c) asynchronous code (async/await or Promises) → review propagation in async chains. [C · CRITERIA] No infrastructure error should propagate to the client without transformation. Trade-off: diagnostic information vs. security — never expose stack traces or internal data to the end client. DoD: zero unhandled exceptions in the system's critical path, verified in code review.
spec-desarrollo_revision_concurrencia_ra: [S · SITUATION] A system with multiple concurrent threads or processes shows intermittent behavior in production: corrupted data, sporadic deadlocks under high load, and inconsistent results in operations that should be atomic. The team suspects race conditions but does not know how to identify them systematically in their code. [P · REQUEST] Review the provided concurrent code snippet and identify: (a) potential race conditions with a description of the failure scenario, (b) synchronization issues (deadlock, livelock, starvation), (c) incorrect use of concurrency primitives, (d) safe refactoring with justification for the chosen synchronization mechanism, (e) suggested concurrency test cases. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Systems engineer specialized in concurrent and parallel programming, with experience debugging race conditions in Java, Go, and Python systems in production. ASSUMPTIONS: environment = multithreaded or asynchronous depending on the code; critical operations require eventual or strong consistency depending on the business context; if confidence < 0.85, declare and continue. INPUTS: code snippet with concurrency pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify shared resources: variables, collections, connections, files. 2. Trace the threads or coroutines that access those resources. 3. Identify points where two or more threads could access simultaneously without synchronization. 4. Classify each issue: race condition, deadlock, livelock, starvation, visibility (memory model). 5. Propose refactoring with the simplest effective mechanism (lock, atomic, concurrent collection, channel, actor model). 6. Design concurrency test cases: load scenarios and interleaving conditions. OUTPUT: concurrency problem table + safe refactored code block + suggested test cases in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (a) code with no explicit concurrency → look for implicit concurrency (ORM, reactive frameworks) and flag it; (b) language with GIL (Python) → adjust analysis for I/O bound vs. CPU bound operations; (c) distributed code (microservices) → scale analysis to distributed race conditions (TOCTOU, double write). [C · CRITERIA] Each identified race condition must have a concrete failure scenario (what happens, when, with what probability). Trade-off: performance vs. concurrency safety — do not over-synchronize at the expense of throughput. DoD: zero race conditions in the critical path verified with a load test.
spec-desarrollo_plan_pruebas_unitarias: [S · SITUATION] A development team has low unit test coverage (< 40%) because developers do not know where to start, write brittle tests that break with any refactoring, and do not follow a consistent pattern. The tech lead wants to establish a solid unit testing practice using the Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) pattern. [P · REQUEST] Given the provided code snippet, generate: (a) an inventory of required unit test cases grouped by scenario (happy path, errors, edge cases), (b) complete implementation of the 3 most critical tests using AAA with the framework of the detected language, (c) a guide of 5 principles for writing maintainable unit tests for the team, (d) an estimate of achievable line and branch coverage with the proposed tests. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Software quality engineer with 10 years implementing testing strategies in product teams, specialized in fast, deterministic, and maintainable unit tests. ASSUMPTIONS: test framework = most common for the detected language (JUnit/pytest/Jest/NUnit); mocks = Mockito/unittest.mock/Jest.mock depending on language; minimum coverage target = 80% lines and 70% branches; if confidence < 0.85, declare and continue. INPUTS: code snippet or function/method to test pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify the unit under test (function, method, class). 2. List all possible test cases: valid input, invalid input, numeric edge cases, null/undefined, expected exceptions. 3. Prioritize the 3 most critical for immediate implementation. 4. Implement each test with the AAA pattern explicitly commented. 5. Draft the guide of 5 principles. 6. Estimate achievable coverage. OUTPUT: case inventory (table) + 3 implemented tests (code) + principles guide (list) + coverage estimate in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (a) function with external dependencies → use mocks and document the double strategy; (b) non-testable code (hardcoded dependencies) → flag it and indicate the minimum refactoring needed; (c) private method → test through the public interface and indicate it. [C · CRITERIA] Each test must be: fast (< 100ms), deterministic (no external dependencies), independent (no execution order), with a name that describes the scenario. Trade-off: maximum coverage vs. maintainability — prefer tests that survive refactorings over tests that maximize the number of covered lines. DoD: test suite approved in PR, green in CI, and with coverage >= 80% in the reviewed module.
spec-desarrollo_test_driven_development: [S · SITUATION] A team wants to adopt Test-Driven Development (TDD) to develop a new business feature, but developers struggle to get started: they do not know which test to write first, how much production code to write in the green step, or when to refactor without breaking the tests. They need a practical guide with a concrete example applied to their user story. [P · REQUEST] Given the provided business requirement, run a complete TDD red-green-refactor cycle with: (a) decomposition of the requirement into testable behaviors, (b) step-by-step implementation of 3 cycle iterations (failing test → minimal code → refactor), (c) final production code and resulting tests, (d) reflection on when to stop the cycle (completion criterion). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert developer in TDD and emergent design, extreme programming practitioner with experience guiding TDD katas in teams adopting the practice for the first time. ASSUMPTIONS: language = as indicated by the user or TypeScript by default; test framework = Jest for TypeScript, pytest for Python, JUnit for Java; each cycle iteration must produce the minimum code needed to pass the test; if confidence < 0.85, declare and continue. INPUTS: business requirement description pasted by the user (e.g., 'calculate shopping cart discount'). STEPS: 1. Break the requirement into a list of testable behaviors ordered from simplest to most complex. 2. Select the simplest behavior for the first iteration. 3. Iteration 1: write failing test → minimal code that passes it → refactor if applicable. 4. Iteration 2: next behavior → test → minimal code → refactor. 5. Iteration 3: edge or error case → test → minimal code → refactor. 6. Present final consolidated code with all tests. 7. Define the cycle completion criterion for this requirement. OUTPUT: list of testable behaviors + 3 iterations in numbered code blocks + final consolidated code + completion criterion in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (a) ambiguous requirement → request clarification on the expected behavior before starting; (b) complex requirement with multiple dependencies → use mocks from the start and indicate it; (c) UI requirement → apply TDD to business logic only and indicate the separation. [C · CRITERIA] Each iteration must explicitly show the three cycle steps. The production code in the green step must be the minimum necessary, not the final solution. Trade-off: development speed vs. emergent design — trust that the cycle leads to the right design. DoD: all tests green, no production code without a backing test, coverage >= 90% of the developed module.
spec-desarrollo_behavior_driven_gherkin:
[S · SITUATION] A development team works with Behavior-Driven Development and needs to translate user stories and acceptance criteria into executable Gherkin scenarios (Given/When/Then) that serve as a living contract between business and technology.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete set of Gherkin scenarios ready to implement, covering the happy path, variants, and edge cases of the described feature, with Feature, Background if applicable, and organizational tags.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior BDD analyst with 8 years of experience writing executable specifications in enterprise software agile projects.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no language is specified, assume English for the scenarios. If no tool is indicated, assume Cucumber/SpecFlow. If no acceptance criteria are detailed, derive them from the pasted user story. Ask only if the user story is absent or ambiguous on more than one critical point (maximum 2 questions).
INPUTS: User story and acceptance criteria pasted in the thread; optionally business rules or additional examples.
STEPS:
1. Analyze the user story and identify actors, preconditions, and expected outcomes → list of key behaviors.
2. Group behaviors into a Feature with a one-line functional description.
3. Draft Background if there are shared preconditions between scenarios.
4. Write Scenario or Scenario Outline for each behavior: happy path, data variants, anticipated errors.
5. Add tags @smoke, @regression, @negative according to the nature of the scenario.
6. Review that each Given/When/Then step is atomic, declarative, and without implementation logic.
OUTPUT: Complete .feature file with Feature, Background (if applicable), minimum 4 scenarios (happy path + 3 variants/edge cases), Examples table for Scenario Outline, classification tags. Gherkin code block format.
EDGE CASES:
- Story with multiple actors: create one Feature per actor or main flow, do not mix.
- Contradictory acceptance criteria: flag the contradiction and assume the more restrictive version until clarified.
- Feature with complex state: use Background to initialize shared state and avoid repetition.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each scenario is autonomous (does not depend on execution order).
- Steps use business domain vocabulary, not technical implementation.
- There is at least one negative or error-validation scenario.
- A developer can implement the step definitions without asking the author.
- Trade-off: depth of coverage vs. maintainability; prefer concise scenarios over exhaustive ones.
- DoD: the .feature file passes Gherkin syntax validation and is reviewed and approved by the Product Owner.

Protocolo MetodologIA: specify the user story → receive executable Gherkin scenarios ready for the sprint.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_pruebas_integraci:
[S · SITUATION] An engineering team maintains a service architecture (microservices, REST/gRPC APIs, or internal modules) and needs an integration test plan that verifies communication contracts, error handling between services, and data consistency across integration points.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver an integration test design document with: map of integrations to cover, test categories by coupling type, concrete test cases (name, precondition, action, expected result, assertion type), and environment strategy (real, container, double).

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior quality architect with experience in distributed systems testing and integration strategy design for enterprise platforms.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no stack is specified, assume REST services with JSON. If no environment is indicated, assume Docker containers with Testcontainers. If the service diagram is not attached, request a minimal description of the services and their dependencies (maximum 2 questions if confidence in the architecture is < 0.85).
INPUTS: Description or diagram of the services involved, API contracts (OpenAPI/Swagger or description), and any relevant performance or SLA requirements pasted in the thread.
STEPS:
1. Identify all integration points: input/output contracts, protocols, and data formats.
2. Classify integrations by criticality (blocking for business flow vs. optional).
3. Design test cases by category: happy path, network error, unexpected provider response, timeout, invalid data.
4. Define environment strategy for each category (real service, mock/stub, ephemeral container).
5. Specify verifiable assertions: HTTP code, response schema, response time, database state.
6. Order cases by execution priority in CI/CD pipeline.
OUTPUT: Integration test case table (name, source service, destination service, precondition, action, expected result, environment type, priority) + environment strategy section + suite approval criteria. Markdown format with tables.
EDGE CASES:
- Circular integration between services: design cases with a double to break the cycle without losing coverage.
- External third-party service without sandbox: document as manual test with verification checklist.
- Variable latency in the integration environment: set explicit timeout threshold and mark test as flaky if it exceeds 3 non-deterministic failures.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each test case has an observable and automatically verifiable expected result.
- Cases cover at least one failure scenario for each critical integration.
- The environment strategy is executable in the CI/CD pipeline without access to production.
- Trade-off: exhaustive coverage vs. execution time; prioritize integrations in the critical business flow.
- DoD: the document is reviewed by the tech lead and the cases are implemented or scheduled in the backlog.

Protocolo MetodologIA: describe the services and their connections → receive the complete integration test design.
spec-desarrollo_contract_testing_pact:
[S · SITUATION] A team develops microservices with dependencies between API consumers and providers. They need to implement contract testing with Pact to ensure that changes in the provider do not break consumers, without requiring full integration tests on every build.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) design of the Pact contracts for the identified consumer-provider interactions, (2) step-by-step implementation guide for consumer and provider, (3) publication and verification strategy on Pact Broker.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior quality engineer specialized in consumer-driven contract testing and microservice architectures with experience in Pact Framework.
