The deliverable is the model design (variables, transformations, validation) or interpretation of results if model outputs are already available, together with an ROI table by channel and a justified reallocation plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Econometrician specializing in Marketing Mix Modeling with experience in regression models with Adstock effects, saturation, and control variables. ASSUMPTIONS: if no historical data are provided, design the conceptual model and describe the minimum required data; if no analysis horizon is specified, use 2 years of weekly data as the minimum recommended; if no channels are indicated, assume the most common ones (paid search, social media, email, organic). INPUTS: paste below the available data (sales/conversion time series, spend by channel per week, control variables such as seasonality, price, distribution, or others) or describe the context for conceptual design. STEPS: 1. Define the dependent variable (sales, conversions, revenue) and the analysis period. 2. Identify independent variables: spend by channel, control variables (price, distribution, seasonality, competition), and dummy variables for special events. 3. Specify Adstock transformations (advertising memory) and saturation curves (diminishing returns) by channel. 4. Describe the estimation process (Bayesian or frequentist linear regression) and fit metrics (R², MAPE). 5. If model results are available: extract percentage contributions by channel, calculate ROI = (attributed sales × margin) / spend by channel, identify over-invested and under-invested channels relative to the saturation point. 6. Produce budget reallocation recommendations with estimated impact on sales. OUTPUT: model design with technical specification of variables and transformations; or results table with (Channel, Spend, Attributed sales, Contribution %, Estimated ROI, Position on saturation curve, Recommendation); reallocation plan with percentage change per channel and estimated sales impact. EDGE CASES: (a) if the data horizon is less than one year, warn about the inability to capture full seasonality; (b) if there are channels with very sporadic or episodic spend, recommend excluding or aggregating them; (c) if adjusted R² is below 0.70, recommend incorporating additional control variables before interpreting contributions. [C · CRITERIA] Adstock and saturation transformations are justified by channel type; contributions sum to 100% or the residual organic component is explained; reallocation recommendations have a quantified impact; causality is not asserted without cross-validation. DoD: complete technical model specification, ROI table by channel, reallocation plan with estimated impact.

Protocolo MetodologIA: specify model transformations before interpreting results; separate measured contribution from estimation with [ASSUMPTION] where necessary; and quantify the expected impact of each reallocation recommendation.
spec-marketing_plan_tagueo_utm_taxonomia:
[S · SITUATION] A digital marketing team manages campaigns across multiple channels (Google Ads, Meta, email, affiliates, organic social, and others) and needs to standardize how it tags its URLs with UTM parameters so that data in Google Analytics, Adobe Analytics, or another web analytics tool are comparable, clean, and useful for decision-making. Currently there are naming inconsistencies that cause channels and campaigns to appear duplicated or misclassified in reports. [P · REQUEST] Design a complete UTM tagging plan with a standardized campaign taxonomy, a naming convention applicable to all channels, an allowed-values table per parameter, and an implementation guide with examples. The deliverable is a tagging governance document that serves as the team's single reference and eliminates ambiguity. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Digital analytics specialist with experience implementing UTM tagging plans for multichannel marketing teams. ASSUMPTIONS: use the 5 standard UTM parameters (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_content, utm_term); if no analytics tool is indicated, design compatible with Google Analytics 4; if no channels are specified, cover the most common (paid_search, paid_social, email, organic_social, affiliate, display). INPUTS: describe below the active channels, advertising platforms used, types of campaigns that run habitually, and the most frequent naming problems. STEPS: 1. Define allowed values for utm_source by channel (e.g.: google, meta, mailchimp, linkedin) in lowercase without spaces. 2. Define allowed values for utm_medium by traffic type (e.g.: cpc, cpm, email, organic_social, affiliate). 3. Design the naming convention for utm_campaign with hierarchical structure: [year]-[quarter or month]-[campaign-name]-[audience or product]. 4. Define when to use utm_content (creative differentiation) and utm_term (manual keywords). 5. Build a table of prohibited or non-standard source-medium combinations (e.g.: source=google with medium=email is incorrect). 6. Produce complete URL examples for each primary channel. 7. Define the approval and quality-control process before launching campaigns. OUTPUT: allowed-values table per UTM parameter; campaign naming convention with examples; valid and invalid source-medium combinations table; 5–8 tagged URL examples per channel; QA checklist before launch; taxonomy maintenance and update process. EDGE CASES: (a) if there are already-active campaign URLs with inconsistent tagging, describe the correction process without breaking the history in the analytics tool; (b) if the team uses a platform that auto-appends parameters (ValueTrack, Meta), specify how to coexist with manual UTMs; (c) if there are multiple markets or countries, define whether the taxonomy is global or includes market prefixes. [C · CRITERIA] Values for each parameter are in lowercase, without spaces, without special characters; source-medium combinations are internally coherent; examples cover all primary channels; the document is self-contained and usable without additional context. DoD: complete values table, campaign naming convention defined, minimum 5 URL examples, QA checklist.

Protocolo MetodologIA: define utm_source and utm_medium values first as a controlled vocabulary; the entire campaign taxonomy is built on that foundation to ensure consistency in analytics reports.
spec-marketing_analisis_funnel_conversio: [S · SITUATION] The digital marketing team of a B2B SaaS company has historical data from its acquisition funnel with volumes and conversion rates between stages (visits → leads → MQL → SQL → opportunities → customers), but has not conducted a structured diagnosis to identify where the most relative value is lost, nor what prioritized actions would improve closing revenue. [P · REQUEST] Written diagnosis of conversion rates by funnel stage, with identification of the stage with the greatest relative loss, a sectoral benchmark reference, and a roadmap of 3 initiatives prioritized by impact/effort to improve global conversion by at least 15 percentage points in the critical stage. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior growth and funnel optimization analyst with experience in B2B SaaS and revenue operations methodologies. ASSUMPTIONS: if no data is provided, assume a standard 5-stage funnel with illustrative fictitious rates; sectoral benchmark from the B2B midmarket software industry; sales cycle of 30–90 days — declare these assumptions upfront and proceed without asking unless confidence is below 0.85. INPUTS: funnel data pasted in the thread (volumes by stage, analysis period, segment or channel if available). STEPS: 1. Calculate step-by-step and cumulative global conversion rates — produce a table with columns: Stage, Inputs, Outputs, Rate, Benchmark, GAP. 2. Identify the bottleneck stage with the greatest weighted value loss by volume — justify in 3 lines. 3. Analyze probable root causes of the critical stage using a condensed 5 Whys framework. 4. Compare rates against the B2B SaaS sectoral benchmark — flag deviations >5 pp. 5. Formulate 3 improvement initiatives ordered by an impact/effort matrix — for each: name, 2-line description, success KPI, estimated timeline. 6. Project an optimistic conversion scenario if all 3 initiatives are executed. OUTPUT: structured document with sections: Current rates vs benchmark table / Bottleneck diagnosis / Root causes / Initiative roadmap / Improved scenario projection. EDGE CASES: (a) if the funnel has fewer than 3 stages, infer standard intermediate stages and note it; (b) if volumes are very low (<50 leads/month) warn about statistical significance before drawing conclusions; (c) if all rates are above the benchmark, redirect the analysis to identify the improvement ceiling and prioritize retention over acquisition. [C · CRITERIA] Every calculated rate must be reproducible from the input data; the bottleneck must be justified with a calculation of lost value (volume × rate delta × value per customer); initiatives must have SMART KPIs; the document should not exceed 800 words of prose plus tables. DoD: all sections complete, no assertions without data or declared assumption. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions upfront, calculate first, interpret afterward, zero assertions without evidence or [ASSUMPTION] label.
spec-marketing_modelo_forecast_demanda_m: [S · SITUATION] The marketing team of a company with an active sales pipeline needs to build a demand forecast model that projects the volume of leads, MQLs, and opportunities for the next 3 to 6 months, integrating historical conversion data, observed seasonality, and planned advertising investment budget, so that the commercial team can plan capacity and the CFO can validate revenue assumptions. [P · REQUEST] Forecast model in the form of a projected monthly table (3 base months + 2 scenarios: conservative and optimistic) with explicit formulas, declared assumptions, and a 150-word executive note to present to the CFO. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior demand generation and revenue forecasting specialist with experience in bottom-up models for SaaS and B2B services companies. ASSUMPTIONS: if no historical data is provided, use B2B SaaS benchmark conversion rates (visit→lead 2%, lead→MQL 25%, MQL→SQL 30%, SQL→customer 20%); reference monthly marketing budget 10,000 USD; average cost per lead 50 USD — declare upfront and proceed. INPUTS: monthly lead and conversion history (minimum 3 months), projected marketing budget per month, any known seasonal factor. STEPS: 1. Calculate average historical conversion rate per stage and coefficient of variation to estimate reliability. 2. Identify seasonality (monthly index) if at least 6 months of data exist, or declare neutral seasonality [ASSUMPTION]. 3. Build a bottom-up model: investment → impressions → clicks → leads → MQL → SQL → opportunities, with an explicit formula at each step. 4. Generate a monthly projection table for 3 months in the base scenario. 5. Apply a conservative adjustment (−20% in lead→MQL conversion rate) and optimistic (+20%) for the two alternative scenarios. 6. Write an executive note of ≤150 words covering: key premises, range of projected opportunities, main risk, recommended action. OUTPUT: model table with visible formulas + three scenarios in comparative columns + executive note. EDGE CASES: (a) if the marketing budget varies more than 30% between months, model each month independently rather than using an average; (b) if the historical series has fewer than 3 data points, warn about low reliability and widen the uncertainty interval to ±40%; (c) if the sales cycle exceeds 90 days, adjust the lag between MQL and opportunity in the model and note it. [C · CRITERIA] Formulas must be reproducible by any analyst from the declared assumptions; the three scenarios must differ by at least one clearly labeled distinct assumption; the executive note must be readable by a CFO without marketing technical knowledge; no number without a declared origin. DoD: complete table with 3 scenarios, explicit formulas, executive note, list of assumptions upfront. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions before calculating, labeled scenarios, executive language without technical jargon in the note.
spec-producto_north_star_metric: [S · SITUATION] A digital product team that has been tracking scattered operational metrics (page views, registrations, transactions, NPS) needs to align the entire organization around a single North Star Metric (NSM) that captures the value delivered to the user and predicts long-term growth, supported by a tree of 6 to 10 actionable inputs that different teams can directly influence. [P · REQUEST] North Star Metric definition document that includes: the proposed NSM with its formula or measurement description, justification of why it captures value for the user and the business, a two-level input tree (primary inputs and secondary inputs), a responsibility matrix by team (who can move each input), and 3 warning signals that would indicate the chosen NSM is incorrect. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Product director or senior metrics strategy consultant with experience defining NSMs in digital consumer and B2B companies. ASSUMPTIONS: if the product is not described, assume a B2B SaaS productivity platform with a monthly subscription model; the default NSM candidate is 'number of active users who complete at least one high-value task per week' — declare and proceed if confidence > 0.85. INPUTS: product or service description, business model (freemium, subscription, transactional), currently available metrics, product stage (growth, maturity). STEPS: 1. Identify what user action generates real (not vanity) value from the product description — produce 3 NSM candidates with pros and cons of each. 2. Select the optimal NSM applying 4 criteria: measurable, actionable, reflects user value, predicts revenue — justify in a comparative table. 3. Define the NSM formula or measurement protocol with operational precision (what counts, what doesn't, frequency). 4. Build the input tree: level 1 (3–4 direct inputs that compose the NSM) and level 2 (2–3 sub-inputs per level-1 input). 5. Create a responsibility matrix: for each input, the responsible team and the metric that represents it. 6. Formulate 3 warning signals (anti-patterns) that would indicate the chosen NSM is creating perverse incentives or measuring the wrong thing. OUTPUT: document with sections: Candidate evaluation / Selected NSM with formula / Input tree (textual diagram + table) / Responsibility matrix / Warning signals. EDGE CASES: (a) if the product has multiple user segments with distinct behaviors, propose one NSM per segment and flag the tension; (b) if the candidate NSM is not measurable in the current stack, flag the data gap and propose a bridge NSM; (c) if the team already has a defined NSM, evaluate the existing one against the 4 criteria before proposing changes. [C · CRITERIA] The NSM must meet all 4 evaluation criteria with an explicit score; the input tree must cover at least 80% of the levers that move the NSM; each input must have a responsible team assigned; warning signals must be concrete and observable, not generic. DoD: all sections complete, NSM with operational formula, tree of at least 6 total inputs, warning signals written. Protocolo MetodologIA: evaluate candidates before selecting, input tree as an organizational alignment tool, warning signals to prevent gaming.
spec-producto_arbol_metricas_aarrr: [S · SITUATION] A product and growth team at a digital company needs to organize all its metrics under the AARRR framework (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) in the form of a hierarchical tree that connects the North Star Metric with the metrics at each stage and with the tactical actions each team can execute, avoiding the dispersion of context-free metrics and enabling identification of where business growth is breaking down. [P · REQUEST] Complete AARRR metrics tree in tabular and textual format with: one primary metric per AARRR stage, 2–3 secondary metrics per stage, the tactical actions that move each secondary metric, the responsible team for each branch, and the recommended review frequency. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Growth engineering and metrics systems design expert with experience in digital startups and scale-ups applying Dave McClure's pirate framework. ASSUMPTIONS: if the product type is not provided, assume a consumer mobile application with a freemium model; target activation rate of 40% of new registrations; primary revenue through conversion to paid plan — declare upfront and proceed. INPUTS: product or service description, business model, growth stage (pre-product market fit, growth, scale), any currently available metrics. STEPS: 1. Map the user journey for the described product identifying the activation event, retention behavior, and referral trigger. 2. For each AARRR stage define: primary metric (1), secondary metrics (2–3) with formula or calculation description, and reference benchmark for the product type. 3. Identify 2–3 concrete tactical actions the team can execute to improve each secondary metric. 4. Assign a responsible team to each branch (e.g.: acquisition → marketing, activation → product + onboarding, retention → customer success + product). 5. Recommend review frequency for each stage (daily, weekly, monthly) based on its nature. 6. Flag the 2 most common trap metrics (vanity metrics) in the analyzed product type and explain why they should not be in the tree. OUTPUT: AARRR tree structured as a table with columns: Stage / Primary Metric / Secondary Metrics / Tactical Actions / Team / Frequency — plus a section on trap metrics to avoid. EDGE CASES: (a) if the product has both online and offline channels, build two differentiated acquisition sub-branches; (b) if there is no organic referral mechanism, replace that stage with an account expansion metric (upsell/cross-sell); (c) if the model is B2B with a long cycle, adjust the activation stage to reflect the moment of first value for the customer team, not the individual. [C · CRITERIA] All metrics must be measurable with standard analytics tools; each stage must have a reference benchmark cited or declared as [ASSUMPTION]; tactical actions must be specific and actionable within ≤30 days; the table must be self-sufficient to present to a team without additional explanation. DoD: all 5 AARRR stages covered, at least 10 total metrics, tactical actions per secondary metric, assigned teams, trap metrics identified. Protocolo MetodologIA: user journey first, metrics afterward, tactical actions at the end — from strategic to operational.
spec-producto_heart_framework: [S · SITUATION] A product team is about to launch or evaluate a specific feature and needs a user experience quality measurement system that goes beyond operational metrics (visits, clicks), using Google's HEART framework (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task Success) to define goals, signals, and concrete metrics per dimension before launch, so the team has agreed success criteria and does not evaluate the feature ad hoc afterward. [P · REQUEST] Complete HEART table for the described feature with: goal (qualitative objective), signal (observable behavior that indicates progress toward the goal), and metric (quantifiable indicator with formula) for each of the 5 dimensions, plus a decision on which 2–3 dimensions to prioritize for this feature with justification. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: UX researcher or senior product manager with experience applying Google's HEART framework in feature evaluation in large-scale digital products. ASSUMPTIONS: if the feature is not described, assume an interactive onboarding feature in a B2B SaaS application; default HEART dimension priority: Adoption and Task Success for new features — declare and proceed if confidence > 0.85. INPUTS: feature description (what it does, for which user, in what usage context), feature's business goal, current behavioral data if available. STEPS: 1. Describe in 3 lines the value the feature delivers to the user and the problem it solves. 2. For each HEART dimension, define: Goal (1 sentence of the desired user state), Signal (1–2 observable behaviors that evidence that state), Metric (quantifiable formula or KPI with measurement frequency). 3. Justify which 2–3 dimensions are most relevant for this specific feature using the criteria of: impact on the business goal, ease of measurement, relevance to the user journey at that moment. 4. Recommend measurement tools (analytics, survey, event logs) for each prioritized metric. 5. Formulate a success hypothesis: 'If the feature works well, in [timeframe] we should see [metric] at [value]'. OUTPUT: HEART table with 5 rows (dimensions) × 3 columns (Goal / Signal / Metric) + section on prioritized dimensions with justification + recommended tools + success hypothesis. EDGE CASES: (a) if the feature is an incremental improvement of something existing, include baseline vs new state comparison metrics; (b) if the feature impacts users of different profiles, separate Task Success metrics by segment; (c) if no instrumentation is available, prioritize metrics measurable from a survey and note it. [C · CRITERIA] Each metric must have an explicit formula or measurement protocol; the prioritized dimensions must be justified based on the specific feature, not generically; the success hypothesis must have a concrete timeframe and numerical value or be declared as [ASSUMPTION]; the table must be usable as a team alignment artifact before launch. DoD: 5 complete dimensions, 2–3 prioritized with justification, recommended tools, success hypothesis formulated. Protocolo MetodologIA: define goals before metrics, prioritize based on the specific feature not generically, quantified success hypothesis.
spec-producto_curva_retencion_cohortes: [S · SITUATION] The product team of a digital application has usage data for its users grouped by registration cohorts (month of first use) and wants to understand whether retention is improving over time, in which week or month users tend to drop off the most, whether certain cohorts retain better than others, and what product actions might explain the observed differences between cohorts. [P · REQUEST] Cohort retention curve analysis including: reading of the pasted retention matrix, identification of the inflection point (week/month where retention drops most sharply), comparison between the worst and best-retaining cohort with causal hypotheses, diagnosis of whether the product has found product-market fit based on curve shape, and 3 product recommendations prioritized to improve retention in the critical period. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior product analyst specializing in retention analysis and cohort behavior with experience in digital products with subscription or recurring engagement models. ASSUMPTIONS: if no real data is provided, use an illustrative 6-cohort × 8-week matrix with typical consumer app declining retention (week 1: 40%, week 4: 20%, week 8: 12%) and note it as [ASSUMPTION]; define retention as the percentage of users who return to use the product in that week/month relative to the users in the cohort. INPUTS: retention matrix in table format (rows=cohorts, columns=weeks/months since registration, cells=% of active users), or export from an analytics tool (Mixpanel, Amplitude, etc.). STEPS: 1. Read the matrix and identify the general shape of the curve: does it drop to zero (bad), flatten out (good), or show a rebound? 2. Calculate the weekly/monthly drop rate to identify the period of greatest drop-off (inflection point). 3. Compare the best-retaining cohort vs the worst at week 4 and week 8, calculate the delta, and formulate hypotheses about what product change or context might explain the difference. 4. Assess whether the curve flattens to a stable value (> 0) or keeps declining: determine whether there are signs of product-market fit based on this standard retention analysis criterion. 5. Propose 3 product initiatives prioritized for the period of greatest drop-off, each with: initiative description, impact hypothesis, and success metric to measure. OUTPUT: narrative summary of the curve (3–4 lines) + comparative table of best/worst cohorts + PMF diagnosis + table of 3 initiatives with hypothesis and success metric. EDGE CASES: (a) if there are fewer than 3 cohorts, warn that the comparison is not statistically robust and treat conclusions as hypotheses to validate; (b) if week 1 retention exceeds 60%, explore whether there is a retention event definition problem (too easy to trigger); (c) if cohort sizes vary greatly (>5x), normalize by size before comparing rates. [C · CRITERIA] All calculations must derive from the pasted matrix or the declared illustrative example; the PMF diagnosis must be based on the curve shape, not opinion; improvement initiatives must target the period of greatest drop-off identified in the analysis, not be generic recommendations. DoD: curve reading, inflection point identified, cohort comparison, PMF diagnosis, and 3 initiatives with hypothesis and metric. Protocolo MetodologIA: read the curve first, calculate the inflection point, PMF diagnosis based on curve shape, initiatives targeting the critical period.
spec-producto_definir_activacion_aha: [S · SITUATION] A digital product team knows that many users register but only a small fraction reaches the core product value and becomes recurring users. The team needs to identify precisely what the Aha moment is (the first time the user experiences the promised value), define the observable activation event in the product that marks that moment, and design an onboarding flow that takes new users to that event in the shortest possible time. [P · REQUEST] Aha moment and activation event definition document including: the Aha moment phrased in terms of the user's experience (not the system's), the technical activation event with its operational definition, the optimal time window to reach that event (Time-to-Activate), an analysis of the barriers preventing users from reaching that event, and a 3-step onboarding plan to reduce Time-to-Activate by at least 20%. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Product onboarding and growth specialist with experience identifying Aha moments in SaaS and consumer apps through behavioral analysis and correlating events with retention. ASSUMPTIONS: if the product is not described, assume a project management tool in which the Aha moment is 'inviting a team member and completing the first assigned task'; Time-to-Activate target ≤ 10 minutes from registration — declare and proceed. INPUTS: product description and core value proposition, current onboarding flow if it exists, available behavioral event data (or textual description of what retaining vs non-retaining users do). STEPS: 1. Formulate the Aha moment in the user's first person: 'The moment a new user understands this product is worth it is when [concrete action that generates real value]'. Propose 2 candidates. 2. Select the best Aha moment candidate using criteria: is it observable as a technical event?, is it correlated with higher retention in available evidence or assumption?, can it happen in a single session?. 3. Define the technical activation event: event name, key parameters, trigger condition (exactly when it is recorded), time window since registration. 4. Identify the 3 main barriers preventing a new user from reaching the activation event (registration friction, UI complexity, lack of initial content, etc.). 5. Design a 3-step onboarding plan targeting each barrier: step name, action asked of the user, reason why this step accelerates reaching the Aha. 6. Propose an activation metric: '% of new users who reach the activation event within the first [N] days' with target and measurement method. OUTPUT: document with sections: Formulated Aha moment / Technical activation event / Identified barriers / 3-step onboarding plan / Activation metric with target. EDGE CASES: (a) if the product has multiple use cases, define one Aha moment per main segment and note the difference; (b) if the Aha requires more than one session, split the onboarding into sessions and use a first-session activation proxy; (c) if there is no behavioral data, base the Aha on user interviews or declare it as a hypothesis to validate with an A/B test. [C · CRITERIA] The Aha moment must be in user language, not system language; the technical event must have an unambiguous trigger condition; barriers must be specific to the described product, not generic; the onboarding plan must directly target the identified barriers; the metric must have a numerical target. DoD: Aha formulated, technical event defined, 3 barriers, 3-step plan, metric with target. Protocolo MetodologIA: Aha in the user's language first, technical event afterward, onboarding designed to attack the real barriers.
spec-producto_dau_mau_stickiness: [S · SITUATION] The product team of a digital application wants to understand how 'sticky' their product is — that is, how frequently monthly active users are also active daily — using the DAU/MAU ratio as the primary stickiness indicator, comparing it against sectoral benchmarks, and deriving product actions to improve habitual usage frequency. [P · REQUEST] Product stickiness diagnosis with: calculation of the current DAU/MAU ratio, interpretation of its position against sectoral benchmarks, segmentation of stickiness by user type or cohort if data is available, diagnosis of the product factors that determine usage frequency, and 3 product experiments prioritized to increase the ratio by ≥5 percentage points. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior product analyst with experience measuring engagement and stickiness in mobile and web applications with high-frequency usage models. ASSUMPTIONS: if no data is provided, use DAU=10,000, MAU=80,000 (ratio=12.5%) for an entertainment consumer app as an illustrative example — declare and proceed; reference benchmark: social networks 50%+, utility apps 20–30%, B2B SaaS 10–20% — declare source as industry reference [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: DAU and MAU values for the analyzed period (or a time series for the last 3 months), product type (social, entertainment, productivity, B2B SaaS), expected natural usage frequency of the product. STEPS: 1. Calculate the DAU/MAU ratio using the provided data or example, round to one decimal. Classify the result: low (<10%), medium (10–30%), high (>30%) by product type. 2. Compare against the declared sectoral benchmark — calculate the gap in percentage points. 3. If there is a time series of 3+ months, calculate the trend (improving, stable, deteriorating). If not, note it as a limitation. 4. Diagnose the 3 product factors that most influence usage frequency for this type of application: notifications, new content, formed habit, recurring use case, social proof, etc. 5. Design 3 product experiments to increase stickiness: for each, experiment name, hypothesis ('if we do X, the DAU/MAU ratio will increase by Y% because Z'), success metrics, main risk, and estimated duration. OUTPUT: calculation and benchmark section / factor diagnosis / table of 3 experiments with hypothesis, metrics, risk, and duration. EDGE CASES: (a) if DAU and MAU do not have the same 'active user' definition, flag the inconsistency before calculating; (b) if the ratio is above the sectoral benchmark, redirect the analysis to identifying whether there is a risk of overuse or user fatigue; (c) if the product is B2B with expected weekly use (not daily), propose DAU/WAU or WAU/MAU as a more appropriate metric. [C · CRITERIA] The ratio must be calculated with explicit arithmetic; the benchmark must be labeled [ASSUMPTION] if no primary source is cited; experiments must have falsifiable hypotheses with metric and timeline; the factor diagnosis must be specific to the analyzed product type, not generic. DoD: ratio calculated, benchmark compared, factors diagnosed, 3 experiments with complete hypotheses. Protocolo MetodologIA: calculate first with visible arithmetic, benchmarks always labeled, experiments with falsifiable hypotheses.
spec-producto_metricas_contrapeso: [S · SITUATION] A product or business team has defined a set of primary success metrics (growth, conversion, activation, or engagement KPIs) but has no counterweight metrics that detect when those primary metrics are being met at the cost of degrading the user experience, product quality, or long-term business health. Without counterweight metrics, teams may aggressively optimize the primary metric generating unwanted side effects ('gaming'). [P · REQUEST] Counterweight metrics system for the provided set of primary KPIs: for each primary KPI, at least one counterweight metric with its operational definition, the specific gaming risk it contains, the recommended alert threshold, and the review frequency. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Metrics systems designer and product strategy consultant with experience preventing organizational dysfunctions caused by poorly designed metric incentives in technology companies. ASSUMPTIONS: if no primary KPIs are provided, use as an example: (1) new user activation rate, (2) NPS, (3) trial-to-paid conversion rate — declare and proceed. INPUTS: list of current primary KPIs of the team or product, description of the team context (product, marketing, sales, customer success team), incentives or bonuses associated with those metrics if known. STEPS: 1. For each primary KPI, identify the most likely gaming behavior: what would a team do to artificially improve that metric without delivering real user value? (example: improving activation rate by forcing onboarding vs making it more valuable). 2. For each identified gaming risk, define the counterweight metric that would detect it: must be difficult to manipulate simultaneously with the primary metric and must capture the quality or sustainability of the result. 3. Define for each counterweight metric: name, formula or calculation description, alert threshold (value that would indicate gaming is occurring), review frequency (weekly, monthly). 4. Design the review structure: propose a team ritual (e.g.: monthly review of primary + counterweight metrics simultaneously) to prevent counterweight metrics from being ignored. 5. Identify if any primary+counterweight pair could create a genuine strategic dilemma (real trade-off) and flag it with a recommendation for resolving the tension. OUTPUT: table of primary KPI / gaming risk / counterweight metric / alert threshold / frequency pairs + review ritual section + genuine trade-offs section. EDGE CASES: (a) if the primary metric is already difficult to manipulate (e.g.: audited net revenue), note it and propose quality metrics for that revenue instead of a counterweight; (b) if there are strong financial incentives associated with a metric (bonus), escalate the urgency of having a counterweight and propose including the counterweight in the same incentive scheme; (c) if the team has more than 6 primary KPIs, recommend reducing them first before adding counterweights. [C · CRITERIA] Each gaming risk must be specific to the analyzed KPI, not generic; each counterweight metric must be difficult to manipulate simultaneously with the primary (independence principle); alert thresholds must be numerical or have a clear decision rule; the review ritual must be concrete (frequency, who attends, what is decided). DoD: complete pairs table, review ritual defined, genuine trade-offs identified. Protocolo MetodologIA: identify the gaming first, design the counterweight so it is independent of the primary, review both metrics simultaneously.
spec-producto_cuadro_mando_producto: [S · SITUATION] A digital product team has metrics scattered across multiple tools and dashboards without a hierarchical structure that allows the different organizational levels (C-suite, product leaders, feature teams) to see the right information at the appropriate level of detail, generating long meetings with irrelevant information for some participants and making fast data-driven decision-making difficult. [P · REQUEST] Product dashboard design at three hierarchical levels (strategic, tactical, and operational) with: metrics assigned to each level with their definition and update frequency, the recommended visualization format for each block, the escalation rules (when data at the operational level must escalate to the strategic level), and the specification of the review meeting associated with each level. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Head of product or organizational design consultant with experience designing multi-level metrics systems for product teams in technology companies of 50 to 500 employees. ASSUMPTIONS: if the product is not described, assume a B2B SaaS platform with subscription model, three feature teams, one product leader, and one CPO — declare and proceed. INPUTS: product description, product team structure (roles and hierarchical levels), currently available metrics, current analytics tools. STEPS: 1. Define the three dashboard levels with their audience and purpose: Level 1 Strategic (CPO, CEO, CFO — business view, monthly frequency), Level 2 Tactical (product leaders and squad leads — product health, weekly frequency), Level 3 Operational (feature teams — sprint execution, daily frequency). 2. For each level, select 3–5 representative metrics for the analyzed product type with: name, operational definition, formula or calculation protocol, data update frequency, recommended visualization format (highlighted number, line chart, table, traffic light). 3. Design escalation rules: concrete conditions under which operational-level data must escalate to tactical or strategic (e.g.: 'if the checkout error rate exceeds 2% for 2 consecutive hours, escalate to tactical level'). 4. Specify the review meeting for each level: name, participants, frequency, duration, format (synchronous, asynchronous with comments), typical decision made. 5. Recommend the most appropriate tool or dashboard configuration for each level based on existing tools or the most common in the market (Mixpanel, Tableau, Notion, Looker, etc.). OUTPUT: three-level table with metrics, visualizations, and meetings + escalation rules section + tool recommendations. EDGE CASES: (a) if the product team has fewer than 5 people, collapse the tactical and operational levels into one and note it; (b) if there are multiple product lines, add a level 0 portfolio above the strategic level; (c) if current tools do not support level segmentation, propose a minimum-effort solution using manual exports as a bridge. [C · CRITERIA] Each level must have a distinct, non-overlapping audience and purpose; escalation rules must have concrete numerical or time-based conditions; each meeting specification must include participants, frequency, and typical decision; tool recommendations must be justified in one line. DoD: three levels defined with 3–5 metrics each, escalation rules, meeting specifications, and tool recommendation. Protocolo MetodologIA: hierarchical structure first, metrics assigned to levels afterward, escalation rules as the coordination mechanism.
spec-producto_l28_engagement: [S · SITUATION] The product team of a digital application wants to go beyond the DAU/MAU ratio and measure engagement with greater granularity using the L7 and L28 models (distribution of users according to how many of the last 7 or 28 days were active), which allow classifying users into usage frequency categories (daily, frequent, occasional, at-risk) and detecting engagement trends before they are reflected in retention or churn metrics. [P · REQUEST] Engagement analysis using the L7 and L28 models that includes: operational definition of both models for the analyzed product, classification of users into frequency categories with the provided data, interpretation of the resulting distribution compared to a healthy distribution, identification of at-risk segments, and 3 re-engagement initiatives prioritized by impact potential. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior product analyst with experience in frequency engagement models (Lxx) in high-usage digital products and consumer platforms. ASSUMPTIONS: if no data is provided, use an illustrative L28 distribution: L28=28 (5%), L28=21-27 (10%), L28=14-20 (20%), L28=7-13 (30%), L28=1-6 (25%), L28=0 (10%) for a productivity app — declare as [ASSUMPTION] and proceed. INPUTS: distribution of users by number of active days in the last 7 days (L7) and/or last 28 days (L28), or user counts by frequency cohort if available. STEPS: 1. Define classification criteria for the specific product: what counts as an 'active day' (minimum usage event), and what are the relevant frequency categories for the context (e.g., for L28: Core 21+, Power 14–20, Casual 7–13, At-Risk 1–6, Dormant 0). 2. Calculate the percentage of users in each category with the provided data or illustrative distribution. 3. Compare the resulting distribution against the 'healthy' distribution for the product type (e.g., a daily productivity app should have >30% in the Core category) — declare benchmark as [ASSUMPTION]. 4. Identify the highest-risk segments: calculate how many users are in At-Risk and Dormant categories and their potential impact on MAU in the next period if 10% of them are reactivated. 5. Propose 3 re-engagement initiatives: for each one, target segment, mechanism (notification, email, in-app message, new feature), impact hypothesis, and success metric. OUTPUT: operational definition of L7 and L28 for the product + user distribution table by category + comparison with healthy distribution + at-risk segment analysis + table of 3 re-engagement initiatives. EDGE CASES: (a) if the product has expected weekly use (not daily), adapt L7 categories to L4 (last 4 weeks) instead of days; (b) if distribution data is unavailable but DAU and MAU are known, infer L28 distribution using the ratio estimation method and flag the imprecision; (c) if the Core category is >50%, evaluate whether the 'active day' definition is too permissive (lower the session threshold). [C · CRITERIA] The 'active day' definition must be product-specific, not generic; frequency categories must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive; the re-engagement impact analysis must include a numerical calculation of the potential recovered users; initiatives must be directed at the identified segment, not be generic product recommendations. DoD: L7 and L28 models operationally defined, distribution calculated, risk analysis with numbers, 3 initiatives with segment and metrics. Protocolo MetodologIA: define 'active' precisely before calculating, complete distribution before interpreting, re-engagement directed at the identified at-risk segment.
spec-producto_quick_ratio_growth: [S · SITUATION] The product or growth team of a digital company wants to evaluate the quality of its active user growth using the Quick Ratio (also known as Startup Growth Ratio), which measures whether the product is growing efficiently by comparing the new and reactivated users gained in a period against the users lost to churn or inactivity, expressing the proportion as a single number that summarizes growth health. [P · REQUEST] Calculation and interpretation of the growth Quick Ratio with the data from the provided period, its comparison with reference benchmarks, a diagnosis of the components most dragging down the ratio (acquisition, reactivation, churn, inactivity), and 3 specific prioritized initiatives to improve the Quick Ratio in the next period. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior growth analyst with experience in growth quality metrics for digital startups and scale-ups, including the Quick Ratio analysis framework popularized by Mamoon Hamid and Casey Winters. ASSUMPTIONS: if no data is provided, use as an example: new users=500, reactivated users=100, churned users=200, inactive users=150 for a monthly period — declare and proceed; Quick Ratio >4 is considered excellent, 2–4 healthy, <2 poor according to industry benchmarks — declare as reference [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: for the analyzed period: number of new users (first use in the period), reactivated users (returned after inactivity), churned users (canceled or have no intention of returning), inactive users (did not use the product in the period but did not formally cancel). STEPS: 1. Calculate the Quick Ratio: QR = (New + Reactivated) / (Churned + Inactive). Show the values of each component, the numerator and denominator separately before the final result. 2. Interpret the result: is the product growing (QR>1), stagnating (QR=1), or contracting (QR<1)? Compare against the declared benchmarks. 3. Calculate the relative weight of each component in the numerator and denominator: does growth depend more on new or reactivated users? Is the drag more from churn or inactivity? 4. Identify the highest-leverage component: improving which component by 20% would yield the greatest impact on the Quick Ratio? Perform the scenario calculation. 5. Propose 3 initiatives prioritized by highest-leverage component: for each one, component it targets, initiative description, expected impact on the Quick Ratio (estimated calculation), tracking metric, and timeline. OUTPUT: detailed Quick Ratio calculation with components / interpretation and benchmark / relative weight analysis / leverage scenario / table of 3 initiatives. EDGE CASES: (a) if churn cannot be separated from inactive in the data, calculate the Quick Ratio with a combined definition and flag the interpretation limitation; (b) if the Quick Ratio is >10, explore whether there is a definition problem with 'inactive' that underestimates the denominator; (c) if the analyzed period is quarterly rather than monthly, adjust the benchmark interpretation according to the natural usage frequency of the product. [C · CRITERIA] The calculation must show each component separately before the final result; the relative weight analysis must have calculated percentages; the leverage scenario must include the improved Quick Ratio calculation; initiatives must target the highest-leverage component identified, not be generic. DoD: Quick Ratio calculated with component decomposition, interpretation with benchmark, leverage analysis with scenario, 3 initiatives with expected impact calculation. Protocolo MetodologIA: calculate with visible decomposition, identify the highest-leverage component before proposing initiatives, numerical scenario before recommending.
spec-producto_metrica_proxy_validar:
[S · SITUATION] The product team uses a proxy metric (e.g., button clicks, time on screen, open rate) as a leading indicator of the real business outcome (retention, conversion, revenue). There is suspicion that the real correlation is weak or spurious, and evidence is needed to decide whether the proxy metric should be kept, adjusted, or replaced.

[P · REQUEST] A structured report that evaluates the validity of the proposed proxy metric against the declared business outcome, with an actionable verdict (keep / adjust / replace) and classified alternative metrics.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product analyst with experience in north star metrics, OKRs, and statistical causality in digital products.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no historical data is provided, assume the analysis is qualitative-structural; if the proxy metric and outcome are not specified, request both before proceeding; if the product context is not declared, infer B2C SaaS sector.
INPUTS: Description of the proxy metric (name, formula, measurement frequency) and the real business outcome (name, time horizon, data source).
STEPS:
1. Formally define the proxy metric and the real outcome with their formulas and measurement intervals.
2. Evaluate conceptual correlation: list the plausible causal mechanisms that would connect proxy → outcome.
3. Identify validity threats: confounders, temporal lag, selection biases, gaming.
4. If data is available, calculate Pearson/Spearman correlation and coefficient of determination; if not, assign qualitative evidence level (high / medium / low).
5. Issue verdict: keep / adjust (specify how) / replace.
6. Propose up to 3 alternative metrics with justification and trade-offs.
OUTPUT: Document in sections: Definitions → Causal mechanism → Validity threats → Evidence → Verdict → Alternatives → Next steps. Maximum length 600 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If the proxy and outcome are the same variable: alert to tautology and request clarification.
- If historical data shows negative correlation: document the finding and explore whether the proxy acts as an inverse indicator.
- If no quantifiable business outcome exists: help formulate one before evaluating the proxy.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the verdict includes a revision condition with a suggested date; each validity threat has a proposed mitigation.
Trade-off documented: sensitivity (detects real changes) vs. specificity (does not generate false alarms).
DoD: the report can be delivered to an executive stakeholder without additional editing.
spec-producto_definir_power_user_curve:
[S · SITUATION] The product team needs to understand the actual distribution of usage frequency to identify who the power users are, what behaviors distinguish them, and how to design mechanics that move casual users toward that segment.

[P · REQUEST] A structured analysis that produces: (1) operational definition of the power user for the specific product, (2) segmentation of the user base into at least 3 frequency bands, (3) hypotheses about the differential behaviors of each band, and (4) at least 2 design / growth interventions to move users between bands.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior growth analyst with experience in cohort analysis, user segmentation, and retention mechanic design in digital products.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no real data is provided, build a reference framework with suggested thresholds based on the product type; if the product type is not specified, assume a productivity application with ideal daily use; only ask if the key action unit (core action) is not defined.
INPUTS: Product description, the key action that defines 'use' (core action), and optionally a statistical summary of session or action frequency.
STEPS:
1. Define the core action to be measured as the frequency unit (e.g., completed task, sent message).
2. Propose the band distribution: dormant / casual / regular / power (with thresholds of actions/week or actions/month).
3. Describe the expected behavioral profile of each band: motivations, use contexts, observable signals.
4. For the power band: list 3-5 differential behaviors that distinguish them.
5. Propose interventions to move casual → regular and regular → power with mechanism and success metric.
6. Define how movement between bands would be measured in a monthly cohort.
OUTPUT: Band segmentation table + profile descriptions + interventions table. Maximum length 700 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If the core action is too generic (e.g., 'session opened'): suggest a more specific action and continue with assumption.
- If the expected distribution is bimodal (use or no use): adapt bands to 2 and explain why the product does not generate gradual behavior.
- If the product has seasonal use: add a note about threshold adjustment by season.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each band has explicit numerical thresholds; each intervention has a success metric measurable in less than 30 days.
Trade-off documented: defining power users by frequency vs. by value generated.
DoD: the analysis can be presented in a product weekly without additional work.
spec-producto_prd_una_pagina:
[S · SITUATION] A product team needs to align engineering, design, and executive stakeholders on a new feature or product before starting the development cycle. Preliminary information is available (brief, conversation, discovery notes) but no formal document yet exists.

[P · REQUEST] A PRD of exactly one page (600-800 words) ready to distribute, covering problem, solution, metrics, scope, dependencies, and success criteria without ambiguity.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product manager with experience writing PRDs for agile teams in technology companies.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user problem is not provided, infer from available context and mark as [ASSUMPTION]; if success metrics are not mentioned, propose 2 generic metrics for the product type; if the target audience is unknown, assume engineering team + product leadership.
INPUTS: Brief, discovery notes, feature description, or any available context pasted in the chat.
STEPS:
1. Draft Context and Problem section (3-4 sentences): who, what problem, quantitative evidence if it exists.
2. Draft Proposed Solution section (4-5 sentences): what will be built, high-level implementation approach, what is not included.
3. Draft Success Metrics section: 2-3 metrics with target value and review date.
4. Draft Scope section: 2-column table (In Scope / Out of Scope), minimum 3 items per column.
5. Draft Dependencies and Risks section: list of 2-4 items with impact and mitigation.
6. Draft Acceptance Criteria section: 3-5 verifiable criteria.
7. Verify total does not exceed 800 words; adjust if necessary.
OUTPUT: PRD document with the 6 sections in that order, headed with feature name, version, and date. Without excessive markdown, suitable for Notion or Confluence.
EDGE CASES:
- If the brief is so scarce that the problem cannot be inferred: ask for at least 2 sentences describing the user's pain before continuing.
- If the feature already has an existing PRD: request the current document and propose a diff of improvements instead of rewriting from scratch.
- If the scope is too broad for one page: segment into phases and draft the PRD only for Phase 1.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the PRD can be reviewed and approved in a 30-minute meeting without clarification questions about the problem or the solution.
Trade-off documented: technical depth vs. executive accessibility.
DoD: the PRD has the feature name, version 0.1, current date, and all sections complete without [PENDING] markers.
spec-producto_press_release_inverso:
[S · SITUATION] The product team wants to apply the Amazon Working Backwards technique to validate whether an initiative has real value before committing engineering resources. An idea or user need exists but there is no formal product definition yet.

[P · REQUEST] A fictional working backwards press release (as if the product were already launched) of 400-500 words, followed by a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) section with 3-5 Q&As that reveal the hardest design decisions.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product manager with experience in the Amazon Working Backwards methodology and customer-oriented product communication.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the product name is not provided, use a descriptive provisional name; if the target audience is not specified, assume a professional user at a mid-sized company; if the main benefit is not mentioned, infer the most obvious one from context and mark it [ASSUMPTION].
INPUTS: Description of the product idea or user need, market context if available.
STEPS:
1. Draft the press release headline: imaginary city, future fictional launch date, product name.
2. Paragraph 1 (hook): what problem it solves and for whom, in terms of the end user.
3. Paragraph 2 (product description): how it works simply, without technical jargon.
4. Paragraph 3 (customer quote): invented quote from a prototypical user expressing the value received.
5. Paragraph 4 (call to action): how to access it, where to get more information.
6. FAQ: 3-5 questions representing the hardest design tensions (e.g., why didn't they do X?, what happens with case Y?), each answered in 2-3 sentences.
7. Add footer note: 'This press release is an internal Working Backwards exercise; not for external distribution.'
OUTPUT: Press release with journalistic structure + clearly separated FAQ section. Without excessive markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the idea describes technology instead of a user benefit: reframe the hook from the user's perspective before continuing.
- If the FAQ reveals that the product has no clear value proposition: flag the finding explicitly and propose 2 reformulations of the problem.
- If the idea is too vague to invent a realistic customer quote: ask for at least the target user profile.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the press release can be read by someone without technical context and they understand what the product does and why it matters in less than 3 minutes.
Trade-off documented: launch aspiration vs. realism of the value proposition.
DoD: the document includes press release + FAQ + footer note, and the customer quote contains a specific and measurable benefit.
spec-producto_definir_alcance_no_alcance:
[S · SITUATION] The product team is about to start development of a feature or system and needs to define precisely what will be built and, crucially, what is left out to avoid scope creep, stakeholder misunderstandings, and engineering rework.

[P · REQUEST] A scope document with two explicit sections — In Scope and Out of Scope — in a verifiable list format, with justification for the highest-ambiguity items, and a Pending Decisions section that requires confirmation before start.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product manager with experience in scope management in agile environments and in scope negotiation with engineering teams and executive stakeholders.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no feature context is provided, ask for a 3-5 sentence description before continuing; if no technical constraints are mentioned, assume standard web architecture with REST API; if delivery time is not specified, assume a 2-week sprint as the reference unit.
INPUTS: Feature or system description, known constraints, decisions already made by the team.
STEPS:
1. List minimum 5 In Scope items with action verb in infinitive (e.g., 'Allow the user to edit their profile').
2. List minimum 5 Out of Scope items with brief justification (1 sentence) for the 3 most controversial or ambiguous.
3. Identify 2-4 Pending Decisions: questions the team must answer before the sprint starts, with suggested owner and suggested deadline.
4. Add an 'Inclusion Criterion' note: how it was decided what is in and what is out (e.g., MVP, time constraint, technical debt).
5. Format as a 2-column table for the main sections.
OUTPUT: In/Out Scope table + Pending Decisions list + Inclusion Criterion. Maximum length 500 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If the described feature is so broad it does not fit in a sprint: suggest segmentation into phases and draft scope only for Phase 1.
- If an out-of-scope item contradicts a requirement already committed to a stakeholder: flag it as a conflict and do not include it in the list until resolved.
- If the feature description is ambiguous: list the 2 possible interpretations and ask for confirmation before assigning items.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: any team engineer can read the document and determine without consulting the PM whether a specific task is in or out of scope.
Trade-off documented: completeness of the first version vs. delivery speed.
DoD: the document has a header with feature name and version, both tables with minimum 5 items each, and at least 1 Pending Decision with an owner.
spec-producto_criterios_aceptacion_gherk:
[S · SITUATION] The product and QA team needs formal acceptance criteria for a user story or feature, written in Gherkin language (Given / When / Then) so they can be used directly as the basis for automated tests and as a delivery contract between product, engineering, and QA.

[P · REQUEST] A set of complete and self-contained Gherkin scenarios for the described story or feature, covering the happy path, at least 2 alternative paths, and at least 2 error paths, with priority tags.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior QA engineer with experience in Behavior-Driven Development (BDD), Gherkin scenario writing, and test case design for web and mobile applications.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the feature does not specify the actor, assume authenticated user; if the technology context is not mentioned, assume web application; if the number of scenarios is not indicated, produce between 5 and 8 scenarios.
INPUTS: Description of the user story or feature, known business rules, expected behaviors.
STEPS:
1. Identify the Feature Name and write the high-level description (Feature: ... / As a... / I want... / So that...).
2. Write the happy path scenario (Happy Path) with complete Given / When / Then.
3. Write 2 alternative path scenarios (valid variations of the main flow).
4. Write 2 error or edge scenarios (failed validation, denied permissions, invalid data).
5. Add Cucumber tags: @high-priority / @medium-priority, @smoke for critical ones, @regression for regression ones.
6. Verify that each Then has an observable and verifiable result (not vague like 'the system responds correctly').
OUTPUT: Formatted Gherkin code block with Feature, Background (if applicable), and all numbered Scenarios. No explanations outside the Gherkin block except a summary table at the end.
EDGE CASES:
- If the story has multiple user roles: create one scenario per role with the same flow but different Given context.
- If a business rule is contradictory: flag it explicitly outside the Gherkin block and do not include the scenario until resolved.
- If the feature has state that persists across sessions: add Background to initialize the prior state.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each scenario can be executed by a QA engineer without asking the PM what the Then means.
Trade-off documented: exhaustive coverage vs. test suite maintainability.
DoD: at least 1 scenario tagged @smoke, all Thens have a measurable result, and error scenarios have specific validation messages.
spec-producto_historias_usuario_invest:
[S · SITUATION] The agile team has a set of requirements, ideas, or features that need to be converted into well-formed user stories for the product backlog. Current stories are too large, dependent on each other, or have vague acceptance criteria, making estimation and sprint planning commitment difficult.

[P · REQUEST] A set of user stories that meet the INVEST criterion (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable), with explicit evaluation of each INVEST dimension per story and basic acceptance criteria.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product manager or Scrum Master with experience in backlog refinement and user story writing in agile teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the input is a list of technical requirements, transform them to user language before writing the stories; if size is not specified, aim for stories completable in 3-5 development days; if the user role is not mentioned, ask once before continuing.
INPUTS: List of requirements, discovery notes, feature descriptions, or previously poorly formed stories pasted in the chat.
STEPS:
1. For each input item, draft the story in format: 'As a [role], I want [action], in order to [benefit].'
2. Evaluate each INVEST dimension with a traffic light (green / yellow / red) and a justification sentence.
3. If any dimension is red, propose the specific correction (split the story, reframe the benefit, etc.).
4. Add 2-3 basic acceptance criteria per story (without full Gherkin, just verifiable bullets).
5. Add a suggested relative estimation in story points (1 / 2 / 3 / 5 / 8) with a 1-sentence justification.
OUTPUT: Table with columns: Story → INVEST (traffic light per dimension) → Acceptance criteria → Suggested estimation. One row per story.
EDGE CASES:
- If the input is an epic story (too large for a sprint): split into sub-stories before applying INVEST.
- If two stories are dependent on each other: flag the dependency and propose sequence or refactoring.
- If the benefit ('in order to') is the same in all stories: alert that they may collapse into a single epic; ask if intentional.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the team can estimate each story in less than 5 minutes in a planning poker session.
Trade-off documented: optimal granularity vs. management overhead of many small stories.
DoD: each story has all 6 INVEST dimensions evaluated, at least 2 acceptance criteria, and a suggested estimation.
spec-producto_definition_of_ready:
[S · SITUATION] The agile team experiences that backlog items arrive at sprint planning without sufficient information to be estimated or committed, causing interruptions, rework, and lack of focus during the sprint. A formal and agreed Definition of Ready (DoR) is needed.

[P · REQUEST] A complete and operational Definition of Ready for the specified backlog item type (user story, bug, spike, etc.), with a verifiable checklist and a documented exception criterion.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Scrum Master with experience in Definition of Ready facilitation, backlog refinement, and agile maturity in software development teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the item type is not specified, assume user story; if the team context is not described, assume a 6-8 person team with 2-week sprint cycles; if the technology stack is relevant to any criterion, ask before including it.
INPUTS: Description of the team (size, context, product type), backlog item type, current problems observed during sprint planning.
STEPS:
1. Define the purpose of the DoR in 2-3 sentences: what problem it solves for this specific team.
2. Draft checklist of 8-12 verifiable criteria, each formulated as a yes/no question (e.g., 'Does the story have an acceptance criterion with at least one error scenario?').
3. Classify criteria as: Mandatory (block sprint planning) and Desirable (enrich but do not block).
4. Define the decision process: who can declare an item 'Ready' and with what quorum.
5. Document 1-2 exception criteria: conditions under which the DoR can be bypassed with recorded justification.
6. Add a 'How to refine toward Ready' section: 3-4 concrete actions the team can take to mature an item.
OUTPUT: DoR document with: Purpose + Classified checklist (Mandatory / Desirable) + Decision process + Exceptions + How to refine. Maximum length 500 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If the team has no refinement ceremony: add a note about the necessary precondition for the DoR to be effective.
- If the item type is a critical production bug: adapt the DoR to allow fast start with less documentation, with minimum criteria.
- If the team is distributed: include a criterion about product owner availability for asynchronous questions.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: in the next sprint planning session, the team can verify the DoR of any item in less than 3 minutes.
Trade-off documented: DoR rigor vs. agility to respond to urgencies.
DoD: the document has purpose, checklist with minimum 8 classified criteria, decision process, and at least 1 documented exception.
spec-producto_definition_of_done:
[S · SITUATION] The development team has no explicit, agreed Definition of Done (DoD), which generates inconsistent deliveries: some stories are closed without automated tests, without code review, or without updated documentation. This produces accumulated technical debt and friction with QA and product.

[P · REQUEST] A complete Definition of Done, specific to the team's context, with criteria classified by level (story / sprint / release), an update process, and adherence metrics.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Engineering manager or senior Scrum Master with experience establishing delivery quality standards in agile software teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the technology stack is not mentioned, assume a web application with an API backend and SPA frontend; if the team has no CI/CD, include the criterion but mark it as "aspirational"; if the maturity level is not described, assume a growing team with 6–12 months of joint work.
INPUTS: Description of product type, main technology stack, current team practices (what they already do well), recurring quality problems.
STEPS:
1. Draft the Story-level DoD (8–12 criteria): what each individual item must meet before being closed.
2. Draft the Sprint-level DoD (3–5 criteria): what the increment must meet at the end of the sprint.
3. Draft the Release-level DoD (3–5 criteria): what must be met before reaching production.
4. Classify each criterion as Blocker (cannot be closed without it) or Desirable (debt is recorded if missing).
5. Define the DoD update process: when to review it, who can propose changes, how agreement is reached.
6. Propose 2 DoD adherence metrics: how the team knows whether they are truly meeting it.
OUTPUT: DoD document structured at 3 levels + update process + adherence metrics. Maximum length 600 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If the team has no CI/CD or automated tests: include those criteria as aspirational with a suggested target date.
- If the product is a B2B service with contractual SLAs: add an SLA verification criterion at the Release level.
- If the team works with multiple stacks (mobile + web + backend): create a DoD variant per stack rather than a single generic one.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: any team member can verify the DoD of a story in less than 5 minutes at the end of the sprint.
Documented trade-off: high quality standards vs. initial delivery speed.
DoD: the document has the 3 levels, Blocker / Desirable classification, update process, and 2 adherence metrics.
spec-producto_spec_tecnico_funcional:
[S · SITUATION] The product team has business requirements or discovery notes that must be translated into a functional specification the engineering team can use directly to design, estimate, and implement without needing multiple rounds of clarification.

[P · REQUEST] A structured functional specification that translates business requirements into verifiable system behaviors, including data flows, formalized business rules, system states, and high-level interface contracts.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Technical product manager or senior business analyst with experience writing functional specifications for software engineering teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If requirements are in pure business language, translate them into system behaviors without losing the intent; if the technology stack is not mentioned, avoid implementation decisions and describe behaviors only; if actors are not defined, ask once before continuing.
INPUTS: Business requirements, discovery notes, product brief, or feature description in free text.
STEPS:
1. List system actors (users, external systems, time/events).
2. Describe main functional flows: textual diagram or numbered walkthrough of each user flow from start to finish.
3. Formalize business rules: numbered list in the format "BR-001: If [condition] then [system behavior]".
4. Define possible states of the system or main entity with allowed transitions.
5. Specify high-level interface contracts: input data, expected output, error conditions for each main operation.
6. List relevant non-functional requirements (performance, security, accessibility) if mentioned in the input.
OUTPUT: Functional specification document with numbered sections: Actors → Functional Flows → Business Rules → States and Transitions → Interface Contracts → Non-Functional Requirements. Maximum length 800 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If requirements contradict each other: flag the contradiction explicitly and propose a resolution before specifying.
- If the requirement implies an architecture decision: describe the expected behavior and add a note "Implementation decision for the engineering team".
- If the input mixes requirements from multiple features: separate into independent specification modules.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: an engineer can read the specification and estimate the work without asking the PM about the expected behavior in any main flow.
Documented trade-off: specification completeness vs. writing time.
DoD: the specification has at least 3 numbered business rules, 1 textual flow diagram, and contracts for the 2–3 most critical operations.
spec-producto_edge_cases_estados_error:
[S · SITUATION] The product and engineering team is specifying or reviewing a feature and needs to systematically identify edge cases and error states before they reach production as bugs or degraded user experiences.

[P · REQUEST] An exhaustive catalog of edge cases and error states for the described feature, with severity, user impact, expected system behavior, and handling recommendation for each case.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior QA engineer or technical product manager with experience in edge-case analysis, error handling design, and feature hardening in digital products.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the feature does not specify main flows, infer them from the description and list them as [ASSUMPTION]; if the technology context is not mentioned, assume a web application with authenticated users; if the document's audience is not specified, assume engineering and QA teams.
INPUTS: Feature description, known main flows, business rules if available.
STEPS:
1. Identify edge-case categories: invalid input, empty states, concurrency, data limits, permissions, external dependencies, network/timeout.
2. For each category, list 2–4 cases specific to the described feature.
3. For each case: descriptive name, triggering condition, severity (critical / high / medium / low), user impact, current expected system behavior, recommended behavior.
4. Identify the 3 highest-risk cases and mark them as priority.
5. Add a "Suggested test coverage" section: list the 5 cases that should have mandatory automated tests.
OUTPUT: Edge-case table with columns: Case → Category → Condition → Severity → Impact → Recommended Behavior. Separate section for priorities and suggested coverage. Maximum length 700 words.
EDGE CASES OF THE ANALYSIS ITSELF:
- If the feature is very simple (single flow, no state): note that the edge-case list is short and propose adding the feature to a basic regression test suite.
- If the feature integrates with external services: mandatory inclusion of the timeout and partial-response category.
- If the team has no current test coverage: add a note on test debt and how to prioritize it.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the QA team can use the catalog directly to write test cases without additional investigation.
Documented trade-off: exhaustive coverage vs. time available to implement error handling.
DoD: the catalog has at least 10 cases in at least 4 different categories, the 3 priority cases are marked, and the suggested coverage section has a minimum of 5 cases.
spec-producto_one_pager_feature:
[S · SITUATION] The product team needs to present a proposal for a new feature to executive stakeholders or product leadership to obtain alignment, prioritization, or budget. There is no time for a full PRD, but more than a bullet list is needed.

[P · REQUEST] A 400–500-word feature proposal one-pager covering the problem, the solution, the expected value, the main risks, and the call to action, designed to be read in under 3 minutes and to generate a decision in the meeting where it is presented.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product manager with experience in executive communication, product proposal presentation, and stakeholder management in technology companies.
ASSUMPTIONS: If quantifiable benefit is not mentioned, use well-described qualitative benefits and mark them [ASSUMPTION]; if the audience is not specified, assume product and technology leadership; if the delivery horizon is not mentioned, assume one quarter.
INPUTS: Description of the idea or user need, problem context, expected benefit, any available data.
STEPS:
1. Write the header: feature name, document version, date, author.
2. Section The Problem (3–4 sentences): who has it, what causes it, what happens if it is not resolved.
3. Section The Solution (3–4 sentences): what is proposed, how it solves the problem, what is not included in this version.
4. Section Expected Value: 2–3 bullets with measurable or well-described qualitative benefit (user + business).
5. Section Risks and Dependencies: 2–3 bullets with risk, probability, and a one-sentence mitigation.
6. Section Call to Action: what is being asked of the stakeholders present (approval, feedback, resources, prioritization), with a suggested decision date.
OUTPUT: One-pager with 6 sections in that order, without excessive tables or bullets, suitable for printing on A4 or presenting on screen. Total 400–500 words.
EDGE CASES:
- If the proposed solution is a technology bet without user validation: flag the risk in the Risks section and recommend a discovery phase first.
- If multiple solution options exist: present the recommended option and mention the discarded alternatives in 1 sentence.
- If the one-pager is presented without a prior meeting: add a context paragraph at the beginning for a cold audience.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: a stakeholder can read the one-pager in 3 minutes and ask at least 1 decision question to the PM.
Documented trade-off: urgency of the problem vs. complexity of the proposed solution.
DoD: the document has all 6 sections, the call to action has a decision date, and the value section has at least 1 user benefit and 1 business benefit.
spec-producto_spec_revision_checklist:
[S · SITUATION] The product team has just written or updated a PRD (Product Requirements Document) for a new feature or product. Before passing it to design or engineering, it needs a structured review that detects ambiguities, missing requirements, inconsistencies, and sections that do not meet quality standards.

[P · REQUEST] Audit the provided PRD using an exhaustive review checklist and deliver a report with (a) score per section, (b) prioritized findings list with severity, and (c) concrete improvement recommendations.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: You are a Senior Product Manager with 10 years of experience auditing product specifications in B2B and B2C software companies; expert in PRD standards, user stories, and acceptance criteria.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the PRD does not indicate the target audience, assume end users of a web/mobile enterprise application. If the technology stack is not specified, assume technical constraints do not apply to this review. If the metrics section is absent, mark it as a critical finding rather than inferring metrics.

INPUTS: The full text of the PRD pasted after this prompt.

STEPS:
1. Read the full PRD and identify the sections present (objective, context, users, functional requirements, non-functional requirements, acceptance criteria, success metrics, dependencies, risks, glossary).
2. For each section, apply the checklist: clarity, completeness, verifiability, absence of ambiguity, alignment with the overall objective.
3. Assign a score of 1–5 to each section and record findings with severity (Critical / Major / Minor).
4. Generate a prioritized findings list (descending severity) with exact location in the document.
5. Write specific improvement recommendations for each Critical and Major finding.
6. Calculate the overall PRD score (weighted average).

OUTPUT: Structured report with: (1) Score table by section, (2) Findings list with severity and location, (3) Improvement recommendations, (4) Overall score and verdict (Approved / Requires revision / Rejected).

EDGE CASES:
- Very short PRD (<500 words): indicate that the audit is incomplete due to lack of content and list all missing sections as Critical.
- PRD with multiple mixed products: request separation before auditing, indicating which sections belong to which product.
- PRD without acceptance criteria: mark all functional requirements as unverifiable and escalate severity.

[C · CRITERIA] Each finding must be actionable and referenceable in the original document. The overall score must reflect the PRD's ability to guide development without additional clarification meetings.
