Protocolo MetodologIA: status and required action visible without additional clicks; balance across strategic perspectives.
spec-consulting_data_storytelling_para_a: [S · SITUATION] An analytics or consulting team has relevant quantitative data (survey results, performance metrics, statistical analyses, benchmark comparisons) that it needs to communicate to a non-technical audience—executives, commercial staff, operational personnel—who have no background in statistics or data science. The data is correct but presented in inaccessible technical format. Without a clear narrative, the audience will ignore the data or reach wrong conclusions. [P · REQUEST] Transform technical data into a data storytelling narrative in English, accessible to a non-technical audience, combining a clear central message, everyday analogies or metaphors, the recommended visualization for each key data point, and an actionable conclusion. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data storytelling specialist with experience communicating analytical insights to executive and commercial audiences without statistical training in Latin American mass consumer, banking, and retail companies. ASSUMPTIONS: the input is the technical data or findings provided by the user; if the user provides tables or statistics without narrative context, that is the primary input; if no specific audience is defined, assume mid-level executives (area managers) with no analytical background; only ask for clarification if confidence in the central message drops below 0.85. INPUTS: data, tables, statistics, or technical findings pasted in the thread, plus the audience profile. STEPS: 1) Identify the central message: what the audience must understand and remember in one sentence. 2) Select the 3-5 most relevant data points to support that message. 3) For each data point: translate the statistic into everyday language with an analogy or metaphor from a familiar context. 4) Recommend the optimal visualization for each data point (chart type and why). 5) Build the narrative sequence: context → tension/problem → data as evidence → actionable conclusion. 6) Draft the closing paragraph with the practical implication for the audience. OUTPUT: structured narrative in text (max. 600 words) with: Central message → Context → 3-5 data points with accessible translation and recommended visualization → Actionable conclusion. EDGE CASES: (a) if data shows negative trends, frame as an opportunity without minimizing reality; (b) if there is significant statistical uncertainty, communicate it with range language ('between X and Y') without technical jargon; (c) if the audience has low visual literacy, favor a single simple visualization per message. [C · CRITERIA] A manager without analytical training must understand the central message and be able to repeat it in their own words. Analogies must come from the audience's work or daily context, not from academic settings. DoD: narrative max. 600 words, central message in the first sentence, minimum three data points translated with analogy, recommended visualization for each data point, actionable conclusion. Protocolo MetodologIA: data in service of the message, not the message in service of the data; if there is tension between statistical precision and accessibility, prioritize accessibility with a technical footnote.
spec-consulting_seleccion_de_grafico_seg: [S · SITUATION] An analyst or consultant has data ready to visualize and must choose the chart type that best communicates the specific message they want to convey. Choosing the wrong chart can distort the message, confuse the audience, or understate the impact of the finding. There is no single rule: the selection depends on the message (comparison, trend, composition, distribution, relationship) and the audience. [P · REQUEST] Given the message the consultant wants to communicate and the type of data available, recommend the optimal chart type in English with justification, secondary alternatives, common errors to avoid with that data, and basic visual configuration guidance (labels, colors, annotations). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data visualization expert applied to consulting reporting, with command of Dona Wong's, Alberto Cairo's, and Big Four chart selection frameworks (McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte, KPMG). ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the visualization tool, assume PowerPoint/Excel; if the message is not explicit, infer the type of analysis (comparison, trend, composition, distribution, relationship) from the data description and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; only ask for clarification if confidence drops below 0.85. INPUTS: description of the message to communicate, type and structure of the data (e.g. 5 categories with one value each, 12-month monthly time series, two continuous variables with 100 observations). STEPS: 1) Identify the message type: comparison / trend / composition / distribution / relationship / deviation. 2) Select the optimal primary chart for that message with a two-sentence justification. 3) List two secondary alternatives with situations where they would be preferable. 4) Flag two common errors with that data (e.g. using a pie chart with more than 5 categories, truncating the Y axis). 5) Provide visual configuration guidance: data labels (yes/no, position), recommended color palette (max. 3 colors), key annotation to highlight. OUTPUT: structured response with: Message type → Recommended chart + justification → Secondary alternatives → Errors to avoid → Visual configuration guide. EDGE CASES: (a) if data is multidimensional (more than 3 variables), recommend small multiples or a matrix of charts; (b) if the audience is non-technical, favor simplicity over informational richness; (c) if the most important data point is a ratio of two values, consider a simple 'big number' with comparison context instead of a chart. [C · CRITERIA] The chart justification must be directly tied to the message, not to aesthetics. Errors to avoid must be specific to the provided data. The configuration guide must be implementable in less than 10 minutes. DoD: recommended chart with justification, two alternatives, two specific errors, implementable configuration guide. Protocolo MetodologIA: the chart serves the message, not sophistication; if there is tension between clarity and visual richness, prioritize clarity.
spec-consulting_appendix_de_soporte_anal: [S · SITUATION] A consulting team has delivered or will present a recommendation proposal to an executive client. After the presentation, the client—or their technical and financial team—will request detailed evidence to support each claim in the main body. Without a well-structured appendix, the team will lose credibility or have to improvise answers under pressure. The appendix is the evidence repository that turns a persuasive recommendation into a demonstrable one. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete structure of the analytical support appendix in English for a consulting presentation, including the section index, the purpose of each section, the type of evidence each section must contain, and the referencing convention to link the presentation body to the appendix. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior analytical methodology consultant with experience structuring appendices for transformation proposals, feasibility studies, and due diligence reports for large companies in Latin America. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the presentation type, assume a strategic recommendations deck; if main body slides are not available, design the standard appendix structure for that type of presentation; if the user provides main body claims, design appendix sections directly aligned to those claims; only ask for clarification if confidence in the type of evidence required drops below 0.85. INPUTS: presentation type, main body claims or findings requiring support, audience that will review the appendix (technical, financial, legal). STEPS: 1) Identify the categories of main body claims (market data, benchmarks, financial analysis, operational findings, model assumptions, methodology). 2) For each category, design the corresponding appendix section with: name, purpose, content type, expected source, and suggested number of slides. 3) Define the referencing convention (e.g. 'See Appendix A, slide 3'). 4) Design the appendix index slide. 5) Flag the three most likely questions from the technical/financial client and the appendix section that answers them. OUTPUT: appendix index with section table (Section | Purpose | Content type | Source | Suggested no. of slides) + referencing convention + list of likely questions with appendix referral. EDGE CASES: (a) if the presentation is confidential, include a data usage restrictions section; (b) if there are model assumptions, dedicate a specific section to an assumptions table with sensitivities; (c) if the audience is legal, include a methodological warnings and limitations section. [C · CRITERIA] Every main body claim must be traceable to a specific appendix section. The team must be able to answer any technical client question in less than 90 seconds by navigating the appendix. DoD: complete index, minimum five appendix sections, referencing convention defined, three likely questions anticipated. Protocolo MetodologIA: evidence traceability over volume; each appendix section exists to answer a specific client question.
spec-consulting_nota_de_avance_quincenal: [S · SITUATION] A consulting team has an active engagement with a client and must send a biweekly progress note (every two weeks) to keep the client informed of progress, alert about risks or blockers that require client-side attention, and maintain trust in the team. The note reaches the project sponsor and possibly the client's management team. A poorly structured note generates anxiety, too many follow-up questions, or the perception that the project is in trouble. [P · REQUEST] Draft the biweekly progress note in English (max. 350 words) in structured format communicating: progress vs. plan in the period, key accomplishments, status of active risks, required client action items, and upcoming activities for the next period, with a professional and trustworthy tone. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Consulting engagement manager with experience in proactive communication with sponsors of 6-18 month transformation projects in technology, banking, and manufacturing sectors in Latin America. ASSUMPTIONS: the input is the team's progress notes or project status for the period; if the user does not provide detailed status, draft the note with sections and [COMPLETE] markers; if progress vs. plan is not quantified, use qualitative descriptors with a traffic light (green/yellow/red) and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; only ask for clarification if confidence in the project status drops below 0.85. INPUTS: period progress notes, risk status, pending client items, planned activities for the next period. STEPS: 1) Draft opening line with overall project status (traffic light + one sentence). 2) 'Period progress' section: 3-5 concrete accomplishments with perfective past-tense verb. 3) 'Risk status' section: traffic-light table with risk, status, and current mitigation action. 4) 'Required client actions' section: numbered list with owner and deadline. 5) 'Upcoming activities' section: 3-5 activities with tentative date. 6) Closing with team availability for queries. OUTPUT: structured text note with five sections, max. 350 words, ready to send by email. EDGE CASES: (a) if the period had significant delays, frame with root cause and recovery plan, not with justifications; (b) if there are conflicts with the client, maintain a neutral and factual tone; (c) if the project is at critical risk, use an explicit alert opening with a proposal for an emergency call. [C · CRITERIA] The sponsor must be able to read and understand the project status in 90 seconds. Client action items must have an owner and date, not be generic. Tone: professional, direct, trustworthy, never defensive. DoD: five complete sections, max. 350 words, action items with owner and date, overall status on the first line. Protocolo MetodologIA: status first, context after; client action items visible and differentiated from team progress.
spec-consulting_informe_final_de_engagem: [S · SITUATION] A consulting team is closing a 3-12 month engagement and must deliver the final report to the client. This document is the formal close of the contract, the evidence of value delivered, and the guide the client will use to implement or continue the work without the consulting team. The report must balance analytical rigor, executive clarity, and knowledge transfer to the client. A weak final delivery risks the client reference and the possibility of engagement extension. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete structure of the final engagement report in English, including the detailed index with each section's purpose, the content of the executive section, the findings and recommendations sections with evidence level, the implementation and roadmap section, and the knowledge transfer closing. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Consulting director with experience closing strategic, operational, and technology transformation engagements for mid-size and large companies in Latin America, with emphasis on deliverables the client can use independently of the consulting team. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the engagement type, assume a strategic diagnosis and recommendations; if engagement scope is not detailed, design the standard structure with [ADAPT TO SCOPE] markers; if previous engagement deliverables are mentioned, integrate them into the structure; only ask for clarification if confidence in the final report objective drops below 0.85. INPUTS: engagement type, original project scope and objectives, key findings and recommendations, implementation status at close, confidentiality restrictions. STEPS: 1) Define the final report message (governing thought of the full document). 2) Design the section structure: cover, executive summary, engagement context, methodology, findings by area, prioritized recommendations, implementation roadmap, monitoring metrics, lessons learned, technical appendix. 3) For each section: purpose, primary audience (executive/technical), expected content, approximate length. 4) Design the executive summary (max. 2 pages) as a self-contained document. 5) Define the knowledge transfer section: documents to deliver, suggested training, post-engagement governance model. OUTPUT: detailed report index with section table (Section | Purpose | Audience | Content | Length) + two-page executive summary outline + list of knowledge transfer elements. EDGE CASES: (a) if the engagement had scope deviations, include a change management and lessons learned section; (b) if recommendations were not implemented during the engagement, clearly separate findings from pending recommendations; (c) if the client has confidentiality restrictions with third-party data, design a data use warnings section. [C · CRITERIA] The executive summary must be self-contained and understandable without reading the rest of the report. The implementation roadmap must be executable by the client team without consulting support. DoD: complete index with 10+ sections, executive summary outline, knowledge transfer list, document message defined. Protocolo MetodologIA: the report belongs to the client, not the consultant; language and structure must empower the client team to continue without dependency.
spec-consulting_business_case_con_van_ti:
[S · SITUATION] An executive team needs to support with numbers the decision to invest in a strategic initiative (expansion, technology, new product, or operational improvement). They have revenue and cost projections but lack the structured financial analysis required by the approving board. [P · REQUEST] Build a complete financial business case that includes a 5-year projected cash flow, Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and payback period, with sensitivity on the highest-impact variable, ready for executive presentation. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior financial analyst with experience in investment project valuation and strategic consulting. ASSUMPTIONS: discount rate 12% annually if not specified; user's local currency; 5-year horizon; initial investment in year 0; if confidence in any datum is below 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: project description, estimated investment amount, projected revenues year by year, and annual operating costs pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Validate and structure input data in a gross cash flow table. 2. Calculate annual free cash flow (revenues − costs − capex). 3. Discount flows at the defined rate and calculate NPV. 4. Calculate IRR by interpolation or internal function. 5. Determine simple payback and discounted payback. 6. Run one-dimensional sensitivity analysis on the highest-impact variable (±10%, ±20%). 7. Write a two-paragraph executive summary with recommendation. OUTPUT: cash flow table (5 years), financial indicators (NPV, IRR, simple payback, discounted payback), sensitivity chart in text or table, and recommendation paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) negative NPV → flag minimum revenue threshold for viability; (2) non-convergent IRR → use bisection method and report; (3) incomplete data for any year → interpolate and declare assumption. [C · CRITERIA] NPV and IRR must be calculated with the same discount rate; discounted payback always greater than or equal to simple payback; the recommendation must cite at least two metrics; the analysis must be reproducible with the data provided. Trade-off: precision vs. speed → prioritize arithmetic accuracy; if data is missing, declare assumption before estimating. DoD: deliverable reviewable by CFO without arithmetic corrections.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Finance · Business Case · NPV-IRR-Payback · Strategic consulting
spec-consulting_modelo_de_costo_benefici:
[S · SITUATION] An organization evaluates whether an intervention (process, system, program, or policy) generates more value than it consumes in resources. The team needs to structure all costs (direct, indirect, opportunity) and all benefits (tangible and monetizable intangible) in a comparative model that justifies or rejects the investment before decision-makers. [P · REQUEST] Build a structured cost-benefit model with identification, quantification, and comparison of costs versus benefits, benefit-cost ratio (BCR), and viability conclusion, presented in a table and executive narrative. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior financial consultant with experience in program evaluation and cost-benefit analysis for public and private sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: analysis horizon 3 years if not specified; all values in base year (no inflation) unless indicated; intangible benefits monetized with explicitly declared methodology; declare assumption and continue if confidence < 0.85. INPUTS: description of the intervention or initiative, list of known costs and expected benefits pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Classify all items into categories: implementation costs, recurring operating costs, directly quantifiable benefits, indirect benefits. 2. Monetize each item with the appropriate methodology (market value, willingness to pay, equivalent savings). 3. Total costs and benefits by year and cumulatively. 4. Calculate BCR = Total Benefits / Total Costs. 5. Calculate net benefit = Benefits − Costs. 6. Write a viability conclusion with limit conditions. OUTPUT: two-column table (costs vs. benefits) with subtotals and category totals, BCR, net benefit, and conclusion paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) BCR < 1 → indicate what benefit level would need to be reached for viability; (2) dominant intangible benefit → warn about result sensitivity to monetization; (3) undeclared opportunity costs → ask the user if they are relevant, maximum one question. [C · CRITERIA] Each item must have a declared valuation source or methodology; BCR calculated coherently with totals; conclusion must mention the highest-weight item on each side. Trade-off: exhaustiveness vs. parsimony → include only quantifiable items with sufficient confidence. DoD: model reviewable by a financial manager without needing to recalculate manually.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Finance · Cost-Benefit · BCR · Value consulting
spec-consulting_estimacion_de_tam_sam_so:
[S · SITUATION] A company or startup needs to size the market it is targeting in order to support decisions about investment, expansion, or an investor pitch. Without a structured quantification of the total addressable market, serviceable available market, and obtainable market, growth plans lack an objective anchor. [P · REQUEST] Produce a documented estimate of TAM (total market), SAM (serviceable available market), and SOM (realistic obtainable market) with top-down and bottom-up methodology, including explicit assumptions, referenced sources, and a confidence range per level. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior market analyst with experience in sizing for startups, corporates, and investment funds. ASSUMPTIONS: if no secondary source data is provided, use bottom-up methodology with target segment data declared as assumption; reference year = current year; currency USD or local as per user context; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: product or service description, operating geography, target segment, unit price or average ticket, available market data pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Define the total universe of the problem (TAM) with a top-down approach from sector figures. 2. Narrow the TAM to the segment accessible with current channels and capabilities to obtain SAM. 3. Project the realistic share capturable in 12-36 months to obtain SOM. 4. Validate with bottom-up approach: segment × average ticket × frequency. 5. Contrast top-down vs. bottom-up and reconcile differences. 6. Synthesize in a table with optimistic/conservative range for each level. OUTPUT: TAM/SAM/SOM table with absolute and percentage values, methodology narrative (2-3 paragraphs), numbered assumptions list, and confidence range per level. EDGE CASES: (1) emerging market without data → use declared geographic or sectoral proxies; (2) SOM > SAM → automatic correction with explanation; (3) multiple geographies → disaggregate by region before consolidating. [C · CRITERIA] SOM always ≤ SAM ≤ TAM; each level must have at least one documented source or assumption; the optimistic/conservative range cannot differ by more than 3× without justification. Trade-off: precision vs. speed → prefer honest ranges over point estimates without basis. DoD: estimation defensible in an investor session without additional data.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Markets · TAM-SAM-SOM · Sizing · Growth consulting
spec-consulting_analisis_de_punto_de_equ:
[S · SITUATION] A company or business unit needs to know exactly how many units it must sell, or how much revenue it must generate, to cover all fixed and variable costs without losing or making money. This threshold is critical for pricing decisions, minimum viable volume, and production planning. [P · REQUEST] Calculate the break-even point in units and in monetary value, with a breakdown of fixed and variable costs, contribution margin per unit, break-even chart in text (volume tranche table), and analysis of what happens if price or costs vary ±10%. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior financial management analyst with experience in CVP (Cost-Volume-Profit) analysis for manufacturing, services, and trade industries. ASSUMPTIONS: selling price and variable costs expressed per unit; fixed costs expressed per period; if the user does not specify a period, assume monthly; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: unit selling price, unit variable cost, total fixed costs for the period, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Calculate unit contribution margin (CM = Price − Variable Cost). 2. Calculate contribution margin ratio (CMR = CM / Price). 3. Calculate break-even in units (BE = Fixed Costs / CM). 4. Calculate break-even in revenue (BE$ = Fixed Costs / CMR). 5. Build volume vs. profit table for 0%, 50%, 100%, 150% of the break-even point. 6. Run sensitivity analysis: price ±10% and variable cost ±10%. 7. Write a managerial implications paragraph. OUTPUT: component table (price, VC, FC, CM, CMR), break-even in units and value, volume-profit table, sensitivity table, implications paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) negative contribution margin → alert that the price does not cover the variable cost; (2) multiple products → apply weighted break-even by sales mix; (3) semi-fixed costs → ask the user for classification in a single question. [C · CRITERIA] Break-even in units and in value must be coherent with each other; the sensitivity table must show the percentage impact on the break-even point; the implications must guide an actionable decision. Trade-off: precision vs. usefulness → prioritize interpretive clarity over excessive decimal places. DoD: the financial manager can use the analysis to set a minimum price or minimum sales volume.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Finance · Break-Even · CVP · Profitability management
spec-consulting_modelo_de_escenarios_bas:
[S · SITUATION] A leadership team needs to evaluate the range of possible results of an initiative before committing resources. Rather than working with a single point forecast, they require three quantitative scenarios (pessimistic, base, optimistic) that reveal risk exposure and the breadth of upside, in order to make robust decisions under uncertainty. [P · REQUEST] Build a three-scenario model (pessimistic, base, optimistic) over the key variables of a project or business, with quantified results per scenario, assigned probabilities, weighted expected value, and a comparative table with a qualitative risk traffic light. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Strategic planning consultant with experience in scenario analysis for investment projects, product launches, and organizational transformations. ASSUMPTIONS: base scenario reflects the most likely projection; optimistic scenario assumes materialization of the main positive drivers; pessimistic scenario assumes materialization of the main risks; default probabilities 20%-60%-20% (pessimistic-base-optimistic) are adjustable; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: project or business description, identified key variables (minimum 2-3), base values per variable, possible variation ranges pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify and list the 3-5 variables of highest uncertainty and impact. 2. Define values per variable for each scenario with justification. 3. Calculate the main financial result or KPI for each scenario. 4. Assign probabilities and calculate weighted expected value. 5. Build comparative table with delta between scenarios. 6. Assign risk traffic light (green/yellow/red) based on the pessimistic result. 7. Write a 1-paragraph narrative per scenario and a strategic conclusion. OUTPUT: variable table with values per scenario, financial results table per scenario, weighted expected value, risk traffic light, and three narrative paragraphs plus conclusion. EDGE CASES: (1) optimistic scenario implies a pessimistic financial result → alert the user; (2) probabilities do not sum to 100% → normalize and declare; (3) correlated variables → group into a single risk factor with a note. [C · CRITERIA] Probabilities must sum to 100%; the expected value must fall between the pessimistic and optimistic; each scenario must have at least one variable that distinguishes it quantitatively. Trade-off: statistical rigor vs. usability → three discrete scenarios are preferable to continuous distributions for executive communication. DoD: the table can be presented to the board without additional preparation.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Strategy · Scenarios · Uncertainty management · Risk consulting
spec-consulting_cuantificacion_de_benefi:
[S · SITUATION] In many transformation, cultural improvement, training, or technology projects, the most important benefits are difficult to measure directly: higher employee satisfaction, reduced turnover, improved brand reputation, reduced human errors, or increased perceived productivity. Without monetizing these benefits, the financial analysis underestimates the real value of the investment. [P · REQUEST] Systematically monetize a list of soft (intangible) benefits using financial proxy techniques, willingness to pay, replacement cost, productivity impact, and risk reduction value, producing a table with method, assumption, estimated value, and confidence range per item. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Value and benefits analyst with experience in change management consulting, human capital, and digital transformation. ASSUMPTIONS: when historical data is unavailable, use sector benchmarks declared as assumptions; express results as a range (min-max) rather than a point value; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: list of identified soft benefits, project context (sector, organization size, number of people impacted) pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Categorize each soft benefit (human capital, reputation, operational risk, process efficiency). 2. Select the most appropriate monetization method per category. 3. Identify the necessary proxy data (employee replacement cost, productive hour value, historical error rate, etc.). 4. Calculate estimated value with minimum-maximum range. 5. Synthesize in a table with columns: benefit, category, method, key assumption, min value, max value, confidence. 6. Write a methodological warning on the limitations of each monetization. OUTPUT: monetized soft benefits table, subtotals per category, consolidated total range, and methodological warning paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) benefit not monetizable by any proxy → include as a qualitative risk with a note; (2) sector data unavailable → use a wide range with declared low confidence; (3) benefits with potential double counting → group and flag. [C · CRITERIA] Each item must have an explicit method; the range must not be narrower than ±20% without sufficient data; the methodological warning must mention the item of highest uncertainty. Trade-off: inclusiveness vs. rigor → prefer to include with declared uncertainty rather than omit. DoD: the analysis can be incorporated into a business case without generating methodological objections.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Value · Intangible benefits · Monetization · Change management consulting
spec-consulting_analisis_de_cadena_de_va:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs to identify in which activities of its value chain it generates real competitive advantage and in which it consumes resources without creating differential value for the customer. Without this diagnosis, investment, outsourcing, or improvement decisions are made without strategic grounding in the processes that truly matter. [P · REQUEST] Produce a value chain analysis following Porter's framework adapted to the business context, identifying primary and support activities, value generation level per activity, critical linkages, and prioritized optimization recommendations. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior strategic consultant with experience in competitive analysis and organizational design based on value chain. ASSUMPTIONS: if cost information per activity is not provided, evaluate qualitatively on a high/medium/low scale; if sector is not specified, infer from the business description and declare; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: business or company description, known main activities, perceived sources of competitive advantage, and main operational pain points pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Map primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, after-sales service). 2. Map support activities (infrastructure, talent management, technology development, procurement). 3. Evaluate value contribution (differentiation or cost) and current performance level per activity. 4. Identify the three most critical linkages between activities (where the performance of one significantly affects another). 5. Detect low-value, high-cost activities as candidates for optimization or outsourcing. 6. Write recommendations prioritized by impact on competitive advantage. OUTPUT: table of primary and support activities with value and performance evaluation, map of critical linkages, list of activities candidates for improvement/outsourcing, and list of prioritized recommendations. EDGE CASES: (1) service company → adapt operations categories to service delivery; (2) multiple business lines → build value chain per line or flag the intersection; (3) insufficient data → make declared qualitative evaluation. [C · CRITERIA] All activities in Porter's framework must be represented; recommendations must be linked to specific activities; the analysis must distinguish between differentiation advantage and cost advantage. Trade-off: exhaustiveness vs. practical usefulness → prioritize activities with highest strategic impact. DoD: the analysis can guide a strategic prioritization workshop without additional preparatory work.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Strategy · Value chain · Porter · Competitive advantage
spec-consulting_modelo_de_madurez_de_pro:
[S · SITUATION] An organization wants to understand the maturity level of its critical processes in order to plan realistic improvements, establish a diagnostic baseline, and communicate the evolution status to leadership. Without a structured maturity model, process improvement initiatives are launched without an objective reference on the starting point or the desired destination. [P · REQUEST] Evaluate the indicated processes against a five-level maturity model (initial, repeatable, defined, managed, optimized), produce a maturity profile per process, identify gaps between the current state and the target level, and deliver a prioritized improvement roadmap. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior process improvement consultant with experience in CMMI-type maturity models, BPM Maturity, and derivatives for technology, services, and manufacturing sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: use a 5-level scale if no other model is specified; default target level = level 3 (defined) if not indicated; evaluate with evidence provided or justified estimation; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: list of processes to evaluate, description of the current state of each (documentation, indicators, automation, governance), desired target level pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Define the criteria for each maturity level adapted to the organization's context. 2. Evaluate each process against the criteria for each level with evidence or estimation. 3. Assign current maturity level (1-5) with justification. 4. Calculate the gap between current and target level. 5. Identify the enabling capabilities to develop to close each gap. 6. Prioritize improvements by strategic impact and required effort. 7. Write a roadmap with phases and milestones. OUTPUT: maturity profile table per process (current level, target level, gap, justification), enabling capabilities table, improvement roadmap with phases, and executive conclusion paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) process without documentation or data → assign level 1 with a note; (2) process already at level 5 → identify maintenance and regression risk; (3) more than 8 processes → group by domain and prioritize the 3-5 most critical. [C · CRITERIA] Each level must have context-specific observable criteria; the roadmap must be sequential (no skipping levels without justification); priorities must consider both impact and feasibility. Trade-off: rigor vs. speed → favor applicable criteria over purist frameworks. DoD: the maturity profile can be presented to a continuous improvement committee for validation and roadmap approval.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Operations · Process maturity · BPM · Continuous improvement
spec-consulting_analisis_make_or_buy:
[S · SITUATION] An organization faces the decision of whether to develop a capability, product, or service internally versus acquiring or contracting it externally. This decision has implications for total costs, delivery speed, strategic control, vendor dependency, and core competencies that must be evaluated holistically before committing resources. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured make-or-buy analysis comparing both options on financial dimensions (total cost of ownership) and strategic dimensions (control, agility, risk, core competency), with a justified recommendation and conditions under which the decision would change. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Operations and strategy consultant with experience in outsourcing analysis, build-vs-buy decisions, and strategic vendor management. ASSUMPTIONS: analysis horizon 3 years if not specified; include hidden costs (maintenance, integration, governance) in the make option; include dependency and switching costs in the buy option; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: description of the capability to evaluate, estimated internal development costs, available market options with prices if known, relevant strategic criteria pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Define the exact scope of what is being evaluated (what make includes, what buy includes). 2. Calculate total cost of ownership (TCO) for make: development, implementation, maintenance, staffing, opportunity. 3. Calculate TCO for buy: license/service, integration, support, vendor dependency, switching cost. 4. Evaluate strategic dimensions: control, speed, risk, alignment with core competency. 5. Build multidimensional comparative table with weighted criteria. 6. Formulate recommendation with boundary conditions (threshold price, time, internal capacity). OUTPUT: TCO table (make vs. buy by year and total), weighted strategic evaluation table, recommendation with justification and boundary conditions. EDGE CASES: (1) similar TCO for both options → decide by strategic control criterion; (2) core competency → recommend make by default with a note; (3) market without mature providers → flag buy risk. [C · CRITERIA] The TCO must include at least 4 cost categories per option; the strategic evaluation must have explicit weighted criteria; the recommendation must be a single option with argumentation. Trade-off: exhaustive analysis vs. decision speed → complete with assumptions before stalling for lack of data. DoD: the analysis can be presented to the investment committee for approval without complementary analysis.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Operations · Make-or-Buy · TCO · Outsourcing decisions
spec-consulting_modelo_de_capacidad_y_de:
[S · SITUATION] An organization faces imbalances between the available capacity of its resources (people, equipment, systems) and the demand it must serve. Without a model that quantifies the gap, leaders make hiring, investment, or prioritization decisions without objective visibility into where the real constraints are and when they will occur within the planning horizon. [P · REQUEST] Build a capacity vs. demand model that compares the supply of available resources against projected demand period by period, identifies saturation and deficit points, and proposes adjustment alternatives (hiring, prioritization, outsourcing, automation) with impact analysis. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Operations and resource planning consultant with experience in capacity models for IT areas, manufacturing, and professional services teams. ASSUMPTIONS: monthly analysis period if not specified; capacity expressed in person-hours or resource units; demand expressed in the same unit type; resource efficiency 80% if not indicated; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: number and type of available resources, maximum capacity per resource and period, projected demand period by period, known constraints or reserves pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Calculate total installed capacity per period (resources × hours × efficiency). 2. Calculate net available capacity (discounting reserves, absences, and non-productive activities). 3. Record projected demand per period. 4. Calculate capacity gap (available − demand) per period. 5. Identify saturation periods (negative gap) and slack periods. 6. Model adjustment alternatives with impact on gap and cost. 7. Synthesize into a table and text bar chart. OUTPUT: period-by-period table of installed capacity, available capacity, demand, and gap; bottleneck identification with severity; adjustment alternatives table with impact and estimated cost; recommendations paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) variable demand with seasonal peaks → flag critical period and calculate maximum gap; (2) multiple resource types → build model per type and consolidate; (3) uncertain future demand → apply optimistic/pessimistic range in a variant. [C · CRITERIA] The gap must be calculated consistently in the same units; alternatives must cover both the short term (0-3 months) and medium term (3-12 months); the recommendation must prioritize the lowest total cost alternatives for the same gap coverage. Trade-off: precision vs. practicality → prefer monthly granularity over weekly unless the context requires it. DoD: the model can be used in a resource planning meeting to make hiring or reassignment decisions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Operations · Capacity and demand · Resource planning · Bottlenecks
spec-consulting_analisis_de_canibalizaci:
[S · SITUATION] A company is considering launching a new product, channel, service, or pricing model that could compete with its current offering, reducing sales of existing lines rather than generating purely incremental revenue. Without quantifying the cannibalization effect, the revenue projection of the new launch overstates the real net impact on the business. [P · REQUEST] Quantify the projected revenue cannibalization effect, estimating the percentage of sales of the new product that come from customers abandoning existing lines versus new customers or additional markets, and calculate the real net incremental revenue after cannibalization. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Portfolio strategy analyst with experience in product launches, business line management, and substitution analysis in consumer and B2B markets. ASSUMPTIONS: if historical substitution data is not available, use sector benchmarks declared as assumptions; typical cannibalization rate for product launches 20-40% if no other is indicated; margin of cannibalized lines equal to that of the new product if no difference is specified; if confidence < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: new product sales projection, description of existing lines at risk of substitution, new product customer profile, historical substitution data if it exists, margins of each line pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify existing product lines at risk of substitution. 2. Estimate the cannibalization rate (% of new product sales coming from current customers). 3. Calculate the volume and value of cannibalized sales per existing line. 4. Calculate the margin loss from cannibalization. 5. Calculate net incremental revenue = new sales − cannibalized revenue. 6. Analyze the impact on the portfolio's consolidated margin. 7. Evaluate whether the launch is profitable net of cannibalization. OUTPUT: sales projection table of gross vs. net post-cannibalization by year, cannibalization breakdown by affected line, net incremental margin, and recommendation on whether to proceed with the launch or adjust positioning. EDGE CASES: (1) total cannibalization (>80%) → repositioning recommendation; (2) positive cannibalization (migration to higher-margin product) → flag as a benefit; (3) insufficient data → pessimistic/optimistic range with sensitivity. [C · CRITERIA] Net incremental revenue must be calculated after deducting cannibalization and compared against the new product's margin; the analysis must cover at least 3 years; the recommendation must include a minimum profitability condition. Trade-off: precision vs. speed → use ranges before waiting for perfect data. DoD: the analysis can be presented to the product team for a launch decision without additional analysis.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Portfolio strategy · Cannibalization · Net revenue · Product management
spec-consulting_evaluacion_de_opciones_c:
[S · SITUATION] A leadership team faces a strategic decision where multiple viable options exist along with several relevant evaluation criteria of varying relative importance. Informal discussion tends to prioritize the preferences of the most vocal participant or the most recently mentioned criterion, without a structured comparison that makes the team's values and the reasoning behind the choice transparent. [P · REQUEST] Build a weighted decision matrix that evaluates all options against the defined criteria, with explicit weights assigned to each criterion, a score for each option per criterion, total weighted score, and a sensitivity analysis to detect whether the winning option changes when the most uncertain weights are adjusted. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Strategic decision facilitator with experience in multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDM) tools, criteria weighting, and communication of decision reasoning to executive teams. ASSUMPTIONS: scoring scale 1-5 by default; weights expressed as percentages summing to 100%; if weights are not provided, ask the user in a single question before proceeding; if confidence in any criterion < 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: list of options to evaluate, list of criteria with their weights (or instruction to suggest them), score for each option per criterion or data to infer it, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Confirm or suggest the criteria weights with justification. 2. Build the matrix with options in rows and criteria in columns. 3. Record the raw score (1-5) of each option on each criterion. 4. Calculate the weighted score per cell (score × weight). 5. Sum weighted scores per option to obtain the total score. 6. Rank the options from highest to lowest total score. 7. Run sensitivity analysis: vary ±20% the weight of the two most uncertain criteria and observe whether the winning option changes. 8. Write a decision conclusion with explanation of the reasoning. OUTPUT: complete weighted matrix table, option ranking, weight sensitivity table, and decision conclusion paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) tie between two options → flag and request a tiebreaker criterion; (2) option dominant across all criteria → flag as a clear consensus; (3) more than 7 options → reduce to the 4-5 most viable before the matrix. [C · CRITERIA] Weights must sum to 100%; each cell must have a documented score; the sensitivity analysis must cover the two highest-weight criteria; the conclusion must identify the recommended option with its margin over the second. Trade-off: quantitative rigor vs. qualitative transparency → show both the final number and the reasoning behind each score. DoD: the matrix can be presented in a decision-making session and the recommendation can be defended before any participant.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Decisions · Weighted matrix · MCDM · Strategic facilitation
spec-consulting_diagrama_sipoc_de_proces: [S · SITUATION] A continuous improvement team needs to map a business process from end to end before starting an optimization or certification project. No structured documentation exists and knowledge is fragmented across areas. [P · REQUEST] Build a complete SIPOC diagram of the indicated process, identifying the 5 columns (Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers) with at least 3-5 entries per column, ready for stakeholder validation. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior operational excellence consultant with experience in Lean Six Sigma and enterprise process mapping. ASSUMPTIONS: the process has between 5 and 8 high-level steps; the scope starts from the most upstream external or internal supplier and ends at the final customer; if no industry is indicated, assume financial services; proceed declaring assumptions without asking unless confidence is below 0.85. INPUTS: process description pasted in the chat or screenshot of the current flow. STEPS: 1) Identify the name and purpose of the process (output: scope definition in one sentence). 2) List the Customers and their key needs (output: column C with 3-5 customers/segments). 3) Define the Outputs received by customers (output: column O with measurable deliverables). 4) Break down the Process into 5-8 high-level steps using action verbs (output: column P with numbered steps). 5) Identify the Inputs required by the process (output: column I with inputs/data/materials). 6) Map the Suppliers that provide each Input (output: column S with internal/external suppliers). 7) Format the final SIPOC table with notes on detected gaps and ambiguities. OUTPUT: SIPOC table in markdown format with 5 clearly delimited columns + "Key observations" section with 3-5 findings + list of declared assumptions. EDGE CASES: (a) highly technical process with insufficient description → build tentative SIPOC with explicit [ASSUMPTION] and request validation; (b) cross-functional process with multiple variants → map the main flow and annotate variants in observations; (c) customer and supplier are the same entity → indicate it and clearly differentiate roles. [C · CRITERIA] Each column has at least 3 concrete and specific entries; Outputs are measurable or verifiable; process steps use action verbs; the table is consistent left to right; DoD: cross-consistency review S→I→P→O→C approved with no logical gaps. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions before delivery, prioritize specificity over exhaustiveness, mark with [ASSUMPTION] every unconfirmed inference.
spec-consulting_value_stream_mapping: [S · SITUATION] An organization that produces a recurring product or service wants to visualize and analyze the complete value stream to identify where wastes, bottlenecks, and improvement opportunities exist before designing the future state. [P · REQUEST] Build a Value Stream Map (VSM) of the indicated flow in structured text format, including the current state with key metrics (lead time, process time, inventory/queue, value-added percentage), waste identification, and a summary of the target future state. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Lean consultant with experience in VSM for manufacturing and service flows. ASSUMPTIONS: if no real metrics are provided, use typical sector ranges marked with [ASSUMPTION]; the flow has between 4 and 8 main stages; the customer is external unless otherwise indicated; assume a services industry if not specified; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: process or flow description pasted in the chat, with or without time metrics. STEPS: 1) Define the product/service and the final customer (output: demand sheet: estimated takt time and volume). 2) Identify each stage of the flow with its process time and wait time (output: stage table with CT, WT, queue). 3) Calculate total lead time, value-added time, and VA% (output: consolidated metrics). 4) Identify information flows and material/data flows between stages (output: description of triggers and channels). 5) Mark the wastes (mudas) detected per stage (output: classified list by type). 6) Propose the future state with priority improvements (output: future VSM with highlighted changes). OUTPUT: Structured VSM document with: (a) current state table per stage, (b) consolidated metrics, (c) information flow map, (d) identified wastes, (e) proposed future state with 3-5 improvements. EDGE CASES: (a) process without time metrics → build qualitative VSM with [ASSUMPTION] on each metric; (b) flow with multiple product families → choose the highest-volume family and note it; (c) flow shared across areas without clear coordination → flag the handoff as a critical point. [C · CRITERIA] Total lead time is the verifiable sum of CT + WT per stage; VA% is calculated correctly; the future state addresses the 3 main wastes; DoD: mathematical and logical consistency review of the flow completed. Protocolo MetodologIA: show intermediate calculations, mark [ASSUMPTION] on every metric not provided, connect findings with concrete actions in the future state.
spec-consulting_identificacion_de_desper: [S · SITUATION] A process-improvement team needs to perform a rapid Lean waste diagnostic on an operational process to prioritize what to improve first and justify a transformation project to management. [P · REQUEST] Analyze the described process applying the 8 Lean wastes framework (Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects, Unused Talent) and deliver a waste catalog with: type, specific description, estimated impact (High/Medium/Low) and one improvement recommendation per waste. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Certified Lean consultant (Black Belt or equivalent) with experience eliminating waste in service and manufacturing processes. ASSUMPTIONS: the process is analyzed as it operates today (current state); impact is estimated qualitatively if there is no data; assume all 8 muda types are candidates for review; proceed without asking, declaring assumptions with confidence >= 0.85. INPUTS: textual description of the process or a VSM fragment pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1) Read and summarize the process in 2-3 sentences (output: confirmed scope). 2) Systematically walk through the 8 mudas and detect concrete instances in the process (output: findings table with textual evidence). 3) Estimate the impact of each waste on lead time, cost or quality (output: H/M/L impact column with brief justification). 4) Formulate a concrete improvement recommendation for each waste found (output: recommended action column). 5) Prioritize the 3 highest-impact wastes with the argument for why to address them first (output: top-3 priorities section). OUTPUT: Waste table with 5 columns (Muda, Specific description, Evidence in the process, Impact H/M/L, Recommendation) + Top-3 priorities section with prioritization argument + declared assumptions. EDGE CASES: (a) very sparse description → identify probable mudas with [ASSUMPTION] and request validation of the 2 most critical; (b) digitized process with no physical handling → omit physical Transportation and Motion but analyze their digital equivalents; (c) more than 15 muda instances → group by type and report the 3 most recurrent per category. [C · CRITERIA] Each detected muda has concrete textual evidence from the process; recommendations are actionable within 90 days without major investment; the top-3 is ranked by impact; DoD: no muda type omitted in the analysis (even if only to declare it does not apply). Protocolo MetodologIA: exhaustive analysis of all 8 mudas, specific evidence mandatory, recommendations prioritized by impact.
spec-consulting_mapa_as_is_de_proceso_bp: [S · SITUATION] A transformation team needs to formally document how an organizational process operates today to create a baseline before redesigning, automating or certifying it under ISO or CMMI. The documentation exists scattered across emails, wikis or in the minds of subject-matter experts. [P · REQUEST] Generate the as-is map of the indicated process in BPMN 2.0 notation using XML pseudocode or equivalent structured description, with pools, lanes, start/end events, tasks, gateways and sequence flows clearly identified, ready to import into Bizagi, Camunda or Lucidchart. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior process architect with BPMN 2.0 certification and experience documenting processes for digital transformation projects. ASSUMPTIONS: the process has between 5 and 12 tasks; the main actors form the pool lanes; exceptions are modeled as intermediate events; if the target tool is not specified, generate a universal structured description; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: textual description of the process, list of actors or roles involved (if available), and target BPMN tool if known. STEPS: 1) Identify pools and lanes from the actors (output: organizational structure of the diagram). 2) Define the start event with its trigger and the end event with its closing condition (output: delimited events). 3) Map the tasks in sequential order with names in verb+object format (output: numbered list of tasks per lane). 4) Identify decision gateways with their branching conditions (output: list of gateways with yes/no conditions). 5) Establish sequence flows and messages between pools if any (output: connectors with labels). 6) Write the structured BPMN description or XML pseudocode (output: final importable artifact). OUTPUT: Structured BPMN description with: (a) pool and lane declaration, (b) element table (ID, type, name, description, connections), (c) convention notes, (d) import instructions for the indicated tool. EDGE CASES: (a) process with more than 12 tasks → decompose into collapsed sub-processes; (b) unknown actors → group in generic lanes (Requester, Approver, Executor) marked with [ASSUMPTION]; (c) flow with cycles or rework → model with join gateway and annotate as loop. [C · CRITERIA] Every task has a verb+object name; every gateway has at least 2 outputs with labeled conditions; the diagram has exactly one start event and at least one end event; DoD: completeness review (no orphan tasks or gateways without condition) approved. Protocolo MetodologIA: fidelity to current state without improvements, name elements with strict BPMN convention, flag real-process ambiguities as notes.
spec-consulting_rediseno_to_be_de_proces: [S · SITUATION] An organization has the as-is map of a process and has identified its main problems (wastes, bottlenecks, recurring errors). It needs to design the future state (to-be) that eliminates those problems, is feasible to implement in the short to medium term, and serves as a blueprint for the implementation team. [P · REQUEST] Design the redesigned to-be process, documenting the changes with respect to the as-is, the design decisions made and the expected impact on key metrics (lead time, cost, quality), together with a map of the future process in structured format. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Process transformation consultant with experience in Lean-Digital redesign and organizational change management. ASSUMPTIONS: the redesign must be implementable without changing the organizational structure unless indicated; the implementation horizon is 6-12 months; if there is no baseline data, impact is expressed as an estimated improvement percentage with [ASSUMPTION]; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: description of the as-is process or existing map + list of identified problems + improvement objectives if available. STEPS: 1) Summarize the as-is and the main problems to solve (output: diagnostic summary in 5 bullets). 2) Define the to-be design principles (e.g. eliminate redundant approvals, digitize manual captures) (output: 3-5 guiding principles). 3) Design the to-be flow step by step indicating changes vs. as-is (output: as-is vs. to-be comparative table by stage). 4) Identify the required enablers (technology, training, new policies) (output: list of enablers with priority). 5) Estimate the expected impact on lead time, cost and quality (output: impact table with estimated baseline and projected improvement). 6) Document design decisions and their discarded alternatives (output: design decisions section). OUTPUT: To-be design document with: (a) diagnostic summary, (b) design principles, (c) as-is vs. to-be comparative table, (d) structured future process map, (e) required enablers, (f) expected impact, (g) documented design decisions. EDGE CASES: (a) no as-is information → request a minimum description of the current process before proceeding; (b) changes requiring unavailable new technology → mark as critical dependency and propose a transitional manual alternative; (c) redesign that eliminates roles → flag change management impact and recommend a communication plan. [C · CRITERIA] Each to-be change has justification linked to an as-is problem; enablers have an assigned owner or responsibility category; impact is quantifiable even if estimated; DoD: organizational feasibility review completed and no change without an identified enabler. Protocolo MetodologIA: each design decision documented, explicit trade-offs, [ASSUMPTION] on all impact without real data.
spec-consulting_analisis_de_tiempos_de_c: [S · SITUATION] An operational or continuous-improvement team needs to understand how much time each stage of a process consumes, where the bottlenecks are and what the relationship between value-added time and total cycle time is, in order to make data-driven optimization decisions. [P · REQUEST] Perform the complete cycle time analysis of the indicated process: break down CT (cycle time) per stage, calculate total lead time, identify the bottleneck, calculate the value-added time percentage and propose the 3-5 priority improvement actions with estimated time impact. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior operations analyst with experience in time-and-motion analysis, Six Sigma and process simulation. ASSUMPTIONS: if no real times are provided, use sector typical ranges marked with [ASSUMPTION]; the bottleneck is the stage with the highest CT relative to takt time; if takt time is unknown, calculate it from the indicated volume and available time; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: list of process stages with process and waiting times (if available) + volume of units per period + available operating time. STEPS: 1) Build the time table per stage (process CT, waiting CT, total CT, %VA per stage) (output: time table). 2) Calculate total lead time by summing all CTs (output: consolidated lead time). 3) Calculate total value-added time and the %VA for the complete process (output: efficiency metrics). 4) Calculate takt time if demand and available time were provided (output: takt time with comparison vs. CT of each stage). 5) Identify the bottleneck and its impact on process capacity (output: bottleneck diagnosis). 6) Propose 3-5 improvement actions ordered by impact on time reduction (output: improvement table with target CT). OUTPUT: Time analysis report with: (a) time table per stage, (b) consolidated metrics (LT, %VA, takt time), (c) bottleneck diagnosis, (d) prioritized improvement table with estimated impact, (e) declared assumptions. EDGE CASES: (a) no time data → build qualitative analysis with typical ranges all marked [ASSUMPTION]; (b) process with high variability → indicate average and range and recommend statistical distribution analysis; (c) multiple bottlenecks → prioritize the one blocking the highest value flow. [C · CRITERIA] LT and %VA calculations are mathematically verifiable; the identified bottleneck has numerical evidence; proposed improvements are specific and have a quantified target CT; DoD: time table reviewed and consistent, no addition errors. Protocolo MetodologIA: show all intermediate calculations, [ASSUMPTION] on all estimated metrics, improvement proposals with numerical impact.
spec-consulting_matriz_raci_de_proceso: [S · SITUATION] In an organizational process there are ambiguities about who does what: tasks performed by multiple people without coordination, decisions made by the wrong person and the absence of a clear owner in critical stages. An improvement team or project leader needs to formally clarify roles and responsibilities. [P · REQUEST] Build the complete RACI matrix of the indicated process, assigning for each task or activity the roles of Responsible (R), Accountable (A), Consulted (C) and Informed (I), with RACI consistency validations included and a findings summary on gaps or overlaps. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organization and process management consultant with experience in governance structure design and responsibility matrices. ASSUMPTIONS: each task must have exactly one R and exactly one A; if there are multiple Rs on a task, it is a gap to report; roles are functional (position or area), not persons; assume between 5 and 15 activities and 3-8 roles if not specified; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: list of activities or tasks in the process + list of roles or areas involved; or textual process description from which both will be inferred. STEPS: 1) List all process activities in logical order (output: activity column). 2) Identify all participating functional roles (output: role header row). 3) Assign R, A, C, I for each task-role intersection (output: complete matrix in table). 4) Validate RACI rules: exactly 1 R per task, exactly 1 A per task, at least 1 assignment per role (output: validation table). 5) Identify gaps (task without R or A), overlaps (multiple Rs) and roles without assignments (output: findings section). 6) Write recommendations to resolve critical gaps (output: 3-5 prioritized recommendations). OUTPUT: RACI matrix in markdown table (rows=activities, columns=roles) + rule validation table + findings and gaps section + prioritized recommendations + declared assumptions. EDGE CASES: (a) description without explicit roles → infer generic roles (Requester, Manager, Approver, Support) marked with [ASSUMPTION]; (b) more than 20 activities → group into macro-activities and detail the critical ones; (c) same role with R and A in the same task → flag as governance risk and recommend separation. [C · CRITERIA] Each activity has exactly 1 R and 1 A; no role has an empty column; gaps are numbered and prioritized; DoD: RACI rule validation completed with no assignment errors on critical activities. Protocolo MetodologIA: RACI rule validation before delivery, gaps prioritized by criticality, [ASSUMPTION] on inferred roles.
spec-consulting_identificacion_de_oportu: [S · SITUATION] An organization wants to explore which parts of its operational processes are candidates for automation (via RPA, APIs, AI or workflow automation) to reduce manual work, errors and cycle times, but lacks clear criteria to prioritize or evaluate technical and business feasibility. [P · REQUEST] Analyze the indicated process or set of processes to identify, classify and prioritize automation opportunities, indicating for each: recommended automation type, eligibility criteria met, estimated benefit, implementation complexity and priority. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Automation and digital transformation consultant with experience in RPA (UiPath/Automation Anywhere), systems integration and AI-powered process automation. ASSUMPTIONS: use standard RPA eligibility criteria (clear rules, high repeatability, structured data, significant volume); if volume is unknown, estimate it as [ASSUMPTION]; benefit is expressed in hours/month saved or % error reduction; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: process description or list of activities + technology context if available (systems used, ERP, CRM). STEPS: 1) Identify all manual or semi-manual activities in the process (output: list of candidate activities). 2) Evaluate each activity against eligibility criteria (rules, repeatability, data, volume, stability) (output: eligibility matrix). 3) Classify the most suitable automation type per activity (RPA, API, workflow, AI/ML, hybrid) (output: type column). 4) Estimate the expected benefit in hours/month or % error reduction per activity (output: benefit column). 5) Estimate implementation complexity (Low/Medium/High) with justification (output: complexity column). 6) Calculate priority as the benefit/complexity ratio and order the automation backlog (output: prioritized ranking). OUTPUT: Automation opportunity matrix with columns (Activity, Criteria met, Automation type, Estimated benefit, Complexity, Priority) + top-5 opportunities with business case description + declared assumptions. EDGE CASES: (a) fully manual process without systems → recommend prior digitization as a prerequisite; (b) activities with frequent exceptions → classify as assisted automation or AI rather than classic RPA; (c) regulated process → add auditability and traceability criterion. [C · CRITERIA] Each opportunity has at least 3 eligibility criteria evaluated; priority reflects the benefit/complexity ratio; automation type is justified; DoD: top-5 with business case sufficient for a preliminary investment decision. Protocolo MetodologIA: eligibility criteria applied systematically, [ASSUMPTION] on estimated volumes, top-5 justified with business impact.
spec-consulting_analisis_de_capacidad_de: [S · SITUATION] An operations team needs to determine whether a process has sufficient capacity to meet current and projected demand, identify where capacity bottlenecks arise and what actions to take to align supply and demand before the system collapses or fails service levels. [P · REQUEST] Perform the capacity analysis of the indicated process: calculate theoretical and effective capacity per stage, compare with demand, identify constraints and bottlenecks, and propose an action plan to close capacity gaps with priority and estimated effort. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior capacity and operations analyst with experience in Theory of Constraints (TOC), capacity planning and line balancing. ASSUMPTIONS: effective capacity is 85% of theoretical capacity if no OEE or real efficiency is indicated; if demand data is not provided, estimate it as 20% annual growth over current volume [ASSUMPTION]; the analysis covers a 12-month horizon if not specified; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: description of process stages with cycle times or capacity per hour + current or projected demand data + number of resources (people, machines) per stage. STEPS: 1) Calculate the theoretical capacity of each stage (units/hour or units/day) (output: theoretical capacity table). 2) Apply efficiency factor to obtain effective capacity (output: effective capacity table). 3) Compare effective capacity with current and projected demand (output: capacity gap table). 4) Identify the main bottleneck and secondary constraints (output: TOC diagnosis). 5) Propose actions to close the gaps: optimization, resource addition, outsourcing, automation (output: action table with effort and priority). 6) Model the impact of proposed actions on effective capacity (output: projected post-improvement capacity). OUTPUT: Capacity report with: (a) theoretical and effective capacity table per stage, (b) gap vs. current and projected demand table, (c) constraint diagnosis, (d) action plan with priority and effort, (e) projected post-improvement capacity. EDGE CASES: (a) no cycle time data → perform qualitative constraint analysis with [ASSUMPTION] on all metrics; (b) multiple product lines → analyze the highest-volume one and indicate that the others require separate analysis; (c) external constraint (supplier) → include it in the analysis and treat it as a bottleneck. [C · CRITERIA] Capacity calculations are verifiable; the bottleneck has numerical evidence; proposed actions have quantified capacity impact; DoD: capacity gap closed 100% in the proposed improvements scenario or residual gap explained. Protocolo MetodologIA: show all calculations, [ASSUMPTION] on estimated metrics, connect each action to the constraint it eliminates.
spec-consulting_diseno_de_indicadores_de: [S · SITUATION] A process has been documented or redesigned, but it has no formal performance indicators to measure whether it is operating correctly, detect deviations in time and make data-driven improvement decisions. The management team needs an operational indicator dashboard for the process. [P · REQUEST] Design the process indicator set for the indicated process: define between 5 and 10 KPIs/KQIs with a complete technical data sheet (name, formula, target, measurement frequency, data source, owner, alert traffic light) aligned to the dimensions of efficiency, quality, speed and customer satisfaction. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Performance management consultant with experience designing measurement systems for operational processes and scorecards. ASSUMPTIONS: indicators cover the dimensions of efficiency, quality, speed and CX unless otherwise specified; the target is expressed as a numerical value with green/yellow/red threshold; if there is no historical data, the target is estimated with [ASSUMPTION] using sector benchmarks; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: process description, business objectives related to the process, and available data sources if known. STEPS: 1) Identify the critical dimensions of the process to measure (output: dimension map: efficiency, quality, speed, CX). 2) Generate 5-10 candidate indicators with descriptive names in the format "% of / Time of / Number of" (output: list of candidate KPIs). 3) Develop the technical data sheet for each indicator (output: table with name, formula, target, frequency, source, owner). 4) Define the alert traffic light for each indicator (green/yellow/red with numerical thresholds) (output: traffic light column). 5) Validate that the set covers the 4 dimensions and that the indicators are balanced (minimal side effect) (output: coverage map). 6) Recommend the review frequency and the minimum viable dashboard (output: measurement governance section). OUTPUT: Indicator data sheet with a table of 5-10 KPIs (Name, Formula, Unit, Target, Frequency, Source, Owner, Traffic light) + dimensional coverage map + measurement governance recommendation + declared assumptions. EDGE CASES: (a) process without defined data sources → design indicators and indicate "pending instrumentation" in the source column; (b) internal support process without external customer → replace CX with internal customer satisfaction; (c) more than 15 candidate indicators → apply Pareto criterion and select the 5-10 with greatest impact on business objectives. [C · CRITERIA] Every indicator has a verifiable formula and an identified data source; the set covers at least 3 of the 4 dimensions; traffic lights have numerical thresholds; DoD: dimensional coverage review and absence of duplicate indicators or indicators with negative side effects. Protocolo MetodologIA: verifiable formulas, targets with [ASSUMPTION] if no historical data, balanced dimensional coverage.
spec-consulting_swimlane_de_handoffs_ent: [S · SITUATION] An organizational process involves multiple areas or teams that pass work between them. The transfer points (handoffs) are a source of errors, delays and information loss because they are not formally documented nor do they have clear acceptance criteria. An improvement team needs to visualize and analyze all handoffs to detect the most problematic ones. [P · REQUEST] Build the swimlane diagram of the indicated process in structured textual format, representing each area in its lane, the handoffs between them with the transferred artifacts and acceptance criteria, and identify the riskiest handoffs with mitigation recommendations. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Process and organizational design consultant with experience in cross-functional workflow mapping and inter-area interface analysis. ASSUMPTIONS: each lane corresponds to an area or team, not a person; handoffs are identified when a task moves from one lane to another; if acceptance criteria are not specified, they will be inferred with [ASSUMPTION]; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: process description mentioning the actors or areas involved + sequence of activities if available. STEPS: 1) Identify the lanes (areas/teams) and arrange them logically in the diagram (output: list of lanes). 2) Map the activities in their corresponding lane (output: activity table per lane). 3) Identify all handoffs (moments when responsibility passes from one lane to another) (output: list of handoffs with origin-destination). 4) Describe the artifact or deliverable transferred in each handoff and its acceptance criteria (output: handoff data sheet). 5) Evaluate the risk of each handoff (risk of information loss, delay, rejection) with H/M/L level (output: risk table per handoff). 6) Propose improvement mechanisms for High-risk handoffs (checklist, SLA, digital confirmation, etc.) (output: prioritized recommendations). OUTPUT: Structured swimlane description with: (a) list of lanes, (b) activity table per lane, (c) handoff data sheet with artifact and acceptance criteria, (d) risk table per handoff, (e) recommendations for High-risk handoffs. EDGE CASES: (a) process with a single area → swimlane does not apply, recommend a simple process map; (b) handoff with multiple recipients → model as a broadcast handoff and flag as coordination risk; (c) handoff with unknown acceptance criteria → mark with [ASSUMPTION] and include in recommendations to formally define them. [C · CRITERIA] Every handoff has an identified artifact and at least one acceptance criterion; High-risk handoffs have a mitigation recommendation; the flow is coherent from start to finish; DoD: flow continuity review with no orphan activities and no handoffs without an identified receiving owner. Protocolo MetodologIA: handoffs as primary analysis points, explicit acceptance criteria, risks prioritized by impact on the end customer.
spec-consulting_quick_wins_operativos: [S · SITUATION] A team or organizational area needs to show tangible improvement results in the short term (less than 90 days) to build trust and momentum in a transformation project, without waiting for long-term initiatives to mature. Leadership wants to know what immediate actions can generate visible impact with low implementation effort. [P · REQUEST] Identify, evaluate and prioritize operational quick wins for the indicated process or area: improvement actions implementable in less than 90 days, without major technology investment, with tangible and measurable impact on efficiency, quality or user experience, delivering a concrete action plan for the top-5. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Continuous improvement and change management consultant with experience identifying short-term opportunities and managing momentum in transformation projects. ASSUMPTIONS: "without major investment" means without capital budget approval or changes to core systems; impact is estimated qualitatively if there is no data; implementable quick win = assignable to an owner this week; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: description of the process, area or problem + list of recurring complaints, frequent errors or already-identified wastes if they exist. STEPS: 1) Collect or infer the main problems and frustrations of the current process (output: list of pain points). 2) Generate a broad list of possible improvement actions without filtering (output: long list of improvements). 3) Filter by quick-win criteria: visible impact < 90 days + no major investment + assignable this week (output: short list of candidates). 4) Score each candidate on impact (1-5) and effort (1-5) and calculate the impact/effort index (output: prioritization matrix). 5) Select the top-5 with the highest index and develop the action plan for each (owner, deadline, success metric, done criterion) (output: quick-win data sheets). 6) Estimate the aggregate impact of the top-5 if implemented in parallel (output: expected impact summary). OUTPUT: Prioritized quick-win matrix (Action, Impact, Effort, Index, Priority) + top-5 action plan data sheets (What, Who, When, Success metric, Done criterion) + expected aggregate impact summary. EDGE CASES: (a) all problems require major investment → identify process or behavioral actions without investment and flag the limitation; (b) team with no immediate implementation capacity → adjust the horizon to 90-120 days and note it; (c) quick win with negative impact on another process → flag the side-effect risk and recommend prior validation.
