[C · CRITERIA] Each top-5 quick win has an assigned owner, deadline and measurable success metric; none requires major budget approval; impact is observable within 90 days; DoD: complete action data sheets reviewed against the validated quick-win criterion. Protocolo MetodologIA: quick-win criterion applied rigorously, impact/effort quantified, concrete action plan with owner and metric.
spec-consulting_propuesta_tecnica_comerc: [S · SITUATION] A technology consulting firm needs to deliver a complete technical-commercial proposal to the client to support a professional services sale, covering the identified business problem, solution scope, proposed team and commercial terms. [P · REQUEST] Draft a technical-commercial services proposal ready to send to the client, with all its standard sections completed, in structured format and professional consultative tone. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior presales consultant with 15 years of experience developing winning proposals in enterprise technology. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not provide the client's name, industry or specific scope, assume a mid-sized company in the financial sector with a digital transformation need and proceed declaring the assumptions; ask only if the absence of a data point makes the document unviable. INPUTS: discovery meeting notes, RFP, or client brief pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Read the inputs and identify the client's core problem and declared evaluation criteria. 2. Draft executive summary (problem, proposed solution, expected value). 3. Develop business understanding and challenge section. 4. Describe the technical solution scope (phases, deliverables, explicit exclusions). 5. Present the methodological approach and key tools. 6. Detail the proposed team with roles and allocations in FTE-months [ASSUMPTION if not specified]. 7. Include high-level timeline (milestones by phase). 8. Add credentials and analogous case studies section. 9. Establish commercial conditions (contracting model, payment terms, validity). 10. Draft proposed next steps. OUTPUT: Word-ready document with titled sections, executive paragraphs, role/timeline tables and footer with validity. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client already has an incumbent provider, add an explicit differentiation section; (b) If the scope is too broad for a single proposal, segment into phases with entry options; (c) If there is no client budget information, omit figures and leave space for negotiation. [C · CRITERIA] The proposal must address all sections of the RFP or brief, use the client's language, not include unit prices (only FTE-months with a note that rates are to be negotiated), and an independent reviewer must be able to understand the value without additional context. Protocolo MetodologIA: structure the proposal in layers — business → solution → team → commercial — and validate coherence between each layer before closing.
spec-consulting_statement_of_work_sow: [S · SITUATION] A consulting engagement is about to begin and the presales team needs to formalize the scope, deliverables, responsibilities and acceptance conditions in a Statement of Work (SOW) that is binding and clear to both parties. [P · REQUEST] Draft a complete project SOW ready for legal review and signature, with all standard sections covered and unambiguous language. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Solutions architect and technical contract drafter with experience at world-class consulting firms. ASSUMPTIONS: if no specific dates are provided, assume start four weeks after signature and relative durations; if no pricing model is specified, use time & material with FTE-month cap; declare both assumptions at the start. INPUTS: approved technical-commercial proposal or client letter of intent pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Extract from the inputs the agreements already reached (scope, parties, payment model). 2. Draft background and purpose section of the SOW. 3. Define detailed work scope (in-scope) with a numbered list of activities. 4. List explicit exclusions (out-of-scope). 5. Describe deliverables with name, brief description and acceptance criterion for each. 6. Establish roles and responsibilities of both parties (simplified RACI). 7. Define milestone timeline with relative dates. 8. Specify the change-of-scope process (change request process). 9. Include acceptance, billing and payment milestone clauses. 10. Add critical assumptions and dependencies. OUTPUT: SOW document with section numbering, deliverable/RACI/milestone tables, ready for signature insertion. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client demands deliverables not agreed upon, refer to the change request process defined in the SOW; (b) If there are multiple parallel contracts, identify the interfaces and dependencies between them; (c) If the scope has third-party components, clarify who manages those licenses or services. [C · CRITERIA] Every deliverable must have an observable acceptance criterion; out-of-scope must be specific enough to prevent disputes; the document must be interpretable without additional verbal context. Protocolo MetodologIA: each deliverable must have a unique name, description, primary owner and measurable acceptance criterion.
spec-consulting_enfoque_metodologico_de_: [S · SITUATION] A technology consulting proposal requires a methodological approach section that explains to the client how the work will be carried out: which reference framework guides the project, how work is organized by phases, what artifacts are produced and how quality is assured. This section is key to building trust and differentiating the firm. [P · REQUEST] Draft the complete methodological approach section, ready to insert in a proposal, describing the framework, engagement phases, key artifacts and quality control mechanisms. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Principal Consultant specializing in delivery methodology design for digital transformation projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if the project type is not specified, assume a diagnosis and roadmap engagement; if the client's preferred framework is not mentioned, use a hybrid agile-structured approach and declare it. INPUTS: description of the project type or scope section of the proposal pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the engagement type and the client's methodological constraints. 2. Select or design the appropriate methodological framework (agile, waterfall, hybrid, design thinking, etc.). 3. Describe the project phases with their objective, relative duration and key deliverables. 4. Explain the decision-making and escalation process. 5. Detail the management artifacts (minutes, dashboards, progress reports). 6. Describe the deliverable review and acceptance process. 7. Include an integrated risk and change management mechanism. 8. Add a process flow diagram (structured text description if no graphical support is available). OUTPUT: Proposal section of 400-600 words with subtitles, phase description in table format, artifact list and methodological differentiation paragraph. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client imposes their own methodology, adapt the approach to that framework and note the complementary additions; (b) If the engagement is purely advisory with no software deliverables, adapt the artifacts to the context; (c) If multiple client teams are involved, include how inter-team coordination is managed. [C · CRITERIA] The reader must understand in 5 minutes how the work will be carried out, what they will receive and when; phases must have observable objectives; methodological differentiation must be concrete, not generic. Protocolo MetodologIA: explicitly connect each phase to an expected business outcome for the client, not just a technical deliverable.
spec-consulting_estimacion_de_esfuerzo_e: [S · SITUATION] A presales team needs to build the effort estimation for a consulting project in FTE-months to include in the proposal or SOW, broken down by role and phase, with the appropriate level of certainty and documented estimation assumptions. [P · REQUEST] Prepare an FTE-month effort estimation table broken down by role, phase and total, with explicit estimation assumptions and confidence notes per line item. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior delivery manager with expertise in parametric and analogical estimation for technology and consulting projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if no detailed scope is provided, work with the macro scope provided and estimate ranges (pessimistic/expected/optimistic); if no available profiles are indicated, use standard consulting profiles (Analyst, Consultant, Senior Consultant, Manager, Director); declare both at the start. INPUTS: project scope, phases and deliverables description pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify project phases and main activities per phase. 2. List the required roles and their expected participation per phase. 3. Estimate effort in FTE-months per role and phase using analogy or expert judgment; mark with [ASSUMPTION] where applicable. 4. Calculate totals by role and by phase. 5. Document estimation assumptions (hours/day, days/month, dedication percentage). 6. Include uncertainty ranges (+/- %) per line item with confidence level. 7. Add project management, QA and change management line items if not already in scope. 8. Present executive summary of total effort. OUTPUT: Estimation table with columns Role / Phase 1 / Phase 2 / ... / Total FTE-months, plus assumptions section and confidence notes. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client asks for a price, respond that FTE-month effort is the basis and the rate is negotiated separately; (b) If scope changes, the estimation must be revised through a change request; (c) If there are third-party components (licenses, cloud), exclude them from the FTE estimation and note them as separate costs. [C · CRITERIA] The table must be self-explanatory; estimation assumptions must be explicit; the FTE-month total must match the sum of the cells; every line item with high uncertainty (>30%) must be flagged. Protocolo MetodologIA: document the estimation method used (analogy, parametric, expert judgment) and the global confidence level before presenting the table.
spec-consulting_caso_de_credenciales_y_e: [S · SITUATION] A consulting proposal needs to include a credentials and relevant experience section that demonstrates the firm has solved problems similar to the client's, increasing credibility and reducing perceived risk in the purchase of professional services. [P · REQUEST] Draft one or several credentials and relevant experience cases (summarized case studies) ready to include in the credentials section of the proposal, with the appropriate format and a clear differentiating message. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Business development consultant with experience in proposal storytelling and positioning of consulting firms. ASSUMPTIONS: if no real cases are provided, build cases with full structure leaving specific placeholders [CLIENT], [INDUSTRY], [QUANTITATIVE RESULT]; if a partial real case exists, complete it with [ASSUMPTION] on each inferred data point. INPUTS: description of the current client challenge and, if available, notes from relevant previous projects, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the relevance dimensions of the current challenge (industry, problem type, technology, scale). 2. Select or build 2-3 cases that cover those dimensions. 3. For each case, structure: client context (industry, size, no name if confidential), the challenge they faced, the firm's approach, results achieved (quantitative whenever possible) and an explicit connection to the current client's challenge. 4. Draft each case in 150-200 words in concise narrative format. 5. Add credentials summary table (case, industry, key technology, highlighted result). OUTPUT: 2-3 credentials cases in narrative format with summary table, ready to insert in proposal. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client is in the same sector as a confidential case, mention industry and scale without a name; (b) If there is no direct industry experience, emphasize the transferability of the approach; (c) If the result cannot be quantified, use process metrics (time reduced, cycles eliminated). [C · CRITERIA] Each case must have at least one quantitative or quantifiable result; the connection to the current challenge must be explicit; the reader must perceive that the firm has already solved something similar before. Protocolo MetodologIA: close each case with a direct connection line to the current client's challenge so that relevance is unambiguous.
spec-consulting_propuesta_de_valor_difer: [S · SITUATION] In a competitive provider selection process for consulting services, the firm needs to clearly articulate why it is the best option: what differentiates it from competitors, what specific value it delivers to the client and why that value is relevant to the organization's current moment and context. [P · REQUEST] Draft the differentiated value proposition section, ready to include in the proposal or use in the pitch, that articulates the firm's concrete differentiators versus generic alternatives and connects them to client value. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Positioning strategist with experience in B2B consultative sales of professional technology services. ASSUMPTIONS: if competitors are not specified, assume global technology consultancies are competing; if the firm's strengths are not described, build differentiators typical of specialized firms (speed, sector specialization, knowledge transfer, client proximity) and mark with [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: description of the firm's strengths, client profile and competitive context pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the client's decision priorities (speed, risk, cost, innovation, etc.). 2. List the firm's real differentiators versus alternatives. 3. Connect each differentiator to a specific client priority. 4. Draft the core value message in 2-3 sentences. 5. Develop 3-5 differentiators in brief narrative format with evidence or example for each. 6. Include implicit comparison table (without naming competitors) with key dimensions. 7. Close with the value promise of the specific engagement. OUTPUT: 300-500 word section with core message, developed differentiators and implicit comparison table. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client already works with an incumbent competitor, emphasize complementarity or improvement differentiators over the current state; (b) If differentiators are similar to those of the competition, deepen the specificity of the evidence; (c) If the process is very price-sensitive, reframe the differentiator toward risk-of-failure reduction and total project cost. [C · CRITERIA] The core message must be memorable and specific; each differentiator must have concrete evidence, not generic claims; the reader must be able to explain in one phrase why this firm and not another. Protocolo MetodologIA: formulate the core message as a value equation — what problem it solves + for whom + with what concrete differential advantage — in a single sentence.
spec-consulting_respuesta_a_rfp: [S · SITUATION] A client organization has issued a formal Request for Proposal (RFP) with requirements, evaluation criteria and expected response format. The consulting firm must respond in a structured manner, ensuring that every RFP requirement is covered, the response is evaluable and it maximizes the score on the declared criteria. [P · REQUEST] Prepare a structured response to the provided RFP, covering each section and evaluation criterion, with the tone, format and level of detail required by the evaluating client. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Proposals Director (Bid Manager) with experience responding to government and private sector technology RFPs. ASSUMPTIONS: if the RFP does not specify a page limit, use 20-30 equivalent pages; if there are no explicit evaluation criteria, infer them from the RFP's language and declare the inferred ones with [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: full RFP text or its most relevant sections pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Read the full RFP and identify: required sections, evaluation criteria with weightings if any, format restrictions and necessary clarifying questions. 2. Build compliance map: RFP requirement → response section. 3. Draft executive cover letter. 4. Respond to each RFP section in the requested order, using the RFP's headings. 5. Ensure each evaluation criterion has explicit evidence in the response. 6. Include requirements compliance table (requirement, response section, status: complies/partially complies/not applicable). 7. Review consistency and coherence between sections. OUTPUT: RFP response with mirror structure of the RFP, compliance table and cover letter. EDGE CASES: (a) If a requirement cannot be met, state it explicitly with an alternative plan; (b) If the RFP has very specific technical questions without an available answer, note the assumption and commit to elaborating during negotiation; (c) If there is a contradiction between RFP sections, request formal clarification before responding to that section. [C · CRITERIA] The compliance table must have 100% of requirements mapped; no RFP section must be left unanswered; the evaluator must be able to assign a score without inferring information not provided. Protocolo MetodologIA: build the compliance map as a skeleton first before drafting any narrative section.
spec-consulting_modelo_de_gobierno_del_e: [S · SITUATION] A medium- or large-scale consulting project requires a clear governance model that defines how decisions will be made, how problems will be escalated, who participates at each governance level and what the review rhythms are to keep the engagement on track with alignment between the parties. [P · REQUEST] Design and document the engagement governance model, with the committee structure, roles, meeting frequencies, escalation mechanisms and decision flow, ready to include in the SOW or project plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Program Manager with experience in governance structure design for medium- and large-scale technology consulting engagements. ASSUMPTIONS: if the project scale is not specified, assume a 3-12 month engagement with 5-15 people from both parties; if the client's stakeholders are not indicated, define three levels: executive sponsor, client project manager, operational team; declare both. INPUTS: project description, involved parties and available organizational structure of the client, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the necessary governance levels (strategic, tactical, operational). 2. Define the committees or instances per level with name, purpose, participants and frequency. 3. Establish the decisions that belong to each level. 4. Design the escalation mechanism: how an issue moves from operational to tactical to strategic. 5. Define the governance artifacts (standard agenda, minutes, status dashboard, decision log). 6. Establish the alert criteria for activating escalation. 7. Include a governance flow diagram (structured description if no graphical support is available). OUTPUT: Governance model document with instance table, escalation flow, artifacts and alert criteria, ready to insert in SOW or project plan. EDGE CASES: (a) If the client has a rigid corporate governance structure, adapt the model to that structure without duplicating instances; (b) If the engagement is small, simplify to two levels and a single weekly review meeting; (c) If there are multiple providers, include how governance is coordinated among them. [C · CRITERIA] Every decision must have a single governing-level owner; escalation must have clear (unambiguous) criteria; the model must be operational from day one of the project. Protocolo MetodologIA: each governance instance must have a standard agenda of no more than 5 items and an explicit decision rule to avoid paralysis.
spec-consulting_pitch_de_apertura_de_opo: [S · SITUATION] A consultant or account executive is about to have the first formal meeting with a prospect or an existing client to open a new business opportunity. They need a 5-10 minute opening pitch that generates interest, demonstrates understanding of the client's context and opens a productive discovery conversation. [P · REQUEST] Draft the opportunity opening pitch script with narrative structure, key talking points, discovery questions to activate the prospect and the closing call to action for the meeting. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Consultative sales director with experience opening technology service opportunities in B2B markets. ASSUMPTIONS: if the prospect's industry is not specified, assume a mid-sized company in the services sector; if the interlocutor's role is not provided, assume a CIO or IT Director; declare both. INPUTS: prospect profile, industry context and, if available, any prior research on the company, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Define the meeting objective (what must happen by the end?). 2. Build the opening hook: a relevant insight about the industry or the prospect's context. 3. Draft the credibility bridge: who we are, why we are relevant to this interlocutor (30 seconds). 4. Present the industry challenge the firm helps solve (no selling yet). 5. Propose 3-5 discovery questions that activate the interlocutor and reveal their priority. 6. Describe the proposed next step with date and format. 7. Draft the opening variant for when the pitch time is less than 3 minutes. OUTPUT: Pitch script with labeled sections (hook, credibility, challenge, questions, next step), estimated time per section and short variant. EDGE CASES: (a) If the prospect is skeptical from the start, have an acknowledgment + pivot to discovery questions ready; (b) If the interlocutor wants to go directly to price, reframe toward the value conversation before discussing cost; (c) If there is little time, use the short opening variant directly. [C · CRITERIA] The hook must be relevant to the interlocutor, not generic; the discovery questions must be open-ended and reveal priorities; the next step must be specific (date + format). Protocolo MetodologIA: the hook must be an insight based on the prospect's industry, not a presentation of the firm — the client first, the firm second.
spec-consulting_plan_de_cuenta_y_expansi: [S · SITUATION] A consulting firm has an active or recent client and wants to build an account expansion strategy: identify additional business opportunities, strengthen relationships with new stakeholders and plan concrete actions to grow client value over time. [P · REQUEST] Prepare an account and expansion plan for the indicated client, with a stakeholder map, expansion opportunity analysis, priority actions and tracking metrics, ready to use in quarterly account management. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Account Manager with experience in relationship management and technology consulting account expansion in enterprise markets. ASSUMPTIONS: if no active or past projects are provided, assume an engagement completed in the IT area with high client satisfaction; if the client's organization is unknown, build a typical stakeholder map (CIO, CFO, affected business units) and mark it with [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: history of the relationship with the client, projects completed, known contacts and strategic client context pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Summarize the current state of the relationship (depth, breadth, health). 2. Build the stakeholder map with relationship level and influence level for each. 3. Identify areas of the client organization without a current relationship (expansion white spaces). 4. Identify 3-5 expansion opportunities based on the client's strategic context. 5. Prioritize opportunities by attractiveness and probability of success. 6. Define the quarterly action plan: relationship activities + sales activities per opportunity. 7. Establish tracking metrics (Net Revenue Retention, new stakeholders reached, pipeline generated). OUTPUT: Account plan with stakeholder map, prioritized opportunity table, quarterly action plan and tracking metrics. EDGE CASES: (a) If the current relationship is strained due to delivery issues, prioritize recovery actions before expansion; (b) If the client has formal RFP processes for new projects, plan pre-positioning before the process opens; (c) If a competitor is active in the account, include a displacement or coexistence strategy. [C · CRITERIA] The action plan must have concrete actions with an owner and date; opportunities must be prioritized with explicit criteria; the stakeholder map must distinguish between contact relationships and influence relationships. Protocolo MetodologIA: classify each opportunity with the attractiveness × probability matrix and only develop the action plan for those that fall in the high-high quadrant.
spec-consulting_diseno_de_workshop_de_co: [S · SITUATION] A consulting team needs to design a co-creation workshop with the client to address a strategic or solution-design challenge collaboratively, generating alignment, ownership, and concrete results in a half-day or full-day working session. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete co-creation workshop: objective, participants, block agenda with facilitated activities, required materials, and a mechanism to consolidate results at the end of the session. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Facilitator and organizational learning experience designer with expertise in Design Thinking, Liberating Structures, and corporate workshop facilitation. ASSUMPTIONS: if duration is not specified, design for half a day (4 hours); if number of participants is not indicated, assume 8-12 mixed people (client + consultants); declare both. INPUTS: description of the challenge to address in the workshop, participant profile, and time and format constraints, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Define the SMART objective of the workshop: what decision or artifact must exist at the end. 2. Design the session energy curve (opening, divergence, convergence, closing). 3. Select appropriate facilitation dynamics for each moment (brainwriting, dot voting, journey mapping, prioritization, etc.). 4. Detail each agenda block with: name, duration, objective, activity, facilitator role, and materials. 5. Design the results-capture mechanism (templates, digital or physical, responsible party). 6. Define the workshop deliverable (decision, prototype, prioritized backlog, roadmap, etc.). 7. Include a contingency plan for a dynamic that does not work. OUTPUT: Complete workshop design with detailed block agenda, facilitator guide per activity, and list of required materials. EDGE CASES: (a) If the group has prior conflicts, prioritize dynamics that neutralize hierarchy (e.g. 1-2-4-All from Liberating Structures); (b) If time is reduced at the last minute, have a 2-hour version with the critical blocks; (c) If there are remote participants, adapt dynamics to hybrid format. [C · CRITERIA] The workshop must end with a concrete artifact (not just insights); each block must have an observable objective; the energy curve must include movement or break moments every 60-90 minutes. Protocolo MetodologIA: the design must follow the diverge-converge curve and each dynamic must be justified by the type of result it produces.
spec-consulting_agenda_de_sesion_de_alin: [S · SITUATION] A consulting team and its client need to hold a strategic alignment session to synchronize expectations, priorities, and pending decisions at a key engagement moment (kick-off, phase close, milestone review, or inflection point). The session must be productive, generate concrete decisions, and leave all participants aligned on next steps. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete agenda for the strategic alignment session, with objectives per item, timings, block owners, and a facilitation dynamic for moments requiring convergence on decisions. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior delivery consultant with experience facilitating executive alignment sessions in technology consulting projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if duration is not specified, design for 2 hours; if the engagement moment is not indicated, assume kick-off of a new phase; declare both. INPUTS: description of the engagement moment, pending decision or alignment topics, attendee profile, and time constraints, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the main purpose of the session and the minimum expected result. 2. List topics to cover ordered by priority (decisions first, informational last). 3. Assign time to each topic with a discussion buffer. 4. Define the responsible party to present or facilitate each block. 5. Identify decision points in the agenda and design a convergence mini-dynamic for each (vote, consent decision, options table). 6. Design the opening (context + session objective in 3 minutes) and closing (agreements + actions + next session date). 7. Include preparation materials attendees must review before the session. OUTPUT: Session agenda with Hour / Block / Objective / Responsible / Dynamic table, plus pre-reads and closing agreements template. EDGE CASES: (a) If there are conflicting topics that may dominate the agenda, establish a maximum time rule per topic before the session; (b) If some attendees are remote, adapt convergence dynamics to hybrid format; (c) If the session runs longer than planned, have the trimmed version with only critical decision points ready. [C · CRITERIA] The agenda must have more time for decisions than presentations; each item must have an observable result; the closing must produce a list of agreements with owner and date. Protocolo MetodologIA: include an explicit parking lot at the start of the agenda to capture topics that arise outside the session scope and do not hijack the time.
spec-consulting_dinamica_de_priorizacion: [S · SITUATION] A consulting or facilitation team is running a workshop with multiple options, ideas, or initiatives under discussion and needs participants to reach a visual, democratic consensus on what to prioritize using the dot voting technique. [P · REQUEST] Design and execute a complete dot voting dynamic: clear rules, point distribution per participant, options board, vote count, and ordered priority table with a recommendation for next steps. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior facilitator with experience in collaborative prioritization workshops and group decision-making. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the list of options or initiatives to prioritize; if the number of participants is not specified, assume 8; each participant receives 5 distributable points; up to 3 points may be accumulated on a single option; if confidence in any parameter is below 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: list of options/initiatives pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Review and normalize the list of options (remove duplicates, clarify ambiguous statements). 2. Define the dynamic rules (points per person, per-option limit, voting duration). 3. Build the voting board in table format with option column and accumulated points column. 4. Simulate or record the vote (if real votes are provided, tabulate them; if not, generate an illustrative example marked as [ASSUMPTION]). 5. Order results from highest to lowest score. 6. Identify natural cutoffs (clusters) between high, medium, and low priority options. 7. Draft a next-step recommendation for the top-3. OUTPUT: options table with descending scores + classification into three bands (high/medium/low priority) + immediate-action recommendation paragraph. EDGE CASES: (a) tie in score between critical options → apply tiebreaker via documented show-of-hands vote; (b) list of more than 20 options → group into categories before voting to reduce cognitive fatigue; (c) absent participant → redistribute their points proportionally or leave blank with a note. [C · CRITERIA] The table must faithfully reflect the recorded votes; priority bands must have an explicit numerical criterion (e.g. top 30% = high); the recommendation must include a concrete action verb and a suggested owner. DoD: complete table, three bands defined, recommendation drafted. Trade-off: speed of consensus vs. depth of deliberation — in short sessions prioritize rule clarity over extended debate. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that each option in the list has an assigned score and that the total sum of points is consistent with participants × individual points before delivering.
spec-consulting_facilitacion_de_design_t: [S · SITUATION] A consultant or facilitator must guide a multidisciplinary team through a design thinking session aimed at solving a specific business or user experience problem, covering the five classic stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete facilitation guide for the session: timed agenda, instructions per stage, trigger questions, specific activities, and output artifacts per phase. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior certified design thinking facilitator with experience in corporate contexts and teams of 6 to 15 people. ASSUMPTIONS: default duration is a full-day workshop (8 effective hours); the design challenge is defined in the pasted input; the team is mixed (business + technology + user) unless otherwise indicated; if any parameter is not specified, declare assumption and continue without asking. INPUTS: design challenge description pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Frame the central challenge in a single HMW (How Might We) sentence. 2. Design the detailed agenda with time blocks per stage. 3. For each stage write: block objective, main activity (with technique name), step-by-step facilitator instructions, trigger questions (minimum 3 per stage), and expected output artifact. 4. Include energy moments (breaks, brief dynamics) in the agenda. 5. Add a section on required materials and space setup. 6. Close with a synthesis and commitments protocol. OUTPUT: Structured facilitation document with agenda, per-stage guide, trigger questions, expected artifacts, and materials list. EDGE CASES: (a) virtual/remote session → replace physical activities with digital equivalents (Miro, Jamboard) with specific instructions; (b) poorly defined challenge → dedicate 20 additional minutes to the empathize stage to delimit the problem; (c) team resistant to the methodology → start with an icebreaker that demonstrates the value of the user perspective. [C · CRITERIA] Each stage must have a measurable objective, a named activity, and a concrete artifact; the agenda must sum to exactly the indicated total duration; trigger questions must be open and non-leading. DoD: complete guide, five stages covered, artifacts defined. Trade-off: depth of empathy vs. available time — in short workshops compress empathize and define into an integrated block. Protocolo MetodologIA: confirm that the sum of agenda times matches the total workshop duration before delivering.
spec-consulting_taller_de_construccion_d: [S · SITUATION] A management or leadership team of an organization needs to build or renew its vision statement through a facilitated workshop, ensuring alignment, collective ownership, and an aspirational, realistic, and motivating formulation. [P · REQUEST] Design and facilitate the complete vision-building workshop: starting-point diagnosis, exploration activities, collective synthesis, iterative drafting of the vision statement, and validation plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior strategic consultant with experience facilitating organizational identity and strategic planning workshops. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains available organizational context (sector, size, current situation); default duration is 4 hours; the group is 8 to 12 leaders; if no organizational context is available, declare assumption about the type of organization and continue. INPUTS: organizational context pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Analyze the organizational context and identify key strategic tensions. 2. Design the workshop agenda with blocks: framing, exploration of desired future, core values identification, collaborative drafting, validation, and agreements. 3. For each block: objective, facilitation technique, time, and output artifact. 4. Provide a vision statement template with criteria (aspirational, time-bound, brief, memorable, inclusive). 5. Include an evaluation rubric for the statement (5 criteria on a 1-3 scale). 6. Draft a vision statement based on available context (mark as [ASSUMPTION] if context is incomplete). 7. Propose a 3-step validation plan with key stakeholders. OUTPUT: workshop agenda with block instructions + statement template + evaluation rubric + vision draft + validation plan. EDGE CASES: (a) group with very divergent positions → introduce a "10-year ideal future" activity before drafting to align expectations; (b) organization in crisis → focus the vision on stabilization before aspiration; (c) remote workshop → use a collaborative digital whiteboard with real-time voting. [C · CRITERIA] The final vision statement must be between 15 and 30 words; it must score above 4/5 on the rubric; the validation plan must include at least two stakeholder groups. DoD: workshop designed, vision draft written, rubric applied, validation plan defined. Trade-off: aspiration vs. feasibility — prefer ambitious visions anchored in current capabilities. Protocolo MetodologIA: evaluate the vision draft with the provided rubric and report the score before delivering.
spec-consulting_sesion_de_brainstorming_: [S · SITUATION] A facilitator or consultant needs to run a brainstorming session that goes beyond the chaos of free ideas and social inhibition, using a methodological structure that maximizes the quantity and quality of ideas generated, fosters equitable participation, and facilitates convergence toward actionable options. [P · REQUEST] Design and facilitate a complete structured brainstorming session: operating rules, selected technique, facilitation script, organized idea capture, and synthesis with categorization and top ideas. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior facilitator in creativity and innovation with mastery of techniques such as brainwriting 635, SCAMPER, De Bono's 6 Thinking Hats, and round-robin. ASSUMPTIONS: the challenge or focus question is in the pasted input; if no technique is specified, use brainwriting 635 by default (reduces social inhibition and generates more ideas in less time); default duration 90 minutes; group of 6 people; if any parameter is missing, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: focus question or challenge pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Reformulate the focus question in a clear, neutral trigger format. 2. Select and justify the most appropriate brainstorming technique. 3. Write the session operating rules (quantity over quality, no judgments, build on others' ideas, time-limited). 4. Design the facilitation script by moments: framing, generation, sharing, grouping, voting. 5. Create an idea-capture template (table with columns: idea, author, category). 6. Define the categorization criterion (by topic, feasibility, impact). 7. Select the top-5 ideas based on explicit criteria or a vote simulation. 8. Write an executive synthesis with the 5 winning ideas and a proposed next step per idea. OUTPUT: facilitation script + operating rules + capture template + synthesis with top-5 ideas and next steps. EDGE CASES: (a) very hierarchical participants → use silent brainwriting to equalize voices; (b) overly broad challenge → dedicate 15 initial minutes to delimiting scope with "what is in/out?"; (c) repetitive ideas → activate a random provocation technique (random object + how does it inspire us?). [C · CRITERIA] The session must produce a minimum of 30 captured ideas; categorization must have between 3 and 5 groups; the top-5 ideas must have an explicit justification of the selection criterion. DoD: complete script, top-5 ideas justified, next steps defined. Trade-off: quantity of ideas vs. synthesis time — in short sessions prioritize generation speed and agile synthesis. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that the reformulated focus question is open, neutral, and does not suggest the answer before continuing.
spec-consulting_dinamica_de_priorizacion: [S · SITUATION] A project, product, or consulting team faces a list of requirements, features, or initiatives that exceed the available budget or time, and needs to prioritize with a shared criterion using the MoSCoW technique (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time). [P · REQUEST] Facilitate the complete classification of all list items into the four MoSCoW categories, with explicit classification criteria, an ordered result table, load analysis per category, and scope recommendations for the sprint or deliverable in question. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior product management and project scoping consultant with experience in agile prioritization and scope negotiation techniques. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the list of items to classify; if the context is not specified (project, product, consulting), assume a software development project; the time constraint is a 2-week sprint unless otherwise indicated; a Must have item cannot exceed 60% of total capacity; if confidence in any parameter is below 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: list of items to prioritize pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Review and normalize items (remove duplicates, clarify ambiguities). 2. Define and document the classification criteria for each MoSCoW category. 3. Classify each item with a one-line justification. 4. Build the table with columns: item, MoSCoW category, justification. 5. Calculate the percentage distribution per category and alert if Must have exceeds 60%. 6. Identify dependencies between Must and Should items. 7. Draft a scope recommendation for the current iteration indicating what to exclude and why. OUTPUT: complete MoSCoW table with justifications + percentage distribution + dependency analysis + one-page scope recommendation. EDGE CASES: (a) more than 70% of items classified as Must → facilitate a "what happens if we don't do it?" session to reclassify; (b) items without sufficient information → classify as Could and mark for refinement; (c) conflicts between stakeholders on classification → document the conflict and propose resolution based on end-user impact. [C · CRITERIA] All items must have a classification and justification; Must items must not exceed 60% of the total; the scope recommendation must include an explicit list of included and excluded items. DoD: complete table, distribution calculated, recommendation drafted. Trade-off: completeness vs. delivery speed — prefer classifying doubtful items as Could to keep Must focused. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that no item is left unclassified and that the percentage distribution sums to 100% before delivering.
spec-consulting_retrospectiva_facilitada: [S · SITUATION] At the close of a project, sprint, or relevant stage, the team needs a facilitated retrospective that goes beyond an informal meeting, systematizing learnings, identifying root causes of problems, and defining concrete, measurable improvement commitments for the next cycle. [P · REQUEST] Design and conduct the complete retrospective: session format, facilitation script with a structured technique, findings capture, root-cause analysis for critical problems, and improvement commitments table with owner and date. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior agile facilitator with experience in high-performance team retrospectives and organizational transformation. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the project or sprint context (achievements, incidents, available metrics); default duration 90 minutes; team of 5 to 12 people; default technique 4L (Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for) for its balance between positive and improvement aspects; if any parameter is missing, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: project or sprint context pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Review the context and synthesize the key milestones of the period. 2. Select and justify the most appropriate retrospective technique. 3. Design the session agenda with blocks and times. 4. Create guiding questions for each dimension of the technique. 5. Tabulate available input data in the technique's categories. 6. Apply root-cause analysis (5 Whys or Fishbone) to the 2 most critical problems. 7. Build an improvement commitments table: description, owner, deadline, success indicator. 8. Write a one-page retrospective executive summary. OUTPUT: session agenda + per-dimension guide + findings table + root-cause analysis of the 2 critical problems + commitments table + executive summary. EDGE CASES: (a) team with interpersonal conflicts → use anonymous retrospective format (nameless digital sticky notes) and redirect to systems, not people; (b) team's first retrospective → dedicate 10 additional minutes to explaining the purpose and psychological safety rules; (c) no quantitative data → base the analysis on qualitative perceptions and mark as [ASSUMPTION]. [C · CRITERIA] The commitments table must have a minimum of 3 actions with owner and date; the root-cause analysis must reach at least the third level of why; the executive summary must fit on one page. DoD: agenda designed, findings tabulated, root causes analyzed, commitments defined, summary written. Trade-off: thoroughness vs. team energy — in long retrospectives prioritize the 3 areas with the greatest impact. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that each improvement commitment has an owner, date, and success criterion before delivering.
spec-consulting_minuta_y_acuerdos_de_wor: [S · SITUATION] At the end of a consulting, strategy, or design workshop, the team needs a formal minutes document that precisely captures the participants, topics covered, decisions made, agreements reached, and committed tasks, so that it serves as an official reference and follow-up tool. [P · REQUEST] Draft the complete workshop minutes from available notes or transcript: formal header, attendees, agenda covered, discussion summaries per item, explicit decisions, agreements with owner and date, and task follow-up table. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project management consultant specializing in high-precision executive documentation for corporate environments. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the workshop notes or transcript; if no explicit date is given, use today's date as assumption; if a responsible party is not identified, mark as "To be defined"; if confidence in any data point is below 0.85, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: workshop notes or transcript pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Extract event metadata (date, location/modality, duration, convener, workshop objective). 2. List participants with name and role if available. 3. Reconstruct the agenda covered in chronological order. 4. For each agenda item: write a discussion summary (3-5 lines), decisions taken (positive and precise formulation), and agreements with owner and deadline. 5. Build the task follow-up table: number, task description, owner, deadline, status (pending). 6. Identify topics that remained open or pending for the next session. 7. Add a next-steps section and next-meeting date if agreed upon. OUTPUT: structured minutes with header, participants, agenda, per-item summary, decisions, agreements, task table, and next steps. EDGE CASES: (a) incomplete or confusing notes → mark the section as [VERIFY] and indicate what information is missing; (b) multiple owners for a task → assign one primary owner and list support parties; (c) workshop with more than 5 agenda items → group related items into thematic sections to streamline reading. [C · CRITERIA] Each decision must be formulated positively and unambiguously; each task must have an owner and a date; the document must be usable as a reference without consulting the original notes. DoD: complete minutes, task table populated, next steps defined. Trade-off: thoroughness vs. readability — summarize discussions to 3-5 lines per item, do not transcribe verbatim. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that all decisions identified in the notes are captured and that no task is left without an owner before delivering.
spec-consulting_diseno_de_pre_lectura_de: [S · SITUATION] A consultant or facilitator who has designed a workshop or working session needs to prepare the pre-reading material that participants will receive in advance, so they arrive aligned, with the necessary context, and with the right mindset to make the most of the in-person time. [P · REQUEST] Create the session pre-reading document: purpose and session objectives, relevant background context, key concepts participants must know, prior reflection questions, participation expectations, and optional reference material. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior instructional designer and facilitation consultant with experience preparing corporate audiences for high-impact workshops. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the session agenda or description for which the pre-reading is prepared; the document is delivered 3 to 5 days in advance; the audience consists of corporate professionals at executive or senior technical level; target reading time is 10-15 minutes; if any parameter is missing, declare assumption and continue. INPUTS: session agenda or description pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Analyze the session agenda or description and identify the 3-5 key concepts or contexts participants must master. 2. Draft the purpose section: what will be achieved in the session and why it matters now. 3. Draft the background context section (maximum 300 words): the situation that gives rise to the session. 4. Develop the key concepts section with a brief definition and practical relevance for each. 5. Formulate 3-5 prior reflection questions that activate critical thinking and the participant's personal perspective. 6. Draft the participation expectations section (what the participant is expected to bring, decide, or share). 7. List optional reference materials for those who want to go deeper. OUTPUT: 1-2 page pre-reading document with sections: purpose, context, key concepts, reflection questions, expectations, and references. EDGE CASES: (a) highly technical topic → simplify technical concepts with analogies and avoid undefined jargon; (b) participants with little time → create a 5-minute version with only purpose + reflection questions as an executive summary; (c) pre-reading for a sensitive organizational change session → write in an invitation tone, not an imposition tone, underlining the participants' protagonist role. [C · CRITERIA] The document must be readable in less than 15 minutes; reflection questions must be open and provocative, not obviously answerable; the tone must be motivating and respectful of the reader's time. DoD: complete document, six sections covered, reflection questions formulated, reading time estimated. Trade-off: depth of context vs. cognitive load — prefer sufficient context to participate vs. exhaustive context that overwhelms. Protocolo MetodologIA: estimate the reading time of the produced document and adjust if it exceeds 15 minutes before delivering.
spec-consulting_evaluacion_de_disposicio: [S · SITUATION] An organization is implementing a significant change (new system, restructuring, cultural transformation) and needs to assess the readiness level of its employees and leaders using the ADKAR model (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement) to identify gaps and design targeted interventions. [P · REQUEST] Design the ADKAR assessment instrument, analyze available results, identify critical gaps by dimension and team, and produce a prioritized intervention plan with concrete actions for each detected gap. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior change management consultant certified in PROSCI/ADKAR with experience in organizational readiness diagnostics and change intervention design. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the change context and/or available assessment data; if no data exists, design the instrument and provide result-scenario interpretation; assessment scale of 1 to 5 per dimension; critical gap when dimension average is below 3; if any parameter is missing, declare the assumption and continue. INPUTS: change description and/or assessment results pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Briefly describe the change and impacted groups. 2. Design the ADKAR instrument: 3 questions per dimension with a Likert 1–5 scale. 3. If assessment data exists, tabulate results by dimension and group. 4. Calculate the average score per dimension and per group. 5. Identify critical gaps (dimensions with an average below 3). 6. Analyze the most likely cause of each gap. 7. Design the intervention plan: for each gap, one specific action, owner, deadline, and success metric. 8. Write the executive summary with a readiness traffic light per dimension (green ≥4, yellow 3–3.9, red <3). OUTPUT: ADKAR instrument + results table with traffic light + gap analysis + intervention plan + one-page executive summary. EDGE CASES: (a) no assessment data → deliver the complete instrument with illustrative interpretive scenarios labeled [ASSUMPTION]; (b) critical gap in Awareness → prioritize a communication campaign before any other intervention; (c) documented active resistance → include listening sessions as the first intervention before training. [C · CRITERIA] The instrument must have 15 questions (3 per dimension); the intervention plan must have at least one action per detected gap; the executive summary must include a visual traffic light per dimension. DoD: instrument designed, results tabulated or scenarios provided, gaps identified, intervention plan written. Trade-off: diagnostic depth vs. speed of action — begin with Awareness and Desire gaps before Knowledge and Ability. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that each ADKAR dimension has exactly 3 questions in the instrument and that each critical gap has at least one intervention before delivering.
spec-consulting_analisis_de_actores_y_re: [S · SITUATION] An organizational change initiative faces multiple actors with different levels of power, interest, and readiness, and the change management team needs a complete stakeholder map that identifies who are allies, who are neutral, and who are resistant, with analysis of the causes of resistance and differentiated engagement strategies. [P · REQUEST] Produce the complete stakeholder and resistance analysis: power/interest map, classification of actors by position toward the change, diagnosis of causes of resistance by actor or group, and an engagement plan with specific tactics to neutralize resistance and strengthen alliances. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior change management and stakeholder analysis consultant with experience in complex organizational environments and power dynamics. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the change description and the list of relevant actors; if actors are not listed, identify them from the change context; the power/interest map uses a 2×2 grid (high/low power × high/low interest); if any parameter is missing, declare the assumption and continue. INPUTS: change description and actor list pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify and list all relevant actors (individuals, groups, areas). 2. Assess each actor's level of power and interest in the change (high/low). 3. Build the stakeholder map table with columns: actor, power, interest, quadrant, position toward the change (champion/neutral/resistant), level of influence over other actors. 4. For each resistant or neutral actor with high power, analyze the causes of resistance (3 categories: rational, emotional, political). 5. Design differentiated engagement tactics by quadrant and resistance type. 6. Build the engagement plan: actor, primary tactic, management owner, contact frequency. 7. Identify the 3 key allies to strengthen first. OUTPUT: stakeholder map table + resistance analysis by actor/group + engagement plan + list of key allies to activate. EDGE CASES: (a) actor with maximum power and active resistance → escalate to the executive sponsor before any direct tactic; (b) collective resistance from an entire area → treat as a group with its own dynamics, not as isolated individuals; (c) actors with unknown position → label as [TO BE ASSESSED] and prioritize sounding conversations. [C · CRITERIA] The map must include all high-power actors; each resistant high-power actor must have a specific tactic; the engagement plan must have at least one action per critical actor. DoD: complete map, resistance causes diagnosed, engagement plan written, key allies identified. Trade-off: depth of analysis vs. speed of action — begin with high-power quadrants regardless of interest level. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that no high-power actor is left without a defined engagement tactic before delivering.
spec-consulting_plan_de_comunicacion_del: [S · SITUATION] An organization implementing a significant change needs a structured communication plan that guides the different stakeholder groups with appropriate messages, at the right moments, through the appropriate channels, and from the most credible spokespersons, to reduce uncertainty, manage expectations, and sustain commitment throughout the entire change process. [P · REQUEST] Develop the complete change communication plan: key messages by audience segment, communications calendar, channel and spokesperson matrix, critical message templates, and feedback mechanisms. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior organizational communication and change management consultant with experience in communication strategies for high-impact corporate transformations. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the change description, available audience groups, and the time horizon; if the time horizon is not defined, assume a 3-month plan; default channels are corporate email, team meetings, and monthly newsletter; if confidence in any parameter is below 0.85, declare the assumption and continue. INPUTS: change description, audiences, and time horizon pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Analyze the change and identify the 3–5 key messages to be communicated throughout the process. 2. Segment the audiences and define the specific information needs of each segment. 3. Adapt the key messages to each audience segment (tone, emphasis, level of detail). 4. Design the communications calendar with milestones (before/during/after the change), date, message, channel, spokesperson, and communication objective. 5. Build the channel matrix: channel, target audience, frequency, owner. 6. Write 2–3 critical message templates (initial announcement, progress update, closing message). 7. Design the feedback mechanism (form, direct line, Q&A session). OUTPUT: key messages + communications calendar + channel and spokesperson matrix + message templates + feedback mechanism. EDGE CASES: (a) change with negative impact on some groups → prepare empathetic honesty messages before the formal announcement; (b) organization with low communication culture → simplify the plan to 3 channels maximum and increase face-to-face frequency; (c) urgent change with little preparation time → prioritize direct leader communication over mass communication. [C · CRITERIA] The calendar must cover the full time horizon of the change; each audience segment must have at least one adapted message; templates must be usable with minimal editing. DoD: complete plan, calendar with milestones, templates written, feedback mechanism defined. Trade-off: message centralization vs. local adaptation — keep key messages consistent but allow tone adaptation by local spokesperson. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that each audience segment has at least one adapted message in the calendar before delivering.
spec-consulting_modelo_de_cambio_de_kott: [S · SITUATION] An organization needs to structure and execute a significant organizational change process using Kotter's 8-step model (urgency, coalition, vision, communication, empower, early wins, consolidate, anchor) to maximize the probabilities of sustained adoption and minimize the risk of reverting to the previous state. [P · REQUEST] Develop the complete change plan based on Kotter's model: diagnosis of the change situation, concrete activities and deliverables for each of the 8 steps, verification milestones, responsible roles, and progress metrics for monitoring the process. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior organizational transformation and change management consultant with certification and extensive practice in Kotter's model and its applications in Latin American business contexts. ASSUMPTIONS: the pasted input contains the description of the change to be implemented; the default horizon is 12 months; the organization has between 50 and 500 employees unless otherwise indicated; if any parameter is missing, declare the assumption and continue. INPUTS: description of the change to be implemented pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Analyze the change and identify the real urgency level and organizational readiness. 2. For each of Kotter's 8 steps: a) name and objective of the step, b) 2–3 concrete activities with operational description, c) expected artifact or deliverable, d) step completion criterion, e) primary responsible role, f) estimated duration. 3. Build the schedule for the 8 steps with natural overlaps (some steps are sequential, others parallel). 4. Define 3 global progress metrics for the change process. 5. Identify the 2–3 most frequent critical risks for this type of change and their mitigation plans. 6. Write a 1-page executive summary of the change plan. OUTPUT: readiness diagnosis + 8-step plan with activities, deliverables, criteria, and roles + schedule + metrics + risks + executive summary. EDGE CASES: (a) urgency nonexistent or manufactured → dedicate additional activities in step 1 to build genuine urgency with data; (b) weak leadership coalition → prioritize step 2 and do not advance to step 3 until at least 3 committed leaders are in place; (c) early wins difficult to achieve → select low-risk, high-visibility pilot changes that can be completed in 60–90 days. [C · CRITERIA] The plan must cover all 8 steps without omissions; each step must have a minimum of 2 operational activities; the schedule must show overlaps where applicable; metrics must be quantifiable. DoD: 8 steps developed, schedule built, 3 metrics defined, risks identified, executive summary written. Trade-off: implementation speed vs. solidity of each step — do not skip steps even under time pressure; compress activities, do not eliminate steps. Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that all 8 steps are developed and that none lacks a completion criterion before delivering.
spec-consulting_diseno_de_red_de_agentes:
[S · SITUATION] A medium- or large-scale organization is undergoing a significant transformation (technological, cultural, structural, or process-based) and needs to identify, select, and articulate an internal network of influential individuals who accelerate change adoption from within, reducing resistance and increasing ownership. The consulting or change management team has access to information about the organizational structure, key stakeholders, and the type of transformation underway.

[P · REQUEST] Design a complete and operational change agent network: selection criteria, role map by level/area, activation protocol, agent enablement plan, and follow-up mechanisms, delivered as a structured document ready to validate with the sponsor.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior consultant specializing in organizational change management with experience in large-scale transformations, change management methodologies (Prosci/ADKAR, Kotter, Satir), and design of internal influence networks.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the transformation type is not specified, assume a digital transformation with a cultural component. If the size is not indicated, assume an organization of 500–2,000 people. If no organizational structure is given, assume a functional hierarchy with 3–4 levels. Only ask if: (1) the geographic scope is critical (multinational vs. local), (2) a corporate change methodology has already been adopted, or (3) there are confidentiality restrictions that limit the mapping. Otherwise, declare the assumptions and proceed.

INPUTS: Paste in the thread the transformation description, the org chart or description of impacted areas, and any resistance diagnosis or climate survey available.

STEPS:
1. Analyze the scope and impact of the transformation to define the network dimensions (coverage by area, hierarchical level, geography).
2. Define agent selection criteria: informal influence, change readiness, technical credibility, relationship network.
3. Design the network architecture: differentiated roles (executive champion, area change agent, operational ambassador), responsibilities, and links between levels.
4. Develop the activation and onboarding protocol for agents: selection communication, kick-off session, enablement materials.
5. Design the training and support plan for agents throughout the transformation.
6. Propose follow-up mechanisms: periodic pulses, adoption metrics by area, barrier escalation.
7. Consolidate in an executive document with a visual network map, role sheets, and activation schedule.

OUTPUT: Structured markdown document with: (a) selection criteria with evaluation table, (b) network architecture with role descriptions, (c) step-by-step activation protocol, (d) enablement plan with sample agenda, (e) follow-up metrics and indicators, (f) textual visual network map by level.

EDGE CASES:
- If the organization already has previous change agents: adapt the design to re-energize and formalize the existing network, avoid role duplication.
- If resistance to change is very high in middle management: reinforce the area agent level with greater density and resources, and include a detractor neutralization tactic.
- If the schedule is very short (less than 3 months): prioritize a minimum viable network with the top 20% most influential agents and agile activation.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The network covers at least 80% of the areas impacted by the transformation.
- Each role has clear, non-overlapping responsibilities with its own performance metrics.
- The activation protocol is executable within the first 2 weeks of the project.
- The enablement plan is realistic in terms of workload (maximum 8 hours in the first month per agent).
- Trade-off: depth vs. speed of activation — if time is limited, prioritize rapid coverage over exhaustive training.
- DoD: document reviewed by the sponsor, with at least one nominated agent per critical area and an approved activation schedule.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Apply the ADKAR framework to validate each layer of the network before scaling to the next activation level.
spec-gestion-proyectos_acta-constitucion:
[S · SITUATION] A project has been formally approved or is in the process of approval within an organization. The team needs a Project Charter that officially authorizes the project, establishes its high-level scope, designates the project manager, defines measurable objectives, and commits initial resources. Without this document, the project lacks formal authorization and the manager has no authority to allocate resources.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete Project Charter ready for the sponsor's signature, with all standard PMI components, adapted to the specific context of the described project.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: PMP-certified project manager with experience structuring projects across various industries, expert in PMI/PMBOK standards and in drafting executive authorization documents that balance formal rigor with operational practicality.

ASSUMPTIONS: If no methodology is indicated, assume a predictive (waterfall) approach. If no sector is specified, assume services or technology sector. If no budget figures are provided, indicate 'To be defined' with a note that it must be completed before signing. If no sponsor is mentioned, assume an executive sponsor from the requesting area. Only ask if: (1) there are regulatory or compliance restrictions affecting scope, (2) there are interdependent projects that must be referenced, or (3) the project already has an internally assigned code or project number.

INPUTS: Paste in the thread the project description, its purpose or business problem it solves, the sponsoring area, expected high-level deliverables, known constraints, assumptions, and names of key stakeholders.

STEPS:
1. Identify and structure the business purpose and justification from the information received.
2. Define the SMART project objectives with their success metrics.
3. Establish high-level requirements and main deliverables.
4. Describe the high-level scope including what is explicitly out of scope.
5. Identify high-level risks with preliminary impact and probability.
6. Define the high-level milestone schedule.
7. Establish the summarized budget and key resources required.
8. Identify key stakeholders with their role and interest in the project.
9. Designate the project manager with authority levels.
10. Draft the complete charter in executive format with a signature section.

OUTPUT: Project Charter document in markdown with sections: purpose and justification, SMART objectives, high-level requirements, scope and exclusions, initial risks, high-level milestones, summarized budget, key stakeholders, project manager and authority levels, approval section with space for the sponsor's signature.

EDGE CASES:
- If the project is agile or hybrid: adjust the scope section to reflect iterative deliverables and replace fixed milestones with high-level releases or sprints.
- If there is insufficient information to define SMART objectives: draft preliminary objectives labeled [PENDING VALIDATION] with specific questions for the sponsor.
- If the project has multiple sponsors or an external sponsor: include a shared governance section with differentiated decision-making roles.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The charter must be readable and signable by an executive in under 10 minutes.
- All objectives must be measurable with at least one quantifiable success metric.
- Scope and exclusions are written to avoid contractual ambiguities.
- The document meets the components required by PMBOK 7th edition.
- Trade-off: completeness vs. speed — if critical information is missing, prioritize a functional charter with explicit pending labels rather than blocking the start.
- DoD: document reviewed by the project manager, no unjustified empty fields, with at least one sponsor signature or documented verbal approval note.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Validate that each objective in the charter has a measurable baseline before closing the document.
spec-gestion-proyectos_caso-de-negocio-b:
[S · SITUATION] An organization is evaluating the feasibility and advisability of undertaking a project or investment. The sponsor or analysis team needs a Business Case that justifies the investment decision with quantitative and qualitative evidence, compares alternatives, and recommends the path forward. Without this document, senior leadership has no objective basis for approving the budget or prioritizing the project against other initiatives.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a structured and complete Business Case that includes analysis of the current situation, evaluated options, benefits and costs, financial analysis (ROI, NPV, payback), risks, and a substantiated recommendation, presented as an executive document ready for an investment committee.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior business analyst and investment evaluation expert with experience in project financial analysis, alternative comparison techniques, and structuring documents for management committees and approval boards.

ASSUMPTIONS: If no exact financial figures are provided, build estimated ranges labeled [ASSUMPTION] with explicit estimation rationale. If no time horizon is specified, assume 3–5 years. If no discount rates are indicated, use 10% as the reference WACC. If no alternatives are mentioned, generate at least three: do nothing (status quo), minimum solution, and complete proposed solution. Only ask if: (1) there are regulatory restrictions that eliminate any alternative, (2) there are confidential financial figures that must not appear explicitly in the document, or (3) the receiving committee requires a specific format.

INPUTS: Paste in the thread the description of the business problem or need, the scope of the proposed solution, expected benefits (quantitative and qualitative), known costs, constraints, identified risks, and the target audience for the document.

STEPS:
1. Describe the current situation and the business problem or need with the consequences of inaction.
2. Identify and compare at least three solution alternatives with weighted criteria.
3. Detail the quantitative and qualitative benefits of the recommended alternative.
4. Build the cost structure: initial investment, recurring operating costs, and transition costs.
5. Calculate or estimate the key financial indicators: ROI, NPV (net present value), payback period, and IRR if applicable.
6. Identify the main risks with probability, impact, and preliminary mitigation plan.
7. Formulate the executive recommendation with clear justification.
8. Write the executive summary of no more than one page.

OUTPUT: Business Case document in markdown with: executive summary, current situation and problem, evaluated alternatives with comparison table, benefits and cost analysis, financial indicators (table), risk analysis, recommendation, and next steps.

EDGE CASES:
- If the initiative is strategic or regulatory in nature (does not generate direct ROI): replace financial return metrics with strategic value, compliance, or risk reduction metrics.
- If the receiving committee is technical, not financial: simplify the financial section and expand the technical alternative comparison.
- If the available financial data is highly uncertain: build a base, optimistic, and pessimistic scenario with ROI and payback ranges for each.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The executive summary communicates the recommendation and its justification in under one page.
- Each evaluated alternative has explicit, weighted comparison criteria.
- Financial indicators are calculated with documented rationale and declared assumptions.
- The risk analysis covers at least the 3 highest-impact risks.
- Trade-off: financial precision vs. delivery speed — prefer documented ranges over delayed exact figures.
- DoD: document reviewed by the sponsor, with at least the financial analysis of the recommended alternative validated by finance or the responsible area.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Contrast the calculated NPV with the cost of capital opportunity cost before issuing the final recommendation.
spec-gestion-proyectos_enunciado-trabajo:
[S · SITUATION] An organization is going to contract an external vendor or formalize the scope of work for an internal team to execute a specific project or service. A Statement of Work (SOW) is needed that precisely defines what will be done, how, when, and under what conditions, so that it serves as a contractual basis or formal scope document that prevents disputes and ambiguities.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete, precise, and contractually sound Statement of Work that covers the work scope, deliverables with acceptance criteria, schedule, resources, responsibilities of both parties, and payment or completion conditions.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Project manager and professional services contract expert with experience drafting SOWs for consulting, technology, and implementation projects, familiar with PMI standards and procurement contracting practices.

ASSUMPTIONS: If it is not specified whether the SOW is for an external vendor or internal team, assume an external vendor. If quality standards are not indicated, assume the industry standards for the described sector. If there is no payment condition information, use a milestone structure as reference. Only ask if: (1) the context is regulated and requires specific compliance clauses, (2) there are intellectual property or confidentiality restrictions that must be included, or (3) there are dependencies with other contracts or ongoing SOWs.

INPUTS: Paste in the thread the description of the service or work to be contracted, expected deliverables, tentative schedule, required vendor resources, roles and responsibilities of both parties, and expected acceptance or quality conditions.

STEPS:
1. Define the work purpose and scope in precise, unambiguous language.
2. Detail each deliverable with its description, delivery format, acceptance criteria, and deadline.
3. Establish the work schedule with start dates, intermediate milestones, and end date.
4. Specify required resources: vendor profiles, materials, accesses, and tools.
5. Define the responsibilities of the vendor and the client (contracting organization) in a differentiated manner.
6. Establish quality standards and deliverable review and approval procedures.
7. Describe payment conditions tied to approved milestones or deliverables.
8. Include clauses on scope changes, dispute resolution, and termination conditions.
9. Draft the complete SOW with a signature section and effective date.

OUTPUT: SOW document in markdown with sections: work purpose and scope, deliverable description with acceptance criteria table, work schedule (milestone table), required resources and profiles, vendor and client responsibilities, quality standards and approval, payment conditions, change management and termination, and signature section.

EDGE CASES:
- If the work is iterative or agile: reformulate the deliverables section as releases or sprints with per-iteration acceptance criteria and replace the fixed schedule with agreed capacity.
- If multiple vendors are involved: include an interfaces and dependencies section between vendors to avoid responsibility conflicts.
- If the SOW is for an internal team without a contractual relationship: adapt the language by removing contractual clauses and focus it as an Internal Scope Agreement with service levels (SLA).

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each deliverable has objective and verifiable acceptance criteria, not subjective ones.
- Vendor and client responsibilities are mutually exclusive and without gaps.
- The schedule has at least 3 control points (milestones) with associated deliverables.
- Document language is clear, precise, and free of contractual ambiguities.
- Trade-off: legal thoroughness vs. negotiation agility — include standard clauses without overloading the document with unnecessary legalese.
- DoD: document reviewed by the legal or procurement area, with all deliverables defined and dates agreed by both parties.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Verify that each SOW deliverable has at least one binary acceptance criterion (meets/does not meet) before closing the document.
spec-gestion-proyectos_orden-de-cambio-v:
[S · SITUATION] During project execution, the team receives a change request (Change Request or Change Order) that may affect the scope, budget, schedule, or objectives originally approved in the Project Charter. Before approving or rejecting the change, it is necessary to validate whether the change order is aligned with the project's strategic objectives or whether it represents a deviation that requires formal re-baselining or even a new charter.

[P · REQUEST] Perform a comparative analysis between the proposed change order and the current Project Charter, determine the level of impact on each project dimension (scope, time, cost, quality, risk), issue a substantiated recommendation on approval, rejection, or escalation, and if approved, generate the approved change record.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: PMP-certified project manager with experience in integrated change management, impact analysis, and change control processes in complex technology, consulting, and infrastructure projects.
