[P · REQUEST] Draft the Formal Acceptance Record for the deliverable: an official document that details the delivered item, confirms compliance with acceptance criteria, records observations or minor pending defects with their remediation plans, and includes the formal signature of the authorized acceptor.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: You are a senior project manager with experience in contractual deliverable management and closure documentation for complex projects.
SUPUESTOS: If no deliverable or acceptance criteria are provided, use as an example the delivery of the analysis phase of an ERP implementation project with its design documents [ASSUMPTION]; if approved criteria are not known, generate industry-standard criteria for the described deliverable type [ASSUMPTION]; proceed if confidence ≥0.85.
INSUMOS: Paste below the deliverable description, the agreed acceptance criteria, the results of tests or reviews performed, and the list of known defects or pending items.
PASOS:
1. Complete the record header → record number, date, project, phase, deliverable, provider/team, authorized acceptor.
2. Describe the accepted deliverable → name, version, functional description, delivery date, composition (included artifacts).
3. Verify criteria compliance → table: Acceptance criterion | Result obtained | Status (Met / Met with observation / Not met).
4. Record observations and minor defects → table: ID | Description | Severity (Critical/Major/Minor) | Remediation plan | Deadline | Responsible party.
5. Declare the acceptance type → Full acceptance / Conditional acceptance (with pending items list) / Rejection with causes.
6. Include effects clause → what rights and obligations are activated upon signature (payment, warranty, start of next phase, etc.).
7. Include signatures section → authorized acceptor (client/sponsor), project manager, witness if applicable.
SALIDA: Formal Markdown document with all sections in the specified order, in appropriate executive and contractual language, ready for signature.
CASOS BORDE:
- If there are unresolved critical defects: the record must indicate Partial Rejection and cannot be used to release associated payments; add a required action note before re-acceptance.
- If the client refuses to sign without documented cause: add a unilateral delivery notification section with a record of the acceptance attempt.
- If the deliverable is intangible (consulting, training, process): adapt the "criteria compliance" language to observed performance evidence and results validation.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the signed document has legal and administrative validity to activate the next contract payment milestone.
- Trade-off: contractual formality vs. agility; for internal deliverables the language can be less formal, for contractual deliverables use precise language.
- DoD: the record is signed by the authorized acceptor, has a unique reference number, and is archived in the project document management system.

Protocolo MetodologIA: verify that each acceptance criterion has an explicit status and that the declared acceptance type is consistent with the results before producing the record.
spec-gestion-proyectos_priorizacion-mosc:
[S · SITUATION] The team of a software development or organizational transformation project has collected a list of candidate requirements or features. The sponsor is pressing for immovable dates and the team needs to agree with stakeholders on what is in and what is out of the delivery scope.

[P · REQUEST] Classify the full list of requirements into the four MoSCoW categories (Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have) and produce a signable prioritization document that includes justification per item, cutoff criteria, and an executive summary of committed scope.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior consultant in scope management and stakeholder facilitation with 15 years of experience in IT and transformation projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not paste the requirements list, assume it must be requested before continuing — this is the only case where a question is asked. If no time or budget constraints are indicated, assume the main constraint is the delivery date agreed with the sponsor. If no voting method is specified, use facilitated consensus with tiebreaker by impact on business objective.

INSUMOS: List of requirements or backlog pasted in the thread; any available project objectives context.

PASOS:
1. Review the requirements list and identify classification criteria: impact on primary project objective, omission risk, technical dependencies — produce weighted criteria table.
2. Classify each requirement as Must / Should / Could / Won't with a one-sentence justification each — produce classification table.
3. Calculate the percentage of effort in each category and verify that Must Have does not exceed 60% of available capacity — produce feasibility traffic light.
4. Draft the committed scope executive summary (max. 150 words) with confirmed Must Haves and Won't Haves explicitly out of scope.
5. Generate a list of validation questions for the stakeholder session.

SALIDA: Structured document with: (a) weighted criteria table, (b) full MoSCoW table with justifications, (c) feasibility traffic light, (d) scope executive summary, (e) validation questions.

CASOS BORDE:
- If more than 70% of items fall in Must Have: alert about inflated scope risk and propose a re-prioritization session using business value criterion.
- If there are requirements with circular dependencies: flag them explicitly and suggest resolution before classifying.
- If the user has no requirements list: stop and request the list before continuing.

[C · CRITERIA] The classification is observable: each item has a category + one-sentence justification. Must Have does not exceed 60% of estimated effort. The executive summary can be approved by the sponsor without ambiguity. DoD: complete table, green traffic light or documented warning, executive summary drafted.

Protocolo MetodologIA: MoSCoW classification ready → declare assumptions used → deliver table + traffic light + executive summary.
spec-gestion-proyectos_lista-actividades:
[S · SITUATION] A project director has just defined the work scope through a WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) and needs to decompose it into concrete, plannable activities in order to build the project schedule.

[P · REQUEST] Generate the schedule activity list with a unique identifier, precise description, WBS work package to which it belongs, assigned responsible party, and additional attributes (assumptions, constraints, required resources) for each activity, in a format directly usable in scheduling tools.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project planning and control specialist, PMP/PMI-SP certified, with experience in activity decomposition for complex engineering and IT projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the WBS, request it before continuing — it is the only blocking field. If no sector or project type is indicated, assume a technology project with analysis, design, development, testing, and deployment phases. If no granularity level is specified, assume activities between 8 and 40 hours in duration (8/80 rule). If no responsible parties are named, leave the field blank with a [TO BE ASSIGNED] indicator.

INSUMOS: WBS or list of work packages pasted in the thread; any available scope document.

PASOS:
1. Review the received WBS and identify all leaf work packages (with no children) — produce count of packages to decompose.
2. For each work package, decompose into 2–6 activities applying the 8/80 criterion; assign hierarchical code (e.g., 1.2.3-A01) — produce draft activity table.
3. Add to each activity: description in verb+object format, relevant assumptions, constraints, and estimated required resources.
4. Validate that the sum of activities covers 100% of the work package (completeness test).
5. Generate the final exportable table in markdown format with columns: Code | Activity Name | WBS Package | Responsible Party | Assumptions | Constraints | Resources.

SALIDA: Activity list in markdown table, plus list of identified implicit milestones and note on activities with high omission risk.

CASOS BORDE:
- If a work package cannot be decomposed into 8–40 h activities (black-box work): mark it as a "hammock" activity and document the reason.
- If there are duplicate activities across different packages: alert about possible scope overlap.
- If the WBS has more than 5 levels: process only leaf levels and document intermediate levels as groupers.

[C · CRITERIA] Each activity has a unique code, verb+object description, and at least one assumptions or constraints field. The sum of activities covers 100% of the WBS scope. The format is importable into MS Project, Jira, or similar without manual reformatting. DoD: complete table, documented completeness test, implicit milestones identified.

Protocolo MetodologIA: WBS received → activities decomposed with attributes → exportable table + completeness validation.
spec-gestion-proyectos_secuenciacion-dep:
[S · SITUATION] A planning team has a schedule activity list and needs to establish the logical execution order to build the schedule model. It is required to identify and document all dependencies between activities using the Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM) with its four relationship types: Finish-to-Start (FS), Start-to-Start (SS), Finish-to-Finish (FF), and Start-to-Finish (SF).

[P · REQUEST] Produce the activity sequencing table with all dependencies documented (relationship type, lead or lag in days, dependency type: mandatory/discretionary/external), and the schedule network diagram in text/ASCII format or a structured description ready to import into scheduling software.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project planner specialized in scheduling techniques and activity network analysis, with experience in construction, IT, and supply chain projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not paste the activity list, request it before continuing. If no project type is specified, assume that mandatory dependencies are the evident techno-logical ones (cannot test without developing, cannot install without acquiring). If no lead or lag is indicated, assume lead/lag = 0 days unless the work logic requires it. If there are no activities with an SF (Start-to-Finish) relationship, do not force it.

INSUMOS: Activity list with their codes and descriptions; any already-known sequence constraints.

PASOS:
1. Review the activity list and identify the logical precedence network; classify each dependency as mandatory, discretionary, or external — produce dependency draft.
2. Assign to each dependency the correct PDM type (FS/SS/FF/SF), lead/lag in days, and a one-sentence justification.
3. Build the complete precedence table: Predecessor Activity | Successor Activity | Relationship Type | Lead/Lag (days) | Dependency Type | Justification.
4. Describe the network diagram in structured text format (nodes and arcs) or importable pseudocode.
5. Flag activities with no predecessors (network start) and no successors (network end), and alert if there is more than one start node or more than one end node.

SALIDA: Complete sequencing table + network diagram description + warnings list (circular dependencies, orphan nodes, unusual SF relationships).

CASOS BORDE:
- If a circular dependency is detected: flag it with the names of the involved activities and propose a breakage.
- If there are activities with no connected dependency: mark them as orphans and request confirmation.
- If the number of activities exceeds 50: process in groups by phase and deliver a per-phase network plus an integration network.

[C · CRITERIA] Each pair of dependent activities has PDM type, lead/lag, and dependency type documented. There are no circular dependencies. The network's start and end nodes are identified. The table is importable into MS Project, Primavera, or similar. DoD: complete table, network diagram described, warnings documented.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Activity list → dependencies classified by PDM type → sequencing table + network diagram.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-duraci:
[S · SITUATION] A planning team has a schedule activity list and needs to estimate durations more reliably than with a point estimate. Experts or historical experience are available to distinguish an optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic scenario for each activity.

[P · REQUEST] Calculate the expected duration (te) and standard deviation (σ) of each activity using the PERT formula (te = (O + 4M + P) / 6; σ = (P − O) / 6), and produce an estimation table with an uncertainty analysis per activity and a summary of the activities with the highest variance.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior schedule analyst and project estimator with mastery of PERT techniques, Monte Carlo simulation, and uncertainty management in complex projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the three values per activity (O, M, P), request them before continuing — it is the only blocking field. If units are not specified, assume working days. If no risk threshold is indicated, assume an activity is high-uncertainty if σ > 20% of te. If not stated whether to use standard or triangular PERT, use standard Beta PERT (formula with 4M weight).

INSUMOS: Table with activity, code, optimistic (O), most likely (M), and pessimistic (P) estimate pasted in the thread.

PASOS:
1. Validate that values O ≤ M ≤ P for each activity; mark inconsistencies — produce list of inconsistencies to correct.
2. Calculate te = (O + 4M + P) / 6 and σ = (P − O) / 6 for each activity — produce result columns.
3. Calculate variance σ² per activity and classify as low (σ < 10% of te), medium, or high uncertainty (σ > 20% of te).
4. Identify the 5 activities with the highest σ² and document them as candidates for contingency reserve or additional analysis.
5. Generate the final table and executive uncertainty summary: total expected duration (if the list is the critical path), 95% confidence range (te ± 2σ accumulated), and recommendations.

SALIDA: Complete table with O, M, P, te, σ, σ², uncertainty level per activity; high-variance activity summary; confidence range if the critical path is provided.

CASOS BORDE:
- If O > M or M > P for any activity: stop that item, alert, and request correction before calculating.
- If an activity has O = M = P: indicate that the estimate is deterministic and provides no uncertainty information.
- If the user wants to use triangular distribution instead of Beta PERT: calculate te = (O + M + P) / 3 and document it explicitly.

[C · CRITERIA] Each activity has te and σ calculated with the correct formula. O ≤ M ≤ P inconsistencies are identified. The uncertainty level is classified. The 95% range is calculated for the critical path if provided. DoD: complete table, uncertainty classification, high-variance activity summary.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Three points per activity → PERT calculated → table with classified uncertainty + risk summary.
spec-gestion-proyectos_calculo-ruta-crit:
[S · SITUATION] A planning team has the schedule activity network with estimated durations and needs to determine which is the least-float path that defines the project's minimum duration and the points where any delay directly impacts the end date.

[P · REQUEST] Run the Critical Path Method (CPM) applying the forward pass (ES and EF calculation) and backward pass (LS and LF calculation), calculate the total and free float for each activity, identify the full critical path, and produce the documented analysis with interpretation for decision-making.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Project control and scheduling specialist with mastery of CPM, PERT, and scheduling tools, with experience in network analysis for engineering, construction, and IT projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the activity network with durations, request it before continuing. If no start date is specified, assume t=0 (day 0). If there are multiple start nodes, create a fictitious start node with duration 0. If there are multiple end nodes, create a fictitious end node with duration 0. If not stated whether durations are deterministic or probabilistic, assume deterministic.

INSUMOS: Activity network (predecessor list per activity) with each activity's duration; or PDM sequencing table with FS relationships.

PASOS:
1. Build the activity list with predecessors and durations; identify start node and end node — produce base table.
2. Run forward pass: calculate ES (Early Start) = max(EF of predecessors) and EF (Early Finish) = ES + duration for all activities — produce ES and EF columns.
3. Run backward pass: calculate LF (Late Finish) = min(LS of successors) and LS (Late Start) = LF − duration for all activities — produce LF and LS columns.
4. Calculate total float (TF = LS − ES = LF − EF) and free float (FF = ES of earliest successor − EF of the activity).
5. Identify the critical path (all activities with TF = 0), calculate the total project duration, and list the critical activities in sequence.
6. Produce summary table and interpretation paragraph for the project director.

SALIDA: Complete CPM table with ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF per activity; list of critical path activities in execution order; total project duration; managerial interpretation paragraph.

CASOS BORDE:
- If there is more than one path with TF = 0: document all critical paths and indicate the project's degree of criticality.
- If any activity has a negative TF: detect a network inconsistency (possibly external constraints) and alert.
- If the network has SS, FF, or SF dependencies (not only FS): apply the generalized CPM algorithm and document the treatment of complex dependencies.

[C · CRITERIA] Each activity has ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, and FF correctly calculated. The critical path is the sequence of activities with TF = 0. The total project duration corresponds to the EF of the final node. The managerial interpretation indicates which activities are critical and how much float the non-critical ones have. DoD: complete table, critical path identified, interpretation documented.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Network with durations → CPM forward/backward → float table → critical path identified + managerial interpretation.
spec-gestion-proyectos_compresion-crashi:
[S · SITUATION] The approved schedule of a project cannot be met by the required date and the team needs to reduce the total project duration without changing scope. Additional budget is potentially available (for crashing) and it can be evaluated whether there are parallel activities on the critical path (for fast-tracking).

[P · REQUEST] Analyze schedule compression options by applying crashing (assigning additional resources to critical activities with the lowest cost per accelerated day) and fast-tracking (parallelizing sequential critical activities), calculate the incremental cost and associated risks for each option, and produce a recommended compression plan that achieves the target duration reduction.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project control and schedule optimization consultant, with experience in cost-duration analysis (crashing curve) and compression risk management.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the critical path with durations and costs, request it before continuing. If the target reduction in days is not indicated, assume the user wants the maximum possible reduction within a reasonable budget — the available budget will be asked before proceeding if not indicated (single blocking question). If crashing costs per activity are not known, use a relative cost estimate of low/medium/high. If risk tolerance is not specified, assume medium tolerance.

INSUMOS: Critical path with activities, durations, normal costs, and if available, crashing costs and minimum durations; day reduction target.

PASOS:
1. Review the critical path and identify activities with the highest crashing potential (lowest cost per accelerated day) — produce candidate ranking.
2. For each crashing candidate: calculate incremental cost per accelerated day = (crash cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − crash duration) — produce cost-crashing analysis table.
3. Identify critical activities that can run in parallel (fast-tracking) and estimate the rework or defect risk that parallelization introduces.
4. Build the optimal compression plan: apply crashing first to the lowest-cost-per-day activities, then fast-tracking where the risk is acceptable, until the reduction target is reached.
5. Calculate total compression cost, days reduced, and net risks. Produce a crashing vs. fast-tracking vs. combination comparison.

SALIDA: Crashing analysis table (cost/day per activity), fast-tracking analysis with risks, recommended compression plan with days reduced and total cost, and options comparison table.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the reduction target exceeds the compressible duration of the critical path (maximum crash point): alert that the target is unachievable without scope changes.
- If crashing an activity creates a new parallel critical path: recalculate and adjust the plan.
- If crashing cost data is unavailable: use the analysis with relative estimates and recommend the user obtain real data before committing.

[C · CRITERIA] The compression plan achieves the target day reduction. The incremental cost is calculated per activity. Fast-tracking risks are qualitatively quantified. The comparison table enables the sponsor to make an informed decision. DoD: complete crashing table, compression plan documented, options comparison.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Critical path + target → crashing/fast-tracking analysis → compression plan with cost and risk + options comparison.
spec-gestion-proyectos_nivelacion-recurs:
[S · SITUATION] A project's schedule presents peaks of resource demand in certain periods that exceed the team's actual availability, generating over-assignment. The project manager needs to redistribute activities to adjust the workload to capacity limits without compromising (or minimally compromising) the finish date.

[P · REQUEST] Apply resource leveling techniques (resource leveling, which may extend the project duration) and resource smoothing (which does not modify the finish date but uses floats), identify the activities that must shift, the impact on project duration, and the resulting load profile.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior specialist in project resource planning and control, with experience in workload optimization in MS Project, Primavera, and manual methods.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the schedule with resource assignments and availability by period, request it before continuing. If which technique to apply first is not specified, start with smoothing (resource smoothing) to preserve the finish date, and if over-assignment persists, apply leveling. If maximum availability per resource is not indicated, assume 8 hours/day per person. If interchangeable and specialized resources are not distinguished, assume each person has a unique, non-interchangeable role.

INSUMOS: Schedule with activities, durations, ES/EF dates, floats, and resource assignments per activity; availability profile for each resource.

PASOS:
1. Build the current load histogram by resource and by period; identify all periods with over-assignment — produce demand peak table.
2. Apply resource smoothing: shift non-critical activities within their total float to reduce peaks; record which activities shift and by how many days.
3. Verify whether over-assignment was resolved; if it persists, apply resource leveling to activities of lower strategic priority, accepting a possible extension of the project duration.
4. Calculate the new leveled load profile and compare it with the original profile.
5. Produce change table: activity | original ES date | new ES date | days shifted | float consumed | resource freed.

SALIDA: Date change table, original vs. leveled load histogram (in text/ASCII or table by period), impact on project duration, and summary of decisions made.

CASOS BORDE:
- If over-assignment cannot be resolved without extending the project beyond an acceptable threshold: present scenarios with different extension thresholds and their implications.
- If there are resources with over-assignment on the critical path: document that leveling will affect the finish date and quantify the impact.
- If there are resources shared with other projects: flag the activity as dependent on external negotiation and exclude it from automatic leveling.

[C · CRITERIA] The resulting load profile does not exceed the maximum availability of any resource in any period. It is documented which technique was used for each shifted activity. The impact on project duration is quantified. DoD: leveled histogram, complete change table, finish date impact documented.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Over-assigned schedule → smoothing + leveling → leveled load profile + change table + duration impact.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-hitos-milest:
[S · SITUATION] A project team needs to communicate progress and delivery commitments to the sponsor and stakeholders in a synthetic, results-oriented way. The Milestone Plan is the high-level communication artifact that defines the project's key control points with their committed dates.

[P · REQUEST] Define the project milestones (events without duration that mark the completion of a phase or the availability of a key deliverable), assign them target dates, owners, and observable acceptance criteria, and produce the milestone plan in a format communicable to the steering committee.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project manager with experience in executive communication and strategic milestone planning for transformation and technology projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the list of deliverables or project phases, request it before continuing — it is the blocking field. If dates are not indicated, derive them from the schedule if available, or mark as [DATE TO BE CONFIRMED]. If the number of milestones is not specified, identify between 5 and 12 milestones for a typical-duration project (fewer for short projects, more for complex ones). If no output format is specified, produce executive table + textual milestone diagram.

INSUMOS: List of phases, key deliverables, or reference schedule for the project; project start and end dates.

PASOS:
1. Review the project content and identify the natural control points (end of phase, approved deliverable, go/no-go decision, regulatory approval, etc.) — produce preliminary list of candidate milestones.
2. Filter and prioritize the milestones of greatest communicative value: those representing decisions, contractual commitments, or verifiable deliverables.
3. For each milestone: assign a clear name in "[Deliverable] [approved/completed/available]" format, target date, owner (role), and an observable acceptance criterion in one sentence.
4. Verify temporal coherence between milestones (no milestones in impossible sequence) and alignment with the project's critical path.
5. Produce executive milestone table and description of the milestone diagram in a textual timeline.

SALIDA: Milestone table with name, date, owner, and acceptance criterion; textual timeline diagram; risk notes for milestones with adjusted dates or without a confirmed owner.

CASOS BORDE:
- If two milestones have ambiguous or mutually dependent acceptance criteria: flag it and propose clarification.
- If the number of milestones exceeds 15: recommend grouping them into management milestones (executive level) and control milestones (team level).
- If the project does not have a clearly defined end: document it as a risk and propose a formal closure milestone.

[C · CRITERIA] Each milestone has a name in deliverable+status format, date, owner, and observable acceptance criterion. Milestones are in coherent temporal sequence. The plan is understandable by the steering committee without additional context. DoD: complete milestone table, timeline diagram, risk notes.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Deliverables and phases → milestones with observable criteria → executive table + timeline + risk notes.
spec-gestion-proyectos_diagrama-gantt-na:
[S · SITUATION] The project team has completed schedule planning and needs to communicate it visually and understandably to both technical and executive audiences. The Gantt chart is the standard schedule representation, but without narrative it remains a table of dates with no context for why the project flows the way it does.

[P · REQUEST] Build the project Gantt chart in structured text format (ASCII representation or markdown table with time bars) and accompany it with an explanatory narrative that describes the sequence logic, phases, key milestones, critical dependencies, and the highest schedule risk points.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project planner and technical communicator, expert in translating complex schedules into understandable visualizations with decision-oriented narrative.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the list of activities with start and end dates, request it before continuing. If the temporal granularity of the Gantt is not specified, use weeks as the base unit for 1–6 month projects, months for longer projects. If whether to include the critical path is not indicated, mark it with a visually differentiated symbol. If the audience level is not specified, produce two sections: executive view (milestones and phases) and team view (detailed activities).

INSUMOS: List of activities with code, name, start date, end date, and predecessor(s) if available; identified milestones; critical path if calculated.

PASOS:
1. Organize activities by phase or by start order; calculate the time scale (number of periods to represent) — produce draft structure.
2. Build the Gantt visual representation in markdown table format: activity column + period columns (weeks or months) with filled cells for the execution period; mark milestones with "◆" and critical activities with "█" vs. non-critical activities with "░".
3. Draft the executive narrative (max. 200 words): description of the main phases, sequence logic, and key control points.
4. Draft the team narrative: description of the most important dependencies, critical activities that cannot be delayed, and the highest schedule risk points.
5. Flag in the narrative any period of high concentration of parallel activities or resource scarcity.

SALIDA: Gantt table in markdown with time scale, milestones, and visual differentiation of critical path; executive narrative (max. 200 words); team narrative with dependencies and schedule risks.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the project has more than 30 activities: build a summary view with phases and milestones, and propose that the detailed view be generated per separate phase.
- If there is significant overlap of activities in a period: alert it in the narrative as a high-pressure period.
- If the critical path was not previously calculated: build the Gantt without criticality differentiation and recommend it as the next step.

[C · CRITERIA] The Gantt is readable in plain text. Milestones are visually differentiated. The executive narrative is understandable without viewing the Gantt. The team narrative identifies at least 3 critical dependencies and 2 risk points. DoD: complete Gantt table, executive narrative, team narrative.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Activities with dates → textual Gantt with milestones and criticality → executive narrative + team narrative.
spec-gestion-proyectos_linea-base-cronog:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has completed the development and review of the schedule and needs to formalize the approved baseline that will serve as the reference for measuring project performance throughout its lifecycle. The schedule baseline is the official starting point against which actual dates will be compared.

[P · REQUEST] Generate the schedule baseline document with the committed dates (planned start and finish) by activity and milestone, the associated change control procedure, the tracking indicators (SPI, SV), and the conditions under which the baseline must be formally revised.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: PMP-certified project manager specializing in performance control and schedule baseline management in medium and high-complexity projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the schedule with approved ES/EF dates, request it before continuing. If it is not indicated whether the schedule was approved by the sponsor, assume it is pending approval and include a signature section. If the tracking tool is not specified, define the indicators in a tool-agnostic format applicable to any tool. If the variation threshold for requesting a baseline change is not indicated, assume ±10% SPI variation or deviation of more than 5 days on critical activities.

INSUMOS: Complete schedule with activities, planned start and end dates, milestones, critical path, and sponsor name.

PASOS:
1. Extract the planned start and end dates of all activities and milestones; organize by phase — produce baseline table.
2. Define tracking indicators: SPI (Schedule Performance Index = EV/PV) and SV (Schedule Variance = EV − PV) with formula, measurement frequency, and alert threshold.
3. Document the change control procedure for the baseline: who can request a change, who approves, what documentation is required, and what conditions justify a re-baselining.
4. Define the formal baseline revision conditions (approved scope change, force majeure, significant resource addition).
5. Produce the complete document with formal cover page, baseline table, indicators, change procedure, and approval section.

SALIDA: Schedule baseline document with: table of committed dates by activity and milestone, SPI/SV indicator definition, change control procedure, revision conditions, and approval section.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the schedule has more than 100 activities: include in the baseline only the milestones and critical path activities; the full detail is referenced as an annex.
- If the schedule still has unconfirmed dates: mark it as "DRAFT" and do not process it as a baseline until all dates are available.
- If the project has no identified sponsor: document it as a governance risk and propose a baseline owner.

[C · CRITERIA] Each activity and milestone has recorded planned start and end dates. The SPI and SV indicators have a formula, threshold, and measurement frequency. The change control procedure is concrete and actionable. The document has an approval section. DoD: complete baseline table, indicators defined, change procedure documented, approval section included.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Approved schedule → baseline table + SPI/SV indicators + change control procedure → formal document ready to sign.
spec-gestion-proyectos_programacion-cade:
[S · SITUATION] A project has a CPM-built schedule that systematically runs late because teams consume all the individual floats of each activity (student syndrome, Parkinson's law). The manager wants to apply Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) to eliminate individual floats, aggregate them as project and feeding buffers, and improve the probability of meeting the finish date.

[P · REQUEST] Apply the CCPM method to the schedule: identify the critical chain (critical activities considering resource constraints), eliminate individual safety floats (reduce durations to 50% of the PERT estimate or the aggressive estimate), calculate the size of the project buffer (PB) and the feeding buffers (FB) for non-critical chains, and produce the CCPM schedule with the buffer schedule.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Specialist in Theory of Constraints and Critical Chain Project Management with experience implementing CCPM in manufacturing, construction, and product development projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the schedule with PERT durations or safe estimates, request it before continuing. If aggressive durations (50%) are not provided, calculate them as 50% of the safe duration — declare this assumption. If the project buffer size is not specified, use the 50% of the critical chain method as a starting point. If it is not indicated whether resources are assigned per activity, assume there are resource constraints that modify the critical chain relative to pure CPM.

INSUMOS: Schedule with activities, safe durations (PERT or conservative estimate), and predecessors; resource assignment per activity if available.

PASOS:
1. Identify the critical chain: start from the CPM path and adjust for resource conflicts (if two consecutive activities require the same resource, the resource constraint makes that sequence part of the critical chain).
2. Reduce individual durations to the aggressive estimate (50% of safe) and eliminate all individual safety floats.
3. Calculate the project buffer (PB) = sum of floats removed from the critical chain × 50% (cut and paste method); or calculate with standard deviation if PERT estimates were used.
4. Identify the feeding chains (non-critical activities that feed the critical chain) and calculate the feeding buffer (FB) for each one = 50% of the sum of floats removed from that chain.
5. Build the CCPM schedule: critical chain + buffers + feeding chain start schedule delayed as late as possible (back scheduling).

SALIDA: CCPM schedule with aggressive durations, identified critical chain, calculated PB, FBs calculated per feeding chain, and comparative table CCPM vs. original CPM (duration, buffers, finish date).

CASOS BORDE:
- If the critical chain changes significantly from the CPM critical path due to resource constraints: explain the difference and its impact on project management.
- If the resulting project buffer is less than 25% of the critical chain: alert that the buffer may be insufficient and recommend revisiting estimates.
- If the team is not familiar with CCPM: include a 3-essential-behavioral-rules orientation section for the team (do not add individual floats, report remaining time not time consumed, start activities as soon as possible).

[C · CRITERIA] The critical chain is identified considering resource constraints. The PB is calculated with an explicit method. Each feeding chain has its FB. The CCPM schedule shows aggressive durations with explicit buffers. The comparison vs. CPM is present. DoD: critical chain identified, PB and FBs calculated, CCPM schedule built, comparison documented.

Protocolo MetodologIA: CPM schedule → critical chain with resource constraints → aggressive durations + PB + FBs → CCPM schedule with comparison.
spec-gestion-proyectos_planificacion-ola:
[S · SITUATION] A medium or long-duration project operates in an environment with significant uncertainty in future phases, making it impossible or imprudent to plan all activities at the same level of detail from the start. The project manager needs to establish a rolling wave planning strategy that defines what is planned in detail now and what will be planned progressively as the project advances and better information is available.

[P · REQUEST] Design the rolling wave plan for the project: define the planning horizons (detail window, summary window, and beyond), the maturity criteria for advancing from wave to wave, the artifacts updated in each wave, the re-planning calendar, and the uncertainty thresholds that justify keeping activities at summary level.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior program manager with experience in adaptive planning, portfolio management, and rolling wave planning for R&D, digital transformation, and new product development projects.

SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the project description and its phases, request it before continuing. If the total project duration is not specified, assume the detail horizon is the current quarter (3 months) and the summary horizon is the following quarter. If the re-planning frequency is not indicated, assume re-planning at the start of each phase or every 4 weeks, whichever comes first. If the level of detail for the near horizon is not specified, assume 1–5 day activities for the detail horizon.

INSUMOS: Project description, list of known phases or deliverables, total estimated duration, uncertainty level per phase if known.

PASOS:
1. Identify the project phases or work blocks and classify them by certainty level: high certainty (plan in detail), medium uncertainty (plan at work package level), high uncertainty (plan only at milestone level) — produce certainty map by phase.
2. Define the three planning horizons: (a) detail horizon (near window, granular activities), (b) summary horizon (medium window, work packages), (c) beyond the horizon (milestones and assumptions).
3. Establish the maturity criteria that allow a phase to advance from the summary horizon to the detail one (e.g., previous deliverable approved, requirements confirmed, resources assigned).
4. Define the re-planning calendar: trigger event + artifacts updated in each wave (WBS, activity list, schedule, assumptions register).
5. Produce the rolling wave planning strategy document and the horizon summary table.

SALIDA: Certainty map by phase, definition of the three planning horizons, maturity criteria for transition between waves, re-planning calendar, and summary table.

CASOS BORDE:
- If all phases have high uncertainty: recommend an agile approach with sprints instead of rolling wave, and document the justification.
- If stakeholders press for a complete schedule from the start: document the risk of premature planning and propose committing only to phase milestones.
- If the project has contractual commitments in high-uncertainty phases: flag them as critical risks requiring explicit contingency reserves.

[C · CRITERIA] Planning horizons are clearly defined with differentiated granularity. Maturity criteria are observable and verifiable. The re-planning calendar is concrete (dates or trigger events). The strategy justifies the uncertainty of future phases to stakeholders. DoD: complete certainty map, horizons defined, maturity criteria documented, re-planning calendar established.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Project with phases and certainty levels → rolling wave planning horizons → maturity criteria + re-planning calendar + documented strategy.
spec-gestion-proyectos_simulacion-montec:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has a schedule with estimated durations for each activity and needs to quantify the probability of meeting the committed delivery date given the uncertainty of actual durations.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a Monte Carlo schedule simulation report with: probability distributions per activity, P10/P50/P80/P90 percentiles of the project completion date, frequency histogram and cumulative probability S-curve, and identification of the three activities with the greatest contribution to total variance.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior expert in quantitative project risk analysis, PMI-RMP certified, with mastery of Monte Carlo simulation applied to schedules (PERT, Triangular, Beta-PERT).
SUPUESTOS: If the user does not indicate the simulation tool, assume manual/Excel calculation with Triangular distribution (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic). If no number of iterations is provided, use 10,000. If correlations between activities are not specified, assume independence. Declare these assumptions at the start; only ask if confidence in the distribution type is less than 0.85.
INSUMOS: List of activities with optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic duration (pasted in the thread), or attached table.
PASOS:
1. Review the list of activities and identify the base critical path.
2. Assign a probability distribution to each activity based on the three provided points.
3. Run 10,000 iterations (or simulate analytically if data is sufficient) calculating the total project duration in each iteration.
4. Calculate P10, P50, P80, and P90 percentiles of the completion date.
5. Build frequency histogram and cumulative probability curve.
6. Calculate each activity's contribution to total variance (sensitivity analysis / tornado).
7. Draft conclusion with the probability of meeting the committed date and time buffer recommendations.
SALIDA: Structured report with: (a) distribution table by activity, (b) P10–P90 percentile table, (c) textual description of histogram and S-curve, (d) tornado diagram with top 3 critical activities, (e) schedule buffer recommendation expressed in days.
CASOS BORDE:
- Activities with high correlation (e.g., same team): declare assumption of correlation 0.7 and sensitize result.
- Insufficient data (only one duration per activity): use ±20% as triangular range and warn of limitation.
- Project already started with partial progress: exclude completed activities and recalculate only the remainder.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Percentiles must be reproducible with the same input data.
- The tornado diagram must identify at least three activities with >10% contribution to variance.
- The buffer recommendation must express absolute days and percentage over the base duration.
- Trade-off: more iterations = greater precision but higher computational cost; 10,000 is sufficient for standard error <1% at P50.
- DoD: the report is acceptable when the manager can make a decision to accept or reject the committed date with quantitative evidence.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_analisis-holgura-:
[S · SITUATION] The project team has a schedule with defined activities, dependencies, and durations, and needs to identify which activities have start/end flexibility and which cannot be delayed without affecting the delivery date.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete float and slack analysis that includes: calculation of total float (TF) and free float (FF) per activity, identification of the critical path, table of activities with the highest risk of chained delay, and float management recommendations to protect the delivery date.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior expert in project planning and control with mastery of CPM (Critical Path Method), forward/backward pass calculation, and proactive float management.
SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide the complete precedence network, build it from the ordered list of activities with their predecessors. If no work calendar is indicated, assume 5 days/week with no holidays. If dependency type is not specified, assume Finish-to-Start (FS) with zero lag. Declare these assumptions at the start; only ask if there is ambiguity in more than 3 critical dependencies.
INSUMOS: List of activities with duration, predecessors, and dependency type (pasted in the thread).
PASOS:
1. Build the network diagram (activity nodes) from the dependency list.
2. Execute the forward pass: calculate ES (Early Start) and EF (Early Finish) for each activity.
3. Execute the backward pass: calculate LS (Late Start) and LF (Late Finish) for each activity.
4. Calculate total float (TF = LS − ES) and free float (FF = ES_successor − EF_activity) for each activity.
5. Identify the critical path (TF = 0) and subcritical paths (TF ≤ 2 days or specified threshold).
6. Build summary table: activity / ES / EF / LS / LF / TF / FF / Critical?
7. Draft risk analysis: activities whose delay chains impacts, and float management recommendations.
SALIDA: (a) Complete CPM table with ES/EF/LS/LF/TF/FF per activity, (b) list of critical path activities, (c) list of subcritical activities with TF ≤ threshold, (d) float management recommendations (e.g., freeze early start on critical activities, protect buffers on subcritical ones).
CASOS BORDE:
- Activities with multiple successors: calculate FF using the minimum ES of all successors.
- Network with loops or circular dependencies: detect and report error before calculating.
- Project with multiple critical paths of equal duration: report all and warn of greater fragility.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each activity must have TF and FF calculated explicitly, not estimated.
- The critical path must be contiguous from project start to project end.
- Management recommendations must be actionable (what to do, not just what to avoid).
- Trade-off: publishing TF to teams can create Parkinson's Law behavior; recommend reserved float management.
- DoD: the manager can prioritize resources and advance/delay decisions based on the delivered table.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-costos:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has a WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) with defined work packages and needs to build a detailed cost estimate starting from the lowest level of the WBS upward to obtain the total project budget.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a bottom-up cost estimate that includes: estimated cost per work package and per deliverable, summary by WBS level, total aggregated budget, and a backup sheet with the basis of estimate for each line.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior expert in project cost estimation and control, with mastery of bottom-up methodology, resource costing (labor, materials, equipment, subcontracts), and documentation of basis of estimate per PMI standards.
SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide resource rates, use [ASSUMPTION] and request rates or ask the user to complete them. If currency is not indicated, assume USD. If effort levels are not specified, derive them from the activity descriptions; only ask if there is ambiguity in more than 2 work packages. If contingency reserve is not indicated, do not include it in this estimate (managed separately).
INSUMOS: WBS with work packages and description of required resources (pasted in the thread).
PASOS:
1. Review the WBS and list all work packages at the lowest level.
2. For each work package, identify the resource types: people (role, hours), materials (quantity, unit), equipment (usage, days), and subcontracts.
3. Calculate the cost of each resource: quantity × unit rate.
4. Sum costs per work package to obtain the total cost of the package.
5. Aggregate package costs within each WBS deliverable/component.
6. Aggregate deliverable costs to obtain the total project budget (without reserves).
7. Document basis of estimate: rate source, effort assumptions, exclusions.
SALIDA: (a) Detailed cost table by work package with resource breakdown, (b) summary table by WBS level, (c) total aggregated budget in one line, (d) basis of estimate section with declared assumptions and explicit exclusions.
CASOS BORDE:
- Work package with ambiguous scope: estimate range (minimum–maximum) and mark as [ASSUMPTION] with justification.
- Resources shared between packages: prorate by hours dedicated to each package.
- Costs in multiple currencies: convert to base currency using specified exchange rate or [ASSUMPTION] with reference date.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each cost line must have its basis of estimate documented.
- The sum of work packages must exactly equal the total of the superior deliverable.
- Exclusions must be explicit to avoid double-counting with other estimates.
- Trade-off: more detail = greater accuracy but more preparation time; bottom-up is the most precise method but requires a mature WBS.
- DoD: the sponsor can approve or challenge the budget based on the delivered backup sheet.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-analog:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager needs a quick cost or duration estimate for a new project or phase, having historical data from similar projects and/or productivity metrics (parameters) from the organization.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a cost or duration estimate using analogous and/or parametric techniques, with: selection and justification of the historical reference project(s), calculation of the adjustment for scale or complexity differences, estimate result with confidence range (±%), and basis of estimate sheet documenting the method, source data, and applicability limits.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior expert in project estimation with mastery of analogous techniques (expert judgment + historical analogy) and parametric techniques (regression models, complexity factors, CERs — Cost Estimating Relationships).
SUPUESTOS: If the user does not provide historical projects, request at least one comparable one before calculating. If no scale parameter is indicated (m², lines of code, function points, units), infer from the project context and declare [ASSUMPTION]. If no preferred technique is specified, use both and compare results. Only ask if it is not possible to infer the scope of the new project with confidence ≥ 0.85.
INSUMOS: Description of the new project/phase, data from similar historical projects and/or productivity parameters (pasted in the thread).
PASOS:
1. Analyze the new project description and identify the main cost/duration drivers (size, complexity, technology, geography).
2. Select the most comparable historical project and calculate the adjustment factor for differences (scale, complexity, inflation if applicable).
3. Apply analogous estimate: cost/duration of the historical project × adjustment factor.
4. If parameters are available (rate per unit, team speed), apply parametric estimate: parameter × number of units of the new project.
5. Compare both results and justify which has greater reliability.
6. Express the estimate as a central value ± % uncertainty based on the maturity of information.
7. Document bases: reference projects, parameter source, applied adjustments, exclusions, and validity conditions.
SALIDA: (a) Comparative table of analogous vs. parametric estimate (if both apply), (b) recommended estimate with confidence range, (c) basis of estimate sheet with method, source data, adjustments, assumptions, and exclusions, (d) estimate reliability traffic light (High/Medium/Low) with justification.
CASOS BORDE:
- Project without a comparable historical reference: use parametric with sector benchmark and mark reliability as Low.
- Multiple historical references with highly dispersed results: present wide range and recommend bottom-up if dispersion exceeds 30%.
- Significant inflation between the historical reference and the new project: adjust with price index and declare source.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Historical reference projects must be comparable in scope, technology, and context.
- The uncertainty range must reflect the actual maturity of the information (±5–15% for mature analogous, ±30–50% for parametric at conceptual stage).
- Exclusions must be explicit.
- Trade-off: analogous is faster but less precise than bottom-up; recommended only in early stages or for sanity check.
- DoD: the sponsor can use the estimate for a go/no-go decision with full awareness of the uncertainty level.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_linea-base-costos:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has the approved cost estimate by work package and needs to build the cost baseline by distributing spending over time to generate the reference S-curve that will serve as the comparison baseline during execution.

[P · REQUEST] Produce the project cost baseline including: temporal distribution of planned spending (PV) by period, planned-value S-curve, cumulative cost table by month/week, and description of the distribution criteria applied.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in project financial planning with mastery of cost baseline construction, distribution of spending over time, and S-curve generation in accordance with the PMI standard (PMBOK® 7th edition).
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide the detailed schedule, distribute costs linearly within the duration of each activity or work package. If no reporting period is indicated, use months. If no distinction is made between direct and indirect costs, treat all as direct in the baseline. If the management reserve is not mentioned, do not include it in the baseline (it goes in the total budget but outside the baseline). Declare assumptions at the beginning.
INPUTS: Approved cost estimate by work package with start and end dates, or schedule with durations (pasted in the thread).
STEPS:
1. Review the cost estimate and the baseline schedule for each work package.
2. Distribute each work package's cost across the periods of its duration according to the appropriate criterion (linear, front-loaded, back-loaded, or milestone-based).
3. Sum the distributed costs by period to obtain the monthly/weekly planned spending (periodic PV).
4. Calculate the cumulative PV period by period to generate the S-curve.
5. Build the baseline table: period / periodic PV / cumulative PV.
6. Describe the distribution criteria applied and the timing assumptions.
7. Identify spending peaks and the periods of highest financial exposure in the project.
OUTPUT: (a) Cost baseline table with columns: Period / Periodic PV / Cumulative PV, (b) S-curve description (shape, peaks, inflection), (c) identification of the 3 highest-spending periods and their cause, (d) notes on distribution criteria and assumptions.
EDGE CASES:
- Activities spanning multiple periods with milestone payments (e.g. fixed-price contract): distribute cost at payment milestones, not linearly.
- Projects with procurement costs (large purchases): record in the commitment period or delivery period according to the declared accounting policy.
- Parallel activities that create a spending peak >40% of the budget in one period: warn of cash flow risk and recommend leveling.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The total of the S-curve at project end must exactly equal the approved work budget (BAC).
- Each period must have its periodic and cumulative PV stated explicitly.
- Distribution criteria must be documented and reproducible.
- Trade-off: linear distribution is simple but may not reflect the actual consumption curve; milestone-based distribution is more precise but requires a detailed schedule.
- DoD: the control team can use the S-curve to compare against actual EV at each control point.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_reservas-continge:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has the project base budget and needs to calculate and justify the contingency reserve (for identified risks) and the management reserve (for unknown risks), so that the total approved budget covers the real uncertainty of the project.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a reserves document that includes: calculation of the contingency reserve based on the quantified risk register, calculation of the management reserve using the appropriate percentage over the base budget, summary table of the total budget (BAC + reserves), and justification of the percentages applied.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in quantitative risk management and project finance, with mastery of the budget determination process per the PMBOK and reserve quantification techniques (expected monetary value, Monte Carlo analysis, percentage over base budget).
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide a quantified risk register, calculate the contingency reserve using the sector standard percentage (10–15% for medium-complexity projects, 20–25% for high complexity) and declare [ASSUMPTION]. If no management reserve percentage is specified, use 5% over the base budget plus the contingency reserve. If the project complexity level is not indicated, infer it from context. Declare all assumptions at the beginning.
INPUTS: Project base budget (BAC without reserves), risk register with probability and monetary impact if available (pasted in the thread).
STEPS:
1. Review the base budget and the available risk register.
2. For each quantified risk: calculate the Expected Monetary Value (EMV = probability × impact).
3. Sum all EMVs to obtain the minimum recommended contingency reserve.
4. If no quantified register exists, apply the standard percentage over the base budget.
5. Calculate the management reserve: 5% (or agreed percentage) over the base budget + contingency reserve.
6. Build the total budget table: Base budget / Contingency reserve / Management reserve / Total authorized budget.
7. Justify each amount with the methodology applied, the risks it covers, and the conditions of use.
OUTPUT: (a) EMV calculation table by risk (if a register exists), (b) total budget table with the four components, (c) justification of the calculation methodology for each reserve, (d) access and release conditions for each reserve (who authorizes, under what condition).
EDGE CASES:
- Project with no risk register: use percentage over base budget and urgently recommend creating the register.
- Risks with very high impact (>30% of base budget): review whether the risk should be managed with a specific response plan rather than just reserving funds.
- Fixed-price projects: clarify that the reserve is internal to the vendor team, not the client's.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The contingency reserve must be backed by the risk register or by a justified percentage.
- The management reserve is not included in the cost baseline but is included in the total authorized budget.
- The conditions of use for each reserve must be explicit and approved by the sponsor.
- Trade-off: very high reserves protect the project but reduce competitiveness; very low reserves expose the project to cost overruns.
- DoD: the sponsor approves the total budget with a full understanding of what each component covers.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_seguimiento-presu:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager is in the execution phase and receives actual cost reports for the period. They need to compare actual spending (AC) against planned spending (PV) by period and cumulatively, identify deviations, and generate a budget monitoring report that allows corrective decisions to be made in time.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a budget monitoring report that includes: comparison table of planned vs. actual budget by period and cumulatively, calculation of absolute and percentage variances, identification of the line items with the greatest deviation, budget status traffic light, and corrective action recommendations.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in project financial control with mastery of budget monitoring, variance analysis, and preparation of financial performance reports for steering committees.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide the cost baseline, request it before calculating variances. If no cutoff period is indicated, use the most recent period available in the data. If actual data includes commitments (open purchase orders), treat them as projected AC and declare it. If no alert threshold is specified, use ±10% variance as the attention threshold and ±20% as the critical alert threshold.
INPUTS: Cost baseline (PV by period) and actual cost report (AC by period) up to the cutoff date (pasted in the thread).
STEPS:
1. Align the cost baseline with the actual cost report by period and line item.
2. Calculate the periodic variance: Variance = PV_period − AC_period.
3. Calculate the cumulative variance: Variance_cum = PV_cum − AC_cum.
4. Calculate the deviation percentage: (Variance / PV) × 100.
5. Apply the traffic light: Green (deviation < 10%), Yellow (10–20%), Red (>20% or growing trend).
6. Identify the 3–5 line items with the greatest absolute deviation and analyze their probable causes.
7. Draft corrective action recommendations for line items in Yellow or Red status.
OUTPUT: (a) Monitoring table: Line Item / Cumulative PV / Cumulative AC / Variance $ / Variance % / Traffic Light, (b) textual trend chart (planned vs. actual S-curve), (c) analysis of line items with the greatest deviation and probable causes, (d) prioritized corrective action recommendations.
EDGE CASES:
- AC > PV but project is ahead of schedule: interpret correctly using EV if progress data is available.
- Line item with AC = 0 even though the period has passed: investigate whether it is a recording omission or an activity that has not started.
- Report with missing data for some periods: interpolate with the average of adjacent periods and warn of the limitation.

[C · CRITERIA]
- All variances must be expressed both in absolute value and as a percentage.
- The traffic light must be applied consistently with the declared threshold.
- Recommendations must be actionable, specific to the deviating line items, and include a suggested responsible party.
- Trade-off: focusing only on cost variance may hide scope problems; recommend complementing with EVM if progress data is available.
- DoD: the committee can make budget reallocation or corrective action decisions based on the report.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_pronostico-presup:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has performance data from a project in execution (PV, EV, AC, BAC) and needs to project the total cost the project will have upon completion, using the Estimate at Completion (EAC) formulas from the Earned Value method.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a cost Estimate at Completion (EAC) forecast report that includes: EAC calculation using the four standard PMI formulas, selection and justification of the most appropriate EAC based on the project scenario, calculation of ETC (Estimate to Complete) and VAC (Variance at Completion), and recommendation of actions to close the gap if VAC is negative.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in Earned Value Management (EVM) analysis with mastery of EAC, ETC, VAC, and TCPI metrics, and the ability to interpret different forecast scenarios according to real project conditions.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide all EVM values (PV, EV, AC, BAC), calculate what is possible with the available data and warn which are missing. If no expected scenario for the second half of the project is specified, calculate all four EACs and recommend the most prudent one. If CPI < 0.8, additionally recommend the TCPI to assess recovery feasibility.
INPUTS: Project EVM data at the cutoff date: BAC, PV, EV, AC (pasted in the thread or in a table).
STEPS:
1. Verify that the four base EVM values are available (BAC, PV, EV, AC).
2. Calculate the four standard EACs:
   a. EAC1 = BAC / CPI (assuming past performance will continue)
   b. EAC2 = AC + (BAC − EV) (assuming remaining work will be executed at budget)
   c. EAC3 = AC + [(BAC − EV) / CPI] (assuming remaining work will follow the current CPI)
   d. EAC4 = AC + [(BAC − EV) / (CPI × SPI)] (assuming combined impact of cost and schedule)
3. Calculate ETC for the selected EAC: ETC = EAC − AC.
4. Calculate VAC = BAC − EAC (negative = projected cost overrun).
5. Calculate TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC) to assess the efficiency required for remaining work.
6. Select and justify the most appropriate EAC based on project context (can the team improve?, are there scope changes?, is CPI stable?).
7. If VAC < 0, draft corrective action recommendations to reduce the projected cost overrun.
OUTPUT: (a) Table with the four calculated EACs, (b) recommended EAC with justification of the assumed scenario, (c) ETC, VAC, and TCPI, (d) interpretation of TCPI (is it realistic to achieve that efficiency level?), (e) action recommendations if VAC < 0.
EDGE CASES:
- CPI > 1 (project under budget): still calculate all four EACs; the most conservative forecast is EAC1.
- Project with scope changes not integrated into BAC: recalculate with adjusted BAC before forecasting.
- TCPI > 1.1: indicate that recovering efficiency is very difficult; recommend replanning the BAC.

[C · CRITERIA]
- All four EACs must be calculated explicitly with their formulas.
- The recommended EAC must be accompanied by a justification based on the real project behavior.
- TCPI must be interpreted qualitatively (easy/difficult/impossible to recover).
- Trade-off: EAC1 is the most conservative and common in projects with a stable CPI; EAC2 is optimistic and valid only if the causes of the overrun have already been resolved.
- DoD: the sponsor can decide to intervene, replan, or accept the cost overrun based on the report.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_business-case-ref:
[S · SITUATION] A project has been in execution for several months and the sponsor or steering committee requires an update to the original business case to confirm that the investment continues to be justified in light of changes that have occurred: cost overruns, delays, scope changes, market variations, or newly available alternatives.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a business case update report that includes: comparison of the current state vs. original business case assumptions, recalculation of key financial indicators (NPV, ROI, payback, IRR), continuous viability analysis, evaluation of options (continue / replan / cancel), and a reasoned recommendation for the committee.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in business analysis and portfolio management with mastery of project financial evaluation (NPV, IRR, ROI, payback), continuous viability analysis, and presentation to steering committees.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide the original business case, build the comparison with available data and indicate the gaps as [ASSUMPTION]. If updated cash flows are not provided, recalculate using available actual cost data and EAC/ETC forecast. If no discount rate is specified, use 10% [ASSUMPTION] to calculate NPV. Ask the user only if more than 3 critical financial data points are missing.
INPUTS: Original business case (or summary), current performance data (actual costs, progress, EAC/ETC forecast), and context changes that have occurred since the start (pasted in the thread).
STEPS:
1. Review the key assumptions of the original business case: expected benefits, total cost, schedule, original IRR/NPV/ROI.
2. Update the assumptions with current information: new projected cost (EAC), new delivery date, changes in expected benefits.
3. Recalculate the financial indicators with the updated assumptions.
4. Compare the original vs. updated indicators in a side-by-side table.
5. Analyze the causes of the deviations and assess whether they are temporary or structural.
6. Evaluate three options: (a) continue as planned, (b) replan scope/budget, (c) cancel the project.
7. Draft the committee recommendation with justification based on updated indicators and option analysis.
OUTPUT: (a) Comparative table: original vs. current assumptions by indicator, (b) financial indicators table: NPV / IRR / ROI / payback — original vs. updated, (c) option analysis with pros/cons of each, (d) committee recommendation with explicit reasoning and next steps.
EDGE CASES:
- Updated NPV remains positive despite the overrun: recommend continuing with a recovery plan.
- Updated IRR falls below the cost of capital: recommend replanning or canceling with a cancellation cost analysis.
- Market changes affecting expected benefits: quantify the impact on NPV and present pessimistic/base/optimistic scenarios.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The original vs. updated comparison must be explicit for each financial indicator.
- The recommendation must be based on quantitative evidence, not just intuition.
- The option analysis must include the cancellation cost if applicable.
- Trade-off: sunk cost bias can lead to continuing non-viable projects; the analysis must be based only on future cash flows.
- DoD: the committee can make an informed decision to continue, replan, or cancel with the information provided.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_valor-ganado-pv-e:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager is in the execution phase and needs to calculate the three fundamental values of the Earned Value method (EVM) at the cutoff date: Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC), to establish the basis for all subsequent performance analyses.

[P · REQUEST] Produce the EVM metrics table with PV, EV, and AC calculated for each activity or work package at the cutoff date, with the project total summary and the progress measurement methodology applied to each activity.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in Earned Value Management (EVM) with mastery of baseline metric calculation, progress measurement methods (0/100, 50/50, weighted milestones, percentage complete, completed units), and application of the technique in accordance with the PMI Practice Standard for EVM.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not specify the progress measurement method per activity, use percentage complete as reported by the team (declare [ASSUMPTION]). If there is no actual cost data per activity, use the total actual cost for the period and distribute it proportionally to EV (declare [ASSUMPTION]). If the user does not indicate the cutoff date, use the most recent one available in the data.
INPUTS: List of activities or work packages with: BAC for each, percentage of progress reported at the cutoff date, and actual costs incurred (pasted in the thread).
STEPS:
1. For each activity: calculate PV = BAC_activity × (planned percentage at the cutoff date per the baseline schedule).
2. For each activity: calculate EV = BAC_activity × (actual progress percentage at the cutoff date).
3. For each activity: record AC = actual cost incurred up to the cutoff date.
4. Sum PV, EV, and AC for all activities to obtain the project total values.
5. Document the progress measurement method used for each activity.
6. Present the three values in a structured table with totals.
7. Flag any activity where the measurement method is questionable or unreliable.
OUTPUT: (a) EVM table with columns: Activity / BAC / Planned % / PV / Actual % / EV / AC / Measurement method, (b) project totals row: total PV / total EV / total AC, (c) notes on the reliability of progress data per activity.
EDGE CASES:
- Activity with reported 100% progress but actual costs still flowing: EV = BAC but AC can keep growing; warn about the impact on performance indices.
- Activity not started even though it should be progressing per the schedule: PV > 0, EV = 0; flag as a critical delay.
- Activities with 0/100 method: EV is 0 until completed; warn that it may distort indices in intermediate periods.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each activity must have its three values (PV, EV, AC) calculated explicitly.
- Project totals must be the exact sum of all activity values.
- The progress measurement method must be declared per activity to ensure reproducibility.
- Trade-off: percentage complete is flexible but subjective; weighted milestones are more objective but require prior milestone definition.
- DoD: the three project total values are ready to calculate variances (CV, SV) and indices (CPI, SPI) in the next step.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_indices-desempeno:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has the EVM values for the project at the cutoff date (PV, EV, AC) and needs to calculate the cost performance index (CPI) and schedule performance index (SPI) to evaluate project efficiency and communicate its status to stakeholders.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an EVM performance index report with: calculation of CPI and SPI by period and cumulatively, qualitative interpretation of each index, status traffic light, trend of the indices over time (if prior period data is available), and action recommendations based on the CPI/SPI combination.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in Earned Value Management with mastery of the interpretation of CPI and SPI performance indices, their significance ranges, and their behavior as predictive indicators of future performance.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide historical data from prior periods, calculate only the cumulative indices and warn that trend analysis is not possible. If no traffic light thresholds are specified, use: Green (CPI/SPI ≥ 0.95), Yellow (0.80–0.94), Red (< 0.80). If only cumulative and not periodic data is available, calculate cumulative only. Declare assumptions at the beginning.
INPUTS: EVM values at the cutoff date: cumulative PV, cumulative EV, cumulative AC (and values from prior periods if available).
STEPS:
1. Calculate CPI = EV / AC (cost efficiency index: how much earned value per unit of actual cost).
2. Calculate SPI = EV / PV (schedule efficiency index: how much earned value per unit of planned value).
3. If prior period data is available, calculate CPI and SPI for each period to analyze the trend.
4. Apply the traffic light to each index according to the defined thresholds.
5. Qualitatively interpret the CPI/SPI combination (4 quadrants: over cost + behind schedule / under cost + behind schedule / over cost + ahead of schedule / under cost + ahead of schedule).
6. Calculate the expected cumulative CPI for the last 20% of the project (final CPI tends to converge toward the current cumulative CPI).
7. Draft action recommendations based on the project's CPI/SPI quadrant.
OUTPUT: (a) Index table: cumulative CPI / cumulative SPI / period CPI / period SPI / CPI traffic light / SPI traffic light, (b) project position quadrant (2×2 CPI vs. SPI), (c) qualitative interpretation of project status, (d) trend of indices (if historical data exists), (e) specific action recommendations.
EDGE CASES:
- SPI converges to 1.0 at project end (known SPI limitation based on time): recommend using SPI(t) based on schedule if date data is available.
- CPI < 1 but SPI > 1 (moving fast but spending too much): analyze whether the schedule advance can turn into savings or aggravates the overrun.
- CPI > 1 and SPI > 1 (project performing well): assess whether there is a risk of sacrificed quality or underestimated scope.

[C · CRITERIA]
- CPI and SPI must be calculated with two decimal places of precision.
- The quadrant interpretation must be explicit and connected to the real project situation.
- Recommendations must differentiate actions for CPI (cost) and SPI (schedule).
- Trade-off: SPI tends to 1 toward project end, so it loses predictive power; complement with SPI(t) in late stages.
- DoD: the manager can present project status to stakeholders with objective metrics and concrete recommendations.

Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze → structure → deliver artifact → validate criteria before closing.
spec-gestion-proyectos_variaciones-cv-sv:
[S · SITUATION] The project manager has the EVM values for the project at the cutoff date (PV, EV, AC) and needs to calculate the absolute cost variances (CV) and schedule variances (SV) to quantify in monetary terms how much the project is deviating from the plan and communicate the status to stakeholders with precise figures.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an EVM variance report with: calculation of CV and SV by period and cumulatively, expression of variances in absolute value and percentage, qualitative interpretation, root cause analysis of the deviations, and a response plan with prioritized corrective actions.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior expert in project control with mastery of EVM variance analysis, root cause identification, and formulation of response plans aimed at recovering project performance.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not provide prior period data, calculate only cumulative variances. If no causes for deviations are specified, infer the most probable ones from the project context and label them as [INFERENCE] for the manager to confirm. If no significance threshold is declared, report any variance >5% as significant.
