ASSUMPTIONS: if no relational data is provided, generate a network of ten typical stakeholders for a cultural transformation program in healthcare (medical director, nursing manager, administrative director, IT chief, medical union, administrative union, executive sponsor, project team, patients/community, regulatory body) with plausible relationships [ASSUMPTION]; relationships are represented in structured text format (edge list) due to lack of graphical tool [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: stakeholder list with role descriptions and indications of relationships between them, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. List all stakeholders as nodes. 2. Identify and note each relationship with direction (A→B) and type (alliance, influence, tension, dependency). 3. Detect nodes with the highest in-degree (influenced by many) and out-degree (influence many). 4. Identify bridge nodes (critical intermediaries). 5. Design two activation routes: one to gain allies from the resistant central node, another to isolate the main blocker. 6. Present the network as a Markdown edge list and an analytical summary. OUTPUT: Nodes section (table: Stakeholder | Role | Type); Edges section (table: Source | Target | Relationship Type | Intensity 1-3); Network Analysis section (central nodes, bridges, blockers); Activation Routes section (two routes with concrete steps). EDGE CASES: (a) stakeholder with high influence but hidden position (non-hierarchical): mark as Hidden Influencer and prioritize private approach; (b) very dense network (>15 relationships): summarize by clusters; (c) contradictory relational data: indicate ambiguity and propose verification. [C · CRITERIA] Each relationship must have an explicit type and direction; central nodes must be identified with a quantitative criterion (degree); activation routes must have concrete sequential steps; DoD: all sections present, nodes and edges complete, routes with at least three steps each.
spec-gestion-proyectos_resumen-ejecutivo: [S · SITUATION] A project director needs to present the current status of their project to a C-Suite-level key stakeholder (e.g., CFO or COO) who has not participated in the last three weeks of meetings and has only fifteen minutes available. The stakeholder makes budget decisions and needs to understand risk, progress, and pending decisions without diving into technical details. [P · REQUEST] Draft a one-page Executive Summary (maximum 450 words) adapted to the profile and priorities of the indicated key stakeholder: include project status (RAG), key advances for the period, risks relevant to them, decisions requiring their participation, and next critical milestones. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project manager with executive communication skills, capable of translating technical and operational complexity into clear, decision-oriented business messages. ASSUMPTIONS: if no project data is provided, assume a digital transformation project in the execution phase with 55% progress, a moderate-to-high budget risk, and a critical go-live milestone in six weeks [ASSUMPTION]; the stakeholder is the CFO with priority on cost and return [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if the required tone is unusually formal or if there are confidentiality restrictions that limit what can be written (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: project status data (progress, risks, milestones) and stakeholder profile, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the three questions the stakeholder would ask when reading this summary. 2. Build the central message (one sentence that answers status + decision needed). 3. Draft the sections: RAG status with justification; Period advances (max. 3 bullets); Risks relevant to the stakeholder (max. 2, in business language); Required decisions (concrete, with deadline); Next milestones (max. 3, with date). 4. Review tone: executive, direct, no technical jargon. OUTPUT: one-page document with header (Project | Period | Date | To | Prepared by), sections with traffic light icons for RAG, short bullets, and a final call to action. EDGE CASES: (a) project status is Red: the summary must start with the problem, not with achievements; (b) stakeholder is technical (CTO): may include more architecture detail without losing brevity; (c) multiple urgent decisions: prioritize the most blocking one and defer others to an annex table. [C · CRITERIA] Maximum 450 words; no paragraph longer than three lines; each risk must be expressed in terms of business impact (cost, time, reputation), not in technical terms; DoD: all sections present, final call to action with date, executive tone verified.
spec-gestion-proyectos_gestion-expectati: [S · SITUATION] A human resources process redesign project faces an active conflict between the HR director (who wants the simplest possible system to avoid training their team) and the IT director (who demands architecture standards that complicate the solution). The project manager is in the middle and needs to manage both parties' expectations and resolve the conflict before it escalates to the steering committee. [P · REQUEST] Design an expectations management and conflict resolution plan for the described conflict: diagnose the type and root of the conflict, propose an interest-based negotiation strategy (not position-based), develop a conversation script for the alignment meeting, and define a formalizable expectations agreement. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organizational conflict resolution consultant and negotiation facilitator with experience in projects with multiple sponsors in conflict. ASSUMPTIONS: if no conflict context is provided, assume the HR vs. IT scenario described above [ASSUMPTION]; Fisher and Ury's interest-based negotiation framework is applied [ASSUMPTION]; the project manager acts as neutral mediator [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if there is a prior conflict history that materially changes the dynamics (<=2 questions, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: conflict description, positions of each party, project context, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Diagnose the conflict type (resources, values, process, relationship). 2. Identify the underlying interests of each party (what do they really need behind their position?). 3. Design three solution options that satisfy the interests of both parties. 4. Develop a conversation script: neutral opening, interest exploration, options presentation, close with agreement. 5. Draft a one-page Expectations Agreement with specific commitments from each party. 6. Define a follow-up mechanism if the agreement is not fulfilled. OUTPUT: Conflict Diagnosis section; Underlying Interests section (table: Party | Position | Real Interest); Solution Options section (3 options with pros/cons); Conversation Script (with turn labels: Mediator/HR Director/IT Director); Draft Expectations Agreement; Follow-up Mechanism. EDGE CASES: (a) conflict with political/power component (one executive wants to block the other): include recommendation to escalate to the sponsor as a prior step to mediation; (b) one party refuses to meet: propose shuttle diplomacy process (separate mediation); (c) conflict about verifiable facts: recommend independent technical validation before negotiating. [C · CRITERIA] The script must be realistic (not a perfect dialogue): include possible objections and the mediator's responses; solution options must be truly different, not variants of the same idea; the agreement must have commitments with owner and date; DoD: all sections present, script with at least four conversation turns, agreement with a minimum of three commitments.
spec-gestion_proyectos_plan_comunicacion: [S · SITUATION] A twelve-month logistics distribution center construction project needs a formal Communications Plan that guides how, when, and through which channels information will be transmitted to each audience throughout the entire lifecycle. The sponsor has requested the document before the official start of the planning phase. [P · REQUEST] Develop the complete Project Communications Plan per PMI standard: define audiences, key messages per audience, channels, frequencies, emission owners, and feedback mechanisms, all organized in a documentally valid structure. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Project communications management specialist with PMP certification and experience in large-scale infrastructure and logistics projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if no project information is provided, assume a twelve-month logistics distribution center construction project with five main audiences (steering committee, project team, contractors, local community, regulatory body) [ASSUMPTION]; predictive methodology is applied [ASSUMPTION]; available channels: email, in-person meetings, project portal, group WhatsApp for operational team [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if there are legal restrictions on communication with the community or the regulator (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: project charter, stakeholder list, description of available channels, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify and segment audiences with their information needs. 2. Define key message per audience and project phase. 3. Select optimal channel per audience (based on formality, urgency, access). 4. Establish frequency and owner of each communication. 5. Define format/template for each type of communication. 6. Establish feedback and escalation mechanism. 7. Structure the plan in a document with standard PMI index. OUTPUT: document with sections: Plan Objective and Scope | Audience Register (table) | Communications Matrix (table: Audience | Message | Channel | Frequency | Owner | Format) | Escalation Guidelines | Feedback Mechanism | Plan Control and Update. EDGE CASES: (a) audience with limited technology access (field contractors): use physical or WhatsApp channels, not the portal; (b) crisis or scope change communication: emergency communication process outside the regular plan; (c) regulatory audience: communications must pass legal review before being issued. [C · CRITERIA] The matrix must have at least one communication per audience per project phase; owners must be roles, not persons (so the plan survives team changes); formats must be named (not "report", but "Biweekly Progress Report v1.0"); DoD: all sections present, complete matrix with no empty cells, operational feedback mechanism.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-comunicaci: [S · SITUATION] A project manager with six distinct audiences (steering committee, technical team, end users, vendors, compliance area, and external community) needs an operational tool that allows them to see at a glance what to communicate, to whom, when, through which channel, and in what format during project execution, without relying on an extensive communications plan. [P · REQUEST] Build a ready-to-operate Communication Matrix by Audience: a dense, precise table that maps each recurring project communication with its audience, essential message, channel, frequency, emitting owner, deliverable format, and communication success criterion. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Project manager specializing in communications management in medium and large projects, with command of hybrid communication tools (in-person and digital). ASSUMPTIONS: if no project context is provided, assume a nine-month CRM system implementation project with the six audiences mentioned [ASSUMPTION]; available channels are: meeting, corporate email, online dashboard, PDF report, and team instant messaging [ASSUMPTION]; base frequencies are: daily (technical team), weekly (manager and key users), bi-weekly (vendors), monthly (steering committee) [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if there are channel restrictions due to corporate policy or regulation (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: audience list, project description, available channels, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Enumerate all audiences with their power and interest level. 2. For each audience, identify the recurring communications of the project lifecycle. 3. For each communication, define: essential message (in one sentence), channel, frequency, emitting owner (by role), deliverable format, success criterion (how you know the communication was effective). 4. Organize everything in a Markdown table. 5. Add a maintenance note: when and who updates the matrix. OUTPUT: Markdown table with columns Audience | Communication | Essential Message | Channel | Frequency | Owner | Format | Success Criterion; Maintenance Notes section; Exception Communications section (scope change, crisis, escalation). EDGE CASES: (a) an audience requires the same message through two different channels (intentional redundancy): mark it explicitly; (b) communication with external audience subject to legal review: add Legal Review Required column; (c) project with more than ten audiences: group by cluster before building the matrix. [C · CRITERIA] The success criterion for each communication must be observable (open rate, confirmed response, registered attendance, not just "received"); formats must be named; the matrix must cover the entire project lifecycle (initiation to closing); DoD: complete table with no empty cells, exceptions section present, maintenance note with owner and update frequency.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estatus-semanal-e: [S · SITUATION] A project manager needs to deliver every Monday the weekly team status report to the sponsor and the steering committee. The report must reflect what was completed the previous week, what is in progress, active blockers, emerging risks, and the plan for the following week, all in a standardized format that the team can complete in under twenty minutes. [P · REQUEST] Generate the complete Weekly Team Status Report for the indicated week: include a three-line executive summary, week's achievements (completed), work in progress with percentage of progress, blockers with resolution owner, new or updated risks, and next week's plan with owner per task. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Project manager with structured communication habits and the ability to synthesize the work of a ten-person team into a one-page actionable report. ASSUMPTIONS: if no week information is provided, assume a software development project in the build phase, week 8 of 20, with three completed deliverables, two tasks in progress, and one technical dependency blocker [ASSUMPTION]; the team uses agile methodology with two-week sprints [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if the format must follow a specific corporate template (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: standup notes, list of completed and incomplete tasks, blockers reported by the team, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Draft a three-line executive summary (overall status, most relevant achievement, main risk). 2. List the week's achievements with evidence (deliverable or milestone, not just activity). 3. List in-progress tasks with percentage and estimated close date. 4. Document each blocker with description, impact, resolution owner, and expected date. 5. Update risks (new or changed status). 6. List next week's plan with task, owner, and completion criterion. OUTPUT: structured report with header (Project | Week | Period | Prepared by | RAG Status), Markdown sections with clean bullets, blockers table, and weekly plan table. EDGE CASES: (a) week with zero achievements: report as a technical debt or systemic blocker week; do not omit the section; (b) more than five blockers: group by critical vs. non-critical impact; (c) RAG status change from previous week: indicate what changed and why. [C · CRITERIA] The executive summary must not repeat data from the detail sections; each achievement must be a deliverable or milestone, not an activity ("payment integration completed" not "worked on payments"); blockers must have an owner and date; DoD: all sections present, RAG status declared, next week's plan with owners.
spec-gestion-proyectos_reporte-estado-ra: [S · SITUATION] A portfolio committee reviews monthly the status of ten active projects. Each project manager must deliver a RAG (Red/Amber/Green) Status Report of maximum half a page that the committee reads in two minutes and that allows them to decide whether the project needs intervention. The format must be consistent across all projects in the portfolio. [P · REQUEST] Generate the Executive RAG Status Report for the project for the committee review: classify the overall status and the five control axes (scope, time, cost, quality, risks), justify each classification with an observable data point or indicator, indicate the action or decision the committee must take (if applicable), and project the status for the next period. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Project manager with experience reporting to portfolio committees, mastery of earned value metrics, and the ability to synthesize the status of a project in executive decision-oriented language. ASSUMPTIONS: if no project data is provided, assume a data platform construction project in the execution phase, month 5 of 10, with SPI=0.88 (schedule delayed), CPI=1.02 (cost under control), stable scope, three active medium-high-level risks [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if the classification depends on confidential data that must not appear in the report (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: progress data, cost and time metrics, risk status, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Determine the RAG status of each axis using a quantitative criterion (Green: under control; Amber: manageable deviation; Red: critical deviation requiring committee action). 2. For each axis, write a one-line justification with the indicator that supports the classification. 3. Determine the overall RAG status (the most critical axis determines the overall status if it is Red). 4. Draft the Action/Decision required section (if applicable) with the name of who must decide and the deadline. 5. Project the status for the next month in one line. 6. Compress everything into half a page with a standard header. OUTPUT: header (Project | Period | Manager | Overall RAG Status + icon); RAG axis table (Axis | Status | Indicator | Justification); Action/Decision section (if applicable); Next Period Projection section. EDGE CASES: (a) all axes Green but the manager has an intuition of an emerging risk: include an Early Warning Signal section; (b) Red cost status with a recovery plan already in execution: indicate in the justification that the corrective action is already active; (c) project paused by committee decision: special status "On Hold" with expected resume date. [C · CRITERIA] Each RAG classification must be backed by a quantitative indicator or verifiable event (not perception); the overall status cannot be Green if any axis is Red; the action/decision must name the responsible party; DoD: complete axis table, overall status consistent with axes, maximum half a page of content.
spec-gestion-proyectos_flash-report-hito: [S · SITUATION] A systems integration project has just completed a critical milestone (for example, approval of the architecture design or completion of a pilot with users). The project manager needs to communicate this achievement immediately to key stakeholders via a brief, impactful, momentum-oriented message that reinforces confidence in the project without sounding like internal propaganda. [P · REQUEST] Draft the Milestone Flash Report: a communiqué of maximum 200 words that celebrates the achievement with concrete data, contextualizes its importance for the project, reports the impact on schedule and overall progress, and anticipates the next milestone with a date. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Project manager with executive communication skills and experience in maintaining momentum for teams and sponsors during long projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if no milestone data is provided, assume successful approval of the technical architecture design of a data platform in week 6 of a twenty-week project, with participation of eight reviewers and zero critical observations [ASSUMPTION]; recipients are the sponsor, the steering committee, and the project team [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if there are restrictions on broadcasting the achievement for contractual or confidentiality reasons (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: milestone name, achievement data (number of participants, time invested, validation result), schedule impact, next milestone, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Open with the achievement statement in one impactful sentence (no euphemisms). 2. Contextualize: why does this milestone matter for the project's success? (2-3 lines). 3. Include a quantitative data point that anchors the achievement. 4. Report the impact on the overall progress of the project (percentage, current vs. planned week). 5. Announce the next milestone with a date. 6. Close with a brief acknowledgment of the team (brief, without names unless indicated). OUTPUT: communiqué of maximum 200 words in plain text or simple Markdown, with suggested email subject and recommended recipient list. EDGE CASES: (a) milestone reached with delay: report the achievement honestly, include the delay as data, and focus on recovery; (b) partially completed milestone: do not qualify it as completed; use "milestone in advanced state of completion" and give a percentage; (c) audience hostile to the project: adapt the tone to be factual and avoid excessive celebratory language. [C · CRITERIA] The communiqué cannot exceed 200 words; it must include at least one quantitative data point of the achievement; the next milestone must have a specific date; DoD: communiqué ready to send, email subject included, tone calibrated to the project context.
spec-gestion-proyectos_minuta-reunion-ac: [S · SITUATION] A project team held a forty-five-minute follow-up meeting with the sponsor, three area managers, and the technical team. Progress, blockers were discussed, and several decisions were made. After the meeting, no one is clear on exactly who was left responsible for each action or what the formal agreements were. The project manager needs structured minutes that faithfully capture the commitments and enable follow-up. [P · REQUEST] Draft the complete Meeting Minutes with Agreements and Actions: meeting data, attendees, agenda items with discussion summary, formal agreements, actions table with owner and date, and next meeting. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Project manager with discipline in meeting documentation and commitment management, capable of transforming disorganized notes into actionable minutes in less than fifteen minutes. ASSUMPTIONS: if no meeting notes are provided, generate typical minutes for a weekly digital transformation project follow-up meeting with five agenda items, two formal agreements, and four actions with different owners [ASSUMPTION]; the meeting was virtual via Teams [ASSUMPTION]; PMI minutes format applies [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if there is disagreement among attendees about what was agreed and the user has not provided the correct version (<=1 question, confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: meeting notes (disorganized or in bullet form), list of attendees, date and time, agenda if it exists, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Complete the header (project, meeting type, date, time, venue/platform, facilitator, secretary). 2. List attendees with role and confirm absences with justification if known. 3. For each agenda item: write a 2-4 line discussion summary, neutral and in third person. 4. Extract formal agreements (decisions that change something: scope, budget, schedule, responsibilities). 5. Build actions table: Action | Owner | Deadline | Completion Criterion. 6. Note next meeting (date, time, platform, tentative agenda). OUTPUT: minutes in Markdown format with standard header, attendees section, agenda items section per item, Formal Agreements section (numbered), Actions table, and Next Meeting section. EDGE CASES: (a) action with no clear owner: assign to the project manager role as escalation owner and mark with a note; (b) agreement that contradicts the project scope: mark with an alert note and recommend validation with the sponsor; (c) attendee who did not actively participate: record as present but without documented intervention. [C · CRITERIA] Agreements must be formulated in active present voice ("The committee approves...", not "It was agreed that it could..."); actions must have a specific deadline (not "as soon as possible"); the completion criterion for each action must be observable; DoD: all sections present, complete actions table with no empty owners, numbered agreements in active voice.
spec-gestion-proyectos_comunicado-cambio:
[S · SITUATION] An organization undergoing transformation needs to communicate a significant change — area restructuring, new operating model, team merger, or leadership change — to its employees. The announcement must reduce uncertainty, build trust, and guide action. [P · REQUEST] Produce a formal organizational change announcement ready to distribute, with a complete narrative structure: context of the change, strategic reason, impact on employees, concrete next steps, and a questions channel. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior consultant in change management and organizational communication with experience in corporate transformations. ASSUMPTIONS: if no audience is indicated, address the entire organization; professional-close tone; maximum length 400 words; if no effective date is specified, use 'in the coming weeks'. Ask only if the type of change is unclear (confidence <0.85). INPUTS: description of the change pasted in the thread or in this message. STEPS: 1. Identify the type of change and target audience. 2. Draft header with sender, date, and specific subject. 3. Write context paragraph: what is changing and why now. 4. Develop impact section: what it means for the affected people. 5. List three to five concrete next steps with owners and approximate dates. 6. Close with a support message and official questions channel. 7. Review tone: eliminate euphemisms that obscure the real message. OUTPUT: Announcement in continuous text, format ready for email or intranet, without visible section markers, with suggested subject on the first line in brackets. EDGE CASES: (1) If the change involves layoffs, add a support paragraph and available support resources. (2) If the audience is senior leadership only, adjust to a strategic tone and omit basic operational explanations. (3) If the change is not yet finalized, draft in anticipation mode without committing to definitive dates. [C · CRITERIA] The announcement is approved if: a reader without prior context understands what is changing, why, and what they should do; it contains no ambiguities that generate rumors; the tone balances directive firmness with human empathy. Trade-off: clarity > brevity when the change is sensitive. DoD: text reviewed, suggested subject included, next steps with action verb.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions used, indicate if any edge case applies, and list the suggested next steps for the sender.
spec-gestion-proyectos_one-pager-ejecuti:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager needs to present the status, scope, and value of their project to an executive committee or sponsor in a single-page format. The reading time of the document must not exceed three minutes and it must allow decisions to be made or resources approved without reviewing the full plan. [P · REQUEST] Produce an executive project one-pager with all essential elements on one A4 page or equivalent screen: name, objective, RAG status, key milestones, value metrics, main risks, and required decision. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project management consultant with experience presenting to steering committees of mid-size and large companies. ASSUMPTIONS: structured text format with delimited sections; RAG status defaults to Amber if not indicated; currency in USD if not specified; project horizon in the current quarter if not mentioned. Ask only if the project name or objective are unknown. INPUTS: project data pasted in this message (name, objective, milestones, metrics, risks, pending decision, budget executed vs. planned). STEPS: 1. Write header with project name, responsible leader, and update date. 2. Draft objective in one sentence (what + for whom + by when). 3. Indicate RAG status with a two-line justification. 4. List three to five key milestones with date and status (completed/in progress/pending). 5. Present two or three value metrics (budget executed vs. planned, NPS, delivery velocity). 6. Summarize the two most critical risks with probability and mitigation. 7. Formulate the decision or approval required from the executive in one direct sentence. OUTPUT: Text document with clearly delimited sections, high information density, no lengthy narrative paragraphs; each section occupies a maximum of three lines. EDGE CASES: (1) If the project is in red (RAG Red), start the document with the alert and the required decision before the objective. (2) If no milestones are defined, substitute with deliverables from the next sprint or phase. (3) If the project is internal with no financial metrics, use adoption or satisfaction metrics. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: it can be read in less than three minutes; the executive can make the required decision with the information presented; there are no redundant data or empty sections. Trade-off: completeness < executive clarity. DoD: all sections complete, RAG status justified, required decision formulated.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions used, indicate the RAG status applied, and list the required decision in bold at the end.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-mala:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager or area leader must communicate significant bad news to their team, client, or sponsor: delivery delay, cost overrun, scope cancellation, technical failure, or quality incident. The way it is communicated determines whether trust is maintained or the relationship is eroded. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured plan to communicate the bad news, including: central message, segmented audiences, optimal channel and timing, conversation script, anticipation of reactions, and post-communication follow-up plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior consultant in crisis management and project communication with experience in high-pressure environments and corporate clients. ASSUMPTIONS: if no audience is indicated, generate a plan for two segments (internal team + client/sponsor); default channel is synchronous meeting followed by backup email; honest-constructive tone. Ask only if the bad news is not described (confidence <0.85). INPUTS: description of the problematic situation pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Summarize the bad news in one sentence without euphemisms. 2. Segment audiences and define what information each receives and when. 3. Select the optimal channel and time window for each audience. 4. Draft a three-act conversation script: acknowledgment of the problem, honest causes, remediation actions. 5. List three to five possible emotional reactions or difficult questions with prepared responses. 6. Define follow-up plan: who does what in the 24-72 hours after. 7. Establish escalation criteria if the reaction exceeds what was anticipated. OUTPUT: Document with sections: Executive summary of the news / Audience map / Conversation script / Anticipated reactions and responses / Follow-up plan. EDGE CASES: (1) If the bad news implies legal risk, add a section for review with legal counsel before communicating. (2) If the team is distributed across time zones, specify a synchronization protocol to prevent the news from arriving via rumor. (3) If the client has a contractual penalty clause, separate the operational communication from the contractual negotiation. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: the receiver of the news understands what happened, why, and what will be done; the communicator does not end up on the defensive; follow-up is scheduled with an owner and date. Trade-off: speed of communication > perfection of the message (delayed news amplifies the crisis). DoD: script reviewed, audiences segmented, follow-up plan with dates.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions used, indicate the highest emotional-risk segment, and list follow-up actions with suggested dates.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-asignacion:
[S · SITUATION] A project team has defined activities or deliverables but no clarity on who does what, who approves, and who should be informed. The absence of a RACI matrix generates duplication of effort, blocked decisions, and accountability gaps. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete RACI matrix for the indicated project or process, with deliverables/activities in rows, roles/people in columns, and one RACI cell per intersection, plus an operating rules glossary. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project management and organizational design specialist with experience building RACI matrices for technology, operations, and consulting projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if no roles are listed, infer the typical ones for the project type (PM, technical lead, sponsor, team, client); maximum one 'R' per row; if not indicated, Markdown table format. Ask only if the main activities cannot be inferred (confidence <0.85). INPUTS: list of project deliverables or activities, and team roles or names, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Identify and list all activities or deliverables in rows (maximum 20, group if more). 2. Identify unique roles as columns. 3. Assign RACI letter to each intersection: R=Responsible, A=Accountable/Approver, C=Consulted, I=Informed. 4. Verify that each row has exactly one 'A' and at least one 'R'. 5. Identify and flag rows with 'R' overload or columns with excess 'A'. 6. Draft a glossary of four matrix operating rules. 7. Flag the three most likely friction points. OUTPUT: RACI table in Markdown with rows=activities and columns=roles, plus an operating rules section and assignment risk analysis. EDGE CASES: (1) If a role is overloaded (more than 40% of 'R'), suggest redistribution. (2) If there are activities without 'A', escalate them as a pending design decision. (3) If the team is distributed, add a time zone column next to each role. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: each activity has exactly one 'A'; no rows without 'R'; roles are recognizable by the team. Trade-off: activity granularity vs. table readability. DoD: complete table, glossary drafted, overloads flagged.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare inferred role assumptions, flag detected overloads, and list the three most likely friction points.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-recu:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager needs to formalize how human, technological, and material resources will be identified, acquired, developed, and released during the project lifecycle. Without a documented resource management plan, teams face availability gaps, assignment conflicts, and cost overruns. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete resource management plan covering: resource categories, acquisition strategy, required roles and profiles, availability schedule, control mechanisms, and release criteria. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior PMI/PMP certified project director with experience in resource planning for digital transformation and professional services projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if no methodology is indicated, use a hybrid approach (predictive for physical resources, adaptive for the team); plan horizon equals the project's; if no material resources are specified, focus on human resources. Ask only if the project type and duration are completely unknown. INPUTS: project description, WBS/deliverable list, available roles and budget constraints, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Classify resources into three categories: human, technological, material. 2. For human resources: list roles, competency profiles, quantity, and dedication per phase. 3. Define acquisition strategy for each critical resource (internal, external, subcontracted). 4. Create an onboarding and release schedule by resource or profile. 5. Establish monitoring mechanisms: capacity meetings, utilization dashboard, alert threshold (>85% load). 6. Document escalation criteria for resource gaps. 7. Define release protocol at phase or project close. OUTPUT: Structured document with six sections + key resources table (role, quantity, start phase, dedication %, acquisition source). EDGE CASES: (1) If a key resource has limited market availability, add a contingency plan with an alternative resource. (2) If the project has overlapping phases, flag possible assignment conflicts. (3) If the resource budget is fixed, add a scope-vs-resources trade-off analysis. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: all critical resources have a defined acquisition strategy; an overload alert mechanism exists; the plan can be reviewed by a PMO without ambiguities. Trade-off: profile detail vs. elaboration speed. DoD: complete resource table, release criteria defined, alert mechanism documented.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare methodology and horizon assumptions used, flag high-dependency critical resources, and list the detected assignment conflicts.
spec-gestion-proyectos_planificacion-cap:
[S · SITUATION] A team lead or project manager needs to determine whether their team has sufficient capacity to absorb the planned workload demand in the coming weeks or sprints, avoiding overloads that generate burnout, poor quality, and delays. [P · REQUEST] Produce a team capacity vs. demand analysis with: available capacity per person and period, estimated demand per initiative, identified gap, and adjustment recommendations (redistribution, prioritization, or resource onboarding). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Scrum Master or Agile Coach with experience in capacity planning for software development and operations teams. ASSUMPTIONS: if no period is indicated, use the next four weeks; default capacity 6 productive hours/person/day discounting ceremonies and meetings; if no vacations are listed, assume none. Ask only if the team size is unknown. INPUTS: list of team members, initiatives or prioritized backlog with effort estimate, known absences, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Calculate gross capacity: people x days x productive hours. 2. Discount absences, holidays, and meeting overhead to obtain net capacity. 3. Map demand: sum estimated effort per initiative or task. 4. Calculate gap: net capacity - total demand. 5. Identify people who are overloaded (>90%) and people with slack (<70%). 6. Propose three adjustment scenarios: redistribute, descope, or onboard. 7. Present a summary capacity vs. demand table per person and period. OUTPUT: Markdown capacity table per person + gap analysis + three adjustment scenarios with explicit trade-offs. EDGE CASES: (1) If the gap is greater than 30%, flag as a critical risk and escalate to the sponsor. (2) If people have less than 50% utilization, investigate whether they have undeclared work before reassigning. (3) If the period has holidays or corporate events, automatically adjust net capacity. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: the gap is quantified in hours or days; each scenario has an explicit trade-off; the team can use the analysis without manually recalculating. Trade-off: estimation precision vs. analysis speed. DoD: complete table, gap calculated, three scenarios documented.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare productive hours and period assumptions, flag overloaded people, and list the three adjustment scenarios with their trade-offs.
spec-gestion-proyectos_histograma-recurs:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager needs to visualize the distribution of team workload over time to detect overload periods, under-utilization valleys, and assignment conflicts between parallel projects. The resource histogram is the standard tool for this visualization. [P · REQUEST] Produce a resource assignment histogram in text/Markdown table format showing, per person and period (week or sprint), the assigned dedication percentage vs. available capacity, with visual identification of overloads and valleys. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Resource management and project planning specialist with experience in PMO tools and portfolio management. ASSUMPTIONS: if no period is indicated, use 8 weeks; maximum capacity 100% = 40 hours per week; mark rows exceeding 90% with an alert symbol; if the source project for each assignment is not indicated, group as 'Project A', 'Project B'. Ask only if minimum assignment data is unavailable. INPUTS: list of people, projects they are assigned to, and dedication percentage per week or sprint, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Build the table header: columns = periods (weeks or sprints), rows = people. 2. Fill each cell with the total assignment percentage for that period. 3. Add a totals row per period (aggregate team demand). 4. Mark cells >90% with an alert symbol and cells <60% with a slack symbol. 5. Add a secondary table with project breakdown for the three most heavily loaded resources. 6. Calculate and report: maximum load peak, minimum valley, and average team deviation. 7. Flag the two or three highest-risk periods for schedule delays due to overload. OUTPUT: Main histogram table + secondary project-breakdown table + three-metric analysis (peak, valley, deviation) + leveling recommendations. EDGE CASES: (1) If any person exceeds 100%, mark in red and suggest resource leveling. (2) If all resources are below 60% in some period, suggest pulling work forward or incorporating new demand. (3) If parallel projects share the same key resource, flag the priority conflict. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: overload is visible at a glance; the project breakdown allows tracing the source of load; recommendations are actionable. Trade-off: weekly vs. monthly granularity depending on project duration. DoD: complete table, calculated metrics, documented leveling recommendations.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare capacity and period assumptions, identify the three most critical resources, and list leveling recommendations with specific periods.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-staffing-ram:
[S · SITUATION] A medium- or large-scale project needs to onboard staff progressively over time, with a ramp curve that reflects the onboarding pace, productivity acquisition, and the optimal onboarding moment for each profile. Without an explicit staffing plan, projects start slowly or onboard staff before there is meaningful work for them. [P · REQUEST] Produce a staffing plan with a ramp curve specifying: profiles to onboard, onboarding date and condition, estimated time to full productivity, ramp cost, and a visual month-by-month schedule. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project director with specialization in professional-services contract management and phased staffing models. ASSUMPTIONS: if no duration is indicated, use 12 months; default ramp time to full productivity is 4 weeks for operational profiles and 8 weeks for senior technical profiles; if no cost is indicated, omit the cost column and note it. Ask only if the minimum project profiles cannot be inferred. INPUTS: project description, required profiles, key phase start dates or deliverables, onboarding conditions, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. List all required profiles with headcount per profile. 2. Define onboarding condition (milestone, date, or load level). 3. Assign the onboarding week or month for each profile. 4. Estimate ramp weeks to full productivity per profile. 5. Build a month-by-month table of active headcount and productive headcount. 6. Calculate the team productivity curve as a percentage of maximum potential per month. 7. Identify the month of greatest productive gap risk and the corrective action. OUTPUT: Onboarding schedule table (profile, headcount, start month, ramp weeks, condition) + text/ASCII productivity curve chart + critical-month analysis. EDGE CASES: (1) If the project requires onboarding more than two profiles in the same month, flag the onboarding saturation risk. (2) If a profile has low market availability, add a contingency plan with an alternative resource. (3) If the project is agile with short sprints, adjust the ramp curve to sprint velocity instead of months. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: each profile has a clear onboarding date and condition; the productivity curve is visible and the critical month is identified; the plan can be reviewed by a financial director and an operations manager. Trade-off: profile detail vs. flexibility in the face of scope changes. DoD: complete table, productivity curve calculated, critical month identified with corrective action.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare ramp assumptions per profile, identify the month of greatest risk of productive gap, and list the suggested corrective actions.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-habilidade:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager or team leader needs to identify which critical skills their team possesses and which are absent or underdeveloped to meet the project objectives or area strategy. The skills matrix enables visualizing gaps and planning development, hiring, or training actions. [P · REQUEST] Produce a skills matrix and gap analysis showing: skills required by the project, each person's current level in each skill, the required level, the calculated gap, and a closure plan for critical gaps. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Talent development leader and organizational capacity management specialist with experience in technology and consulting projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if no scale is indicated, use 1-4 (1=basic, 2=functional, 3=advanced, 4=expert); critical gap = difference ≥2 or current level ≤1 in a skill required at ≥3; if not all people are listed, build the matrix for the team described. Ask only if the required skills are completely unknown. INPUTS: list of team members, critical project skills, and required level for each skill, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Build a table with people as rows and skills as columns. 2. Fill in the estimated or reported current level per skill and person. 3. Calculate the gap per cell: required − current. 4. Calculate the average gap per person (individual readiness index). 5. Calculate the average gap per skill (skill maturity index for the team). 6. Identify the three most critical gaps in the team. 7. Propose a closure action for each critical gap (training, mentoring, hiring, or reallocation). OUTPUT: Markdown skills table + readiness index table + analysis of three critical gaps with closure action and estimated time. EDGE CASES: (1) If more than 50% of the team has a critical gap in the same skill, escalate it as a project risk. (2) If a person has an average readiness index <1.5, flag them for an intensive development plan. (3) If a required skill does not exist in any team member, recommend immediate hiring or subcontracting. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: the gap is quantified per person and per skill; the three critical gaps have a closure action with owner and time. Trade-off: precision of self-assessment vs. speed of construction. DoD: complete table, indices calculated, closure actions with owner and estimated time.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare rating scale assumptions, identify the three critical gaps, and list closure actions with owner and estimated time.
spec-gestion-proyectos_modelo-desarrollo:
[S · SITUATION] A team leader or project manager is working with a team that has undergone recent changes (new hires, turnover, restructuring) or that shows signs of dysfunction such as frequent conflicts, low productivity, or disconnection from the objective. The Tuckman model (Forming-Storming-Norming-Performing-Adjourning) provides a diagnostic and intervention framework. [P · REQUEST] Produce a diagnosis of the team's Tuckman stage and an intervention plan with concrete actions to accelerate progress toward the Performing stage, with observable progress indicators. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organizational coach and high-performance team facilitator with experience in agile team development and transformation projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if the team's behavior is not described, infer Storming stage as the most common starting point; interventions mapped to the first four stages; if the team is in Adjourning, focus on positive closure and learning retention. Ask only if there is no description of the team whatsoever. INPUTS: team description (tenure, composition, observed behaviors, project context), pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Analyze observed signals and diagnose the current Tuckman stage with justification. 2. Describe the characteristics of the current stage and the next (for context). 3. Identify the three main obstacles slowing progress to the next stage. 4. Propose five concrete intervention actions with owner, format (workshop, conversation, practice), and frequency. 5. Define three observable indicators that the team has advanced to the next stage. 6. Flag one alert signal that would indicate regression to the previous stage. 7. Propose a team ritual that reinforces sustained progress. OUTPUT: Document with: stage diagnosis + description of current and next stage + three obstacles + five interventions + three progress indicators + regression signal + suggested ritual. EDGE CASES: (1) If the team has members at different stages (some in Norming, others in Storming), propose segmented interventions. (2) If the team has frequent turnover (>30% in the last 3 months), flag a reset Tuckman cycle and an acceleration strategy for Forming. (3) If the organizational context involves high pressure or uncertainty, adapt interventions for low-time-availability environments. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: the diagnosis has observable justification; interventions are feasible without additional budget; progress indicators are verifiable within the next two weeks. Trade-off: depth of diagnosis vs. speed of implementation. DoD: justified diagnosis, five interventions with owner and format, progress indicators defined.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare stage diagnosis assumptions, identify the three main obstacles, and list the five interventions with owner and format.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-reconocimien:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager or area leader needs to design a structured plan to recognize team achievements and maintain motivation during a long-duration project or in a high-pressure context. Without deliberate recognition actions, teams experience fatigue, disengagement, and loss of key talent. [P · REQUEST] Produce a recognition and motivation plan that includes: team motivator diagnosis, a menu of formal and informal recognition actions, a recognition milestone schedule, a continuous feedback mechanism, and effectiveness metrics. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: People management and organizational culture specialist with experience in high-demand projects and talent retention in technical teams. ASSUMPTIONS: if no budget is indicated, design 80% of actions at no cost; if team size is not indicated, assume 5 to 15 people; default motivators according to McClelland's theory: achievement, affiliation, and power; plan horizon equals the project's or six months if not indicated. Ask only if the team context is completely unknown. INPUTS: team description, project context, relevant recent achievements, and budget constraints, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Identify two or three dominant team motivators based on the described context. 2. Design a menu of five informal recognition actions (no cost, immediate) and three formal recognition actions (with or without cost, periodic). 3. Align formal recognition actions with project milestones. 4. Design a continuous feedback mechanism (weekly pulse, individual check-in, recognition board). 5. Define two plan effectiveness metrics (eNPS, retention, ceremony participation). 6. Establish who is responsible for executing each type of action. 7. Include a monthly adjustment protocol based on disengagement signals. OUTPUT: Document with: identified motivators + action menu (informal and formal) + milestone schedule + feedback mechanism + effectiveness metrics + owners. EDGE CASES: (1) If the team is in crisis or sustained high-pressure mode, prioritize load relief actions before celebration. (2) If there are significant cultural differences in the distributed team, adapt recognition formats to each person's cultural context. (3) If budget is zero, build a plan 100% based on verbal recognition, visibility, and autonomy. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: the plan has at least five actions executable next week; metrics are measurable without additional tools; the schedule is aligned with project milestones. Trade-off: recognition frequency vs. impact of each action. DoD: complete menu, aligned schedule, metrics defined with baseline.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare motivator and budget assumptions, identify the three highest-immediate-impact actions, and list effectiveness metrics with a suggested baseline.
spec-gestion-proyectos_acuerdo-trabajo-e:
[S · SITUATION] A project team works in a distributed manner: different time zones, cities, or countries, with mixed modes (in-person and remote). Without an explicit working agreement, communication problems, inefficient meetings, undocumented decisions, and cultural disconnection arise. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete working agreement for the distributed team, covering: communication norms, synchronous availability windows, channels by message type, meeting protocol, asynchronous decision-making, document management, and agreement review mechanism. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Agile Coach specializing in distributed teams and global remote work, with experience in technology and international consulting projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if time zones are not indicated, assume a team with a maximum difference of up to 3 time zones; default working language is English with technical English permitted; default collaboration tools are Slack/Teams + Zoom/Meet + Confluence/Notion; if size is not indicated, assume between 5 and 20 people. Ask only if the team composition and time zones are completely unknown. INPUTS: team composition (people, locations, time zones, mode), available tools, project context, pasted in this message. STEPS: 1. Define the common synchronous availability window (time-zone overlap). 2. Establish communication rules per channel: what goes in chat, what goes in email, what requires a meeting. 3. Define maximum response times by message type (urgent, normal, informational). 4. Establish meeting protocol: prior agenda, recording, minutes with decisions, maximum duration. 5. Design asynchronous decision-making process with a response deadline. 6. Define shared documentation structure: file names, folders, versions. 7. Establish agreement review cadence (monthly or per phase). OUTPUT: 'Working Agreement of Team [Name]' document with seven sections, format ready to share and digitally sign (or acknowledge at a team meeting). EDGE CASES: (1) If the time-zone difference exceeds 8 hours, design the workflow as predominantly asynchronous. (2) If there are significant language barriers, include a rule for simplifying written language. (3) If the team includes external consultants and internal staff, differentiate access levels to channels and documents. [C · CRITERIA] Approved if: any new member can onboard using the agreement as the sole reference; the agreement is specific (not generic) to the team and project; all sections have concrete examples. Trade-off: completeness of the agreement vs. team adoption (fewer rules = higher compliance). DoD: seven complete sections, concrete examples in each section, review mechanism with a defined date.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare time-zone and tool assumptions, identify the most critical communication risk, and list the three norms with the greatest impact on team productivity.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-cali:
[S · SITUATION] A project in execution needs a formal document establishing how quality of deliverables will be planned, assured, and controlled, reducing rework and client or sponsor rejections.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a complete Quality Management Plan, in structured document format, with all components required by project management good practices (metrics, tools, roles, QA and QC activities, and acceptance criteria).

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: You act as a Senior PMO with PMP certification and experience in quality assurance for technology and transformation projects.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not paste the project charter or WBS, assume a medium-complexity software project with a team of 8-15 people and a 6-month duration. Declare assumptions at the beginning. Ask questions only if the industry type or applicable quality standard (ISO, CMMI, etc.) cannot be inferred with confidence ≥0.85.

INPUTS: Project context pasted in the thread (name, scope, industry, applicable standard if any).

STEPS:
1. Identify the project context and declare key assumptions.
2. Define the project quality policy (1 paragraph).
3. Establish measurable quality objectives (minimum 3, with a numerical acceptance threshold).
4. List applicable standards and regulations.
5. Describe quality assurance (QA) activities: reviews, audits, frequency.
6. Describe quality control (QC) activities: inspections, tests, sampling.
7. Define quality metrics: name, formula, frequency, owner, green/yellow/red threshold.
8. Assign quality roles and responsibilities (simplified RACI).
9. Document the tools and techniques to be used.
10. Establish the non-conformance management and corrective action process.

OUTPUT: Structured document with numbered sections, tables for metrics and RACI, and a one-page executive summary at the beginning.

EDGE CASES:
- If the project already has an active quality plan: propose only the missing sections or specific improvements, do not rewrite everything.
- If the standard is regulatory (FDA, ISO 13485): add a requirements traceability and records management section.
- If the quality budget is not defined: include an effort estimation section in hours per activity.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each metric has an explicit formula, frequency, and owner.
- Trade-off: QA/QC rigor level proportional to project risk; do not generate unnecessary bureaucracy.
- DoD: the document can be approved by the sponsor without additional questions about how quality will be controlled.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions before developing, cite applicable standards, and deliver an artifact ready for approval.
spec-gestion-proyectos_metricas-calidad-:
[S · SITUATION] An ongoing project needs executive and operational visibility on quality status, with indicators that allow detecting deviations early and making decisions before defects escalate into failed deliveries.

[P · REQUEST] Design a project quality metrics dashboard: definition of each indicator, calculation formula, data source, measurement frequency, owner, traffic-light thresholds (green/yellow/red), and recommended visualization.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: You act as a quality metrics and project analytics specialist with experience implementing dashboards for PMOs.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the project type is not specified, assume a software development project. If no visualization tool is indicated, assume the dashboard will be exported to a table/spreadsheet and you may suggest alternatives. Declare assumptions at the beginning and proceed without asking if confidence in the project type is ≥0.85.

INPUTS: Project context and list of deliverables or phases pasted in the thread.

STEPS:
1. Identify relevant quality dimensions: functional, process, product, satisfaction.
2. Select 8-12 key metrics, prioritizing the actionable ones.
3. For each metric specify: name, one-sentence definition, calculation formula or rule, data source, frequency, reporting owner, green/yellow/red threshold, and recommended chart type.
4. Group the metrics into dashboard sections: Process Quality, Product Quality, Resolution Speed.
5. Propose the dashboard visual structure (section layout, indicator hierarchy).
6. Describe the dashboard review cycle: who reviews it, how often, and what actions each alert level triggers.

OUTPUT: Master metrics table (columns: name, definition, formula, source, frequency, owner, green, yellow, red, chart) + dashboard layout description + review cycle in text.

EDGE CASES:
- If the project has fewer than 3 months remaining: reduce to 5-6 essential metrics and weekly frequency.
- If no historical data is available: indicate what baseline must be established in the first 2 weeks and how.
- If the client requests satisfaction metrics: add delivery NPS and deliverable acceptance rate.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each metric has an explicit formula and quantitative threshold.
- Trade-off: 8-12 metrics is the optimal range; more generates noise, fewer creates blind spots.
- DoD: the dashboard can be populated by the project team with current data on the same day as the session.

Protocolo MetodologIA: prioritize actionable metrics, define precise numerical thresholds, and deliver a structure ready to implement.
spec-gestion-proyectos_lista-verificacio:
[S · SITUATION] A project team needs an operational quality control tool to systematically inspect deliverables before handing them over to the client or passing to the next phase, reducing escaped defects and rejections.

[P · REQUEST] Create a quality control checklist (QC checklist) applicable to the project's deliverables, with binary (pass/fail) or scale criteria, grouped by category, with usage instructions and traceability log.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: You act as a senior quality inspector with experience in quality control of deliverables for software, consulting, and engineering projects.

ASSUMPTIONS: If deliverables are not specified, assume a software project with typical deliverables: requirements document, technical design, source code, test cases, user manual, and release. Declare assumptions at the beginning. Ask questions only if the deliverable type or client acceptance criteria are completely unknown and cannot be inferred.

INPUTS: Project description and list of deliverables pasted in the thread; acceptance criteria if available.

STEPS:
1. Identify and list the deliverables to be controlled.
2. For each deliverable, define 5-10 verification criteria grouped by category (completeness, correctness, format, approvals, consistency).
3. Establish the verification type: binary (Yes/No) or scale (1-3).
4. Add registration columns: verified by, date, observations, final status (Approved/Rejected/Conditional).
5. Include usage instructions in an initial section: who applies the checklist, at what point, what to do if an item fails.
6. Add a closing section: inspector signature, deliverable owner signature, closing date.

OUTPUT: Checklist table per deliverable (ready to copy into Word/Excel) + usage instructions + signature section + guide on what to do with rejected items.

EDGE CASES:
- If the deliverable is source code: include code review criteria (naming standards, test coverage, basic security).
- If the client has their own acceptance criteria: map checklist items to those criteria with a cross-reference.
- If the project is agile: adapt the checklist as a Definition of Done per user story type.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each checklist item is verifiable by an inspector without ambiguity.
- Trade-off: maximum 10 items per deliverable to keep it usable; critical criteria first.
- DoD: the team can apply the checklist in less than 15 minutes per deliverable.

Protocolo MetodologIA: design unambiguous criteria, include usage instructions, and deliver a format ready to operate on the same day.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-adqu:
[S · SITUATION] A project requires contracting external goods, services, or works (software, hardware, consulting, specialized resources) and needs a formal plan defining what is acquired, how suppliers are selected, what contract types will be used, and how contract execution is supervised.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete Procurement Management Plan covering: procurement needs, strategy, contract types, selection process, procurement documents, roles and responsibilities, and contract supervision.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: You act as a senior procurement manager with PMP training and experience in public and private contracting for technology projects.

ASSUMPTIONS: If items to be acquired are not detailed, assume software development services, licenses, and specialized consulting. If it is not indicated whether it is public or private sector, assume private. Declare assumptions at the beginning. Ask only if the legal contracting regime is critical and cannot be inferred.

INPUTS: Project context, WBS or list of work packages requiring external procurement, pasted in the thread.

STEPS:
1. Identify procurement items from the context.
2. Classify each item: good, service, or work; one-time or recurring acquisition.
3. Define the procurement strategy per item: open competition, direct invitation, justified sole-source.
4. Select the most appropriate contract type per item: fixed price, time and materials, cost-reimbursable.
5. List the procurement documents to prepare: RFI, RFP, SOW, terms and conditions.
6. Define the supplier evaluation and selection process: criteria, weightings, committee.
7. Establish the procurement schedule aligned with the project schedule.
8. Assign roles and responsibilities (RACI).
9. Describe the contract supervision and closure process.

OUTPUT: Structured document with procurement items table, schedule, RACI, and supervision section; format ready to be included in the Project Management Plan.

EDGE CASES:
- If there are severe budget constraints: prioritize critical items and propose a phased procurement strategy.
- If the project is public: add a regulatory framework and tendering process section.
- If a supplier is already pre-selected: document sole-source justification and monitoring conditions.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each procurement item has an explicit contract type, selection criteria, and owner.
- Trade-off: formality level proportional to the amount and risk of the procurement.
- DoD: the plan can be executed by the procurement team without additional queries to the PM.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about regime and sector, align the procurement schedule with the project schedule, and deliver a self-contained artifact.
spec-gestion-proyectos_criterios-evaluac:
[S · SITUATION] A project needs to select one or more external vendors from among several received proposals. An objective evaluation matrix is required to prevent decisions based on personal preferences and to allow the selection to be justified before the sponsor or a procurement committee.

[P · REQUEST] Design a vendor evaluation criteria matrix with categories, specific criteria, weights, a scoring scale, calculation method, and a scoring template ready to populate with the proposals received.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: You act as a procurement and vendor evaluation specialist with experience on technology and professional services selection committees.

SUPUESTOS: If the vendor type or service is not specified, assume software development and technology consulting services. If no eliminatory criterion is indicated, assume all criteria are weighted. Declare assumptions at the outset. Ask only if the budget ceiling or regulatory criteria are unknown and critical.

INSUMOS: Description of the goods or services to be procured, number of vendors to evaluate, and key constraints (budget, timeline, technical), pasted into the thread.

PASOS:
1. Identify the evaluation dimensions relevant to the contract type.
2. Define 4–6 criteria categories (e.g., technical capability, experience, economic proposal, methodology, support, compliance).
3. For each category, define 2–4 specific criteria with a description of what each one evaluates.
4. Assign a percentage weight to each category (total sum = 100%).
5. Define the scoring scale (e.g., 1–5 with a description for each level).
6. Establish whether there are eliminatory criteria (pass/fail) prior to the weighted scoring.
7. Design the scoring template: table with vendors in columns, criteria in rows, score, and weighted score.
8. Describe the evaluation process: who evaluates, how scores from multiple evaluators are consolidated, how it is documented.

SALIDA: Complete evaluation matrix (table) + scoring scale with descriptors + scoring template ready to populate + evaluation procedure in text.

CASOS BORDE:
- If price is the dominant criterion (public sector): increase economic weight to 40–50% and document justification.
- If there is only one viable vendor: redesign as a conformity evaluation (pass/fail) with a minimum requirements checklist.
- If evaluators come from different areas: include an evaluator role column and a weighted average section per evaluator.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the scoring template allows calculating the final score for each vendor with simple arithmetic.
- Trade-off: 4–6 categories balances objectivity with practicality; more criteria dilute real differences.
- DoD: the evaluation committee can complete the matrix in a 2-hour session and produce a justifiable ranking.

Protocolo MetodologIA: weight criteria according to risk and contract type, include scoring descriptors, and deliver an operational template ready for the committee.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-cont:
[S · SITUATION] A project has one or more active contracts with external vendors and needs a formal plan to administer them: monitor compliance, manage payments, control contractual changes, resolve disputes, and close contracts upon completion.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a Contract Administration Plan covering: contract inventory, roles and responsibilities, vendor performance monitoring process, payment and milestone management, contractual change control, dispute resolution, and closure process.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: You act as a senior contract administrator with experience in contractual management of technology and professional services projects.

SUPUESTOS: If active contracts are not detailed, assume 2–3 software service contracts (development, support, licenses). If contract type is not indicated, assume fixed price with payment milestones. Declare assumptions at the outset. Ask only if penalty clauses or the legal framework are critical and unknown.

INSUMOS: List of active contracts (vendor, scope, amount, term, payment milestones, status) and project context, pasted into the thread.

PASOS:
1. Prepare the contract inventory: vendor, scope, contract type, value, term, payment milestones, status.
2. Assign contractual administration roles and responsibilities (RACI): contract administrator, project PM, legal area, finance area.
3. Define the performance monitoring process: contractual KPIs, review frequency, vendor report format.
4. Describe the payment authorization and recording process linked to milestones or deliverables.
5. Establish the contractual change control process: who can request, how it is evaluated, who approves, how it is formalized.
6. Define the dispute resolution process: escalation, mediation, timelines.
7. Describe the contract closure process: deliverable acceptance, settlement, document archiving.

SALIDA: Structured document with inventory table, RACI, contractual change flowchart (textual description or step table), closure process, and contract closure meeting minutes template.

CASOS BORDE:
- If contracts include delay penalties: add an early warning management section before the penalty is triggered.
- If the project has multiple interdependent contracts: add a section for managing interfaces between contracts.
- If the vendor is from another country: include applicable law considerations and exchange rate provisions.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each contract has defined performance KPIs and a payment process.
- Trade-off: level of formality proportional to the value and risk of each contract; smaller contracts with a simplified process.
- DoD: the contract administrator can operate the plan without consulting the PM for routine operational decisions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: separate operational administration from strategic oversight, define clear escalation processes, and deliver a usable closure template.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-make-or-bu:
[S · SITUATION] A project or business area must decide whether to develop certain components, capabilities, or services internally, or to acquire them from external vendors. The decision impacts costs, timelines, quality, and strategic dependency, so it requires a structured and documented analysis.

[P · REQUEST] Develop a make-or-buy analysis matrix for the indicated items, with quantitative and qualitative evaluation criteria, weighted scoring, a recommendation per item, and decision justification.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: You act as a chief operating officer or strategic PMO with experience in insourcing and outsourcing decision analysis at technology companies.

SUPUESTOS: If the items to analyze are not specified, assume 4–6 typical software project components: custom development, infrastructure platform, reporting module, third-party integration, technical support, training. If no cost data is available, request rough estimates or use ranges. Declare assumptions at the outset. Ask only if the items or available budget cannot be inferred.

INSUMOS: List of items to analyze, team internal capabilities, budget and time constraints, and project strategic context, pasted into the thread.

PASOS:
1. List the items to analyze in the matrix rows.
2. Define the evaluation criteria for each dimension: total cost, development/delivery time, expected quality, risk, available internal capacity, strategic dependency, scalability.
3. Assign a percentage weight to each criterion (sum = 100%).
4. Score each item for both the MAKE and BUY option per criterion (scale 1–5, where 5 = most favorable).
5. Calculate the total weighted score per option.
6. Issue a recommendation per item (Make / Buy / Hybrid) with justification in 2–3 sentences.
7. Add a risk analysis section per decision and long-term strategic considerations.

SALIDA: Make-or-buy matrix table with weighted scores + recommendations table with justification + strategic considerations section.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the item is a strategic differentiating asset: recommend Make even if the cost is higher, with competitive advantage justification.
- If internal capacity is at its limit: include an opportunity cost analysis for building the item internally.
- If hybrid options exist (buy and customize): include a third option in the matrix.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each item's recommendation is supported by the matrix's weighted score, not by preferences.
- Trade-off: analysis rigor proportional to the economic value and strategic risk of the item.
- DoD: the executive committee can approve the make-or-buy decisions based on the matrix without requiring additional analysis.

Protocolo MetodologIA: weight criteria according to the strategic context, make cost and capacity assumptions explicit, and deliver a matrix with a justified recommendation.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-direccion-pr:
[S · SITUATION] An approved project needs its governing document: the Project Management Plan (PMP), which integrates all subsidiary plans (scope, schedule, costs, quality, resources, communications, risks, procurement, stakeholders) into a coherent document that serves as the foundation for execution, monitoring, and closure.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete and integrated Project Management Plan, following the PMBOK structure, with all subsidiary plans referenced or outlined, defined baselines, and a plan change control process.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: You act as a PMP-certified project manager with more than 10 years of experience in technology and organizational transformation projects.

SUPUESTOS: If no project charter or WBS is provided, assume a 9-month digital transformation project, medium budget, 12-person team, predictive methodology with phase reviews. Declare all assumptions explicitly before developing. Ask only if the project's scope and objectives are completely unknown.

INSUMOS: Project charter, WBS, stakeholder register, and any existing subsidiary plans, pasted into the thread.

PASOS:
1. Write the introduction section: PMP purpose, methodology, validity, and update process.
2. Document the baselines: scope (summarized WBS), schedule (key milestones), and cost (budget by phase).
3. For each subsidiary plan, develop a 1–2 page summary: scope, schedule, costs, quality, human resources, communications, risks, procurement, stakeholders.
4. Define the integrated change control process: who can request, how impact is evaluated, who approves, how the PMP is updated.
5. Establish the PMP review and update process: frequency, responsible parties, versioning.
6. Include the glossary of terms and references to supporting documents.

SALIDA: Structured document with index, baseline sections, 9 subsidiary plans in summary, change control process, and glossary; format suitable for the project repository.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the project is agile or hybrid: adapt the schedule and scope sections to sprints/releases and add an agile governance section.
- If subsidiary plans already exist and are approved: reference them with version number instead of rewriting them.
- If the project exceeds 18 months: include a phase review and periodic re-planning process.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each subsidiary plan is represented with its key elements; no sections are empty without justification.
- Trade-off: depth of each section proportional to the complexity and risk of the area; not all plans require the same level of detail.
- DoD: the PMP can be distributed to the team and sponsor as a reference document without additional revisions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: integrate subsidiary plans with internal consistency, declare assumptions about scope and methodology, and deliver a versioned and distributable document.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-bene:
[S · SITUATION] A project has been approved based on benefits promised to the business (cost reduction, revenue increase, efficiency improvement, regulatory compliance, etc.), but without a formal plan to materialize, measure, and sustain those benefits. Without this plan, the benefits remain on paper and the ROI is never verified.

[P · REQUEST] Develop a Benefits Management Plan that defines the expected benefits, their realization metrics, responsible parties, measurement schedule, and the conditions necessary for benefits to be sustained after project closure.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: You act as a Benefits Realization Manager with experience in digital transformation and operational improvement projects.

SUPUESTOS: If project benefits are not specified, infer the most common ones for the described project type (operational efficiency, cycle time reduction, NPS improvement, error reduction). If no baseline data is available, indicate how to establish it before the start. Declare assumptions at the outset. Ask only if the benefit type cannot be inferred with confidence ≥0.85.

INSUMOS: Business case or project justification, related strategic objectives, and current baseline metrics if available, pasted into the thread.

PASOS:
1. Identify and list the project's expected benefits (minimum 4).
2. For each benefit define: description, type (financial/non-financial), beneficiary, quantified expected value, and current baseline.
3. Define the realization metric for each benefit: indicator, formula, data source.
4. Establish the measurement schedule: when the benefit is expected to begin materializing, measurement milestones, full realization date.
5. Assign the responsible party (owner) for each benefit and the conditions necessary for its materialization.
