Assign influence level (high / medium / low). 4. Determine position toward the purchase with justification. 5. Propose a specific relationship strategy per person. 6. Identify power dynamics or alliances among stakeholders. OUTPUT: per-stakeholder table + textual relationship diagram + prioritized action plan. EDGE CASES: (a) if a blocker is identified, escalate the strategy for that actor; (b) if there is no clear decision-maker, flag the risk and propose how to identify one; (c) if there are more than 8 stakeholders, group into priority levels. [C · CRITERIA] Each stakeholder has a specific (non-generic) strategy; the highest-risk actor is identified; the action plan has at least 3 steps with a time-bound owner; DoD: the executive can present the map at a QBR without embarrassment. Protocolo MetodologIA: in complex sales, the deal is won or lost in relationships, not in the proposal.
spec-ventas_identificar_champion: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive has an active opportunity at a corporate account but has not yet identified a person inside the prospect who will act as an internal champion: someone who sells the solution internally when the salesperson is not present. They have information about several client contacts with varying levels of access and influence. [P · REQUEST] Produce an analysis of available contacts to identify the most likely champion candidate, with a profile of the attributes they must meet and an action plan to develop them: sequence of conversations, materials to provide, and validation criteria confirming the champion is active. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are an enterprise sales director specializing in internal relationship development within key accounts and complex sales methodologies such as MEDDIC and Miller Heiman. ASSUMPTIONS: if access to the decision-maker is not mentioned, assume the champion is the primary bridge; if personal motivation data is absent, infer from title and deal context; if there are multiple candidates, analyze the three most relevant. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: description of known contacts and interaction notes, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Define the 5 key attributes of an effective champion in this specific context. 2. Score each candidate on the 5 attributes. 3. Identify the strongest candidate with justification. 4. Design a champion development plan: 3-5 key conversations with an objective each. 5. List materials and enablers to give the champion. 6. Define 3 indicators that the champion is active and acting. OUTPUT: champion profile + candidate scoring + development plan in table + activation indicators. EDGE CASES: (a) if no candidate meets the minimum threshold, propose how to identify new contacts; (b) if the champion candidate lacks access to the decision-maker, design a parallel strategy; (c) if the potential champion has recently changed stance, flag the risk and a reconquest strategy. [C · CRITERIA] The analysis distinguishes between a friendly contact and a real champion; the development plan is specific and executable in 3 weeks; activation indicators are observable and verifiable; DoD: the executive knows exactly who to develop and what to do tomorrow. Protocolo MetodologIA: without a champion there is no deal; the champion is not named — they are built with evidence.
spec-ventas_comprador_economico: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive has spent weeks working with technical or operational contacts at a prospect account but has not managed to access the person with real authority to approve the budget and close the purchase (the economic buyer). The opportunity is at risk of stalling or closing with a no due to lack of executive coverage. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete strategy to access the economic buyer: how to identify them if not yet clear, how to obtain an introduction through the current contact, and a first-contact script (email and meeting opening) adapted to the executive profile. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are an enterprise VP of Sales with 20 years closing deals above USD 500k that required executive navigation in Fortune 1000 accounts and leading LATAM companies. ASSUMPTIONS: if the economic buyer is not identified, assume they are the C-suite of the beneficiary area (CFO for efficiency deals, CTO for technology, CEO if the deal is strategic); if the current contact does not have a direct relationship with the executive, assume they can make an email introduction. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: deal description, current contact, and reason why the economic buyer has not been accessed, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Identify the probable economic buyer with their title and typical motivation. 2. Design the argument to request the introduction from the current contact (1 paragraph). 3. Draft a first-contact email with the economic buyer (maximum 120 words). 4. Design a 3-minute meeting opening oriented toward business impact. 5. Anticipate the 3 most probable objections from the executive and their responses. OUTPUT: strategy + introduction script + email + meeting opening + objection handling. EDGE CASES: (a) if the current contact resists making the introduction, propose an alternative direct access strategy; (b) if the economic buyer is the CEO, adjust the level of abstraction of the message; (c) if there are multiple economic buyers (e.g., in a board of directors), prioritize the one with the greatest urgency. [C · CRITERIA] The email is no more than 120 words and ends with a single closing question; the meeting opening does not mention product features; each objection has a response under 60 words; DoD: the executive can send the email without modification. Protocolo MetodologIA: the economic buyer makes decisions with business data, not with demos; reaching them late means arriving when they have already decided.
spec-ventas_criterios_decision: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive is in the active evaluation phase with a prospect. The client will compare proposals from several vendors, but the criteria by which they will make the decision have not been explicitly stated or have been communicated vaguely. The executive needs to understand precisely what the client will evaluate, with what weight, and who will judge each criterion. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured list of decision criteria inferred from the prospect context, organized by category and relative weight, with validation questions to confirm them in the next conversation and a salesperson positioning strategy against each criterion. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a sales strategy consultant specializing in RFP evaluation processes and vendor comparison in B2B technology and services markets. ASSUMPTIONS: if no explicit criteria are mentioned, infer them from the sector and solution type using the most common evaluation standards (TCO, implementation, support, integration, scalability, referenceability); if the prospect has not given weights, use the sector's typical distribution. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: deal context, solution type, and any prospect comments about what they value, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Categorize criteria into: technical, commercial, relational, and risk. 2. List the most probable criteria per category with estimated relative weight. 3. Draft 2 validation questions per criterion (to confirm in conversation). 4. Propose a salesperson positioning strategy for each criterion. 5. Identify the 3 criteria where the salesperson has the greatest competitive advantage. OUTPUT: criteria table with weight + validation questions + positioning strategy per criterion. EDGE CASES: (a) if the prospect is in a formal RFP process, adjust the analysis to the typical structure of a tender document; (b) if there are multiple evaluators with different criteria, segment the table by evaluator profile; (c) if the salesperson is at a disadvantage on a key criterion, design a neutralization strategy. [C · CRITERIA] Criteria sum to 100% weight; each criterion has at least one validation question and one positioning action; the 3 advantage criteria are context-specific (not generic); DoD: the executive can use the table to prepare the next evaluation meeting. Protocolo MetodologIA: whoever defines the evaluation criteria defines the outcome; early capture is the first act of selling.
spec-ventas_evento_critico: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive has an opportunity with a good relationship and identified problem, but without real urgency: the prospect is interested but there is no concrete date or reason forcing a decision soon. The deal is at risk of extending indefinitely or dying by inertia. [P · REQUEST] Produce a critical buying event analysis: identify or construct the concrete fact (internal or external to the prospect) that creates real urgency to decide before a given date, and design the conversation to connect that event to the salesperson's proposal so the prospect recognizes it as their own. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a consultative sales director specializing in sales cycle management and legitimate urgency creation in B2B technology and enterprise services deals. ASSUMPTIONS: if no clear external event is mentioned, identify the most common for the sector (fiscal year-end, contract expiration, product launch, regulatory audit, leadership change); if no deadline is mentioned, propose a 90-day horizon as reasonable urgency. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: deal description, prospect sector, known client or market events, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Identify 3-5 candidate critical events (internal and external) relevant to this prospect. 2. Select the strongest one with justification. 3. Calculate the implicit deadline of the event. 4. Design the argument to connect the event to the purchase decision (2 paragraphs). 5. Draft the conversation question so the prospect recognizes the event as urgent on their own. 6. Include the risk of ignoring the event (cost of arriving late). OUTPUT: candidate event analysis + recommended event + connection argument + conversation question + deadline calculation. EDGE CASES: (a) if the prospect has explicitly said there is no urgency, design a strategy to challenge that stance; (b) if the critical event is external and the prospect can ignore it, build a vulnerability argument; (c) if there are multiple events, create a sequence of escalating urgency. [C · CRITERIA] The critical event is specific to the prospect (not a generic industry event); the conversation question does not sound manipulative; the deadline calculation is realistic; DoD: the executive can use the argument on the next call without the prospect feeling artificial pressure. Protocolo MetodologIA: urgency is not imposed — it is discovered; the critical event is the clock the prospect already has without knowing it.
spec-ventas_value_hypothesis: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive is about to make first contact with a new prospect or has just received limited information about them. Before the first meeting they need to formulate a value hypothesis: a structured assumption about the impact their solution can generate for that specific client, so they arrive with a provocative value proposition instead of a generic product presentation. [P · REQUEST] Produce a documented initial value hypothesis: assumed problem, estimated economic impact, solution mechanism, key assumptions that must be validated in discovery, and the opening message for the first conversation. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a Challenger Sale sales consultant specializing in building provocative value hypotheses that force the prospect to think differently before having given any brief. ASSUMPTIONS: if the sector is not specified, use B2B enterprise technology; if the interlocutor's title is not indicated, assume VP or Director of the relevant function; if no company data exists, infer the context of a mid-size company of 200–1,000 employees with typical sector challenges. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: company name or sector, type of solution the seller offers, and any available prospect information, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Identify the prospect's most probable problem given their sector, size, and market moment. 2. Quantify the potential impact of solving that problem (with [ASSUMPTION] where applicable). 3. Articulate the mechanism by which the seller's solution generates that impact. 4. List the 5 key assumptions that must be validated in the discovery meeting. 5. Draft the opening message for the first conversation (maximum 80 words). OUTPUT: value hypothesis card with: Assumed problem / Estimated impact / Mechanism / Assumptions to validate / Opening message. EDGE CASES: (a) if the prospect already has a competitor's solution, adapt the hypothesis to that solution's typical gaps; (b) if the company has had a recent event (merger, CEO change, expansion), connect the hypothesis to that event; (c) if the solution is completely new to the sector, design the hypothesis as a problem reframe (not a solution reframe). [C · CRITERIA] The hypothesis is specific to the prospect (not a generic presentation); the opening message provokes a reaction of recognition or curiosity; the assumptions are questions that discovery must answer; DoD: the executive can use the card as a guide for the entire first meeting. Protocolo MetodologIA: arriving with a hypothesis means arriving as an advisor; arriving without one means arriving as a salesperson.
spec-ventas_resumen_discovery: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive has just finished a discovery meeting with a prospect. They have raw notes or a transcribed recording of the conversation. They need to convert those notes into a structured document that serves two purposes: sharing it with the prospect as a confirmation of what was understood (alignment and credibility) and using it internally to update the CRM, prepare the proposal, and align the team. [P · REQUEST] Produce a post-discovery summary in two versions: (1) external version to share with the prospect (confirms understanding, builds trust, proposes next steps), and (2) internal version for the CRM and sales team (MEDDIC/situation/impact/next action/risks). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior account executive specializing in post-discovery communication that maximizes the perception of competence and accelerates deal progress. ASSUMPTIONS: if notes are fragmented, infer context and identify information gaps; if next steps are not mentioned, propose the most probable ones given the deal stage; if no follow-up date was agreed, propose one within 5–7 business days. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: raw notes or transcript of the discovery meeting, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Extract the core problem, declared impact, and buying motivations. 2. Identify stakeholders mentioned and their roles. 3. Capture decision criteria and the buying process mentioned. 4. Record critical information gaps. 5. Draft external version (maximum 400 words, professional and warm tone). 6. Complete internal MEDDIC card with available data. OUTPUT: external version ready to send + internal MEDDIC card. EDGE CASES: (a) if the meeting revealed an unanticipated blocker, highlight it in both versions; (b) if the prospect gave negative signals, record them in the internal version without reflecting them in the external one; (c) if multiple next steps were agreed, prioritize them by urgency. [C · CRITERIA] The external version contains no internal sales jargon; the MEDDIC card identifies missing fields; next steps have an owner and a date; DoD: the executive can send the external version within 30 minutes of the meeting without significant editing. Protocolo MetodologIA: the post-discovery summary is the moment where the seller demonstrates they listened more than they talked.
spec-ventas_preparacion_demo: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales executive has a product or solution demo scheduled with a prospect within the next 3–7 days. They have discovery information about the client's problems, the stakeholders who will attend, and the evaluation criteria identified. They need to structure the demo so it is not a feature presentation but a value demonstration oriented to the client's specific problem. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete demo preparation plan: narrative structure for the presentation, key scenes to show aligned with the prospect's problems, necessary preparation materials, sales team role assignment, and pre-demo validation checklist. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior solutions engineer (pre-sales) with 10 years designing consultative demos that convert technical evaluations into purchase decisions in B2B technology markets. ASSUMPTIONS: if demo duration is not specified, assume 60 minutes; if the number of client attendees is not indicated, assume 4–6 people with technical and business profiles; if there are no explicit evaluation criteria, infer them from the sector and type of solution. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: discovery notes, type of solution to demonstrate, attendee profile, and known evaluation criteria, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Define the demo's narrative arc (problem → friction → solution → outcome). 2. Design 3–5 key scenes tied to the prospect's specific pains. 3. Identify moments for client participation within the demo. 4. Assign sales team roles (facilitator, demonstrator, note-taker). 5. List necessary preparation materials (client data, demo environment, sample data). 6. Create the validation checklist for the 24 hours before. OUTPUT: complete demo plan with narrative structure + scenes + roles + materials + checklist. EDGE CASES: (a) if attendees are primarily technical, increase the depth of architecture scenes; (b) if it is a virtual demo, add technical contingencies; (c) if the prospect has already seen a previous demo, redesign to show only what has not been seen with a new narrative. [C · CRITERIA] Each scene is tied to a specific prospect pain (not a generic feature); the demo has at least 2 moments of interaction with attendees; the checklist covers technical, narrative, and logistical aspects; DoD: the sales team can execute the demo without improvising. Protocolo MetodologIA: a demo without prior discovery is a catalog; a demo with discovery is a diagnosis with evidence.
spec-ventas_demo_basada_valor: [S · SITUATION] A B2B sales team has a demo scheduled with a prospect and there is a risk of falling into the usual pattern of showing product features instead of demonstrating the business impact the prospect will obtain. The team wants to structure and execute a demo that the prospect experiences as a mirror of their own problem solved, not as a demonstration of technical capabilities. [P · REQUEST] Produce a value-based demo script: conversation structure with narrative transitions, problem-anchoring phrases before each technical scene, impact questions during the demo, and the close of the presentation oriented to concrete next steps. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a pre-sales director and product evangelist specializing in narrative demo methodologies (SNAP, Command of the Message, Challenger) in B2B enterprise technology markets. ASSUMPTIONS: if the solution is not specified, assume an enterprise software platform with operational efficiency modules; if there is no prospect data, assume a manufacturing or logistics company of 500–2,000 employees with friction in manual processes; if demo time is not indicated, assume 45 active minutes. Ask no more than 2 questions if confidence is below 0.85; otherwise declare assumptions and continue. INPUTS: name of the solution to demonstrate, identified prospect pains, and attendee profile, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Build the narrative opening that connects with the prospect's world before showing anything (2 minutes, no screens). 2. Design 3–4 demo scenes, each with: pain-anchoring phrase + technical transition + subsequent impact question. 3. Create participatory validation moments (questions the prospect answers while watching the demo). 4. Design the demo close oriented to next steps with a tentative date. 5. Prepare 3 responses to frequent technical objections during the demo. OUTPUT: complete value-based demo script with opening + scenes + questions + close + objection handling. EDGE CASES: (a) if the prospect interrupts to request unplanned features, include a narrative redirection protocol; (b) if attendees are only technical, adapt impact questions to operational metrics instead of financial ones; (c) if the demo is asynchronous (recorded), adapt the script to narrative monologue without live questions. [C · CRITERIA] Each technical scene is preceded by a pain-anchoring phrase for the prospect; the close does not say "what did you think?" but proposes a concrete action; validation questions have short answers (yes/no or a number); DoD: any member of the pre-sales team can execute the script without having been in the discovery. Protocolo MetodologIA: showing to impress is a catalog; showing to recognize is a sale.
spec-ventas_guion_demo_tell_show_tell:
[S · SITUATION] A sales or pre-sales executive must present a software or service demo before a prospect's evaluation committee. Without a structured script, the demo loses its narrative thread, the prospect disengages, and the key differentiators are buried under features. [P · REQUEST] Create a complete narrative script for the demo, with clearly delimited Tell-Show-Tell sections, exact phrases for the presenter, on-screen instructions and transitions, ready for rehearsal and execution. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior sales enablement consultant with 12 years designing winning demos for B2B software companies. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify total duration, assume 30 minutes; if they do not indicate the number of modules, assume 3 main functional modules; if they do not detail the audience profile, assume CTO + functional manager; proceed declaring these assumptions without asking unless confidence is below 0.85 on any of them. INPUTS: the user will paste a description of the product or service, the prospect's main pain, and up to 3 key differentiators. STEPS: 1. Identify the core pain and the hero of the story (the prospect, not the product). 2. Draft the opening TELL section: problem context + value promise in ≤3 sentences. 3. For each module: draft the introductory TELL (why they will see this), the SHOW with step-by-step navigation instructions + transition phrases + emphasis points, and the closing TELL (what they just saw + business impact). 4. Draft the global narrative close: recap + concrete call to action. 5. Include a presenter notes column with body language cues and silence management. OUTPUT: script document in a three-column table (Time | What the presenter says | What is shown on screen) plus margin notes section, ~600–900 words of script content. EDGE CASES: (a) complex product with 10+ modules: select only the 3 most relevant to the declared pain and add an optional modules appendix; (b) purely technical audience: increase architecture depth and reduce business metaphors; (c) demo in a language other than Spanish: produce the script in the requested language while maintaining the structure. [C · CRITERIA] Each TELL section is ≤45 seconds of reading aloud. Each SHOW has an actionable on-screen instruction. The script passes the whisper test: someone unfamiliar with the product can execute it alone. Trade-off: technical depth vs. narrative clarity; prioritize clarity. DoD: script reviewed, times summed = agreed duration ±10%.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions used, number each step executed, and close with acceptance criterion verified.
spec-ventas_demo_tell_show_tell:
[S · SITUATION] A seller or pre-sales person has a demo already prepared or a draft screen flow, but the presentation lacks narrative structure: it jumps straight to features without context and does not close each module with impact. The prospect is left with a "feature catalog" feeling instead of a solution to their problem. [P · REQUEST] Apply the Tell-Show-Tell pattern to the existing demo flow: reorganize or supplement the content so that each segment has an entry TELL, a demonstrable SHOW, and a closing TELL with business impact, delivering the result as a restructured demo map. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a B2B demo architect with experience in enterprise SaaS, specializing in adapting existing flows to the Tell-Show-Tell pattern without rewriting the demo from scratch. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not deliver the existing flow, ask for a minimum list of modules or screens before continuing; if they do not indicate the audience title, assume decision-maker + operational user; if they do not specify time per module, distribute proportionally over the declared total time; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence is below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste the current demo flow (can be a list of screens, index, or description of steps) and the prospect's context (industry, pain, title). STEPS: 1. Analyze the delivered flow and identify the 3–5 natural "show" moments. 2. For each show moment, draft the entry TELL (problem + specific promise in ≤2 sentences). 3. Describe the SHOW with the concrete on-screen actions and verbal emphasis points. 4. Draft the closing TELL (what they just saw + metric or concrete benefit). 5. Assemble the complete map in table format and estimate time for each block. 6. Flag if any current module does not fit the pattern and propose a reframe or elimination. OUTPUT: restructured demo map in table format (Block | Entry TELL | SHOW description | Closing TELL | Est. Time) + list of recommended adjustments vs. original flow. EDGE CASES: (a) flow with more than 8 modules: group into a maximum of 5 thematic blocks before applying the pattern; (b) demo without screens (pure service): use visual artifacts, data, or cases as substitutes for the SHOW; (c) executive audience with <20 min: compress to a maximum of 3 blocks with a SHOW of ≤60 seconds each. [C · CRITERIA] Each entry TELL contextualizes the pain before showing any feature. Each closing TELL mentions a measurable or verifiable benefit. The map can be executed without the original demo author. Trade-off: feature coverage vs. narrative flow; prioritize flow. DoD: map delivered with time per block and list of adjustments.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions applied, number steps executed, and confirm DoD at the end.
spec-ventas_personalizar_demo:
[S · SITUATION] A pre-sales team has a generic product demo that shows all features in a standard way. The prospect has a specific use case with their own language, processes, and metrics. Presenting the generic demo generates low resonance and the prospect perceives that the solution was not designed for them. [P · REQUEST] Produce a demo personalization plan: what data to change, which flows to prioritize, what terminology to adapt, and what scenarios to build so the demo faithfully reflects the prospect's operational environment, delivered as a personalization checklist + adjustment script. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior pre-sales engineer specializing in demo personalization for enterprise software, with experience mapping client processes to product flows. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not provide prospect information, request at least industry, decision-maker title, and one or two critical processes before continuing; if the product is not specified, assume a generic enterprise management platform and declare it; if there is no real client data, assume representative fictitious data will be used; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: the user will paste prospect information (industry, size, key processes, terminology used, pains identified in discovery) and a description of the product or base demo. STEPS: 1. Extract the 3–5 prospect processes most relevant to the product. 2. Map each process to a module or flow in the base demo. 3. For each mapped module, specify: field names to rename, sample data to substitute, client-specific metrics to incorporate, navigation flow to prioritize or simplify. 4. Identify features of the generic demo that do not apply and mark them as "hide in this demo." 5. Draft the adjustment script: ordered list of changes with exact field, current value, and proposed value. 6. Propose a narrative scenario of 2–3 paragraphs using the prospect's language. OUTPUT: (A) personalization checklist in table format (Module | Change | Field/element | Proposed value | Priority) and (B) personalized narrative opening scenario. EDGE CASES: (a) prospect in a regulated sector (banking, health): add a compliance note next to each proposed fictitious data point; (b) technical demo with data in a real database: add a section with sample data loading scripts; (c) preparation time <2 hours: prioritize only the 3 highest-visual-impact changes. [C · CRITERIA] The personalized demo makes the prospect hear their own language in the first 60 seconds. Each change has a concrete proposed value, not a vague recommendation. The checklist can be executed by someone other than the person who conducted the discovery. Trade-off: fidelity to the client's real environment vs. preparation time; balance at the level of "recognizable, not perfect." DoD: complete checklist + narrative scenario delivered.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions applied, number steps, and confirm DoD.
spec-ventas_demo_descubrimiento:
[S · SITUATION] The sales team faces a prospect whose real problem is not fully defined: the client knows something is failing but cannot articulate what solution they need. A standard product demo closes doors before opening them. A conversational demo format is needed that discovers and validates needs in real time while showing capabilities. [P · REQUEST] Design a 45–60 minute iterative discovery demo session: agenda, discovery questions per module, pivots based on the prospect's response, and a protocol for capturing insights live — delivered as an actionable session guide. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a consultative sales consultant with SPIN Selling certification and experience in discovery demos for complex enterprise technology solutions. ASSUMPTIONS: if the client's vertical is not specified, assume a mid-size professional services company and declare it; if there is no prior discovery information, assume this is the first contact; if the number of prospect attendees is not specified, assume 3–4 people from different roles; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence is below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste available prospect context (industry, size, expressed symptom or problem, primary contact) and a description of the product or portfolio to explore. STEPS: 1. Design a 5-min opening: frame the session as a joint exploration, not a presentation. 2. For each product capability area (maximum 4), design: a situation question, a problem question, a 3–5 minute mini-show, and an implication question at the close of the module. 3. Design a pivot matrix: if the prospect shows high interest → go deeper; if they show indifference → skip to the next module; if they identify an uncovered pain → note it and promise follow-up. 4. Design a live capture sheet: table to note the prospect's verbatim quotes, pain level (1–5), and associated module. 5. Design a 5-min close: synthesis of what was discovered, confirmation of priorities with the client, and proposal of a concrete next step. OUTPUT: session guide with (A) agenda with times, (B) question bank per module, (C) simplified pivot matrix, (D) live capture sheet in table format. EDGE CASES: (a) senior executive prospect: reduce questions to 2 per module and increase listening time; (b) remote session: add instructions for a real-time collaboration tool; (c) prospect already informed about the product: skip basic situation questions and go directly to implication. [C · CRITERIA] The seller speaks less than 40% of the time in the session. Each module generates at least one captured verbatim quote. The agreed next step is a dated action, not "we'll stay in touch." Trade-off: breadth of discovery vs. depth in modules; prioritize discovering 2–3 deep pains over covering all capabilities. DoD: complete guide with the four listed deliverables.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions used, number steps executed, and confirm DoD.
spec-ventas_manejo_objeciones_demo:
[S · SITUATION] During a product demo before a prospect, objections arise in real time: price, implementation complexity, comparison with competitors, doubts about integrations, or skepticism about ROI. A presenter without a trained protocol can get stuck, unnecessarily cede ground, or lose the narrative thread of the demo. [P · REQUEST] Create a bank of responses to frequent objections during a demo, with a 4-step protocol for handling them in real time and response templates by objection category, ready for memorization and practice. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior sales coach with experience training pre-sales teams for enterprise software, specializing in objection handling in demo contexts. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the type of solution, assume a B2B enterprise software platform with a medium-to-high ticket; if they do not indicate the business's recurring objections, generate the 8 most common ones in that context; if there is no information about the mentioned competitor, include a generic differentiation response structure; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: the user can paste the most frequent objections their team receives, product context, and prospect segment. STEPS: 1. Define the 4-step protocol for any objection: (1) Acknowledge and validate ("It makes sense to ask about that…"), (2) Clarify the real source of the objection with a question, (3) Respond with evidence or a reframe, (4) Resume the demo thread. 2. Categorize objections into: price/budget, implementation complexity/risk, competitor comparison, technical integration/compatibility, demonstrable ROI/value, timing/priority. 3. For each category, write 2 response templates: one for the economic decision-maker and one for the technical user. 4. For competitor objections, draft a response that acknowledges the competitor without attacking them and reframes around the key differentiator. 5. Draft pocket cards: one per category with the protocol summarized in ≤5 lines. OUTPUT: (A) 4-step protocol illustrated with an example, (B) objections bank in table format (Category | Typical objection | Decision-maker response | Technical user response), (C) 6 pocket cards in plain text format. EDGE CASES: (a) objection that requires escalation to an architect or director: "buy time" protocol + commitment to respond within 24h; (b) repeated objection in the same session: indicate when to propose a parking lot and continue; (c) objection that invalidates a complete module: protocol for reorganizing the demo in real time. [C · CRITERIA] The presenter does not abandon the demo for any objection; they always resume the thread. Each response acknowledges the concern before responding. No response attacks a competitor by name. Trade-off: completeness of the bank vs. memorability; prioritize 8 mastered objections over 20 superficial ones. DoD: bank of ≥8 objections, protocol, and cards delivered.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, number steps executed, and confirm DoD.
spec-ventas_cierre_demo:
[S · SITUATION] A product demo has concluded its demonstration segment. The presenter needs to close the session in a way that consolidates perceived value, identifies the prospect's level of interest, and agrees on a concrete next step that advances the sales cycle. Without a structured close, the session ends in an ambiguous "we'll be in touch" and momentum is lost. [P · REQUEST] Design a demo closing protocol of 8–10 minutes: sequence of value confirmation questions, interest signal reading technique, next step proposals differentiated by level of interest, and exact phrases to agree on the next action — delivered as a ready-to-use closing guide. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a sales director with experience in consultative sales cycles for enterprise software, specializing in designing demo closes that convert interest into commitment. ASSUMPTIONS: if the stage of the sales cycle is not specified, assume it is the first formal demo; if there is no information about the interlocutor's level of authority, assume a decision-maker with influence but not the final signatory; if the CRM is not indicated, assume manual registration; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence is below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste what was shown in the demo, the prospect's observed reactions, and any known information about their decision process. STEPS: 1. Draft a 2-minute value summary: recap of the 3 "show" moments linked to the pains expressed by the prospect. 2. Design 3 value confirmation questions ("Does this resolve the problem you mentioned about X?", "What generated the most impact from what you saw?", "Is there anything that wasn't clear?"). 3. Design a signal reading table: verbal and non-verbal indicators of high, medium, and low interest, with the recommended closing action for each level. 4. Design a next step menu by level of interest: (high) schedule a technical session or proposal in <5 days; (medium) send a success case + follow-up call in 7 days; (low) ask openly what is blocking progress + offer a value resource. 5. Draft exact phrases to propose the next step without pressure: "Based on what we saw today, the best step would be…". 6. Design a commitment confirmation protocol: who does what by when, with a post-demo follow-up email format. OUTPUT: (A) 2-min value summary script, (B) confirmation question bank, (C) interest signal table, (D) next step menu with exact phrases, (E) post-demo follow-up email template. EDGE CASES: (a) clearly uninterested prospect: honest closing protocol that preserves the relationship for future opportunities; (b) decision-maker absent from the demo: protocol for closing with those present and securing the bridge to the decision-maker; (c) prospect asks for price at the close: protocol to redirect to a formal proposal without giving a number cold. [C · CRITERIA] The session ends with an agreed dated action, not a vague commitment. Each confirmation question has an expected answer that informs the next step. The follow-up email can be sent in less than 5 minutes post-demo. Trade-off: pressure to advance vs. long-term relationship; prioritize relationship. DoD: all 5 listed deliverables are complete.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, number steps, and confirm that the close ends with a dated action.
spec-ventas_poc_plan:
[S · SITUATION] After a successful demo, the prospect or sales team wants to move forward with a Proof of Concept (PoC) to validate that the solution works in the client's real environment before purchase. Without a formal plan, the PoC becomes an endless project, success criteria remain implicit, and the effort does not translate into a purchase decision. [P · REQUEST] Draft a structured PoC plan: technical and business scope, timeline, responsibilities, measurable success criteria, required resources, and an exit agreement, delivered as a plan document ready to review and sign with the client. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a technical pre-sales manager with experience structuring and managing enterprise software PoCs for mid-market and enterprise prospects. ASSUMPTIONS: if PoC duration is not specified, assume 30 calendar days; if there is no information about the client's technical environment, assume basic integration with one existing system as the first milestone; if the client team is not specified, assume a 2-person technical team and a business sponsor; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence drops below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste: product or module description, client pain points and objectives declared in discovery, known constraints (technical, time, resource). STEPS: 1. Define the PoC scope: which modules or capabilities are tested, which specific use cases are validated, and what is explicitly out of scope. 2. Set the week-by-week timeline: preparation + setup, use-case execution, evaluation and decision. 3. Define the responsibility matrix (simplified RACI): what the vendor does, what the client does. 4. Draft success criteria in the format "the PoC is successful if..." with verifiable metrics. 5. Identify required resources: test data, access, infrastructure, people's time. 6. Draft the exit clause: conditions under which the PoC is stopped early and what happens to commitments. 7. Include the post-PoC decision-making process: who decides, in what timeframe, and with what criteria. OUTPUT: structured PoC plan document in sections: (1) Objective and scope, (2) Timeline with milestones, (3) Responsibility matrix, (4) Success criteria, (5) Required resources, (6) Exit clause and decision agreement. EDGE CASES: (a) PoC in the client's production environment: add a risk management and reversibility section; (b) multiple business units involved: add a stakeholder matrix and escalation channel; (c) competitive PoC (parallel evaluation with another vendor): add a section on confidentiality agreements and fair access. [C · CRITERIA] Success criteria are binary (met / not met) or have a numerical threshold. The document can be reviewed and signed by the client without requiring additional explanation. The plan has no ambiguities about who does what. Trade-off: plan detail vs. speed of start; balance at "enough detail to commit, not so much that it delays the kick-off." DoD: document with all 6 sections complete.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, number the steps, and confirm that the success criteria are verifiable.
spec-ventas_criterios_exito_poc:
[S · SITUATION] A PoC (Proof of Concept) between vendor and client is about to start or has just begun. The most frequent cause of PoC failure is not technical: it is the absence of success criteria agreed upon by both parties. Each side has different expectations, and when the PoC ends, neither can declare whether it was successful or not. [P · REQUEST] Create a mutual success criteria document for the PoC, agreed upon and signed by vendor and client, with verifiable metrics, measurement method, owner, and success threshold for each criterion, ready to include in the PoC agreement. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a pre-sales architect with experience negotiating success criteria for enterprise software PoCs, specializing in building agreements that protect both parties and facilitate the purchase decision. ASSUMPTIONS: if client objectives are not specified, request them before continuing since without them the document loses validity; if the number of criteria is not indicated, use between 4 and 6 to maintain focus; if there is no information about the technical environment, add an environment validation criterion as the first point; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence drops below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste the client's business objectives, pain points expressed in discovery, the product capabilities to be tested, and any known constraints or conditions. STEPS: 1. Map each client business objective to a product capability. 2. For each mapping, draft the success criterion in an observable format: "Considered successful when [subject] [observable verb] [measurable result] under [condition]." 3. Define the measurement method for each criterion: which tool, which data point, who captures it. 4. Assign the validation owner: vendor, client, or both. 5. Set the minimum success threshold and the target threshold for each criterion. 6. Identify blocking criteria (if not met, the PoC cannot be declared successful) vs. desirable criteria. 7. Draft the agreement section: "The parties agree that the PoC is declared successful if all blocking criteria are met at the minimum level." OUTPUT: success criteria document with table (Criterion | Associated business objective | Measurement method | Owner | Minimum threshold | Target threshold | Blocking Y/N) + signature agreement section. EDGE CASES: (a) client wants subjective criteria ("should look easy to use"): convert to an observable criterion with a usability test or adoption rate; (b) technical criterion impossible to measure in the PoC environment: flag the limitation and propose a proxy criterion; (c) more than 6 criteria requested: prioritize the 6 with the greatest weight on the purchase decision and move the rest to "observations." [C · CRITERIA] Each criterion is verifiable by a third party without ambiguity. Blocking criteria are those strictly necessary for the solution to be viable. The document can be presented at a review meeting without requiring additional explanation. Trade-off: exhaustiveness of criteria vs. focus on what is decisive; prioritize 4-6 strong criteria over 10 weak ones. DoD: complete table with ≥4 criteria, blocking/desirable classification, and agreement section.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare applied assumptions, number the steps, and confirm that all blocking criteria are verifiable.
spec-ventas_storytelling_caso_exito:
[S · SITUATION] The sales team has data from a client who successfully implemented the solution, but they present it as a list of metrics or a technical summary. The prospect does not connect emotionally with the numbers: they need to see themselves reflected in the story of another client who faced the same problem and overcame it with the solution. [P · REQUEST] Transform the raw data of a success story into a structured storytelling narrative ready to use in demos, proposals, and sales conversations, with a problem opening, transformation development, and impact close. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a content marketing and B2B sales storytelling specialist with experience converting technical success stories into impact narratives for executive and technical audiences. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not provide outcome metrics, draft the impact with qualitative description and mark estimated values with [ASSUMPTION]; if there is no information about the protagonist's role, assume operations manager or equivalent; if the case's sector is not indicated, infer it from the client's name or description; proceed declaring assumptions. INPUTS: the user will paste the success story data: client (may be anonymous), industry, initial problem, solution implemented, results obtained (quantitative and qualitative), implementation time. STEPS: 1. Identify the "crisis moment" or maximum pain point of the client before the solution. 2. Build the 3-act narrative arc: (A) The world before: the problematic situation and the consequences of the pain; (B) Transformation: how the decision was made and how the implementation worked; (C) The world after: concrete results + a real or reconstructed client quote. 3. Draft the long version (400-500 words) for written proposals. 4. Draft the short version (90-120 words) for verbal use in demos. 5. Extract 3 impact bullets for a reference slide. 6. Identify the most relevant element of the story for the current prospect (if the user indicates their profile). OUTPUT: (A) long narrative, (B) short narrative, (C) 3 impact bullets, (D) relevance note for the current prospect. EDGE CASES: (a) client wants anonymity: replace name with sector and size ("a mid-sized manufacturing company in Mexico"); (b) results only qualitative: build the impact with a description of how the situation changed and add a validation note; (c) client story from a different sector than the prospect: add an analogy bridge at the end of the short version. [C · CRITERIA] The long narrative makes the reader feel they know the protagonist. The impact bullets have a number or percentage (real or marked [ASSUMPTION]). The short version can be read aloud in 30-40 seconds. Trade-off: narrative detail vs. brevity; the short version prioritizes brevity, the long version prioritizes depth. DoD: all 4 deliverables completed.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare applied assumptions, number the steps, and confirm that metrics are marked as real or [ASSUMPTION].
spec-ventas_propuesta_comercial:
[S · SITUATION] The sales team needs to present a formal commercial proposal to the prospect after the discovery and demo stage. Poorly structured proposals mix technical description with price, lack a value thread, and are perceived as generic quotes rather than solutions designed for the client. [P · REQUEST] Create the complete structure of a persuasive commercial proposal: section index, key content for each section, length and focus criteria for each block, and a document presentation message template, ready to use as a working framework for drafting the proposal. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a sales director with experience structuring winning commercial proposals for mid-to-high-ticket B2B technology and services solutions. ASSUMPTIONS: if the solution type is not specified, assume software as a service (SaaS) with an implementation component; if there is no information about the prospect's decision process, assume an evaluation committee with technical and business criteria; if no desired length is indicated, assume 8-12 pages excluding cover and appendices; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence drops below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste the prospect's information, pain points and objectives identified in discovery, the modules or services to propose, known commercial conditions, and the reference budget if applicable. STEPS: 1. Design the proposal index in order of greatest to least importance for the decision-maker. 2. For each section, draft: a value-oriented title (not descriptive), expected key content, recommended length, and tone. 3. Ensure that the "problem understanding" section precedes the "proposed solution" section. 4. Design the investment section to appear after value has been established, never as the second section. 5. Include a next steps section with dates and owners. 6. Draft the proposal delivery message template (email/message in ≤150 words). OUTPUT: (A) complete index with a description of each section (name | key content | length | tone), (B) list of format and design recommendations, (C) delivery message template. EDGE CASES: (a) proposal for a formal tender with a prescribed format: adapt the index to the required format while maintaining value principles; (b) proposal in English or another language: produce the index in the requested language; (c) proposal for a single buyer with no committee: shorten to 5-6 sections with emphasis on the decision-maker's personal ROI. [C · CRITERIA] The decision-maker can understand the value of the proposal by reading only the executive summary. The investment section appears after the value section. Next steps have a date and an owner. Trade-off: technical detail vs. executive clarity; produce two versions (executive summary + technical appendix) if there are mixed audiences. DoD: complete index + delivery message.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare applied assumptions, number the steps, and confirm that the investment appears after the value.
spec-ventas_executive_summary:
[S · SITUATION] A commercial proposal is almost ready, but the executive summary is generic: it lists product features, repeats the vendor's company name several times, and does not articulate why this solution is the answer to this specific client's problem at this specific moment. The executive who reads only the summary does not understand the value and cannot defend the decision internally. [P · REQUEST] Draft a commercial proposal executive summary of at most one page (250-350 words) that articulates the client's problem, the proposed solution, the expected value, and the call to action, calibrated for an executive reader with 90 seconds of attention. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a senior commercial proposal writer with experience in executive communication for complex technology solution sales. ASSUMPTIONS: if the complete proposal draft is not provided, request at least: the client's core problem, the proposed solution, 2-3 value metrics, and the desired call to action before continuing; if the client has no hard ROI data, use qualitative value description and mark any projection with [ASSUMPTION]; if the reader's role is not indicated, assume CEO or general manager; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence drops below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste the client context (problem, objectives), the proposed solution, the strongest value arguments, and the desired next step. STEPS: 1. Open with a sentence that names the client's problem without mentioning the vendor (first sentence, first paragraph). 2. Paragraph 2: articulate the proposed solution in the client's language, not in product jargon. 3. Paragraph 3: present the 3 strongest reasons why this solution is the right answer for this client at this moment. 4. Paragraph 4: expected impact quantified or described with evidence (analogous case if there are no own data points). 5. Closing sentence: concrete call to action (schedule a review, approve the proposal, start a PoC). 6. Check that the vendor's name appears at most 2 times and the client's name or their problem appears at least 4 times. OUTPUT: finalized executive summary in prose, 250-350 words, with no bullets or intermediate subheadings, ready to copy into the proposal. EDGE CASES: (a) evaluation committee with multiple perspectives: add a bridge sentence that acknowledges both the technical and the business perspective; (b) competitive proposal where there is another finalist: include a differentiation sentence without naming the competitor; (c) client who already knows the product: omit the solution description paragraph and add more weight to the expected impact. [C · CRITERIA] Can be read aloud in 90 seconds or less. The client's problem is the first idea. No sentence starts with the vendor's name. Contains an explicit call to action. Trade-off: persuasion vs. neutrality; calibrate to the client's tone (conservative or innovative). DoD: finalized text of 250-350 words with the 5 structural elements present.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare applied assumptions, number the steps, and confirm that the executive summary has the 5 structural elements.
spec-ventas_business_case:
[S · SITUATION] The prospect's internal sponsor is convinced of the solution's value but needs to justify the investment before the CFO or executive committee with a solid business case. Without this document, the project stalls in budget approval indefinitely. The vendor who helps build the business case accelerates the decision and positions itself as a strategic partner, not just a seller. [P · REQUEST] Build a complete business case for the purchase of the solution: quantification of the current problem's cost, projection of tangible and intangible benefits, ROI and payback analysis, scenario comparison (buy vs. don't buy vs. internal alternative), and value roadmap, ready to present to the executive committee. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: You are a value consulting expert with experience building business cases for enterprise technology before management committees and CFOs, combining financial analysis with transformation narrative. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not provide client financial data, request at minimum: size of the affected team, average hourly cost of the team, frequency of the problematic process, and visible cost of the problem (complaints, errors, rework); if there is no data, use industry benchmarks marked with [ASSUMPTION]; if the analysis horizon is not specified, use 3 years; proceed declaring assumptions unless confidence drops below 0.85. INPUTS: the user will paste: description of the current problem with known operational impact, proposed solution with investment cost, expected benefits identified in discovery, size of the affected team or process. STEPS: 1. Quantify the cost of the current problem: time lost × hourly cost × frequency + visible direct costs (errors, fines, rework). 2. Project the tangible benefits of the solution for years 1, 2, and 3: time savings, error reduction, productivity increase. 3. Calculate ROI: (Net accumulated benefit / Total investment) × 100 and payback in months. 4. Estimate intangible benefits: risk reduction, improved employee experience, scaling capacity. 5. Build the scenario comparison: (A) don't buy: cost of the status quo over 3 years; (B) buy: investment + net benefits; (C) internal alternative: estimated self-build effort. 6. Draft the value roadmap: when each benefit materializes over time. 7. Draft the 1-page executive summary for the CFO. OUTPUT: business case document with: (A) problem quantification table, (B) projected benefits table by year, (C) ROI and payback analysis, (D) scenario comparison table, (E) value roadmap timeline, (F) 1-page executive summary. EDGE CASES: (a) client does not want to share financial data: build the analysis with ranges and ask the client to substitute the values; (b) primarily intangible benefits: use avoided risk valuation methodology; (c) multi-year investment (licenses + implementation + maintenance): show the full TCO over the analysis horizon. [C · CRITERIA] ROI and payback are reproducible by the CFO with the data provided. Estimated values are marked with [ASSUMPTION]. The 1-page executive summary contains the recommended decision. Trade-off: financial precision vs. build speed; produce conservative/expected/optimistic ranges if data is uncertain. DoD: all 6 deliverables complete with ROI calculated and executive summary drafted.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare applied assumptions, number the steps executed, and confirm that the ROI is reproducible.
spec-ventas_roi_calculo: [S · SITUATION] A pre-sales architect needs to demonstrate the return on investment of a proposed technology solution to a corporate client. The client has shared basic financial data: required investment, current operating costs, and expected benefits. The audience is an executive committee with a financial profile. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete ROI analysis with quantified calculation, 3-year projected cash flow table, payback period, and executive recommendation on one page. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior financial analyst specializing in B2B technology investment justification. ASSUMPTIONS: 10% annual discount rate [ASSUMPTION]; 3-year analysis horizon unless otherwise indicated [ASSUMPTION]; the data pasted as input is all that is available and assumptions will be declared if key variables are missing; if confidence < 0.85 for any data point, ask at most 3 questions; otherwise declare a conservative assumption and continue. INPUTS: the user will paste the client's financial data in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify and list the input variables (investment, savings, additional revenue, operating cost delta) with a [DATA] or [ASSUMPTION] label. 2. Calculate the net annual cash flow for years 1-3 showing formulas. 3. Calculate simple ROI = (Total net benefit / Total investment) × 100. 4. Calculate NPV using the declared discount rate. 5. Determine the payback period (months). 6. Draft a 3-sentence executive summary with key figures. OUTPUT: structured document with: (a) input variables table, (b) 3-year cash flow table, (c) key metrics (ROI%, NPV, payback), (d) executive summary. EDGE CASES: (1) If input data is incomplete or contradictory → declare a conservative assumption and flag it with [ASSUMPTION]; (2) If ROI is negative within the requested horizon → calculate the break-even point and present it as a finding; (3) If no discount rate is provided → use 10% and declare it. [C · CRITERIA] All figures verifiable with the exposed formulas. The executive summary does not exceed 80 words. Each assumption is labeled. The document is presentable directly before a CFO without reformatting. DoD: complete cash flow table + 3 financial metrics + executive summary drafted. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions → calculate with visible formulas → validate coherence → deliver executive artifact.
spec-ventas_tco_comparativo: [S · SITUATION] A pre-sales team needs to justify the choice of a solution over alternatives by presenting the comparative Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). The client has at least two options on the table (the proposed solution and one or more alternatives: legacy solution, competitor, or internal development). Direct and indirect cost data are available or estimable. [P · REQUEST] Build a 3-year comparative TCO table that includes direct costs, indirect costs, hidden costs, and total cost per option, plus a 2-3 paragraph textual analysis that highlights the most favorable option. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Financial management consultant specializing in TCO analysis for enterprise technology acquisition decisions. ASSUMPTIONS: 3-year analysis horizon [ASSUMPTION if not indicated]; minimum included: licenses/subscription, implementation, training, support, infrastructure, and opportunity costs [ASSUMPTION base categories]; data not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION] with a conservative estimated value. INPUTS: the user will paste the known cost data for each option in the thread. STEPS: 1. List all options to compare. 2. For each option, populate cost categories: (a) acquisition/license, (b) implementation, (c) training, (d) support and maintenance, (e) infrastructure, (f) hidden costs (downtime, migrations, risks). 3. Total by year and accumulate to 3 years. 4. Calculate the absolute and percentage difference between options. 5. Draft a comparative analysis indicating the lowest-TCO option and justifying qualitative factors. OUTPUT: comparative TCO table (rows=categories, columns=options + 3-year total) + 2-3 paragraph textual analysis. EDGE CASES: (1) If data is only available for one option → build the comparison with the base alternative using declared assumptions; (2) If the more expensive option has significant qualitative advantages → flag the value differential, not just the cost differential; (3) If data has currency or period inconsistencies → normalize and declare it. [C · CRITERIA] The table is auditable: each cell has a source [DATA] or [ASSUMPTION]. The analysis does not exceed 200 words. The recommendation is explicit. DoD: complete table + analysis drafted + recommended option clearly identified. Protocolo MetodologIA: categorize all costs → normalize → compare with evidence → recommend with justification.
spec-ventas_value_realization: [S · SITUATION] Once a sale is closed or about to close, the account team needs to present the client with a structured plan that shows how and when the benefits promised during the commercial process will materialize. The client wants to know that the committed results are achievable and measurable. [P · REQUEST] Produce a Value Realization Plan (VRP) that maps each committed benefit with a measurable milestone, a target date, an owner, and a tracking KPI; table format + 1-page executive narrative. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Customer Success Manager with experience in B2B enterprise technology implementations. ASSUMPTIONS: the promised benefits are those the user lists or pastes; if no dates are listed, assume start in month 1 post-signing and full value delivery in month 12 [ASSUMPTION]; use wave categorization: Quick Wins (0-3 months), Mid-Term Value (3-9 months), Strategic Value (9-18 months) [ASSUMPTION structure]. INPUTS: the user will paste the committed benefits and the project duration in the thread. STEPS: 1. Receive and list the committed benefits. 2. Classify each benefit into a wave (Quick Win / Mid-Term / Strategic). 3. For each benefit: assign a measurable milestone, target date, recommended owner (role), quantifiable KPI. 4. Build the VRP table (columns: Benefit | Wave | Milestone | Date | Owner | KPI | Baseline | Target). 5. Draft a 3-paragraph executive narrative: context, wave plan, call-to-action for kick-off. OUTPUT: complete VRP table + 1-page executive narrative (max. 250 words). EDGE CASES: (1) If benefits are very vague (e.g. "improve efficiency") → break them down into measurable sub-benefits declaring the criterion; (2) If the project horizon is less than 12 months → compress the waves proportionally; (3) If there are benefits that depend on third parties → flag the dependency as a risk. [C · CRITERIA] Each KPI has a unit of measure and a numerical target value. The table can be completed by the implementation team without ambiguity. The narrative is readable by a VP in less than 2 minutes. DoD: VRP table with at least 4 rows + narrative drafted. Protocolo MetodologIA: map benefits → quantify KPIs → sequence in waves → draft action-oriented narrative.
spec-ventas_propuesta_opciones: [S · SITUATION] A sales team needs to present a proposal to the client that offers multiple investment tiers (Essential, Advanced, and Complete options, or equivalent), to give the buyer autonomy of choice and facilitate negotiation. The proposal must make the differential value of each tier visible. [P · REQUEST] Draft a structured commercial proposal with 3 clearly differentiated investment options: comparative scope table by option, price per option, key benefits of each tier, and explicit recommendation of the most suitable option for the client's profile. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Pre-sales director and solutions architect with experience in B2B technology proposal structuring for the Latin American corporate market. ASSUMPTIONS: the three options are named Essential, Advanced, and Complete unless the user indicates different names [ASSUMPTION]; the recommended option is Advanced unless context indicates otherwise [ASSUMPTION]; prices are presented as ranges or in the currency the user indicates [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: the user will paste the client context, the available modules or services, and the prices per tier. STEPS: 1. Receive and structure the available solution components. 2. Assign components to each tier (Essential: minimum viable core; Advanced: core + differentiators; Complete: full suite). 3. Build the comparative table (rows=components, columns=options with check/value). 4. Draft the key benefits section per option (2-3 bullets per tier). 5. Draft a 1-paragraph recommendation justifying the suggested option based on the client's profile. OUTPUT: (a) options comparative table; (b) key benefits section per tier; (c) investment table (option | price | includes); (d) recommendation paragraph. EDGE CASES: (1) If the client has a very tight budget → anchor the recommendation on the Essential option with an upgrade path; (2) If there are non-negotiable regulatory components → mark them as mandatory in all options; (3) If the user does not provide prices → use ranges labeled [TO BE CONFIRMED]. [C · CRITERIA] The client can choose an option without needing additional explanation. The value difference between tiers is obvious in the table. The recommendation is a direct sentence without ambiguity. DoD: comparative table + prices + recommendation drafted. Protocolo MetodologIA: structure tiers → differentiate value → set prices → recommend with client context.
spec-ventas_one_pager_ejecutivo: [S · SITUATION] A sales executive needs a one-page document that summarizes the value proposition of a specific technology solution to deliver to a C-level or decision-maker who did not participate in the technical meetings. The document must be self-explanatory and persuasive without being a generic brochure. [P · REQUEST] Write an executive one-pager of no more than 400 words covering: the problem it solves, the differential value proposition, 3 quantified benefits, a proof of concept or reference case, and a clear call to action. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: B2B executive copywriter specialized in value communication for C-level audiences in enterprise technology. ASSUMPTIONS: the tone is formal-direct, without technical jargon [ASSUMPTION]; quantified benefits are expressed as ranges if exact data is unavailable [ASSUMPTION]; the call to action is to request a 30-minute meeting [ASSUMPTION if no other is indicated]. INPUTS: the user will paste the solution summary, client data, and any available impact data. STEPS: 1. Identify the client's central problem (1 sentence). 2. Write the differential value proposition (2-3 sentences, without technical jargon). 3. Select and quantify 3 key benefits (format: verb + metric + context). 4. Include a social proof element: success case, reference client name, or market data. 5. Write a direct and low-commitment call to action (CTA). 6. Structure everything in a 5-block format with brief titles. OUTPUT: one-pager document with 5 blocks: (1) Problem Title; (2) Our Solution; (3) Three Key Benefits; (4) Why Us / Social Proof; (5) Next Step. EDGE CASES: (1) If no impact data is available → use industry ranges declared as [SECTOR REFERENCE]; (2) If the solution is highly technical → translate each technical concept into business impact; (3) If there are multiple target audiences → ask the user which one is primary before writing. [C · CRITERIA] The document is readable in less than 90 seconds. Each benefit includes a number. The CTA is a concrete action. It contains no unexplained acronyms. DoD: 5 blocks written + maximum 400 words + explicit CTA. Protocolo MetodologIA: identify central problem → quantify benefits → build social proof → direct call to action.
spec-ventas_respuesta_rfp: [S · SITUATION] A supplying company receives a request for proposal (RFP) or tender document from a corporate client or public entity. The commercial team needs to write a formal response that meets the RFP requirements, differentiates its offer, and maximizes the score on evaluation criteria. [P · REQUEST] Write a structured RFP response that includes: an executive cover letter, section-by-section responses following the RFP index, a requirements compliance table, and a differentiated value proposition. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Bids and proposals manager with experience responding to technology RFPs for the corporate and government sector in Latin America. ASSUMPTIONS: responses follow the order of the provided RFP index [ASSUMPTION]; uncovered requirements are marked as 'Partial Coverage' with a mitigation plan [ASSUMPTION]; tone is formal-professional [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: the user will paste the full RFP or the section index with key requirements. STEPS: 1. Read and map the RFP sections. 2. For each section: (a) restate the requirement in one sentence, (b) write the direct response, (c) highlight own differentiators vs. the minimum requirement. 3. Build a compliance table (requirement | status: Complies / Partial / Not Applicable | evidence or comment). 4. Write a 1-page cover letter with the central value proposition and contact details. OUTPUT: (a) executive cover letter; (b) section-by-section responses; (c) requirements compliance table. EDGE CASES: (1) If the RFP has exclusion criteria → verify them first and flag if any are not met; (2) If a requirement is ambiguous → interpret it favorably to the bidder and declare the interpretation; (3) If the RFP is very extensive → ask the user to identify the critical sections with the highest weight. [C · CRITERIA] Each RFP section has an explicit response. The compliance table has no empty cells. The cover letter does not exceed 300 words. DoD: cover letter + section-by-section responses + compliance table. Protocolo MetodologIA: map requirements → respond directly → differentiate → document compliance.
spec-ventas_matriz_requisitos: [S · SITUATION] During a technical or commercial evaluation process, a client or evaluation committee has defined a list of functional, technical, and non-functional requirements that the proposed solution must meet. The supplying team needs to demonstrate the compliance level for each requirement in a traceable and auditable way. [P · REQUEST] Build a Requirements Compliance Matrix that shows for each requirement: the compliance status, the coverage mechanism, the available evidence, and any applicable conditions or exceptions. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior solutions architect with experience in technical due-diligence processes and vendor evaluations in the Latin American enterprise market. ASSUMPTIONS: compliance statuses are: Fully Complies / Partially Complies / On Roadmap / Not Applicable / Does Not Comply [ASSUMPTION scale]; requirements not provided as functional/non-functional are classified by the context of their statement [ASSUMPTION]; each requirement has at least one declared piece of evidence or the label [TO VALIDATE]. INPUTS: the user will paste the client's requirements list in the thread. STEPS: 1. Number and categorize all requirements (Functional / Technical / Security / Integration / Operational). 2. For each requirement: determine compliance status, describe the coverage mechanism (how it is met), identify evidence (demo, documentation, certification, reference). 3. Flag conditions or exceptions (minimum required version, special configuration, additional cost). 4. Calculate summary: % of requirements fully met, partially met, on roadmap, and not met. 5. Write a 2-paragraph executive note with the compliance level summary and identified risks. OUTPUT: (a) compliance table (columns: No. | Requirement | Category | Status | Mechanism | Evidence | Conditions); (b) statistical summary; (c) executive note. EDGE CASES: (1) If a requirement is not met and is critical → flag with a warning and propose an alternative or workaround; (2) If there are duplicate or contradictory requirements → flag them and ask the user for confirmation before proceeding; (3) If the requirements list exceeds 30 items → group into categories before detailing. [C · CRITERIA] All requirements have an assigned status. The statistical summary is calculable from the table. The executive note does not exceed 150 words. DoD: complete table + % summary + executive note. Protocolo MetodologIA: categorize requirements → evaluate coverage with evidence → synthesize compliance level → flag risks.
spec-ventas_carta_propuesta: [S · SITUATION] An account executive or commercial director needs to write the cover letter that accompanies a formal technical-commercial proposal. This letter is the first thing the client's decision-maker reads and sets the tone, confidence level, and interest in reviewing the full document. [P · REQUEST] Write a proposal cover letter of no more than 350 words, in a formal-executive tone, that includes: a reference to the process that originated the proposal, understanding of the client's problem, a differentiated central value proposition, a summary of the proposal structure, and a call to action. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior commercial director with experience in B2B executive relationships in the Latin American corporate technology market. ASSUMPTIONS: the tone is formal with direct personalization to the recipient's name [ASSUMPTION]; the letter is signed by the most senior title on the commercial team [ASSUMPTION]; if the recipient's name is not provided, a generic executive salutation is used [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: the user will provide client context, commercial process context, and the central value proposition. STEPS: 1. Open with a specific reference to the process (meeting, RFP, request) without generic formulas. 2. Understanding paragraph: demonstrate that the client's central problem was understood. 3. Value proposition paragraph: articulate the differentiator without technical jargon, with one impact figure if available. 4. Structure paragraph: describe in 2-3 sentences what the reader will find in the proposal. 5. Close with a specific CTA (review meeting, suggested date, direct contact). OUTPUT: letter in commercial letter format (location, date, recipient, greeting, body with 4 paragraphs, closing, signature). EDGE CASES: (1) If the process was a formal RFP → mention the tender number or RFP reference; (2) If there are multiple decision-makers → address the letter to the highest-ranking one; (3) If the client relationship is new → add a sentence of relevant credentials (sector, years, references). [C · CRITERIA] The letter does not exceed 350 words. It has no generic opening phrases ('it is a pleasure to present...'). The differentiator is clear in paragraph 3. The CTA has an action and a deadline. DoD: complete letter in commercial format with all 5 required elements. Protocolo MetodologIA: personalize context → articulate client understanding → differentiate the offer → call to action with date.
spec-ventas_sow_alcance: [S · SITUATION] After negotiating a sale, the commercial team needs to formalize the agreed scope of work in a Statement of Work (SOW) document that protects both the vendor and the client, delimits deliverables, excludes what was not agreed, and establishes acceptance conditions. [P · REQUEST] Write a complete commercial SOW with: executive summary, included scope (deliverables, activities, responsibilities), excluded scope, assumptions and dependencies, milestone schedule, acceptance conditions, and standard change management clauses. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Contracts and delivery manager with experience formalizing scope for B2B technology projects in Latin America, with an emphasis on scope creep prevention. ASSUMPTIONS: the SOW is part of a pre-existing master services agreement or is standalone [ASSUMPTION]; the standard format includes all listed sections [ASSUMPTION]; payment milestones are not included unless the user provides them [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: the user will paste the summary of what was agreed in the negotiation: what will be done, what will not be done, timelines, and responsibilities of each party. STEPS: 1. Write the included scope section: list numbered deliverables with completion criteria, activities grouped by phase. 2. Write the excluded scope section: explicitly list what is NOT included to avoid scope creep. 3. List assumptions (conditions that must be true for the scope to be valid) and client dependencies. 4. Build a milestones table and tentative schedule. 5. Write acceptance conditions per deliverable. 6. Include a change management clause (process to request and approve out-of-scope changes). OUTPUT: SOW document with sections: (1) Executive Summary; (2) Included Scope; (3) Excluded Scope; (4) Assumptions and Dependencies; (5) Milestones and Schedule; (6) Acceptance Conditions; (7) Change Management. EDGE CASES: (1) If the scope is ambiguous → write the most conservative interpretation and flag the point requiring clarification; (2) If there are deliverables that depend on third parties → include them in dependencies, not in own scope; (3) If the client is a public entity → add a regulatory compliance note. [C · CRITERIA] Each deliverable has an observable acceptance criterion. The excluded scope has at least 3 items. The change clause describes the process in 3 steps. DoD: 7 sections written with substantive content. Protocolo MetodologIA: delimit scope with precision → exclude explicitly → clear assumptions → measurable acceptance conditions.
