Explicit trade-off: depth of review vs. time available before the merge.
DoD: no Critical or High finding is left without an actionable recommendation.
spec-vibe-coding_auditoria-de-seguridad-:
[S · SITUATION] A team developing with AI assistance needs to perform a rapid security audit of their web application before a launch or client review, covering the most critical vulnerabilities from the OWASP Top 10 without spending weeks on a full pentest.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a rapid security audit report based on the OWASP Top 10: verification checklist per category, findings detected in the provided code or configuration, remediation recommendations with priority and effort estimate.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior web application security engineer experienced in OWASP Top 10-based audits for Node.js and React applications.
ASSUMPTIONS: Next.js/Node.js stack; application with user authentication; SQL database by default; if the user provides specific code or configuration, analyze those artifacts directly.
INPUTS: Paste relevant code snippets (authentication, database queries, user input handling) or description of the application architecture.
STEPS:
1. Map the application to the OWASP Top 10 version 2021 and identify the 5 most probable risks given the stack.
2. Verify A01 Broken Access Control: roles, permissions, and authorization at route and API level.
3. Verify A02 Cryptographic Failures: password storage, tokens, sensitive data in transit.
4. Verify A03 Injection: parameterized queries, input validation, output sanitization.
5. Verify A05 Security Misconfiguration: HTTP headers, CORS, cookies, CSP.
6. Verify A07 Authentication Failures: rate limiting, account lockout, session management.
7. Produce a report with findings by OWASP category, severity, and remediation recommendation.
OUTPUT: (a) Findings table by OWASP category with severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low). (b) Remediation code for critical findings. (c) Post-remediation verification checklist. (d) Tool recommendations to automate detection.
EDGE CASES:
- No access to source code: audit only header configuration and observable behavior.
- Dependencies with known CVEs: indicate how to verify with npm audit or equivalent.
- Authentication delegated to third parties (Auth0, Supabase): focus on integration configuration.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: all Critical findings have remediation code ready to apply.
Explicit trade-off: rapid audit coverage vs. depth of a full pentest.
DoD: no A01, A02, or A03 finding is left without an actionable recommendation.
spec-vibe-coding_detectar-secretos-filtr:
[S · SITUATION] A developer suspects or has confirmed that secrets (API tokens, private keys, passwords) have been compromised by being accidentally included in the code repository, in CI/CD logs, or in commit messages, and needs to detect the scope of the leak, revoke the affected secrets, and prevent recurrence.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a secret leakage response plan: commands to scan the Git history and current code, revocation procedure by secret type, Git history cleanup, and configuration of automated prevention tools.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior security engineer specialized in secret exposure incident response and repository hardening.
ASSUMPTIONS: Git repository on GitHub; Node.js/TypeScript language; scanning tool gitleaks or truffleHog by default; if the user indicates another cloud provider, adapt the revocation procedure.
INPUTS: Description of the secrets suspected of having been leaked and the platform or service they belong to (AWS, Stripe, database, etc.).
STEPS:
1. Scan the complete repository history with gitleaks to detect secrets in past commits.
2. Scan the current working directory to detect secrets in untracked files.
3. Classify the found secrets by type and urgency of revocation.
4. Revoke and regenerate each affected secret on the corresponding platform; document steps per service.
5. Clean the Git history with git filter-repo to eliminate commits that contained secrets.
6. Configure a pre-commit hook with detect-secrets and GitHub Secret Scanning to prevent recurrence.
7. Force rotation of active tokens and verify that there was no unauthorized access in service logs.
OUTPUT: (a) Scanning commands ready to execute. (b) Revocation procedure by secret type with links to relevant panels. (c) Git history cleanup commands. (d) Prevention tool configuration. (e) Post-remediation verification checklist.
EDGE CASES:
- Secret in a very old commit with many subsequent merges: warn about rebase complexity and recommend BFG Repo-Cleaner.
- Secret published in an already-closed public pull request: contact GitHub Support for cache purge.
- Repository already cloned by third parties: assume compromise and revoke immediately without waiting for confirmation.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: gitleaks detects no secret in the history or working directory after remediation.
Explicit trade-off: speed of revocation (immediate) vs. time to clean the history (may take hours).
DoD: all detected secrets are revoked, the history is clean, and prevention tools are active before the incident is considered closed.
spec-vibe-coding_validacion-y-sanitizaci:
[S · SITUATION] A web application in production receives user data (forms, URL parameters, HTTP headers, JSON/XML payloads) without systematic validation or sanitization, exposing code paths to SQL injection, XSS, command injection, and insecure deserialization.

[P · REQUEST] Audit every entry point of the application and produce: (1) attack surface map with severity, (2) corrected code snippets with strict validation and contextual sanitization, (3) rules for a reusable central validator, (4) test suite with representative malicious cases.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Application security engineer with 10+ years in OWASP Top 10 and secure code review.
ASSUMPTIONS: backend technology is that of the pasted code; if no code is pasted, assume Node.js/Express with PostgreSQL; testing framework is the stack's native one. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask questions only if the technology is ambiguous or if there are multiple SQL dialects and the difference affects the solution (maximum 2 questions).
INPUTS: source code pasted in the thread or a representative snippet of controllers/routes.
STEPS:
1. List all identified entry points (field, data type, possible injection vector) → table with columns: Entry point | Type | Risk | Severity.
2. For each high/critical risk point, show the vulnerable code and the corrected code with inline comments.
3. Design a central validation module/class with reusable rules (whitelist, type, length, format).
4. Write 5–8 automated test cases with classic malicious payloads (SQLi, XSS, traversal) and the expected result.
5. List 3 additional defense-in-depth controls (CSP, prepared statements, output encoding).
OUTPUT: structured document with numbered sections, code in language-tagged blocks, severity table, test suite ready to run.
EDGE CASES:
- If the code uses an ORM that already abstracts SQL, focus on XSS and command injection instead of SQLi.
- If no code is available, generate canonical examples for the assumed stack.
- If there are free-text fields (comments, bios), document why sanitization must be contextual to the destination (HTML vs. DB vs. CLI).

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: every high-severity entry point has corrected code with explicit validation.
- Trade-off: do not use blacklists (fragile); prefer whitelist and contextual encoding.
- DoD: test suite is runnable without modification; central module is importable from any controller; zero test payloads pass without an explicit rejection.

Protocolo MetodologIA: audit → map surface → fix with code → test with payloads → deliver reusable module.
spec-vibe-coding_revision-de-dependencia:
[S · SITUATION] A software project has a dependency manifest file (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, go.mod, Gemfile, or other) with third-party libraries that may contain known CVEs, outdated versions, or unmaintained packages that represent supply-chain risk.

[P · REQUEST] Analyze the pasted dependency manifest and produce: (1) prioritized list of dependencies with known vulnerabilities or high risk, (2) recommended safe version or alternative for each, (3) concrete migration snippets or update commands, (4) minimum dependency management policy for the team.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Software security architect specialized in supply-chain analysis and dependency management in production projects.
ASSUMPTIONS: the ecosystem is that of the pasted manifest; if none is pasted, assume npm/Node.js; referenced CVEs come from NIST NVD and official ecosystem advisories. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if there are multiple manifests and the user does not indicate which to prioritize (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: content of the manifest file pasted in the thread.
STEPS:
1. Identify the package manager and ecosystem from the manifest → declare in one line.
2. Classify dependencies into three groups: (A) known vulnerability with CVE, (B) severely outdated (>2 major versions behind), (C) no updates in >18 months or archived.
3. For group A, list: package | current version | CVE | CVSS severity | recommended safe version.
4. For groups B and C, list with recommendation: update, replace, or accept documented risk.
5. Generate the exact update commands for the 5 highest-risk dependencies.
6. Draft a 5-rule policy for dependency management (review frequency, severity threshold to block CI, recommended scanning tool).
OUTPUT: tables by risk group, executable commands in a code block, policy as a numbered list.
EDGE CASES:
- If the manifest is very large (+100 dependencies), prioritize direct dependencies over transitive ones.
- If a vulnerable dependency has no safe version available, indicate alternative mitigations (sandboxing, security wrapper, replacement).
- If the ecosystem has no public CVE but has a maintainer advisory, mention it with its date.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each identified CVE has its safe version or documented mitigation.
- Trade-off: do not recommend major version upgrades without warning about potential breaking changes.
- DoD: update commands are executable without modification in the detected ecosystem; policy is adoptable without paid tools.

Protocolo MetodologIA: detect ecosystem → classify risks → recommend safe versions → generate commands → deliver team policy.
spec-vibe-coding_verificar-alucinaciones:
[S · SITUATION] A developer has code generated by an AI tool (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor, or another) that includes references to APIs, methods, packages, or behaviors that may not exist in the declared version of the framework or library, creating silent errors or runtime failures that are hard to diagnose.

[P · REQUEST] Audit the pasted AI-generated code and produce: (1) list of verifiable claims (APIs used, methods, imports, versions), (2) classification of each as confirmed, questionable, or invented, (3) corrections with the documented real API, (4) list of warning signs for detecting hallucinations in future sessions.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior software engineer with experience in auditing AI-generated code and verifying it against official documentation across multiple ecosystems.
ASSUMPTIONS: the language and versions are those declared in the pasted code or imports/package; if versions are not declared, assume the most recent LTS of the detected ecosystem. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if there is critical version ambiguity that changes the answer (maximum 2 questions).
INPUTS: AI-generated code snippet pasted in the thread, optionally with the framework version.
STEPS:
1. Extract all verifiable external references: imports, library method calls, API URLs, package names, configuration parameters → table: Reference | Type | Declared source.
2. For each reference, classify: CONFIRMED (exists in the official docs for the version), QUESTIONABLE (exists in different versions or with different behavior), INVENTED (does not exist in any known version).
3. For QUESTIONABLE and INVENTED references, show the equivalent real API with a corrected code snippet.
4. Identify hallucination patterns present: plausible but nonexistent method names, version mixing, parameters with wrong names, imports of nonexistent submodules.
5. Deliver a checklist of 8 warning signs for identifying AI hallucinations in future code.
OUTPUT: classification table, corrected code in blocks, warning-sign checklist as a list.
EDGE CASES:
- If the code mixes two mutually incompatible libraries, indicate it explicitly as a composition error.
- If an invented API has a real functional equivalent, propose the real alternative instead of just flagging it as an error.
- If all the code is correct, confirm it with evidence and add the warning signs anyway.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: every external reference has an explicit classification with a source or justification.
- Trade-off: prioritize accuracy over speed; if there is uncertainty between versions, indicate both.
- DoD: corrected code compiles and runs without errors in the declared ecosystem; checklist is actionable without additional tools.

Protocolo MetodologIA: extract references → classify by truthfulness → fix with real API → deliver warning-sign checklist.
spec-vibe-coding_rate-limiting-y-abuso:
[S · SITUATION] An API or web application exposed to the internet has no rate limiting controls or abuse protection, making it vulnerable to brute-force attacks, mass scraping, computational resource denial of service, and enumeration of private resources.

[P · REQUEST] Design and implement a complete rate limiting and anti-abuse strategy for the pasted application, producing: (1) endpoint map with risk profile and recommended thresholds, (2) rate limiting implementation code per layer (global, per route, per user/IP), (3) response strategy for detected abuse, (4) minimum load tests to validate the thresholds.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: API infrastructure and security architect with experience in high-availability systems and protection against distributed attacks.
ASSUMPTIONS: the stack is that of the pasted code; if no code is pasted, assume Node.js/Express with Redis as the counter store; default thresholds are conservative (10 req/s global, 3 req/min on authentication routes). Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if the expected user volume is critical for calibrating thresholds (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: API route/controller code pasted in the thread, optionally with expected traffic.
STEPS:
1. List all identified endpoints and classify them by risk profile: authentication, sensitive data, costly operations, public read endpoints → table: Endpoint | Method | Risk profile | Recommended threshold.
2. Implement rate limiting per layer: (a) global per IP, (b) per route based on profile, (c) per authenticated user with burst allowance.
3. Design the abuse response: correct HTTP codes (429), Retry-After headers, logging of blocked IPs, optional alerts.
4. Add anti-enumeration protections on authentication routes: constant response time, failed attempt limit with exponential backoff.
5. Write 3 simplified load tests (with curl or a stack tool) to verify that the thresholds work.
OUTPUT: endpoint table with thresholds, implemented code in per-layer blocks, response strategy, executable tests.
EDGE CASES:
- If the API is public without authentication, apply IP-based rate limiting with more permissive thresholds and document the alert threshold.
- If there are multiple server instances (horizontal scaling), use a shared store (Redis) for distributed counters.
- If Redis cannot be used, propose an in-memory alternative with a warning about its multi-instance limitation.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: every endpoint has documented thresholds and active rate limiting code.
- Trade-off: conservative thresholds protect better but may affect legitimate users during spikes; document how to adjust.
- DoD: code is deployable without modification; 429 responses include Retry-After; tests demonstrate that the threshold is applied.

Protocolo MetodologIA: classify endpoints by risk → implement layered rate limiting → design abuse response → validate with tests.
spec-vibe-coding_manejo-de-errores-consi:
[S · SITUATION] An application has scattered and heterogeneous error handling: some modules throw uncaught exceptions, others return ad hoc error codes, HTTP error responses expose stack traces in production, and there is no centralized logging or standard error response format for the client.

[P · REQUEST] Audit the error handling of the pasted code and design a consistent strategy, producing: (1) inventory of current failure points with classification, (2) centralized error handling architecture with an error type hierarchy, (3) implemented error middleware or interceptor, (4) standard API error response format, (5) 6-rule guide for the team.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior software architect specialized in application resilience, observability, and developer experience in distributed systems.
ASSUMPTIONS: the stack is that of the pasted code; if nothing is pasted, assume Node.js/Express; the production environment must not expose stack traces; logging with levels (error, warn, info). Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if it is unclear whether the app is a REST API, GraphQL, or a server-side rendering application (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: source code pasted in the thread (controllers, services, existing middleware).
STEPS:
1. Identify all current error-handling patterns in the code → table: Pattern | Module | Problem.
2. Design a class/type hierarchy: ApplicationError base with subclasses (ValidationError, NotFoundError, AuthorizationError, ExternalServiceError, DatabaseError) with associated HTTP code and business code.
3. Implement centralized error middleware/interceptor with: structured logging, sanitized client response, dev vs. production environment distinction.
4. Define the standard JSON error response format: mandatory fields (status, code, message, requestId) and optional ones (details, path).
5. Refactor a representative controller from the pasted code to adopt the new architecture.
6. Draft 6 team rules for consistent error handling.
OUTPUT: inventory table, class hierarchy with code, implemented middleware, JSON response schema, refactored controller, team rules.
EDGE CASES:
- If the code has uncaught asynchronous errors (Promises without catch), identify them explicitly and add the corresponding global handler.
- If there are integrations with external services, design error wrapping to avoid exposing third-party details to the client.
- If the app is a monolith with server-rendered views, adapt the error response to HTML vs. JSON depending on the Accept header.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: a single centralized error-handling point processes all uncaught errors.
- Trade-off: error messages useful to the developer in dev vs. generic safe messages in production.
- DoD: stack traces do not reach the client in production; all errors have structured logging; the response format is consistent throughout the API.

Protocolo MetodologIA: inventory current patterns → design hierarchy → implement centralized middleware → define standard format → encode team rules.
spec-vibe-coding_checklist-de-listo-para:
[S · SITUATION] A development team is about to deploy a new application or a major version to a production environment. There is a risk of overlooking critical controls in security, performance, observability, failure recovery, and compliance that are only discovered after deployment, when there is already impact on users.

[P · REQUEST] Generate an exhaustive, prioritized production-readiness checklist tailored to the described stack and application type, producing: (1) structured checklist by domain with actionable items, (2) criticality classification for each item (blocker / important / recommended), (3) guide on how to verify each blocker item, (4) approval gate template for the team.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior site reliability engineer (SRE) with experience onboarding systems to production in high-availability environments.
ASSUMPTIONS: stack and application type are as described by the user; if not described, assume a REST API web application in a Docker container deployed to the cloud. Declare assumptions at the start. Do not ask questions if the stack is generic enough; ask a maximum of 2 if there are critical unspecified infrastructure components.
INPUTS: description of the stack, application type, and business domain (or assume defaults).
STEPS:
1. Structure the checklist across 8 domains: Security | Configuration and secrets | Observability and logging | Performance | Resilience and recovery | Data and migrations | CI/CD and deployment | Compliance and privacy.
2. For each domain, list actionable items with an imperative verb + verification criterion + criticality: BLOCKER, IMPORTANT, RECOMMENDED.
3. For each BLOCKER item, add a column with the specific command, tool, or manual check to verify it.
4. Generate an approval gate template: table with columns Item | Owner | Status (Pending/OK/N/A) | Evidence.
5. Add a section of the 5 most common errors in the first production deployment with their mitigation.
OUTPUT: domain-based checklist in a markdown table, verification guide for blockers, approval gate template, common errors section.
EDGE CASES:
- If the application handles personal or financial data, add specific GDPR/CCPA or PCI-DSS items in the compliance domain.
- If there are database migrations, add rollback, pre-backup, and staging-test items.
- If it is a microservice, add circuit breaker, timeout, and graceful degradation items.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: all BLOCKER items have a specific verification method.
- Trade-off: do not include items redundant with others already covered; prefer items that add differential value.
- DoD: checklist is executable by the team without additional expert knowledge; approval gate template is adoptable in the release process.

Protocolo MetodologIA: structure by domain → classify by criticality → document blocker verification → generate approval gate → list common errors.
spec-vibe-coding_cumplimiento-de-privaci:
[S · SITUATION] An application collects, stores, or processes personal user data (names, emails, locations, usage behavior, or other) without having implemented the minimum privacy controls required by regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, or equivalent local laws, exposing the organization to fines and loss of trust.

[P · REQUEST] Audit the described code and data architecture and produce: (1) inventory of personal data collected with its recommended legal basis, (2) list of missing privacy controls with severity, (3) implementation of the 5 most critical controls, (4) internal technical privacy policy template for the team.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Technical privacy advisor with experience implementing GDPR/CCPA compliance in digital product engineering teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: the primary regulation is GDPR if not specified; the stack is that of the pasted code or Node.js/Express if no code is provided; personal data identified is what appears in database models/schemas. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if the jurisdiction materially affects the required controls (maximum 2 questions).
INPUTS: database schemas, data models, or controller code pasted in the thread.
STEPS:
1. Identify all fields that constitute personal or sensitive data in the schema → table: Field | Type of personal data | Sensitivity | Recommended legal basis.
2. Evaluate existing privacy controls against those required: explicit consent, right to erasure, portability, data minimization, retention with TTL, encryption at rest and in transit, access logs.
3. Classify missing controls by severity: CRITICAL (requires immediate implementation), IMPORTANT, RECOMMENDED.
4. Implement code for the 3–5 most critical controls: complete user deletion function, data anonymization in exports, consent header in the API, access logging for sensitive data.
5. Draft a one-page internal technical privacy policy with: types of data collected, maximum retention, permitted access, procedure for exercising data subject rights.
OUTPUT: personal data inventory table, controls list with severity, implementation code, internal technical policy.
EDGE CASES:
- If the data includes special categories (health, religion, sexual orientation), mark them as CRITICAL and add additional encryption and restricted access controls.
- If the app has analytics or behavioral tracking, include the corresponding consent and opt-out controls.
- If no database schema is available, infer it from the API forms or endpoints and indicate it as an assumption.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: every identified personal data field has a documented legal basis and an associated technical control.
- Trade-off: do not delete data that has a legal retention obligation (fiscal, security); document the exception.
- DoD: user deletion function deletes or anonymizes all personal data; access logging for sensitive data is active; technical policy is reviewable by the DPO or equivalent.

Protocolo MetodologIA: inventory personal data → classify missing controls → implement critical controls → document internal technical policy.
spec-datos_sql_consulta_desde_lenguaje_n:
[S · SITUATION] A data analyst or developer needs to retrieve specific information from a relational database but lacks the time or sufficient SQL mastery to accurately translate a natural language business requirement into a correct, efficient, and safe SQL query.

[P · REQUEST] Translate the natural language business requirement into a correct, executable SQL query, producing: (1) the SQL query with explanatory comments, (2) step-by-step logic explanation, (3) performance considerations, (4) alternative variants if applicable.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior data engineer with expert mastery of SQL across multiple engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake) and experience translating business requirements into optimized queries.
ASSUMPTIONS: the SQL engine is PostgreSQL if not specified; table and column names are exactly those in the pasted schema; if no schema is pasted, declare assumptions about the structure and note it explicitly. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if the requirement's ambiguity produces two interpretations with materially different results (maximum 2 questions).
INPUTS: business requirement in free text and schema of the relevant tables (CREATE TABLE or column descriptions).
STEPS:
1. Restate the requirement in precise technical terms (which tables, which conditions, which aggregations, which period).
2. Write the SQL query with: explicit SELECT (no SELECT *), typed JOINs, clear WHERE conditions, GROUP BY if there is aggregation, ORDER BY if the order matters to the business.
3. Add inline comments explaining each non-obvious section of the query.
4. Explain the logic in 3–5 steps in natural language.
5. Point out potential performance issues (full table scan, missing index, cartesian product) and how to mitigate them.
6. If there is more than one valid interpretation, show the alternative variant with a description of when to choose each one.
OUTPUT: SQL query in a code block with the dialect specified, numbered explanation, performance considerations section.
EDGE CASES:
- If the requirement involves data from multiple time periods, use CTEs for clarity instead of nested subqueries.
- If there are columns with ambiguous names across multiple tables, always use table aliases.
- If the result could return millions of rows, add a LIMIT clause with a warning and a pagination recommendation.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the query runs without syntax errors on the declared engine and returns exactly what the requirement describes.
- Trade-off: clarity over brevity; prefer named CTEs over nested subqueries for complex queries.
- DoD: query has comments understandable by someone with basic SQL; performance considerations are documented; no SELECT * is used.

Protocolo MetodologIA: restate the requirement → write commented SQL → explain the logic → flag performance → offer alternative variant.
spec-datos_sql_optimizar_query_lenta:
[S · SITUATION] A SQL query in a production or analytical system takes too long to execute (seconds or minutes), affecting user experience or report latency. The team suspects missing indexes, full table scans, inefficient JOINs, or correlated subqueries, but doesn't know where to start.

[P · REQUEST] Analyze the pasted slow SQL query and its execution plan and produce: (1) diagnosis of slowness causes with evidence from the plan, (2) optimized version of the query, (3) recommended indexes with exact DDL, (4) expected improvement estimate, (5) reusable SQL optimization checklist.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Relational database optimization expert with experience in performance tuning on PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQL Server at scale of millions of records.
ASSUMPTIONS: the engine is PostgreSQL if not specified; if no EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan is pasted, proceed with heuristic analysis of the query and indicate that the diagnosis is inferred. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if the data volume (order of magnitude of rows) is unknown and critical for the index recommendation (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: slow SQL query pasted in the thread, optionally with EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and DDL of the involved tables.
STEPS:
1. Read the execution plan and identify the most costly nodes (Seq Scan, Nested Loop with many rows, Sort without index) → table: Node | Cost | Estimated vs. actual rows | Root cause.
2. Identify anti-patterns in the query: SELECT *, correlated subqueries, functions on WHERE columns, OR on indexed conditions, JOINs over columns of different type.
3. Rewrite the optimized query with the corrections applied, with comments indicating each optimization.
4. Generate the necessary CREATE INDEX statements with the correct columns, index type (B-tree, Hash, GIN, etc.) and a description of why.
5. Estimate the expected improvement in execution time (order of magnitude: 10x, 100x) with justification based on the plan.
6. Deliver a 10-item reusable SQL optimization principles checklist.
OUTPUT: diagnosis table, optimized query in a code block, index DDL, improvement estimate, checklist.
EDGE CASES:
- If the problem is in the total data volume and not in the query, recommend partitioning or materialization as a long-term solution.
- If there are multiple slow queries in the same module, indicate the common pattern and how to resolve it systematically.
- If the optimization requires schema changes (denormalization, computed columns), indicate it as an advanced option with pros and cons.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the optimized query uses indexes in the execution plan (Index Scan instead of Seq Scan) on the main filter conditions.
- Trade-off: more indexes improve reads but slow down writes; document the impact on insert/update operations.
- DoD: index DDL is executable without modification; optimized query produces the same result as the original; improvement estimate is justified.

Protocolo MetodologIA: read the plan → identify anti-patterns → rewrite the query → generate index DDL → estimate improvement → deliver checklist.
spec-datos_sql_refactor_subqueries_a_cte:
[S · SITUATION] A SQL query has multiple nested subqueries that make the code hard to read, maintain, and debug. Deep nesting prevents quickly understanding the business logic, hinders collaboration in code reviews, and can mask logical errors or inefficiencies.

[P · REQUEST] Refactor the pasted SQL query with nested subqueries into an equivalent version using Common Table Expressions (CTEs), producing: (1) refactored query with semantically named CTEs, (2) explanation of each CTE's logic, (3) logical equivalence verification, (4) guide on when to use CTEs vs. subqueries vs. views.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior data engineer with experience writing readable and maintainable SQL for analytics and data engineering teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: the engine is PostgreSQL if not specified (CTEs are SQL:1999 standard and work across all major engines); CTE names must reflect the entity or transformation they represent in the business domain. Declare assumptions at the start. Do not ask questions unless the business domain of the subqueries is completely opaque and affects naming (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: SQL query with nested subqueries pasted in the thread.
STEPS:
1. Map the current nesting structure: identify each subquery, its inferred purpose, and its nesting level → visual tree in text.
2. Assign a semantic name to each subquery that describes what data it represents (not "subquery1" but "sales_by_region").
3. Extract each subquery as a CTE in logical order (from the innermost outward, or from the most independent to the most dependent).
4. Write the complete refactored query with CTEs, a one-line comment on each CTE explaining its purpose.
5. Verify logical equivalence: list the filter conditions, aggregations, and JOINs from the original vs. the refactored version.
6. Draft a 1-page guide: CTEs vs. inline subqueries vs. temporary views — when to choose each option.
OUTPUT: nesting tree, refactored query in a code block with comments, equivalence verification table, decision guide.
EDGE CASES:
- If the subquery is correlated (references columns from the outer query), explain how to handle it with LATERAL JOIN or keep it inline with justification.
- If there are CTEs used more than once in the final query, mention the WITH RECURSIVE or MATERIALIZED clause depending on the engine.
- If the engine is SQL Server or pre-8.0 MySQL, indicate CTE syntax differences.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the refactored query produces the same result as the original in all implicit test cases.
- Trade-off: CTEs improve readability but some engines do not materialize them by default; indicate when to force materialization.
- DoD: every CTE has a semantic name and a purpose comment; the final query without the CTEs is a simple, readable SELECT; decision guide is actionable.

Protocolo MetodologIA: map nesting → name CTEs semantically → extract in logical order → verify equivalence → deliver decision guide.
spec-datos_sql_window_functions_ranking:
[S · SITUATION] A data analyst needs to calculate rankings, running totals, moving averages, or row-to-row comparisons (lag/lead) in SQL, but the solutions they have attempted with GROUP BY and subqueries are incorrect or inefficient because individual rows are not preserved alongside the aggregated result.

[P · REQUEST] Design SQL queries with the appropriate window functions for the described analysis requirement, producing: (1) a correct and executable window function query, (2) an explanation of each window clause (PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, frame), (3) a comparison with the equivalent subquery approach to illustrate the advantage, (4) a catalog of 8 typical window function use cases with minimal examples.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Data analysis specialist with advanced SQL, proficient in window functions in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, and Snowflake.
ASSUMPTIONS: the engine is PostgreSQL if not specified; sample data is from the pasted schema or, if no schema, a synthetic dataset representative of the described use case is generated. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if the window type (ROWS vs. RANGE) is ambiguous and materially affects the result (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: description of the desired analysis (ranking, running total, moving average, lag/lead comparison) and schema or sample data.
STEPS:
1. Identify the required window function type: ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK for rankings; SUM/AVG over window for running totals and moving averages; LAG/LEAD for row-to-row comparisons.
2. Design the OVER clause: define PARTITION BY (grouping without collapsing rows), ORDER BY (order within the partition), and frame clause (ROWS BETWEEN) if applicable.
3. Write the complete query with the window function, including a sample data CTE to make it self-contained and executable.
4. Explain each part of the OVER clause with business analogies (e.g. "PARTITION BY region is like resetting the counter for each region").
5. Show the correlated subquery equivalent to illustrate why the window function is more efficient and readable.
6. Deliver a catalog of 8 typical use cases: ranking by category, top-N per group, running total by date, 7-day moving average, percentage change vs. prior period, distribution percentile, first/last occurrence per group, dense rank.
OUTPUT: self-contained query in a code block, explanation of each OVER clause, comparison with subqueries, catalog of 8 use cases.
EDGE CASES:
- If ranking with ties is required (same position for equal values), use DENSE_RANK instead of ROW_NUMBER and explain the difference.
- If the engine is MySQL pre-8.0 (no window function support), indicate it and provide the user-variable alternative.
- If the partition has a single group (no PARTITION BY), clarify that the window operates over the entire table.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the query executes without errors and produces the expected result with the included sample data.
- Trade-off: window functions compute over all rows before filtering; use as a subquery or CTE if filtering on the window result is needed.
- DoD: query is self-contained with sample data; catalog has executable code for each case; explanation is understandable by analysts with intermediate SQL.

Protocolo MetodologIA: identify the window type → design the OVER clause → write self-contained query → explain with analogies → deliver use case catalog.
spec-datos_sql_pivot_unpivot_tabular:
[S · SITUATION] An analyst or data engineer needs to transform query results from rows to columns (PIVOT) or from columns to rows (UNPIVOT) to build tabular reports, cross-tables, or formats required by visualization tools or Excel exports, but the syntax varies significantly between SQL engines and many lack native support.

[P · REQUEST] Build the appropriate PIVOT or UNPIVOT query for the described transformation, producing: (1) a self-contained, executable query with sample data, (2) a native version with PIVOT/UNPIVOT if the engine supports it and a portable version with CASE WHEN / UNION ALL, (3) handling of dynamic values (when column values are not known in advance), (4) a comparative guide by SQL engine.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Data engineer with experience in relational data transformations and building tabular reports for business intelligence on multiple SQL engines.
ASSUMPTIONS: the engine is PostgreSQL if not specified (PostgreSQL has no native PIVOT; CASE WHEN with GROUP BY will be used); the pivot column values are those from the schema or sample data; if values are dynamic, generate a dynamic SQL version and warn about injection risk. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask only if the number of PIVOT columns is very high (>20) and could affect the solution design (maximum 1 question).
INPUTS: description of the desired transformation (which column becomes the header, what values are aggregated, which dimensions are kept) and schema or sample data.
STEPS:
1. Identify the transformation components: row key column, column whose values become headers (pivot column), value to aggregate (value column), aggregation function (SUM, COUNT, MAX, MIN).
2. Write the portable version with CASE WHEN and GROUP BY, self-contained with a sample data CTE.
3. If the engine supports native PIVOT (SQL Server, Oracle, BigQuery), write that version as well with a readability comparison.
4. If PIVOT values are dynamic (not known at design time), generate the dynamic SQL with safe string construction and an injection warning.
5. For UNPIVOT, use UNION ALL or native UNPIVOT depending on the engine, with sample data showing the inverse transformation.
6. Deliver a comparison table: SQL Engine | Native PIVOT support | Recommended syntax | Limitations.
OUTPUT: self-contained queries in code blocks (one portable, one native if applicable), dynamic SQL if applicable, comparison table by engine.
EDGE CASES:
- If there are NULL values in the pivot column, use COALESCE(value, 0) or COALESCE(value, '') depending on type and document the desired behavior.
- If the number of values to pivot is dynamic and very large, recommend performing the transformation in the application layer or the BI tool.
- If the PIVOT query will be used frequently, suggest materialization as a view or calculated table.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the self-contained query executes without errors and produces the expected cross-table with the sample data.
- Trade-off: native PIVOT is more readable but less portable; CASE WHEN is universally compatible but more verbose with many columns.
- DoD: portable version with CASE WHEN works on any standard SQL engine; dynamic SQL includes a security warning; comparison table covers the 4 main engines.

Protocolo MetodologIA: identify PIVOT components → write portable version → write native version if applicable → handle dynamic values → deliver comparison table by engine.
spec-datos_sql_deteccion_duplicados: [S · SITUATION] A relational database table contains duplicate records — either exact duplicates (all columns equal) or partial duplicates (same business entity, different surrogate key) — that distort reports, KPIs, and data integration processes. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) a SQL query that identifies all duplicate groups, indicating how many occurrences each group has and which rows are candidates for deletion; (2) a second deduplication query that retains exactly one record per group (the most recent version, or the one with the smallest ID if there is no date field) and deletes or flags the rest; (3) an index or constraint recommended to prevent future duplicates. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data engineer with 10+ years of SQL optimization in relational databases at scale. ASSUMPTIONS: default engine is PostgreSQL; if the user does not specify business columns that define duplication, assume they are all columns except the primary surrogate key; retention criterion: most recent record by audit column `updated_at` or `created_at`; if no date column exists, retain the minimum ID — declare these assumptions at the start of the response. INPUTS: DDL or table description pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Analyze the DDL and identify business candidate-key columns → produce an explicit list. 2. Write `duplicates` CTE with GROUP BY on candidate-key and HAVING COUNT(*)>1 → show count per group. 3. Write detail query using ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY candidate-key ORDER BY criterion) to tag rows to delete (rn > 1). 4. Write a safe delete statement (DELETE with subquery or CTE) or a flagging statement with an `is_duplicate BOOLEAN` column. 5. Propose CREATE UNIQUE INDEX or constraint for future prevention with a note on write impact. OUTPUT: three SQL blocks formatted with inline comments, preceded by a table of adopted assumptions; at the end, a precaution note about executing in a transaction with possible ROLLBACK. EDGE CASES: (a) table without a surrogate key — use CTID (PostgreSQL) or equivalent rowid, indicate it; (b) chained duplicates where the "original" is also a duplicate of another — ROW_NUMBER with consistent ORDER BY resolves it, explain; (c) table with millions of rows — add batch execution hint with LIMIT/OFFSET or temporal partitioning. [C · CRITERIA] All three queries must execute without error on the declared engine; the DELETE must not remove more records than those identified in the detection step; the index must not break referential integrity; the response includes at least one resolved edge case. Protocolo MetodologIA: detect → tag → delete safely → prevent.
spec-datos_sql_recursive_jerarquias: [S · SITUATION] A database table stores a self-referential hierarchical structure (org chart, category tree, bill of materials, chart of accounts) using an adjacency list pattern: each row has an `id` and a `parent_id` pointing to the parent node; the root has `parent_id = NULL`. Navigating that hierarchy — obtaining descendants, ancestors, or the complete path — is required without loading all data into the application. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) a recursive CTE that traverses the full hierarchy from a configurable root node down to the leaves, exposing depth level, ID path, and name/label path as computed columns; (2) a variant that traverses in reverse (from leaf to root); (3) a query that detects cycles to avoid infinite loops; (4) a brief explanation of the anchor + recursive term mechanism. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data engineer specializing in advanced SQL and hierarchical data structures. ASSUMPTIONS: default engine is PostgreSQL (WITH RECURSIVE); table named `nodes` with columns `id INTEGER`, `parent_id INTEGER`, `name TEXT`; default root node is the one with `parent_id IS NULL`; maximum guard depth is 50 levels to prevent loops — declare these assumptions at the start. INPUTS: DDL or description of the hierarchical table pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Confirm or adjust table structure based on DDL. 2. Write the descending recursive CTE with anchor (root node) and recursive term (JOIN with child nodes); compute columns `level`, `path_ids` (array or delimited string), `path_names`. 3. Write the ascending variant (leaf → root) with the same pattern. 4. Write a cycle detection query using the visited IDs array and the condition `id = ANY(path)`. 5. Add comments explaining the anchor term, recursive term, and termination condition. OUTPUT: four SQL blocks with inline comments; initial assumptions table; note on configurable recursion limit in each engine. EDGE CASES: (a) tree with orphan nodes (parent_id points to non-existent ID) — add LEFT JOIN with IS NULL filter to detect them; (b) very deep hierarchy (>100 levels) — explain adjusting `max_recursion` in MySQL or depth in SQL Server; (c) multiple roots in the same table — show how to adapt the anchor with `parent_id IS NULL` or a list of roots. [C · CRITERIA] The descending CTE must complete without timeout on hierarchies up to 20 levels deep; cycle detection must return zero rows in a cycle-free table; the mechanism explanation must be understandable without prior knowledge of recursive CTEs. Protocolo MetodologIA: anchor → expand → detect cycles → expose paths.
spec-datos_sql_traducir_dialectos: [S · SITUATION] A data engineering team needs to migrate or port SQL queries written for one database engine (source) to another engine with a different dialect (target). Dialect differences include date/time functions, window functions, data types, NULL handling, identifier quoting, string functions, CTEs, UPSERT, and result size limits. An incorrect manual translation produces errors or silently different results. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) the received original query, annotated with marks on each construct that requires adaptation; (2) the query translated to the target dialect, fully functional, with inline comments explaining each change; (3) an equivalence table for the modified functions/constructs (columns: original, target equivalent, semantic difference note). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect with migration experience across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, and Redshift. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the target engine, ask only for that data before proceeding; if the source engine is not specified, infer it from the query dialect and declare it as an assumption; translations must preserve exact semantics, never sacrifice correctness for brevity. INPUTS: original SQL query pasted in the chat; source and target engines specified by the user or inferred. STEPS: 1. Identify the source engine (declare as assumption if inferred). 2. Parse the query and list all dialect-dependent constructs (functions, types, special syntax). 3. Produce an annotated version of the original query with comments `-- [ADAPT: reason]`. 4. Write the translated query with comments `-- [TRANSLATED: from X to Y]` on each change. 5. Build the equivalence table. 6. If there are constructs with no direct equivalent, propose a workaround with a limitation note. OUTPUT: three clearly separated sections — annotated query, translated query, equivalence table — followed by warnings about non-trivial semantic differences. EDGE CASES: (a) proprietary functions without an equivalent (e.g. BigQuery's QUALIFY in PostgreSQL) — propose a CTE wrapper or equivalent subquery; (b) differences in NULL handling in comparisons — add an explicit note; (c) different recursion or result size limits between engines — document. [C · CRITERIA] The translated query must execute without syntax errors on the target engine; the semantics (results) must be identical to the original except for explicitly documented cases; the equivalence table covers 100% of the adapted constructs. Protocolo MetodologIA: annotate source → translate with traceability → document semantic differences.
spec-datos_sql_explicar_query_heredada: [S · SITUATION] A data team inherits a complex SQL query — between 50 and 500 lines — written by someone who is no longer available. The query has no comments, uses cryptic aliases, combines multiple JOINs and subqueries, and no one is entirely certain what it produces or why it was written that way. The team needs to understand it before modifying or replacing it. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) a one-sentence executive summary describing what the query calculates; (2) a section-by-section breakdown explaining in plain language what each CTE, subquery, or JOIN does and what columns it contributes to the final result; (3) an alias dictionary — table with alias used in the query, inferred full name, and business description; (4) a data flow diagram in text (ASCII or Mermaid) showing how sources flow to the result; (5) a list of business domain assumptions the query appears to make, marked as [INFERENCE]. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data engineering analyst specializing in reading and documenting high-complexity legacy SQL. ASSUMPTIONS: if the engine is not specified, infer it from the dialect and declare it; tables referenced without DDL are described by name and inferred context, always marked as [INFERENCE]; it is assumed the query is correct and has no bugs — the goal is to understand, not to correct. INPUTS: inherited SQL query pasted in the chat; optionally DDL of the involved tables. STEPS: 1. Identify the engine and declare as assumption if inferred. 2. Segment the query into logical blocks (CTEs, subqueries, main JOINs, WHERE/HAVING/ORDER clauses). 3. Write the one-sentence executive summary. 4. Document each block with: purpose, source tables, produced columns, filtering or aggregation logic. 5. Build the alias dictionary. 6. Generate the flow diagram in Mermaid (flowchart LR). 7. List inferred business assumptions. OUTPUT: structured document with five numbered sections; Mermaid diagram in a code block; assumptions marked with [INFERENCE]. EDGE CASES: (a) query with complex conditional logic (nested CASE WHEN) — explain each branch separately; (b) unknown proprietary functions — document with [ASSUMPTION] and note that verification is required; (c) query with embedded optimizer hints or technical comments — include them in the documentation as historical context. [C · CRITERIA] The executive summary must be understandable to someone from the business side without SQL knowledge; the breakdown must cover 100% of the logical blocks; business assumptions must be clearly distinguished from facts observable in the code. Protocolo MetodologIA: segment → explain → map flow → document assumptions.
spec-datos_sql_cohorte_retencion: [S · SITUATION] A product or analytics team needs to measure user retention over time by grouping them into acquisition cohorts (week, month, or quarter of their first action). Cohort analysis allows identifying whether retention improves or worsens across user generations and at which periods the greatest churn occurs. The query must run directly in the database without relying on external BI tools. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) a complete SQL query that calculates the cohort table: rows = acquisition cohort, columns = periods 0 through N since acquisition, values = percentage retention rate; (2) an auxiliary query that calculates the size of each cohort (unique users in period 0); (3) a brief explanation of the logic (how the relative period and retention rate are calculated). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data analyst specializing in product metrics and window SQL. ASSUMPTIONS: events table named `events` with columns `user_id`, `event_date DATE`; monthly cohort granularity by default; maximum follow-up period 12 months; retention defined as a user who records at least one event in relative month N counted from their month of first activity — declare these assumptions at the start. INPUTS: description or DDL of the events table pasted in the chat; optionally desired granularity and number of periods. STEPS: 1. Calculate `first_activity` per user with MIN(event_date). 2. Calculate `cohort` by truncating first_activity to the month (or specified granularity). 3. Calculate relative period (event_month - cohort in months). 4. Count active users per (cohort, period). 5. Join with cohort sizes and calculate rate = active / cohort_size * 100. 6. Pivot the result (using CASE WHEN or CROSSTAB if available) to matrix format. OUTPUT: two SQL blocks with inline comments; assumptions table; note on how to adapt granularity to weeks or quarters. EDGE CASES: (a) users with events in multiple months but no activity in period 0 (register and immediately churn) — include in cohort with retention 0 in periods > 0; (b) engine without native pivot support (PostgreSQL) — use CASE WHEN with MAX; (c) recent cohorts with incomplete periods — add `is_complete_period` column or precaution note. [C · CRITERIA] Period-0 cohort must always show 100% retention; the sum of users in any period N must be ≤ cohort size; the query must be adaptable to weekly or quarterly granularity with a single parameter change. Protocolo MetodologIA: first activity → relative period → rate per cohort → pivoted matrix.
spec-datos_sql_gap_islands: [S · SITUATION] A database table records events or states with a timestamp (or date) for entities such as users, devices, sessions, or contracts. It is necessary to identify: (a) islands — contiguous or overlapping periods where the entity was active or in a given state; (b) gaps — time intervals between islands where the entity was inactive or in a different state. This pattern appears in session analytics, system availability, active contracts, continuous geolocation, and anomaly detection. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) a SQL query that identifies and labels each island (contiguous period) with its start date/time, end date/time, and duration; (2) a SQL query that identifies each gap between consecutive islands with its duration; (3) an explanation of the algorithm used (classic row-number difference or lag/lead method). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data engineer specializing in analytical SQL and time series. ASSUMPTIONS: table named `events` with columns `entity_id`, `start_date DATE`, `end_date DATE`; if events are point events (no end_date), assume a duration of 1 day; gap tolerance = 0 days (periods that touch are considered contiguous) — declare these assumptions at the start; if the user specifies a different tolerance, apply it. INPUTS: DDL or description of the events table pasted in the chat; optionally gap tolerance and state column to filter. STEPS: 1. Use LAG() to compare start_date with the previous event's end_date per entity. 2. Mark the start of a new island when the gap > tolerance. 3. Calculate the island group_id with SUM() OVER of the start marks. 4. Aggregate by (entity_id, group_id) to obtain each island's range. 5. Calculate gaps as LAG(end_date) in the islands CTE. OUTPUT: two SQL blocks with inline comments; assumptions table; explanation of the algorithm in three conceptual steps. EDGE CASES: (a) overlapping events (end_date of one is after start_date of the next) — merge into the same island using GREATEST(end_date) in the aggregation; (b) entities with a single event — island of a single point, empty gap; (c) events without end_date (in progress) — treat end_date as NOW() or the current date, flag it. [C · CRITERIA] The islands query must not produce entity duplicates within the same island; the calculated gaps must equal the difference between the previous island's end and the next island's start; the algorithm must work correctly with overlapping events. Protocolo MetodologIA: detect change → group contiguous → calculate islands → calculate gaps.
spec-datos_sql_revisar_inyeccion: [S · SITUATION] A development team has code that builds or executes SQL queries and needs to verify that it is correctly protected against SQL injection attacks. The code can be in any backend language (Python, Java, Node.js, PHP, etc.) and may use an ORM, native drivers, or ad-hoc query builders. SQL injection vulnerabilities are the most common database attack vector and can compromise confidentiality, integrity, and availability. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) analysis of each point in the code where SQL is built or executed, indicating whether it is safe, vulnerable, or requires manual review, with severity (CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW); (2) for each vulnerability found: explanation of the risk, sanitized attack payload example (without active exploitation instructions), and a concrete fix with corrected code; (3) a best-practices parameterization checklist for the specific technology stack. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior security engineer specializing in application and database security with OWASP Top 10 expertise. ASSUMPTIONS: if the language is not specified, infer it from the code and declare it; correct parameterization = use of prepared statements or query builders with parameter binding; string concatenation or interpolation of external variables into SQL = at least HIGH vulnerability. INPUTS: code fragment that builds or executes SQL pasted in the chat; optionally the technology stack and database engine. STEPS: 1. Identify all SQL construction or execution points in the code. 2. For each point: classify as safe/vulnerable/requires-review + severity + justification. 3. For each vulnerability: explain risk + show conceptual example payload + write corrected code. 4. Generate the stack best-practices checklist. OUTPUT: findings table (code point, classification, severity); correction sections with code diff or before/after; final checklist. EDGE CASES: (a) ORM usage that appears safe but with raw() or execute() for dynamic queries — mark as requires-review and explain risk; (b) indirect inputs (DB columns used as parameters in subsequent queries) — flag second-order injection risk; (c) dynamic IN lists — show safe pattern with array binding. [C · CRITERIA] The analysis must cover 100% of the SQL execution points in the provided fragment; example payloads must illustrate the risk without constituting active attack instructions; the corrected code must be functionally equivalent to the original. Protocolo MetodologIA: identify SQL points → classify risk → correct with parameterization → verify with checklist.
spec-datos_modelo_estrella_dimensional: [S · SITUATION] An analytics or data warehouse team needs to design a star schema to enable high-performance analytical reports and queries on a specific business process (sales, operations, logistics, marketing, etc.). The star schema is the foundation of Kimball dimensional modeling: a central fact table with quantitative metrics surrounded by denormalized dimension tables representing the axes of analysis. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) identification of the dimensions of the described business process (who, what, when, where, how); (2) design of the fact table with its metrics, foreign keys to dimensions, and declared grain; (3) design of each dimension table with descriptive attributes and surrogate key; (4) SQL DDL for the complete schema; (5) Mermaid diagram of the star schema. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect specializing in dimensional modeling and data warehouse design (Kimball methodology). ASSUMPTIONS: fact table grain = transactional level (one record per individual transaction) if no other is specified; all dimensions include surrogate key `dim_*_key BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` and load date `load_date`; time dimension always present with at least: date, year, quarter, month, week, day of week — declare these assumptions at the start. INPUTS: description of the business process and its main metrics pasted in the chat; optionally a list of known dimensions. STEPS: 1. Identify the business process and declare the fact table grain. 2. List the dimensions (minimum: time, one main subject dimension). 3. Design the fact table with additive, semi-additive, and non-additive metrics clearly classified. 4. Design each dimension table with its descriptive attributes. 5. Write the complete DDL in PostgreSQL by default. 6. Generate the Mermaid erDiagram. OUTPUT: five numbered sections; DDL in a code block; Mermaid diagram in a code block; metric classification table (additive/semi-additive/non-additive). EDGE CASES: (a) process with multiple grains (order header + line item) — design two separate fact tables; (b) calculated metrics that should not be stored (ratio, percentage) — document them as derived metrics, not columns; (c) dimension with high cardinality (millions of customers) — recommend partitioning or an index on the natural key. [C · CRITERIA] The fact table must not contain descriptive attributes (only metrics and foreign keys); each dimension must have at least one natural key and one surrogate key; the Mermaid diagram must reflect all the DDL relationships. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare grain → identify dimensions → design facts → DDL → diagram.
spec-datos_modelo_snowflake_normalizado: [S · SITUATION] A data architecture team faces the decision of choosing between a star schema (denormalized dimensions) and a snowflake schema (dimensions normalized into sub-tables) for a data warehouse or data mart. The choice affects query performance, ease of maintenance, storage consumption, and the team's learning curve. There is no universal answer: the decision depends on the specific context. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) a structured comparative analysis of star vs. snowflake across the axes: query performance, ease of maintenance, storage consumption, ease of use for analysts, and management of attribute changes; (2) a decision tree or questionnaire of 5–7 context questions to guide the choice; (3) a concrete recommendation for the context described by the user, with justification based on their answers; (4) a DDL example for one dimension of the same process modeled in both schemas, to illustrate the practical difference. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect specializing in dimensional modeling with experience on multiple analytical platforms (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, Synapse). ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not describe the context, present the comparative analysis and decision tree first, and ask for answers to the questionnaire before making the recommendation; modern platforms with columnar storage favor the star schema for scan performance. INPUTS: data warehouse context description (data scale, platform, team, frequency of dimension changes) pasted in chat. STEPS: 1. Present star vs. snowflake comparative table across the five axes. 2. Formulate a decision tree with questions about scale, platform, team, cardinality, and frequency of changes. 3. If the user has provided context: evaluate answers and issue a justified recommendation. 4. Write a DDL for one dimension (e.g., customer or product dimension) in both schemas. 5. Point out when a hybrid schema (partial snowflake) makes sense. OUTPUT: comparative table; decision tree in Mermaid; recommendation (if context is available); DDL example in two versions. EDGE CASES: (a) columnar MPP platform (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake) — explain why star generally outperforms snowflake on these platforms; (b) dimension with stable, high-cardinality sub-hierarchies (geography, product category) — this is the most legitimate case for snowflake; (c) team with non-technical BI profiles — star reduces complexity of ad-hoc queries. [C · CRITERIA] The comparative table must cover at least five axes; the decision tree must lead to one of three options (star, snowflake, hybrid); the recommendation must be grounded in the context's characteristics, not generic preferences. Protocolo MetodologIA: compare axes → decide by context → illustrate difference with DDL.
spec-datos_modelo_scd_tipo2: [S · SITUATION] A data warehouse team needs to track the history of attribute changes in a dimension — for example, changes in a customer's category, a product's price, a salesperson's region, or an employee's department. With SCD Type 2 (Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2) the complete history is preserved: each change generates a new row, and historical facts remain linked to the correct version of the dimension at the time of the event. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) design of the dimension table with SCD Type 2 support, including all necessary control columns; (2) complete SQL DDL for the dimension and its staging table; (3) MERGE/UPSERT logic to load changes detected via the staging table, distinguishing inserts of new entities, attribute updates that generate a new version, and attribute updates that do not require history (selective Type 1); (4) a query to obtain the current active version of all records. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect specializing in Kimball dimensional modeling and ETL patterns for data warehouses. ASSUMPTIONS: standard SCD2 control columns: `dim_key BIGINT` (surrogate), `natural_key`, `validity_start_date DATE`, `validity_end_date DATE` (9999-12-31 for active record), `is_active BOOLEAN`, `version INT` — declare these assumptions at the start; default engine PostgreSQL; change detection strategy is MD5 hash comparison of tracked attributes. INPUTS: description of the dimension to model (entity, attributes, which are Type 2 and which are Type 1) pasted in chat. STEPS: 1. List the dimension's attributes and classify them: Type 2 (history), Type 1 (overwrite), Type 0 (do not change). 2. Design dimension table with SCD2 control columns. 3. Design staging table. 4. Write MERGE statement for: (a) new entities → INSERT, (b) changes in Type 2 attributes → close prior version (end_date, is_active=false) + INSERT new version, (c) changes in Type 1 attributes → in-place UPDATE. 5. Write active-version query. OUTPUT: DDL for three objects (dimension, staging, recommended indexes); documented MERGE/load logic; active-version query; attribute classification table. EDGE CASES: (a) initial load (bulk load) — treat all records as new entities with start_date = load date; (b) feedback of historical changes with an effective date different from the load date — use `effective_date` from staging as `validity_start_date`; (c) multiple active versions due to load error — add UNIQUE constraint (natural_key, is_active) with partial filter. [C · CRITERIA] At any given point in time, the JOIN of the fact table with the dimension by date range must return exactly one version per fact; the MERGE must not create orphan records; the active-version query must return exactly one record per natural_key. Protocolo MetodologIA: classify attributes → design SCD2 control → MERGE with traceability → query active version.
spec-datos_modelo_normalizacion_3fn: [S · SITUATION] A development or data architecture team has a relational schema that presents problems of redundancy, update anomalies, insertion anomalies, and deletion anomalies — symptoms of not being normalized. The schema must be brought to Third Normal Form (3NF) to eliminate these anomalies and guarantee data integrity without unnecessary redundancy. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) diagnosis of the received schema: identify violations of 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF present, with concrete examples of the anomalies each violation can produce; (2) step-by-step normalization process to 3NF with the resulting DDL at each stage; (3) Mermaid erDiagram of the final schema in 3NF; (4) table of functional dependencies identified during the process. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior relational database architect specializing in normalization theory and OLTP schema design. ASSUMPTIONS: default engine PostgreSQL; if the schema has no PKs defined, infer them from context and declare them as an assumption; the target is 3NF — not BCNF or 4NF unless the user explicitly requests it; preserve sample data if the user provides it to illustrate the anomalies. INPUTS: DDL of the current schema or description of the tables with columns pasted in chat; optionally, sample data. STEPS: 1. Analyze the DDL and list all detected functional dependencies. 2. Check 1NF: identify repeating groups or non-atomic values — correct. 3. Check 2NF: identify partial dependencies (attributes dependent on part of a composite key) — decompose. 4. Check 3NF: identify transitive dependencies (non-key attribute that determines another non-key attribute) — decompose. 5. Write DDL for the final 3NF schema with PKs, FKs, and constraints. 6. Generate Mermaid diagram. OUTPUT: diagnosis with anomaly examples; DDL in three stages (1NF, 2NF, 3NF); final Mermaid diagram; functional dependencies table. EDGE CASES: (a) multi-valued attributes (list of phone numbers, list of tags) — normalize to a separate table with FK; (b) composite candidate key of more than two columns — identify all partial dependencies; (c) schema already in 3NF — confirm and justify that there are no violations. [C · CRITERIA] The final 3NF schema must not contain transitive dependencies; every eliminated redundancy must be recoverable via JOIN; the DDL must be syntactically correct in the declared engine; each decomposition must preserve the original information (lossless join). Protocolo MetodologIA: diagnose anomalies → normalize by stages → verify without redundancy → diagram.
spec-datos_modelo_denormalizacion_olap: [S · SITUATION] A data team has a normalized relational schema (3NF or higher) designed for OLTP transactional workloads and needs to create a denormalized version optimized for OLAP analytical queries in a data warehouse, data mart, or analytics layer. Strategic denormalization reduces costly JOINs, improves scan performance on columnar engines, and simplifies analyst queries, at the cost of higher storage consumption and greater pipeline loading complexity. [P · REQUEST] Deliver: (1) analysis of the received OLTP schema: identify frequent JOINs in analytical queries and performance bottlenecks that justify denormalization; (2) design of the denormalized OLAP schema with justification for each denormalization decision; (3) DDL of the resulting analytical schema; (4) update strategy: how to keep the source OLTP schema and the OLAP schema synchronized when data changes; (5) guide to when NOT to denormalize (trade-offs to consider). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect specializing in analytical layer design and performance optimization on OLAP columnar platforms. ASSUMPTIONS: default OLAP destination engine BigQuery or Snowflake (columnar); default update strategy: materialized table or daily snapshot; denormalization preserves semantics — information is never lost through denormalization — declare these assumptions at the start. INPUTS: DDL of the normalized OLTP schema + description of the most frequent analytical use cases, pasted in chat. STEPS: 1. Analyze the DDL and analytical use cases: identify JOIN patterns, columns most queried in filters and aggregations. 2. Classify OLTP tables as: dimensions to flatten, facts to keep, lookup tables to embed. 3. Design the OLAP schema: wide tables, arrays of structs for 1:N relationships, pre-calculated derived columns. 4. Write DDL for the analytical schema. 5. Design synchronization strategy (incremental MERGE, full snapshot, or materialized table). 6. Document trade-offs and when keeping the normalized schema is better. OUTPUT: analysis of frequent JOINs; section-by-section justified design; analytical DDL; synchronization strategy; trade-offs table with columns "denormalize" vs. "keep normalized". EDGE CASES: (a) 1:N relationships of high cardinality (facts per customer) — do not flatten, use a separate fact table; (b) frequently changing attributes — decide between current-state column or historical snapshot; (c) columnar engine with ARRAY/STRUCT support (BigQuery) — leverage nested types for secondary relationships. [C · CRITERIA] The OLAP schema must reduce the number of JOINs needed for the declared analytical use cases; denormalization must not lose information recoverable from the OLTP source; the synchronization strategy must be implementable with standard ETL/ELT tools; the trade-off guide must cover at least four scenarios where denormalization is not advisable. Protocolo MetodologIA: analyze JOINs → denormalize strategically → synchronize source → document trade-offs.
spec-datos_modelo_erd_desde_requerimient: [S · SITUATION] The data engineering team received a functional specification in text — user stories, business rules, or domain description — and needs to convert it into a normalized entity-relationship diagram (ERD) before beginning database implementation. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete ERD in Chen or Crow's Foot notation with all entities, attributes (indicating primary and foreign keys), cardinalities, and relationships identified from the pasted requirements text. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect with experience in relational modeling and normalization to 3NF. ASSUMPTIONS: if the text does not mention cardinalities, assume 1-N by default; if there is ambiguity in entities, select the most conservative reading (fewer entities) and document it; ask the user only if the ambiguity affects more than 30% of the model, maximum 3 questions. INPUTS: requirements text pasted in the message. STEPS: 1) Identify noun candidates for entities and verb candidates for relationships — list findings. 2) Apply normalization rules (1NF → 2NF → 3NF) — document decisions. 3) Define natural or surrogate primary keys with justification. 4) Diagram in Mermaid erDiagram syntax with all attributes and relationships. 5) Deliver summary table: entity, attributes, PK, FK, cardinalities. OUTPUT: Mermaid erDiagram block + Markdown table. EDGE CASES: (a) weak entity without its own PK → use composite PK or surrogate and annotate; (b) M:N relationship → decompose into bridge table with composite PK; (c) multi-valued attributes → create dependent entity. [C · CRITERIA] The diagram must compile in Mermaid without errors; all relationships from the requirements text must be represented; the structure must be in 3NF or document the exception. DoD: renderable diagram + summary table delivered. Protocolo MetodologIA: identify assumptions with [ASSUMPTION], evidence with [CODE] or [DOC], and mark DoD at close.
spec-datos_modelo_data_vault: [S · SITUATION] An analytical engineering team must build an auditable historical storage layer to integrate multiple operational sources into an enterprise data warehouse. The business requires change traceability, parallel loading, and the ability to add sources without redesigning the model. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete Data Vault 2.0 model: identify hubs, links, and satellites from the provided inventory of business entities and relationships; deliver conceptual DDL in pseudo-SQL and a Mermaid diagram with all three object types clearly distinguished. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data warehouse architect certified in Data Vault 2.0. ASSUMPTIONS: if the load source is not specified, assume daily batch; if the inventory does not indicate descriptive attributes, create a generic satellite per hub with a description field; ask the user only if business keys cannot be inferred, maximum 2 questions. INPUTS: entity and relationship inventory pasted in the message. STEPS: 1) Identify business keys per entity → define one Hub for each. 2) Identify M:N relationships between hubs → define one Link for each. 3) Identify descriptive and audit attributes → define Satellites (one per source per Hub/Link). 4) Add standard DV2.0 metadata columns: LOAD_DTS, RECORD_SOURCE, HASH_KEY. 5) Draft conceptual DDL (pseudo-SQL) for each object. 6) Diagram in Mermaid erDiagram. OUTPUT: conceptual DDL + Mermaid diagram. EDGE CASES: (a) business hierarchy → use Hierarchy Link; (b) attributes that change over time → Effectivity Satellite; (c) sources with different keys for the same entity → Bridge or same Hub with differentiated RECORD_SOURCE. [C · CRITERIA] Each Hub has exactly one business key; each Link references a minimum of two Hubs; each Satellite has a FK to its Hub or Link and DV2.0 audit columns. DoD: DDL + diagram delivered and conformant with DV 2.0. Protocolo MetodologIA: tag assumptions with [ASSUMPTION] and mark DoD at close.
spec-datos_modelo_one_big_table: [S · SITUATION] An analytics team is debating whether to model their consumption data in a single denormalized table (One Big Table, OBT) or in a classic dimensional model (star/snowflake) for a data mart on a modern columnar platform (BigQuery, Snowflake, or Redshift). The decision affects query performance, storage costs, and long-term maintainability. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured comparative analysis between OBT and the dimensional model for the described use case: a trade-off matrix, a justified recommendation with measurable criteria, and, if OBT is recommended, a schema of the resulting table. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect with experience in columnar platforms and analytical modeling. ASSUMPTIONS: if the platform is not specified, assume BigQuery; if the volume is not indicated, assume tens of millions of rows per month; proceed with those assumptions without asking. INPUTS: description of the use case, entities, and main metrics, pasted in the message. STEPS: 1) Summarize the use case in one sentence and list the key entities and metrics. 2) Evaluate OBT across dimensions: read performance, storage cost, ease of maintenance, analytical onboarding time, risk of null rows or duplicated values. 3) Evaluate the dimensional model across the same dimensions. 4) Build a comparative table with a 1-5 score per dimension. 5) Issue a recommendation with quantitative justification; if OBT wins, design the table schema (column names and types). OUTPUT: Markdown comparative table + recommendation + OBT schema if applicable. EDGE CASES: (a) very high cardinality in dimensions → favor dimensional model; (b) small analytics team without advanced SQL knowledge → point in favor of OBT; (c) data from multiple domains with separate governance → dimensional model mandatory. [C · CRITERIA] The comparative table covers at least five dimensions; the recommendation cites at least two quantitative metrics; the OBT schema (if applicable) has column names in snake_case and explicit data types. ROLE: Senior data architect with experience implementing lakehouses with Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Hudi on platforms such as Databricks, Azure Synapse, AWS Lake Formation, or Google Cloud Storage + BigQuery.
