Without this mapping, the data team does not know what to implement to satisfy auditors, and the legal team cannot verify that technical controls comply with the regulation. [P · REQUEST] Build a regulatory compliance map to data controls: requirement table by regulation, corresponding technical and operational controls, required compliance evidence, owners, and implementation status, delivered as an auditable compliance matrix. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data compliance and governance consultant with experience mapping regulations to technical controls on data platforms, privacy audits, and security certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2). ASSUMPTIONS: if no applicable regulations are specified, assume GDPR + LGPD + ISO 27001 as the base set; if no technology stack is indicated, assume a cloud data platform with Snowflake + S3/Azure Blob; if no data inventory is provided, assume the presence of customer PII, financial data, and employee data; declare assumptions at the start; ask only if there are very specific local regulations from a non-standard sector (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: list of applicable regulations and norms with their geographic scope, pasted in the chat; optionally prior audits or identified gaps. STEPS: 1. Enumerate the key articles and requirements of each applicable regulation for data → requirements table grouped by regulation and topic (consent, access, retention, security, lineage, breach notification). 2. Map each requirement to specific implementable technical controls on the data stack → requirement → technical control mapping table with tool or mechanism. 3. Map each requirement to operational controls (policies, processes, training) → operational controls table with process and frequency. 4. Define the compliance evidence required for each control: logs, reports, certificates, consent records → evidence inventory. 5. Assign owner (Data Owner, CISO, DPO, Engineering) and status (not started / in progress / implemented / audited) to each control → implementation status table. 6. Identify critical gaps and develop a prioritized remediation plan by regulatory risk → gap table with priority and closing deadline. OUTPUT: compliance matrix in Markdown with six sections, exportable as a table for tracking in Jira or Excel. EDGE CASES: (a) two regulations with contradictory requirements → document the conflict and recommend the most restrictive interpretation after consulting legal counsel; (b) technical control not available in the current stack → propose a compensating control and a technical improvement roadmap; (c) new regulation or in a grace period → indicate the applicability date and include it in the preventive remediation plan. [C · CRITERIA] Each control has an objective verification criterion that an auditor can check; the matrix has no gaps without a closure plan; the owner is a specific person or role, not a generic team; the remediation plan has concrete dates; DoD: the DPO and CISO can use the matrix to prepare an external audit without additional work. Protocolo MetodologIA: tag with [DOC] each normative article referenced and with [ASSUMPTION] each requirement interpretation not confirmed by legal counsel.
spec-datos_gobierno_linaje_trazabilidad: [S · SITUATION] A data team needs to document how data flows from the original sources (transactional systems, external APIs, files) to the consumption artifacts (dashboards, ML models, regulatory reports), passing through all intermediate transformations. Without this lineage, it is impossible to trace the origin of an error, assess the impact of a schema change, or demonstrate the traceability required by auditors. [P · REQUEST] Document end-to-end data lineage for a specific data flow: lineage diagram, transformation table, field-level impact analysis, and continuous lineage maintenance process, delivered as a technical lineage document. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data engineer with specialization in data lineage, metadata, and data observability tools (OpenLineage, Marquez, DataHub, Atlan, dbt docs, Apache Atlas). ASSUMPTIONS: if no specific data flow is provided, assume a sales flow from OLTP system (PostgreSQL) → raw ingestion in S3 → dbt transformations → Snowflake data mart → Tableau dashboard; if no lineage tool is indicated, assume manual capture plus dbt docs for the transformation layer; declare assumptions at the start; ask only if there are transformations in proprietary tools without OpenLineage support (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: description of the data flow (source systems, transformation tools, consumption destinations, key traced fields), pasted in the chat; optionally existing diagrams. STEPS: 1. Map all nodes in the data flow: source systems, ingestion pipelines, transformation layers, intermediate tables, consumption artifacts → lineage diagram in text format (Mermaid). 2. For each transformation, document: source system, input fields, transformation logic (formula or business description), output fields, destination system → transformation table. 3. Document field-level lineage for the 5-10 most business-critical fields → field lineage table with each hop. 4. Design the impact analysis: given a change in a source field, which transformations, tables, and dashboards are affected → impact analysis template with applied example. 5. Define the lineage maintenance process: who updates the lineage when changes occur, in what tool, how often, how it is validated → maintenance guide with checklist. 6. Specify the integration of lineage into the metadata catalog: how to link the lineage document to the catalog, which metadata fields are populated automatically vs. manually → integration plan. OUTPUT: technical lineage document in Markdown with Mermaid diagram, transformation tables, field-level lineage, and maintenance guide. EDGE CASES: (a) transformations in a BI tool (Tableau or Power BI calculations) → document as a presentation layer with formula description even if not capturable by OpenLineage; (b) external data sources without schema access → document the known interface and mark the node as a black box with a functional description; (c) ML transformations that generate features → treat the feature store as a node in the lineage graph with a description of the transformation algorithm. [C · CRITERIA] The diagram is readable by a non-technical person in fewer than 5 minutes; each transformation has a business description (not just technical); the impact analysis can be executed in fewer than 15 minutes given a real change; the maintenance process has an explicit owner and frequency; DoD: a new analyst can trace the origin of any dashboard field using only this document. Protocolo MetodologIA: tag with [INFERENCE] each transformation whose logic is inferred from context and with [ASSUMPTION] each flow node not explicitly confirmed.
spec-datos_gobierno_catalogo_metadatos: [S · SITUATION] An organization with a growing data lake or data warehouse needs a data catalog that allows analysts, engineers, and decision-makers to find the data they need, understand what it means, know who is responsible for it, and trust its quality. Without a structured catalog, knowledge about data lives in silos, is lost with staff turnover, and effort is duplicated. [P · REQUEST] Structure a data and metadata catalog: metadata model (what fields are documented for each asset), population and maintenance process, catalog quality standard, and adoption plan, delivered as a ready-to-execute catalog implementation guide. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data architect with experience implementing data catalogs (Collibra, Alation, DataHub, Amundsen, dbt docs) and designing enterprise metadata models. ASSUMPTIONS: if no catalog tool is specified, assume DataHub Open Source or dbt docs depending on stack maturity; if no asset types to catalog are indicated, assume tables in Snowflake/BigQuery, dashboards in Tableau/Power BI, and pipelines in dbt; if no maturity level is indicated, assume a non-existent catalog being built from scratch; declare assumptions at the start; ask only if there are unusual asset types (ML models, streaming, APIs) that require a highly specialized metadata model (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: list of data asset types to catalog with estimated volume, current stack tools, and available data team, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Design the metadata model: what fields each asset type documents (table, column, dashboard, pipeline) → metadata schema by asset type with field, type, required status, and description. 2. Prioritize the most critical assets for the first cataloging cycle → prioritization matrix by business value and usage frequency. 3. Define the catalog quality standard: what constitutes a well-documented asset, what fields are required, how the completeness score is measured → quality rubric with score. 4. Design the initial population process: who loads what, in what tool, with what template, on what schedule → population plan with owners and sprints. 5. Define the continuous maintenance process: update triggers (schema change, new source, owner change), owner and frequency → maintenance flow with checklist. 6. Develop the adoption plan: how to get analysts and data scientists to actively use the catalog → adoption strategy with success metrics (searches per week, assets documented at 80%+). OUTPUT: implementation guide in Markdown with six sections, metadata schema, quality rubric, and documentation templates. EDGE CASES: (a) small data team (<5 people) → simplify the metadata model to essential fields and automate population via schema scraping scripts; (b) external data sources without direct access → document only the metadata of the ingestion point and flag as unmanaged external source; (c) assets with multiple active versions → implement metadata versioning with a current version field and archive of prior versions. [C · CRITERIA] The metadata model has fewer than 15 required fields to avoid discouraging adoption; the quality rubric is applicable in fewer than 5 minutes per asset; the adoption plan has measurable weekly metrics; the guide can be executed by a Data Steward with no prior catalog tool experience; DoD: at the end of the first sprint, at least 30% of critical assets are documented with a score >=70 on the rubric. Protocolo MetodologIA: tag with [ASSUMPTION] each metadata field whose required status you assume without confirming with catalog users and with [INFERENCE] each asset prioritization based on the provided context.
spec-datos_gobierno_acceso_minimo_privil: [S · SITUATION] An organization with a cloud data platform (data warehouse, data lake, or lakehouse) needs to implement an access control model based on the principle of least privilege: each user, role, or process receives exactly the permissions needed for their function and nothing more. The absence of this model generates excessive access, risk of sensitive data exposure, and difficulty demonstrating compliance to auditors. [P · REQUEST] Design the least-privilege access control model: access role taxonomy, permission matrix by role and data layer, access request and approval process, periodic review process, and technical configuration in the data stack — delivered as an access control policy with implementation guide. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data security architect with experience designing RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) and ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) models in modern data platforms (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, AWS Lake Formation). ASSUMPTIONS: if the stack is not specified, assume Snowflake as data warehouse with AWS S3 as the raw layer; if the current role model is not indicated, assume all users have overly broad roles or direct table access without intermediate roles; if the preferred access model is not specified, assume RBAC with functional roles by domain and layer; declare assumptions upfront; ask only if there are very dynamic access requirements that would require ABAC with real-time context attributes (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: description of user types and their access needs (engineers, analysts, data scientists, business users, automated processes), data layers (raw, staging, marts), and business domains, pasted in chat. STEPS: 1. Design the functional role taxonomy: roles by user type and business domain → role tree with inheritance in Snowflake. 2. Build the permission matrix: which role has access to which database/schema/table with which privilege (SELECT, INSERT, MODIFY) → permission matrix by layer and domain. 3. Define additional constraints: column-level security for PII, row-level security by business unit, dynamic masking of sensitive data → advanced constraints table with technical implementation. 4. Design the access request and approval process: request form, approval criteria, SLA, tool, notification, automatic provisioning → process flow with diagram. 5. Define the periodic access review process (access review / certifications): frequency, responsible parties, revocation criteria, off-boarding process → process guide with semi-annual checklist. 6. Document the technical configuration in Snowflake: SQL commands to create roles, assign permissions, and apply column masking → commented configuration script as an example. OUTPUT: access control policy with implementation guide in Markdown, permission matrix, and example SQL script. EDGE CASES: (a) automated process (dbt or Airflow pipeline) → create service accounts with write-only permissions on the target schema and read-only on source schemas, never human roles; (b) temporary user (external consultant) → temporary role with expiration date and access to masked data; (c) user with multiple roles across different domains → assign secondary roles with explicit scoping to prevent privilege escalation. [C · CRITERIA] The permission matrix has no blank cells or roles with access to everything; the request and review processes have defined SLAs; the SQL script is executable without additional modifications as a starting point; the policy satisfies a compliance audit trail; DoD: a new engineer can be provisioned with the correct permissions in less than one business day using only this policy. Protocolo MetodologIA: label with [CONFIG] every Snowflake-specific technical configuration and with [ASSUMPTION] every permission assigned without confirmation from the domain Data Owner.
spec-datos_gobierno_retencion_ciclo_vida: [S · SITUATION] An organization that accumulates data in data lakes, data warehouses, and operational systems lacks a formal policy defining how long each type of data is retained, when it is archived, when it is deleted, and who approves these decisions. This absence generates unnecessary storage costs, legal risks from retaining data longer than necessary (especially PII), and risks of losing data that had to be preserved due to regulatory obligation. [P · REQUEST] Define a data retention and lifecycle policy: retention periods by data type and domain, lifecycle states, archival and deletion criteria and processes, and technical configuration in the storage stack — delivered as an implementable formal policy. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior data governance and regulatory compliance specialist with experience designing retention policies that balance legal, regulatory, operational, and cost requirements on modern data platforms (AWS S3, Snowflake, Azure Data Lake). ASSUMPTIONS: if applicable regulations are not specified, assume GDPR/LGPD (5-year maximum for PII without business justification plus the 90-day grace period for deletion) and accounting regulations (7 years for financial documents); if the storage stack is not specified, assume AWS S3 (object storage) + Snowflake (data warehouse); if the data inventory is not indicated, assume categories: customer PII, financial transactions, system logs, employee data, marketing data, and product data; declare assumptions upfront; ask only if there are sector-specific regulations with very specific non-standard retention periods (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: inventory of data categories with applicable regulations and operational retention needs, pasted in chat; optionally existing retention policies. STEPS: 1. Design the data lifecycle state taxonomy: Active → Inactive → Archived → Deleted → with definition and transition criteria → state diagram. 2. Define retention periods by data category: PII, financial, operational, logs, marketing, employees → retention table with active period, archived period, regulatory or operational justification, and legal basis. 3. Design transition processes: who approves archival, who approves deletion, how deletion is documented (certificate of destruction) → process flows with responsible parties and SLA. 4. Specify the technical implementation in AWS S3: lifecycle policies (Standard → IA → Glacier → deletion) with days configuration → configuration table by bucket/prefix and S3 policy script. 5. Specify the technical implementation in Snowflake: Time Travel, Fail-safe, Dynamic Data Masking, WHERE clauses for date partitions → configuration guide with examples. 6. Design the retention compliance audit process: how to verify data was correctly deleted, deletion records, periodic reports → quarterly audit checklist with required evidence. OUTPUT: retention policy in Markdown with six sections, period table, configuration scripts, and audit checklist. EDGE CASES: (a) data subject to active litigation or investigation → apply legal hold that suspends the normal lifecycle until the process is resolved; (b) data under multiple regulations with conflicting periods → retain the longest period and document the justification; (c) data in offline backup or tape → include the backup deletion process as part of the complete deletion process. [C · CRITERIA] Every retention period has a cited legal or operational justification; configuration scripts are executable without modification as a starting point; the deletion process generates auditable evidence; the policy covers 100% of the organization's data categories; DoD: the storage team can configure the automatic lifecycle and the DPO can use the policy to respond to right-to-erasure requests. Protocolo MetodologIA: label with [DOC] every retention period based on specific regulation and with [ASSUMPTION] every period based on assumed business practice.
spec-datos_gobierno_data_mesh_dominios:
[S · SITUATION] An organization with multiple business lines generates data in departmental silos; the central data team is a bottleneck and the business domains do not have clear ownership over their data. It is necessary to design a federated governance model inspired by Data Mesh that defines data domains, their owners, contracts, and the shared global standards.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a federated governance design document that includes: (1) catalog of identified data domains with their domain owner, (2) data contract template per domain (schema, SLA, quality, access), (3) RACI responsibility matrix between domains and central platform, (4) mandatory global standards (security, PII, minimum quality), (5) three-phase implementation roadmap.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Architect specialized in Data Mesh, with experience in multi-domain organizations and federated governance.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the sector is not specified, assume manufacturing or retail with 4-8 typical domains (Sales, Logistics, Finance, Product, Customers, Operations); if no technological platform is indicated, assume a cloud-agnostic stack with data catalog capabilities (DataHub, Collibra, or similar). Declare adopted assumptions. Ask only if there are specific regulatory constraints (GDPR, financial data) or a very atypical number of domains (fewer than 2 or more than 15).
INPUTS: Paste business description, business lines, existing source systems, and known constraints.
STEPS:
  1. Identify and name data domains with justification (output: domain list + delimitation criteria).
  2. Define ownership structure per domain: data product owner, technical steward, primary consumers (output: role table per domain).
  3. Design data contract template: data product name, public schema, availability SLA, access policy, PII classification, minimum quality metrics (output: reusable YAML template or table).
  4. Build RACI matrix for key decisions: schema definition, breaking changes, quality incidents, sensitive data access (output: RACI table).
  5. List non-negotiable global standards: identifier format, PII handling, retention, mandatory lineage (output: global policies section).
  6. Trace three-phase roadmap (Foundation, Expansion, Optimization) with milestones, dependencies, and advancement criteria (output: phase table with estimated timeline).
OUTPUT: Structured Markdown document with six numbered sections; tables for RACI and contract template; half-page executive summary at the beginning.
EDGE CASES:
  - Very small domain (1-2 people): merge with adjacent domain and document the decision.
  - Cross-cutting data (MDM, shared customers): create a master data domain with special governance.
  - Cultural resistance to ownership: include in the roadmap a two-step change management plan.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each domain has a named owner, a contract with schema and SLA, and appears in the RACI.
Trade-off: domain autonomy vs. global consistency — prioritize interoperability in identifiers and PII classification over internal schema freedom.
DoD: document reviewable by a CDO with no open questions about responsibilities; roadmap actionable in a 2-week sprint.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Ontology-first → design based on business evidence → actionable deliverable with no ownership ambiguity.
spec-datos_gobierno_madurez_evaluacion:
[S · SITUATION] An organization wants to understand at what maturity level its data governance and analytics capabilities are before launching a transformation initiative. No formal prior assessment exists; maturity perceptions vary between technical and business teams.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a data governance and analytics maturity assessment report that includes: (1) diagnosis by dimension with a 1-5 score and evidence, (2) maturity heatmap, (3) gap between current state and target state, (4) top 5 initiatives prioritized by impact/effort, (5) 12-month roadmap.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior data governance consultant with expertise in DMBOK, DAMA, and maturity models such as DCAM or CMM adapted to data.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no maturity model is specified, use five standard dimensions: Strategy and Governance, Data Quality, Architecture and Management, Analytics and Use, Culture and Competencies. Default target state: level 3 (Defined) across all dimensions within 12 months. If there is no quantitative evidence, work with declared qualitative evidence and mark with [ASSUMPTION]. Ask only if the sector has very specific data regulations that would change the dimensions (e.g. banking, health).
INPUTS: Paste questionnaire diagnosis answers, summarized interviews, or free description of the current state by area.
STEPS:
  1. Map the received information to the five maturity dimensions (output: evidence table per dimension).
  2. Score each dimension on a 1-5 scale with evidence-based justification (output: maturity scorecard).
  3. Build a visual heatmap in text (table with descriptive colors: Red/Yellow/Green) (output: maturity heatmap).
  4. Define target state per dimension and calculate the gap (output: gap table with delta per dimension).
  5. Generate a long list of initiatives per dimension and prioritize the top 5 with an impact/effort matrix (output: prioritized table with justification).
  6. Build a 12-month roadmap with quarterly milestones (output: Q1-Q4 roadmap table).
OUTPUT: Structured Markdown report; scorecard as a table; heatmap as a table with descriptive cells; roadmap by quarter.
EDGE CASES:
  - Very scarce information: assign score 1 (Initial) as a conservative baseline and mark maximum gaps.
  - Organization with very heterogeneous units: score by unit and average with a dispersion note.
  - Very high declared maturity without evidence: flag discrepancy and suggest validation with a data audit.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each dimension has a score, evidence, and quantified gap; the top 5 initiatives have explicit prioritization criteria.
Trade-off: diagnosis thoroughness vs. speed to action — prioritize clarity on the two most critical dimensions for the business objective.
DoD: report presentable to a steering committee with conclusions in less than one executive page; roadmap with suggested dates and owners.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Evidence-based diagnosis → quantified gap → prioritization by business impact.
spec-datos_gobierno_glosario_negocio:
[S · SITUATION] An organization detects that the same data terms have different definitions depending on the area using them (e.g. "active customer" means something different in Sales, Finance, and CRM), which generates inconsistent reports and conflicts between teams. It is necessary to build a formal business glossary that unifies definitions, identifies critical terms, and establishes a maintenance process.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a complete business glossary with: (1) master table of terms with canonical definition, domain owner, synonyms, related technical field, and usage example; (2) classification of terms by criticality (High/Medium/Low); (3) register of conflicting terms with proposed resolution; (4) governance process for additions, removals, and modifications of terms; (5) template in exportable format (Markdown or CSV).

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Steward or Data Governance Analyst with experience building business glossaries in tools such as Collibra, Alation, DataHub, or Confluence.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no terms are listed, infer the 15-20 most common for the indicated sector (e.g. Sales: customer, opportunity, revenue, conversion rate; Finance: recognized revenue, margin, accounting close). If no domain owner is named, assign the most logical business area. Ask only if there is highly specialized niche regulatory terminology (e.g. Basel III, medical HL7) that fundamentally changes the definitions.
INPUTS: Paste list of conflicting terms, existing glossary (if any), sector description, and business areas.
STEPS:
  1. Inventory received terms or infer initial list by sector (output: candidate term list).
  2. For each term: draft a clear canonical definition in business language (not technical), identify the domain owner, list synonyms and equivalent terms (output: draft table per term).
  3. Map each term to its main technical field or entity in the source systems (output: technical reference column in the table).
  4. Classify by criticality: High (impacting regulatory reports or executive KPIs), Medium (impacting operational decisions), Low (internal area use) (output: criticality column + justification).
  5. Identify definition conflicts between areas and propose resolution with suggested arbiter (output: conflict table with status).
  6. Define the governance process: roles (Owner, Steward, Approver), change request flow, review cadence (output: process section in Markdown).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with master table (Term | Definition | Domain Owner | Synonyms | Technical Field | Criticality | Usage Example), conflicts section, and governance process section. Include CSV-friendly version of the master table.
EDGE CASES:
  - Term with completely different definition in two areas: create two entries with domain prefix (e.g. "Customer [Sales]" vs "Customer [Finance]") and flag for executive resolution.
  - Technical term without a clear business equivalent: describe in functional language and flag for validation with area owner.
  - Outdated existing glossary: keep the original entry as "legacy version" and add a new canonical version.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each term has a unique definition, assigned owner, and concrete usage example; conflicts have a proposed resolution.
Trade-off: technical precision vs. business readability — prioritize that any business analyst understands the definition without needing additional technical documentation.
DoD: glossary importable into a data catalog tool; governance process approvable in a 30-minute meeting.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Ontology-first → canonical definitions with evidence trail → sustainable maintenance process.
spec-datos_warehouse_arquitectura_capas:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs to build or redesign its data warehouse to support reports, dashboards, and advanced analytics. Data comes from multiple source systems (ERP, CRM, operational databases) and must be available to business users with different access and latency needs.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a layered data warehouse architecture design document that includes: (1) descriptive diagram of the layers (Landing/Raw, Staging, Core/DWH, Data Marts, Serving); (2) responsibilities, technologies, and recommended patterns per layer; (3) definition of transformation zones and data lineage; (4) partitioning and versioning strategy; (5) design decisions with documented trade-offs.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Architect with experience designing modern data warehouses on cloud platforms (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no platform is specified, assume Snowflake as the reference with transferable principles. If no data volume is indicated, assume medium scale: 1-10 TB of data processed per day, dozens of sources. If no latency requirement is mentioned, assume batch analytics with daily update as the baseline, with near-real-time possibility at the serving layer. Declare assumptions. Ask only if there are data sovereignty constraints (mandatory on-premise) that fundamentally change the architecture.
INPUTS: Paste source system description, approximate volume, target BI tools, number of analytical users, and latency constraints.
STEPS:
  1. Define the appropriate number and name of layers for the context (output: text ASCII diagram or hierarchical layer description).
  2. For each layer: describe purpose, storage type, allowed transformations, latency, access, and recommended tools (output: per-layer table).
  3. Design the lineage flow from source to serving with quality checkpoints (output: textual flow diagram).
  4. Define partitioning strategy (by date, by domain, by size) and data versioning (SCD type 1/2/3 where applicable) (output: strategy section with examples).
  5. Document key design decisions with considered alternatives and trade-offs (output: simplified Architecture Decision Records table).
  6. List technical risks and mitigations (output: risk table).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with six sections; text diagrams; layer table; ADR table. Length: 800-1200 words of technical content.
EDGE CASES:
  - Source with unstructured data (logs, images): add a specialized processing sub-layer before Staging.
  - Strict real-time access requirement (< 5 min): include a parallel streaming path that feeds directly into the Serving layer.
  - Extreme cost constraint: collapse Landing and Staging layers into a single raw zone partitioned by ingestion date.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each layer has a single responsibility, assigned technology, and data advancement criteria between layers.
Trade-off: schema flexibility vs. query performance — in early layers prioritize flexibility (schema-on-read), in serving layers prioritize performance (schema-on-write).
DoD: document usable as a technical reference for an engineering team with no open questions about which layer stores which type of data.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Layered architecture with single responsibility → decisions documented with trade-offs → scalable design from day one.
spec-datos_warehouse_lakehouse_vs_dwh:
[S · SITUATION] An organization is evaluating which data storage architecture to adopt to support both traditional analytics (BI, reports) and modern workloads (ML, unstructured data, streaming). There is pressure to modernize but it is unclear whether a classic data warehouse, a data lake, or a lakehouse architecture is the right decision given their context.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a structured decision analysis that includes: (1) objective comparison of the three paradigms across key dimensions; (2) decision tree with weighted criteria; (3) justified recommendation for the specific context; (4) phased migration or adoption plan; (5) risks and conditions for reviewing the decision.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Solutions Architect with experience evaluating and migrating between storage paradigms: relational data warehouses, object-storage data lakes, and lakehouse platforms (Databricks, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, BigQuery Omni).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no current stack is specified, assume no consolidated data platform exists (greenfield). If no volume is mentioned, assume medium-high scale (10-100 TB). If there are no explicit ML requirements, assume they are a future aspiration, not an immediate requirement. Declare assumptions. Ask only if budget is the dominant constraint, as it significantly changes the recommendation.
INPUTS: Paste description of the current state, types of analytical workloads, available teams (data engineers, data scientists), current technology stack, and 3-year business objectives.
STEPS:
  1. Build a three-column comparative table (DWH / Data Lake / Lakehouse) by dimensions: schema, supported workloads, latency, cost, tool maturity, learning curve, ideal use cases (output: comparative table).
  2. Design a textual decision tree with weighted questions: Is ML a current or future requirement? Is data primarily structured? Does the team master SQL vs Python? Does the budget favor managed services? (output: decision tree with paths).
  3. Apply the tree to the user's specific context and arrive at a clear recommendation with justification (output: recommendation section with evidence).
  4. Design a three-phase adoption plan with milestones, specific tools, and advancement criteria (output: phase table).
  5. List the five main risks of the decision and the conditions that would justify revisiting it in the future (output: risk table and review triggers).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with comparative table, decision tree, recommendation with justification, phase plan, and risk table. Length: 700-1000 words.
EDGE CASES:
  - SQL-only team without Python: recommend modern DWH with native lakehouse capabilities (Snowflake, BigQuery) before a Spark-based platform.
  - Regulated data with strict access requirements: prioritize DWH with granular RBAC over object-access data lake.
  - Very limited budget: evaluate open-source options (DuckDB + Parquet, Apache Iceberg on S3) as a pragmatic alternative.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the recommendation is specific (platform name or pattern), has at least three justifications based on the context, and the adoption plan has time-bound milestones.
Trade-off: flexibility/modernity (lakehouse) vs. simplicity/operational maturity (DWH) — the recommendation must explicitly state which is prioritized and why in this context.
DoD: document that allows a Technical Committee to make the decision in a 60-minute session without needing additional information.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Decision based on real context → explicit tree with weights → actionable recommendation with adoption plan.
spec-datos_warehouse_modelado_kimball_in:
[S · SITUATION] A data engineering team must choose between Kimball's dimensional modeling approach (star schema, data marts first) and Inmon's enterprise integration approach (normalized 3NF, single EDW) for the design of their organization's data warehouse. The decision has a direct impact on delivery speed, query performance, and long-term maintainability.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a modeling approach selection document that includes: (1) technical description of both approaches with their modern variants; (2) comparative table by key criteria; (3) contextualized decision tree; (4) justified recommendation with example design for the given context; (5) five-step initial implementation guide.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Architect specialized in data warehouse modeling, with hands-on experience in Kimball and Inmon implementations, and knowledge of modern hybrid approaches (Data Vault 2.0, Anchor Modeling).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no dominant use case is specified, assume sales and finance analytics as the main scenario. If no team profile is indicated, assume three data engineers with intermediate-to-advanced SQL proficiency. If there is no explicit requirement of delivery agility vs. enterprise consistency, prioritize fast value delivery as the first criterion. Declare assumptions. Ask only if there is a regulatory requirement that mandates a single audited enterprise source of truth (e.g. Basel III).
INPUTS: Paste description of the main analytical use case, number and complexity of business processes to model, team profile, and expected first delivery timeline.
STEPS:
  1. Describe Kimball (star/snowflake schema, facts and dimensions, conformed dimensions) and its modern variants, then Inmon (3NF, ODS, EDW, derived data marts) and Data Vault as a hybrid alternative (output: technical comparative section).
  2. Build comparative table by: initial delivery speed, analytical query performance, ease of maintenance, support for business changes, enterprise integration, team learning curve (output: table with score and notes).
  3. Design decision tree: Does the team master dimensional SQL? Are data marts the first deliverable? Is an audited corporate EDW required? Does the business change frequently? (output: decision tree with paths).
  4. Apply the tree to the context and recommend an approach with justification; design a minimal example schema (2-3 fact tables, 4-5 dimensions) for the indicated use case (output: recommendation + example schema in text).
  5. List five initial implementation steps with a completeness criterion per step (output: numbered step list).
OUTPUT: Structured Markdown document with five sections; tables and tree in text; example schema with table and key column names.
EDGE CASES:
  - Organization with very heterogeneous business units: evaluate Data Vault 2.0 as an alternative combining Inmon integration with Kimball agility.
  - New team without dimensional modeling experience: prefer Kimball with simplified star schema over Inmon to reduce the initial learning curve.
  - Migration from existing model: inventory the current model before recommending, to assess refactoring cost.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the recommendation names the approach, justifies with at least three context-based criteria, and the example schema is concrete (real domain table names).
Trade-off: data mart delivery speed (Kimball) vs. long-term enterprise consistency and integration (Inmon) — the recommendation must explicitly state which is prioritized and why.
DoD: document that allows the engineering team to begin modeling in the following week without needing another design session.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Technical decision with explicit tree → concrete domain example → actionable five-step implementation.
spec-datos_warehouse_capa_servicio_bi:
[S · SITUATION] An organization has a data warehouse with consolidated transformation layers, but business users and BI tools access internal tables with complex schemas directly, which generates slow queries, inconsistencies between reports, and high engineering dependency for any change. A serving layer needs to be designed to abstract the complexity and optimize access for different consumer profiles.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a serving layer design document that includes: (1) object catalog for the layer (views, aggregated tables, semantic layer, APIs); (2) organization strategy by audience and use case; (3) access and security policies by profile; (4) performance strategy (materialization, indexes, caching); (5) stability contract with consumers.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior BI and Data Architect with experience designing serving layers on modern platforms (Snowflake, dbt, LookML, dbt Semantic Layer, Cube.dev, certified Power BI datasets).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no BI tool is specified, assume Power BI or Tableau as primary destinations. If no consumer profile is described, assume three standard profiles: business analyst (basic or no SQL), data scientist (advanced Python/SQL), and external system (API/connector). If there is no performance information, assume queries of up to 10 million records with a response expectation under 10 seconds. Declare assumptions. Ask only if there are specific RLS (Row Level Security) requirements that affect the view design.
INPUTS: Paste description of the existing data model (current layers), BI tools and consumers, most-queried KPIs or metrics, and current performance or access problems.
STEPS:
  1. Map consumer profiles and their access needs: frequency, granularity, expected metrics (output: consumer profile table).
  2. Design the serving layer object catalog: denormalized views for BI, pre-calculated aggregated tables for executive KPIs, API exposure for external systems (output: object table with type, description, and audience).
  3. Define access and security strategy: database roles, RLS by sensitive dimension, PII data masking (output: access matrix by profile and object).
  4. Design performance strategy: which objects are materialized vs. calculated in real time, clustering/index strategy, caching policy (output: performance strategy table by object).
  5. Draft stability contract: which fields are part of the public interface, deprecation policy, breaking change notification process (output: service contract section in Markdown).
  6. Define serving layer health metrics: average response time, usage rate by object, failure frequency (output: operational KPI table for the layer).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with six sections; object table; access matrix; performance table; contract section. Include a sample SQL view for the most-queried KPI.
EDGE CASES:
  - KPI calculated with very complex logic: materialize in a calculated table with a scheduled update process instead of a view.
  - External consumer without SQL capability: design a REST API or data endpoint with service authentication.
  - Data with strict privacy requirements (PII): implement dynamic data masking and RLS before exposing to any serving layer.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each object has a defined audience, update strategy, and access policy; the contract specifies the deprecation process.
Trade-off: performance by materialization (storage and processing cost) vs. data freshness (latency cost) — document the decision by KPI type.
DoD: a business analyst can connect their BI tool to the serving layer and build a report without engineering assistance in the first session.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Abstraction by audience → performance guaranteed by contract → consumer autonomy without engineering dependency.
spec-datos_warehouse_real_time_analytics:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs real-time or near-real-time analytics capabilities for use cases such as fraud detection, operational monitoring, live personalization, or business alerts. The current batch architecture does not satisfy the required latency (seconds to minutes) and an architecture must be designed that processes continuous events without abandoning historical analytical capabilities.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a real-time analytics architecture document that includes: (1) architecture diagram with key components; (2) selection and justification of technologies for ingestion, processing, and serving; (3) integration patterns with the historical data warehouse (Lambda or Kappa architecture); (4) consistency guarantees and fault tolerance strategy; (5) operational cost estimation and scaling criteria.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Data Architect specialized in streaming and real-time analytics, with experience in Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, Spark Structured Streaming, ksqlDB, Kinesis, Pub/Sub, and HTAP analytical platforms (ClickHouse, Apache Druid, Pinot).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no cloud platform is specified, assume AWS or cloud-agnostic with alternatives across the three main providers. If no required latency is indicated, assume near-real-time (1-5 minutes as the objective, 30 seconds as the aspiration). If no event volume is described, assume 10,000-100,000 events per second at peak. Declare assumptions. Ask only if the use case requires strict transactional consistency (ACID) over real-time data, as it fundamentally changes the technology choice.
INPUTS: Paste description of the real-time use case (what the business needs to know and in what timeframe), event sources (transactional systems, IoT, logs), estimated event volume, and latency constraints.
STEPS:
  1. Define the real-time use case with latency SLA, data granularity, and query profile (output: requirements section with SLA).
  2. Design the layered architecture diagram: Sources → Ingestion/Broker → Stream Processing → Hot Analytical Storage → Serving/API → Consumers (output: ASCII text or descriptive diagram with arrows).
  3. Select and justify technologies for each layer with alternatives (output: component table with primary technology, alternative, and justification).
  4. Design integration with the historical data warehouse: Lambda pattern (separate batch + stream processing with serving-layer join) vs. Kappa (stream only, history rehydrated from log) — recommend with justification (output: historical integration section).
  5. Define guarantee strategy: exactly-once vs at-least-once, late event handling, time windows (tumbling, sliding, session), and failure recovery (output: guarantees section).
  6. Estimate monthly operational costs for the indicated volume and define horizontal scaling criteria (output: cost estimation table [ASSUMPTION] with variability note).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with six sections; textual architecture diagram; technology table; historical integration section; estimated cost table with assumption disclaimer.
EDGE CASES:
  - Frequently out-of-order events (IoT, sensors): implement windows with configurable watermark and late data discard policy past a threshold.
  - Historical drill-down requirement over streaming data: implement dual materialization in hot storage (Druid/Pinot) and historical storage (DWH/Lakehouse).
  - Very limited budget: evaluate simplified architecture with Kafka + ClickHouse as a cost-effective solution vs. Kinesis + Redshift.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the diagram has all components named with assigned technology; the latency SLA is defined with tolerance; historical integration has an explicit pattern.
Trade-off: minimum latency (Kappa with hot storage) vs. separation of concerns and operability (Lambda with consolidated batch) — the recommendation justifies the choice for this context.
DoD: document that allows a data engineering team to present the architecture to their CTO in a 45-minute session and begin the prototype within two weeks.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Latency SLA as first constraint → event-driven architecture → explicit integration with historical data.
spec-datos_warehouse_reverse_etl:
[S · SITUATION] An organization has enriched data, customer segments, and calculated metrics in its data warehouse, but marketing, sales, and operations teams continue using operational tools (CRM, email marketing tools, support platforms) with outdated data or without the metrics calculated by the data team. A Reverse ETL flow is needed to reliably and consistently bring warehouse data back to operational tools.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a Reverse ETL design document that includes: (1) flow map: what data leaves the warehouse to which tools and at what frequency; (2) Reverse ETL tool selection and justification; (3) design of the activation models layer; (4) incremental synchronization strategy and change management; (5) quality, reconciliation, and observability policies.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Engineer specialized in data activation pipelines and Reverse ETL, with experience in tools such as Census, Hightouch, Polytomic, and with activation models in dbt.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the Reverse ETL tool is not specified, evaluate and recommend among Census, Hightouch, and a custom solution with Airflow/Python based on the context. If the synchronization frequency is not indicated, assume hourly synchronization as a baseline with near-real-time option for critical cases. If destination tools are not listed, assume CRM (Salesforce or HubSpot) and email marketing tool (Brevo, Klaviyo or similar) as primary destinations. Declare assumptions. Ask only if there are API restrictions (rate limits, per-call costs) that fundamentally change the approach.
INPUTS: Paste the list of destination operational tools, data or segments to synchronize, desired update frequency, and the current warehouse data model.
STEPS:
  1. Map the activation flows: for each destination, which warehouse object is synchronized, which fields, at what frequency, and under what update condition (output: activation flow table).
  2. Evaluate and select Reverse ETL tool with a criteria comparison: compatibility with destinations, incremental support, observability, cost, ease of configuration (output: comparison table + recommendation).
  3. Design the activation models: dbt views or models prepared for synchronization, with universal identifier column, last-modified timestamp, and segmentation fields (output: activation model schema with example SQL).
  4. Design the incremental synchronization strategy: change detection (CDC vs timestamp vs hash), deletion handling (soft delete vs hard delete at destination), deduplication by universal identifier (output: incremental strategy section).
  5. Define quality and observability policies: validations before synchronizing, alerts for failures or rejected records, periodic reconciliation between warehouse and destination, synchronization audit log (output: table of policies and observability metrics).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with five sections; flow table; tool comparison table; example activation model SQL schema; observability table.
EDGE CASES:
  - Destination tool with no standardized API: design synchronization via CSV+SFTP file export as fallback.
  - Very high volume of records (millions of rows): implement incremental synchronization in batches with configurable time window to avoid overloading the destination API.
  - Update conflict: the CRM has more recent data than the warehouse in some fields — define merge policy with explicit precedence field.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each flow has a defined frequency, activation condition, and owner; activation models have a universal identifier and change timestamp.
Trade-off: freshness of data in operational tools (frequent synchronization) vs. load on destination system APIs (rate limits) — document the balance chosen per flow.
DoD: a data team can implement the first Reverse ETL flow in less than one week using this document as a guide.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Data activation oriented to the operational use case → reliable incremental synchronization → observability from day one.
spec-datos_warehouse_feature_store:
[S · SITUATION] A data science or ML Engineering team needs to design a feature store that centralizes the creation, storage, and serving of features for machine learning models, eliminating the duplication of transformation logic across notebooks, training pipelines, and production inference systems.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a feature store design document that includes: (1) architecture with offline and online storage; (2) feature catalog with schema and metadata; (3) feature creation, registration, and versioning process; (4) offline-online synchronization strategy; (5) integration with training and inference pipelines; (6) feature governance policies.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior ML Engineer or Data Architect with specialization in feature stores and MLOps, with experience in Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks, Vertex AI Feature Store, or custom implementations on Snowflake/Redis/DynamoDB.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the platform is not specified, evaluate Feast (open-source) vs Hopsworks vs managed solution based on the context. If inference scale is not indicated, assume batch and online inference with serving latency < 50ms for hot features. If there is no information about the team, assume a team of 2-5 data scientists supported by 1-2 data engineers. Declare assumptions. Ask only if there are differential privacy or regulatory compliance requirements on the features that change the storage architecture.
INPUTS: Paste description of current or planned ML models, required feature types (temporal aggregations, entity features, session features), inference scale, and the team's technology stack.
STEPS:
  1. Define the storage architecture: offline store (for training, historical) vs. online store (for real-time inference, low latency) with specific technologies for each (output: textual architecture diagram with two layers).
  2. Design the feature catalog: for each feature, name, associated entity (user, product, session), transformation type, aggregation period, data source, owner, freshness SLA, usage tags (output: example feature catalog table with 8-12 representative features).
  3. Define the lifecycle process: creation (who can create them, in which repository), quality review, catalog registration, semantic versioning, deprecation (output: process diagram and versioning policy).
  4. Design the offline-online synchronization strategy: which features are materialized in the online store, at what frequency, how consistency between training and inference is guaranteed (training-serving skew) (output: synchronization strategy section).
  5. Define integration interfaces: how a data scientist consumes features for training (historical point), how the inference system serves features in real time (output: Python/SQL integration code examples).
  6. Establish governance policies: who can register features, approval process, feature lineage to source data, usage audit (output: feature governance section).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with six sections; textual architecture diagram; feature catalog table; integration code examples; governance section.
EDGE CASES:
  - Feature with very expensive computation (1-year temporal window): pre-calculate in offline store with daily scheduled materialization and do not include in online store.
  - Detected training-serving skew: implement automated validation that compares the distribution of features in training vs. inference in production.
  - Small team without capacity to operate complex infrastructure: recommend managed solution (Vertex AI Feature Store, Databricks Feature Store) over custom implementation.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the catalog has at least 8 features with all metadata; the synchronization strategy defines the frequency and consistency mechanism; code examples are executable.
Trade-off: operational complexity of a full feature store (Feast/Tecton) vs. simplified solutions (tables in warehouse + snapshots) — the recommendation must justify the investment level based on team maturity.
DoD: a data scientist can start creating and consuming features in the store in their first week using this document.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Training-inference consistency as the guiding principle → catalog as single source of truth → governance that scales with the team.
spec-datos_warehouse_estimacion_capacida:
[S · SITUATION] An architecture or finance team needs to estimate the storage capacity, operating cost, and growth projection of a data warehouse or analytical data platform for the next 1-3 years. The estimate must support budget decisions, service tier selection, and cloud provider negotiations.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a capacity and cost estimation report that includes: (1) inventory of sources and current volumes; (2) growth model with projections at 12, 24, and 36 months; (3) cost estimate broken down by component (storage, compute, data transfer, licenses); (4) optimization scenarios with their cost impact; (5) tier and configuration recommendations per usage scenario.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Data Architect or FinOps Analyst with experience in cost estimation for cloud data platforms (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks) and in analytical cost optimization.
ASSUMPTIONS: All monetary estimates are marked with [ASSUMPTION] and are based on the indicated provider's public on-demand prices without contract discounts. If the provider is not indicated, use Snowflake as a reference with Enterprise edition pricing in the us-east-1 region. If the current volume is not specified, assume a starting point of 1 TB of compressed data in the warehouse. The default growth rate is 40% annually if none is indicated. Declare all assumptions. Ask only if there are existing contractual commitments with the provider that change the cost model.
INPUTS: Paste the data source inventory (name, type, current volume in GB/TB), number of concurrent users, query frequency, and processing pipeline (batch, streaming, frequency).
STEPS:
  1. Build the current data inventory: for each source, calculate raw volume and estimated compressed volume in warehouse (default 3:1 compression ratio for tabular data) (output: inventory table with volumes).
  2. Apply growth model: project stored volume at 12, 24, and 36 months with the indicated growth rate; include pessimistic (+60%) and optimistic (+20%) scenarios (output: projections table with three scenarios).
  3. Estimate costs by component: storage ($ per TB/month), compute (credits or compute hours per workload), data transfer, complementary tool licenses (dbt, Fivetran, etc.) [ASSUMPTION on all values] (output: cost table broken down by year).
  4. Identify three optimization scenarios: additional compression, intelligent partitioning, storage and compute separation, reserved capacity agreements — calculate the estimated savings of each (output: optimizations table with estimated % savings [ASSUMPTION]).
  5. Recommend platform tier and configuration per growth scenario: warehouse size, auto-suspend policy, workload separation (output: configuration recommendations table per scenario).
OUTPUT: Markdown report with five sections; all monetary figures in USD with disclaimer note; projections table with textual chart; optimizations table. Visible note at the beginning: "All estimates are indicative, based on public on-demand prices, and must be validated with the provider."
EDGE CASES:
  - Unstructured data (images, video, audio) as part of the inventory: estimate separately with cold storage tier (S3 Glacier, GCS Archive) and do not include in the warehouse compute.
  - Very pronounced seasonal usage peaks: design a variable cost model with separation between base load and peak load; evaluate serverless vs. dedicated warehouse.
  - Cloud provider change under consideration: add a comparative TCO analysis section between two providers [ASSUMPTION on both estimates].

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: each figure has a reference source or [ASSUMPTION] mark; projections have three scenarios; optimizations have an estimated savings percentage.
Trade-off: estimation accuracy vs. delivery speed — prioritize the correct order of magnitude with explicit ranges over precise figures without basis.
DoD: report presentable to a CFO or budget committee that allows approving or rejecting the investment without requesting additional information.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Estimation with explicit ranges and assumptions → optimizations prioritized by ROI → budget decision with evidence.
spec-datos_avanzado_forecasting_demanda:
[S · SITUATION] An analytics or data science team needs to build a demand forecasting model based on time series to support inventory, production, or budget decisions. Historical demand data is available but no formal forecasting process exists; current projections are made manually using linear trends or moving averages without capturing seasonality or external variables.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a technical implementation plan for the forecasting model that includes: (1) exploratory analysis of the time series (trend, seasonality, noise); (2) selection and justification of the modeling approach; (3) data pipeline and features design; (4) model evaluation and validation strategy; (5) production deployment plan and drift monitoring.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Data Scientist specialized in time series and forecasting, with experience in statistical models (ARIMA, SARIMA, ETS), ML models for forecasting (Prophet, LightGBM with temporal features, N-BEATS), and MLOps frameworks for production time series models.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the tool is not specified, use Python with Prophet as the base model and LightGBM with temporal features as the higher-performance alternative. If temporal granularity is not indicated, assume weekly forecasting with a 12-week horizon. If there is no information about external variables, assume that only historical demand data is available as input. If the number of series to forecast is not mentioned, assume between 50 and 500 SKUs or units of analysis. Declare assumptions. Ask only if the forecast horizon is greater than 6 months, as that fundamentally changes the model selection.
INPUTS: Paste description of historical data (granularity, temporal coverage, format), target variable (demand of which entity: SKU, store, customer), available external variables (price, promotions, weather, holidays), and business metric for evaluating the forecasting.
STEPS:
  1. Design the series exploratory analysis: trend and seasonality charts, STL decomposition, autocorrelation analysis (ACF/PACF), outlier and missing data detection (output: analysis checklist with example Python code per step).
  2. Select the modeling approach with justification: evaluate classical statistical models (SARIMA), probabilistic models (Prophet), ML models with temporal features (LightGBM/XGBoost), deep learning models (N-BEATS, TFT) based on series volume, horizon, and available data (output: approach comparison table with recommendation).
  3. Design the features pipeline: temporal features (day of week, month, quarter, holidays), lag features (demand N periods ago), rolling window features (mean, deviation in 4/8/12-week window), available external features (output: features table with name, type, and example calculation code).
  4. Design the evaluation strategy: walk-forward validation with multiple windows, error metrics (MAPE, RMSE, SMAPE, forecast bias), benchmark against naive model (historical average) (output: evaluation schema with walk-forward validation code).
  5. Design the production plan: retraining frequency, pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Prefect), forecast storage, forecast serving API, statistical drift monitoring (PSI, distribution test) and degradation alerts (output: production pipeline diagram and monitoring table).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with five sections; exploratory analysis checklist; model comparison table; features table with Python example code; evaluation schema; production pipeline diagram.
EDGE CASES:
  - Series with very little historical data (< 2 years): prioritize models with few parameters (ETS, Prophet) over ML models that require more data.
  - Many series with heterogeneous patterns: implement hierarchical forecasting or series clustering before training models by group.
  - Frequent or irregular missing data: implement seasonality-based imputation before modeling and document the imputation policy.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the plan has executable Python code for at least two steps; the evaluation metric is defined before training the model; the production pipeline has retraining frequency and drift alert criterion.
Trade-off: model interpretability (SARIMA, Prophet) vs. predictive performance (LightGBM, N-BEATS) — the recommendation must align the choice with the team's capabilities and the business's explainability requirement.
DoD: a data scientist can run the exploratory analysis and a baseline model in the first two days using this plan as a guide.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Exploratory analysis first → simplest model that works → production with drift monitoring from the start.
spec-liderazgo_one_on_one_agenda_colabor:
[S · SITUATION] A team leader holds periodic 1:1 meetings (weekly or biweekly) with each direct report. Meetings often lose relevance because the leader imposes the agenda unilaterally, reducing the contributor's engagement and openness. A structure is needed that distributes ownership of the space between both parties.

[P · REQUEST] Co-constructed 1:1 agenda template ready to use, with sections for the contributor and the leader, space for tracking previous commitments, and a shared priority field, exportable as an editable document.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior specialist in leadership conversation design and high-performance team development.
ASSUMPTIONS: 45-60 minute meeting; plain text format compatible with Notion/Confluence; if the sector is unknown, assume technology/services; proceed declaring assumptions if confidence ≥ 0.85.
INPUTS: Paste here the team context, desired frequency, and any recurring topic you want to include (or leave blank for generic version).
STEPS:
1. Define proportional time blocks (contributor ≥ 60% of the time).
2. Draft the opening section with a temperature-check question.
3. Create the contributor's block: own topics, blockers, wins.
4. Create the leader's block: organizational context, feedback, follow-up.
5. Design closing with SMART commitments and review date field.
6. Add instructional note on how to prepare the agenda before each session.
OUTPUT: Agenda document with header, 5 numbered sections, commitment table (who / what / when), and usage note.
EDGE CASES:
- Only a 20-minute meeting: reduce to 3 sections and remove organizational context.
- Very reserved contributor: add suggested open questions in each block.
- First 1:1: replace commitment tracking with a mutual expectations section.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the agenda can be filled in independently by both parties before the meeting; each section has a visible usage instruction.
Trade-off: simplicity > exhaustiveness; better for a field to be missing than for the agenda to be intimidating.
DoD: at least 3 sections with explicit owner (contributor/leader/both), functional commitment table, preparatory note.

Protocolo MetodologIA: delivery in Spanish, without unnecessary jargon, with sections clearly labeled by owner.
spec-liderazgo_one_on_one_primer_encuent:
[S · SITUATION] A leader has just onboarded a new direct report (either through external hiring or internal transfer). They have the first 1:1 scheduled in the coming days and want to use that meeting to build trust, understand mutual expectations, and lay the foundations of a productive relationship, without falling into an interrogation or a monologue.

[P · REQUEST] Structured script for the first 1:1 with a new report: opening, key questions to get to know the person, communication of leadership style, expectations agreement, and closing with concrete commitments. Target duration: 60 minutes.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior executive coach specialized in leader onboarding and building relationships in corporate environments.
ASSUMPTIONS: Technology or professional services company context; new report with 0-30 days in the role; leader with average experience in formal 1:1s; proceed declaring assumptions if confidence ≥ 0.85.
INPUTS: Paste the new report's name/role and team context here, or leave blank for a generic version.
STEPS:
1. Draft a warm opening (2-3 sentences) that establishes the tone of psychological safety.
2. Design the mutual knowledge block: 4-5 open questions about trajectory, motivations, and preferred work style.
3. Create the leader transparency block: communicate style, availability, how to give and receive feedback.
4. Design the expectations block: what the leader expects in the first 30/60/90 days and what the contributor needs to succeed.
5. Draft closing with 2-3 concrete commitments from the leader to the contributor.
6. Add margin notes with facilitation tips (suggested time per block, what to avoid).
OUTPUT: Script with 5 blocks, suggested timings, formulated questions, facilitation notes, and final commitment table.
EDGE CASES:
- New report from a more senior hierarchical role: adjust tone to acknowledge their prior experience.
- Meeting reduced to 30 minutes: consolidate blocks 2 and 3, remove facilitation notes.
- Report with a history of poor relationships with previous leaders: add an explicit question about what has and has not worked in the past.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the script can be followed without additional preparation; each block has an assigned time that totals 60 minutes; questions are open and non-directive.
Trade-off: warmth > efficiency in this first session.
DoD: 5 complete blocks, at least 4 open questions, facilitation notes in each block, commitment table.

Protocolo MetodologIA: human and direct tone, neutral Latin American Spanish, facilitation notes in brackets.
spec-liderazgo_one_on_one_preguntas_skip:
[S · SITUATION] A director or area manager holds periodic skip-level meetings: individual conversations with people who report to their direct leaders, without those leaders present. The goal is to obtain direct signals about climate, blockers, and intermediate leadership effectiveness, without creating paranoia or undermining the authority of the direct leaders.

[P · REQUEST] Categorized bank of 20-25 questions for skip-level meetings, grouped by objective (team climate, direct leader effectiveness, operational blockers, development and growth, culture), with usage notes for each category.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior specialist in organizational design and team climate diagnosis in technology companies.
ASSUMPTIONS: Technology or services company with between 50 and 500 people; skip-level conducted by director/VP; contributors with 3+ months on the team; proceed declaring assumptions if confidence ≥ 0.85.
INPUTS: Paste here the organizational context, main reason for the skip-level, or warning signals you want to explore; or leave blank for a generic version.
STEPS:
1. Define 5 categories each with a clear objective.
2. Draft 4-5 open questions per category, ordered from least to most depth.
3. Add a usage note per category: when to prioritize, recommended tone, warning signals in the response.
4. Add an opening section (2 warm-up questions) and closing (1 closing question that leaves agency with the contributor).
5. Include a list of questions NOT to ask and why.
OUTPUT: Document with 5 categorized sections, 20-25 numbered questions, usage notes, opening/closing section, and prohibited questions list.
EDGE CASES:
- Contributor who has worked with the direct leader for less than 1 month: avoid questions about the leader's effectiveness; focus on expectations and first impressions.
- Signal of active conflict in the team: prioritize climate and blocker categories; omit development questions.
- Clearly uncomfortable contributor: step back to warm-up questions and offer to continue in another session.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: all questions are open; none induces a response about the direct leader; usage notes have at least one concrete warning signal.
Trade-off: diagnostic breadth > efficiency; better to have more questions than will be used in a single session.
DoD: 5 categories, 20+ questions, usage notes per category, prohibited section with at least 5 examples.

Protocolo MetodologIA: reusable bank, descriptively named categories, actionable usage notes in Spanish.
spec-liderazgo_one_on_one_check_in_estad:
[S · SITUATION] At the start of each 1:1, a leader wants to do a quick and authentic check-in of the contributor's emotional state and workload using the RAG model (Red/Amber/Green). Many leaders skip this step or do it superficially ('how are you?'), losing valuable information about the team's wellbeing and real capacity.

[P · REQUEST] 5-minute RAG check-in protocol for the start of a 1:1: question sequence, visual scale, signal interpretation guide, and facilitation decisions based on the color declared by the contributor.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior specialist in organizational wellbeing and leadership conversation facilitation with a focus on psychological safety.
ASSUMPTIONS: 1:1 meeting between 30 and 60 minutes; leader-contributor relationship with at least 2 weeks of history; check-in will take a maximum of 5 minutes; proceed declaring assumptions if confidence ≥ 0.85.
INPUTS: Paste team context, 1:1 frequency, or observed stress signals here; or leave blank for a generic version.
STEPS:
1. Define the RAG scale with concrete behavioral descriptors (not just colors).
2. Draft 2-3 check-in questions for each contributor openness level (high, medium, low).
3. Design the facilitator decision tree: what to do if the contributor declares Red, Amber, or Green.
4. Add a guide to non-verbal signals that contradict the declared color.
5. Include transition phrases to move from the check-in to the rest of the agenda based on the result.
OUTPUT: Protocol with descriptive RAG scale, 3 question sets (by openness), decision tree, non-verbal signals table, and transition phrases.
EDGE CASES:
- Contributor who always says Green even when showing signs of exhaustion: add an indirect calibration question.
- Contributor in Red with a personal crisis: decision tree includes option to suspend agenda and offer a containment space.
- First RAG check-in with this contributor: add instruction to present the model before applying it.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the protocol can be applied without additional preparation; the decision tree covers all 3 RAG colors; transition phrases sound natural.
Trade-off: authenticity > speed; if the contributor is in Red, the check-in may extend and that is acceptable.
DoD: RAG scale with descriptors, 3 question sets, complete decision tree, at least 4 non-verbal signals, 3 transition phrases.

Protocolo MetodologIA: practical tool in Spanish, visual decision tree with emojis or symbols if it aids readability.
spec-liderazgo_one_on_one_carrera_largo_:
[S · SITUATION] A leader wants to dedicate a specific 1:1 session to exploring a contributor's long-term professional aspirations: where they want to be in 3-5 years, what gaps they need to close, and what role the current team can play in that journey. This conversation is often avoided due to lack of structure or fear of generating expectations that cannot be met.

[P · REQUEST] Structured script for a long-term career conversation 1:1: exploration of aspirations, gap diagnosis, identification of opportunities in the current role, and agreement on concrete next steps. Duration: 60-75 minutes.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Corporate career coach with specialization in talent development in technology and services organizations.
ASSUMPTIONS: Contributor with 6+ months on the team; leader with authority to open project and learning opportunities (not necessarily to promise promotions); exploratory, non-evaluative conversation; proceed declaring assumptions if confidence ≥ 0.85.
INPUTS: Paste the contributor's name/role, team context, and any prior signals about their aspirations here; or leave blank for a generic version.
STEPS:
1. Design opening that establishes the exploratory (non-evaluative) purpose of the conversation.
2. Create aspirations block: 4-5 open questions about long-term vision, dream roles, and deep motivations.
3. Create gap diagnosis block: questions to identify skills, experiences, and networks the contributor recognizes as missing.
4. Create opportunities block in the current role: co-construct 2-3 concrete initiatives that close the gap without leaving the team.
5. Design closing with 90-day plan and quarterly review agreement.
6. Add facilitation notes: how to handle aspirations that seem unachievable or imply leaving the company.
OUTPUT: Script with 5 blocks, suggested timings, questions per block, opportunities table and 90-day plan, facilitation notes.
EDGE CASES:
- Contributor who doesn't know what they want long-term: add values and energizers exercise before the aspirations block.
- Aspiration that implies leaving the company in less than 1 year: handle honestly; the leader can still support from a place of transparency.
- Contributor who wants the leader's current role: manage without defensiveness; explore what specific skills of that role attract them.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the contributor leaves with at least 2 concrete next steps and a review date; the leader leaves with actionable information about the contributor's development.
Trade-off: depth > breadth; better to explore few aspirations in detail than to sweep many superficially.
DoD: 5 complete blocks, at least 4 aspirations questions, opportunities table with owner, 90-day plan, facilitation notes for the 3 edge cases.

Protocolo MetodologIA: development conversation script, Spanish, focus on contributor agency not on the leader as opportunity provider.
spec-liderazgo_one_on_one_notas_seguimie:
[S · SITUATION] After each 1:1, a leader has scattered notes in free text: discussed topics, verbal commitments, contributor concerns, and pending actions. Without a synthesis process, these inputs are lost before the next session, commitments are not fulfilled, and the contributor perceives that the conversation had no impact.

[P · REQUEST] Structured synthesis of raw 1:1 notes: executive summary of key topics, commitment table (who/what/when/status), follow-up points for the next session, and attention signals that the leader should monitor. Format ready to share with the contributor or archive.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Executive leadership assistant expert in managing team conversations and tracking organizational commitments.
ASSUMPTIONS: Free text notes in Spanish or Spanglish; 1:1 of 30-60 minutes; commitments can be from the leader, the contributor, or shared; if notes are ambiguous, infer and declare the assumption; proceed if confidence ≥ 0.85.
INPUTS: Paste the raw 1:1 notes here (free text, shorthand, unordered bullets, etc.).
STEPS:
1. Read the raw notes and identify: discussed topics, verbal commitments, mentioned emotions, and blockers.
2. Draft 3-5 bullet executive summary (key topics without internal jargon).
3. Build the commitment table with columns: Who / Commitment / Deadline / Status.
4. Draft the follow-up section for the next session (pending open questions, progress to verify).
5. Identify 1-2 attention signals (disengagement risks, systemic blockers, unresolved needs) with action recommendation.
6. Add next session date and time field.
OUTPUT: Structured document with: 3-5 bullet summary, commitment table, follow-up section, attention signals, and next session field. Ready to share.
EDGE CASES:
- Empty or very sparse notes: generate a blank template and request the 3 minimum data points: date, contributor name, and 1 discussed topic.
- Commitments without a date: assign a default date of 7 days and mark it as [ASSUMPTION] for validation.
- Sensitive topic detected in notes (resignation, interpersonal conflict): exclude from the shareable document and create a private section for the leader.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the commitment table has at least 1 row with owner and date; the document can be shared with the contributor without additional editing; attention signals have a recommended action.
Trade-off: clarity > exhaustiveness; the summary must be readable in 30 seconds.
