SUPUESTOS: if industry is not specified, assume B2B software company; if size is not mentioned, assume 8-15 person team; if culture is not described, infer high-performance, autonomy, and continuous learning culture — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: team description, recent achievements, tech stack, and values pasted in the chat; if missing, proceed with declared assumptions. PASOS: 1) Identify the team's unique differentiators from the inputs. 2) Draft the EVP focused on impact, growth, and culture. 3) Write the team description with an authentic voice, free of corporate clichés. 4) Create LinkedIn posts with an emotional hook and call to action. 5) Formulate interview questions that reveal genuine cultural alignment. SALIDA: structured document with four sections, each labeled and ready to copy-paste. CASOS BORDE: (a) new team with no track record — focus on vision and opportunity; (b) team with high turnover — omit phrases about stability and focus on accelerated learning; (c) company with no recognized brand — amplify the project and impact rather than the name. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: each piece can be read independently without additional context. Trade-off: authenticity > corporate polish. DoD: all four artifacts are complete, without placeholders, and in a consistent tone. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions before writing, use evidence from the input, and label each section.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_niveles_autori: [S · SITUATION] A leader delegating responsibilities to their team faces ambiguity: team members do not know how far they can decide on their own, what they must consult before acting, and what requires explicit approval. This creates excessive dependency or unauthorized decisions. [P · REQUEST] Produce a delegation matrix with explicit authority levels for a specific responsibility or area: (1) table with five authority levels (inform, recommend, decide with consultation, decide with notification, decide autonomously), (2) assignment of each key activity to the corresponding level, (3) 5-minute conversation guide to communicate the matrix to the team member. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Senior executive coach specializing in delegation structure design for technical and management team leaders. SUPUESTOS: if the area is not specified, assume software project management; if the team member's level is not mentioned, assume a professional with 2-4 years of experience; if activities are not listed, infer the five most common for the area — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: area or responsibility to delegate, list of key activities, and team member level pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1) List the key activities of the responsibility to delegate. 2) Assign each activity to one of the five authority levels with a brief justification. 3) Build the formatted table. 4) Draft the conversation guide with concrete, non-generic phrases. 5) Include an example of how to escalate if the team member exceeds their level. SALIDA: markdown table + conversation guide, both ready to use in a 1:1 meeting. CASOS BORDE: (a) new team member — use levels 1-3 only; (b) very senior team member — use levels 3-5 with emphasis on notification; (c) decisions with legal or financial impact — always minimum level 2. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: each activity has exactly one assigned level with justification. Trade-off: clarity > exhaustiveness. DoD: complete table with no empty cells and conversation guide with literal phrases. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, assign levels with evidence from context, deliver ready-to-use artifacts.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_matriz_eisenho: [S · SITUATION] A leader has a list of responsibilities and tasks they manage personally, but their time is limited and they need to prioritize which ones to retain, delegate, eliminate, and schedule. The absence of this analysis creates overload and bottlenecks in the team. [P · REQUEST] Apply the Eisenhower matrix (urgent-important) to the leader's task list and produce: (1) classification of each task in the four quadrants with a 1-sentence justification, (2) explicit action recommendation for each task (delegate + to whom/profile, eliminate, schedule, or retain), (3) an immediate delegation plan for tasks in the "urgent + not important" quadrant. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Executive productivity strategist with experience optimizing leader time in high-pressure environments. SUPUESTOS: if the available team is not specified, assume a 5-person team with generalist roles; if the time horizon is not specified, assume the current week; if a task has insufficient context to classify, assume "important + not urgent" and declare it — declare all assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: list of the leader's current tasks and responsibilities pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1) Read and understand each task on the list. 2) Classify into the four quadrants with explicit criteria. 3) For each task, assign an action: delegate (with suggested profile), eliminate (with justification), schedule (with suggested window), or retain (with justification). 4) Build the immediate delegation plan for the urgent + not important quadrant. 5) Deliver the markdown table sorted by quadrant. SALIDA: markdown table with four columns (task, quadrant, action, notes) plus immediate delegation plan. CASOS BORDE: (a) all tasks are urgent — flag the systemic problem and propose eliminating one task for every two urgent ones; (b) strategic tasks without a visible owner — recommend temporary retention with a review date; (c) repetitive tasks — flag them as automation or SOP candidates. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: each task has a quadrant and action assigned without ambiguity. Trade-off: speed of decision > perfection of analysis. DoD: complete table, immediate delegation plan with at least three concrete actions. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, classify with explicit criteria, deliver actionable artifacts.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_brief_resultad: [S · SITUATION] A leader is going to delegate a task or project to a team member and wants to ensure the team member understands exactly what is expected, when, with what resources, and with what success criteria, without the need for subsequent micromanagement. [P · REQUEST] Draft a result-oriented delegation brief that includes: (1) context and purpose of the work (why it matters), (2) expected result with observable and measurable success criteria, (3) explicit scope (what is included and what is excluded), (4) available resources and constraints, (5) follow-up milestones with dates, (6) authority level assigned for this work, (7) escalation protocol if the team member gets blocked. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Senior consultant in performance management and delegation systems design for team leaders. SUPUESTOS: if duration is not specified, assume two weeks; if the team member's level is not mentioned, assume a professional with 3 years of experience; if constraints are not detailed, assume standard team tools and budget access — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: description of the task or project to delegate, assigned team member, and relevant context pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1) Draft the context and purpose in 2-3 sentences focused on the impact of the work. 2) Define the expected result with metrics or observable criteria. 3) Delimit the scope with at least two explicit exclusions. 4) List available resources and real constraints. 5) Propose three follow-up milestones with relative dates. 6) Assign an explicit authority level for key decisions. 7) Define the escalation protocol with clear conditions. SALIDA: structured brief document in seven sections, format ready to share in writing with the team member. CASOS BORDE: (a) highly operational task — simplify to four sections (result, scope, milestones, escalation); (b) strategic project with high ambiguity — add a team member assumptions section to validate; (c) remote team member — add communication channel and frequency. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the team member can start work by reading only the brief, without an additional meeting. Trade-off: clarity > brevity. DoD: seven complete sections, measurable result, and escalation protocol with at least one concrete condition. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions at the start, use result-oriented language, deliver brief ready to share.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_monkey_managem: [S · SITUATION] A leader constantly receives problems from their team that team members should solve on their own or with minimal guidance. Every time a team member brings a problem without a proposed solution, the leader ends up carrying the work (the "monkey" returns to the leader). This creates dependency, leader overload, and under-development of the team. [P · REQUEST] Produce a practical system for the leader to return ownership of problems to their team members, including: (1) return conversation protocol (concrete phrases for 3 typical situations), (2) "next move" rule to require the team member to arrive with options, (3) assigned monkey tracking table, (4) 1-page guide to communicate the dynamic change to the team. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Senior executive coach specializing in organizational behavior, team dynamics, and development of team member autonomy. SUPUESTOS: if the sector is not specified, assume technology or professional services teams; if the number of team members is not mentioned, assume five; if the current dependency level is not described, assume high dependency — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: description of the typical situations where problems bounce back to the leader, pasted in the chat; if not provided, proceed with the most common patterns. PASOS: 1) Identify the three typical problem-bounce-back patterns. 2) Draft the conversation protocol with literal phrases for each pattern. 3) Define the next-move rule with clear criteria (minimum two options with pros/cons). 4) Design the monkey tracking table (team member, problem, date assigned, next move, deadline). 5) Write the 1-page guide to communicate the change to the team in a constructive, non-blaming tone. SALIDA: four independent artifacts, each labeled and ready to use. CASOS BORDE: (a) team member in genuine crisis — distinguish between a legitimate monkey and a genuine emergency; exception protocol included. (b) team with institutionalized escalation culture — add a note on how to manage resistance. (c) problems with client impact — maintain leader visibility without taking on the monkey. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the leader can use the conversation protocol without additional preparation. Trade-off: team autonomy > short-term comfort. DoD: all four artifacts are complete with literal phrases, a table with headers, and a guide without generic advice. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, use actionable phrases, distinguish emergency from dependency.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_seguimiento_si: [S · SITUATION] A leader who has delegated tasks or projects to their team wants to stay informed about progress without creating a sense of constant surveillance or eroding the team member's trust and autonomy. Micromanagement destroys motivation and delegation loses its value. [P · REQUEST] Design a delegation follow-up system that includes: (1) contact-point cadence differentiated by risk level and team member maturity, (2) three high-value follow-up questions for each contact point (that generate information without creating an interrogation), (3) status update format that the team member fills out autonomously (max 5 fields), (4) early warning signals that justify increasing frequency without appearing as distrust. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Senior specialist in performance management system design and leadership of high-autonomy teams. SUPUESTOS: if the number of active delegations is not specified, assume five; if the confidence level in team members is not described, assume medium level; if the organizational context is not specified, assume a mid-size technology company — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: list of active delegations, maturity or confidence level for each team member, and team context, pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1) Define the follow-up cadence based on two variables: work risk and team member maturity (2x2 matrix → four cadences). 2) Draft three high-value follow-up questions that do not sound like control. 3) Design the autonomous status update format with a maximum of five fields (no empty checkboxes). 4) List five early warning signals with the recommended response for each. SALIDA: four structured and labeled artifacts, ready to implement. CASOS BORDE: (a) team member who does not report without a reminder — include a non-intrusive automatic reminder mechanism; (b) high-risk delegation with new team member — justify high cadence without damaging the relationship; (c) remote team — adapt all formats to asynchronous communication. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the system can be implemented this week without additional meetings. Trade-off: leader visibility > team member autonomy for high-risk delegations, reversed for low-risk delegations. DoD: four complete artifacts, follow-up questions without the verbs "report" or "explain," warning signals with concrete response. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, design for autonomy by default, deliver implementable artifacts.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_liderazgo_situ: [S · SITUATION] A leader manages team members with different levels of competence and motivation in specific tasks. Applying the same leadership style to everyone creates friction: too much control with experts, too much freedom with beginners. Situational leadership resolves this by adapting the style to the team member's development level in each specific task. [P · REQUEST] Produce a situational leadership application guide that includes: (1) evaluation of a team member's development level in a specific task (D1-D4 by Blanchard), (2) description of the corresponding leadership style (E1-E4) with concrete behaviors, (3) three conversation opening phrases for each style, (4) transition table: when and how to move from one style to the next. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Executive coach certified in situational leadership with experience in technical and management team development. SUPUESTOS: if the task and team member are not specified, assume a new team member on a complex technical task; if the organization is not specified, assume a professional services company — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: description of the team member, the specific task, and team context pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1) Evaluate the team member's development level (D1-D4) for the described task, with justification of two indicators. 2) Assign the corresponding leadership style (E1-E4) with a description of concrete behaviors. 3) Draft three conversation opening phrases for that style. 4) Build the complete transition table (four rows, four columns: level, advancement signal, setback signal, leader action). SALIDA: four structured and labeled sections, with emphasis on concrete phrases and behaviors. CASOS BORDE: (a) team member with D4 in competence but D1 in motivation — describe E3 style and the re-engagement conversation; (b) new task for an expert team member in other areas — apply D1 without damaging their self-esteem; (c) forced transition due to organizational change — include re-diagnosis protocol. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the leader can identify the development level and select the style without prior training in the model. Trade-off: diagnosis precision > speed of application. DoD: evaluation with two justified indicators, three conversation phrases per style, and complete transition table. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, justify the diagnosis with observable indicators, use literal phrases.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_empoderar_deci: [S · SITUATION] A leader wants their team to make more decisions autonomously, but it is currently unclear what kinds of decisions they can make without consulting the leader, which ones require advance notification, and which ones are exclusive to the leader. This lack of clarity generates paralysis, unnecessary escalations, or unauthorized decisions. [P · REQUEST] Produce a documented decision perimeter for the team that includes: (1) taxonomy of three decision categories (autonomous, with advance leader notification before acting, reserved for the leader), (2) at least five examples per category adapted to the team context, (3) perimeter update protocol when circumstances change, (4) 30-minute alignment session: agenda and facilitation questions to present and validate the perimeter with the team. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Senior consultant in organizational design and empowerment of high-autonomy teams. SUPUESTOS: if the team's decision types are not described, assume a technology team with technical, process, and stakeholder communication decisions; if size is not specified, assume six people — declare assumptions at the start. INSUMOS: team description, types of decisions made, and organizational context pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1) Define the three categories with an explicit classification criterion. 2) Generate five examples per category with language specific to the team. 3) Draft the update protocol (who can propose changes, how frequently, and how it is approved). 4) Design the alignment session agenda with time allocations, facilitation questions, and validation method. SALIDA: decision perimeter document with four sections + session agenda, all ready to present to the team. CASOS BORDE: (a) team in high-uncertainty context — reduce the autonomous category and expand the leader-notification category; (b) conflict over who decides — include a temporary arbitration mechanism; (c) distributed team — adapt the update protocol to asynchronous channels. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: any team member can classify a new decision in under 2 minutes by consulting the document. Trade-off: perimeter clarity > exhaustiveness of examples. DoD: document with three defined categories, fifteen total examples, and a 30-minute agenda with concrete facilitation questions. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, use examples from the real context, deliver ready-to-present artifacts.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_stretch_assign: [S · SITUATION] A leader wants to accelerate a collaborator's development by assigning them a responsibility one level above their current comfort zone (stretch assignment). If poorly designed, the assignment generates failure and demotivation; if well designed, it produces accelerated growth, greater engagement, and readiness for roles of greater responsibility. [P · REQUEST] Design a complete stretch assignment for a specific collaborator that includes: (1) diagnosis of the development gap the assignment will close, (2) description of the assignment with scope, expected outcome, and duration, (3) leader support plan (check-ins, resources, support network), (4) success criteria that are also learning criteria, (5) contingency plan if the collaborator gets stuck midway. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert in accelerated talent development and design of on-the-job learning experiences for high-demand organizations. ASSUMPTIONS: if the collaborator is not described, assume a professional with 3–5 years of experience with leadership potential; if duration is not indicated, assume three months; if the organizational context is not described, assume a growing technology company — declare assumptions at the start. INPUTS: description of the collaborator (strengths, development areas, aspirations), description of current work and team context, pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1) Identify the development gap with evidence from the input (2 strengths to leverage + 1–2 areas to develop). 2) Design the assignment with defined scope, observable outcome, and duration. 3) Propose the leader's support plan: check-in frequency, resources, and at least one person from the support network. 4) Define dual success criteria: what the collaborator delivers + what they learn. 5) Design the contingency plan with two blocking scenarios and the leader's response in each. OUTPUT: stretch assignment document in five sections, ready to present to the collaborator in a 1:1. EDGE CASES: (a) collaborator with low confidence — reduce scope and increase support; (b) assignment with high business impact — add organizational safety net (executive sponsor); (c) collaborator already aware of the stretch — reframe as leading the initiative, not just participating. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the collaborator can accept the assignment understanding exactly what is expected, what support they have, and how their success will be measured. Trade-off: sufficient challenge > excessive safety; not so high as to generate failure. DoD: five complete sections, dual success criteria, and contingency plan with two scenarios. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, design for real growth not leader convenience, deliver artifact ready for 1:1.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_documentar_tra: [S · SITUATION] A leader or collaborator is going to transfer a responsibility to another person (through rotation, promotion, reassignment, or departure from the team). Without adequate documentation, the receiver arrives blind: they do not know the historical context, pending decisions, key stakeholders, or latent risks. This generates operational disruptions and loss of institutional knowledge. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete responsibility handover document that includes: (1) description of the responsibility and its purpose, (2) current status with in-progress, pending, and blocked tasks, (3) key historical context (decisions made, reasons, lessons learned), (4) stakeholder map with type of relationship and interaction frequency, (5) active risks and pending commitments with dates, (6) recommended accompaniment period (with or without overlap), (7) verification checklist confirming the receiver is ready to assume independently. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior consultant in knowledge management and operational continuity for high-demand teams. ASSUMPTIONS: if the responsibility is not described, assume management of an ongoing software project; if the duration of available overlap is not indicated, assume two weeks; if stakeholders are not listed, assume three types: internal client, technical team, and management — declare assumptions at the start. INPUTS: description of the responsibility, current status, stakeholders, and relevant context pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1) Describe the responsibility with its purpose in 2–3 sentences. 2) Document the current status with three columns: in progress, pending, blocked. 3) Capture the historical context: three key decisions with justification and lesson learned. 4) Build the stakeholder map in table format. 5) List active risks and pending commitments with due dates. 6) Propose the accompaniment period with transfer milestones. 7) Generate the 10–12 item verification checklist. OUTPUT: structured handover document in seven sections, in a format ready to share with the receiver. EDGE CASES: (a) urgent handover without overlap — prioritize sections 1, 2, 5, and 7; (b) responsibility with highly specialized tacit knowledge — add a "receiver's frequently asked questions" section; (c) unplanned departure — two-page emergency template. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the receiver can assume the responsibility independently at the end of the accompaniment period. Trade-off: practical utility for the receiver > exhaustive completeness. DoD: seven complete sections, 10–12 item checklist, and at least three documented risks. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, document with focus on the receiver not the transferring party, deliver a shareable artifact.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_recuperar_dele: [S · SITUATION] A leader delegated a responsibility or project to a collaborator and the result is not meeting expectations: the work is behind, the quality is insufficient, the collaborator is blocked or overwhelmed, or the trust relationship has deteriorated. The leader needs to recover the work without destroying the relationship or the collaborator's motivation, and without taking everything back themselves. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured recovery plan that includes: (1) diagnosis of root causes of failure (minimum three hypotheses with diagnostic questions), (2) recovery conversation: three-part script (acknowledge, redirect, agree), (3) adjusted re-delegation plan with greater support or reduced scope, (4) emergency escalation protocol if the deadline is critical, (5) prevention actions for the next delegation. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior executive coach specializing in leadership interventions, difficult conversation management, and recovery of failed projects. ASSUMPTIONS: if the failed delegation is not described, assume a technical project with a deadline in two weeks; if the probable cause is not indicated, assume a combination of ambiguous brief and lack of support; if the relationship with the collaborator is not specified, assume a trust relationship at risk — declare assumptions at the start. INPUTS: description of what went wrong, current status of the work, and what is known about the causes, pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1) List three root-cause hypotheses with one diagnostic question per hypothesis. 2) Write the three-part conversation script with literal phrases. 3) Propose the adjusted re-delegation plan: what changes (scope, support, milestones) and why. 4) Define the emergency escalation protocol with activation conditions. 5) List three prevention actions for the next delegation. OUTPUT: five structured and labeled sections, with emphasis on literal phrases for the difficult conversation. EDGE CASES: (a) collaborator in a personal crisis that affected the work — separate the professional conversation from the human support conversation; (b) failure caused by the leader (ambiguous brief, lack of resources) — begin the conversation by acknowledging your own responsibility; (c) deadline expired with no possible recovery — closure and learning protocol. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the leader can have the recovery conversation without additional preparation using the script. Trade-off: trust relationship > speed of recovery. DoD: five complete sections, three-part script with literal phrases, and at least three concrete prevention actions. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, produce literal phrases for the difficult conversation, distinguish leader causes from collaborator causes.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_diagnostico_fue: [S · SITUATION] A leader observes tension, friction, or explicit conflict between members of their team. Before intervening, they need to understand the real source of the conflict because the wrong intervention can make it worse. Team conflicts can originate in scarce resources, value differences, role ambiguity, poorly defined interdependencies, historical grievances, or incompatible work styles. [P · REQUEST] Produce a diagnosis of the conflict source that includes: (1) five-category framework of conflict sources with observable indicators per category, (2) primary and secondary source hypotheses based on the conflict description, (3) diagnostic interview plan: three questions per party involved (neutral, non-leading), (4) decision tree to choose the type of intervention based on the diagnosed source, (5) initial intervention recommendation with justification. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior specialist in organizational conflict resolution and team dynamics with training in mediation and organizational psychology. ASSUMPTIONS: if the conflict is not described, assume a conflict between two collaborators over role overlap in a project; if the escalation level is not indicated, assume a latent, unexpressed interpersonal conflict — declare assumptions at the start. INPUTS: description of the observed conflict, parties involved, relevant history, and team context, pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1) Present the five-category framework with 2–3 observable indicators per category. 2) Analyze the conflict description and propose the primary source hypothesis (with evidence) and secondary (with assumptions). 3) Write the diagnostic interview plan with three neutral questions per party (non-leading, non-accusatory). 4) Build the intervention decision tree: four sources → four intervention types with activation condition. 5) Issue the initial intervention recommendation with a two-sentence justification. OUTPUT: five structured and labeled sections, with emphasis on literal interview questions and decision tree in visual format (text). EDGE CASES: (a) conflict with client impact — escalate diagnosis and add urgency criterion; (b) conflict with a harassment or discrimination component — refer to HR immediately, do not continue the diagnosis; (c) systemic conflict involving the entire area — expand interviews to at least five people. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the leader can start the diagnostic interviews this week with the questions from the document. Trade-off: precise diagnosis > fast intervention. DoD: five complete sections, hypotheses with evidence, twelve neutral interview questions, and decision tree with at least four branches. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions, base hypotheses on evidence from the input, deliver literal neutral questions.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_mediacion_dos_p:
[S · SITUATION] You are the leader of a work team and two of your direct collaborators maintain an interpersonal conflict that is affecting collaboration, team climate, and area results. The conflict may have its origin in differences in work style, misunderstandings about responsibilities, or unresolved accumulated friction. [P · REQUEST] Design a step-by-step mediation plan between the two people involved: structure of prior individual conversations, facilitated joint session, and written closing agreements, all in a single actionable page. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior consultant in conflict management and organizational development with 15 years facilitating mediations in high-performance teams. ASSUMPTIONS: Both people continue working together and there is no violence or formally reported harassment; the leader has authority to facilitate the session; if no specific conflict context is provided, assume disagreement about task responsibilities — declare this assumption at the start. INPUTS: description of the conflict pasted in the thread or provided by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify the type of conflict (task, relationship, process) and its intensity based on described signals. 2. Design individual interview guide with each person (5 key questions, active listening, no judgment). 3. Structure joint session agenda (neutral opening, exposure of perspectives, search for common interests, agreements). 4. Draft post-mediation working agreement template with 2-week follow-up. 5. Include warning signals indicating need to escalate to HR. OUTPUT: Document in sections: Initial Diagnosis | Individual Interview Guide | Joint Session Agenda | Agreement Template | Escalation Criteria. EDGE CASES: (a) One person refuses to participate — protocol for forced individual conversation with clear consequences. (b) The conflict reveals a structural role design problem — redirect to responsibilities redesign. (c) There is a history of repeated conflicts — add formal improvement plan clause. [C · CRITERIA] The plan is executable in less than 2 weeks; agreements are observable and measurable; the joint session has a maximum duration of 90 minutes; the document fits on one A4 page; trade-off: psychological depth vs. operational practicality — prioritize practicality. DoD: the leader can execute the plan without additional external support.

Protocolo MetodologIA: apply systemic listening, facilitative neutrality, and verifiable behavioral agreements.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_estilos_thomas_:
[S · SITUATION] A leader faces a specific conflict situation on their team or in their organization and needs to decide which management style to apply to maximize the positive outcome. The Thomas-Kilmann model defines five styles: compete, collaborate, compromise, avoid, and accommodate, each appropriate based on the level of assertiveness and cooperativeness the context requires. [P · REQUEST] Given the described conflict, analyze which of the five Thomas-Kilmann styles is most appropriate, explain why you discarded the other four, and deliver an opening script to start the conversation using the recommended style. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Executive coach certified in conflict diagnosis and organizational facilitation with mastery of the Thomas-Kilmann model and its practical applications in leadership contexts. ASSUMPTIONS: The conflict involves at least two parties with divergent interests; if the user does not describe the conflict with sufficient detail, assume it is a disagreement about project priorities between peers of equal hierarchy — declare the assumption. INPUTS: conflict description pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Map the conflict on the assertiveness/cooperativeness axes of the TK model. 2. Identify the optimal style justifying with at least two situational criteria. 3. Discard the other four styles with one concrete reason each. 4. Write a 3–5 sentence opening script to start the conversation with the chosen style. 5. Warn about the most common risk when applying that style in this context. OUTPUT: TK analysis section (table of 5 styles with assessment) + recommended style with justification + opening script + risk warning. EDGE CASES: (a) The conflict has high emotional charge — recommend temporarily avoiding as a prior step before the main style. (b) The power differential is asymmetric — adjust the recommended style considering the position of lesser power. (c) The conflict is recurring — signal that no tactical style will resolve the root problem without systemic intervention. [C · CRITERIA] The analysis explicitly cites all five TK styles; the script is usable without editing in the real conversation; the justification includes at least two concrete situational criteria; trade-off: resolution speed vs. long-term relationship quality — the analysis must make this tension explicit. DoD: the leader can choose and apply the style within the next 24 hours.

Protocolo MetodologIA: rigorous situational mapping with the Thomas-Kilmann model and a ready-to-use opening script.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_desactivar_tens:
[S · SITUATION] During a team meeting, planning session, or results review, the discussion escalates emotionally: two or more people raise their voices, interrupt each other, or make comments that threaten to break the group dynamic and halt the work. The leader or facilitator must intervene in real time to defuse the tension without invalidating either party or losing the thread of the conversation. [P · REQUEST] Deliver a three-phase intervention protocol (before, during, after) with literal phrases ready to use in neutral Latin American Spanish, applicable within the next 2 minutes of a real meeting. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert facilitator in group dynamics and emotional management in high-performance environments, with training in nonviolent communication and de-escalation techniques. ASSUMPTIONS: The meeting is in-person or synchronous virtual with at least 4 people; the facilitator has legitimate authority to intervene; if no specific context is described, assume a technology team meeting in a sprint review — declare assumption. INPUTS: description of what happened in the meeting pasted by the user, or the user requests generic phrases. STEPS: 1. Identify the trigger of the tension (technical disagreement, personality clash, external pressure) from the context. 2. Design Phase 1 intervention: pause the dynamic (neutral interruption phrase + legitimate reason for the pause). 3. Design Phase 2: redirect the energy (acknowledgment of emotions + reframe toward common goal). 4. Design Phase 3: restore collaboration (minimum viable agreement + concrete next step). 5. Include 3 emergency phrases for the first 30 seconds. OUTPUT: Three-phase intervention card with numbered literal phrases, emergency phrases in a highlighted box, and adjustment note if the meeting is virtual. EDGE CASES: (a) A person leaves the room — formal pause protocol and individual follow-up. (b) The conflict involves the facilitator themselves — indicate how to momentarily hand off the role. (c) The tension is passive-aggressive rather than explicit — adapted phrases for that mode. [C · CRITERIA] The phrases are usable without editing; they do not blame any person; they reframe toward goals; the complete protocol is executed in less than 5 minutes; trade-off: speed of de-escalation vs. resolution of the underlying issue — prioritize de-escalation now, resolution later. DoD: the facilitator can read the emergency phrases from their phone if necessary.

Protocolo MetodologIA: three-phase intervention with literal phrases in neutral Spanish ready for an ongoing meeting.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_conversacion_no:
[S · SITUATION] A leader or collaborator has received or issued a complaint, grievance, or criticism that is formulated accusatorially, reactively, or with emotional charge that makes it difficult to listen and resolve. Reframing that complaint using the four components of Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication (NVC) — observation, feeling, need, and request — allows the message to be transformed into communication the interlocutor can receive without becoming defensive. [P · REQUEST] Given the original complaint, deliver: (a) NVC analysis of the original message identifying what each component violates, (b) reframed NVC version ready to use, and (c) tips on tone and body language for in-person or virtual delivery. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Certified practitioner in Nonviolent Communication with experience coaching leaders and teams, trained in the Rosenberg method and its applications in corporate environments. ASSUMPTIONS: The complaint is between people who maintain an ongoing working relationship; if the user does not paste the complaint, assume a leader saying to a collaborator: "You always deliver late and you do not care about the team" — declare assumption. INPUTS: the literal complaint pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify in the original complaint the violations of the four NVC components (judgments, generalizations, demands, disguised feelings). 2. Extract the concrete observation free of judgment. 3. Identify the real feeling beneath the accusation. 4. Articulate the legitimate unmet need. 5. Formulate the specific, positive, present-tense request. 6. Write the complete NVC version in 2–4 sentences. 7. Add 3 delivery tips (tone, posture, appropriate timing). OUTPUT: NVC analysis table (original vs. reframed by component) + NVC version ready to use + delivery tips. EDGE CASES: (a) The complaint involves repeated behaviors — add distinction between pattern and single episode. (b) The complaint comes from a superior to a subordinate — adjust the request component to make it more directive without being authoritarian. (c) The context is written (email or chat) — adapt the delivery tips for text. [C · CRITERIA] The NVC version contains no judgments, generalizations, or accusations; the request is specific and actionable within 48 hours; the analysis cites all four components; trade-off: emotional authenticity vs. diplomacy — the NVC version must sound genuine, not forcedly positive. DoD: the user can use the reframed version exactly as written in the next conversation.

Protocolo MetodologIA: transform accusatory complaints into four-component nonviolent communication ready to use.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_acuerdos_trabaj:
[S · SITUATION] A work team has no explicit collaboration rules and conflicts emerge from misunderstandings about unwritten norms: response times, decision-making, ways of giving feedback, managing disagreements, use of communication channels. Establishing co-constructed and documented working agreements prevents future conflicts and creates a reference framework the team can return to when friction arises. [P · REQUEST] Facilitate the creation of a working agreements document for the described team: generate facilitating questions for the co-construction session, propose baseline agreements per thematic area, and deliver the final template ready to sign or share. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organizational development and team culture design consultant, with experience facilitating working agreement sessions in technology, product, and services teams. ASSUMPTIONS: The team has between 4 and 12 people; the leader will facilitate the session; if the type of team is not described, assume a software development team at a technology company — declare assumption. INPUTS: description of the team, its main frictions or work context pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Identify the most critical thematic areas for the described team (communication, decisions, feedback, meetings, conflicts, deliverables). 2. Generate 2–3 facilitating questions per thematic area for the co-construction session. 3. Propose 2–3 baseline agreements per area as a starting point (not imposed). 4. Structure the agreements document with sections, format, and a periodic review clause. 5. Add instructions to facilitate the 60–90 minute co-construction session. OUTPUT: Session facilitation guide (questions by area) + agreements document template with proposed baseline agreements + process instructions + quarterly review clause. EDGE CASES: (a) The team is distributed across multiple time zones — add asynchrony-specific agreements. (b) There are new and veteran members — include an onboarding process to the agreements. (c) Previous agreements were ignored — add a peer-to-peer accountability mechanism. [C · CRITERIA] Each agreement is observable, verifiable, and does not depend on subjective interpretation; the template fits on one page; the co-construction session lasts a maximum of 90 minutes; trade-off: exhaustiveness vs. adherence — fewer well-maintained agreements outperform many ignored ones. DoD: the team can sign the document at the end of the facilitated session.

Protocolo MetodologIA: co-construction of observable behavioral agreements to prevent conflicts with an integrated review mechanism.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_silos_entre_are:
[S · SITUATION] Two or more areas, departments, or teams in an organization operate with objectives, metrics, or cultures that generate chronic friction: they accuse each other of lack of collaboration, do not share information, inadvertently sabotage each other, or compete for resources. Inter-silo friction reduces delivery speed, duplicates work, and damages the experience of internal and external clients. [P · REQUEST] Design a 4-week intervention plan to reduce friction between the two described areas: root cause diagnosis, alignment activities, permanent coordination mechanisms, and success metrics. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior consultant in organizational design and team integration with experience in change interventions at medium and large organizations in technology and services sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: Both areas have leaders willing to participate in the intervention; if the areas are not described, assume friction between the Software Development team and the Operations/Infrastructure team — declare assumption. INPUTS: description of the two areas in conflict and the observed frictions. STEPS: 1. Diagnose the root causes of friction (misaligned incentives, unmanaged dependencies, lack of mutual visibility, history of incidents). 2. Design initial alignment activities (joint dependency-mapping session, "a day in your area" exercise). 3. Propose permanent coordination mechanisms (synchrony forums, shared dashboards, internal service level agreements). 4. Establish 3–5 observable success metrics at month 1 and month 3. 5. Include a communication plan to manage team resistance. OUTPUT: 4-week plan in table format (week, objective, activities, responsible party, deliverable) + permanent mechanisms + success metrics + resistance management plan. EDGE CASES: (a) An area leader sabotages the intervention — escalation protocol to management with business arguments. (b) The friction has its origin in a previous organizational decision (merger, restructuring) — contextualize the intervention as part of cultural integration. (c) The areas have different work cultures (agile vs. waterfall) — include a methodology translation workshop. [C · CRITERIA] The plan is executable with internal resources without hiring external consultants; the metrics are quantifiable; the permanent mechanisms require less than 2 additional hours of weekly meetings; trade-off: speed vs. depth of cultural change — prioritize rapid structural changes over slow cultural transformation. DoD: by month 1 there is at least one documented improved coordination metric.

Protocolo MetodologIA: systemic 4-week intervention with root causes, permanent mechanisms, and success metrics to reduce silos.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_personalidad_di:
[S · SITUATION] A leader has a team member whose behavior creates persistent friction with the team: this could be a person who dominates conversations, responds with hostility to feedback, undermines decisions in private, repeatedly fails to honor commitments, or demotivates the team with a chronically negative attitude. The leader needs a specific strategy to manage this dynamic without prematurely escalating to a disciplinary process and without damaging the climate for the rest of the team. [P · REQUEST] Given the described behavior, deliver: diagnosis of the behavioral pattern, structured direct conversation strategy, and a support plan with improvement indicators and escalation decision points. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Executive coach specializing in leadership of difficult people and performance management, with training in organizational psychology and experience in behavioral interventions in corporate environments. ASSUMPTIONS: The team member has been on the team for more than 3 months; the behavior does not constitute formal harassment; if the user does not describe the behavior, assume a team member who responds with hostility to feedback and undermines team decisions — declare that assumption. INPUTS: description of the team member's specific behavior. STEPS: 1. Classify the behavioral pattern (hostility, passive-aggressiveness, repeated non-compliance, chronic demotivation, dysfunctional dominance). 2. Identify possible root causes (insecurity, misaligned expectations, external problems, prior history with the leader). 3. Design the direct conversation structure: opening, objective behavioral description, impact on the team, clear expectation, active listening. 4. Propose a 30-day support plan with verifiable behavioral improvement milestones. 5. Define 3 decision points with criteria for escalating to HR or a formal process. OUTPUT: Behavioral pattern diagnosis + direct conversation structure with key phrases + 30-day table plan + escalation decision points. EDGE CASES: (a) The team member has high technical performance despite the behavior — balance talent retention with team protection. (b) The behavior worsened after a specific organizational decision — consider a context conversation before the direct conversation. (c) The rest of the team has already formally reported the problem — accelerate the plan and shorten the timelines. [C · CRITERIA] Conversation phrases are direct without being aggressive; plan milestones are behavioral and observable; the plan does not require more than one additional weekly meeting; trade-off: talent retention vs. team protection — the plan must be explicit about when the balance tips toward protection. DoD: the leader can have the direct conversation in the next week with the plan in hand.

Protocolo MetodologIA: behavioral diagnosis, structured direct conversation, and 30-day plan with escalation decision points.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_post_incidente_:
[S · SITUATION] After an incident, error, or failure involving multiple people or teams, the group needs to review what happened without falling into blame, finger-pointing, or cover-up dynamics. Blameless culture postulates that errors are systemic and that the goal of the post-incident conversation is to learn and improve systems, not to punish people. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete structure of a 60–90-minute blameless post-incident conversation: agenda, facilitating questions per section, participation rules, final document template, and action follow-up mechanism. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert facilitator in continuous learning culture, site reliability engineering (SRE), and blameless practice, with experience facilitating incident post-mortems in technology and operations teams. ASSUMPTIONS: The incident has already occurred and is contained; all those involved will participate in the session; if the incident is not described, assume a production service outage with customer impact lasting less than 4 hours — declare that assumption. INPUTS: description of the incident, areas involved, and basic timeline if the user has it. STEPS: 1. Design an opening that establishes the blameless psychological contract with participants (why we are here, what we will not do). 2. Structure a factual chronological reconstruction section (facts, not interpretations). 3. Design a root cause analysis section using an adapted 5 Whys technique for group context. 4. Structure a learnings and actions section with owner, date, and closure criterion per action. 5. Design a close acknowledging the team's effort in responding to the incident. 6. Create a post-incident document template in a standard format. OUTPUT: Session agenda with timings + facilitating questions per section + participation rules (maximum 5) + document template + weekly action follow-up mechanism. EDGE CASES: (a) One person feels they were unfairly blamed before the session — individual pre-session check-in protocol. (b) The incident reveals a process problem a leader should have resolved earlier — how to name the finding without making accusations. (c) Participants are not honest due to fear of consequences — partial anonymity technique for the initial reconstruction. [C · CRITERIA] The session produces no individual attributions of blame; each action has an owner, a date, and a success criterion; the document template fits in 2 pages; trade-off: completeness of analysis vs. session duration — limit to 90 minutes maximum with root cause prioritization. DoD: the post-incident document is ready by the end of the session.

Protocolo MetodologIA: blameless facilitation with factual reconstruction, root cause analysis, and actions with owner and date.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_disenso_product:
[S · SITUATION] A team tends toward easy consensus, groupthink, or silence on important decisions: people do not express objections for fear of appearing negative, contradicting the leader, or breaking group harmony. This produces lower-quality decisions, surprising implementation problems that were not anticipated, and team members who disengage when they are not heard. [P · REQUEST] Design a set of practices and tools for a team to develop the ability to dissent productively: techniques for decision meetings, facilitation roles, questions that invite questioning, and dissent health metrics. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Specialist in facilitating high-quality group decisions, with experience in leadership team dynamics, collective critical thinking practices, and groupthink prevention patterns. ASSUMPTIONS: The team is a professional work team with autonomy to influence decisions; the leader is willing to model dissent; if the team is not described, assume a product or technology team of 6–10 people — declare that assumption. INPUTS: description of the most frequent types of decisions and the current discussion pattern. STEPS: 1. Diagnose the current dissent inhibition pattern (leader pressure, cultural norm of harmony, fear of consequences, lack of argumentation skills). 2. Design specific techniques for decision meetings (devil's advocate, pre-mortem, anonymous voting, forced round of objections). 3. Propose rotating roles that institutionalize questioning (official challenger, dissent guardian). 4. Generate 10 facilitating questions that invite questioning without creating unnecessary conflict. 5. Define 3 dissent health metrics (participation in discussion, time to first dissent, % of decisions revised post-implementation). OUTPUT: Diagnosis of the inhibition pattern + 4 meeting techniques with usage instructions + description of rotating roles + 10 facilitating questions + 3 health metrics. EDGE CASES: (a) The leader is the main dissent inhibitor — include a specific section on how the leader can model dissent by inviting criticism of their own ideas. (b) The team has pronounced hierarchical differences — partial anonymization techniques. (c) The organizational culture penalizes questioning — complementary psychological safety frameworks. [C · CRITERIA] Techniques are implementable in the next decision meeting; metrics are measurable without special tools; roles require no formal training; trade-off: meeting efficiency vs. decision quality — accept longer meetings in exchange for more robust decisions. DoD: the team has at least one active technique in its next important decision meeting.

Protocolo MetodologIA: institutional practices of productive dissent with rotating roles, meeting techniques, and decision health metrics.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_definir_valores:
[S · SITUATION] A work team has declared values that are abstract, generic, or decorative ("excellence", "integrity", "collaboration") that no one can translate into observable day-to-day behaviors. Values without specific behaviors do not change the culture nor serve as criteria for feedback, selection, or evaluation. The team needs to redefine its values as concrete behavioral commitments that anyone can recognize and verify. [P · REQUEST] Facilitate the process of redefining the team's values: convert abstract values into observable behavioral commitments, generate 3–5 verifiable behaviors per value, and produce the team's final behavioral values document. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organizational culture design consultant with experience in defining behavioral values, values-based performance evaluation, and cultural onboarding in technology and services teams. ASSUMPTIONS: The team already has declared values, even if abstract; the process includes team participation to legitimize the results; if no values are provided, assume generic values: excellence, collaboration, innovation — declare that assumption. INPUTS: list of the team's current values pasted by the user. STEPS: 1. Analyze the current values and identify which are abstract, redundant, or impossible to verify. 2. For each value, generate 3–5 specific behaviors that any team member can observe in daily work. 3. Write each behavior in the first-person plural ("When we disagree, we express disagreement in the meeting, not afterward"). 4. Identify the opposite behavior for each value to clarify the behavioral boundary. 5. Design a 45-minute micro-session to validate and adjust the behaviors with the team. OUTPUT: Values table (abstract value → one-sentence definition → 3–5 observable behaviors → opposite behavior) + validation micro-session guide + note on use in feedback and evaluation. EDGE CASES: (a) The team has more than 7 values — recommend reducing to 3–5 maximum before developing behaviors. (b) Values are imposed by the organization without team participation — design a process of collective ownership. (c) Values are in tension with each other — make the priority hierarchy explicit. [C · CRITERIA] Each behavior is observable by a third party; it contains no subjective adjectives; it is in the first-person plural; trade-off: specificity vs. flexibility — enough specificity to guide behavior without restricting creativity. DoD: any new team member can understand what is expected of them in 10 minutes of reading.

Protocolo MetodologIA: conversion of abstract values into observable behavioral commitments with a behavior table and validation process.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_seguridad_psicolo:
[S · SITUATION] Psychological safety — the shared belief that the team is a safe space for interpersonal risk-taking — is the primary predictor of team performance according to research by Amy Edmondson and Google's Project Aristotle. A team with low psychological safety avoids asking questions, reporting errors, proposing disruptive ideas, or giving honest feedback, which deteriorates innovation, quality, and talent retention. [P · REQUEST] Given the described team, deliver: (a) diagnosis of the level of psychological safety using observable indicators, (b) identifiable root causes of the current level, and (c) 60-day elevation plan with concrete practices and follow-up metrics. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Team psychological safety specialist with training in Amy Edmondson's model, design of leadership interventions, and organizational culture in high-pressure environments. ASSUMPTIONS: The team has been working together for at least 3 months; the leader has real influence over the team's climate; if the team is not described, assume a software engineering team of 6–8 people with symptoms of silence around errors and scarcity of new ideas — declare that assumption. INPUTS: description of the team, observed symptoms, and leader behaviors that the user shares. STEPS: 1. Map observable indicators of low psychological safety (who speaks in meetings, reaction to errors, frequency of questions, level of dissent). 2. Identify root causes of the current level (leader behavior, results pressure, history of negative consequences). 3. Design leader interventions classified into three levers: modeling vulnerability, creating safety structures, responding productively to risk. 4. Develop a 60-day calendar with weekly practice, associated metric, and progress signal. 5. Include 5 diagnostic questions the leader can use in a one-on-one conversation with each member. OUTPUT: Diagnosis with estimated level (low/medium/high) and evidence + root causes + 60-day calendar in table + 5 individual diagnostic questions. EDGE CASES: (a) The leader themselves is the main cause of low safety — plan that begins with changes to the leader's behavior before team activities. (b) A recent incident damaged safety (someone was penalized for speaking up) — trust repair intervention prior to the elevation plan. (c) The organization has a high-control culture — distinguish what the leader can do within that context from what requires systemic change. [C · CRITERIA] Calendar practices are concrete and executable weekly; metrics do not require formal surveys; the diagnosis cites specific observable behaviors; trade-off: speed of change vs. authenticity — do not force leader behaviors that are not genuine. DoD: by day 30 there is at least one psychological safety metric with a documented positive signal.

Protocolo MetodologIA: diagnosis with behavioral evidence, three intervention levers, and 60-day calendar with psychological safety metrics.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_team_charter:
[S · SITUATION] A new team or one going through a moment of significant change (new leader, new members, new strategic mandate) needs to formalize its collective identity: purpose, mission, work norms, mutual commitments, ways of making decisions, and how to measure success. A team charter is the foundational document that aligns the group from the start and serves as a reference in moments of friction or ambiguity. [P · REQUEST] Facilitate the creation of a complete team charter for the described team: generate the document structure with each section developed, facilitating questions to co-construct it with the team, and the final document ready to adopt. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: High-performance team development consultant with experience facilitating team constitution sessions, culture design, and strategic alignment in technology and services organizations. ASSUMPTIONS: The team has between 4 and 15 people; the leader will facilitate the session or participate actively; if the team is not described, assume a digital product team at a growing technology company with members from different disciplines (product, design, engineering) — declare that assumption. INPUTS: description of the team, its purpose or creation context, and any relevant organizational constraints. STEPS: 1. Define the required sections of the team charter (purpose, mission, behavioral values, work norms, decision-making, communication, meetings, team metrics, mutual commitments). 2. Develop each section with proposed content based on the team's context. 3. Generate 2–3 facilitating questions per section for the co-construction session. 4. Design the agenda for the 2–3-hour co-construction session. 5. Include a semi-annual review clause and a new member onboarding process. OUTPUT: Complete team charter document with all sections developed + facilitating questions per section + co-construction session agenda + review and onboarding clause. EDGE CASES: (a) The team is brand new and has no history — prioritize the purpose, norms, and commitments sections. (b) The existing team has unresolved dynamics — add an "elephants in the room" section at the start of the session. (c) The team is globally distributed — add a specific section on asynchronous work norms. [C · CRITERIA] The document is adoptable in a single 2–3-hour session; each section has concrete content, not just empty questions; norms are behavioral and verifiable; trade-off: completeness vs. usability — a maintained 2-page charter beats a filed 10-page one. DoD: the team can sign the charter at the end of the session and use it as a reference from the next day onward.

Protocolo MetodologIA: foundational team charter with purpose, behavioral norms, decision-making, and semi-annual review process.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_rituales_equipo:
[S · SITUATION] A team leader of 6–12 people wants to institutionalize recurring practices — meetings, celebrations, check-ins — that translate the team's declared values into observable everyday behaviors, rather than leaving culture to chance.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a catalog of 5 team rituals ready to implement: evocative name, frequency, duration, facilitator, step-by-step mechanics, and explicit link to the cultural value it reinforces.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior organizational culture consultant with experience in ritual design in technology and professional services companies.
ASSUMPTIONS: The team works in hybrid mode (in-person + remote); the team's values will be pasted in the INPUTS field; if no values are provided, the assistant infers 3 typical high-performance team values (collaboration, continuous learning, recognition) and declares them before continuing.
INPUTS: Paste here the team's values or cultural principles and any existing ritual that already works or has failed.
STEPS:
1. Read the inputs and identify the 3 values with the largest gap between what is declared and what is lived [INFERENCE if no gap is declared].
2. For each selected value, design at least 1 ritual; complete up to 5 rituals covering different frequencies (daily, weekly, monthly).
3. For each ritual describe: name, objective, frequency, duration, suggested facilitator, 3–5-step mechanics, minimum materials, adoption indicator.
4. Include 1 quarterly "cycle close" ritual that integrates learnings.
5. Add a summary table with the 5 rituals and their key attributes.
OUTPUT: Document in numbered sections: assumed context → 5 detailed rituals → summary table → note on gradual implementation (do not launch all at once).
EDGE CASES:
- If the team is 100% asynchronous and distributed across multiple time zones: propose asynchronous versions (Loom, Slack thread) for each synchronous ritual.
- If the team has been together for less than 3 months: prioritize trust-building rituals before performance ones.
- If existing rituals are mentioned: evaluate them with a cultural reinforcement criterion before adding new ones.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each ritual has mechanics executable in less than 30 minutes without special preparation.
- The value↔ritual link is explicit and verifiable by an external observer.
- The summary table allows the leader to choose 1–2 rituals to start with without reading the entire document.
- Trade-off: depth of each ritual vs. number; if space requires it, reduce to 4 rituals with greater detail.
- DoD: 5 rituals described, table delivered, at least 1 ritual per frequency (daily/weekly/monthly).

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions → design rituals → link values → deliver actionable table.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_reconocimiento_si:
[S · SITUATION] A leader or culture owner in an organization of 20–200 people detects that recognition of work well done depends almost exclusively on the direct manager, which generates inequity, invisibilization of lateral contributions, and low intrinsic motivation. They want to design a peer recognition system that is sustainable, authentic, and does not become an empty point-scoring game.

[P · REQUEST] Design a peer recognition system: design principles, operational mechanics, channels, frequency, recognition categories, roles, and an 8-week launch plan.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior specialist in recognition system design and employee experience with expertise in motivational psychology (self-determination theory) and organizational culture.
ASSUMPTIONS: The organization uses a messaging tool such as Slack or Teams; if no platform is specified, the design is for Slack with a Teams equivalent; the budget for incentives is symbolic (non-monetary) unless otherwise indicated.
INPUTS: Paste here the team size, available platforms, cultural values, and any prior recognition attempt and why it did not work.
STEPS:
1. Define 4–6 system design principles (e.g., timeliness, specificity, equity, authenticity).
2. Design 3–5 recognition categories aligned with the declared values.
3. Describe the operational mechanics: who can give recognition, when, how (form, channel, message format), what is published and where.
4. Establish cadence: spontaneous recognition vs. collective celebration moment (e.g., Friday kudos).
5. Define roles: cultural champion, moderator, metrics owner.
6. Create an 8-week launch plan: milestones, communications, activation workshops, adoption review.
7. Include 3 measurable success indicators at 90 days.
OUTPUT: Structured document: principles → categories → mechanics → cadence → roles → 8-week plan → success metrics → warnings about common anti-patterns (inflationary recognition, visible favoritism).
EDGE CASES:
- If the culture is highly hierarchical: add a leadership sensitization phase before the open launch.
- If the team is smaller than 15 people: simplify to 3 categories and a single channel; omit the moderator role.
- If there were prior failed attempts: start with a diagnosis of why it failed before proposing the new system.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The system can operate without additional budget in the base version.
- Recognition categories are defined with concrete examples to avoid ambiguity.
- The 8-week plan includes a date, owner, and deliverable per milestone.
- Trade-off: coverage vs. depth; if the team is large, prioritize automation over personalization.
- DoD: principles documented, complete operational mechanics, 8-week plan with milestones, 3 success metrics.

Protocolo MetodologIA: principles first → operational mechanics → gradual plan → adoption metrics.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_equipo_remoto_per:
[S · SITUATION] A distributed team leader across at least 2 different time zones experiences disconnection signals: uneven participation in meetings, little interaction outside tasks, higher-than-average turnover, and statements like "I feel alone" or "I don't know who my colleagues are". The team has between 6 and 20 people and rarely — or never — meets in person.

[P · REQUEST] Design a 90-day strategy to build a sense of belonging in the remote team, with concrete actions for 3 pillars: interpersonal connection, visibility of contributions, and shared meaning.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior remote work and distributed team culture consultant with experience in all-remote organizations of more than 50 people.
ASSUMPTIONS: The team uses video conferencing (Zoom/Meet) and messaging (Slack/Teams); if no tools are specified, these are assumed. The team has no budget for an in-person retreat in the next 90 days [ASSUMPTION; adjust if budget is available].
INPUTS: Paste here the team size, time zones, available tools, observed disconnection symptoms, and any prior action taken.
STEPS:
1. Diagnose the current state of belonging using the 3-pillar framework (connection, visibility, meaning).
2. For each pillar design 2–3 concrete actions with owner, frequency, and tool.
3. Build the 90-day roadmap: weeks 1–4 (connection foundations), weeks 5–8 (contribution visibility), weeks 9–12 (shared meaning rituals).
4. Include a proposal for a high-energy half-day virtual gathering (virtual offsite) with a detailed agenda.
5. Design 3 proxy belonging metrics measurable without a formal survey (participation in channels, response time, emoji/reaction usage).
6. Flag 3 common mistakes when trying to build remote culture and how to avoid them.
OUTPUT: Strategy structured in 4 sections: diagnosis by pillar → actions per pillar → 90-day roadmap → proxy metrics + common mistakes.
EDGE CASES:
- If the team has 3+ time zones without overlap: design all actions in asynchronous format first, with synchronous only for overlap windows.
- If there are active interpersonal conflicts: prioritize a mediation intervention before collective belonging actions.
- If the team is new (< 6 months): add a cultural onboarding protocol for new members.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each action specifies tool, owner, and frequency; none requires more than 2h/week investment from the leader.
- The roadmap is sequential: it does not launch all actions at once.
- Proxy metrics are observable day-to-day without a survey.
- Trade-off: high-energy actions (high connection but costly in time) vs. asynchronous micro-actions (lower energy but sustainable).
- DoD: 3-pillar strategy complete, 90-day roadmap, virtual offsite agenda, 3 proxy metrics.

Protocolo MetodologIA: diagnose pillars → actions per pillar → gradual roadmap → observable metrics.
spec-liderazgo_cultura_diversidad_inclus:
[S · SITUATION] A team leader or people and culture owner in an organization of 15–150 people recognizes that diversity and inclusion (D&I) declarations remain at the corporate policy level and are not translated into everyday behaviors. Meetings are dominated by the same voices, certain people do not feel heard, and decisions tend to replicate the biases of the most visible group.

[P · REQUEST] Design a catalog of 10 inclusion practices executable in the team's daily operations — meetings, decisions, onboarding, communication — with implementation instructions for each one, without requiring prior training programs.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) specialist focused on low-threshold interventions (nudges) and redesign of everyday processes.
ASSUMPTIONS: The team has not received formal DEI training; the leader has autonomy over their meetings and team dynamics but not over company policies; practices must work both in-person and remotely.
INPUTS: Paste here the team size, observable diverse composition (gender, seniority, native language, time zone), the 2–3 moments where exclusion is most visible, and any inclusion practice already adopted.
STEPS:
1. Identify the 4 operational contexts where exclusion occurs most frequently: meetings, decision processes, onboarding, and written communication.
2. For each context, design 2–3 specific practices: name, description, when to apply, who facilitates, time required (≤10 min for everyday practices).
3. For each practice include: signal that it is working and warning signal that it is not.
4. Order practices from lowest to highest effort to facilitate incremental adoption.
5. Include 3 specific cognitive biases that each practice counteracts (e.g., amplification bias, HIPPO effect, affinity bias).
6. Add a 1-page guide so the leader can introduce the practices without creating resistance.
OUTPUT: Catalog of 10 practices organized by context → comparative table (effort × impact) → resistance-free introduction guide → list of biases counteracted.
EDGE CASES:
- If the team is homogeneous (little visible diversity): focus practices on diversity of perspectives and cognitive styles, not only identity-based.
- If there is strong cultural resistance ("this is political"): use team effectiveness language instead of DEI.
- If the team is small (< 8 people): simplify to 6 practices and remove the highest-friction ones.

[C · CRITERIA]
- No practice requires more than 15 additional minutes in the existing flow.
- Signals of functioning are observable without a survey.
- The catalog's language is operational, not ideological.

spec-liderazgo_cultura_team_health_check:

spec-liderazgo_cultura_disfunciones_lenc:

spec-liderazgo_cultura_team_building_pro:

spec-liderazgo_cultura_etapas_tuckman:

spec-liderazgo_cultura_carta_motivadores:

spec-liderazgo_coaching_modelo_grow:

spec-liderazgo_coaching_preguntas_podero:
[S · SITUATION] A leader, internal coach, facilitator, or agile coach needs a repertoire of high-quality questions to use in coaching conversations, team reflection sessions, performance reviews, and mentoring sessions. The questions must open genuine reflection, not suggest the answer or turn into an interrogation.

[P · REQUEST] Build a bank of 60 powerful coaching questions organized in 6 functional categories (objective, reality, options, commitment, limiting beliefs, learning), with a note on when to use each category and a guide on what makes a question powerful (and not powerful).

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Certified executive coach and coach trainer specializing in designing high-leverage questions and transformational coaching conversations.
ASSUMPTIONS: The bank is for use in 1:1 and group conversations; questions are in Latin American Spanish; the user's experience level varies (from a leader without training to a certified coach).
INPUTS: Indicate the main use context (individual coaching, team session, performance review, mentoring) so that the questions are calibrated to the context.
STEPS:
1. Define in 5 lines what makes a question powerful: technical characteristics (open, short, neutral, coachee-centered, future-oriented).
2. Define in 5 lines what turns a question into a non-powerful one (closed, contains the answer, multiple, projects judgment).
3. Design 10 questions for each of the 6 categories:
   a. Clarity of objective (what do you want to achieve, what for, how will you know you achieved it)
   b. Reality exploration (what is happening, what have you tried, what resources do you have)
   c. Option generation (what alternatives exist, what would you do if you had no fear, what would you tell someone in your situation)
   d. Commitment and action (what will you do, when, what could stop you, how will you support yourself)
   e. Beliefs and limiting assumptions (what do you assume is true, where does that conviction come from, what would happen if it were not true)
   f. Learning and reflection (what did you learn, what would you do differently, what surprised you)
4. For each category include: a note on when to use it, a signal that the question landed (the coachee stops to think), and the most frequent trap when using it.
5. Add 5 rescue questions: what to say when the conversation stalls or the coachee gives superficial answers.
OUTPUT: Framework of what makes a question powerful → 6 categories × 10 questions → usage notes per category → 5 rescue questions.
EDGE CASES:
- If the user is a leader without coaching training: highlight the 20 most versatile questions to start with.
- If the context is a performance review: add a note that in that context the powerful question must coexist with direct feedback.
- If the coachee talks a lot without going deeper: recommend the silence technique + meta-reflection question.

[C · CRITERIA]
- None of the 60 questions contains the implicit answer.
- The questions are formulated in natural Latin American Spanish, not in literal translation from English.
- The framework of what makes a question powerful vs. not powerful is concrete enough for the reader to rewrite their own questions.
- Trade-off: quantity (60) vs. memorability; add "anchor question" markers (1-2 per category that the leader can memorize).
- DoD: 60 organized questions, quality framework, usage notes, 5 rescue questions, anchor questions marked.

Protocolo MetodologIA: quality framework first → questions per category → memorable anchors → rescue for stalls.
spec-liderazgo_coaching_plan_desarrollo_:

spec-liderazgo_coaching_desarrollar_alto:

spec-liderazgo_coaching_skill_will_matri:

spec-liderazgo_coaching_sucesion_rol:

spec-liderazgo_desempeno_evaluacion_anua:

spec-liderazgo_desempeno_calibracion_ses:

spec-liderazgo_desempeno_matriz_9box: [S · SITUATION] A team leader with 6-15 people needs to place each team member on the performance-potential matrix (9-box) for the annual talent review cycle, in order to substantiate development, retention and succession decisions before Human Resources and senior management. spec-liderazgo_desempeno_separar_desempe: [S · SITUATION] A leader or talent committee needs to make development, promotion and succession decisions, but systematically confuses current performance (what the team member achieves today in their role) with future potential (the capacity to take on roles of greater complexity).
