[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a one-page conceptual framework explaining the difference between performance and potential with three observable indicators per dimension; (2) a dual evaluation tool (double-axis table with different diagnostic questions for each dimension); and (3) three illustrative cases (one of high-performance/low-potential conflict, one of low-performance/high-potential, one of full alignment) with the recommended decision for each case. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Specialist in succession planning and leadership development with experience implementing differentiated talent models (HiPo type) in 500-5,000 employee companies in technology and consulting sectors. ASSUMPTIONS: if the type of company is not specified, assume a 500-employee technology company in growth; if the hierarchical level evaluated is not indicated, assume team members from individual technical roles to middle managers; if no specific team member is provided, generate the framework and tools generically applicable to any case. INPUTS: optionally the leader will describe one or more specific team members to calibrate the illustrative cases with real data; if none are provided, generate archetypal examples. STEPS: 1. Draft the one-page conceptual framework with the operational definition of performance and potential, and three observable indicators for each — output: structured text framework. 2. Design the dual evaluation tool: two blocks of 3-4 diagnostic questions, one for performance and one for potential, with a simple response scale (yes/no/partially) — output: evaluation table. 3. Draft the three illustrative cases with context, observed signals and recommended decision — output: three case blocks. OUTPUT: document with three labeled sections: Conceptual framework | Dual evaluation tool | Illustrative cases. EDGE CASES: (a) if the team member being evaluated has recently transitioned roles, warn that the measured performance may not reflect their actual ceiling; (b) if the evaluator has recency bias (only remembers the last 2 months), include in the tool a question that forces a long-term perspective; (c) if the evaluation result shows low-performance/high-potential, indicate the maximum recommended investment time without evidence of improvement before reclassifying. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the performance and potential indicators are mutually exclusive and do not overlap in wording. Trade-off: exhaustiveness of the framework vs. practical usability — prioritize a tool applicable in 30 minutes over academic taxonomy. DoD: a leader without formal HR training can use the dual evaluation tool independently and arrive at a defensible classification before their management. Protocolo MetodologIA: explicitly differentiate in each section when you are talking about performance and when about potential; use [ASSUMPTION] for inferences about the team member or context not provided.
spec-liderazgo_desempeno_documentar_evid: [S · SITUATION] A team leader arrives at the annual evaluation cycle close without continuous performance records for their team members, which forces them to rely on recent memory (recency bias), exposes them to challenged rating decisions and prevents them from building solid arguments for PIPs, promotions or separations. They need a continuous performance evidence documentation system that is simple, sustainable and legally defensible. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) an individual performance evidence log template, for weekly or biweekly use, with minimum fields to capture observable facts, context and impact; (2) a criteria guide to distinguish high-quality evidence (specific, dated, observable) from weak evidence (subjective, generic); and (3) a documentation cadence calendar with recommended alerts for the three key moments of the cycle (start, midpoint, close). [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert in performance management and HR process compliance, with experience designing documentation systems that withstand legal audits and are voluntarily adopted by busy leaders. ASSUMPTIONS: if team size is not specified, assume a team of 6-10 people; if no preferred logging tool is indicated, assume the leader will use free text (notes in any digital format); if no evaluation cycle is specified, assume an annual cycle with a mid-year review. INPUTS: the leader may share the names of their team's roles and the management tool they use (Notion, Excel, Google Docs, etc.) to adapt the template; if nothing is shared, generate a generic template in text table format. STEPS: 1. Design the evidence log template with fields: Date | Team Member | Situation (brief context) | Observable Behavior | Measured or Estimated Impact | Type (achievement/area for improvement) | Evidence Source — output: template in text table. 2. Draft the evidence quality guide with three examples of high-quality vs. low-quality evidence in a comparative format — output: comparative table. 3. Design the cadence calendar with three key moments and the recommended documentation activities for each — output: cadence table. OUTPUT: document with three sections: Evidence log template | Evidence quality guide | Cadence calendar. EDGE CASES: (a) if the leader supervises more than 12 people, simplify the template to the minimum necessary and suggest a rotation of team members to document each week rather than all at once; (b) if the company's HR system already has a logging tool, indicate how to adapt the template to feed into it; (c) if the leader has limited time (less than 15 minutes per week), suggest a maximum 5-line log format per incident. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: each field in the template has a completion instruction that a leader without HR training can follow without ambiguity. Trade-off: thoroughness of the log vs. sustained adoption — prioritize simplicity; an incomplete but consistent log is worth more than a perfect log that is abandoned after two weeks. DoD: the leader can complete the template in less than 10 minutes per incident; the logged evidence can be read aloud in a calibration meeting without needing additional explanation. Protocolo MetodologIA: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the team or the logging tool; in the quality guide explicitly state what types of statements are inadmissible in a legal process.
spec-liderazgo_desempeno_promocion_caso: [S · SITUATION] A leader wants to promote a team member to a higher level but needs to present a formal case before a talent committee, Human Resources or senior management. Without a structured, evidence-based document, the promotion request is perceived as favoritism or an emotional decision, which reduces the probability of approval and the team member's career timeline. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete promotion case document that includes: (1) a one-page executive summary with the recommendation and the three main arguments; (2) comparative performance analysis (last 2-3 periods) with quantified achievements; (3) readiness assessment for the next level using the target role description; (4) business impact analysis if the promotion is approved vs. delayed; and (5) a 90-day post-promotion transition plan. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior Human Resources Business Partner (HRBP) with experience building and approving promotion cases in fast-scaling technology companies, trained in talent committee calibration criteria. ASSUMPTIONS: if no specific performance metrics are provided, draft with [COMPLETE] markers and note what type of data is needed; if the target level is not specified, assume promotion from individual contributor to team leader; if no decision culture is indicated, assume the committee values quantitative evidence over qualitative testimony. INPUTS: the leader will paste the team member's name, current and target role, period achievements with data if available, and any third-party feedback available (clients, peers, other leaders). STEPS: 1. Draft the one-page executive summary with a clear recommendation and three fact-based arguments — output: executive summary. 2. Build the comparative performance table with quantified achievements by period — output: performance table. 3. Draft the readiness assessment for the next level using a target role competencies format with current and required levels — output: competency gap table. 4. Draft the business impact analysis (approval vs. delay) with at least two concrete consequences per scenario — output: impact analysis. 5. Draft the 90-day transition plan with milestones and responsible parties — output: transition plan. OUTPUT: five-section document with formal committee presentation header. EDGE CASES: (a) if the team member has been in the current role less than one year, note that most committees apply a minimum tenure filter and how to argue for an exception; (b) if there are evident competency gaps, do not omit them but include them in the transition plan section with how they will be closed; (c) if there is another internal candidate competing for the same position, include a differentiation note without disparaging the other candidate. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: each argument in the executive summary has at least one supporting quantitative data point. Trade-off: document thoroughness vs. committee reading time — limit the document to 3-4 pages; additional detail goes in optional annexes. DoD: a talent committee member who does not know the team member can read the document and reach the same conclusion as the leader without needing additional oral context. Protocolo MetodologIA: mark with [COMPLETE] where data is missing; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the team member or the committee; never invent performance figures.
spec-liderazgo_desempeno_decision_desvin: [S · SITUATION] A leader or HR manager must make and execute the separation decision for a team member. The situation is legally sensitive, emotionally intense for all parties and operationally critical (the team and the business must continue). Without structured preparation, the conversation can generate legal disputes, damage to the leader's reputation or unnecessary organizational trauma. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a 12-point pre-decision verification checklist to confirm the separation is justified, documented and aligned with the legal process; (2) a 10-15 minute separation conversation script structured in four phases (opening, communicating the decision, logistical information, dignified closing); and (3) a communication plan to the remaining team for the 24 hours after. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Labor attorney and people management consultant with 15 years preparing separation conversations in technology and services companies in Latin America, with a focus on employer legal protection and team member dignity. ASSUMPTIONS: if the separation cause is not specified, assume objective cause of low performance after an unmet PIP; if no legal framework is indicated, assume general Latin American labor legislation with emphasis on cause documentation; if it is not mentioned whether severance is agreed, assume HR has the calculations ready before the conversation. INPUTS: the leader will share the reason for separation, whether prior documentation exists (PIP, warnings) and whether HR participates in the meeting. STEPS: 1. Draft the pre-decision verification checklist grouped into three blocks: justification (documented cause), process (completed steps, HR involved), and logistics (documents, access, assets ready) — output: 12-point checklist with status (yes/no/pending). 2. Draft the four-phase conversation script with exact phrases the leader can use, including recommended pauses and how to handle emotional interruptions — output: annotated script. 3. Draft the communication plan to the remaining team: what to say, when, how to handle questions and how to reinforce team stability — output: 24-hour communication plan. OUTPUT: document with three labeled sections: Pre-decision checklist | Conversation script | Team communication plan. EDGE CASES: (a) if the separation cause is different from low performance (e.g., conduct, restructuring), note that the script and checklist must be significantly adjusted and recommend specific legal counsel; (b) if the team member may react aggressively or unpredictably, add a safety protocol in the script (have HR present, meeting in a room with accessible exit, do not do it by video conference without support); (c) if the separation is due to restructuring (not performance), adapt the language to separate the decision from the person and make it structural. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the script uses no euphemisms that delay the main message by more than two sentences; the complete conversation does not exceed 15 minutes. Trade-off: legal protection vs. humanity of the process — both are non-negotiable; the script must be simultaneously defensible in court and dignified for the team member. DoD: the leader can execute the conversation with the script as a reference without improvising the critical phrases; the remaining team receives communication before end of day. Protocolo MetodologIA: mark with [LEGAL RISK] any situation that requires validation by a labor attorney before proceeding; use [ASSUMPTION] for any inference about the context or the team member.
spec-liderazgo_desempeno_compensacion_co: [S · SITUATION] A leader must communicate to a team member a compensation decision from the salary review cycle: it may be a raise, a bonus, an increase lower than expected or no adjustment. These conversations have a high emotional impact on the team member and affect their motivation, retention and trust in the leader. Without structured preparation, the leader may generate false expectations, resentment or harmful salary comparisons for the team. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a differentiated conversation script for three scenarios (full raise per expectations, raise lower than expected, no salary adjustment), with specific phrases for each case; (2) a protocol for handling difficult questions (why not more? when will it be reviewed? what does it take to earn more?); and (3) a list of common mistakes leaders make in these conversations and how to avoid them. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Leadership coach and compensation communication specialist with experience training frontline managers in technology companies where salary transparency is partial or limited. ASSUMPTIONS: if no compensation scenario is specified, generate the script for all three scenarios; if the company's salary transparency policy is not indicated, assume that salary band details are confidential; if the leader does not have specific figures, draft with [INSERT AMOUNT/PERCENTAGE] markers. INPUTS: the leader will indicate the scenario (full raise / lower / no adjustment), the reason for the decision and whether there is a committed next review milestone. STEPS: 1. Draft for each scenario an opening (30 seconds), direct communication of the decision (1 minute), context and justification (2 minutes) and a future-oriented closing (1 minute) — output: three compact scripts with estimated time. 2. Draft the difficult questions handling protocol with 5 frequent questions and a recommended response for each — output: question/response table. 3. Draft the list of 7 common mistakes with the error pattern and the correct alternative — output: errors and corrections table. OUTPUT: document with three sections: Scripts by scenario | Difficult questions protocol | Common mistakes and alternatives. EDGE CASES: (a) if the team member already knows the outcome before the conversation (through rumors or comparisons), adapt the opening to validate the information without confirming other team members' data; (b) if the compensation decision is noticeably below the market and the leader has no power to change it, include in the script how to acknowledge the gap and what non-monetary compensation can be offered; (c) if the team member receives a raise but has performance that does not justify it (internal pressure), do not pretend performance was excellent — the script must remain consistent with the performance message. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the script does not promise future reviews without concrete dates or percentages without HR authorization. Trade-off: honesty vs. risk of demotivation — prioritize honesty; dishonesty in compensation destroys trust in the long term. DoD: the leader can conduct any of the three scenarios with the script as a reference without improvising the justification phrases; the team member ends the conversation with clarity about the outcome and, if there is no raise, with at least one actionable next step. Protocolo MetodologIA: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the company's salary policy; use [INSERT] for the values the leader must personalize before the conversation.
spec-liderazgo_desempeno_feedback_contin: [S · SITUATION] A team leader operates with an episodic feedback model (annual or semi-annual evaluation) that generates surprises in formal reviews, disconnection between daily performance and recognition, and little opportunity for course correction during the cycle. They need to design a continuous feedback system that is sustainable, consumes no more than 2 hours per week of the leader's time, and builds feedback habits across the entire team. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) the complete design of the continuous feedback system with rhythms (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly), formats and responsible parties for each cadence; (2) a 30-minute weekly 1-on-1 template development-oriented with bidirectional feedback sections; and (3) a system onboarding protocol to adopt it with an existing team in 30 days without resistance. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organizational culture and performance management systems consultant with experience implementing continuous feedback in 5-20 person technology teams, including distributed and remote teams. ASSUMPTIONS: if team size is not specified, assume 6-10 people; if it is not indicated whether the team is in-person or remote, assume a hybrid team; if no communication tool is specified, assume the team uses Slack or Teams and has access to Google Docs or Notion for the template. INPUTS: the leader may share the team size, the communication tool and whether any team ritual is already established to build upon. STEPS: 1. Design the cadence system: table with four levels (daily/weekly/monthly/quarterly), description of the ritual, duration, participants and format — output: cadence table. 2. Design the weekly 1-on-1 template with five sections: mood (check-in), progress on commitments, leader-to-team-member feedback (SBI: Situation-Behavior-Impact), team-member-to-leader feedback, and a concrete action agreement — output: 1-on-1 template. 3. Design the 30-day onboarding protocol: week 1 (present the system), week 2 (first pilot cycle), week 3 (adjustment and brief retrospective), week 4 (full adoption) — output: week-by-week onboarding plan. OUTPUT: document with three sections: Cadence system design | 1-on-1 Template | 30-day onboarding protocol. EDGE CASES: (a) if the team is fully remote across multiple time zones, add asynchronous mechanisms to the cadence design (e.g., a weekly structured message) as an alternative to synchronous rituals; (b) if the leader has more than 12 direct reports, simplify the system to two cadences (weekly and quarterly) and suggest a peer or co-leader model to distribute the load; (c) if the team has a low-feedback culture or prior negative experiences with similar systems, include in the onboarding an expectations calibration session before the pilot. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the complete system demands no more than 2 hours per week from the leader with a team of 10 people. Trade-off: richness of feedback vs. sustainability of the system — prioritize sustainability; a simple adopted system beats a sophisticated abandoned one. DoD: the leader can present the system to their team with the template and onboarding plan without needing additional materials; after 30 days the team can operate the system semi-autonomously. Protocolo MetodologIA: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the team or the tools; include in each cadence the estimated real weekly time commitment for the leader.
spec-liderazgo_reuniones_diseno_agenda: [S · SITUATION] A leader frequently schedules meetings, but many end without a clear outcome, with participants who did not understand why they were there, or run beyond the allotted time without reaching a decision. The average cost of an 8-person team meeting lasting 1 hour at a technology company exceeds $800 USD [ASSUMPTION: average senior salary]; the leader needs a reproducible method to design meetings with an explicit purpose, the right participants and a measurable outcome from the start. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a meeting design template with five required fields (single purpose, expected result in past tense, essential vs. optional participants, timed agenda, and operating agreements); (2) a two-minute decision tree to determine whether a meeting is necessary or can be replaced by an asynchronous message; and (3) a five-point checklist for the facilitator to verify before sending the invitation. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Organizational effectiveness consultant and high-performance meeting facilitation specialist, with experience in technology companies that have reduced meeting time by 30-40% without losing decision quality. ASSUMPTIONS: if no meeting type is specified, assume a weekly team follow-up meeting of 6-10 people; if no collaboration tool is indicated, assume video conference with access to a shared document; if the leader does not provide the topic, generate the template generically with completion instructions. INPUTS: the leader will share the type of meeting they want to design, the participants and the topic or decision that needs to be reached. STEPS: 1. Design the meeting design template with the five required fields, with one-line completion instructions per field and an example — output: template with example. 2. Design the decision tree for whether a meeting is needed: three binary questions (does it require real-time interaction? does the decision need more than one perspective now? does the cost of delay exceed the cost of the meeting?) with yes/no paths to meeting or asynchronous message — output: decision tree in text. 3. Draft the five-point pre-invitation checklist — output: numbered list. OUTPUT: document with three sections: Design template | Decision tree | Pre-invitation checklist. EDGE CASES: (a) if the meeting has more than 10 participants, recommend in the template dividing between vote participants (decision-makers) and listening participants (observers) with explicit roles; (b) if the meeting purpose cannot be stated in one sentence, note that the meeting needs to be split in two or is not ready to be scheduled; (c) if the meeting is recurring (weekly/biweekly), add a quarterly audit field to review whether the meeting is still necessary. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the template can be completed in less than 5 minutes; the expected result is written in past tense ("was decided...", "was prioritized..."). Trade-off: rigor of design vs. speed of scheduling — the decision tree must take no more than 2 minutes. DoD: any meeting participant can read the invitation and know exactly why they are there and what is expected of them before entering the room. Protocolo MetodologIA: include a completed template example for the most common meeting type (team follow-up); use [ASSUMPTION] for any inference about team size or the tool.
spec-liderazgo_reuniones_facilitar_decis: [S · SITUATION] A leader or facilitator must run a meeting where a group of 4-12 people needs to reach a concrete decision before the session ends. Without an explicit method, decision meetings end with apparent consensus that is not real, with the same discussion that was already had before, or with the leader imposing their judgment without having leveraged the group's knowledge. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a group decision facilitation guide with five sequential steps (frame the problem, generate options, evaluate with criteria, converge and decide, record and communicate), with recommended time and facilitation techniques for each step; (2) a comparative table of four group decision-making methods (consensus, majority vote, leader decision with group input, and consultative) with the ideal use context for each; and (3) a 5-minute decision meeting closing protocol that ensures everyone leaves with clarity on what was decided, who executes, and by when. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Facilitator of organizational decision processes and group dynamics designer with experience facilitating critical decisions in technology, product, and strategy teams. ASSUMPTIONS: if the decision topic is not specified, generate the guide in a generic form applicable to any type of operational or tactical decision; if the preferred decision method is not indicated, recommend the consultative method as the default for technical teams; if the total meeting duration is not specified, assume 60 minutes. INPUTS: the facilitator may share the decision topic, the number of participants, the level of prior agreement, and any constraint (deadline, budget, resources) that narrows the options. STEPS: 1. Draft the five facilitation steps with recommended duration (not exceeding 60 minutes total), facilitation technique for each step, and warning signs indicating the group is stuck — output: five-step guide. 2. Build the comparative table of the four group decision methods with columns: method, when to use it, main advantage, main risk, typical time — output: comparative table. 3. Draft the 5-minute closing protocol with the three verification questions the facilitator asks before closing the meeting — output: closing protocol. OUTPUT: three-section document: Decision Facilitation Guide | Methods Table | Closing Protocol. EDGE CASES: (a) if the group includes mixed hierarchies (directors and analysts in the same room), add a facilitation note on how to prevent rank from suppressing perspectives from lower levels; (b) if the decision is urgent (less than 30 minutes available), provide a compressed three-step version of the process; (c) if the group is polarized into two positions with no movement, include a disequilibrium technique (e.g., position reversal: each party defends the opposing argument for 2 minutes) to unblock the conversation. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: at the end of the session, all participants can answer without ambiguity "what was decided?" and "who does what by when?" Trade-off: decision quality vs. speed — the consultative method balances both; if time is critical, the leader decides with prior documented input. DoD: the facilitator can run the session with the five-step guide as a reference without needing prior training in advanced facilitation; the closing protocol produces a written record of the decision before everyone leaves. Protocolo MetodologIA: flag with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the group or the type of decision; if the leader provides the specific topic, adapt the facilitation techniques to that specific context.
spec-comunicacion_email_frio_aida: [S · SITUATION] A sales, business development, or marketing professional needs to send a cold email to a prospect who does not know them, with the goal of obtaining a response: a meeting, a call, or a content download. Generic cold emails have open rates of 15-25% and response rates of 1-5% [ASSUMPTION: B2B industry benchmarks]; a well-structured email using the AIDA framework (Attention-Interest-Desire-Action) can double the response rate if the subject line and first paragraph are properly personalized. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a complete cold email applying AIDA for a specific prospect and offer, with a subject line of maximum 7 words, a body of 100-150 words, and a single measurable call to action (CTA); (2) two variants of the same email (more direct version and more consultative version) for A/B testing; and (3) a one-sentence explanation per section of why each part fulfills its function in the AIDA framework. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: B2B sales copywriting specialist with experience in cold email marketing for technology services, consulting, and SaaS, trained in the Aaron Ross method (Predictable Revenue) and in personalization-at-scale techniques. ASSUMPTIONS: if the type of prospect is not specified, assume an IT or digital decision-maker at a company with 100-500 employees; if the offer is not indicated, assume a digital transformation consulting service; if the prospect's name or company name is not provided, draft with markers [NAME] [COMPANY] that the user must personalize; if the language is not specified, use professional-register neutral Latin American Spanish. INPUTS: the user will provide the prospect's name (or marker), title, company, the problem the offer solves, and the main benefit the prospect will receive. STEPS: 1. Draft the email subject line (maximum 7 words, no emojis, no exclamation marks, activating opening through relevance or curiosity) — output: 3 subject line options with specificity score. 2. Draft the Attention paragraph (first line, personalized, connecting with a specific pain point or context of the prospect) — output: 1-2 sentence paragraph. 3. Draft the Interest paragraph (why this is relevant to the prospect now, with a data point or reference case) — output: 2-3 sentence paragraph. 4. Draft the Desire paragraph (what the prospect will obtain concretely, quantified if possible) — output: 2-sentence paragraph. 5. Draft the single low-friction CTA (a yes/no question or a specific date proposal) — output: CTA sentence. 6. Create the direct variant (shorter, explicit CTA) and the consultative variant (more empathetic, CTA in question form) — output: two variants. 7. Draft the one-sentence explanation per AIDA section — output: justification table. OUTPUT: three sections: Main AIDA Email | A/B Variants | AIDA Justification per Section. EDGE CASES: (a) if the prospect is C-level (CEO, CTO, CFO), adjust the email to be even shorter (maximum 80 words in the body) and center the value on business impact, not service features; (b) if the service or product has a high price or long sales cycle, reduce the CTA ambition to «do you have 15 minutes this week?» instead of trying to close in the first email; (c) if the prospect is in a regulated industry (banking, health, government), avoid guaranteed-result claims and add expectation-management language. [C · CRITERIA] Observable: the subject line has maximum 7 words; the email body has maximum 150 words; there is exactly one CTA. Trade-off: personalization vs. scalability — the email must be personalizable by replacing only 3-5 markers without rewriting from scratch. DoD: the user can copy the email, replace the markers, and send it in less than 5 minutes; the A/B version enables a test with the same audience variables. Protocolo MetodologIA: flag with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the prospect or the industry; with [CUSTOMIZE] the fields the user must complete with real prospect data.
spec-comunicacion_email_seguimiento_secu:
[S · SITUATION] A B2B sales professional or independent consultant sent an initial proposal to a prospect who has not responded. They need a sequence of 5 follow-up emails escalated in tone and urgency to reactivate the conversation without being intrusive.

[P · REQUEST] Draft 5 follow-up emails ready to send, with complete subject line and body, spaced over recommended days, escalating progressively from a friendly reminder to a definitive close, producing a measurable response rate superior to generic follow-up.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior B2B consultative sales specialist and conversion copywriter with 12+ years closing professional services contracts in Latin America.

ASSUMPTIONS: If no proposal context is provided, assume it is a technology consulting service for USD 15,000–50,000, sent 5 business days ago. If the prospect's sector is not indicated, assume a mid-size manufacturing or retail company. Declare assumptions at the start; ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) prospect's name, (2) service offered, (3) urgency of close.

INPUTS: Paste a summary of the sent proposal or the key points of the service offered. If nothing is pasted, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Define cadence: indicate recommended send day for each touch (D+2, D+5, D+9, D+14, D+21).
2. Draft Touch 1 — Friendly reminder: subject + brief body (<120 words), no pressure, with an open-ended question.
3. Draft Touch 2 — Added value: include an insight, success case, or relevant industry data.
4. Draft Touch 3 — Angle shift: focus on the cost of inaction or a real deadline.
5. Draft Touch 4 — Escalation to decision-maker: assume there is a superior or partner involved; CC or mention without excessive pressure.
6. Draft Touch 5 — Definitive close: polite but final tone; leave the door open for the future without further insistence.
7. Deliver summary table: touch | day | subject | objective | CTA.

OUTPUT: 5 blocks formatted as «TOUCH N – Day +X» > Subject: ... > Body: ... | Summary table at the end in Markdown.

EDGE CASES:
- If the prospect already responded negatively: omit touches 4 and 5 and replace with a respectful close email with a future reactivation seed.
- If the proposal has an expired validity date: adjust touch 3 to acknowledge the expiration and offer a quick renewal.
- If the service is highly technical (software, cybersecurity): simplify language in touches 1 and 2 so a non-technical executive can approve them.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Each subject line < 55 characters; mobile-ready.
- No email exceeds 180 words.
- Tone escalates without becoming aggressive: the prospect must feel they can respond «no» without tension.
- DoD: 5 complete emails + summary table delivered in a single block, ready to copy into any email client.

Protocolo MetodologIA: before drafting, declare the assumptions used and the chosen day cadence.
spec-comunicacion_email_disculpa_corpora:
[S · SITUATION] A services company (technology, consulting, logistics, or similar) suffered an incident that affected customers — service outage, delivery error, data failure, critical delay — and needs to communicate the formal apology in a way that preserves trust, accepts responsibility without creating excessive legal liabilities, and makes the remediation steps clear.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a corporate apology email ready to send to the affected segment, with subject line, personalizable greeting, structured body (acknowledgment > impact > summarized root cause > actions taken > compensation/gesture if applicable > next steps > support contact), and a closing that reaffirms the service commitment. Maximum 300 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior Corporate Communications Director with experience in crisis management and regulated communication in high-exposure sectors (fintech, health, enterprise SaaS).

ASSUMPTIONS: If the type of incident is not specified, assume a digital platform service outage for 4 hours during business hours. If no available compensation is indicated, do not invent discounts or credits; instead propose a goodwill phrase without committing numerically. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) nature of the incident, (2) affected segment, (3) whether active remediation is already underway.

INPUTS: Paste the incident description, date/time, estimated impact, and remediation actions already taken. If there are no inputs, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: direct, without euphemisms, < 60 characters.
2. Open with genuine acknowledgment without passive language («we regret the inconvenience» is prohibited).
3. Describe the impact from the affected customer's perspective, in one sentence.
4. Explain root cause in non-technical language, 1–2 sentences.
5. List actions taken (short bullets).
6. If compensation applies, include it clearly; if not, use a goodwill gesture without a specific amount.
7. Indicate next steps and a specific (not generic) support channel.
8. Close with a commitment to improvement and corporate signature.

OUTPUT: Complete email ready to copy — subject line + formatted body, markers [COMPANY], [DATE], [CONTACT] where to personalize.

EDGE CASES:
- If the incident has active legal implications: add a footnote warning that the text must be reviewed by legal counsel before sending.
- If the incident involves personal data (possible GDPR/Data Law breach): add a specific data notification paragraph per applicable regulation.
- If the sender is the CEO vs. the support team: adjust tone and level of personal commitment.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Zero passive euphemisms; the email accepts responsibility in first person plural.
- Formal but human tone: not cold or bureaucratic.
- Does not promise what it cannot deliver; all compensation is verifiable.
- DoD: one complete email with personalization markers, ready to send after minimal edits.

Protocolo Metodología: declare incident assumptions before drafting and flag which elements require legal review if applicable.
spec-comunicacion_email_no_breaker:
[S · SITUATION] A professional receives requests they must decline — joining a project with no budget, accepting conditions outside their scope, granting non-viable discounts, collaborating with someone whose proposal does not fit — and needs to draft an email that says «no» clearly, without burning the relationship, without opening the door to endless renegotiations, and without too many explanations that weaken their position.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a professional email that declines the request with elegance: neutral subject line, acknowledgment of the value of the request, explicit «no» without softening euphemisms, brief and honest reason (without excessive justification), alternative or open door if applicable, and warm closing that preserves the relationship.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Executive assertive communication consultant specializing in professional boundary negotiation in high-pressure corporate environments.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the request to decline is not specified, assume it is a request for free collaboration or a discount greater than 30% above the standard rate. If the relationship with the requester is not indicated, assume a known professional contact who is not an active client. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) the exact nature of the request, (2) whether a real alternative exists to offer.

INPUTS: Paste or describe the received request and the main reason for declining. If there are no inputs, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: neutral and drama-free (not «Re: Rejection of your proposal»).
2. Open acknowledging the request with one genuine sentence (not condescending).
3. Say «no» with a direct and clear sentence in the second line; do not bury it in the final paragraph.
4. Give ONE honest and brief reason (max. 2 sentences); do not invent elaborate excuses.
5. If a genuine alternative exists, offer it in a bullet or one sentence; if not, omit this section.
6. Close with a warm phrase that reaffirms the relationship without creating an expectation of revision.
7. The complete email must not exceed 150 words.

OUTPUT: Complete email (subject line + body) with markers [YOUR NAME], [REQUESTER] where necessary.

EDGE CASES:
- If the request comes from a current client with an active contract: adjust tone to indicate the «no» is about this specific request, not the business relationship.
- If the person has decision-making power over future opportunities for the sender: keep the «no» clear but emphasize the alternative or the next contact point more.
- If the request is overtly abusive or disrespectful: use a more neutral tone and omit the open door.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The «no» appears in the first 3 sentences of the body.
- Zero evasive phrases such as «I'm not sure this is the best time» or «maybe another time».
- The alternative (if it exists) is specific and actionable, not vague.
- DoD: one email < 150 words ready to send with minimal personalization.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the request and the relationship before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_recordatorio_pag:
[S · SITUATION] A company or independent professional has an overdue or nearly due invoice with a client and needs to send a reminder email that keeps the business relationship positive while pressing firmly enough to obtain payment or an explicit commitment to a payment date.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete payment reminder email (subject line + body) in a firm-cordial tone that includes: clear reference to the invoice, amount, and due date, CTA with a response deadline, mild consequences if no response is received (without threatening), and a contact channel for resolving questions. Maximum 200 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior finance and corporate collections manager with 10+ years in professional services companies, expert in maintaining cash flow without deteriorating relationships with strategic clients.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the invoice status is not specified, assume it is 10 business days past due. If the amount is not indicated, use [AMOUNT]. If the reminder number is not specified, assume it is the first. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) days past due, (2) whether there was a prior deferred payment agreement, (3) whether the client relationship is sensitive.

INPUTS: Provide invoice number, amount, issuance and due date, client name, and name of the payments contact. If not provided, use markers.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: mention invoice number and that it is a reminder, < 60 characters.
2. Open with a cordial greeting and direct reference to the outstanding invoice.
3. State amount, invoice number, and due date in the first paragraph.
4. Ask if there is any obstacle or question about the invoice (empathetic opening).
5. Request confirmation of payment date or transfer by a specific deadline.
6. Mention next steps if there is no response (without explicitly threatening).
7. Include account details or payment link if applicable.
8. Close with willingness to resolve any questions.

OUTPUT: Complete email with markers [CLIENT COMPANY], [CONTACT], [INVOICE #], [AMOUNT], [DUE DATE], [RESPONSE DEADLINE], [PAYMENT DETAILS], ready to personalize.

EDGE CASES:
- If this is the third reminder or more: raise the tone to formal-firm, remove the empathetic question, and mention that the matter will move to legal if not settled within X days.
- If the client claimed to have paid: include a verification paragraph and request proof of payment.
- If the invoice has an ongoing dispute: do not send a collections reminder; indicate that the dispute must be resolved first.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Firm but non-aggressive tone; the client must feel urgency, not threat.
- The response deadline is concrete, not «as soon as possible».
- DoD: one complete email with all markers identified, ready to personalize in < 2 minutes.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the invoice status and the reminder number before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_introduccion_dob:
[S · SITUATION] A professional or network connector wants to introduce two people who do not know each other because they believe the connection will generate mutual value — business opportunity, collaboration, expert advice, market access — and needs to do so in a way that both parties want to respond, without the connector remaining a permanent intermediary or creating an unwanted obligation.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete double introduction email (subject line + body) that presents both people with their roles and the specific reason for the connection, makes the mutual value clear, transfers the thread to both so they can continue autonomously, and does not exceed 200 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior professional network connector with expertise in entrepreneurship, technology, and consulting ecosystems in Latin America; specialist in high-impact introductions that generate conversations.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the people are not specified, assume an introduction between a fintech startup founder and an innovation director at a mid-size bank in search of alliances. If the connection reason is not indicated, assume a technology pilot opportunity. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) roles and names of both people, (2) specific reason for the mutual value.

INPUTS: Provide name, role, and company of person A and person B, and the concrete reason for the introduction. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: «[Name A], meet [Name B]» or a direct variant < 65 characters.
2. Open with «I am introducing you both» or «I would like you to meet» without a long preamble.
3. Introduce person A: name + role + one relevant skill/achievement for the connection, in 2 sentences.
4. Introduce person B: name + role + one relevant need or project for the connection, in 2 sentences.
5. Articulate the mutual value in ONE clear sentence: «I believe [A] can help [B] with X because Y».
6. Hand off the thread: «I will leave this in your hands» or similar; avoid remaining as an intermediary.
7. Optionally include a question or suggested action to break the ice between them.
8. Brief closing of no more than 2 lines.

OUTPUT: Complete email with subject line and body, markers [NAME A], [ROLE A], [COMPANY A], [NAME B], [ROLE B], [COMPANY B], [REASON], ready to personalize.

EDGE CASES:
- If one of the parties does not know they will be introduced (no opt-in): add a line indicating the sender has already spoken with both and both agreed to the introduction, or flag that it is recommended to confirm before sending.
- If the connection could be perceived as a conflict of interest for the connector: add a brief neutrality statement.
- If both people know each other vaguely: change the focus from «introducing them» to «deepening the connection» and adjust the subject line accordingly.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The mutual value is explicit and specific; not generic like «they have a lot in common».
- The email does not make the connector the permanent point of contact.
- Body < 200 words.
- DoD: complete email with markers, ready to personalize and send.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the profiles and the connection reason before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_solicitud_referi:
[S · SITUATION] A professional or services company wants to activate their network of satisfied contacts (current clients, former clients, allies, colleagues) to obtain referrals or recommendations to new prospects, and needs an email that makes the request in a direct way, without being uncomfortable or transactional, that facilitates action for the recipient and minimizes friction.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete referral request email (subject line + body) that briefly recalls the relationship or shared positive result, concisely explains what type of contact would be ideal, makes the direct request in one sentence, offers to facilitate the introduction, and gives thanks without creating emotional debt. Maximum 180 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior business development consultant specializing in organic referral-based growth in professional B2B services in Latin America.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the relationship with the recipient is not specified, assume they are a satisfied client with a project completed 2–6 months ago. If the ideal referral profile is not defined, assume mid-size companies in the same sector as the current client. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) concrete result achieved with the recipient, (2) desired referral profile.

INPUTS: Provide the recipient's name, shared result or project, and the profile of the type of contact being sought. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: warm and direct, < 55 characters, without mentioning «referral» if it sounds transactional.
2. Open by recalling the value generated in the relationship with a specific phrase (not generic).
3. Ask for the referral directly in ONE sentence without beating around the bush.
4. Describe the ideal contact profile in 1–2 sentences to help the recipient think of someone.
5. Offer to facilitate the introduction (provide text ready to forward or introduce directly).
6. Make it clear that if no one comes to mind right now, there is no problem.
7. Give thanks without creating excessive emotional debt; do not promise anything in return if it is not genuine.

OUTPUT: Complete email with markers [RECIPIENT NAME], [SHARED RESULT], [IDEAL REFERRAL PROFILE], [YOUR NAME], ready to personalize.

EDGE CASES:
- If the recipient is a colleague or ally (not a client): adjust the opening to speak about mutual collaboration instead of results delivered to the client.
- If the company has a referral program with a financial incentive: add mention of the benefit in one sentence at the end, but after the main CTA.
- If the relationship is very recent (< 30 days): postpone the request or focus it on a LinkedIn recommendation before an active referral.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The request is explicit and appears in the first 2 paragraphs.
- It does not sound like a mass campaign; the recipient must feel it is a personalized email.
- Body < 180 words.
- DoD: email with markers, ready to personalize and send with < 2 minutes of editing.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the relationship and the referral profile before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_reactivacion_cli:
[S · SITUATION] A services company has clients who stopped buying or interacting 3 or more months ago without having given explicit negative feedback — they simply went cold. The commercial team needs to reactivate them with an email that recalls the past value, acknowledges the silence without drama, offers a new angle or a fresh reason to reconnect, and leads them to a concrete conversation or action.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete reactivation email (subject line + body) that is personalized, does not sound like a mass campaign, includes a specific reference to the prior relationship, presents a fresh value hook (success case, service update, sector insight), and has a low-friction CTA. Maximum 200 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior commercial director specializing in account retention and reactivation in professional services and B2B technology companies.

ASSUMPTIONS: If the inactivity period is not specified, assume 4–6 months without a transaction or interaction. If the reason for the silence is not known, assume natural drift (no negative incident). If no value hook is provided, invent a plausible one from the technology consulting services sector. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) whether there was an unresolved negative incident, (2) profile of the previously delivered service.

INPUTS: Provide the client's name, last service or project delivered, and if available, a relevant news item or success case. If not, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: personal, referencing the past relationship or the new development, < 60 characters.
2. Open by acknowledging the time without contact naturally, without guilt or drama.
3. Mention the last project or collaboration with a specific detail that demonstrates real memory.
4. Introduce the value hook: service update, result obtained with a similar client, relevant sector insight.
5. Low-friction CTA: propose a 20-minute call or send a free resource, not a full proposal.
6. Close with a warm tone and no pressure; make clear the response can be «not the right time» without consequences.

OUTPUT: Complete email with markers [CLIENT NAME], [LAST PROJECT], [VALUE HOOK], [YOUR NAME], [SPECIFIC CTA], ready to personalize.

EDGE CASES:
- If inactivity was > 12 months: the tone must be more humble; explicitly acknowledge the long time elapsed and do not assume they remember the details.
- If there was an unresolved negative incident: do not send this email; first resolve the incident with an apology/resolution email.
- If the client is in a known restructuring process: focus the hook on cost savings or operational efficiency, not expansion.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The email does not sound like a mass template; at least one specific detail from the client's history is present.
- The CTA requires < 5 minutes of action from the client.
- Body < 200 words.
- DoD: complete email with markers, ready to personalize in < 3 minutes.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the inactivity and the value hook before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_negociacion_prop:
[S · SITUATION] A professional or company received a counter-proposal from a client or vendor — lower price, different conditions, reduced scope, different timeline — and needs to respond by email in a way that keeps the deal alive, defends their position with concrete value arguments, explores points of agreement, and moves the conversation to a next round of negotiation or close, without yielding unnecessarily.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a counter-proposal response email (subject line + body) that: acknowledges the received proposal without outright rejecting it, explains in value terms why the original offer holds or what can be adjusted and under what conditions, identifies one or two possible points of agreement, and proposes a concrete next step (call, meeting, revised version). Maximum 250 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior corporate negotiator specializing in professional services, consulting, and B2B technology contracts; expert in interest-based negotiation techniques (Harvard/BATNA).

ASSUMPTIONS: If the counter-proposal received is not specified, assume the client is requesting a 20% discount on the original proposal without scope changes. If the minimum acceptable position is not defined, assume there is a 10% margin but no more. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 regarding: (1) specific amount or condition of the counter-proposal, (2) whether there is a close deadline for the sender.

INPUTS: Provide a summary of the original proposal and the counter-proposal received, and the minimum acceptable position. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

STEPS:
1. Draft subject line: neutral and constructive, < 60 characters, without unnecessary «Re: Re:».
2. Open by thanking the response and showing willingness to find an agreement.
3. Acknowledge the other side's legitimate interest in obtaining better conditions, without conceding yet.
4. Argue the value of the original proposal with 2–3 concrete points (ROI, differentiator, guarantees), not just price.
5. Propose one or two adjustment alternatives that are not a pure discount: payment term, reduced scope, phases, deferred bonus.
6. Identify the most obvious point of agreement and flag it explicitly.
7. Propose a concrete next step: 30-minute call, meeting, send revised proposal.
8. Close with a collaborative tone, not an ultimatum.

OUTPUT: Complete email with markers [CONTACT NAME], [COMPANY], [COUNTER-PROPOSAL CONDITION], [ALTERNATIVE PROPOSAL 1], [ALTERNATIVE PROPOSAL 2], [NEXT STEP], ready to personalize.

EDGE CASES:
- If the counter-proposal is unreasonable (> 40% discount with no scope change): acknowledge the gap respectfully and request more context before responding with numbers.
- If the close is urgent for the sender: do not show it in the email; maintain position confidently even if there is internal urgency.
- If the counter-proposal comes from a procurement area that does not understand the technical value: redirect the conversation to the end user or technical area in the next step.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The email defends the position with value arguments, not just resistance.
- At least one alternative to a pure discount is proposed.
- Collaborative tone; the recipient must feel the sender wants to reach an agreement.
- DoD: email < 250 words with markers, ready to personalize and send.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the counter-proposal and the minimum acceptable position before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_agradecimiento_p:
[S · SITUATION] After a business meeting — pitch, discovery call, proposal review, kickoff, or progress meeting — the professional who called or led it needs to send a follow-up email that thanks participants for their time, consolidates verbal agreements and commitments in writing, makes it clear who does what and by when, and keeps the momentum of the conversation moving toward the next agreed step.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete post-meeting email (subject + body) that includes: brief and genuine thanks, a summary of key points discussed (3–5 bullets), a table or list of next steps with owner and date, a reminder of the next milestone or scheduled meeting, and a clear CTA to confirm or correct the summary. Maximum 250 words.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project and account manager with 10+ years managing executive client relationships in technology consulting and professional services.

SUPUESTOS: If the meeting type is not specified, assume the first discovery meeting with a prospective consulting client. If the points discussed are not provided, synthesize 4 plausible bullets for that meeting type. If next steps are not given, propose 3 typical actions (proposal submission, technical review, second meeting). Ask only if confidence < 0.85 on: (1) meeting type and participants, (2) specific commitments made.

INSUMOS: Provide meeting type, list of participants, key points discussed, and agreed next steps. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

PASOS:
1. Draft subject: 'Summary and next steps — [meeting] [date]' or similar, < 65 characters.
2. Open with genuine thanks in one sentence (avoid empty phrases like 'it was a pleasure').
3. Include a 'Points discussed' section with 3–5 concise bullets.
4. Include a 'Next steps' section in table or list format: | Action | Owner | Date |.
5. Remind of the next milestone or already-scheduled meeting.
6. Close with CTA: 'Let me know if I should correct anything' or 'Confirm we are aligned'.
7. Ensure the email serves as the written record of verbal commitments.

SALIDA: Complete email with placeholders [MAIN PARTICIPANT NAME], [MEETING TYPE], [MEETING DATE], [POINT 1–5], [ACTION 1–3], [OWNER 1–3], [ACTION DATE 1–3], [NEXT MILESTONE], ready to personalize.

CASOS BORDE:
- If there were unresolved disagreements during the meeting: record them as 'pending definition' in the next steps section, without taking sides.
- If the meeting was very brief or informal: reduce bullets to 2 and remove the table; keep the email < 120 words.
- If there are multiple teams with different responsibilities: create a subsection per team in the next steps.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The email functions as an informal record of minutes: if someone prints it, the commitments are clear.
- No next step lacks an owner or date.
- Body < 250 words.
- DoD: complete email with next-steps table and placeholders, ready to personalize.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the meeting type and agreements before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_onboarding_bienv:
[S · SITUATION] A service company (consulting, SaaS, agency, technology) has just closed a contract with a new client and needs to send the official welcome email at the start of onboarding. This email must set the tone of the relationship, introduce the assigned team, make the first process steps clear, establish realistic expectations about the coming days, and reduce the client's anxiety about what lies ahead.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete onboarding welcome email (subject + body) that conveys genuine enthusiasm, introduces the key team (name + role), details the first 3 process steps in a clear list, indicates the main communication channel and update frequency, and closes with the next concrete milestone. Maximum 280 words.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior Customer Success Director with experience onboarding enterprise clients at technology services companies and consulting firms in Latin America.

SUPUESTOS: If the service is not specified, assume data analytics platform implementation or digital transformation consulting. If the project duration is not given, assume 3 months. If the first steps are not indicated, propose: (1) alignment kick-off, (2) access and documentation collection, (3) diagnostic session. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 on: (1) client name and main contact, (2) assigned team from the provider company.

INSUMOS: Provide client name, contracted service, duration, assigned team, and first steps. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

PASOS:
1. Draft subject: warm and actionable, mentions the client name or the service, < 65 characters.
2. Open with genuine welcome; one sentence conveying pride in having them as a client.
3. Briefly introduce the assigned team: name + role + one line of specialty, in bullets.

SALIDA: Complete email with placeholders [CLIENT NAME], [CONTRACTED SERVICE], [PROJECT LEAD], [MEMBER 2], [STEP 1–3], [COMMUNICATION CHANNEL], [FIRST MILESTONE], [MILESTONE DATE], [DIRECT CONTACT], ready to personalize.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the client is large with multiple stakeholders: include a line inviting them to share the email internally with the team that will be involved.
- If onboarding has a project management platform (Asana, Jira, ClickUp): mention they will receive access within the next 24 hours.
- If this is a client who has previously worked with the company: personalize the welcome acknowledging the prior relationship.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The tone is warm and professional; the client must feel they are in good hands from the first paragraph.
- The first 3 steps are specific and actionable, not generic.
- Body < 280 words.
- DoD: complete email with placeholders, ready to personalize in < 3 minutes.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the service and team before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_escalamiento_int:
[S · SITUATION] A collaborator or manager needs to internally escalate a problem — unresolved risk, project blockage, decision outside their authority, inter-department conflict, at-risk client — to a higher organizational level (director, C-suite, committee) so that action or a decision is taken. The escalation must be perceived as professional, urgent but not alarmist, and must give the recipient all the information needed to act without having to search for it.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete internal escalation email (subject + body) that communicates the problem precisely, includes the minimum necessary context, describes the impact if no action is taken, specifies what is needed from the recipient (decision, resource, authorization, intervention), and proposes a response deadline. Maximum 250 words.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior project and operations manager with experience in executive escalations at technology and consulting companies; expert in high-impact upward communication.

SUPUESTOS: If the problem is not specified, assume a strategic client is at risk of canceling the contract due to delayed deliverables. If the recipient is not indicated, assume the General Director or a VP. If no specific decision is requested, assume authorization is required to reassign resources or grant a deadline extension. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 on: (1) exact nature of the problem, (2) specific decision or action required from the superior.

INSUMOS: Provide problem description, brief chronological context, potential impact, and necessary action from the recipient. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

PASOS:
1. Draft subject: '[ESCALATION]: [short problem description] — decision required before [date]', < 70 characters.
2. Open with a 1-sentence context phrase: when it started and who is involved.
3. Describe the problem in 2–3 sentences without blaming individuals; focus on facts and situation.
4. Indicate the concrete impact if no action is taken (in terms of client, project, money, or reputation).
5. Describe what has already been attempted to resolve without escalating.
6. Specify the decision or concrete action needed from the recipient.
7. Propose a clear deadline: 'I need a response before [date/time]'.
8. Offer availability for an immediate call if necessary.

SALIDA: Complete email with placeholders [RECIPIENT], [PROBLEM], [PROBLEM START], [IMPACT], [PRIOR ACTIONS], [REQUESTED DECISION], [RESPONSE DEADLINE], [YOUR NAME], ready to personalize.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the problem involves an error by another team member: describe without pointing directly; use 'area X' or 'process Y' instead of names.
- If this is the second escalation (the recipient already knows the case): open with 'As I mentioned on [date], the problem persists' and skip to the current status.
- If the problem has legal or contractual implications: explicitly state that a legal counsel review is recommended before acting.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The recipient can act on the information in the email without requesting more context.
- The requested decision or action is specific and unambiguous.
- The tone is urgent but not alarmist or accusatory.
- DoD: email < 250 words with placeholders, ready to send with minimal personalization.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the problem and required action before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_invitacion_event:
[S · SITUATION] A company or professional is organizing an event — webinar, workshop, conference, product launch, executive breakfast, hackathon — and needs to send an email invitation that generates registrations or attendance confirmations (RSVP), conveys the concrete value of the event for the specific recipient, and has a clear, low-friction registration CTA.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a complete event invitation email (subject + body) that includes: the event's value proposition for the recipient in the first sentence, key logistics details (date, time, venue/platform, duration), three specific benefits of attending, speaker(s) or facilitator(s) if applicable, CTA with RSVP button or registration link, and registration deadline. Maximum 220 words in the body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior event marketing and B2B communication specialist with experience generating high-conversion registrations for executive events in Latin America.

SUPUESTOS: If the event type is not specified, assume a 60-minute technology trends webinar with 2 expert speakers. If the audience is not indicated, assume technology and operations directors at medium-to-large companies. If there is no date, use [DATE] as a placeholder. Ask only if confidence < 0.85 on: (1) event topic or value proposition, (2) specific profile of the recipient.

INSUMOS: Provide event name, topic, date/time, platform or venue, speaker(s), and concrete benefits of attending. If not provided, use declared assumptions.

PASOS:
1. Draft subject: generate curiosity or urgency without clickbait, < 60 characters; include date if it is soon.
2. Open with the value proposition for the recipient in the first sentence, before logistics details.
3. Indicate date, time, duration, and platform/venue in 1–2 compact lines.

7. Add a limited-capacity or registration-closing line if real or strategic.
8. Close with a brief line inviting them to share with their team if applicable.

SALIDA: Complete email with placeholders [EVENT NAME], [DATE], [TIME], [DURATION], [PLATFORM/VENUE], [SPEAKER], [BENEFIT 1–3], [RSVP LINK], [REGISTRATION DEADLINE], ready to personalize.

CASOS BORDE:
- If the event is free: highlight this near the CTA without making it the only benefit.
- If the event is paid: do not reveal the price in the initial invitation email; redirect to the landing page for full context.
- If the recipient has previously attended an event in the same series: personalize the opening by acknowledging that prior experience.

[C · CRITERIA]
- The value proposition appears in the first 2 sentences; logistics details are not first.
- The CTA is visible, specific, and has a deadline.
- Body < 220 words.
- DoD: complete email with placeholders, ready to personalize and integrate into a mass-send or individual-send platform.

Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions about the event and recipient profile before drafting.
spec-comunicacion_email_renovacion_contr: [S · SITUATION] A company needs to renew a contract or subscription with a client or supplier whose term is about to expire. The sender wants to maintain the business relationship, highlight the value delivered, and facilitate signing or confirmation without friction. [P · REQUEST] Draft a professional renewal email that achieves: (1) recalling the value received, (2) presenting clear renewal conditions, (3) including a call to action with a deadline, and (4) maintaining the appropriate tone for the type of relationship (formal B2B, friendly SaaS, etc.). Deliverable: email subject line + complete body ready to send. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: Senior commercial communications writer with experience in B2B client retention and contract management. SUPUESTOS: if the user does not provide the relationship type, assume formal B2B [ASSUMPTION]; if no conditions are indicated, assume renewal on the same terms [ASSUMPTION]; if there is no explicit deadline, propose 15 calendar days before expiration [ASSUMPTION]; ask only if the client/product name and expiration date are missing (confidence < 0.85). Extract key data (parties, product/service, dates, conditions) → list of verifiable facts. 3. Draft subject with soft urgency and clear benefit → 1 line ≤ 60 characters. 4. CASOS BORDE: (a) contract with price increase → highlight additional value before the price, frame as investment; (b) deteriorated relationship → reparative tone, offer a prior meeting; (c) multiple client contacts → draft for the economic decision-maker, not the technical contact.
