Trade-off: concrete specificity > generic emotiveness. DoD: opening anecdote written, with delivery notes and bridge, ready to rehearse. Protocolo MetodologIA: differentiate speaker material [REAL] from suggested narrative construction [CONSTRUIDA].
spec-comunicacion_story_storybrand_sb7: [S · SITUATION] A company wants to clarify its brand message so prospects immediately understand what problem it solves, how it solves it, and what they should do next. The current message is confusing, centered on the company rather than the customer. The team needs to apply the 7-block StoryBrand framework to organize communication. [P · REQUEST] A complete BrandScript with the 7 StoryBrand framework blocks (character, problem, guide, plan, call to action, failure avoided, success) plus a 50-word unified message paragraph ready to use in a web header, pitch, or deck. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Brand positioning consultant certified in the StoryBrand framework with experience in messaging for startups and mid-size companies. ASSUMPTIONS: the 7 blocks are (1) A character — ideal customer with desire; (2) Has a problem — external, internal, philosophical; (3) Meets a guide — the brand, with empathy and authority; (4) Who gives them a plan — 3 simple steps; (5) And calls them to action — direct CTA + transitional CTA; (6) That helps them avoid failure — consequences of not acting; (7) And ends with success — concrete positive transformation; if confidence in the ideal customer is below 0.85, ask for the profile before completing block 1. INPUTS: description of the company, its product/service, and its target customer pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Complete block 1: identify the character and their central desire → 2 lines. 2. Complete block 2: articulate external, internal, and philosophical problem → 3 lines. 3. Complete block 3: position the brand as an empathetic guide with authority → 2 lines. 4. Complete block 4: design a plan of 3 simple and memorable steps → 3 bullets. 5. Complete block 5: write direct CTA (buy/demo) and transitional CTA (free resource) → 2 options. 6. Complete block 6: name the main failure the customer wants to avoid → 2 lines. 7. Complete block 7: paint concrete and aspirational success → 2-3 lines. 8. Write a 50-word unified message paragraph → draft + revised version. OUTPUT: "BrandScript SB7" document with the 7 blocks completed, unified paragraph, and suggestions for where to use each block. EDGE CASES: (a) Multiple product lines → build one BrandScript per line and flag the level of fragmentation; (b) Professional services company → adapt the "plan" to a methodology or process; (c) No clear competitor differentiation → flag it in block 3 and propose a unique authority angle. [C · CRITERIA] The character is the customer, never the company. The plan has exactly 3 memorable steps. The unified paragraph can be said in 20 seconds. Trade-off: radical clarity > descriptive completeness. DoD: complete BrandScript with 7 blocks, unified paragraph, and usage suggestions, ready to hand off to the marketing team. Protocolo MetodologIA: mark as [INFERIDO] any block built without explicit data from the user.
spec-comunicacion_story_data_narrativa: [S · SITUATION] An analyst, executive, or corporate communicator has a relevant set of data or statistical results (report, study, business metrics) and needs to transform them into a persuasive narrative that is comprehensible, emotionally resonant, and actionable for a non-technical audience. [P · REQUEST] A data narrative structured in five parts: (1) opening hook with the most impactful figure, (2) context that gives the data meaning, (3) tension or problem the data reveals, (4) solution or recommended action supported by the data, and (5) memorable close with a verbal visualization of the possible future; ready for a presentation, executive report, or article. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data journalist and strategic communicator with experience translating complex analyses into executive and public policy narratives. ASSUMPTIONS: the data are truthful and come from reliable sources; if there are no concrete data, the narrative is built with industry data marked [DATO INDUSTRIA — verify]; the target audience is non-technical unless otherwise indicated; the tone is direct and objective with measured emotional charge; if confidence in the correct interpretation of the data is below 0.85, ask for clarification before continuing. INPUTS: data set, table, report, or statistical summary pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the most impactful figure or data point in the set → opening hook. 2. Add the minimum context needed for the data to make sense (historical comparison, benchmarking, sample n) → 2-3 lines. 3. Articulate the tension or problem the data reveals (what is at stake, who is affected) → 1 paragraph. 4. Connect the data to a concrete and justified action → 1 paragraph with the recommendation. 5. Write the memorable close with a verbal visualization of the future if action is taken → 2-3 lines. 6. Assemble the complete narrative and review for fluency → final artifact of 300-450 words. OUTPUT: Text "Data narrative: [Thematic title]" with the 5 parts clearly structured; figures highlighted in suggested bold; executive-journalistic tone. EDGE CASES: (a) Contradictory or ambiguous data → flag the ambiguity to the user and propose the most conservative interpretation; (b) Sensitive data (about people, vulnerable groups) → use inclusive language and avoid stigmatization; (c) Future projection data → clearly distinguish projection from fact with [PROYECCIÓN]. [C · CRITERIA] The opening figure stops the reader in 5 seconds. The recommendation flows directly from the data, not a generic one. The close is memorable and specific. Trade-off: narrative impact > statistical exhaustiveness. DoD: complete data narrative, in 5 parts, with verified or labeled figures, ready to publish. Protocolo MetodologIA: distinguish [DATO REAL] from [DATO INDUSTRIA] from [PROYECCIÓN] for each figure cited.
spec-comunicacion_story_antes_despues_pu: [S · SITUATION] A communicator, marketer, or consultant needs to build a persuasive message that contrasts the customer's current painful situation with a desirable future situation, and then present their solution as the bridge that makes that transformation possible. The Before-After-Bridge (BAB) structure is one of the highest-converting copywriting formulas in emails, ads, landing pages, and presentations. [P · REQUEST] A complete communication block using the Before-After-Bridge structure in three length versions: short (50-80 words for social media or headline), medium (150-200 words for email or product description), and long (350-450 words for a landing page or proposal section), all ready to copy and adapt. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior direct-response copywriter specializing in BAB, PAS, and AIDA formulas for digital channels and commercial materials. ASSUMPTIONS: the "Before" is the ideal customer's current pain or friction state; the "After" is the desired relief or transformation state; the "Bridge" is the company's specific solution; if the customer's emotional state is not specified, it is inferred from the described pain; the default tone is direct and empathetic; if confidence in the ideal customer is below 0.85, ask for the segment before drafting. INPUTS: product/service description, customer's main pain, and core benefit pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Articulate the "Before" with maximum specificity and emotional resonance → 2-3 lines. 2. Contrast with a concrete and aspirational "After" → 2-3 lines. 3. Present the "Bridge" (the solution) with clarity and credibility → 2-3 lines. 4. Draft the short version (50-80 words) assembling the 3 parts fluently → draft. 5. Expand to medium version (150-200 words) with additional details → draft. 6. Expand to long version (350-450 words) with storytelling, social proof, and CTA → draft. OUTPUT: Document with the 3 versions labeled with their suggested channel; personalization notes for each version; a "BAB Cheat Sheet" of 5 lines with the values of the specific case. EDGE CASES: (a) Product that resolves a desire, not a pain → reframe the "Before" as a state of lack or unsatisfied aspiration; (b) Multiple possible pains → build one BAB version per pain and recommend the most frequent; (c) Technical audience → increase technical specificity in the Bridge and reduce emotional language in the Before. [C · CRITERIA] The "Before" generates immediate recognition ("that is exactly what I feel"). The "After" is concrete, not generic. The "Bridge" connects both states logically and emotionally. Trade-off: pain specificity > breadth of audience. DoD: three versions written and reviewed, with channel notes and cheat sheet, ready to use. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare as [INFERIDO] the customer's emotional state that was not explicitly provided.
spec-comunicacion_story_metafora_analogi: [S · SITUATION] A technical expert, consultant, or science communicator needs to explain a complex, abstract, or specialized concept to an audience that does not share their domain of knowledge. Without a well-built metaphor or analogy, the concept generates confusion, disconnection, or loss of attention. [P · REQUEST] A set of 3 original and concrete metaphors or analogies to explain the specified concept, with: (1) the metaphor stated in one sentence, (2) the development in 3-5 lines, (3) the explicit correspondence point (what maps to what), and (4) the warning of where the metaphor breaks to avoid inducing confusion. Plus a recommendation of which one to use based on the audience. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Scientific communicator and rhetorician specializing in pedagogy of the concept and analogy design for executive, technical, and educational communication. ASSUMPTIONS: the goal of the metaphor is comprehension, not literary decoration; if the audience is not specified, a professional adult without technical domain of the area is assumed; metaphors must come from everyday domains (cooking, construction, travel, sport, nature); if confidence in the concept to explain is below 0.85, ask for a precise definition of the concept before proceeding. INPUTS: technical or complex concept to explain and target audience pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Decompose the concept into its key structural elements → list of 3-5 essential properties. 2. Find an everyday domain that shares the same structure → 3 domain candidates. 3. Develop 3 complete metaphors/analogies, one per candidate → drafts. 4. For each metaphor: identify the explicit correspondence points → mapping table. 5. For each metaphor: identify where the analogy breaks or may confuse → warning. 6. Recommend the best one by audience with justification → final paragraph. OUTPUT: Document "Metaphor set: [Concept]" with the 3 metaphors developed, their correspondence tables, breakage warnings, and final recommendation by audience. EDGE CASES: (a) Concept with no direct physical or everyday equivalent → build composite metaphors (two domains combined) and flag it; (b) Technical audience that knows the domain → use analogies between distinct technical sub-domains; (c) Concept with multiple dimensions → build one metaphor per dimension and warn that no single analogy captures everything. [C · CRITERIA] Each metaphor is understood on the first reading without prior knowledge of the concept. The correspondence points are explicit, not implicit. The breakage warning is exactly 1-2 clear lines. Trade-off: clarity > total technical rigor. DoD: 3 metaphors developed with correspondences, warnings, and recommendation, ready to use in a presentation or text. Protocolo MetodologIA: flag with [SIMPLIFICACIÓN PEDAGÓGICA] any element of the concept that was intentionally simplified for the metaphor to work.
spec-comunicacion_story_arco_emocional: [S · SITUATION] A content creator, speaker, brand writer, or communications director needs to design the emotional arc of a narrative (talk, video, long article, campaign, or content series) so the audience experiences an intentional sequence of emotions that culminates in action or recall. Without a planned emotional arc, narratives are flat, lack tension, or have poorly positioned climaxes. [P · REQUEST] A complete emotional arc design that includes: (1) text diagram of 6-8 emotional nodes with the target emotion, the corresponding narrative stimulus, and the suggested duration or proportion, (2) description of the key moments (opening, point of maximum tension, catharsis/resolution, and close), and (3) an 8-criteria checklist to verify the arc works before publishing. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Creative director and narrative experience designer with expertise in dramatic arcs, audience psychology, and emotional communication for digital and live formats. ASSUMPTIONS: the emotional arc has 6-8 nodes in sequence; available emotions are: curiosity, surprise, tension, empathy, admiration, recognized-frustration, hope, pride, urgency, catharsis, inspiration; the closing node always ends with an activating emotion (inspiration, urgency, hope), never a passive one; if the format and duration are not specified, a video or talk of 10-20 minutes is assumed; if confidence in the narrative topic is below 0.85, ask for the central message before designing. INPUTS: description of the content or narrative (topic, audience, format, central message) pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify the central message that must remain with the audience → 1 sentence. 2. Select the most effective opening emotion for the context → 2-line justification. 3. Map the 6-8 emotional nodes in sequence with their narrative stimulus and duration → table. 4. Identify the point of maximum tension (approx. node 4-5) and its mechanism → description. 5. Design the catharsis or emotional resolution → 2-3 lines. 6. Design the activating close → 2-3 lines. 7. Draft an 8-criteria verification checklist → list. OUTPUT: Document "Emotional arc: [Narrative title]" with the node table, description of key moments, and checklist; technical-creative language. EDGE CASES: (a) Narrative under 5 minutes → compress to 4 essential nodes (opening, tension, resolution, activation); (b) Informational content with no inherent conflict → build tension from cognitive dissonance (surprising fact vs. prior belief); (c) Multi-piece content series → design a macro arc (across the whole series) and micro-arcs per episode. [C · CRITERIA] Each emotional node has a concrete, not generic, narrative stimulus. The point of maximum tension is between 50% and 70% of the total. The close activates without manipulating. Trade-off: emotional intentionality > spontaneous fluency. DoD: arc of 6-8 nodes, key moments described, 8-criteria checklist, ready to guide content production. Protocolo MetodologIA: flag with [SUPUESTO DE AUDIENCIA] each emotion whose receptivity was inferred without prior audience research.
spec-comunicacion_story_pixar_estructura: [S · SITUATION] A communications, marketing, or leadership professional needs to transform a key message — product launch, organizational change, value proposition, or lesson learned — into a memorable story that connects emotionally with the audience. They have the raw message but lack the narrative structure to make it impactful. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete, ready-to-use story applying Pixar's six-step narrative formula (Once upon a time… / Every day… / Until one day… / Because of that… / Until finally… / Ever since that day…), calibrated to the user's specific context. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior narrative writer specialized in corporate storytelling and persuasive communication, with mastery of Pixar's dramatic structures. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste their message or central context; if they do not, apply a generic business transformation example; professional-emotional tone by default; average length per act: 2–4 sentences. INPUTS: message, product, change, or situation the user pastes in the chat. STEPS: 1) Identify the protagonist, central conflict, and transformation from the input. 2) Draft the six Pixar acts with natural transitions and rising tension. 3) Incorporate a sensory detail or statistic in act 3 to anchor credibility. 4) Close act 6 with a hook line linking to the business message. 5) Provide a short version (≤80 words) and a long version (≤300 words). OUTPUT: Two story versions (short and long) with all six acts clearly labeled, plus a suggested usage note. EDGE CASES: (a) very abstract message → ground it in a concrete human anecdote before scaling; (b) story without a clear antagonist → use market friction or internal inertia as the obstacle; (c) mixed audience → write act 5 with a double layer: quantitative result and emotional resonance. [C · CRITERIA] The story must pass the 'why should I care?' test before act 3; each act must advance the tension; the short version must work as a LinkedIn post; DoD: reviewed to contain no empty generalizations or corporate clichés.
spec-comunicacion_story_testimonio_video: [S · SITUATION] A marketing or sales team has information from a satisfied customer — interview, notes, emails, or review — and needs to convert it into a structured script for recording a compelling 60–120 second testimonial video to serve as a conversion asset. [P · REQUEST] Write a complete testimonial video script with a three-act structure (before-situation / transformation / result-proof), with basic camera directions, estimated time per segment, and verbatim lines ready for the customer to read or paraphrase. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior testimonial video scriptwriter with experience producing high-conversion B2B and B2C content. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste customer information (interview, notes, or review); if no data is pasted, use a generic enterprise technology customer profile; warm and authentic tone, not overproduced; target duration 90 seconds unless otherwise indicated. INPUTS: raw customer information (interview, quotes, result metrics). STEPS: 1) Identify the prior problem-situation, the moment of change, and the measurable result. 2) Select the 1–2 most powerful verbatim customer quotes. 3) Draft the script with labeled segments (estimated seconds + text + direction note). 4) Add an opening hook (first 5 seconds) and a close with an implicit call to action. 5) Mark paraphrasing options in brackets to give the customer flexibility. OUTPUT: Script in table format (Segment | Duration | Verbatim Text | Direction Note), plus a flowing text version for the customer to read. EDGE CASES: (a) customer unwilling to share hard data → use perception language ('we felt that…', 'we noticed a change in…'); (b) very long testimonial → highlight the 3 most impactful moments and compress; (c) customer speaks another language → include a localization note. [C · CRITERIA] The hook must capture attention in ≤5 seconds; the result must include at least one concrete indicator; the tone must sound like a real person, not a corporate script; DoD: script tested by reading aloud in ≤120 seconds.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_memo_decision: [S · SITUATION] A leader or management team needs to obtain approval or alignment from a committee or senior executive on a specific decision (investment, process change, hiring, alliance, etc.) and needs a memo of exactly one page that presents the problem, evaluated options, recommendation, and next step, without the recipient needing to read more than necessary. [P · REQUEST] Draft a one-page decision executive memo (≤500 words) with standardized sections, direct C-suite-level language, and an explicit call to action on the last line. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior executive communication advisor with experience drafting memos for boards of directors and management committees. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the decision context; if not, use a technology investment approval example; formal-direct tone; one recommended option among a maximum of three alternatives; fictitious date and signatory if not provided. INPUTS: description of the decision, available options, evaluation criteria, and preferred recommendation. STEPS: 1) Write an executive header (To / From / Date / Subject / Action Required). 2) Draft the 'Context' section in ≤60 words. 3) Draft the 'Options Evaluated' section with a 2–3 row table (Option | Key Benefit | Main Risk). 4) Draft the 'Recommendation' section with justification in ≤80 words. 5) Draft the 'Next Steps' section with 2–3 concrete actions + owner + date. 6) Add a bolded 'Action Required' line as the close. OUTPUT: Ready-to-use memo with all sections completed, in ≤500 words total. EDGE CASES: (a) decision with high political risk → add a 'Critical Assumptions' note before the recommendation; (b) multiple decision-makers → adapt 'To' as a list and reduce technical jargon; (c) extreme urgency → highlight 'Action Required' in the first line as well. [C · CRITERIA] The recipient must understand the decision, options, and recommendation in ≤2 minutes of reading; the recommendation must be a single option with no ambiguity; DoD: memo ≤500 words, one printed page at 11pt.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_resumen_ejecutivo: [S · SITUATION] A professional has a lengthy document — report, study, proposal, research, or technical review — that an executive or committee needs to review but does not have time to read in full. They need a self-contained executive summary that captures the essence of the document in ≤1 page and can be read by the recipient in ≤3 minutes. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured executive summary (≤400 words) with sections: purpose, key findings (3–5 points), strategic implications, recommendations, and next steps; all faithfully extracted from the source document. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior executive communication analyst with experience synthesizing complex reports for management audiences. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the document or its key sections; if not, request the input before proceeding; document is assumed to be in Spanish or will be translated; minimum technical detail in the summary; no claim without support in the source document. INPUTS: complete document or main sections pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1) Read the input and identify the document's central purpose in one sentence. 2) Extract the 3–5 most relevant findings with supporting evidence or figures. 3) Derive 2–3 strategic implications for the organization. 4) Formulate 2–3 actionable recommendations. 5) List 2–3 next steps with a suggested owner. 6) Compose the summary in the indicated order, in ≤400 words. OUTPUT: Complete executive summary with labeled sections, in text format and exportable as a standalone document. EDGE CASES: (a) document without clear conclusions → infer and mark as [INFERENCE]; (b) technical document with specialized jargon → translate to business language; (c) multiple authors with contradictory perspectives → flag the tension in 'Strategic Implications'. [C · CRITERIA] The summary must be understandable without reading the source document; each finding must have explicit support; DoD: ≤400 words, no unsubstantiated opinions, no invented findings.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_brief_proyecto: [S · SITUATION] A sponsor, project manager, or area lead is about to launch a new project and needs an executive kickoff brief that aligns all stakeholders from day one: what will be done, why it matters, who is responsible, what the main milestones are, and what is needed to succeed. The brief must be readable in ≤5 minutes and substantive enough to replace an initial kick-off meeting. [P · REQUEST] Draft an executive project kickoff brief of ≤600 words with standardized sections: strategic context, SMART project objective, scope (in/out), key team and roles, main milestones with tentative dates, initial risks, and success criteria. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project manager with PMP certification and experience in executive communication for initiative launches. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the project description; if no dates are provided, use relative months (Month 1, Month 2, etc.); SMART objective inferred and marked as [ASSUMPTION] if not provided; default team of 3–6 people. INPUTS: project description, objective, available team, key dates, and known constraints. STEPS: 1) Draft strategic context in ≤80 words (why this project now). 2) Formulate the SMART objective in one sentence. 3) List 3–5 in-scope deliverables and 2–3 out-of-scope items. 4) Define key roles in a table (Name/Role | Primary Responsibility | Estimated % Dedication). 5) List 4–6 milestones with tentative dates. 6) Identify 3 initial risks with level (high/medium/low) and suggested mitigation. 7) Define 3–4 measurable success criteria. OUTPUT: Complete brief with all sections, ready to share with the team and sponsors on the first day of the project. EDGE CASES: (a) project without dates → use relative phases and mark as [ASSUMPTION]; (b) project with multiple sponsors → add a 'Governance and Approvals' section; (c) project with high technical component → include a glossary of 3–5 key terms. [C · CRITERIA] The brief must be understandable by any team member without prior knowledge; the objective must be verifiably SMART; DoD: ≤600 words, all sections complete, no unsupported claims.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_actualizacion_est: [S · SITUATION] A project manager or program lead must send a periodic status update to sponsors and the management team. They need a concise status report that uses the RAG traffic-light system (Red / Amber / Green) to communicate project health visually and unambiguously, without the recipient having to read more than one page to understand what is happening and what is needed from them. [P · REQUEST] Produce a RAG traffic-light status report of ≤400 words with sections: period header, overall RAG status with justification, key indicators (schedule / budget / scope / quality / risks) each with its traffic light, period achievements, active blockers, next actions, and a support request if applicable. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior project manager with experience in executive reporting and status communication to management committees. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the period data (progress, issues, metrics); if indicators lack numerical values, assign a qualitative traffic light and mark as [ASSUMPTION]; default period: weekly; Green = on track, Amber = manageable risk, Red = intervention required. INPUTS: period data: progress, issues, schedule/budget/scope metrics. STEPS: 1) Determine overall RAG status based on the most critical indicators. 2) Assign a traffic light to each indicator (schedule, budget, scope, quality, risks). 3) List 2–4 period achievements as bullets. 4) List active blockers with impact and mitigation action. 5) List 3–5 next actions with owner and date. 6) Draft a specific support request if any indicator is Red. OUTPUT: Complete report with traffic-light emojis (🟢🟡🔴) for quick reading, in ≤400 words. EDGE CASES: (a) no budget data → mark that indicator as ⚪ No data; (b) project fully Red → add an 'Escalation Required' note at the top; (c) multiple sub-projects → use a summary table per sub-project before the details. [C · CRITERIA] The recipient must understand project status in ≤90 seconds; every Red indicator must have an identified blocker and a mitigation action; DoD: ≤400 words, all indicators with a traffic light assigned.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_comunicado_cambio: [S · SITUATION] A human resources, internal communications, or general management leader must inform employees about a significant organizational change — restructuring, merger, leadership change, new operating model, headcount reduction, or cultural transformation — and needs an internal announcement that is clear, empathetic, and reduces uncertainty without causing panic or rumors. [P · REQUEST] Draft an internal organizational change announcement of ≤500 words with the following structure: direct subject line, change context, description of the change in plain language, impact on employees, what remains the same, next steps, and a questions channel. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Internal communications and organizational change management specialist with experience in companies of more than 500 employees. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the change details; empathetic-professional tone by default; if no questions channel is defined, suggest an HRBP email or Town Hall; effective date of the change marked as [ASSUMPTION] if not provided; the announcement is signed by the CEO or General Director unless otherwise indicated. INPUTS: description of the change, reasons, expected impact on people and operations, effective date, available communication channels. STEPS: 1) Draft a direct subject line with no euphemisms (≤10 words). 2) Write a context paragraph: why this decision is being made now (≤80 words). 3) Describe the specific change in 2–3 paragraphs, without ambiguity. 4) List in bullets what changes and what does not change for employees. 5) Detail next steps: dates, informational sessions, available resources. 6) Close with a recognition and support paragraph (human tone). 7) Add a questions channel line. OUTPUT: Complete announcement ready to send by email or publish on the intranet, with subject line included. EDGE CASES: (a) headcount reduction → include a paragraph on the support process for affected employees and a confidentiality line; (b) merger/acquisition → do not mention financial details without legal approval (mark as [PENDING LEGAL]); (c) change with high uncertainty → be explicit about what is not yet known and when it will be communicated. [C · CRITERIA] The announcement must answer 'what changes for me?' and 'what do I do now?' before the third paragraph; the tone must be empathetic without being condescending; DoD: ≤500 words, subject line included, no sensitive data left unmarked.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_talking_points: [S · SITUATION] An executive, spokesperson, or area lead must participate in a press interview, panel, client meeting, or public presentation and needs a structured set of talking points that allows them to speak clearly and consistently on a specific topic, anticipate difficult questions, and stay on the key message without improvising dangerous answers. [P · REQUEST] Produce a spokesperson talking points set with: central message (1 phrase), 3–5 main points with supporting evidence, 5–8 anticipated difficult questions with a suggested answer, bridge phrases to redirect toward the central message, and phrases to avoid with alternatives. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior strategic communications and media training advisor with experience preparing spokespersons for media and high-risk audiences. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the topic and context of the appearance; if no specific audience is provided, assume a print press interview; tone according to audience (formal for board, conversational for mass media); minimum 3 difficult questions even if the user does not identify them. INPUTS: topic of the appearance, audience, context (event, crisis, launch), key messages the spokesperson wants to convey, sensitive topics to avoid. STEPS: 1) Define the central message in ≤20 words. 2) Develop 3–5 main points each with supporting evidence or a figure. 3) Draft 5–8 probable difficult questions with a suggested answer of ≤60 words each. 4) Create 3–5 bridge phrases to redirect toward the central message. 5) List 3–5 phrases to avoid with safe alternatives. 6) Add a usage note: when and how to use the document. OUTPUT: Structured talking points document, ready for review and memorization by the spokesperson. EDGE CASES: (a) active crisis → prioritize empathy messages and concrete action over technical explanations; (b) sensitive regulatory topic → add a note 'Validate with legal advisor before use'; (c) international audience → adapt cultural references and avoid local idioms. [C · CRITERIA] The spokesperson must be able to build any answer from the central message in ≤30 seconds; no suggested answer should create greater reputational risk; DoD: central message ≤20 words, all sections complete.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_one_pager_iniciat: [S · SITUATION] An area lead, product manager, or consultant needs to obtain approval, funding, or sponsorship for an internal initiative — new project, program, tool, process, or investment — and their only opportunity is a single page that will reach an executive with little time. The one-pager must sell the initiative in a way that the recipient understands why it matters, what is proposed, and what is expected of them, without needing additional documentation. [P · REQUEST] Draft an initiative sales one-pager of ≤450 words with the following structure: impactful title, problem or gap it addresses, initiative proposal, quantifiable benefits (or estimates), required investment, main mitigated risks, and a clear call to action. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior executive communication and internal sales consultant with experience obtaining initiative approval before management committees. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the initiative description; quantifiable benefits estimated and marked as [ASSUMPTION] if no figures are provided; required investment in orders of magnitude if no exact figures are available; direct-persuasive tone; the decision-maker is a C-suite executive by default. INPUTS: initiative description, problem it solves, expected benefits, approximate investment, identified risks, and desired call to action. STEPS: 1) Draft an impactful title of ≤10 words connecting problem and solution. 2) Describe the problem or gap in ≤80 words with evidence or data. 3) Present the proposal in ≤100 words with a clear solution mechanism. 4) List 3–4 quantifiable benefits (savings, speed, ROI, reduced risk). 5) State the required investment with a high-level breakdown. 6) Name 2 main risks with mitigation in one line each. 7) Close with a specific call to action ('Approve the pilot', 'Assign the team', etc.). OUTPUT: Complete one-pager with all sections, ready to print or send as a PDF. EDGE CASES: (a) no benefit figures → use industry benchmarks and mark as [EXTERNAL REFERENCE]; (b) initiative with cross-functional impact → add a section on areas that benefit; (c) decision-maker with a financial profile → place the estimated ROI in the first visible line. [C · CRITERIA] The executive must understand why to approve in ≤2 minutes of reading; the call to action must be a single, specific one; DoD: ≤450 words, all sections complete, figures or estimates present.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_briefing_prensa: [S · SITUATION] A public relations, corporate communications, or marketing team needs to inform media about a relevant event — product launch, strategic alliance, executive appointment, financial results, event, or social-impact initiative — and requires a press release or media briefing structured according to international journalistic standards to maximize the likelihood of coverage. [P · REQUEST] Draft a press release or media briefing of ≤600 words with standard journalistic structure: headline with an active verb, subheadline that expands, lead (who-what-when-where-why in ≤50 words), inverted pyramid body, spokesperson quote, company boilerplate, and contact details. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior public relations writer with experience in print and digital media and international corporate communications agencies. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the event data to communicate; if there is no real spokesperson quote, draft an attributable quote and mark as [PENDING APPROVAL]; distribution date assumed as immediate; if there is no boilerplate, draft a generic one based on available data. INPUTS: description of the event, who is involved, when it occurs, why it matters, key figures or data, spokesperson quote, and company boilerplate. STEPS: 1) Draft a headline of ≤12 words with an active verb in present or recent past tense. 2) Draft a subheadline that completes or contrasts the headline (≤20 words). 3) Draft a lead with the 5Ws in ≤50 words. 4) Develop the body from most to least important information (inverted pyramid), 2–3 paragraphs. 5) Insert the spokesperson quote with name and title. 6) Add the company boilerplate. 7) Add the PR contact block. OUTPUT: Complete press release ready to distribute, in standard format with a 'FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE' or 'EMBARGO UNTIL [DATE]' line as applicable. EDGE CASES: (a) event with risk of negative interpretation → structure the lead from the benefit and place mitigating context in paragraph 2; (b) multiple spokespersons → designate a primary spokesperson and move additional quotes to paragraph 4; (c) international audience → avoid local idioms and adapt units of measure. [C · CRITERIA] A journalist must understand the news reading only the lead; the headline must be publishable without modification; DoD: ≤600 words, all sections present, no quote without attribution.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_carta_inversionis: [S · SITUATION] A CEO, CFO, or founder must periodically communicate to investors, strategic partners, or key stakeholders the state of the business, the period's results, the important decisions made, and the vision for the future, maintaining trust and credibility even when there is bad news. The letter must be direct, transparent, and calibrated to the financial sophistication of the recipient. [P · REQUEST] Draft a letter to investors or key stakeholders of ≤700 words with the following structure: executive-tone opening, period results summary (with at least 3 key indicators), strategic decisions taken and their rationale, current challenges addressed honestly, vision and priorities for the next period, and a close with a call to confidence. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior financial communications and investor relations advisor with experience in startups, growth-stage companies, and listed companies. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the period data; estimated indicators are flagged as [ASSUMPTION] if exact figures are unavailable; executive-transparent tone by default; quarterly letter by default; signed by the CEO unless otherwise indicated. INPUTS: period results (revenue, growth, key metrics), strategic decisions made, current challenges, vision for the next period, and any relevant milestones. STEPS: 1) Draft an executive opening that sets the tone and frames the period (≤60 words). 2) Summarize results with 3-5 key indicators and a comparison vs. the prior period or target. 3) Explain 2-3 strategic decisions made with their rationale in ≤100 words. 4) Name 2-3 current challenges honestly along with a response plan. 5) Present the vision and 3-4 priorities for the next period. 6) Close with a paragraph of confidence and commitment (≤60 words). OUTPUT: Complete letter with greeting, structured body, and signature, ready to send as a PDF or formal email. EDGE CASES: (a) results below target → be transparent about causes before discussing the recovery plan; (b) material fact not previously disclosed → flag as [REQUIRES LEGAL VALIDATION]; (c) multiple types of investors → use accessible language and add a glossary if technical terms are present. [C · CRITERIA] The investor must understand what happened, why, and what will be done about it before the third paragraph; the letter must contain no unsupported promises; DoD: ≤700 words, minimum 3 indicators with figures or estimates, no promise without supporting evidence.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_mensaje_crisis: [S · SITUATION] An organization faces a crisis situation — product or service failure, security incident, accident, labor conflict, viral communications error, public lawsuit, environmental damage, or any event that threatens its reputation — and needs to issue an urgent, calibrated message within the first hours of the incident to control the narrative, demonstrate accountability, and preserve the trust of key audiences. [P · REQUEST] Draft a crisis communication message of ≤350 words for the primary affected audience (customers, employees, press, regulators, or community as applicable), with the following structure: acknowledgment of the facts, expression of empathy, description of actions taken, update commitment, and contact channel; in an empathetic-responsible tone without premature admission of legal liability. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior crisis communications advisor with experience in reputation management, media relations, and management of high-impact incidents. ASSUMPTIONS: the user will paste the known facts of the incident; if there is uncertainty about the causes, assume they are under investigation; never invent unconfirmed data; if the user does not specify the distribution channel, assume a public statement on the website and social media; empathetic-responsible tone without admission of legal liability. INPUTS: incident description, confirmed facts, affected persons or groups, actions taken to date, intended distribution channel. STEPS: 1) Draft an opening that acknowledges the facts without minimizing or exaggerating them (≤40 words). 2) Express empathy toward those affected in ≤30 words. 3) Describe concrete actions taken or underway (minimum 2 actions). 4) Provide an update commitment with a specific channel and frequency. 5) Add direct contact information for those affected. 6) Review that no phrase implies admission of legal liability and flag sensitive phrases as [VALIDATE WITH LEGAL]. OUTPUT: Complete crisis message, ready to publish or send, with a long version (≤350 words) and a short version for social media (≤280 characters). EDGE CASES: (a) incident with serious victims → prioritize acknowledgment of the people over corporate reputation in the opening paragraph; (b) crisis caused by a third party (supplier, individual employee) → establish distance without evading supervisory responsibility; (c) unconfirmed information → be explicit about what is not yet known and when an update will be provided. [C · CRITERIA] The message must not generate new unanswered questions; empathy must be specific, not generic; DoD: ≤350 words, minimum 2 concrete actions, update commitment with date or frequency, no phrase implying unvalidated legal liability.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_acta_reunion:
[S · SITUATION] The team has just concluded a working meeting (kick-off, sprint review, architecture committee, strategic alignment session, etc.) and needs a formal record that serves as the official document with traceability of decisions made and commitments acquired.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a structured set of minutes that includes: meeting header, list of attendees with roles, agenda covered, summary of key discussions, decisions made (with brief justification), action table (owner, deadline, description), next steps, and an approval section.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior executive writer with experience in corporate governance and agile project documentation.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no organizational format is specified, use a neutral professional format. If no action deadline is indicated, flag as [TO BE DEFINED]. If the level of detail in the input is low, infer reasonable context and declare it.
INPUTS: Raw notes, transcript, or summary of the meeting pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Identify and structure the header (meeting name, date, time, location/platform, convener).
2. List attendees with name, role, and organization.
3. Map the actual agenda covered vs. the planned agenda.
4. Draft a discussion summary per agenda item (2-4 sentences each).
5. Extract and number decisions with a one-line justification.
6. Build the action table: ID, description, owner, deadline, initial status.
7. Draft the next steps section and the date of the next meeting if applicable.
8. Include an approval/signature block.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with clearly demarcated sections, action table in Markdown table format, ready to export to PDF or share in a documentation repository.
EDGE CASES:
- If key attendees are missing: add the note [VERIFY WITH CONVENER] next to the empty slot.
- If there are contradictory decisions in the notes: document both versions and flag [REQUIRES CONFIRMATION].
- If the meeting produced no formal decisions: document it as an 'informational session' and list only actions and next steps.

[C · CRITERIA] The minutes are approvable if: every decision has at least one associated owner; each action has a deadline or an explicit [TO BE DEFINED]; there is no ambiguity about who must act; the document is self-contained (understandable without having attended the meeting). Commitment: executive brevity over exhaustiveness; clarity over formality.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Document with traceability — every decision has an owner, every commitment has a date.
spec-comunicacion_ejec_resumen_bloi:
[S · SITUATION] A professional needs to communicate a complex tactical situation (production incident, analysis result, change proposal, project update) to an executive or multi-level audience that has no time to read lengthy documents and needs to grasp the essentials within the first ten seconds.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a tactical communication using the BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) framework: the conclusion/required action comes first, followed by the minimum necessary context, supporting evidence, and an explicit call-to-action. Maximum 200 words in the main body.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Strategic communicator trained in military and executive communication; expert in high-information-density messages.
ASSUMPTIONS: Primary audience is management or C-level with 60 seconds available. If urgency is not specified, assume medium urgency. If there are multiple audiences, prioritize the highest-ranking one.
INPUTS: Description of the situation, relevant data, and the decision or action needed from the audience, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Extract the most important conclusion or required action — this is the first sentence.
2. Write 1-2 sentences of minimal context (what happened, when, magnitude).
3. Add 2-3 evidence or concrete data points in a list.
4. Draft a specific, measurable call-to-action with a date if applicable.
5. Add a 'For more detail' section with 1-2 optional sentences.
OUTPUT: Structured text block (not necessarily Markdown) of maximum 200 words, with the BLUF line highlighted at the top, evidence list, and final CTA.
EDGE CASES:
- If the message has no clear action: produce it anyway with the CTA flagged [DEFINE ACTION] and a note.
- If the data is contradictory: include only the most conservative figure and flag [ASSUMPTION].
- If the audience is technical rather than executive: maintain the BLUF structure but allow 50 additional technical words.

[C · CRITERIA] The message is valid if: the first sentence expresses the conclusion without ambiguity; a reader can act correctly by reading only the first sentence; the full body is readable in under 60 seconds; the CTA is specific and attributable.

Protocolo MetodologIA: The conclusion first, always — context serves the message, not the other way around.
spec-comunicacion_doc_readme_proyecto:
[S · SITUATION] A development or architecture team has a software repository or technical project that lacks effective initial documentation. New team members take days to understand the purpose, the architecture, the local setup, and the contribution workflows, causing productivity loss and errors in their first days.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete onboarding-oriented README.md that allows a new technical team member to understand the project, set up the local environment, and make their first contribution in under two hours.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior technical writer with experience in documenting open-source and enterprise software projects; familiar with GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket conventions.
ASSUMPTIONS: Technology stack inferred from the provided context. If no license is specified, omit the license section. If no architecture is indicated, describe only the visible entry layer.
INPUTS: Project description, technology stack, known setup commands, and branch structure, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Draft status badge + project name and description in 2-3 sentences.
2. Create a 'What this project does' section with purpose, audience, and main use cases.
3. Write a 'High-level architecture' section with an ASCII diagram or structured text.
4. Document the 'Prerequisites' section with exact versions or ranges.
5. Write the 'Local setup' section with copyable step-by-step commands.
6. Add an 'Environment variables' section with a name/description/default-value table.
7. Document the 'Workflow and branches' section with naming conventions.
8. Include a 'How to contribute' section with steps from fork to PR.
9. Add a 'Contact / Maintainers' section and useful links.
OUTPUT: Complete Markdown file with section anchors, GitHub-compatible automatic table of contents, and formatted code blocks.
EDGE CASES:
- If the project is internal and must not be public: include a confidentiality notice at the top.
- If the stack is heterogeneous (multiple services): create subsections per service in Setup.
- If there is no architecture information: omit the diagram and add a [DIAGRAM PENDING] placeholder.

[C · CRITERIA] The README is valid if: a developer who has never seen the project can complete `git clone` + setup in under 2 hours; every command is copyable without modification; sections are navigable via the table of contents; no instructions assume undocumented prior knowledge.

Protocolo MetodologIA: An effective README is the first day of work for the next team member — write it for someone who does not yet know the project.
spec-comunicacion_doc_guia_usuario:
[S · SITUATION] A functionality, tool, process, or product has been developed or updated and end users need practical documentation that takes them from zero to completing a concrete task without needing human support.

[P · REQUEST] Draft a step-by-step user guide covering everything from prerequisites to verification of the expected result, with suggested screenshots and warning notes at critical points.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: User experience and technical documentation specialist; masters task-based writing style and the minimum progression principle.
ASSUMPTIONS: End user has basic domain knowledge but no prior experience with this specific functionality. If no platform is specified, assume desktop web browser. If no version is indicated, document for the most recent available version.
INPUTS: Description of the functionality or process to document, known steps, system name, and target audience, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Draft the introduction: what the user achieves upon completing this guide (concrete result).
2. List prerequisites: access, permissions, required prior tools.
3. Structure numbered steps with action verbs at the start ('Click on...', 'Enter the value...', 'Select...').
4. Insert [NOTE], [WARNING], and [TIP] callouts at critical points.
5. Add screenshot suggestions with a description in brackets [SCREENSHOT: description].
6. Draft the verification section: how the user knows they completed the process correctly.
7. Add a troubleshooting section with the 3-5 most common errors and their resolution.
OUTPUT: Structured Markdown document with numbering, note/warning callouts, screenshot suggestions, and a verification and troubleshooting section.
EDGE CASES:
- If the process has alternative paths (different roles, different platforms): create explicit branches with headers 'If you are [ROLE A]' / 'If you use [PLATFORM B]'.
- If the process is very long (more than 15 steps): divide into phases with verifiable intermediate objectives.
- If the functionality changes frequently: add a version note and last-verified date.

[C · CRITERIA] The guide is valid if: a new user can complete the task on the first attempt by following only the guide; each step has an action and an observable result; the verification section unambiguously confirms success; the troubleshooting section covers at least the 3 most common errors.

Protocolo MetodologIA: A good user guide eliminates the need to ask — every step anticipates the doubt of the next one.
spec-comunicacion_doc_faq_estructurada:
[S · SITUATION] A product, service, process, or policy generates a recurring volume of repeated questions to the support, sales, or documentation team. These questions come from users with different search intents: some want to understand ('what is it?'), others want to do something ('how do I?'), others compare ('what's the difference between?'), and others solve problems ('why doesn't it work?').

[P · REQUEST] Create a FAQ section structured by search intent categories, with questions phrased as a real user would ask them and direct answers of maximum 120 words each.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Content strategist and technical writer with experience in conversational SEO and knowledge base design; familiar with the Moz and Google search intent taxonomy.
ASSUMPTIONS: Mixed audience (technical and business users) unless otherwise specified. If no question count is specified, generate between 15 and 25. Answers use direct language without internal jargon unless necessary.
INPUTS: Description of the product, service, or process; known frequently asked questions or problematic topics; target audience, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Classify or infer questions into 4 categories: Informational ('What is...?'), Procedural ('How do I...?'), Comparative ('What's the difference between...?'), Problem-solving ('Why doesn't...?').
2. Phrase each question as a real user would write it in a search engine or chatbot.
3. Draft a direct answer (maximum 120 words): answer the question in the first sentence, then briefly expand.
4. Add a suggested internal link or reference if applicable, flagged as [LINK: description].
5. Review that there are no duplicate or overlapping questions.
6. Order questions within each category by estimated frequency (highest to lowest).
OUTPUT: Markdown document with sections by intent category, questions in bold as H3 headers, and answers in paragraph form; include a table of contents anchor.
EDGE CASES:
- If there are sensitive questions (legal, pricing, privacy): draft a conservative answer and flag [VALIDATE WITH LEGAL/COMPLIANCE].
- If a question has no available answer: include it anyway with the response 'This information is available at [LINK] or by contacting [AREA]'.
- If the domain is highly technical: add a glossary of 5-10 terms at the end.

[C · CRITERIA] The FAQ is valid if: each answer responds to the question in the first sentence; no questions are answered with 'it depends' without giving at least two concrete cases; all 4 intent categories are represented; a user can resolve their question without contacting support in at least 70% of cases.

Protocolo MetodologIA: A useful FAQ speaks the user's language, not the organization's — phrase questions the way someone who is searching would ask them.
spec-comunicacion_doc_runbook_operativo:
[S · SITUATION] An operations, DevOps, SRE, or technical support team needs to document a critical procedure (deployment, rollback, incident escalation, backup, credential rotation, etc.) so that any team member can execute it correctly under pressure, even at 3 AM, without needing to consult the original author.

[P · REQUEST] Produce a complete operational runbook with verifiable execution steps, activation conditions, success/failure criteria, and rollback or escalation procedures.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior site reliability engineer (SRE) with experience in operational documentation for high-availability systems; applies the Google SRE runbook standard.
ASSUMPTIONS: Executor has access to the systems mentioned. If no operating system is specified, assume Linux. If there is no rollback information, document the section as [ROLLBACK PROCEDURE PENDING]. If no RTO is indicated, assume expected resolution in under 30 minutes.
INPUTS: Procedure name, systems involved, known steps, required tools, and success criteria, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Document the header: procedure name, owner, version, last-verified date, criticality level.
2. Write the 'When to run this runbook' section: activation conditions with concrete examples.
3. List prerequisites: access, tools, environment variables, permissions.
4. Document numbered execution steps with: exact command in a code block, expected result, verification command, and action if it fails.
5. Add a success verification section with a confirmation command or observable metric.
6. Document the rollback section with ordered steps.
7. Include an escalation section: who to contact, in what order, with what information.
8. Add a change history at the bottom.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with code blocks, escalation contact table, change history section, and criticality header.
EDGE CASES:
- If the procedure has destructive steps (data deletion, restart of critical services): add a [CRITICAL WARNING] block with an explicit confirmation checkpoint.
- If there are dependencies on external systems (third parties): document the fallback if the external system is unavailable.
- If the procedure varies by environment (dev/staging/prod): create a differences table by environment.

[C · CRITERIA] The runbook is valid if: an operator without prior context can execute it without questions; every command has its expected result documented; there is a rollback section even if incomplete; escalation has real names and channels (not generic ones); destructive steps have explicit checkpoints.

Protocolo MetodologIA: A runbook that requires questions during an incident has failed its purpose — write it for someone who hasn't slept and is under pressure.
spec-comunicacion_doc_release_notes:
[S · SITUATION] A product or development team has just published a new version of their software (major, minor, or patch) and needs to communicate the changes in a way that end users understand what improved, what was fixed, and what they need to be aware of, without having to read the commit diff or technical backlog.

[P · REQUEST] Draft user-oriented release notes that communicate the value of the changes, not just their technical existence; with sections differentiated by type of change and clear signaling for changes that require user action.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior product writer with experience in release communications for SaaS products and enterprise software; familiar with the release notes style of Notion, Linear, Figma, and GitHub.
ASSUMPTIONS: Mixed audience (technical and business users). If no version number is specified, use [v0.0.0]. If a technical change has no visible impact for the user, omit it or group it under 'Internal improvements'. If there are no breaking changes, omit that section.
INPUTS: Version number, list of changes (commits, tickets, technical description), release date, and target audience, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Draft the header with version number, date, and the release's value phrase (what this version achieves in business terms).
2. Create the 'New Features' section with new changes explained in user benefit terms (not technical implementation).
3. Create the 'Improvements' section with changes to existing functionality.
4. Create the 'Fixes' section with resolved bugs, describing the symptom the user experienced.
5. If applicable: create a '⚠ Changes requiring your attention' section for breaking changes or required migrations with action steps.
6. Add an optional 'Coming Soon' section with 1-3 upcoming roadmap items.
7. Include a link to the full changelog and support channel.
OUTPUT: Markdown document with optional section emojis, scannable structure, important changes highlighted, and a support CTA at the end.
EDGE CASES:
- If there are breaking changes: they always appear first, with migration steps or a mandatory link.
- If the version only has security fixes: create a security section with a description of the impact without revealing vulnerability details.
- If the technical changelog is very long: group similar changes into a single summary line.

[C · CRITERIA] The notes are valid if: a non-technical user can understand what changed and whether it affects them; breaking changes are visible immediately without needing to read the full document; each 'New Feature' is described in user benefit terms, not implementation terms; fixes describe the symptom, not the technical fix.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Release notes talk about what the user experiences, not what the developer implemented — translate code into value.
spec-comunicacion_doc_politica_interna:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs to formalize a rule, guideline, or internal procedure (acceptable use policy, onboarding procedure, password security policy, remote work policy, incident management procedure, etc.) in a way that is comprehensible, actionable, and applicable by all members without ambiguity.

[P · REQUEST] Draft an internal policy or procedure document that complies with the standard elements of corporate governance: purpose, scope, definitions, responsibilities, procedure, exceptions, sanctions if applicable, and change control.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Corporate governance specialist and organizational policy writer; familiar with ISO 27001, COBIT, and enterprise compliance frameworks.
ASSUMPTIONS: Medium-to-large organization with multiple functional areas. If no effective date is indicated, use [APPROVAL DATE + 1 YEAR]. If no sanctions are specified, include a section with placeholder text. If no responsible area is indicated, assume the area of the person making the request.
INPUTS: Policy or procedure name, topic it regulates, scope of application, known rules, and responsible area, pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Draft the formal header: document code, version, effective date, responsible area, classification.
2. Write the 'Purpose' section: why this policy exists in 2-3 sentences.
3. Write the 'Scope' section: who it explicitly applies to and who it explicitly does not apply to.
4. Draft the 'Definitions' section: glossary of key terms used in the policy.
5. Document the 'Responsibilities' section: role → concrete responsibility table.
6. Draft the 'Policy / Procedure' section: rules or numbered steps, written in mandatory active voice ('Employees must...', 'The IT area ensures...').
7. Include the 'Exceptions' section: how to request an exception and who approves them.
8. Include the 'Non-compliance and sanctions' section if applicable.
9. Add a 'Change History' table and an approval section with signatures.
OUTPUT: Formal Markdown document with document control header, numbered sections, responsibilities table, and approval block.
EDGE CASES:
- If the policy has legal implications (GDPR, labor law, contractual): add a [REQUIRES LEGAL REVIEW] note before approval.
- If there is a conflict with an existing policy: explicitly document which policy it replaces or complements.
- If it applies to multiple countries with different legislation: create an appendix per jurisdiction.

[C · CRITERIA] The policy is valid if: a new employee can read it and know exactly what they must and must not do; every rule is written without ambiguity ('must' for mandatory, 'may' for discretionary, 'must not' for prohibited); responsibilities are assigned by role, not by person's name; a documented exception mechanism exists.

Protocolo MetodologIA: A clear policy is one that no one needs to interpret — write it for someone who was not in the meeting where it was decided.
spec-comunicacion_doc_tutorial_aprendiza:
[S · SITUATION] An education, product, or development team wants users to learn a skill, concept, or feature through a progressive tutorial that combines conceptual explanation with guided practice, so that by the end of the tutorial the learner can apply what they learned independently.

[P · REQUEST] Design and write a guided learning tutorial with a pedagogical structure: learning objective, minimal conceptual context, progressive practical exercises with solutions, comprehension checkpoints, and an applicable final synthesis.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior instructional designer with experience in project-based learning, Bloom's taxonomy, and interactive technical tutorials (Learn.co, freeCodeCamp, exercism.io style).
SUPUESTOS: Learner with prior knowledge of the adjacent domain but no experience with the specific topic. If no duration is specified, design for 30-60 minutes. If no practice environment is indicated, assume web or local terminal according to the domain.
INSUMOS: Tutorial topic, learner level, assumed prior skills, available practice environment, and expected learning outcome, pasted below.
PASOS:
1. Write the header: tutorial title, estimated duration, difficulty level, prerequisites.
2. Write the 'What you will learn' section: 3-5 learning objectives in observable format ('By the end, you will be able to…').
3. Write the 'Context' section (maximum 200 words): the central concept explained with an analogy and the problem it solves.
4. Structure progressive practice modules (3-5 modules): each one with (a) minimal new concept, (b) annotated example, (c) exercise with clear instructions, (d) expandable solution [SOLUTION], and (e) verification checkpoint.
5. Add the 'Final challenge' section: an integrative exercise that combines all modules.
6. Write the 'What you learned' section as a synthesis + connection with the next level of learning.
SALIDA: Markdown tutorial with sections per module, code blocks formatted by language, exercises marked with [EXERCISE], solutions marked with [SOLUTION], checkpoints with [CHECKPOINT], and a final challenge with estimated difficulty.
CASOS BORDE:
- If the domain requires a specific execution environment: include an 'Environment setup' section at the beginning with exact commands.
- If the learner may have a very heterogeneous background: add a 'If you already know X, you can skip to…' section at the beginning.
- If the topic is too extensive for a single tutorial: split into a tutorial series and document the series map.

[C · CRITERIA] The tutorial is valid if: learning objectives are observable and verifiable; each module introduces exactly one new skill; the final challenge cannot be solved without having completed all modules; the solution to each exercise is available but not immediately obvious.

Protocolo MetodologIA: An effective tutorial makes the learner build, not just read — each module ends with something that works.
spec-comunicacion_doc_referencia_api:
[S · SITUATION] A development team has built or updated a functionality, API endpoint, library module, or system component and needs technical reference documentation that serves both as an entry point for new integrators and as a quick reference for experienced developers.

[P · REQUEST] Produce complete reference documentation for the functionality with: purpose description, input parameters with types and validations, response structure with all fields, possible error codes, functional usage examples, and notes on non-obvious behaviors.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Technical writer specializing in API and SDK documentation; knowledgeable in OpenAPI 3.0 standards, Python/TypeScript docstrings, Stripe Docs and Twilio Docs style.
SUPUESTOS: Audience is technical developers with 2+ years of experience. If no API version is specified, document as v1. If there is no rate limit information, include a section with [TO BE DEFINED]. If no authentication is specified, assume standard Bearer Token.
INSUMOS: Name and description of the functionality, HTTP method if applicable, known parameters, response structure, and observed error cases, pasted below.
PASOS:
1. Write the header: functionality name, version, HTTP method if applicable, path/signature, required access level.
2. Write the 'Description' section: what it does, when to use it, and when not to use it.
3. Document the 'Input parameters' section: table with columns name, type, required/optional, description, validations, and default value.
4. Document the 'Response structure' section: table or annotated JSON with all fields, types, and description.
5. Document the 'Response codes' section: table with HTTP code, error name, and description of the scenario that triggers it.
6. Write the 'Usage examples' section: minimum 2 examples (happy path + common error) with complete request and response in code blocks.
7. Add the 'Notes and special behaviors' section: edge cases, idempotency, rate limits, deprecations.
SALIDA: Markdown document with parameter tables, formatted JSON/YAML/cURL code blocks, examples section with complete request+response, and error codes table.
CASOS BORDE:
- If the functionality behaves differently by environment (sandbox vs. production): document differences in a table.
- If there are deprecated fields: mark them with ~~strikethrough~~ and a migration note.
- If the functionality is asynchronous: document the callback or polling mechanism.

[C · CRITERIA] The documentation is valid if: a developer can integrate the functionality using only this reference without consulting the source code; all required parameters are documented with their exact type; examples are executable without modification using test credentials; all known error codes have a description of the scenario.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Reference documentation is the system's contract with the world — each documented field is a promise the system must keep.
spec-comunicacion_doc_adr_decision:
[S · SITUATION] A software or technology architecture team has made a significant technical design decision (database choice, communication pattern, framework, authentication strategy, deployment approach, etc.) and needs to document it in a structured way so that future team members understand the context, the alternatives considered, and the reasons for the chosen path, without needing to interview the decision-makers.

[P · REQUEST] Write a complete ADR (Architecture Decision Record) following Michael Nygard's format with status, date, consequences, and conformance extensions, to serve as a permanent reference in the repository.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Senior software architect with experience in distributed engineering teams; knowledgeable in Michael Nygard, Alexandros Marinos (Y-Statements) ADR formats, and the ADR style of Amazon, Netflix, and Thoughtworks.
SUPUESTOS: Audience is engineers who will join the project in the future. If no date is specified, use the current date. If no alternatives are documented, infer at least 2 reasonable options and mark them [INFERENCE]. If no status is indicated, use 'Proposed'.
INSUMOS: Topic of the decision, technical or business context, options considered, reasons for the choice, and known consequences, pasted below.
PASOS:
1. Write the header: ADR number, descriptive title, status (Proposed/Accepted/Deprecated/Superseded), date, and authors.
2. Write the 'Context' section: the technical or business situation that forces the decision; what would happen if no decision is made.
3. Write the 'Decision' section: the choice in a single direct sentence ('We have decided to use X for Y').
4. Document the 'Alternatives considered' section: table with each option, its advantages, disadvantages, and reason it was rejected.
5. Document the 'Consequences' section: list of positive, negative, and neutral consequences of the decision made.
6. Add the 'Conformance' section: how compliance with this decision is verified (metrics, tools, reviews).
7. Include the 'Notes' section: links to related documents, related ADRs, relevant tickets or PRs.
SALIDA: Markdown document with complete ADR structure, alternatives table, differentiated consequences list (positive/negative/neutral), and conformance section.
CASOS BORDE:
- If the decision is under debate (no consensus): mark status as 'Proposed' and document each position's arguments without bias.
- If a previous decision becomes obsolete: document the new ADR as 'Supersedes ADR-XXX' and update the old ADR with status 'Superseded by ADR-YYY'.
- If the decision is experimental: use status 'Experimental' with a mandatory review date.

[C · CRITERIA] The ADR is valid if: an engineer joining the project 2 years from now can understand why this decision was made without interviewing anyone; the context section explains what problem forces the decision; the alternatives are documented with enough honesty to understand why they were not chosen; the negative consequences are not minimized.

Protocolo MetodologIA: An ADR is a letter to the future team — write the context that seems obvious today, because in two years it no longer will be.
spec-comunicacion_doc_changelog_keepacha:
[S · SITUATION] A software project needs to maintain or generate a CHANGELOG.md file that records in a structured and human-readable way all relevant changes in each version, following the Keep a Changelog standard (keepachangelog.com) and semantic versioning (semver.org), so that users, integrators, and contributors can understand what changed in each release without reading the commit history.

[P · REQUEST] Generate or update a CHANGELOG.md that strictly follows the Keep a Changelog format, with entries organized by version in descending order, correct change categories, and an [Unreleased] section for pending release changes.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROL: Technical writer specializing in release management and semantic versioning; deeply knowledgeable in keepachangelog.com v1.1.0, semver.org v2.0.0, and the conventions of projects like curl, Vue.js, and Rails.
SUPUESTOS: Project uses semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). If no release date is specified, use [YYYY-MM-DD]. If changes are technical descriptions (commits), translate them to user-oriented language. If there is no [Unreleased] section, create an empty one.
INSUMOS: List of changes per version (commits, tickets, or descriptions), version numbers, and release dates, pasted below.
PASOS:
1. Create the CHANGELOG header with a link to keepachangelog.com and semver.org.
2. Create the [Unreleased] section at the top (always present, empty if no pending changes).
3. For each version in descending order: create a `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` header with a commit comparison link.
4. Within each version, classify the changes into the standard categories (include only those with entries): Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security.
5. Write each entry as a bullet point beginning with a past-tense verb ('Added…', 'Fixed…', 'Removed…') describing the impact visible to the user.
6. Add a version comparison links section at the bottom of the file in the format `[X.Y.Z]: https://…`.
SALIDA: Complete and valid CHANGELOG.md file per Keep a Changelog v1.1.0, with [Unreleased] section, versions in descending order, correct categories, and comparison links at the bottom.
CASOS BORDE:
- If an entry has a breaking change: prefix with '**BREAKING CHANGE:**' in bold within the Changed or Removed category.
- If there are multiple similar changes that are hard to distinguish: group similar changes in one entry with a nested list.
- If the project has no prior version history: create only [Unreleased] + [0.1.0] as the first version.

[C · CRITERIA] The CHANGELOG is valid if: it follows Keep a Changelog v1.1.0 format without deviations; each entry describes the impact visible to the user, not the internal implementation; [Unreleased] is always present; breaking changes are in bold; comparison links are present at the bottom.

Protocolo MetodologIA: A changelog is the project's memory for those who were not there — each entry is a transparency contract with users.
spec-comunicacion_doc_glosario_terminos: [S · SITUATION] A product, technology, or consulting team needs an official glossary that unifies the technical and business vocabulary used in their documents, meetings, and systems. The dispersion of synonyms and informal definitions generates misunderstandings and rework. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured canonical glossary with precise definitions, usage notes, synonyms, and related terms for the indicated domain, ready to be published on the team's wiki or portal. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a senior information architect with experience in terminological normalization for technology companies and management consulting firms. SUPUESTOS: If the user does not paste a list of candidate terms, infer the 20 most critical terms for the declared domain and continue; if the audience is not specified, assume mixed technical-business; ask only if the domain is completely ambiguous (confidence < 0.85). INSUMOS: list of candidate terms or domain description pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1. Identify and alphabetically sort the terms to include. 2. For each term write: canonical definition (max. 2 sentences), usage context, accepted and unaccepted synonyms, related terms. 3. Flag ambiguities or usage conflicts with an explanatory note. 4. Generate a Markdown table with columns: Term | Definition | Accepted synonyms | Avoid | Related. 5. Add a maintenance criteria section (who approves changes, review cadence). SALIDA: Markdown document with cover page (domain, version, date, owner), glossary table, maintenance section; between 15 and 40 entries. CASOS BORDE: (a) term has multiple meanings depending on context → document each meaning with a context label; (b) bilingual team → add a column with the equivalent in the other language; (c) term not yet agreed upon → mark it as 'under discussion' with proposed options. [C · CRITERIA] Each definition is falsifiable and free of unexplained jargon; unaccepted synonyms are explicitly listed; table passes review by 3 different roles without ambiguities; deliverable is publishable without additional editing. Trade-off: technical precision over brevity when there is a risk of confusion. DoD: glossary with ≥15 validated entries, maintenance section included, no internal contradictions. Protocolo MetodologIA: define the vocabulary before building the system — terminological imprecision is cognitive debt.
spec-comunicacion_doc_diagrama_flujo_tex: [S · SITUATION] A technical or functional team has created or received a flowchart or process diagram (BPMN, UML activity, swimlane, simple flowchart) and needs a narrative text to accompany it in the official documentation, so that it is understandable for audiences without visualization tools or with accessibility needs. [P · REQUEST] Write a structured textual description of the flow or process represented in the diagram, organized by phases and sequential steps, with actors, branching conditions, and integration points clearly identified. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a senior process analyst and technical writer with experience in enterprise architecture documentation and operational manuals. SUPUESTOS: If the user does not attach the diagram, infer the structure from the verbal description of the process and declare the assumptions; assume a mixed technical-functional audience unless otherwise indicated; ask only if the type of process is completely unknown. INSUMOS: diagram description, screenshot, or list of steps pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1. Identify the process name, objective, and scope. 2. List participating actors or systems. 3. Describe each phase with its steps in order, including inputs, outputs, and responsible party. 4. Document each branch with a [YES/NO] condition or decision criterion. 5. Identify integrations with external systems and start/end events. 6. Write an executive summary paragraph (3-5 sentences). 7. Add a diagram elements table (symbol → meaning) if applicable. SALIDA: Markdown document with executive summary section, actors table, step-by-step description organized by phases, branches table, and integration notes; between 400 and 800 words.
