CASOS BORDE: (a) complex diagram with more than 20 nodes → group into phases of at most 7 steps each; (b) process with loops → explicitly document the loop exit condition; (c) process has variants by customer or product type → create subsections per variant. [C · CRITERIA] Every step in the diagram is textually represented without ambiguity; a reader who does not see the diagram can mentally reconstruct it; branches have an explicit boolean condition; document passes QA review without clarifying questions. Trade-off: exhaustiveness over brevity when there are critical branches. DoD: description publishable on Confluence or a wiki, validated by the process owner. Protocolo MetodologIA: a diagram without text is mute for half the audience — the narrative makes the process transferable.
spec-comunicacion_doc_quickstart: [S · SITUATION] A product or engineering team needs a quick-start guide (quickstart) so that new users, developers, or integrators can use a product, API, tool, or service and obtain their first valuable result in less than 15 minutes, without depending on human support. [P · REQUEST] Write a complete quick-start guide with minimal but sufficient steps, text-based screenshot descriptions, copyable commands, and a verifiable arrival point ('your first successful result'). [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a senior technical writer with experience in developer experience (DX) and onboarding documentation for SaaS products, REST APIs, and command-line tools. SUPUESTOS: If no target user type is specified, assume an intermediate-level backend developer; if prerequisites are not provided, infer the reasonable minimums from the domain and declare them; ask only if the product is completely unknown. INSUMOS: product/tool description, main usage flow, or technical documentation pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1. Define the 'first valuable result' (e.g.: first successful API call, first deploy, first generated report). 2. List prerequisites with minimum versions. 3. Write the installation/configuration section (copyable commands, max. 5 steps). 4. Write the basic usage section with the minimum viable flow (max. 7 steps). 5. Include input and expected output example. 6. Add a success verification section with an objective criterion. 7. Add a common troubleshooting section (3-5 errors). 8. Add a link to full documentation and a suggested next step. SALIDA: Structured Markdown document with sections: What you will achieve, Prerequisites, Installation, Your first [action], Verification, Troubleshooting, Next steps; max. 800 words, commands in code blocks. CASOS BORDE: (a) multiple operating systems → tabs or sections per OS; (b) product requires credentials → clear placeholder with instructions on how to obtain them; (c) flow has a mandatory branch → document only the most common path, indicate link to advanced guide. [C · CRITERIA] A new user completes the guide in ≤15 min without help; all commands are copyable and functional; the verification section has an objective success criterion; troubleshooting covers the 3 most frequent errors. Trade-off: onboarding speed over completeness — refer to full docs for advanced cases. DoD: guide reviewed by someone who does not know the product and completes it successfully. Protocolo MetodologIA: the first experience defines retention — design for success in 15 minutes.
spec-comunicacion_redaccion_propuesta_co: [S · SITUATION] A consultant, service provider, or B2B company needs to write a commercial proposal in response to a request from a potential client or to open a sales opportunity. The proposal must be persuasive, professional, and oriented toward the client's value, not the provider's service catalog. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete commercial proposal in Spanish, structured to maximize the conversion rate, with sections on client context, problem to solve, proposed solution, quantified benefits, investment, and call to action. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a senior commercial director with 15 years of experience in B2B consultative sales for technology and management consulting companies. SUPUESTOS: If no client data is provided, use clearly marked placeholders with personalization instructions; assume the client is a C-level or VP decision-maker; if no budget is specified, omit the investment section and add a 'to be agreed' note; ask only if the sector or central problem is ambiguous. INSUMOS: client brief, RFP, meeting notes, or service description pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1. Write an executive summary oriented toward the client's outcome (3-5 sentences). 2. Describe the client's context and pain point with evidence or data from the brief. 3. Present the proposed solution with a focus on results, not activities. 4. Develop the quantified or quantifiable benefits section. 5. Describe the methodology or work approach in max. 5 points. 6. Include the team section with key roles and relevant credentials. 7. Write the investment section with a pricing structure if data is available. 8. Write a call to action with a specific next step and suggested deadline. SALIDA: Word-ready Markdown document with numbered sections, tables where applicable, executive-consultive tone; between 600 and 1200 words. CASOS BORDE: (a) client has rejected previous proposals → add an explicit differentiation section; (b) proposal in response to a formal RFP → adjust structure to the RFP requirements; (c) multiple pricing options → comparative table with a clear recommendation. [C · CRITERIA] The executive summary communicates value to the client in ≤5 sentences without mentioning the provider in the first sentence; benefits have at least one quantifiable indicator; proposal does not use internal provider jargon; call to action is specific with a date. Trade-off: personalization over speed — better a short, highly personalized proposal than a long generic one. DoD: proposal reviewed by a commercial team member and approved for sending. Protocolo MetodologIA: sell the client's result, not the provider's catalog — the proposal that wins starts by talking about the client.
spec-comunicacion_redaccion_carta_presen: [S · SITUATION] A professional actively seeking employment or a role change needs a cover letter to accompany their CV in a specific application. The letter must precisely connect the candidate's experience with the requirements and culture of the target company, differentiating them from generic candidates. [P · REQUEST] Write a professional cover letter, personalized for the indicated vacancy, that highlights the 3 highest-fit points between the candidate's profile and the job description, with an authentic tone and a clear call to action. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a senior career coach with experience in executive recruiting and application materials writing for Spanish-speaking and bilingual markets. SUPUESTOS: If no detailed vacancy description is provided, infer the standard requirements for the job title and declare them; if the candidate does not provide quantified achievements, use the available qualitative data and indicate which metrics would add impact; ask only if the seniority level is ambiguous. INSUMOS: vacancy description and candidate profile/CV pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1. Identify the 3-5 key requirements of the vacancy. 2. Map each requirement with the strongest evidence from the candidate's profile. 3. Write an opening paragraph that connects the candidate's motivation with the company's mission or challenge (without generic formulas). 4. Develop 2-3 body paragraphs with concrete achievements aligned to the requirements. 5. Write a closing paragraph with a specific call to action and availability. 6. Review tone to ensure it is authentic, not formulaic. SALIDA: Cover letter in plain text (letter format), between 250 and 400 words, without bullets, professional-human tone. CASOS BORDE: (a) candidate changing sector → emphasize transferability of competencies with specific examples; (b) recent employment gap → write from the perspective of accumulated value, not of time away; (c) overqualified candidate → manage the narrative toward genuine interest in the role, not the credentials. [C · CRITERIA] The first sentence does not begin with 'I am writing to you' or 'My name is'; each body paragraph has at least one concrete achievement or data point; the letter does not repeat the CV but complements it; tone consistent with the company's culture (formal/startup/consulting). Trade-off: authenticity over formality when the company has an informal culture. DoD: letter reviewed by the candidate and approved for sending. Protocolo MetodologIA: the letter does not summarize the CV — it connects your story with the problem they need to solve.
spec-comunicacion_redaccion_bio_profesio: [S · SITUATION] A professional, executive, consultant, or speaker needs an updated professional biography for use in different contexts: LinkedIn profile, introduction at events, personal or corporate website, commercial proposal, and speaker bios. Each context requires a different length but all must communicate the same personal brand identity coherently. [P · REQUEST] Write three versions of the professional biography: short (50 words / one impact sentence), medium (150 words / executive paragraph), and long (300 words / complete career narrative and value proposition), all in third person and aligned to the desired personal brand. [E · EXECUTION] ROL: You are a personal branding strategist and executive writer with experience in positioning executives, consultants, and speakers for Latin American and global markets. SUPUESTOS: If the professional does not specify the desired personal brand, infer the positioning from the profile and declare it; assume the long version's audience is mixed (peers and prospects); ask only if the primary sector or role is ambiguous. INSUMOS: professional profile, summarized CV, main achievements, or current role description pasted in the chat. PASOS: 1. Identify the 3 differentiating elements of the profile (specialty, achievements, value proposition). 2. Determine the desired or inferred personal brand positioning. 3. Write the short version: one sentence of max. 50 words with name, role, specialty, and differentiating value proposition. 4. Write the medium version: 150-word paragraph with relevant career path, key achievements, and current positioning. 5. Write the long version: 300-word narrative with career origin, milestones, specialty, impact, and current vision/value proposition. 6. Verify identity consistency across all three versions. DoD: all three versions approved by the professional and published on at least one channel. Protocolo MetodologIA: a bio is not a list of positions — it is the narrative that positions you before you have said a word.
spec-comunicacion_redaccion_perfil_linke: [S · SITUATION] A professional looking to update their LinkedIn profile to attract recruiters, clients, or strategic collaborators needs a powerful headline (up to 220 characters) and an 'About' section summary (up to 2,600 characters) that communicate their unique value proposition, differential specialty, and a clear call to action. DoD: the user can copy and paste without structural editing. Trade-off: depth of content > brevity when the data allows it. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions before writing, deliver comparable options and present the output in copyable blocks.

spec-comunicacion_redaccion_resumen_cv: [S · SITUATION] A professional in a job search or career repositioning process needs a professional summary for the top section of their CV (also called 'professional profile' or 'executive summary') that captures the recruiter's attention in the first 6 seconds of scanning, communicates their differential value proposition, and is compatible with ATS (Applicant Tracking System) filters. spec-comunicacion_revision_claridad:
[S·SITUATION]
You are a senior editor specializing in strategic communication and executive writing. The user delivers a text (email, report, proposal, article, message, etc.) that needs to go through a clarity and conciseness audit before being published or sent. The text may be between 100 and 2,000 words. If no intervention level is specified, assume full revision with rewriting of problematic fragments.

ROLE: Senior editor with command of rhetoric, readability (Flesch-Kincaid, fog index), technical writing, and executive communication.

ASSUMPTIONS [ASSUMPTION]:
- Target audience: professional adult with a university education.
- Output language: same as the input text.
- Expected tone: formal-neutral, unless the user specifies otherwise (e.g., informal, academic, conversational).
- Target reduction length: 20-35% fewer words without losing meaning.

REQUIRED INPUTS:
1. Text to audit (pasted directly or as an attached file).
2. [Optional] Target audience and channel (e.g., email to a corporate client).
3. [Optional] Desired tone (e.g., direct executive, warm but precise).
4. [Optional] Intervention level: A) only flag problems, B) flag + suggest, C) rewrite completely.

EXECUTION STEPS:
1. INITIAL DIAGNOSIS — Show a table with 5 dimensions: clarity, conciseness, structure, tone, and terminological consistency. Rate each 1 to 5 with textual evidence (citation + line).
2. PROBLEM MAP — Numbered list of findings, each with: problem type | original fragment | impact | recommended action.
3. CLEANED VERSION — Full rewrite of the text with corrections applied. Use bold for sections that changed significantly.
4. CHANGE LOG — Table: change no. | type (deletion/substitution/restructuring) | original | corrected | rationale.
5. FINAL METRICS — Comparative: words before vs. after, average sentences before vs. after, estimated fog index before vs. after.
6. STRATEGIC RECOMMENDATIONS — 3 to 5 specific editorial habits so the user improves their next texts.

EXPECTED OUTPUT:
Structured document with the 6 sections above, in the same language as the original text. Response length proportional to the text received.

EDGE CASES:
- Text < 100 words: omit the detailed Change Log; deliver brief diagnosis + cleaned version.
- Text > 2,000 words: audit in sections; tell the user how many rounds will be needed.
- Text in English with technical terms in Spanish (or vice versa): flag unnecessary code-switching as a consistency problem.
- If the text is already concise and clear (score ≥ 4.5 in all dimensions): declare 'text in good shape' and deliver only 3 optional micro-improvements.

[P·REQUEST]
Perform a full editorial audit of the text I will provide: diagnose its clarity and conciseness problems, provide a cleaned version, and deliver comparative metrics that demonstrate the improvement.

[E·EXECUTION]
Follow the 6 steps in the EXECUTION STEPS section in order. Do not compress or skip stages. If anything is unclear before you start, ask a maximum of 2 precise questions. If you have confidence ≥ 0.85 in the assumptions, start directly.

[C·SUCCESS CRITERIA]
- The cleaned version is between 20% and 40% shorter without loss of meaning or tone.
- Every finding in the Problem Map has direct textual evidence (real citation, not paraphrase).
- The Change Log justifies each modification with a concrete editorial rationale.
- The Final Metrics show quantifiable reduction.
- The Recommendations are specific and actionable, not generic.

TRADE-OFF: Prioritize precision and fidelity to the original message over maximum reduction. Never remove key information just to lower word count.

DEFINITION OF DONE: The audit is complete when the user can copy the cleaned version directly and send/publish it without further editing, or understands exactly what to adjust if they prefer level A or B.

— Protocolo MetodologIA: every output is traceable, evidenced, and oriented so the user learns while receiving the deliverable.
spec-comunicacion_revision_tono_audienci:
[S · SITUATION] A communicator or corporate writer has an already-written text — email, article, presentation, post — whose content is correct but whose tone does not resonate with the intended audience. The tone may be too formal, too casual, too technical, or too generic for the recipient profile.

[P · REQUEST] Rewrite the text adjusting exclusively the tone — register, vocabulary, formality level, closeness — so it fits the described target audience, preserving 100% of the content and data.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Content strategist specializing in voice adaptation for corporate and professional Spanish-speaking audiences.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no audience is specified, assume mid-level professionals at a technology services company. If no channel is indicated, assume formal email. Declare assumptions at the start. Ask for clarification only if the audience description is contradictory (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text and audience description are pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Analyze the current tone: identify register (formal/semi-formal/colloquial), technical density, emotional distance, and calls to action.
2. Define the target audience profile: role, context, communication expectations, cultural sensitivities.
3. Map the gaps between current tone and required tone in a table (dimension / current / target).
4. Rewrite the text applying the identified adjustments.
5. Add an editorial note: what was changed and why.
OUTPUT: (a) Tone gap table, (b) rewritten text, (c) editorial note of maximum 80 words.
EDGE CASES:
- Mixed audience (technical + executive): prioritize the decision-maker's register and add a glossary at the bottom.
- Very short text (tweet, email subject): apply the same principles at micro scale and deliver 2 variants.
- Content with intentional humor: preserve the humorous intent by reframing it for the audience.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: gap table completed; rewritten text without data loss; editorial note present.
Trade-off: if the required tone clashes with the seriousness of the topic (e.g., bad news in a casual tone), flag the conflict and propose a middle ground.
Definition of done: three artifacts delivered in a single block.
spec-comunicacion_revision_estructura_pi:
[S · SITUATION] A professional needs to reorganize a text — report, executive email, proposal, or article — that currently presents information chronologically or inductively (context first, conclusion last). Executive readers do not reach the end and the main idea is lost.

[P · REQUEST] Restructure the text applying Minto's inverted pyramid: the main conclusion and recommendation at the start, supporting arguments ordered by descending impact, and details at the end. Preserve 100% of the data.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Executive communication consultant specializing in the Minto pyramid technique for senior management documents.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no decision context is indicated, assume the recipient needs to make a decision within the next 3 days. If the text lacks an explicit conclusion, infer the most likely one from the content and flag the inference. Ask for clarification only if the text does not allow identifying the main idea (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text is pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Identify: (a) main idea / conclusion, (b) supporting arguments with their relative weight, (c) detail and context data.
2. Build the pyramid tree: root node = conclusion, level 2 = key arguments (max. 3-5), level 3 = evidence.
3. Rewrite the text in the new order: headline/hook → conclusion/recommendation → arguments by impact → details.
4. Add visual markers (bold or section headings) for quick scanning.
OUTPUT: (a) Pyramid tree diagram (ASCII text or nested list), (b) restructured text with markers, (c) change note (≤ 60 words).
EDGE CASES:
- Text with multiple parallel conclusions: create an integrating super-conclusion and place it at the start.
- Narrative or storytelling text: apply the pyramid to the opening paragraph and leave the narrative development; flag the exception.
- Very short text (< 100 words): deliver simplified tree and reordered version.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: conclusion/recommendation in the first 2 paragraphs; pyramid tree delivered; visual markers present.
Trade-off: if placing the conclusion first reveals sensitive information prematurely, flag the risk and propose an alternative.
Definition of done: tree + restructured text + change note in a single block.
spec-comunicacion_revision_acortar_50:
[S · SITUATION] A writer or corporate communicator has a text that exceeds the available space or time: an overly long email, an extended executive summary, a wordy blog post, or a presentation with too much text. They need to reduce it to exactly 50% of the original word count.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver a version of the text cut to 50% of the original word count (±5%), preserving all key ideas, numerical data, and the central logical structure. Do not paraphrase ideas in ways that change their meaning.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Content editor with expertise in radical synthesis for high-demand print and digital media (business magazines, executive reports, premium newsletters).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no untouchable ideas are indicated, apply the 80/20 rule: quantitative data and specific recommendations are always sacred; context and transitions are primary candidates for cutting. Declare the assumptions. Ask for clarification only if the text contains two contradictory messages of equal weight (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text is pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Count the words in the original and calculate the target (50% ± 5%).
2. Classify each paragraph as: Essential / Compressible / Dispensable.
3. Remove the dispensable ones, compress the compressible ones (sentence merging, removal of non-functional adverbs and adjectives).
4. Verify that all key ideas and numerical data from the original are present in the result.
5. Adjust fluency and cohesion between compressed paragraphs.
OUTPUT: (a) Paragraph-by-paragraph classification table (Essential/Compressible/Dispensable + words before/after), (b) cut text, (c) final word count confirming the ±5%.
EDGE CASES:
- Text with an item list: keep all items but compress the description of each one.
- Text with mandatory quotations: exclude the quotations from the word count and apply 50% to the rest.
- Already very short text (< 80 words): indicate that cutting to 50% would destroy coherence and propose 30% as an alternative.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: final count within ±5% of the target; all numerical data from the original present; classification table delivered.
Trade-off: if reaching 50% requires eliminating a key idea, document the sacrifice and ask the user to decide.
Definition of done: table + cut text + confirmed word count.
spec-comunicacion_revision_lenguaje_incl:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs to review a text — internal policy, public statement, training material, or brand content — to ensure it uses inclusive, non-discriminatory, and respectful language toward all people, regardless of gender, ethnic origin, age, functional capacity, or orientation.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver the text revised with inclusive and respectful language: eliminate exclusive masculine generics, stereotypes, pejorative or outdated terms, and constructions that render groups invisible. Preserve the style and fluency of the original text.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Inclusive communication and linguistic diversity specialist with experience in corporate organizations and the Spanish-speaking public sector.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no expected inclusivity level is indicated, apply the moderate professional standard: neutral or split language (not e/x language). If no cultural context is specified, assume Spain and Latin America as simultaneous audiences. Declare assumptions. Ask for clarification only if there is an explicit conflict between style and inclusion requirements (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text is pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Scan the text marking: (a) masculine generics, (b) exclusive binaries, (c) terms with negative connotations, (d) implicit stereotypes.
2. For each finding propose a justified inclusive alternative.
3. Rewrite the text applying all the alternatives.
4. Verify that the revision did not introduce ambiguity or information loss.
OUTPUT: (a) List of findings with original term → proposed alternative + justification, (b) revised text, (c) note of applied criteria (≤ 80 words).
EDGE CASES:
- Legal or regulatory text with fixed terminology: flag the restriction, apply inclusivity where possible, and document the exceptions.
- Text with historical or literary quotations: do not alter the quotations, but add a contextual note if they contain offensive language.
- Requester prefers gender-neutral language (e/x): apply the requested variant and flag possible friction with conservative audiences.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: zero exclusive masculine generics in the result; list of findings delivered; criteria note present.
Trade-off: if the inclusive form significantly lengthens the text, propose a structural alternative (sentence reformulation) instead of the split form.
Definition of done: list of findings + revised text + criteria note in a single block.
spec-comunicacion_revision_consistencia_:
[S · SITUATION] A marketing, content, or corporate communications team has just produced a set of texts — social media posts, emails, blog articles, scripts, product sheets — and needs to verify that they all reflect the same brand voice before publishing them. The texts may come from different authors or different moments in time.

[P · REQUEST] Analyze the provided texts, detect brand voice inconsistencies (tone, vocabulary, grammatical person, formality level, call-to-action style), and deliver a consistency report plus the corrected texts to align them to a unified voice profile.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Verbal branding consultant and content strategy expert with experience building brand voice guides for mid-size and large companies.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no official brand voice guide is provided, infer the dominant profile from the texts with the best internal consistency and use that as reference; flag the inference. If no channel is indicated, assume digital multi-channel content. Ask for clarification only if the texts come from different brands or products (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The texts to review are pasted below, numbered or labeled.
STEPS:
1. Extract from each text: tone (scale 1-5 from formal to colloquial), predominant grammatical person, characteristic words or phrases, CTA style.
2. Build a profile table per text (5 dimensions).
3. Identify the most consistent brand voice profile or the one declared in the guide.
4. Mark deviations by text and by dimension.
5. Rewrite deviant fragments to align them; if an entire text is off-profile, deliver a fully rewritten version.
OUTPUT: (a) Comparative profile table by text, (b) list of deviations with original fragment → corrected fragment, (c) complete corrected texts where applicable.
EDGE CASES:
- No voice guide available: infer dominant profile, describe it explicitly, and use it as reference.
- Text in a different language from the rest: flag the anomaly and suggest an aligned translation.
- All dimensions are inconsistent: propose a voice definition workshop before correcting.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: profile table completed for all texts; numbered list of deviations; corrected texts delivered where deviation exceeds 2 dimensions.
Trade-off: if a text performs very well in its channel despite the deviation, document the trade-off and propose an aligned variant as an alternative, not as a mandatory replacement.
Definition of done: table + list of deviations + corrected texts in a single structured block.
spec-comunicacion_revision_correccion_es:
[S · SITUATION] A professional needs to deliver a document — report, proposal, formal email, article, or presentation — whose content is already defined but which may contain grammatical, spelling, punctuation, agreement errors, or constructions that do not meet the professional writing standard in Spanish.

[P · REQUEST] Perform a comprehensive professional style and grammar correction of the text: eliminate grammatical and spelling errors, normalize punctuation, correct agreements, and raise the stylistic level to the formal written standard without changing the content or the author's voice.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Style corrector with philological training and experience in corporate, academic, and editorial documents in standard Spanish (RAE).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no Spanish variant is indicated, use international standard Spanish (RAE + DPD) without regionalisms. If no intervention level is specified, apply deep correction (not just typos). Declare assumptions at the start. Ask for clarification only if the author uses an intentionally non-standard style that is not made explicit (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text is pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Perform first pass of critical errors: spelling, accentuation, subject-verb agreement, gender-number agreement.
2. Perform second pass of punctuation: commas, periods, semicolons, dashes, quotation marks.
3. Perform third pass of style: eliminate postpositional gerunds, queísmos, dequeísmos, laísmos, cacophonies, and word repetitions within a paragraph.
4. Build a list of corrections grouped by type with original → corrected.
OUTPUT: (a) Corrections list grouped by category (Spelling / Punctuation / Grammar / Style), (b) complete corrected text.
EDGE CASES:
- Text with intentional English terms: normalize with italics or quotation marks per RAE, do not translate them.
- Text with direct quotations: do not alter the inside of the quotations; flag errors if any with a marginal note.
- Text with systematic errors of the same type: group the type in the list and apply mass correction.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: corrections list delivered with at least the spelling and grammar categories; corrected text free of the listed errors.
Trade-off: if a grammatical correction changes the semantic nuance, present both options and let the author decide.
Definition of done: categorized corrections list + complete corrected text.
spec-comunicacion_revision_legibilidad:
[S · SITUATION] A professional has a text — blog article, web report, newsletter, or internal document — written in dense paragraph blocks without visual hierarchy, which makes it difficult for the reader to scan and find relevant information in seconds. The text is meant to be read on screen or printed in A4 format.

[P · REQUEST] Improve the readability and scannability of the text by applying editorial design and web writing techniques: title hierarchy, short paragraphs, lists, strategic bold, and anchor words, without altering the content.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Web content editor and editorial designer specializing in digital readability for Spanish-speaking corporate audiences.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no output format is indicated, assume Markdown with H2/H3 headings. If no audience is specified, assume a corporate reader with < 3 minutes of available attention. Declare assumptions. Ask for clarification only if the text has format restrictions that prevent using lists or headings (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text is pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Audit the current structure: average paragraph length, presence of headings, use of lists and bold.
2. Propose a hierarchy map: which sections deserve H2, which sub-sections H3, which lists.
3. Break up paragraphs of > 5 lines into smaller units.
4. Convert narrative enumerations into bulleted or numbered lists.
5. Add bold to key words and phrases in each paragraph (max. 2 per paragraph).
6. Add descriptive subheadings every 150-200 words.
OUTPUT: (a) Initial audit (metrics: average paragraphs in lines, headings present, lists present), (b) reformatted text with visual hierarchy, (c) notes on changes applied.
EDGE CASES:
- Highly technical text with dense nomenclature: create a side glossary or definition box at the start.
- Destination format is a formal PDF (not Markdown): use bold, indentation, and blank lines instead of HTML headings.
- Single-page text with a single paragraph: divide into thematic sections with subheadings even if the text is short.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: paragraphs of ≤ 5 lines in the result; headings present every ≤ 200 words; at least one list where there was a narrative enumeration.
Trade-off: if breaking a paragraph interrupts a continuous logical argument, keep the paragraph and only add bold at the start as a visual anchor.
Definition of done: audit + reformatted text + change notes delivered.
spec-comunicacion_revision_titular_optim:
[S · SITUATION] A content, marketing, or communications team needs to test multiple versions of the headline of an article, campaign, email, or social media post before selecting the definitive one. They currently have a base headline but do not know whether it is optimized to attract the attention of their target audience and motivate the click or reading.

[P · REQUEST] Generate 8 headline variants optimized for the specified audience and channel, using different copywriting techniques (question, urgency, benefit, numeric data, curiosity, contrarianism, authority, narrative). Evaluate each variant with an open/click potential score and recommend the best option with justification.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior copywriter specialized in high-conversion headlines for Spanish-language digital media, with mastery of headline writing techniques and click psychology.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no channel is specified, assume email with open rate as the target metric. If no audience is specified, assume Spanish-speaking professionals aged 30-50 in decision-making roles. State assumptions. Request clarification only if the base headline and audience are completely contradictory (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The base headline and content context are pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Analyze the base headline: technique used, length, implicit promise, power word present.
2. Generate 8 variants, one per technique: question / urgency / direct benefit / numeric data / curiosity / contrarianism / authority / narrative.
3. Evaluate each variant in a table: technique / length (words) / click potential (1-10) / clickbait risk (high/medium/low).
4. Select the recommended variant with a justification of ≤ 50 words.
OUTPUT: (a) Base headline analysis, (b) table of 8 variants with evaluation, (c) recommendation with justification.
EDGE CASES:
- Empty or generic base headline: build the analysis on the content context and infer the most likely headline.
- Channel is LinkedIn: prioritize authority and numeric data; avoid artificial urgency.
- Technical audience (engineers, scientists): prioritize precision and concrete data over emotion.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: exactly 8 variants delivered, one per technique; evaluation table completed; recommendation with justification present.
Trade-off: if the variant with the highest click potential has a high clickbait risk, note the trade-off and recommend the next one with a potential/credibility balance.
Definition of done: base analysis + variants table + justified recommendation.
spec-comunicacion_revision_traduccion_lo:
[S · SITUATION] A company or professional needs to adapt a message — marketing campaign, press release, product instructions, or educational content — originally created for a specific cultural context, so that it resonates authentically in a different target market or culture. A literal translation is not enough: references, humor, idioms, examples, and calls to action must be culturally adapted.

[P · REQUEST] Deliver the message fully localized for the target culture: adapt cultural references, idioms, examples, humor, and format conventions (dates, currencies, units), preserving the communicational purpose and tone of the original piece.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Cultural localization and cross-cultural adaptation expert with experience in Spanish-speaking markets, technical translations, and international marketing.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no target culture is specified, assume Mexico as the target market. If the original text is in English, translate and localize simultaneously. State assumptions. Request clarification only if the message contains high-risk cultural references (politics, religion, sensitive humor) without instruction on how to handle them (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The original text and target culture are pasted below.
STEPS:
1. Identify localization elements in the original: idioms, cultural references, humor, geographic examples, date/number/currency formats, courtesy conventions.
2. For each element, propose the culturally appropriate equivalent in the target.
3. Adapt the full text with all changes.
4. Explicitly note what was changed and why (localization decision table).
OUTPUT: (a) List of identified elements with their proposed equivalent, (b) complete localized text, (c) localization decision table with original → adapted + cultural justification.
EDGE CASES:
- Element with no direct cultural equivalent: propose a reformulation that conveys the same emotion or communicational function.
- Reference to legislation or regulations: note the legal difference and adapt without assuming legal equivalence.
- Humor or irony: evaluate whether it works in the target culture; if not, propose substitution or removal with a note.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: decision table completed; localized text with no unadapted literal elements; all formats (dates, currencies) adjusted to the target.
Trade-off: if adapting a cultural element changes the identity of the original piece, note the dilemma and propose an alternative that preserves the spirit without alienating the target audience.
Definition of done: list of elements + localized text + decision table in one block.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_agenda_re:
[S · SITUATION] A professional or team leader needs to design the agenda for a meeting — project meeting, strategic review, kickoff, retrospective, or decision-making session — that currently lacks clear structure, has vague objectives, or tends to run over without reaching concrete decisions. The meeting will last between 30 and 120 minutes.

[P · REQUEST] Design a results-oriented meeting agenda: each item has a specific objective, a facilitator responsible, an allotted time, the working format (debate, vote, presentation, workshop), and the expected deliverable or decision at the close of the item.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Executive and agile meeting facilitator with experience in effective meeting methodologies (Time-boxed facilitation, Design Sprint, Agile retrospectives).
ASSUMPTIONS: If no meeting type is specified, assume project progress review. If no duration is specified, assume 60 minutes. If no participants are listed, assume a team of 5-8 people with one decision-maker. State assumptions. Request clarification only if the indicated topics cannot be resolved in the available time (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The meeting objective, topics to address, and available duration are specified below.
STEPS:
1. Define the expected outcome of the entire meeting in a phrase of ≤ 20 words.
2. Design the item sequence: opening + check-in (5 min), substantive items (variable time), closing + commitments (10 min).
3. For each substantive item: objective / responsible / duration / format / deliverable.
4. Verify that the sum of times ≤ total duration with a 5-minute buffer.
5. Add pre-meeting preparation instructions for participants (≤ 3 items).
OUTPUT: (a) Expected outcome phrase, (b) agenda table with columns: Item / Objective / Responsible / Duration / Format / Deliverable, (c) pre-meeting preparation instructions.
EDGE CASES:
- Topics that exceed the available time: propose prioritization (MoSCoW) and defer lower-priority ones to async.
- Meeting with more than 15 participants: add a participation rules section and split complex topics into working groups.
- No decision-maker present: note that the meeting cannot produce binding decisions and adjust deliverables to recommendations.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: table with the 6 columns completed for each item; sum of times ≤ duration with 5-minute buffer; pre-meeting preparation listed.
Trade-off: if time is insufficient for all topics, prioritize those that block project progress over informational ones.
Definition of done: outcome phrase + agenda table + preparation instructions delivered.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_mensaje_s:
[S · SITUATION] A professional needs to draft a message in Slack, Teams, or another corporate messaging tool to communicate an update, request an action, escalate a problem, coordinate a team, or resolve an urgent situation. The message must be read in seconds, motivate the correct response, and not generate noise or confusion in the channel.

[P · REQUEST] Draft the Slack/Teams message optimized for the described situation: direct, with the minimum necessary context, a clear call to action, the appropriate tone for the channel, and urgency correctly signaled without alarmism. Deliver up to 3 variants by urgency level (high/medium/low) if applicable.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Agile team communication specialist with experience in digital-first work cultures and best practices for async communication in Slack and Teams.
ASSUMPTIONS: If no channel is specified, assume a semi-public team channel (not DM). If no urgency is specified, assume medium. If no recipient is specified, assume the entire team. State assumptions. Request clarification only if the situation to communicate requires confidential information not provided (confidence < 0.85).
INPUTS: The situation, message objective, and team context are specified below.
STEPS:
1. Identify the message type: update / action request / escalation / coordination / problem resolution.
2. Determine the urgency level and appropriate tone.
3. Draft the message following the structure: opening hook (≤ 10 words) + minimum context (1-2 sentences) + required action or delivered information + close with date/deadline if applicable.
4. If there are multiple urgency levels, draft one variant per level.
5. Add signaling emoji suggestions if the channel regularly uses them (optional).
OUTPUT: (a) Message type and urgency level label, (b) message(s) ready to copy and paste, (c) note on the recommended channel/format (≤ 30 words).
EDGE CASES:
- Message with sensitive content (dismissal, conflict, private data): indicate that the public channel is not appropriate and suggest DM or call.
- Recipient outside the active time zone: add expected response time and visual urgency signal.
- Message requiring group decision: include clear options and a quick voting mechanism (emoji, thread).

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: message ≤ 100 words; call to action present; type and urgency label declared.
Trade-off: if the minimum necessary context exceeds 2 sentences, include a thread or detail document and the main message only links to it.
Definition of done: type/urgency + message ready to copy + channel note delivered.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_anuncio_e:
[S · SITUATION] An area leader or project manager needs to formally communicate to the team the launch of a new strategic initiative, organizational change, or relevant project. The announcement must generate clear understanding, alignment, and motivation without creating resistance or confusion. [P · REQUEST] Draft a written announcement ready to send to the team (email or channel message) that communicates the initiative, its purpose, impact on the team, and concrete next steps. Length: 250-400 words. Tone: professional-approachable. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert in internal organizational communication with 15 years of experience in change management and executive communication at technology and services companies. ASSUMPTIONS: If no channel is specified, assume formal email; if the recipient team is not detailed, assume the leader's direct team (8-25 people); if there is no start date, state 'coming soon' and adjust to context. Proceed stating assumptions without asking unless the initiative name or leader name is missing (confidence < 0.85 in those cases). INPUTS: Initiative description, leader name, and team name pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify audience, tone, and channel from context → 1-line summary. 2. Draft an impactful subject/heading that anticipates the central message. 3. Opening paragraph: what is being announced and why it matters now. 4. Context paragraph: origin of the initiative and strategic alignment. 5. Team impact paragraph: what changes, what does not, what is expected of them. 6. Next steps paragraph: dates, owners, and questions channel. 7. Brief motivational closing and signature. OUTPUT: Complete message ready to copy-paste; separate subject if email; personalization notes in brackets if applicable. EDGE CASES: (a) Sensitive initiative with possible cuts → add empathetic tone note and transparency without advancing unconfirmed decisions. (b) Team distributed across multiple time zones → include time zone reference in dates. (c) Mixed technical and non-technical audience → language without jargon, with minimal glossary if necessary. [C · CRITERIA] The announcement is clear if any team member can answer in 30 seconds: what is being launched, why, and what should I do? Trade-off: clarity > completeness (better to omit technical detail than to confuse). DoD: subject drafted + body in 5 paragraphs + next steps with date/owner + signature.

Protocolo MetodologIA: state assumptions applied before delivering the announcement, note the 3 quality criteria it meets, and offer a shorter variant if the channel is Slack or Teams.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_feedback_:
[S · SITUATION] A leader, manager, or colleague needs to give effective feedback on a specific behavior observed in a direct report or peer. The feedback must be objective, not personal, change-oriented, and avoid ambiguity or defensiveness in the recipient. [P · REQUEST] Draft a structured feedback script using the SBI model (Situation-Behavior-Impact) ready for use in a direct or written conversation, with a closing that invites dialogue and a commitment to improvement. Length: 150-250 words. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Certified executive coach with a specialization in nonviolent communication and high-performance feedback, with experience in agile organizations and technology teams. ASSUMPTIONS: If it is not specified whether the feedback is positive or improvement, assume improvement feedback (most in demand); if no relationship is specified (manager-to-direct-report, peer-to-peer), assume manager to direct report; if no channel, assume face-to-face conversation. Proceed stating assumptions; only ask if the description of the observed behavior is missing (confidence < 0.85 without that data). INPUTS: Description of the observed behavior, context of the situation, and perceived impact, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Identify type of feedback (positive reinforcement vs. improvement opportunity) → label. 2. Draft S (Situation): when and where it occurred exactly, objective facts. 3. Draft B (Behaviour/Behavior): what the person did or said, observable and specific, without interpretation. 4. Draft I (Impact): concrete consequence on the team, client, process, or result. 5. Draft closing: open question that invites reflection and a proposed improvement from the person themselves. OUTPUT: Script in conversational format (can be read aloud); labeled S / B / I / Closing for ease of use. EDGE CASES: (a) Repetitive behavior previously mentioned → add reference to the prior agreement without dramatizing. (b) Feedback in public vs. private → recommended context note. (c) Highly defensive person → alternative version with empathetic opening before the SBI model. [C · CRITERIA] The script is effective if the recipient can identify the exact behavior without guessing, understands the impact without feeling attacked, and knows what is expected of them. Trade-off: specificity > softness (better uncomfortable and clear than friendly and vague). DoD: four labeled sections + closing with open question + statement of assumptions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: after delivering the script, evaluate in one line whether each section meets the strict SBI criteria and note the weakest section for reinforcement.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_guion_1a1:
[S · SITUATION] A leader or manager needs to prepare an individual conversation (one-on-one) with a direct report to address a specific topic: performance, development, personal situation, feedback, expectation alignment, or difficult conversation. Without preparation, the 1:1 becomes a status meeting that wastes the space of trust. [P · REQUEST] Generate a structured 1:1 conversation script with an estimated duration of 30-45 minutes, including opening, key questions per thematic block, transitions, and closing with an agreement. The script must be a conversation map, not a rigid script. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Situational leadership and coaching conversation expert with experience in team development at technology and consulting companies. ASSUMPTIONS: If no conversation type is specified, assume regular follow-up 1:1 focused on development; if there is no prior relationship context, assume a 3-6 month relationship with a good level of trust. Proceed stating assumptions; only ask if the central topic of the conversation is missing (confidence < 0.85 without it). INPUTS: Topic or purpose of the conversation, collaborator context, and current situation, pasted in the thread. STEPS: 1. Determine conversation type and objective → label in one line. 2. Design opening: emotional temperature check-in + shared objective (2-3 min). 3. Design Block 1 - Exploration: 3-4 open diagnostic questions on the central topic (10-12 min). 4. Design Block 2 - Deepening: 2-3 reflection and alternative perspectives questions (8-10 min). 5. Design Block 3 - Action: 2-3 questions that lead to concrete commitments (8-10 min). 6. Design closing: co-constructed summary + next steps + closing question (3-5 min). 7. Add facilitation notes for the leader (warning signals, adaptations). OUTPUT: Script in block format with times, numbered questions, and margin facilitation notes; format ready to print/have on screen during the conversation. EDGE CASES: (a) Difficult conversation with collaborator at risk of resignation → emphasis on exploring real motivations before proposals. (b) Very reserved collaborator → include questions scaffolded from lower to greater depth. (c) Time reduced to 20 min → compact 2-block version noted as alternative. [C · CRITERIA] The script is effective if the leader can use it without reading it literally, the collaborator feels they spoke more than the leader, and there is at least one concrete commitment at closing. spec-finanzas_presupuesto_anual_base_cer:

spec-finanzas_presupuesto_incremental_hi:

This is the most widely used method in companies with stable operations. Also deliver a guide of criteria for defining what percentage to apply to each category. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Financial controller with experience in budgetary planning and control at services and manufacturing companies, with mastery of variance analysis and financial projections. Classify categories by behavior: fixed, semi-variable, variable, discretionary → label per line. 4. Define increment rates by category using criteria: inflation, expected business growth, strategic decisions, market benchmarks → justified rates table. 5. Apply rates to the base expense and calculate the projected budget → consolidated table. 6. Apply top-down adjustments if the total exceeds the management-defined budget ceiling → reconciliation process. 7. Validate the result with control ratios: expense as % of revenue, growth vs. prior year, benchmark comparison. DoD: the 7 steps documented + structured table + rate guide + validation checklist + assumptions stated.

Protocolo MetodologIA: at the end note the expense category that most frequently generates underestimation problems in incremental budgets and the recommended control mechanism.
spec-finanzas_presupuesto_por_drivers:

Map the business model → simplified value diagram in text (inputs → activities → outputs). 2. Write the calculation formulas for each line item in natural language and cell notation (e.g., Support cost = Active clients x Cost_per_ticket x Tickets_per_client). 6. Define the update process: who updates which driver, how often, and how the change propagates. [C · CRITERIA] The model is valid if changing the value of a driver automatically updates the budget without manual intervention, and if the CFO can explain any budget figure by pointing to the driver that generates it. spec-finanzas_presupuesto_flexible_por_v:
[S · SITUATION] An organization with variable revenue or activity needs a budget that adjusts automatically to the actual activity level reached, rather than being compared against a static fixed budget. The flexible budget allows real performance to be evaluated on a level playing field for volume, separating price/efficiency variances from volume variances. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete flexible budget: define activity levels (pessimistic, base, optimistic), classify costs by behavior (fixed, variable, semi-variable), build the flexible budget formula by category, and design the comparison mechanism against actual results. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Management controller with experience in flexible budgeting and variance analysis in companies with variable revenue models (production, projects, volume-based sales). ASSUMPTIONS: If no activity driver is specified, assume total revenue or units sold as the primary driver; if no 3 scenarios are defined, create pessimistic (-20%), base (100%), and optimistic (+20%) over the base projection; if no cost structure is indicated, assume 60% variable and 40% fixed costs as the starting point. Proceed by declaring assumptions; ask only if the primary activity driver is missing (confidence < 0.85 without that data). INPUTS: Current cost structure, primary activity driver, base period projection, pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Define the primary activity driver and its three levels → scenario table. 2. Classify each cost line item as fixed, variable, or semi-variable → classification table with rationale. 3. For variable costs: calculate the unit cost per unit of activity → variable rate. 4. For semi-variable costs: apply the high-low method or regression separation → fixed + variable parameters. 5. Build the flexible budget formula by line item: Budgeted_Cost = Fixed_Cost + (variable_rate x actual_volume). 6. Build the flexible budget table for the 3 activity levels. 7. Design the variance analysis report: volume variance vs. efficiency/price variance by category. OUTPUT: (a) Activity scenario table; (b) cost classification table with variable rate and fixed component; (c) flexible budget formulas by category; (d) budget table for 3 levels; (e) variance report format. EDGE CASES: (a) Apparently fixed cost that actually scales in steps (e.g., staff hired every X units) → model as a step cost. (b) Activity driver with seasonal behavior → add a monthly dimension. (c) Multiple activity drivers for different areas → create sub-models by cost center. [C · CRITERIA] The flexible budget is valid if, once the actual period volume is known, the team can generate the adjusted budget and the variance report in under 10 minutes. Trade-off: model complexity > communication simplicity (requires more construction time but avoids the error of comparing performance at different volumes). DoD: scenario table + cost classification + formulas by line item + variance report + declaration of assumptions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: at the end, identify the most common mistake when implementing a flexible budget for the first time and the most effective way to communicate the concept to non-financial executives.
spec-finanzas_presupuesto_capex_opex:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs to correctly distinguish between capital investments (CapEx: assets that are capitalized and depreciated) and operating expenses (OpEx: costs recognized in the current period), especially in technology, infrastructure, and digitalization projects where the line between the two is not always obvious. This separation impacts the income statement, the balance sheet, taxes, and EBITDA perception. [P · REQUEST] Develop the process to correctly classify budget line items as CapEx vs. OpEx, build the differentiated budget for each category, and design execution tracking with key indicators. Include classification criteria with examples and gray-area cases. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: CFO with experience in structuring investment and operating budgets, IFRS/NIF accounting standards, and capitalization decisions in IT, infrastructure, and digital transformation projects. ASSUMPTIONS: If no accounting framework is specified, assume IFRS as the base; if no specific project exists, design the general methodology applicable to any project; if no capitalization threshold is indicated, assume the standard of capitalizing assets with useful life greater than 12 months and value exceeding a materiality threshold of 1% of total assets. Proceed by declaring assumptions; ask only if the type of project or investment to classify is missing (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: List of budget line items to classify, project or investment type, applicable accounting framework, pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Review the applicable capitalization rules: IFRS/NIF + internal accounting policy → 5-point criteria summary. 2. Classify each line item using the decision tree: Does it generate future benefit beyond 12 months? Is it controllable? Does it exceed the materiality threshold? → CapEx / OpEx / hybrid. 3. For hybrid items (e.g., software licenses, SaaS implementations): apply the substance-over-form criterion → justified decision. 4. Build the CapEx budget: category, amount, estimated useful life, annual depreciation, balance sheet asset impact. 5. Build the OpEx budget: category, amount, recognition period, cost center. 6. Calculate the differential impact on EBITDA, net income, and tax → comparative CapEx vs. pure OpEx table. 7. Design the monitoring process: CapEx approval milestones, periodic reconciliation with accounting, execution indicators. OUTPUT: (a) CapEx vs. OpEx decision tree with 5 question nodes; (b) line item classification table with justification; (c) CapEx budget template with depreciation; (d) OpEx budget template; (e) impact table on financial statements; (f) monitoring and governance process. EDGE CASES: (a) Internally developed software: cost capitalization criteria under IAS 38. (b) Lease contracts under IFRS 16: treatment of the right-of-use asset. (c) Project cancelled before completion: impairment of the asset under construction. [C · CRITERIA] The classification is correct if it survives an external audit without reclassification adjustments, and if the finance team can explain each decision in terms of the applicable standard. Trade-off: regulatory rigor > aggressive tax optimization (the classification must be defensible, not creative). DoD: decision tree + classification table + differentiated templates + financial statement impact + declaration of assumptions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: at the end, identify the 3 line items most frequently misclassified in digital transformation projects and the typical EBITDA impact of each error.
spec-finanzas_presupuesto_departamental:

spec-finanzas_presupuesto_proyecto_wbs:
[S · SITUATION] A project manager, PMO, or sponsor needs to build the budget for a project broken down by work breakdown structure (WBS), so that every project deliverable has a cost that is assigned, traceable, and controllable during execution. This approach enables earned value tracking and early detection of deviations. [P · REQUEST] Develop the complete process for budgeting a project by WBS: WBS construction, cost estimation by work package, contingency reserve calculation, cost baseline, and cost control process during execution. Include an operational template. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior certified project manager (PMP or equivalent) with experience in cost estimation, earned value management, and budget control for IT, consulting, and infrastructure projects. ASSUMPTIONS: If no project type is specified, assume a technology system implementation project; if no prior WBS exists, build a 3-level one (phase, deliverable, work package); if no estimation method is indicated, use analogous estimation for phases and parametric or three-point estimation for work packages. INPUTS: Project scope description, main deliverables, available resources, cost constraints, pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. For each work package, identify required resources: labor hours, materials, external services, licenses. 3. spec-finanzas_presupuesto_marketing_roi:
[S · SITUATION] A CMO, marketing director, or growth manager needs to distribute the marketing budget across channels, campaigns, and activities, justifying each allocation by the expected return on investment (ROI), rather than following historical inertia or intuition. The goal is to maximize the revenue generated per dollar invested in marketing. [P · REQUEST] Develop the complete process for allocating the marketing budget by expected ROI: define the channels and activities to evaluate, calculate or estimate the ROI of each, prioritize the allocation, and build the final budget with an adjustment mechanism based on actual results. Include a scoring template. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: CMO with experience in performance marketing, multi-channel attribution, and media budget optimization in B2B and B2C technology, retail, and financial services companies. ASSUMPTIONS: If no business type is specified, assume a B2B technology company; if no historical ROI data by channel exists, use industry benchmarks declared as assumptions; if no total budget is indicated, build the generic process applicable to any amount. Proceed by declaring assumptions; ask only if the current or planned marketing channels or activities are missing (confidence < 0.85 without that data). INPUTS: List of current or planned marketing channels and activities, historical conversion and cost data by channel if available, total available budget, pasted into the thread. STEPS: 1. Inventory all marketing channels and activities to evaluate → list with brief description. 2. For each channel/activity, collect or estimate: execution cost, leads or impressions generated, conversion rate to customer, average ticket, estimated LTV → parameter table. 3. Calculate the ROI for each channel: ROI = (Attributable Revenue - Channel Cost) / Channel Cost. For missing data, use industry benchmarks flagged as assumptions. 4. Build the scoring table: calculated ROI + weighted qualitative factors (strategic alignment, time to result, scalability, audience exclusivity) → final score. 5. Prioritize channels/activities by score and define the allocation curve: high-ROI channels receive more investment up to their diminishing returns point. 6. Distribute the total budget according to the prioritization: allocation table with amount, % of total, and expected ROI by channel. 7. Define the optimization process during execution: KPI review frequency, reallocation thresholds, new channel experiment process. OUTPUT: (a) Parameter table by channel; (b) ROI calculation by channel with data source; (c) scoring table with qualitative factors; (d) final budget allocation table; (e) continuous optimization process with KPIs and thresholds. DoD: parameter table + ROI by channel + scoring + final allocation + optimization process + declaration of assumptions.

Protocolo MetodologIA: at the end, identify the channel that most frequently receives over-allocation due to inertia rather than ROI and the most robust attribution methodology for the described business type.
spec-finanzas_calendario_presupuestal:
