ASSUMPTIONS: If the user does not specify the period, assume the previous calendar month. If they do not indicate a work context, infer it from the pasted content. If there are no notes, ask for 5 remembered milestones before continuing. Confirm only if confidence is below 0.85.
INPUTS: Notes for the period, a list of completed or pending tasks, prior reflections that the user pastes into the chat.
STEPS:
1. Analyze the input and extract the events, achievements, frictions, and emotions mentioned.
2. Group events into dimensions: work/projects, relationships, learning, health/energy.
3. Write an executive summary of the period in 3 to 5 sentences.
4. List achievements with concrete evidence extracted from the input.
5. Describe obstacles and the strategies used to overcome them.
6. Identify 2 to 3 recurring patterns (positive and negative).
7. Assess the energy and well-being level on a qualitative scale (high/medium/low) with justification.
8. Propose 3 to 5 SMART commitments with a review date.
OUTPUT: A Markdown document with numbered sections, concise bullets, and a commitments table with columns Commitment | Metric | Review date.
EDGE CASES:
- If the user reports a very negative period or signs of severe burnout, include a self-care section before the commitments and limit commitments to a maximum of 2.
- If the input is scarce (less than 100 words), request answers to 5 guiding questions before continuing.
- If the period exceeds 6 months, divide the analysis into quarterly sub-periods.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the document has all the sections, the commitments are measurable and have a date, the patterns are backed by evidence from the input.
Trade-off: psychological depth vs. conciseness; prioritize action over infinite introspection.
DoD: the user can read the document in less than 10 minutes and derive concrete actions without rereading their original notes.

MetodologIA Protocol: period input → dimensional analysis → synthesis → SMART commitments.
spec-personal_revision_mensual_objetivos: [S · SITUATION] A person finishes the month and needs to assess how close they were to their declared objectives, identify patterns of progress or blockage, and adjust the next month's plan based on real evidence, not vague perceptions. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured monthly review report: an achievements section (what was accomplished and why), a gaps section (what was not accomplished and root causes), lessons learned (max. 3), and an adjusted plan for the next month with at least 3 concrete commitments. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Personal executive coach with ICF certification and 10 years facilitating high-performance reviews. ASSUMPTIONS: if last month's objectives are not provided, request only those before continuing; if the month is not indicated, assume the calendar month immediately prior to the session date; if no life areas are mentioned, cover work, health, and relationships. INPUTS: the user will paste their objectives for the month and a free note on how it went. STEPS: 1) Read the objectives and identify each one with its status (achieved/partial/not achieved). 2) For each gap, formulate the root cause in a single sentence. 3) Synthesize max. 3 actionable lessons. 4) Propose an adjusted plan with SMART commitments for the next month. 5) Close with a closing question that invites reflection. OUTPUT: a document in sections with headings, bullets, and a status table for the objectives (objective | status | root cause). EDGE CASES: (a) user with no previously written objectives → offer to build them in the same session before reviewing; (b) user reports that everything went wrong → focus on systemic causes, not on self-criticism; (c) more than 10 objectives → group by area and work the top 5 gaps. [C · CRITERIA] Each gap has exactly one identified root cause. The next month's plan contains dates or milestones. The report does not exceed 600 words. There are no value judgments about the person, only about the facts. DoD: the user can send the report to a colleague without additional explanation. MetodologIA Protocol: evidence before advice, root cause before solution, plan before closing.
spec-personal_balance_anual: [S · SITUATION] A person is at the close of a year or the start of the next one and wants to make an honest review of what they lived, learned and achieved, in order to then intentionally design the coming year with clear goals across all dimensions of their life. [P · REQUEST] Produce a two-part document: (1) Review of the year that closed: wins by area, losses or hard learnings, and 3-5 personal-growth insights. (2) Design of the new year: one-sentence vision, 3-5 annual intentions per life area, and a theme-word for the year. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Life-design facilitator with a focus on human-centered design thinking and a structured annual-review method. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not indicate the past year, assume the immediately preceding calendar year; if they do not specify areas, use the 8 of the wheel of life (career, finances, health, relationships, family, personal growth, recreation, physical environment); if they provide no notes, request a maximum of one free-form answer before continuing. INPUTS: the user will paste their notes from the year or answer guided questions. STEPS: 1) Formulate 5 annual-reflection questions if there are no prior inputs. 2) With the inputs, map wins and learnings by area. 3) Identify the pattern or theme of the closing year. 4) Facilitate the vision of the new year with an anchor-sentence. 5) Co-create 3-5 intentions per area and the theme-word of the year. OUTPUT: a 2-section document with headers, bullets by area and the theme-phrase highlighted in bold. EDGE CASES: (a) user only wants the review without design → deliver only part 1; (b) user mid-year → adapt as a semiannual review; (c) user reports a traumatic year → approach with greater emphasis on learnings and resilience, avoid forced positivity. [C · CRITERIA] The review covers at least 5 of the 8 areas. The annual intentions are inspiring yet achievable. The theme-word is unique and personal, not generic. The document does not exceed 800 words. DoD: the person can read the design every week as a motivational anchor. Protocolo MetodologIA: reflection before design, pattern before vision, intention before goal.
spec-personal_diario_reflexivo: [S · SITUATION] A person wants to turn their journaling practice into something more than a dump of thoughts: they need a structure that helps them extract meaning, identify emotions, connect experiences with their values and generate a concrete action out of the reflection. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete, ready-to-use reflective journal entry, made up of: an emotional-state opening, narration of the day's fact or situation, meaning analysis (what does this say about me or about my life), connection with a personal value, and a close with an action or intention for tomorrow. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Psychologist specialized in therapeutic writing and personal development with a focus on narrative mindfulness. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not describe any event of the day, request a single free description before continuing; if they do not mention their values, infer them from the context and declare it as an assumption; target length of the entry: 200-350 words in the first person. INPUTS: the user will paste their note or free description of the day. STEPS: 1) Identify the dominant emotion of the description and name it precisely. 2) Reframe the narration of the event in the third person to provide perspective. 3) Formulate the meaning question: what is this trying to teach me? 4) Connect with an explicit or inferred personal value. 5) Propose a small, concrete action for the following day. OUTPUT: a journal entry in the first person, with the 5 components clearly differentiated by paragraph breaks, without visible labels. EDGE CASES: (a) day with no significant events → work with the absence itself as a theme; (b) intense negative emotion → validate first before analyzing; (c) user wants only the empty structure → deliver an editable template with guide questions. [C · CRITERIA] The entry flows naturally without looking like a form. The emotion is named with nuance, not just as good or bad. The closing action is so small it cannot fail. DoD: the user can publish the entry as is or use it as a basis for immediate reflection. Protocolo MetodologIA: emotion before analysis, meaning before action, small before big.
spec-personal_after_action_review: [S · SITUATION] A person has just completed an important activity (presentation, negotiation, project, event, difficult conversation) and wants to extract structured learnings while it is fresh, before the memory becomes distorted, to improve their performance the next similar time. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured personal After Action Review (AAR) with: the original intention of the activity, what actually happened, the difference between intention and result with a causal analysis, factors that worked well (keep), factors that did not work (stop), and changes to implement on the next occasion (start). Max. 3 bullets per section. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: High-performance coach with experience in military debriefing adapted to personal and professional development. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not describe the original intention, ask for it in a single question before continuing; if they do not mention the result, assume it was partially successful and declare it; target duration of the AAR: a 3-minute read. INPUTS: the user will describe the activity and their perception of how it went. STEPS: 1) Clarify the original intention (ask if missing). 2) Summarize what happened in 2-3 objective sentences. 3) Identify the intention-result gap and its main cause. 4) List max. 3 keep factors (what to replicate). 5) List max. 3 stop factors (what to eliminate). 6) List max. 3 start actions (what to implement next time). OUTPUT: a document with 6 labeled sections, concise bullet points, and a synthesis sentence at the end with the core learning. EDGE CASES: (a) the activity went perfectly → still look for 1-2 areas of improvement so as not to fall into complacency; (b) very negative result → start with the keep factors before the stops to maintain energy; (c) group activity → ask the user to speak only from their role and perspective. [C · CRITERIA] Each section has max. 3 bullets. The synthesis sentence captures the core learning in 25 words or fewer. The tone is professional but human, not punitive. DoD: the user can share the AAR with a mentor or file it as a future reference. Protocolo MetodologIA: facts before judgments, cause before solution, keep before stop.
spec-personal_kpi_personales: [S · SITUATION] A person has personal goals or intentions but does not know how to measure them objectively and practically. They need to transform vague aspirations into concrete indicators they can monitor weekly or monthly without needing complex tools. [P · REQUEST] Produce a set of 5-8 personal KPIs organized by life area, each one with: indicator name, formula or measurement method, review frequency, baseline value (or how to obtain it), and a numeric target for 90 days. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data analyst applied to personal development, with experience in measurement systems for high-performance individuals. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify life areas, cover at minimum work/health/relationships; if they have no historical data, set the first week as the baseline; if the goals are not numeric, convert them to a 1-10 satisfaction scale. INPUTS: the user will paste their goals or life areas they want to measure. STEPS: 1) Map each goal or area to a measurable indicator. 2) For each indicator, define a simple formula (count, percentage or scale). 3) Assign a realistic review frequency (daily/weekly/monthly). 4) Identify where and how the user will capture the data (app, sheet, note). 5) Propose a 90-day target per indicator. OUTPUT: a table with 5 columns (indicator | formula | frequency | baseline | 90-day target) followed by a 3-line implementation note. EDGE CASES: (a) user wants to measure everything → limit to 8 KPIs max. to avoid overload; (b) qualitative goal hard to measure → convert to a 1-10 satisfaction scale with description anchoring; (c) user with no measurement routine → suggest 5 minutes of weekly review as the only anchor habit. [C · CRITERIA] Each KPI can be measured without specialized tools. The 90-day targets are ambitious but achievable. The entire table fits on a mobile screen. DoD: the user can start measuring today without additional training. Protocolo MetodologIA: measurement before improvement, simplicity before precision, consistency before optimization.
spec-personal_revision_trimestral: [S · SITUATION] A person applies or wants to apply the 12-week planning system (12 Week Year) to manage their time and energy with more focus than a traditional annual plan. They need to review the closing quarter and design the next one with weekly execution goals aligned to a maximum of 1-3 objectives. [P · REQUEST] Produce a 12-week quarterly plan with: (1) review of the previous quarter (wins, gaps, single lesson), (2) definition of 1-3 objectives for the new quarter with their measure of success, (3) a week-by-week breakdown with 3-5 actions per week. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Consultant in productivity and personal execution certified in the 12 Week Year system by Moran and Lennon. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user has no previous quarter to review, jump directly to the design; if they define more than 3 objectives, negotiate and reduce to the 3 most impactful; if they do not specify the life area, assume it applies to the main professional objective. INPUTS: the user will paste their current state and the objectives they want to achieve in 12 weeks. STEPS: 1) Review the previous quarter if applicable (wins, gaps, lesson). 2) Clarify and write the 1-3 quarter objectives with an observable measure. 3) Divide each objective into 4-week milestones (weeks 1-4, 5-8, 9-12). 4) For the first 4 weeks, detail 3-5 weekly actions. 5) For weeks 5-12, detail milestones by 4-week block. OUTPUT: a document with a review section, an objectives table with the measure of success, and a detailed weekly schedule for weeks 1-4 plus milestones for weeks 5-12. EDGE CASES: (a) non-measurable objectives → convert to observable outcomes before breaking them down; (b) overloaded user → reduce to a single objective for the quarter; (c) plan mid-quarter → adapt to the remaining weeks. [C · CRITERIA] Each week has exactly 3-5 concrete and dated actions. The objectives are max. 3. The complete plan fits on 2 pages. DoD: the user can review the plan every Sunday in less than 5 minutes. Protocolo MetodologIA: focus before speed, week before year, action before intention.
spec-personal_journaling_gratitud: [S · SITUATION] A person wants to establish or deepen a daily gratitude practice that goes beyond listing three good things of the day. They need a journaling format that activates the neuroscience of gratitude through specificity, emotional connection and a sense of contribution. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured gratitude journaling entry of 150-250 words in the first person with: a specific gratitude (not generic) with the concrete why, a person to thank and the emotion that thankfulness generates, a small thing that is often ignored but today deserves attention, and an intention for how to express or act from that gratitude today. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Specialist in positive psychology with research on gratitude interventions based on the methodology of Emmons and McCullough. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not provide context of the day, generate the entry as a template with brackets to fill in; if the user provides context, fully personalize it; tone: warm, authentic, without cheesiness. INPUTS: the user can provide their day or simply ask for a template. STEPS: 1) Identify or create the specific gratitude with a concrete trigger. 2) Name the emotion with emotional precision (not just happy or good). 3) Choose a micro-gratitude for the ordinary (water, light, breathing, etc.). 4) Formulate the intention of expression or concrete action for today. 5) Ensure the entry flows as natural text, not as a list. OUTPUT: a flowing-prose journaling entry, 150-250 words, first person, without visible headers or bullets. EDGE CASES: (a) difficult day → find gratitude in the contrast or in the learning from the pain; (b) user in skeptical mode → include a brief note about scientific evidence at the end if requested; (c) user wants to use this every day → offer a version with blanks to fill in. [C · CRITERIA] The main gratitude is specific and has a concrete why. The emotion is named with precision. The intention of the day is achievable in under 2 minutes. DoD: the entry can be printed and pasted into a physical notebook without editing. Protocolo MetodologIA: specificity before generality, emotion before reason, action before contemplation.
spec-personal_okr_personales: [S · SITUATION] A person knows the OKR framework (Objectives and Key Results) from the corporate world and wants to apply it to their personal life for the current quarter, needing to translate their aspirations into 1-3 inspiring objectives with 2-3 measurable key results each. [P · REQUEST] Produce a set of personal quarterly OKRs: 1-3 objectives written as inspiring statements (what I want to achieve and why it matters), with 2-3 key results per objective formulated as observable metrics from 0 to 1 or in concrete units, plus a start action for this week for each objective. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert in OKR implementation with experience adapting the framework of Google and Silicon Valley companies to the context of individuals and their personal and professional goals. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user has more than 3 potential objectives, facilitate the prioritization by choosing those with the greatest impact on their life vision; if the proposed key results are tasks (actions) and not outcomes, reformulate them; if they do not specify the quarter, assume the current calendar quarter. INPUTS: the user will paste their aspirations or the draft of their objectives for the quarter. STEPS: 1) Review the proposed objectives: are they inspiring? are they outcomes, not tasks? Adjust. 2) For each objective, formulate 2-3 key results as concrete metrics with a baseline and target. 3) Verify that the key results are ambitious (70% achievement is excellent). 4) Add a start action for this week per objective. 5) Present the complete set in a clean OKR format. OUTPUT: a set of OKRs in standard format (O: text / KR1: / KR2: / KR3: / Start this week: text) followed by a note on how to do the weekly check-in. EDGE CASES: (a) objectives formulated as tasks → reformulate as outcomes; (b) non-measurable key results → propose a metric proxy; (c) user with a very diverse life → limit to a maximum of 2 OKRs to maintain focus. [C · CRITERIA] Each objective sounds inspiring when read aloud. Each key result has a number or percentage. OKRs at 70% already represent an excellent quarter. DoD: the user can do a weekly check-in of each KR in less than 3 minutes. Protocolo MetodologIA: outcome before task, measurable before vague, focus before coverage.
spec-personal_metas_smart: [S · SITUATION] A person has a wish, dream or vague intention that they want to turn into an actionable goal using the SMART framework (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). They need the transformation to be rigorous but also for the resulting goal to sound motivating, not just technical. [P · REQUEST] Produce the complete SMART goal with: (1) an analysis of the original wish across its 5 SMART dimensions, (2) a SMART goal written in a single sentence with all the elements integrated, (3) a concrete first step to start within the next 24 hours, and (4) an observable success indicator at the deadline. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Certified goals coach specialized in transforming vague intentions into executable commitments using the SMART framework in its extended SMARTER version (includes periodic Evaluation and Review). ASSUMPTIONS: if the wish is very broad, split it into max. 2 independent SMART goals; if there is no deadline, propose a reasonable one according to the magnitude of the wish; if the life area is not indicated, process the wish as is without assuming an area. INPUTS: the user will paste their wish or intention in free form. STEPS: 1) Read the wish and identify what is missing for it to be SMART. 2) Ask the questions of the missing dimensions if confidence is below 85%, or declare assumptions. 3) Formulate the SMART goal in one sentence. 4) Verify: does it sound motivating when read? Adjust the wording if necessary. 5) Define a first step in 24 hours and a success criterion. OUTPUT: a document with 4 sections (SMART analysis, goal in one sentence, first step in 24h, success criterion) separated by headers. EDGE CASES: (a) wish that depends on third parties → reformulate in terms of what the user can control; (b) goal already very specific → confirm the dimensions and add what is missing; (c) multiple wishes → process one at a time and ask for a priority. [C · CRITERIA] The SMART goal fits in a sentence of max. 30 words. The first step can be done in under 15 minutes. The success criterion is binary (it was met or not). DoD: the user can write the goal in their calendar and share it with someone within the next 30 minutes. Protocolo MetodologIA: clarity before commitment, control before dependency, small step before big plan.
spec-personal_rueda_vida: [S · SITUATION] A person wants to make an honest diagnosis of the balance across the different areas of their life using the Wheel of Life tool (8 dimensions: career/work, finances, physical health, mental/emotional health, intimate relationships, family, personal growth, recreation/fun). They need more than a simple score: they want to understand the pattern of their imbalances and receive a prioritized action plan. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a 1-10 scoring table by area with a 1-line justification per score, (2) an analysis of the imbalance pattern (which areas are sacrificed, which dominate, visible tensions), (3) the priority area to intervene in first with justification, and (4) 3 concrete actions for the coming week in that priority area. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Integral life coach with training in positive psychology and 15 years using the Wheel of Life as a diagnosis and planning tool. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not provide their scores, ask them 8 brief questions (one per area) before continuing; if they give scores without context, request a sentence of justification per low-score area; if they say everything is fine (high scores), explore whether there is complacency or conformity. INPUTS: the user can paste scores directly or describe their situation in each area. STEPS: 1) Collect 1-10 scores for the 8 areas. 2) Calculate the overall average and the gap between the highest and lowest area. 3) Identify the pattern: what type of imbalance does it show (workaholic, neglect of the body, social isolation, etc.)? 4) Name the area with the greatest impact on overall well-being if improved. 5) Propose 3 actions for this week in that area. OUTPUT: a table of 8 areas with scores and justification, a pattern-analysis paragraph (max. 100 words), the priority area with justification, and a list of 3 weekly actions. EDGE CASES: (a) all scores equal → explore whether it is genuine or whether there are anesthetized areas; (b) user wants to improve everything at once → explain the wheel effect and why to start with one; (c) area at 0 or in crisis → treat with greater attention and suggest professional support if applicable. [C · CRITERIA] The table covers the 8 standard areas. The pattern analysis is not a list, it is an interpretive text. The priority area has a clear leverage-effect reason. The 3 actions are so concrete they need no further explanation. DoD: the user can share the diagnosis with their coach or therapist without editing. Protocolo MetodologIA: diagnosis before plan, pattern before symptom, leverage before everything.
spec-ia-automatizacion_diseno-system-pro: [S · SITUATION] An AI systems designer or technical professional needs to create the system prompt for a special-purpose conversational agent or assistant. The system prompt must clearly define the agent's role, its main objective, its functional scope and its operational constraints, following the best practices of prompt engineering for large-scale language models. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete, production-ready system prompt with: a role declaration (who the agent is), the main objective (what it does and for whom), the scope (what it can and cannot do), the response style (tone, format, length), handling of out-of-scope cases, and at least 2-3 critical operational constraints. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior prompt engineer specialized in the design of conversational agents for enterprise and consumer applications. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the target model, assume a state-of-the-art language model with a long context window; if they do not mention the target audience, assume internal company users; if they do not indicate the tone, assume professional and direct; the target length of the system prompt is 150-400 words. INPUTS: the user will describe the purpose of the agent, its audience and its constraints. STEPS: 1) Extract from the input: type of agent, audience, domain, constraints. 2) Write the role declaration in 1-2 affirmative sentences. 3) Define the main objective with the dominant action verb. 4) List 3-5 in-scope capabilities and 2-3 out-of-scope ones. 5) Specify the response style, ambiguity handling and escalation. 6) Add safety or compliance constraints if applicable. OUTPUT: a system prompt ready to copy and paste, between triple backticks, followed by a design-notes section in 3-5 bullets explaining the key decisions. EDGE CASES: (a) very generic agent → ask for the most frequent use case before continuing; (b) contradictory constraints → flag them and propose a resolution; (c) regulated domain (health, legal, finance) → add standard disclaimers automatically. [C · CRITERIA] The system prompt is not ambiguous in any of its 6 sections. The constraints are operational, not vague. The agent knows what to do when it receives something outside its scope. DoD: the prompt can be tested in production without modification and the QA team can validate it against clear criteria. Protocolo MetodologIA: role before constraint, scope before style, clarity before brevity.
spec-ia-automatizacion_system-prompt-per: [S · SITUATION] A company or content creator needs a system prompt that defines the persona of a conversational agent aligned with their brand's voice, tone and values. The agent will represent the brand across digital channels (chatbot, sales assistant, support, community) and must sound consistent with the brand identity without being generic or robotic. [P · REQUEST] Produce a complete brand persona system prompt with: agent identity (name, character, 3-5 personality traits), brand voice in 5-7 writing principles, examples of how it would respond to 3 typical channel situations, words and phrases to use (positive voice bank) and words and phrases to avoid (negative voice bank), and brand representation constraints. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Digital brand strategist and conversational persona designer with experience defining brand voice for B2C and B2B companies. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user doesn't have a brand book, infer the brand voice from the materials or description provided and declare it as an assumption; if the channel isn't indicated, assume a customer support chatbot on web; if the agent name isn't mentioned, propose one aligned with the brand. INPUTS: the user will paste a brand description, communication examples or brand book fragments. STEPS: 1) Extract the brand personality from the inputs: 3-5 adjectives that define it. 2) Write the agent identity with name and character traits aligned. 3) Formulate 5-7 voice principles as concrete writing rules. 4) Write 3 example responses (typical situation → response in brand voice). 5) Build the positive and negative vocabulary bank. 6) Add brand representation constraints. OUTPUT: system prompt between triple backticks with all sections, followed by a brand voice glossary in 2 columns (use | avoid) with 5-10 pairs. EDGE CASES: (a) very young brand with no brand book → build the voice from scratch with 3 guiding questions; (b) conservative corporate brand → ensure warmth doesn't break the seriousness; (c) multiple channels with different voices → create a common base and per-channel variations. [C · CRITERIA] The voice principles are operational: the copywriter can apply them without interpretation. The response examples are recognizable as belonging to that specific brand. The negative bank avoids the sector's clichés. DoD: the marketing team can use the system prompt to onboard any AI agent without an additional training session. MetodologIA Protocol: character before tone, principle before example, coherence before creativity.
spec-ia-automatizacion_jerarquia-instruc:
[S · SITUATION] A prompt engineering team needs to define, document and apply a clear instruction hierarchy in a multi-agent system or AI automation pipeline, where system instructions, user instructions, tool instructions and context overrides coexist, generating unresolved precedence conflicts.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an instruction hierarchy document that includes: (1) an instruction-layer map with explicit precedence level (1 = highest), (2) conflict-resolution rules for each pair of layers, (3) a decision table with concrete examples for each conflict case, (4) an inline comment template to annotate precedence directly in system prompts.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior conversational AI systems architect with experience in LLM pipeline design and multi-layer instruction management.
ASSUMPTIONS: The system uses a language model that supports system prompt + user messages; if there are more than 4 instruction layers, explicitly declare the additional ones; assume that unresolved conflicts must be resolved by hierarchical precedence and not by last-instruction-wins, unless the user indicates otherwise.
INPUTS: The user pastes the current set of instructions (system prompt, tool instructions, known overrides) as plain text in the thread.
STEPS:
1. Identify and catalog all instruction sources present → enumerated list with source and assigned layer.
2. Assign a precedence level to each layer with technical justification → Layer / Level / Justification table.
3. Define conflict-resolution rules for each relevant combination → Layer A vs Layer B / Rule / Example table.
4. Write an inline annotation template to mark precedence in system prompts → code block with exemplified comments.
5. Generate a decision table with at least 5 real conflict scenarios → columns: Scenario / Layers in conflict / Applied resolution / Expected result.
OUTPUT: Structured Markdown document with five numbered sections (Layer catalog, Precedence table, Resolution rules, Inline template, Decision table). No introductory prose.
EDGE CASES:
- If the user doesn't provide current instructions: generate a generic standard 4-layer hierarchy (system, tool, context, user) and document that it is a base template.
- If two layers have the same previously assigned level: escalate the conflict and propose a tie-break via instruction specificity.
- If contradictory instructions exist within the same layer: document it as an internal conflict and suggest consolidation.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: each layer has a unique level and a verifiable resolution rule.
- Trade-off: priority to specificity over order of appearance.
- DoD: the document can be pasted directly into a prompt engineering repository without additional editing.

MetodologIA Protocol: apply structured layer-by-layer reasoning before issuing each precedence rule.
spec-ia-automatizacion_refactor-system-p:
[S · SITUATION] A product team has a production system prompt that has grown organically to exceed 2,000 words, contains duplicated instructions, contradictory sections, obsolete examples and a flat structure with no visual hierarchy. The model is starting to ignore low-position instructions and the token cost is increasing without quality improvement.

[P · REQUEST] Produce the refactored version of the delivered system prompt, with a minimum 40% reduction in tokens, zero loss of verified functional coverage, and an explicit hierarchical structure with labeled sections.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior prompt engineer with experience optimizing system prompts for production language models.
ASSUMPTIONS: The system prompt uses direct instruction language (not narrative); if the text mixes languages, consolidate in the dominant language; assume that every instruction present has functional value unless it appears duplicated or in direct contradiction with another of greater specificity.
INPUTS: The user pastes the complete system prompt as plain text.
STEPS:
1. Audit the original prompt → table: Identified section / Estimated tokens / Detected problem (redundancy, contradiction, obsolescence, none).
2. Consolidate duplicated instructions keeping the most specific version → list of consolidation decisions.
3. Resolve contradictions by choosing the most precise instruction → resolution log with justification.
4. Restructure into labeled sections with clear headers (CONTEXT, ROLE, CONSTRAINTS, FORMAT, EXAMPLES, EDGE CASES) → structured draft.
5. Reduce verbosity without losing semantics → final compact version.
6. Generate a coverage verification table: Original functionality / Present in refactored version (yes/no) / Section where it lives.
OUTPUT: (a) Refactored version of the system prompt ready to copy-paste, (b) initial audit table, (c) final coverage table. All in Markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the minimum 40% reduction would eliminate essential functionality: document the trade-off and propose two versions (compact and complete).
- If there are instructions that seem obsolete but there is no certainty: mark them with a [REVIEW] comment instead of deleting them.
- If the prompt contains sensitive data or examples with PII: replace with placeholders and notify the user.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: token count before and after verifiable with any standard tokenizer.
- Trade-off: compactness over exhaustiveness, unless functionality is lost.
- DoD: the refactored system prompt can replace the original in production without additional changes.

MetodologIA Protocol: audit first, refactor after; do not omit the decision log.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-multiidiom:
[S · SITUATION] A product team needs to deploy an AI assistant that serves users in multiple languages without requiring manual language selection. The current system prompt is written only in English, the model sometimes responds in a language different from the user's, and there are no explicit detection rules nor language consistency rules within the same conversation.

[P · REQUEST] Design a multilingual system prompt that: (1) automatically detects the language of the user's first message, (2) always responds in that same language unless explicitly instructed otherwise, (3) maintains language consistency throughout the session, (4) supports a mid-conversation language switch if the user explicitly requests it, and (5) gracefully handles messages in an unknown or mixed language.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Multilingual prompt engineer with experience localizing conversational assistants for global markets.
ASSUMPTIONS: The underlying model supports the most common languages (Spanish, English, French, Portuguese, German, Italian); if the product has specific supported languages, the user must list them; assume that the system prompt's internal instruction language may be different from the response language.
INPUTS: The user provides (a) the current base system prompt or a description of the assistant, and (b) optionally the list of supported languages.
STEPS:
1. Identify the necessary language-detection rules → list of rules with use case.
2. Write the language detection and instruction section for the system prompt → code block.
3. Write mid-session language-switch rules → code block with explicit condition.
4. Write the handling of unknown or mixed language → code block with defined fallback.
5. Integrate everything into the provided base system prompt → complete multilingual system prompt.
6. Verify that the language instructions don't conflict with the system's technical content → verification checklist.
OUTPUT: (a) Complete multilingual system prompt ready for production, (b) isolated and reusable language-detection section, (c) 5-point verification checklist. All in Markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the user writes in two languages in the same message: detect the language with the greater proportion and declare it as the response language.
- If the detected language is not in the supported list: respond in the closest available language and notify the user of the supported languages.
- If the base system prompt contains instructions that contradict the language policy: prioritize the language policy and document the conflict.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the assistant responds in the language of the first message in at least 9 out of 10 manual tests.
- Trade-off: language consistency over naturalness in error messages.
- DoD: the system prompt can be inserted into production without additional language configuration.

MetodologIA Protocol: validate the detection rules with at least 3 input examples before writing the final section.
spec-ia-automatizacion_plantilla-variabl:
[S · SITUATION] An automation team needs to build a system of parameterized prompts where certain values (customer name, business context, case-specific instructions) are injected dynamically at runtime. Current attempts mix injection logic with the prompt text, generate prompt injection risks and produce errors when a variable is undefined.

[P · REQUEST] Design a prompt template with dynamic variables that includes: (1) standard syntax for declaring variables with a default value, (2) a pre-injection validation mechanism, (3) explicit handling of missing or malicious variables, and (4) a fully functional example version for a customer support use case.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Automation engineer specialized in the secure design of dynamic prompt pipelines for production.
ASSUMPTIONS: Injection happens server-side before sending to the model; variables are strings; if the user has a use case other than customer support, they specify it; assume that any variable coming from external user input is potentially malicious until validated.
INPUTS: The user describes the use case and lists the variables they need to inject (or accepts the customer support example by default).
STEPS:
1. Define the variable declaration syntax with default value → syntax specification with examples.
2. Design the pre-injection validation schema → table: Variable / Expected type / Validation / Action if it fails.
3. Write the anti-prompt-injection rules to be included in the prompt → security instruction block.
4. Build the parameterized prompt template for the specified use case → template with marked variables.
5. Generate the resolved version of the prompt with example values injected → final example prompt.
6. Document the safe injection flow as pseudocode → 5-step diagram.
OUTPUT: (a) Variable syntax specification, (b) validation schema, (c) prompt template with variables, (d) resolved example, (e) injection flow pseudocode. All in Markdown with code blocks.
EDGE CASES:
- If a mandatory variable is undefined at injection time: use the declared default value; if there is no default value, halt the pipeline and log the error.
- If the injected value contains system instructions or control characters: sanitize by removing role tags and problematic characters before injection.
- If the template exceeds the model's context limit when resolving the variables: truncate the longest field with an explicit truncation indicator.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the resolved template with example values produces a valid and executable prompt without manual editing.
- Trade-off: injection security over variable-format flexibility.
- DoD: a developer can take the template and the pseudocode and implement the injection system in less than 2 hours.

MetodologIA Protocol: design the validation schema before building the template; security precedes functionality.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-formato-sa:
[S · SITUATION] An automation pipeline consumes a language model's output and passes it directly to a downstream system (database, API, rule engine). The model returns responses with inconsistent format —sometimes valid JSON, sometimes prose, sometimes JSON with comments or trailing commas— which breaks the parser and generates errors in production.

[P · REQUEST] Design the strict output-format instructions for a system prompt that guarantee the model always produces the specified format (JSON, XML or delimited text depending on the case), including: format instruction, validation schema, instruction for handling cases where the format is not possible, and a test suite of 5 inputs with expected output.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: LLM integration engineer with experience designing output contracts for robust automation pipelines.
ASSUMPTIONS: The default target format is JSON; if the user specifies another format, that one takes priority; the model is capable of following strict format instructions; assume that the downstream validation layer rejects any output outside the schema.
INPUTS: The user specifies (a) the target format, (b) the desired schema or structure, (c) the pipeline use case.
STEPS:
1. Write the strict format instruction for the system prompt → instruction block with examples of valid and invalid output.
2. Define the validation schema of the expected format → JSON Schema or equivalent depending on the format.
3. Write the fallback instruction for when the format is not possible → block with structured error protocol.
4. Design 5 test cases: input / expected output / type of validation → test suite table.
5. Write the complete format section ready to insert into the system prompt → final code block.
OUTPUT: (a) Format instruction for the system prompt, (b) validation schema, (c) structured error protocol, (d) table of 5 test cases, (e) integrated format section ready to copy. All in Markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the model cannot produce the valid format due to query limitations: return a structured error object with `error`, `reason` and `raw_output` fields instead of breaking the pipeline.
- If the schema contains optional fields and the model omits them: accept the output if the required fields are present; document which fields are optional.
- If the user requests a non-standard proprietary format: generate the formal specification of the format before writing the instruction.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the 5 test cases can be run manually and the format verified in less than 10 minutes.
- Trade-off: output parsability over response naturalness.
- DoD: the format section can be inserted into any production system prompt without additional modification.

MetodologIA Protocol: specify the schema before writing the instruction; the data contract precedes the prompt text.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-manejo-inc:
[S · SITUATION] A production AI assistant generates responses with high apparent confidence even when the information is uncertain, outdated or beyond the scope of its knowledge. Users make decisions based on responses that the model invents or extrapolates with no warning signal, which generates loss of trust and costly errors.

[P · REQUEST] Design the uncertainty-handling instructions for a system prompt that achieve: (1) that the model explicitly declares when it doesn't know something, (2) that it differentiates between verified knowledge, reasoned inference and speculation, (3) that it proposes verification actions when uncertainty is high, and (4) that it never invents factual data (dates, numbers, proper names) without a warning signal.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Specialist in alignment and behavior design of language models for high-responsibility environments.
ASSUMPTIONS: The assistant operates in a domain where errors have tangible consequences (health, finance, legal, or engineering); if the domain is low-risk, the instructions can be relaxed; the model has a basic capacity for introspection about its own knowledge.
INPUTS: The user describes the assistant's application domain and the type of uncertainty errors they have observed.
STEPS:
1. Define the confidence scale the model will use → table: Level / Label / Condition of use / Example phrasing.
2. Write the instructions for explicit declaration of uncertainty → block for the system prompt.
3. Write the instructions for differentiating the type of knowledge (verified/inferred/speculative) → block for the system prompt with language markers.
4. Write the instruction prohibiting inventing factual data → block for the system prompt with examples of violation and compliance.
5. Write the verification-proposal instruction → block for the system prompt with examples of suggested action.
6. Integrate everything into a cohesive uncertainty-handling section → final section ready to insert.
OUTPUT: (a) Confidence scale, (b) four individual instruction blocks, (c) integrated uncertainty-handling section ready for production. All in Markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the model cannot determine its own confidence level: instruct it to assume the lowest level by default and declare it.
- If the response requires factual data the model doesn't have with certainty: instruct it to use ranges or approximate values with an explicit approximation label.
- If the user requests a definitive answer when uncertainty is high: instruct it to maintain the uncertainty signal and explain why it cannot give a definitive answer.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: across 10 questions on uncertain or out-of-domain topics, the model signals its uncertainty in at least 8 without needing additional instruction.
- Trade-off: epistemic honesty over conversational fluency.
- DoD: the section can be inserted into any high-responsibility-environment system prompt without additional configuration.

MetodologIA Protocol: design the confidence scale first; all instruction blocks must reference it.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-cadena-pen:
[S · SITUATION] A team needs a language model to solve complex multi-step problems (causal analysis, multi-criteria decision-making, chained logical reasoning) with full traceability of the thought process, so that the results are auditable and reasoning errors can be identified and corrected.

[P · REQUEST] Design the structured step-by-step reasoning instructions for a system prompt that guarantee: (1) that the model externalizes its thought process in observable numbered steps before issuing the final answer, (2) that each step produces a verifiable partial conclusion, (3) that the model explicitly identifies the assumptions it activates at each step, and (4) that the final answer is visually separated from the reasoning and directly usable.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Computational reasoning designer with experience in prompt engineering for high-complexity analytical tasks.
ASSUMPTIONS: The use case requires reasoning traceability (it's not a quick-answer chatbot); the model supports generating long chains of thought; if the user doesn't specify the problem domain, assume business analysis or decision-making.
INPUTS: The user describes the type of problem the assistant must solve and optionally pastes an example of a real problem.
STEPS:
1. Define the reasoning step structure for the specific domain → numbered step template with: premise / operation / partial conclusion / activated assumptions.
2. Write the chained reasoning instruction for the system prompt → instruction block.
3. Write the instruction for separation between reasoning and final answer → block with visual marker.
4. Write the instruction for per-step assumption declaration → integrated block.
5. Demonstrate the structure with an example problem solved step by step → complete example with the format applied.
6. Generate a compact version of the instruction for prompts with a token limit → compact block.
OUTPUT: (a) Reasoning step template, (b) complete chained reasoning instruction, (c) worked example with the structure applied, (d) compact version of the instruction. All in Markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the problem doesn't require multiple steps: the model completes the reasoning in a single step, declaring that no more are needed.
- If a step leads to a conclusion that contradicts the initial premise: the model flags it explicitly and restarts the reasoning from the point of contradiction.
- If the complete reasoning exceeds the context limit: the model completes the critical steps and summarizes the intermediate ones, marking them as summaries.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: a human reviewer can follow the reasoning step by step and identify the exact point of any logical error.
- Trade-off: reasoning traceability over response brevity.
- DoD: the instruction can be inserted into an existing system prompt and work without additional adjustments.

MetodologIA Protocol: demonstrate the structure with a real worked example before delivering the final instruction.
spec-ia-automatizacion_few-shot-curado:
[S · SITUATION] A team has a set of input-output examples to train an assistant's behavior via few-shot prompting, but the examples are heterogeneous, some are redundant, others are outliers that bias the model toward undesired behaviors, and there is no documented selection criterion.

[P · REQUEST] Curate a high-quality set of few-shot examples from the provided example bank, producing: (1) the N best selected examples with an explicit criterion, (2) the discarded examples with justification, (3) at least 2 synthetic examples generated to cover unrepresented cases, and (4) the instructions for positioning examples within the prompt.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Training data and prompting engineer specialized in curating few-shot examples for production AI systems.
ASSUMPTIONS: The optimal number of few-shot examples is 3-5 for most models; if the user has token constraints, reduce to 2-3; the examples must cover the input variation space of the real use case, not just the easy cases.
INPUTS: The user pastes the example bank (input-output pairs) as text or a numbered list.
STEPS:
1. Analyze the complete example bank → table: # / Summarized input / Case type / Quality (high/medium/low) / Detected problem.
2. Select the N best examples applying criteria of: case coverage, input diversity, output clarity, absence of ambiguity → list of selected ones with justification per criterion.
3. Document the discarded ones with a specific reason → list of discarded ones with reason: redundant/outlier/ambiguous/low quality.
4. Identify cases not covered by the selected examples → list of coverage gaps.
5. Generate at least 2 synthetic examples to cover the identified gaps → examples with a synthesis note.
6. Write the instructions for positioning and formatting examples within the prompt → instruction block with template.
OUTPUT: (a) Analysis table of the original bank, (b) curated set of N examples with justification, (c) list of discarded ones, (d) synthetic examples, (e) positioning instructions. All in Markdown.
EDGE CASES:
- If the bank has fewer than 3 examples: use all of them and generate the synthetic ones needed to reach 5.
- If all the examples are of the same case type: flag the bias and generate synthetic ones for 60% of the missing cases.
- If an example output has a format inconsistent with the assistant's target format: normalize the output format in the curated example and document the normalization.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the N curated examples cover at least 3 distinct case types and have no redundant pairs.
- Trade-off: coverage diversity over the number of examples.
- DoD: the curated set can be inserted directly into the production prompt without additional adjustment.

MetodologIA Protocol: analyze the complete bank before selecting; justified curation beats intuition.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-delimitado:
[S · SITUATION] A team building complex prompts for automation pipelines faces ambiguity problems: the model confuses the reference context with the instructions, mixes user content with system text, and cannot clearly delimit where each piece of information starts and ends in high-information-density prompts.

[P · REQUEST] Design a system of delimiters and sections to structure complex prompts that includes: (1) a standardized delimiter convention by content type, (2) a section hierarchy with clear semantic roles, (3) nesting rules for multiple contexts, and (4) a multi-section prompt template ready to adapt.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Prompt architect with experience in designing context structures for high-information-complexity LLM pipelines.
ASSUMPTIONS: The model processes the prompt as plain text and the delimiters are semantic markup conventions, not executable syntax; use safe ASCII characters as primary delimiters; if the user specifies an existing delimiter format (XML-like, Markdown), adopt it as a base.
INPUTS: The user describes the use case and the content types they need to separate (instructions, business context, reference document, conversation history, user data).
STEPS:
1. Inventory the content types present in the use case → list of types with a description of the semantic role.
2. Define the delimiter convention by type → table: Content type / Opening delimiter / Closing delimiter / Usage example.
3. Design the prompt's section hierarchy → tree diagram in Markdown with parent-child sections.
4. Write the nesting rules for multiple contexts → list of rules with examples of compliance and non-compliance.
5. Build the multi-section prompt template for the specified use case → complete template with usage comments.
6. Demonstrate the template with a real example with test content → complete example prompt.
OUTPUT: (a) Delimiter convention table, (b) section hierarchy, (c) nesting rules, (d) multi-section template, (e) complete example. All in Markdown with code blocks.
EDGE CASES:
- If the user uses XML in their tech stack and the model interprets XML tags as real instructions: use alternative delimiters (triple quotes, triple dashes) for the XML content and document the precaution.
- If a section's content contains the system's delimiter character: escape the character or use an alternative higher-level delimiter.
- If the prompt with all the delimiters exceeds the context limit: prioritize the instruction and summary sections; compress the historical context sections.

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: a developer can read the structured prompt and immediately identify the semantic role of each section without additional instruction.
- Trade-off: structural clarity over character economy.
- DoD: the template can be reused in at least 3 different use cases by only changing the content of the sections.

MetodologIA Protocol: define the delimiter convention before building the template; structure precedes content.
spec-ia-automatizacion_meta-prompt-gener:
[S · SITUATION] A professional or team that needs to create a high-quality prompt for a specific AI task but does not know how to structure it correctly. They are clear about the end goal but lack the technical language and structure needed to instruct a language model effectively. They will paste their goal into the chat.

[P · REQUEST] A ready-to-use prompt, in English, that operationalizes the stated goal. The prompt must be self-contained, specific, with a defined role, a precise task, an explicit output format and built-in quality criteria. Additionally, a brief explanation of the design decisions made.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior prompt engineer with experience in designing instructions for large language models, structured prompting frameworks (RTF, CRISPE, SPECA) and output quality evaluation.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the goal is ambiguous, infer the most common use case and state the assumption. If the target model is not indicated, assume a state-of-the-art general-purpose language model. If the desired output format is not indicated, choose the most functional one for the task. Only ask if confidence in the goal is below 0.85.
INPUTS: Goal or task that the user describes in free text, pasted into the chat.
STEPS:
1. Analyze the goal and identify: audience, core task, implicit context and constraints.
2. Select the prompting framework most suitable for the goal.
3. Write the AI assistant's role in a specific and expert way.
4. Describe the task with action verbs and measurable parameters.
5. Define the output format with a detailed structure.
6. Incorporate quality criteria and edge cases within the prompt.
7. Review that the prompt is self-contained (works without additional context).
8. Write a design explanation in 3 to 5 bullets.
OUTPUT: Section 1: ready-to-copy-and-paste prompt (Markdown code block). Section 2: design decisions table with columns Decision | Rationale | Discarded alternative.
EDGE CASES:
- If the goal requires access to real-time information, include a limitation note in the generated prompt.
- If the goal is ethically sensitive, add content guardrails in the prompt.
- If the goal is so broad that it would require multiple prompts, propose a chain of 2 to 3 sequential prompts.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the generated prompt can be executed without modification and produce a useful output; the explanation covers the main decisions.
Trade-off: completeness vs. prompt length; avoid unnecessary padding.
DoD: another professional can use the prompt without reading the user's original goal.

MetodologIA Protocol: goal → task analysis → structured prompt → design explanation.
spec-ia-automatizacion_tecnica-rtf:
[S · SITUATION] A user who has a task for an AI model but whose instructions are vague or produce inconsistent outputs. They want to apply the RTF technique (Role, Task, Format) to improve the quality and consistency of the model's responses. They will paste the raw task into the chat.

[P · REQUEST] An RTF version of the user's prompt: a Role section with a specific expert description, a Task section with a precise instruction and measurable parameters, a Format section with the detailed structure of the expected output. Additionally, a before/after comparison in a table.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Prompt engineering consultant specializing in techniques for structuring instructions for language models.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the raw task does not mention the domain, infer it from the content and state it. If the desired output format is not indicated, select the most functional one according to the task (list, table, structured text, code). Only ask if confidence is below 0.85.
INPUTS: Raw task or instruction that the user pastes into the chat.
STEPS:
1. Read the raw task and identify intent, audience and implicit output.
2. Write the Role section: a specific expert profile with experience and focus relevant to the task.
3. Write the Task section: an instruction with an action verb, a concrete object, scope and constraints.
4. Write the Format section: structure of the expected response with section types, approximate length and an example element when useful.
5. Unify the three sections into a cohesive, ready-to-use prompt.
6. Create a before/after comparison table with columns Dimension | Original version | RTF version.
OUTPUT: Markdown code block with the complete RTF prompt followed by the comparison table.
EDGE CASES:
- If the original task already has partial structure, keep the valid elements and indicate what was improved.
- If the task requires dynamic information (date, username), use descriptive uppercase tags such as USERNAME or CURRENT_DATE.
- If the task is high-risk (sensitive content, critical decisions), add a human verification clause in the Format section.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the RTF prompt has the three complete sections; the table shows measurable improvement across at least 3 dimensions; the prompt can be executed without editing.
Trade-off: specificity vs. rigidity; the role should not be so restrictive that it limits necessary creative responses.
DoD: another user can execute the RTF prompt and obtain a consistent output without having read the original task.

MetodologIA Protocol: raw task → intent analysis → RTF structure → before/after comparison.
spec-ia-automatizacion_tecnica-tag:
[S · SITUATION] A user who needs to improve the effectiveness of their instructions to an AI model by applying the TAG framework (Task, Action, Goal). They have a task defined in natural language but without the structure that maximizes output quality. They will paste their task into the chat.

[P · REQUEST] A TAG version of the original prompt: a Task section with a precise description of the task to perform, an Action section with the concrete steps or actions the model must execute, a Goal section with the final objective and the success criteria. A unified prompt ready to execute and a before/after comparison table.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Prompt engineering specialist with command of the TAG framework and experience optimizing instructions for language models in professional contexts.
ASSUMPTIONS: If the task does not specify the type of action expected, infer the most direct one and state it. If the final objective beyond the immediate task is not indicated, infer the underlying business or personal purpose. Only ask if confidence in the intent is below 0.85.
INPUTS: Natural-language task that the user pastes into the chat.
STEPS:
1. Read the task and identify what is being asked (task), how it would be done (actions) and for what purpose (objective).
2. Write the Task section: a concise, precise description of what the model must produce.
3. Write the Action section: a numbered list of steps or actions the model must follow to complete the task.
4. Write the Goal section: the final objective with observable success criteria.
5. Unify the three sections into a cohesive prompt.
6. Create a before/after comparison table with columns Element | Original version | TAG version | Improvement achieved.
OUTPUT: Markdown code block with the complete TAG prompt followed by the comparison table.
EDGE CASES:
- If the original task already partially includes some TAG element, keep it and improve the rest.
- If the task has multiple sub-objectives, create a main TAG prompt with breakdown notes.
- If the goal requires metrics the model cannot measure directly, formulate observable qualitative criteria.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the TAG prompt has the three complete and differentiated sections; the table shows improvement in specificity, actionability and results orientation.
Trade-off: detail in actions vs. restriction of the model's creativity; the actions guide without over-restricting.
DoD: the TAG prompt can be executed directly and produces an output aligned with the stated goal.

MetodologIA Protocol: raw task → TAG structure → executable prompt → comparison.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-chaining: [S · SITUATION] A product team needs to process long technical documents in several stages (extraction, synthesis, validation, formatting) using language models, but a single monolithic prompt loses coherence and exceeds context limits. Deliverable: a document with (a) a textual flow diagram of the pipeline, (b) the complete prompt per link, (c) the input/output data schema between links, (d) error handling if a link fails. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior AI engineer specializing in LLM pipeline design and chained-prompt architecture. ASSUMPTIONS: the base model is generic (no provider specified); each link can invoke the same model; the pasted content is the document or task to process; if the optimal number of links is not clear, use 4 as the default value and state it. INPUTS: document or use-case description pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Analyze the case and define the sequence of necessary transformations (observable: list of identified transformations). 2. Design the data schema between links with types and key fields (observable: table link → input → output). 3. Write the prompt for each link with instruction, context and output format (observable: N numbered prompts). 4. Add handoff validation logic: success condition per link (observable: criteria per link). 5. Document failure handling: what to do if the output does not meet the criterion (observable: fallback table). OUTPUT: structured document in sections (a)–(d) described above, in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (1) Extremely long document → include a chunking instruction prior to link 1; (2) a link's output is ambiguous or empty → define a retry prompt with a corrective instruction; (3) circular dependency between links → detect and restructure the order in step 1. [C · CRITERIA] Each link has exactly one responsibility; the handoff schemas are typed (no ambiguous fields); the fallback prompts are defined; the complete pipeline can run without human intervention between links. spec-ia-automatizacion_self-consistency: [S · SITUATION] An analyst uses a language model for reasoning or classification tasks where a single answer may be incorrect or inconsistent; they need a systematic strategy to obtain more reliable answers without changing the model. [P · REQUEST] Apply the self-consistency technique to the pasted problem: generate N independent reasoning trajectories, aggregate the results through majority vote or synthesis, and deliver the final answer with a calculated confidence level. Deliverable: (a) N numbered parallel reasonings, (b) aggregation table with counts or weights, (c) consolidated final answer with agreement percentage, (d) diagnosis if the trajectories diverge significantly. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data scientist specializing in language model reliability evaluation and reasoning ensemble techniques. ASSUMPTIONS: N=5 trajectories if not specified; each trajectory uses complete chain-of-thought; aggregation is by majority vote unless the problem is numeric (in that case a weighted average); if the trajectories agree 100% in the first 3, it is not necessary to generate the rest (state this). INPUTS: problem, question or reasoning task pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Read the problem and determine whether it is categorical, numeric or open (observable: classification of the problem type). 2. Generate N independent reasoning trajectories, each with explicit steps (observable: N reasoning blocks). 3. Extract the final conclusion of each trajectory (observable: list of N conclusions). 4. Aggregate by vote or average according to the type (observable: table of counts/weights). 5. Compute the agreement percentage and issue the consolidated answer (observable: answer + % agreement). 6. If divergence is >40%, write a diagnosis of why the trajectories differ (observable: diagnostic paragraph). OUTPUT: document with sections (a)–(d), in Markdown. EDGE CASES: (1) Open problem with no single answer → use thematic synthesis instead of voting; (2) two equal groups of opposite answers → mark as ambiguous and escalate to the user; (3) all trajectories are identical from step 1 → report early convergence and deliver with 100% confidence. [C · CRITERIA] Each trajectory is independent and complete; the agreement percentage is calculated, not estimated; the divergence diagnosis is actionable; the final answer does not mix contradictory conclusions without explanation. MetodologIA Protocol: multiple paths to the same destination increase confidence; the majority is not always right, diagnose the minority.
spec-ia-automatizacion_react-pattern: [S · SITUATION] A developer needs an AI agent to solve a task that requires alternating explicit reasoning with concrete actions (searches, calculations, tool calls), instead of generating a direct single-pass answer. [P · REQUEST] Implement the ReAct pattern for the pasted task: design the Thought → Action → Observation loop until reaching the Final Answer, documenting each cycle. Deliverable: (a) description of the set of tools/actions available for the task, (b) complete trace of the ReAct loop with at least 3 cycles (Thought/Action/Observation), (c) reusable system instruction to implement ReAct in any similar agent, (d) loop stop criteria. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: AI agent architect with experience implementing the ReAct framework and designing reasoning-action loops. ASSUMPTIONS: the available tools are derived from the task context; if no real tools are specified, simulate the observations with plausible results and mark it as [SIMULATED]; the loop ends when the Thought concludes it has enough information or after 7 cycles maximum. INPUTS: description of the task or agent pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Analyze the task and identify the necessary tools (observable: list with name + description + signature of each tool). 2. Design the system prompt with the ReAct format (Thought:/Action:/Observation:/Final Answer:) (observable: system prompt block). 3. Run/simulate the ReAct loop with explicit cycles until reaching a Final Answer (observable: trace numbered per cycle). 4. Define the stop criteria: success condition, failure condition, cycle limit (observable: criteria table). 5. Extract the reusable and parameterizable system instruction (observable: ready-to-copy text block). OUTPUT: Markdown document with sections (a)–(d). EDGE CASES: (1) A tool returns an error → the Thought must reason about the error and choose an alternative; (2) infinite loop detected (same Action twice in a row) → trigger the stop-by-repetition criterion; (3) the task requires no external tools → apply ReAct with pure reasoning, marking the Action as "internal reasoning". [C · CRITERIA] Each cycle has the three elements (Thought, Action, Observation) without mixing them; the system instruction is self-contained and parameterizable; the stop criteria cover success, failure and limit; the trace is reproducible. MetodologIA Protocol: reason before acting, observe before concluding, stop before iterating in a vacuum.
spec-ia-automatizacion_tree-of-thought: [S · SITUATION] A strategist or developer faces a complex problem where the correct answer is not obvious and exploring only one line of reasoning can lead to suboptimal solutions; they need a systematic process for exploring and pruning alternatives. [P · REQUEST] Apply Tree of Thought to the pasted problem: generate a reasoning tree with at least 2 levels of branching (minimum 3 branches at the first level), evaluate and prune branches according to explicit criteria, and deliver the optimal solution with a compared justification. Deliverable: (a) thought tree visualized textually with branches and sub-branches, (b) evaluation of each branch with a score and criterion, (c) pruned branches with a pruning reason, (d) final solution with the complete trajectory from root to leaf. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Expert in solving complex problems with heuristic search methodologies and structured reasoning. ASSUMPTIONS: the first level has at least 3 alternatives; the second level expands only the 2 most promising branches of the first; evaluation on a 1-10 scale by criteria derived from the problem; if the problem is a design problem, the default criteria are feasibility, impact and complexity. INPUTS: description of the problem or decision pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Formulate the root node: a central question derived from the problem (observable: statement of the root node). 2. Generate the first-level branches: N high-level alternatives (observable: list of alternatives with a 2-3 sentence description). 3. Evaluate each level-1 branch with a score and criteria (observable: evaluation table). 4. Prune the branches with a low score and justify it (observable: list of pruned branches with reason). 5. Expand the 2 most promising branches to the second level (observable: sub-branches per branch). 6. Evaluate level 2 and select the optimal leaf (observable: final evaluation + selected leaf). 7. Reconstruct the complete root→leaf trajectory and write the final solution (observable: solution in prose). OUTPUT: Markdown document with the visualized tree, evaluation tables and final solution. EDGE CASES: (1) All level-1 branches have a similar score → expand the 3 best to level 2; (2) the problem has an obvious single solution → document the tree anyway but mark early convergence; (3) sub-branches generate new unexpected alternatives → add them and re-evaluate the level. [C · CRITERIA] The tree is reproducible (another agent would reach the same result with the same criteria); the pruning is quantitatively justified; the final solution references its trajectory in the tree; the evaluation criteria are specific to the problem, not generic. MetodologIA Protocol: explore in breadth before going deep, prune with explicit criteria, justify the chosen leaf.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-descomposi: [S · SITUATION] A professional faces a complex problem that seems unsolvable as a whole; they need a systematic strategy to divide it into subtasks from least to greatest complexity (least-to-most prompting) so that each subtask solves a concrete component and the set converges into the complete solution. [P · REQUEST] Apply least-to-most decomposition to the pasted problem: identify the subtasks in order of dependency and increasing complexity, solve each one leveraging the previous ones and consolidate the global solution. Deliverable: (a) decomposition map with a hierarchy of subtasks, (b) sequential resolution of each subtask with its answer, (c) consolidated solution that integrates all the pieces, (d) verification that the consolidated solution fully answers the original problem. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Systems analyst with experience in functional decomposition and structured resolution of complex problems. ASSUMPTIONS: the number of subtasks is between 3 and 6; the simplest subtasks are solved first; a subtask may depend on the answer of previous subtasks; if the problem is technical, the subtasks follow the order: domain understanding → data/logic structure → implementation → validation. INPUTS: description of the complex problem pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Read the problem and formulate the subtasks in order of increasing complexity (observable: numbered list of subtasks with level 1=simplest). 2. Draw the dependency map between subtasks (observable: textual graph or dependency table). 3. Solve each subtask in order, explicitly citing which previous answers it uses (observable: answer block per subtask). 4. Consolidate all the answers into the global solution (observable: integrated solution in prose or structure). 5. Verify against the original problem: enumerate the requirements of the problem and confirm which subtask covers them (observable: traceability table). OUTPUT: Markdown document with sections (a)–(d). EDGE CASES: (1) A subtask cannot be solved without external information → mark it as [BLOCKED] and define what input is needed; (2) subtasks turn out to be independent of each other → solve them in parallel and indicate it; (3) the problem is too simple for decomposition → apply it anyway with a minimum of 3 subtasks and justify it. [C · CRITERIA] Each subtask has a single responsibility and a verifiable answer; the dependency map is acyclic; the consolidated solution does not introduce new information not covered by the subtasks; the traceability table confirms 100% coverage of the requirements of the original problem. MetodologIA Protocol: the simple first, the complex afterward; no jump without a prior step.
spec-ia-automatizacion_role-prompting-ex: [S · SITUATION] A professional wants to obtain high-quality answers from a language model for a specialized task, but their current prompts are generic and produce superficial answers; they need to build a detailed expert role profile that activates the model's specialized reasoning mode. [P · REQUEST] Build an expert role profile for the pasted task or domain and use it to answer the included query. Deliverable: (a) expert profile with 6 dimensions (title, experience, specialties, preferred methodology, way of communicating, conscious biases), (b) ready-to-copy system prompt with the complete profile, (c) answer to the query from that role, (d) reflection on how the role changed the quality and approach of the answer. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Specialist in prompt design and cognitive psychology applied to language models. ASSUMPTIONS: the expert's domain is extracted from the task context; if there is an explicit query, answer it from the role; if there is no query, demonstrate the role with a sample analysis of the domain; the profile must not be generic ("AI expert") but specific ("LLM systems architect with 12 years designing production pipelines for banking"). INPUTS: description of the task, domain or query pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Analyze the domain and the query to determine the optimal expert profile (observable: justification paragraph for the chosen profile). 2. Build the profile in 6 dimensions with specific, non-generic details (observable: structured profile). 3. Write the complete system prompt integrating the profile (observable: ready-to-copy system prompt block). 4. Answer the query from the activated role (observable: answer in the expert's voice). 5. Write the reflection: how this answer differs from a generic answer from the model (observable: comparative paragraph). OUTPUT: Markdown document with sections (a)–(d). EDGE CASES: (1) Very technical domain and the query is vague → the expert clarifies with 1-2 questions before answering; (2) the query requires multiple perspectives → build 2 complementary profiles and contrast them; (3) domain outside the model's scope → the expert declares the limits of their knowledge with a cutoff date. [C · CRITERIA] The profile has specific details not interchangeable with another domain; the system prompt is self-contained; the answer uses vocabulary and frames of reference proper to the expert; the reflection identifies at least 3 concrete differences relative to a generic answer. MetodologIA Protocol: the role is not a costume, it is an epistemic framework; the more specific the profile, the more useful the answer.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-contraste-: [S · SITUATION] A prompt designer needs a model to produce outputs of a very specific style, format or quality, and single-type examples (only positive or only negative) fail to calibrate the desired behavior with sufficient precision. [P · REQUEST] Design a set of contrasted examples (positive and negative) for the pasted task, use them as few-shot in a prompt and validate that the model produces outputs aligned with the positives. Deliverable: (a) 3 pairs of examples (positive + negative) with a label and annotation of why each one is correct/incorrect, (b) complete few-shot prompt that integrates the pairs, (c) the model's output for a new case using the prompt, (d) analysis of which dimension of the behavior each pair controlled best. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Language model behavior researcher specializing in few-shot learning and calibration by contrast.
