- If there are steps that require human approval, include a wait node (Wait) with a confirmation webhook.
- If any integration does not have a native node in n8n, use the HTTP Request node with the configuration of the corresponding API.

[C · CRITERIA]
Observable: the JSON is importable into n8n without syntax errors; all process steps are covered; error handling is present.
Trade-off: flow flexibility vs. maintenance complexity; prefer native nodes over custom code when possible.
DoD: a user with access to n8n can import the JSON and configure the credentials without additional help.

Protocolo MetodologIA: business process → n8n nodes → configuration → exportable JSON.
spec-ia-automatizacion_n8n-nodo-ia-agent:
[S · SITUATION] An automation team needs to add an AI Agent node within an existing workflow in n8n so that the agent can execute external tools, maintain conversational memory between runs, and use a language model configured in the project credentials.
[P · REQUEST] Deliver the complete configuration of the n8n AI Agent node: node JSON parameters, list of required sub-nodes (model, memory, tools), a description of each key option, and an example expression to pass the chat input to the agent.
[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Automation architect with specialization in n8n and AI agents.
ASSUMPTIONS: n8n version >= 1.30; LLM credentials already configured; window memory of 10 messages; if the user does not indicate tools, assume only calculator and HTTP Request [SUPUESTO].
INPUTS: description of the current flow pasted into the chat or a screenshot of the canvas.
STEPS:
1. Identify the flow trigger and the field that contains the user's message.
2. Define the chain of sub-nodes: LLM node (model) → Memory node → Tool node(s).
3. Draft the JSON configuration of the Agent node with all relevant fields.
4. Write the n8n expression to map the input to the agent.
5. Document edge cases and recommendations for temperature and iteration limit.
OUTPUT: JSON code block with the node configuration + Markdown table with key parameters + example expression.
EDGE CASES:
- If the HTTP tool returns a 4xx error, the agent must return a failure message instead of retrying infinitely → limit maxIterations to 5.
- If the memory is empty (first run), the agent must start with no prior context without throwing an exception.
- If the model does not support function calling, omit tools and warn the user.
[C · CRITERIA] The JSON is directly pasteable into the n8n editor without schema errors; the input expression is tested against an example Chat Trigger node; at least one functional documented tool is included.
spec-ia-automatizacion_n8n-webhook-respu: [S · SITUATION] A development team needs an n8n workflow to receive external HTTP requests, process data, and return a structured JSON response to the client that called the webhook, instead of just running tasks in the background. The workflow must respond in less than 30 seconds and handle variable payloads. [P · REQUEST] Design the complete workflow in n8n with the Webhook node configured in 'Respond to Webhook' mode, including the processing node chain and the final response node. Deliver: a node diagram in text, exportable JSON configuration of the workflow, and a testing guide with curl. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior automation engineer with 5 years building APIs with n8n in production. ASSUMPTIONS: the incoming payload is JSON with at least a 'data' field; the expected response is JSON; n8n version 1.x installed; if the specific use case is not mentioned, assume a generic internal API integration — declare the assumption and continue. INPUTS: paste the example payload or use case description here. STEPS: 1) Configure the Webhook node (POST, custom path, Respond to Webhook mode, optional Header authentication). 2) Add a Set or Code node to transform/validate the incoming payload. 3) Add business logic nodes (IF, HTTP Request, etc.) as the case requires. 4) Add a Respond to Webhook node with a structured JSON body and an appropriate HTTP code. 5) Export the workflow as JSON. 6) Write a curl test command with example headers and body. OUTPUT: JSON block of the exported workflow + curl test command + table of response fields with type and description. EDGE CASES: (1) Timeout — if processing exceeds 29 s, return a partial response with status 202 and a task ID. (2) Malformed payload — an IF node at the start validates the structure; if it fails, respond 400 with an error message. (3) Error in an internal node — use an Error Trigger node connected to Respond to Webhook to return 500 with a trace. [C · CRITERIA] The webhook responds in < 30 s with valid JSON. The Respond to Webhook node always executes (even on error). The webhook path is semantically descriptive. Trade-off: simplicity vs. robustness — prefer explicit error handling over compact flows. DoD: workflow importable into a clean n8n and tested with curl without errors. Protocolo MetodologIA: declare assumptions with [SUPUESTO] before generating; deliver an artifact ready to import.
spec-ia-automatizacion_n8n-manejo-errore: [S · SITUATION] A production n8n workflow fails silently when an HTTP Request node receives a 500 or a timeout: items are lost, there is no notification, and the team finds out about the problem hours later. A complete error-handling strategy is needed with automatic retries, notifications, and failure logging. [P · REQUEST] Design and implement in n8n an error-handling and retry strategy for an existing workflow. Deliverables: (1) per-node retry configuration (retry settings), (2) Error Trigger workflow with notification to Slack/email and logging to Google Sheets or a SQL table, (3) step-by-step configuration guide. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior automation architect with experience in data pipeline resilience in n8n. ASSUMPTIONS: n8n version 1.x; if no notification channel is specified, use Slack with a generic webhook and declare it as [ASSUMPTION]; assume the workflow has at least one failure-prone HTTP Request node; continue if confidence > 0.85. INPUTS: paste the JSON of the current workflow or a description of the key nodes here. STEPS: 1) Identify critical nodes and configure Max Tries and Wait Between Tries on each one. 2) Enable 'Continue on Error' on non-critical nodes with fallback logic. 3) Create a separate workflow triggered by an Error Trigger that captures workflowId, nodeId, message, and timestamp. 4) Add a Slack (or Email) node in the error workflow with a structured message. 5) Add a Google Sheets (or Postgres) node to persist the error log. 6) Add an HTTP Request node to retry the failed item if applicable. 7) Document the strategy in a comment block within the workflow. OUTPUT: two exportable JSON workflows (main with retries + error workflow) + retry configuration table per node type. EDGE CASES: (1) Error in the error workflow itself — add a second Error Trigger with direct email notification. (2) Mass failure (>100 items) — group notifications into a summary every 5 min to avoid spam. (3) Node without native retry support — wrap it in a Code node with try/catch and manual retry logic. [C · CRITERIA] Zero items lost without a record. Notification arrives in < 2 min after the failure. Error log is queryable. Trade-off: total coverage vs. complexity — prioritize notification and logging over infinite automatic retries. DoD: importable workflows tested with a simulated failure. spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-respu:
[S · SITUATION] A professional or team receives a high volume of emails that require personalized replies but that follow repetitive patterns (price inquiries, information requests, meeting confirmations). Writing each reply manually consumes daily hours.
[P · REQUEST] Implement an automated flow that detects new emails, classifies them by intent, generates a personalized reply draft with an LLM, and places it as a draft in the email client for the user's manual review and sending.
[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Personal productivity automation specialist with experience in Gmail and LLM integration for inbox management.
ASSUMPTIONS: default email client Gmail [SUPUESTO]; default automation platform Zapier [SUPUESTO]; the draft always remains pending human review before sending [SUPUESTO]; reply tone: professional and cordial [SUPUESTO].
INPUTS: examples of 3-5 typical emails received and the user's usual replies, plus any specific tone or content instructions.
STEPS:
1. Configure the trigger in Gmail (new email in the inbox, excluding spam and newsletters).
2. Extract sender, subject, and body of the email.
3. Classify the email's intent with a first LLM prompt (inquiry / request / confirmation / other).
4. Select the appropriate reply template according to the intent.
5. Generate the personalized draft with a second LLM prompt that includes context from the original email.
6. Create the draft in Gmail via API with the recipient and subject pre-filled.
OUTPUT: flow diagram in text + classification prompt + draft generation prompt + draft structure by intent type.
EDGE CASES:
- If the email contains sensitive information (contracts, financial data), flag and do not generate an automatic draft.
- If the intent is 'other' with low confidence, do not generate a draft and notify the user for manual review.
- If the sender is on the VIP list, prioritize and notify via Slack before creating the draft.
[C · CRITERIA] The draft is created in Gmail without being sent automatically in 100% of cases; the intent classification has at least 4 documented categories; the generation prompt uses the sender's name and the original subject.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-extra:
[S · SITUATION] A finance or accounting team receives invoices in PDF or image format by email or shared folder and must manually enter the key data (supplier, date, invoice number, line items, totals, taxes) into its management system, an error-prone and slow process.
[P · REQUEST] Implement an automated flow that extracts the structured data from each invoice using computer vision or a multimodal LLM, validates it against business rules, and delivers a validated JSON ready for ingestion into the management system.
[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Document processing engineer with experience in invoice data extraction with a multimodal LLM and JSON schema validation.
ASSUMPTIONS: invoices in PDF or JPG of up to 5 pages [SUPUESTO]; default extraction model: gpt-4o with vision capability [SUPUESTO]; default destination system: Google Sheets or Airtable [SUPUESTO]; default currency: USD [SUPUESTO].
INPUTS: a sample invoice (image or PDF pasted/described) and the field schema required by the management system.
STEPS:
1. Configure the trigger (new file in a Drive folder or email with an attachment).
2. Convert the PDF to an image if necessary for the vision model.
3. Write the extraction prompt with JSON output instructions and field schema.
4. Validate the extracted JSON against the schema: required fields present, correct data types, totals add up with the line items.
5. If validation passes, ingest into the destination system. If it fails, send to a manual review queue with the problematic field flagged.
6. Log each extraction with status (successful / review / error).
OUTPUT: extraction prompt + invoice JSON schema + flow diagram in text + documented validation rules.
EDGE CASES:
- If the invoice has multiple pages, process each page and consolidate the line items.
- If the extracted total amount does not match the sum of the lines, flag a discrepancy and send to review.
- If the invoice is in a language other than Spanish or English, detect the language and normalize the fields to the schema.
[C · CRITERIA] The extraction captures at least 8 key fields without errors in 90% of sample invoices; validation detects total discrepancies in 100% of cases; the JSON is directly ingestable by the destination system without additional transformation.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-enriq:
[S · SITUATION] A sales team receives raw leads (name + email + company) from web forms or imports and must manually research each lead to enrich its profile (title, company size, industry, LinkedIn) and qualify it (ICP fit, estimated interest level) before assigning it to a representative.
[P · REQUEST] Design and implement an automated flow that enriches each new lead with data from external sources and an LLM, qualifies it according to defined ICP criteria, and updates the CRM with the enriched data and the qualification score.
[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: RevOps and sales pipeline automation specialist with experience in data enrichment and lead scoring.
ASSUMPTIONS: default CRM HubSpot [SUPUESTO]; default enrichment source: Apollo.io API or web search via Serper [SUPUESTO]; default ICP criteria: B2B company, 50-500 employees, technology or financial services sector [SUPUESTO].
INPUTS: sample of 3-5 raw leads (name, email, company), the business's ICP criteria, the CRM fields where the enriched data will be saved.
STEPS:
1. Configure the trigger (new contact in HubSpot or new row in Google Sheets).
2. Search for company data in Apollo.io or Serper using the name and email domain.
3. Extract and structure the enriched data (industry, size, contact's title, LinkedIn).
4. Send the enriched profile to an LLM to compute an ICP score (1-100) with justification.
5. Update the contact in HubSpot with the enriched data and the score.
6. If the score exceeds the threshold (70 by default), automatically assign to a representative and notify via Slack.
OUTPUT: flow diagram in text + ICP qualification prompt + enrichment JSON schema + assignment rule.
EDGE CASES:
- If the company is not found in the enrichment source, use only the email data (domain) and flag low confidence.
- If the email is from a generic domain (gmail, hotmail), do not attempt to enrich the company and flag for manual review.
- If the ICP score is 0 (does not meet any criterion), move the lead to a discard list and do not assign a representative.
[C · CRITERIA] The enrichment adds at least 4 new fields to the lead's profile; the ICP score has a readable justification of at most 50 words; leads with a score >= 70 are assigned in less than 5 minutes from arrival.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-moder:
[S · SITUATION] A digital platform receives user-generated content (comments, posts, reviews) in high volume and needs to automatically moderate that content to detect and manage messages that violate policies (hate speech, spam, adult content, misinformation) before they become publicly visible.
[P · REQUEST] Design and implement an automated moderation flow that classifies each piece of content by violation type and risk level, executes the corresponding action (approve, hide, delete, escalate to a human moderator), and logs the decision with justification.
[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Trust and safety engineer on digital platforms with experience in content moderation systems with LLM and acceptable use policies.
ASSUMPTIONS: text content (not images by default) [SUPUESTO]; default violation categories: hate speech, spam, adult content, misinformation, none [SUPUESTO]; risk levels: low, medium, high, critical [SUPUESTO]; automatic action only for low and medium risk; high and critical risk always to a human moderator [SUPUESTO].
INPUTS: examples of content to moderate (5-10 cases with different violations) and the platform's acceptable use policies.
STEPS:
1. Configure the trigger (new content on the platform via webhook).
2. Write the classification prompt that identifies violation type and risk level with JSON output.
3. Implement the decision logic: action according to category and risk level.
4. Execute the action via the platform's API (approve, hide, delete, flag for review).
5. Log the decision, justification, and timestamp in a log database.
6. Notify the human moderator if the risk is high or critical.
OUTPUT: classification prompt + output JSON schema + decision matrix (type × risk → action) + flow diagram in text.
EDGE CASES:
- If the content is in a language not supported by the model, flag as 'human review' without classifying.
- If the same user accumulates 3 medium-risk violations in 24 hours, automatically escalate to account review.
- If the platform's API fails to execute the action, retry 3 times and log the failure.
[C · CRITERIA] The prompt produces a correct classification in at least 90% of test cases; the decision matrix covers all combinations of category and risk level; high and critical risk content is NEVER processed without human review.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-tradu:
[S · SITUATION] A product team needs to translate and localize technical documentation, interface strings, and marketing materials into multiple languages systematically, without losing brand terminology or tone consistency across versions.

[P · REQUEST] Produce an automated translation and localization pipeline that includes: (1) an approved terminology correspondence table by language, (2) translated and localized versions of the delivered content, (3) a list of cultural adaptation decisions (dates, currencies, local references), and (4) a linguistic QA checklist with at least 5 verifiable criteria.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior computational linguist with 10+ years in software and digital content localization, certified in XLIFF and TMX flows.

ASSUMPTIONS: The source content is in Spanish or English; the target languages are those indicated in the input (by default: English, Portuguese, and French); the tone is professional-technical unless indicated otherwise; the brand glossary is inferred from the content if not provided; UTF-8 and .md or .txt formats are assumed.

INPUTS: Paste the source text or the content files directly into the conversation thread.

STEPS:
1. Extract a list of key terms and proper nouns → draft glossary by language.
2. Translate segment by segment respecting the glossary; mark cultural localization decisions with the [LOC] tag.
3. Adapt cultural references (dates, units, examples) → adaptations table.
4. Generate final versions per language in clean format.
5. Run the QA checklist: terminological consistency, UI string length, gender markers, pluralization, and encoding.

OUTPUT: (A) Glossary by language in a markdown table; (B) Translated content by section with [LOC] notes; (C) Cultural adaptations table; (D) QA checklist with PASS/FAIL status per criterion.

EDGE CASES:
- Term with no direct equivalent → transliterate and add an explanatory note in parentheses.
- UI string too long after translation → propose a short version and a full version.
- Culturally sensitive content → mark with [REVISAR] and leave the decision to the human reviewer.

[C · CRITERIA] Each glossary term appears consistently in all occurrences (≥95%); cultural adaptations are documented with justification; the QA checklist has no FAIL items without a resolution note; the output is processable by standard CAT tools. Trade-off: speed vs. terminological precision — prioritize precision. DoD: all sections of the input have a version in each target language and the QA checklist is complete.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Translate with terminological precision, document cultural adaptations, and deliver a verifiable QA checklist.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-gener:
[S · SITUATION] An operations or business team needs to convert periodic tabular data (sales, product metrics, operational KPIs) into narrative reports ready to distribute, without relying on analysts to draft each cycle.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) an executive narrative report with Summary, Key Findings, Trends and Recommendations sections; (2) a KPI table with prior-period variation and a RAG traffic light (Red/Amber/Green); (3) up to 3 visualizations described in chart-ready language (type, axes, data); (4) a draft email distribution message.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior data analyst with experience in business intelligence and executive communication, specialized in automating periodic reports.

ASSUMPTIONS: Data is pasted as a CSV or markdown table; the period is monthly unless stated otherwise; the audience is leadership/management; RAG thresholds: Green ≥target, Amber 80-99% target, Red <80% target — adjust if others are specified; targets are inferred from context or flagged as [ASSUMPTION] if not provided.

INPUTS: Paste the tabular data directly into the thread.

STEPS:
1. Read data → identify metrics, periods and key variations.
2. Apply RAG thresholds to each KPI → traffic-light table.
3. Draft the executive Summary (≤5 sentences), Key Findings (bullets), Trends (narrative paragraph) and Recommendations (≤3 concrete actions).
4. Describe up to 3 recommended visualizations with a specification of type and data.
5. Draft the distribution message (subject + body ≤150 words).

OUTPUT: Structured report document in markdown with: Summary section, KPI table with columns Metric/Value/Target/Variation/RAG, Trends section, Recommendations section, chart specifications and distribution message.

EDGE CASES:
- Incomplete data or with gaps → flag the cell with [N/A] and exclude it from the variation calculation.
- Target not provided → mark the KPI as [NO TARGET] and omit the traffic light for that row.
- Data with statistical anomalies (outliers >3σ) → highlight in Key Findings with a [REVIEW DATA] note.

[C · CRITERIA] Each KPI has its variation calculated correctly; the RAG traffic light is consistent with the defined thresholds; the recommendations are actionable and specific (not generic); the distribution message is self-contained and requires no attachments to be understood. Trade-off: brevity vs. depth — prioritize executive clarity. DoD: complete report with all sections, no KPIs left unclassified for RAG (except [NO TARGET]) and a distribution message ready to send.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Turn data into actionable executive narrative with a verifiable RAG traffic light.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-onboa:
[S · SITUATION] An organization needs to reduce the load on the HR team and technical leads during the onboarding of new collaborators, by creating a knowledge-base conversational assistant that answers frequent questions, guides first-day/week tasks and routes only the cases that genuinely require human intervention.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a list of 20 onboarding frequently asked questions classified by category (Administrative, Access, Culture, Technical process); (2) answers for each question using only the internal documentation provided; (3) a routing decision tree (when to answer vs. route to a human); (4) a Day 1 welcome script and a first-week checklist; (5) the assistant's personality configuration (tone, answer limits, closing phrases).

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior employee experience designer with expertise in knowledge management and HR chatbot design.

ASSUMPTIONS: The internal documentation is pasted into the thread; if it is not provided, model answers are generated marked [TEMPLATE – COMPLETE]; the organization is a technology company or consultancy unless stated otherwise; the assistant's language is Spanish; the assistant does NOT handle confidential salary information or disciplinary decisions.

INPUTS: Paste internal onboarding documentation, HR policies and existing FAQs into the thread.

STEPS:
1. Read documentation → extract frequent topics → classify into 4 categories.
2. Draft 20 FAQ questions with a concise answer (≤150 words each) using only the documentation.
3. Build a decision tree: condition → action (answer/route/escalate).
4. Draft a Day 1 welcome script (≤300 words) and a first-week checklist (≥10 items).
5. Define the personality configuration: name, tone, 3 welcome phrases, 3 closing phrases, 5 explicit answer limits.

OUTPUT: Structured document in markdown with the 5 numbered sections, the decision tree in nested-list format, the checklist in checkbox format and the personality configuration block in commented YAML format.

EDGE CASES:
- Question outside the assistant's scope → respond: 'This query is handled directly by [ROLE]. You can contact [CHANNEL]' and indicate the routing.
- Contradictory information in the documentation → flag the ambiguity and mark [REVIEW WITH HR].
- Question about salary, specific benefits or personal situation → always route to HR without answering.

[C · CRITERIA] The 20 FAQs cover the 4 categories (≥4 per category); each answer implicitly cites the source (document section); the decision tree has clear, unambiguous routing criteria; the first-week checklist has actionable items with a suggested owner. Trade-off: completeness vs. answer length — prioritize concise answers and clear routing. DoD: all sections complete, no [TEMPLATE – COMPLETE] if documentation was provided, and a decision tree with no dead-end branches.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Design an onboarding assistant with precise FAQs, a clear routing tree and a coherent personality.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-socia:
[S · SITUATION] A marketing team or content creator needs to transform a single idea or content source into multiple pieces adapted to different social media platforms, maintaining brand voice consistency and saving the time of drafting each piece from scratch.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a content map showing how the source idea branches into the target platforms; (2) ready-to-publish content pieces for each platform (LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Instagram, and one additional if specified); (3) A/B variants for at least 2 platforms; (4) a list of hashtags and CTAs per platform; (5) a suggested 7-day publishing calendar.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior digital content strategist with experience managing multiple brand accounts and producing omnichannel content.

ASSUMPTIONS: The source idea is pasted into the thread; the brand tone is professional-accessible unless stated otherwise; the default platforms are LinkedIn, Twitter/X and Instagram; LinkedIn: ≤1300 characters, Twitter/X: ≤280 characters per tweet, Instagram: caption ≤2200 characters with focus on the first line; the audience is B2B professional unless stated otherwise.

INPUTS: Paste the idea, article, insight or topic into the conversation thread.

STEPS:
1. Analyze the source idea → identify the core message, secondary angles and notable data.
2. Create a content map: core idea → branches per platform with a differentiated angle.
3. Draft a piece per platform respecting character limits and native format.
4. Generate an A/B variant for LinkedIn and Instagram (distinct approach, not paraphrase).
5. List relevant hashtags (≤5 per platform) and 2 CTAs per platform.
6. Propose a 7-day publishing calendar with platform, suggested time and piece type.

OUTPUT: Markdown document with: a visual content map (nested list), sections per platform with main piece and A/B variant, a hashtags/CTAs table and a 7-day calendar table.

EDGE CASES:
- Very short or vague idea → expand with 3 possible angles and ask for confirmation of the preferred one before continuing.
- Sensitive or potentially controversial content → flag with [REVIEW APPROVAL] before publishing.
- Platform not in the defaults → adapt the format if the user specifies it; if there is no clear criterion, ask for limits and style.

[C · CRITERIA] Each piece respects the platform's character limits; the A/B variants offer a genuinely different angle (not just reordering words); hashtags are relevant and do not exceed the defined limit; the calendar is feasible (no more than 2 posts per day per platform). Trade-off: creativity vs. adherence to brand voice — prioritize brand consistency. DoD: all platforms covered, A/B variants for ≥2 platforms and a complete 7-day calendar.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Transform an idea into omnichannel content ready to publish with a consistent brand voice.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-revis: [S · SITUATION] An engineering team has an active CI/CD pipeline and wants to integrate AI-assisted automatic code review before the merge. The human reviewer currently takes between 30 and 90 minutes per pull request and needs a first filter that detects critical problems, technical debt and convention violations. [P · REQUEST] Produce a structured code review report for the pasted diff, including: (1) a prioritized list of findings with severity (CRITICAL / WARNING / SUGGESTION), (2) the exact line or affected code block, (3) an explanation of the problem and an actionable recommendation, (4) a 3-5 line executive summary for the author. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as a senior software engineer with 10+ years reviewing code in production, expert in quality, security and maintainability. ASSUMPTIONS: if no language is specified, infer it from the diff's syntax; if no style standard is indicated, apply the most widespread guides of the detected ecosystem; if the diff is incomplete, state that assumption and review what is available. INPUTS: diff or code fragment pasted into the message. STEPS: 1) Identify the language, context and scope of the change. 2) Scan for potential bugs, security vulnerabilities and race conditions. 3) Evaluate readability, naming and adherence to conventions. 4) Detect technical debt: duplication, excessive coupling, magic values. 5) Generate a list of findings ordered by severity. 6) Draft the executive summary. OUTPUT: Markdown with sections ##Summary, ##Findings (severity/line/description/recommendation table), ##Conclusion. EDGE CASES: empty diff → return a warning and request content; configuration-only diff → adjust criteria to secrets security and value correctness; diff larger than 500 lines → process by logical blocks and notify. [C · CRITERIA] Each finding references a concrete line; recommendations are actionable in under 30 min; the summary is understandable without reading the diff; no obvious false positives. Done when the report has at least 1 finding or explicitly confirms the code passes review with no observations. Protocolo MetodologIA: Reason over the diff before drafting — issue each finding only if you can cite the exact fragment that originates it.
spec-ia-automatizacion_automatizar-inves: [S · SITUATION] A product or strategy team needs to produce a market research report on a specific sector or product quickly, but with high reliability. The main risk is that the AI generates figures or trends without support, which can lead to wrong decisions. An automatable process with integrated adversarial verification is required that distinguishes verified facts from inferences. [P · REQUEST] Generate a complete market research report for the indicated topic, with each claim tagged as [VERIFIED], [INFERENCE] or [ASSUMPTION], plus an adversarial risks section that questions the main conclusions. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as a senior market intelligence analyst with experience in technology sectors and an adversarial methodology for data verification. ASSUMPTIONS: if no sector is indicated, infer it from the topic and state the assumption; if no geographic scope is specified, apply a global perspective with emphasis on Latin America; market data without a date is assumed to be at most 2 years old [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: research topic pasted into the message; optionally sources or base data provided by the user. STEPS: 1) Define scope: segment, geography, analysis period. 2) Identify key players, market size and main trends. 3) Tag each claim with [VERIFIED]/[INFERENCE]/[ASSUMPTION]. 4) Run an adversarial review: generate 3-5 counter-arguments to the main conclusions. 5) Synthesize opportunities and risks. 6) Draft a one-page executive summary. OUTPUT: Structured Markdown with ##Executive Summary, ##Market Context, ##Key Players, ##Trends, ##Adversarial Analysis, ##Opportunities and Risks, ##Declared Sources. EDGE CASES: very broad topic → narrow the scope and state the assumption; topic without public data → indicate information gaps explicitly; user provides contradictory data → flag it in the adversarial section. [C · CRITERIA] Each quantitative claim carries a tag; the adversarial section has at least 3 challenges; the summary is actionable without reading the body; there are no invented figures without an [ASSUMPTION] tag. Done when the report has a summary, an adversarial analysis and at least 3 identified trends. Protocolo MetodologIA: Tag each datum with its certainty level before including it in the final report.
spec-ia-automatizacion_eval-suite-prompt: [S · SITUATION] A team that uses language models in production needs to systematically evaluate the quality of its prompts before deploying them. Without a formal evaluation suite, prompt changes are made blindly and errors reach end users. A reusable test suite is required that covers expected cases, boundary cases and known failure scenarios for a prompt or family of prompts. [P · REQUEST] Design a complete evaluation suite for the described prompt or task: a list of test cases with input, expected output, success criterion and failure severity, plus instructions to run it manually or with a script. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as an AI systems evaluation engineer with experience designing test harnesses for LLMs in production environments. ASSUMPTIONS: if no target model is specified, design the suite model-agnostically; if no scale is indicated, design for 20-50 test cases; if the prompt is not provided, use the task objective as a base and declare the assumption. INPUTS: prompt or task description pasted into the message; optionally examples of good or bad outputs. STEPS: 1) Extract the prompt's main function and its expected variants. 2) Define test categories: typical cases, input variants, boundary cases, adversarial. 3) Draft 15-30 test cases with format: ID / Input / Expected output / Pass-fail criterion / Severity. 4) Add execution instructions (manual and automatable with Python/JS). 5) Define the quality threshold for release: minimum percentage of cases passed by severity. OUTPUT: Markdown with ##Suite Objective, ##Test Categories, ##Test Cases Table, ##Execution Instructions, ##Release Threshold. EDGE CASES: ambiguous prompt → document ambiguities as specific test cases; creative task with no deterministic output → use rubric criteria instead of exact match; more than 3 prompt variants → organize by variant with a prefix in the ID. [C · CRITERIA] The suite has at least 15 cases covering the 4 categories; each case has an objective success criterion; the instructions allow execution without prior knowledge of the prompt; the release threshold is made explicit. Done when someone can run the suite without asking anything. Protocolo MetodologIA: Define the success criterion of each case before drafting the test input.
spec-ia-automatizacion_eval-llm-como-jue: [S · SITUATION] A team that evaluates language model outputs at scale needs to automate quality judgment without relying exclusively on human annotators. The LLM-as-judge technique uses a model to score the outputs of another, but requires a precise rubric and a well-designed judge prompt to avoid position, length and self-confirmation biases. [P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) an evaluation rubric with 3-6 dimensions specific to the indicated task, (2) a complete, ready-to-use judge prompt that instructs the evaluator model to score 1-5 per dimension with justification, (3) instructions to detect and mitigate the 3 most common biases of the LLM-as-judge pattern. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as an LLM evaluation researcher with experience in rubric design and bias mitigation in automated judgment systems. ASSUMPTIONS: if no task is specified, design for evaluating general-purpose assistant responses; if no judge model is indicated, design the prompt to be compatible with any model of the Claude or GPT-4-class family; scoring scale 1-5 by default [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: description of the task or output type to evaluate, pasted into the message. STEPS: 1) Analyze the task to identify relevant quality dimensions. 2) Draft a rubric with name, description and scoring anchors (1, 3, 5) per dimension. 3) Draft a complete judge prompt with instructions to reason before the score. 4) Add anti-bias instructions: position, length and self-confirmation. 5) Include a usage example with the judge's expected output. OUTPUT: Markdown with ##Rubric (table with dimensions and anchors), ##Judge Prompt (code block), ##Bias Mitigation, ##Usage Example. EDGE CASES: creative task with no single correct answer → emphasize coherence and instruction-adherence dimensions instead of factuality; very short output (<50 words) → add a completeness dimension; multiple languages → specify the evaluation language in the judge prompt. [C · CRITERIA] The rubric has observable anchors at each level; the judge prompt requires reasoning before the score (chain-of-thought); the mitigations are concrete and implementable; the example shows real judge output with scores and justifications. Done when the judge prompt can be copied and used without further modification. Protocolo MetodologIA: Draft the rubric anchors before writing the judge prompt to ensure coherence.
spec-ia-automatizacion_eval_comparacion_: [S · SITUATION] A product team has two versions of a prompt (A and B) and needs to decide which to deploy in production. The decision cannot be based on intuition: it requires a structured comparative analysis over a set of representative test cases, with quantitative metrics and a justified verdict. [P · REQUEST] Given Prompt A, Prompt B and the set of test cases provided (or generated if not supplied), produce a comparative A/B analysis that includes: a results table per case, aggregate performance metrics, an analysis of qualitative differences and a deployment recommendation with conditions. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as an AI systems evaluator specialized in comparative prompt analysis with a rigorous experimental methodology. ASSUMPTIONS: if only one prompt is provided, deduce that the user wants to compare against an improved version and request the second; if no test cases are supplied, generate 10 representative cases based on the prompt's objective and declare the assumption; default quality metrics: precision, completeness, instruction adherence, tone [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: Prompt A, Prompt B and optionally test cases with expected outputs, pasted into the message. STEPS: 1) Review both prompts and identify key design differences. 2) Run each test case mentally against A and B (or use provided outputs). 3) Score each result on the defined metrics (1-5 scale). 4) Calculate averages and differences per metric. 5) Identify patterns: on which input types A wins, on which B wins. 6) Draft a recommendation with confidence threshold and conditions. OUTPUT: Markdown with ##Design Differences, ##Results Table per Case, ##Aggregate Metrics (table), ##Pattern Analysis, ##Deployment Recommendation. EDGE CASES: identical outputs in all cases → report a tie and recommend additional criteria; A wins on quality but B on speed → separate recommendations by use case; insufficient test cases (<5) → warn about low statistical confidence. [C · CRITERIA] The results table has a numeric score per metric for each case; the recommendation includes a usage condition; the pattern analysis identifies at least one segment where each prompt is superior or confirms clear dominance. Done when the team can make the deployment decision without additional information. Protocolo MetodologIA: Identify the design differences between prompts before evaluating any test case.
spec-ia-automatizacion_eval-casos-limite: [S · SITUATION] A team developing AI prompts or pipelines needs to identify the input cases that can make its system fail before users encounter them in production. Typical cases are easy to cover; boundary and adversarial cases require systematic reasoning about which extreme or malicious conditions can break the expected behavior. [P · REQUEST] For the described prompt or system, generate a structured catalog of boundary and adversarial cases: a list of cases organized by failure category, with a description of the case, why it is problematic and the correct expected behavior. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as an AI systems red teaming expert with experience in identifying prompt vulnerabilities and LLM pipeline robustness. ASSUMPTIONS: if no priority failure type is specified, cover all the main categories; if no language for the test inputs is indicated, generate cases in Spanish and English; default number of cases 20-30 [ASSUMPTION]. INPUTS: description of the prompt or system to evaluate, pasted into the message; optionally usage context and user types. STEPS: 1) Identify the system's main function and its implicit assumptions. 2) Generate cases per category: empty or malformed inputs, extremely long inputs, instruction injection, deliberate ambiguity, borderline sensitive content, unexpected language, incorrectly formatted inputs, internal contradictions. 3) For each case: write the test input, explain why it is a risk and define the correct expected behavior. 4) Prioritize the 5 most critical cases. OUTPUT: Markdown with ##Risk Categories, ##Cases Catalog (table with Category/Test Input/Risk/Expected Behavior/Priority), ##Top 5 Critical Cases. EDGE CASES: system with content restrictions → expand the jailbreak and bypass category; multi-agent system → add an inter-agent interference category; low-latency system → add cases of inputs that generate excessively long responses. [C · CRITERIA] The catalog has at least 20 cases across 6+ categories; each case has a concrete test input (not just an abstract description); the 5 critical cases include a priority justification. Done when the team can run the cases without additional interpretation. Protocolo MetodologIA: Write the concrete test input before analyzing each case's risk.
spec-ia-automatizacion_eval-regresion-pr: [S · SITUATION] A team maintains prompts in production that evolve over time: instructions are tuned, the model is changed, the system context is modified. Without regression tests, each change can introduce silent degradations in behaviors that previously worked correctly. A regression testing system is needed that automatically detects when a prompt change breaks previously validated behaviors. [P · REQUEST] Design a regression testing system for the described prompt or prompt family: a set of fixed test cases with reference outputs, comparison criteria to detect regressions and a validation protocol before each deployment. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Act as an AI systems reliability engineer with experience designing regression pipelines for LLMs in production. - Trade-off: opacity vs. transparency; document what assistant information CAN be shared with users.
- DoD: insertable self-protection instruction, executable function, documented policy, 6 test cases.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Classify the confidentiality level of the system prompt before designing the protection instructions.
spec-ia-automatizacion_guardrail-confirm:
[S · SITUATION] An AI agent has access to tools that execute actions with real, irreversible consequences: sending emails, modifying database records, making payments, deleting files or calling external APIs. If the agent executes an action by mistake or through manipulation, the damage can be costly or impossible to revert.

[P · REQUEST] Design a high-impact action confirmation mechanism that includes: (1) classification of tools by impact level, (2) an interception function that requests confirmation before executing risky actions, (3) a confirmation flow with the user (text or cryptographic signature), and (4) a cancellation and auditing policy, with executable code.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Autonomous agent architect with experience designing human-in-the-loop security patterns for AI systems with access to external tools.
ASSUMPTIONS: The agent uses the tool-calling (function calling) pattern of an LLM; the confirmation mechanism is conversational text (the user replies "yes" or "no") — state if a cryptographic signature or two-factor authentication is required; the pipeline is in Python. Ask only if: (a) some high-impact actions must be non-interruptible by business design, (b) the confirmation channel differs from chat (email, Slack), (c) multiple approval levels are required (manager approval).
INPUTS: Paste the agent's tool list with its description (name, parameters, effect).
STEPS:
1. Classify each tool into impact levels: LOW (read, query), MEDIUM (reversible write), HIGH (irreversible, financial, external) → table tool / level / justification.
2. Write the Python decorator `@require_confirmation(level="high")` that intercepts execution and requests user confirmation before proceeding.
3. Implement the function `confirmation_flow(action_description: str, params: dict) -> bool` that presents the action in natural language and waits for a response.
4. Define the cancellation policy: what to do if the user rejects, if there is a timeout, if there is an ambiguous response.
5. Implement the auditing function `log_action_decision(action, params, user_response, executed: bool)` with timestamp.
OUTPUT: Python code with decorator, confirmation flow and auditing; tool classification table; documented cancellation policy.
EDGE CASES:
- Agent chains multiple high-impact actions → confirm each one individually; option to "confirm all" with an explicit list.
- Automated user (bot-to-bot) without a human confirmation channel → deny all HIGH-level actions by default or require a pre-authorized token.
- False confirmation via injection ("the user already confirmed") → validate confirmation outside the LLM context (application layer).

[C · CRITERIA]
- Observable: the decorator correctly intercepts HIGH tools and lets LOW ones through without interruption in the test cases.
- Trade-off: UX friction vs. security; document when to use silent vs. explicit confirmation.
- DoD: functional decorator, tested confirmation flow, auditing with timestamp, complete classification table.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Classify each tool by impact level before designing the confirmation mechanism.
spec-ia-automatizacion_guardrail-limites:
[S · SITUATION] An engineering team is designing or auditing an autonomous AI agent that has access to tools with irreversible-impact capability (writing to databases, sending emails, deleting files, executing code in production, calling external APIs with side effects). They need to define explicit guardrails to prevent unauthorized actions.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a taxonomy of tools by risk level (Low/Medium/High/Critical) with classification criteria; (2) a per-level guardrail policy with activation conditions, restrictions and a human approval mechanism; (3) a set of ≥10 guardrail rules in a verifiable format (condition → containment action); (4) a decision flow diagram in structured text so the agent evaluates whether it can use a tool; (5) a list of common anti-patterns and how to detect them.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior AI security engineer specialized in designing secure agentic systems and tool access control.

ASSUMPTIONS: The agent uses a standard tool-calling framework (function calling or MCP); if the stack is not specified, assume a generic architecture; read-only tools are Low risk by default; tools with external or irreversible effects are High/Critical; the human approval threshold activates at High and Critical level.

INPUTS: Paste the agent's available tool list (name, description, permissions) or describe the use case in the thread.

STEPS:
1. Read available tools → classify into the risk taxonomy with justification per tool.
2. Define per-level policy: what the agent can do autonomously vs. what requires confirmation.
3. Draft ≥10 guardrail rules in the format: IF [condition] THEN [containment action].
4. Build the decision flow diagram: input (intent to use a tool) → evaluation nodes → output (proceed/ask for confirmation/block).
5. List ≥5 anti-patterns of tool misuse with a detection signal.

OUTPUT: Markdown document with: risk taxonomy table, per-level policy table, numbered list of guardrail rules, nested-text flow diagram and anti-patterns table with detection signal.

EDGE CASES:
- Dual-use tool (read and write in the same call) → classify by the higher-risk component.
- Chain of tools where the result of one feeds another dangerous one → treat the whole chain at the level of the most dangerous link.
- Agent in test mode vs. production → include a differentiated policy with an environment flag.

[C · CRITERIA] All input tools are classified; the guardrail rules are automatically verifiable (observable condition); the flow diagram has no dead-end nodes; the anti-patterns have a concrete detection signal. Trade-off: security vs. operational autonomy — prioritize security on Critical tools. DoD: complete policy for all levels, ≥10 rules and a flow diagram without ambiguities.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Design tool guardrails with a risk taxonomy, verifiable rules and an explicit approval flow.
spec-ia-automatizacion_guardrail-citas-o:
[S · SITUATION] A team that uses language models to generate high-impact content (analysis reports, legal documents, market research, institutional communications) needs to ensure that every factual claim is backed by a cited and traceable source, eliminating unsupported claims.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a mandatory citation policy with criteria for what constitutes a factual claim that requires a citation; (2) a set of ≥8 guardrail rules to detect and block unsourced claims; (3) a standardized citation format template for use in system prompts; (4) a human review protocol for claims marked as high-criticality; (5) examples of uncited claims transformed into correctly cited claims.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: AI governance and content quality specialist with experience auditing language model outputs and academic and journalistic citation standards.

ASSUMPTIONS: The content to audit is pasted in the thread; if no specific content is provided, the policy and rules are generated generically; sources can be internal documents, URLs or bibliographic references; it is assumed that the model must explicitly state when it infers vs. when it cites.

INPUTS: Paste the text or content to audit, or the available source documents, in the conversation thread.

STEPS:
1. Define factual claim criteria: which types of sentences require a mandatory citation (statistics, dates, attributions, projections).
2. Draft ≥8 guardrail rules in the format: CLAIM TYPE → ACTION (cite/mark [NO SOURCE]/block).
3. Design the citation format template: inline and footnote reference structure for use in system prompts.
4. Define the human review protocol: escalation criteria, responsible roles and resolution deadline.
5. Generate ≥5 transformation examples: uncited claim → correctly cited claim applying the rules.

OUTPUT: Markdown document with: a factual claim criteria section, a guardrail rules table, a citation template block in code, a human review protocol in numbered steps and a before/after examples table.

EDGE CASES:
- Widely accepted common-knowledge claim (e.g.: water boils at 100°C) → exempt from citation but document the exemption criterion.
- Unverifiable source (dead URL, undated document) → mark [UNVERIFIABLE SOURCE] and request a replacement.
- Claim that mixes cited data and inference → split into two sentences and cite only the data.

[C · CRITERIA] The guardrail rules cover at least 4 distinct types of factual claim; the citation template is reproducible without ambiguity; the transformation examples show real application of at least 3 different rules; the human review protocol has defined roles and deadlines. Trade-off: rigor vs. text fluency — prioritize full traceability in high-criticality content. DoD: complete policy, ≥8 rules, functional template, protocol with roles and ≥5 transformation examples.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Ensure traceability of claims with verifiable guardrail rules and standardized citations.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-tool-:
[S · SITUATION] An engineering team is implementing or improving the function/tool calling system of an AI agent and needs to ensure that the function definitions are robust, errors are handled correctly and the agent uses the tools reliably and predictably.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a tool-definition design guide with principles and a checklist; (2) JSON definition schemas for the provided tools, with description, typed parameters, default values and examples; (3) a catalog of common tool calling errors with root cause and solution; (4) a runtime tool error handling protocol; (5) robustness test cases for at least 3 failure scenarios.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior software engineer specialized in LLM integration and design of agent systems with function calling.

ASSUMPTIONS: The reference framework is the Anthropic Claude API with tool_use (JSON Schema); if another framework is indicated (OpenAI, Gemini, LangChain) the syntax is adapted; tool schemas are generated in JSON Schema draft-07; if no concrete tools are provided, representative examples are generated (search, file read, database query).

INPUTS: Paste the description or code of the tools/functions to define, or the agent's context, in the thread.

STEPS:
1. Review the input tools → identify parameters, types, optionality and side effects.
2. Draft the design guide: 5-7 principles of robust definition with a verification checklist.
3. Generate a JSON schema per tool with: name, description, input_schema (type, properties, required, examples).
4. Compile an error catalog: ≥8 error types with cause, symptom and correction.
5. Design a runtime error handling protocol: an IF/THEN flow for each error type.
6. Write robustness test cases: valid input, invalid input, timeout, unexpected response.

OUTPUT: Markdown document with: a principles and checklist section, JSON code blocks for each tool schema, an error catalog table, an error handling protocol in a numbered list and a test cases section with a Given/When/Then structure.

EDGE CASES:
- Tool with mutually exclusive parameters → model with oneOf in JSON Schema and document in the description.
- Tool that can return partial results → include a status and partial_result field in the response schema.
- Tool with a rate limit → include retry handling with exponential backoff in the error protocol.

[C · CRITERIA] Each JSON schema is valid per JSON Schema draft-07; the tool descriptions are sufficient for an LLM to invoke them correctly without additional context; the catalog covers at least type, format, timeout and authentication errors; the test cases have a defined expected result. Trade-off: schema verbosity vs. LLM interpretability — prioritize description clarity. DoD: all schemas are valid, a catalog with ≥8 errors, a protocol with no empty branches and ≥3 complete test cases.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Design self-documenting tool schemas with predictable error handling and robustness test cases.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-mcp-s:
[S · SITUATION] An engineering team needs to integrate an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server with a language model to expose tools, resources and prompts to the agent in a standardized way, and ensure the integration is secure, observable and maintainable.

[P · REQUEST] Produce: (1) a step-by-step integration guide to connect an MCP server to a language model; (2) the specification of the tools, resources and prompts the MCP server will expose; (3) the MCP client configuration (transport, authentication, timeouts); (4) a set of integration tests with success, error and timeout scenarios; (5) a production checklist to validate the integration before deployment.

[E · EXECUTION]
ROLE: Senior software engineer specialized in the MCP protocol and AI agent architectures with external tool integrations.

ASSUMPTIONS: The MCP server uses stdio or SSE transport; the language model is MCP-compatible (Claude or similar); if no server stack is specified, assume Node.js with the official MCP SDK; authentication is OAuth 2.0 or API token; server logs are available for debugging.

INPUTS: Paste the description of the MCP server to integrate (URL, tools it exposes, usage context) or the agent use case in the thread.

STEPS:
1. Define the MCP server's capabilities inventory: tools, resources and prompts with their signatures.
2. Design the client configuration: transport (stdio/SSE), authentication, timeout and retry policy.
3. Draft the integration guide in numbered steps from connection to first successful invocation.
4. Define the specification of each exposed tool: name, description, parameters, expected response.
5. Write integration tests: ≥5 cases (successful connection, valid tool, invalid tool, timeout, failed authentication).
6. Complete the production checklist: ≥10 verifiable items before deployment.

OUTPUT: Markdown document with: a capabilities inventory section, a client configuration block in JSON/YAML, a step-by-step integration guide, tool specifications in a table, test cases in Given/When/Then and a production checklist with checkboxes.

EDGE CASES:
- MCP server exposes tools with names colliding with the model's native tools → prefix with the server namespace.
- SSE transport loses connection → implement automatic reconnection with exponential backoff and a retry limit.
- MCP tool returns a response larger than the model's context window → implement pagination or truncation with a continuation indicator.

[C · CRITERIA] The integration guide lets an engineer with no prior context connect the server in ≤30 minutes; each tool has a sufficient description for the model to invoke it correctly; the integration tests cover at least happy path and error cases; the production checklist includes security validation, timeouts and monitoring. Trade-off: automation vs. explicit control — prioritize explicit and observable configuration. DoD: complete guide, valid configuration, ≥5 tests and a checklist of ≥10 items.

Protocolo MetodologIA: Integrate an MCP server with explicit configuration, complete integration tests and a verifiable production checklist.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-salid:
[S · SITUATION] You are integrating a language model into a backend pipeline where the response must be consumed programmatically by a downstream service. The model tends to mix explanatory text with the JSON, or to return missing fields, breaking deserialization. [P · REQUEST] Generate the complete JSON Schema and the system prompt that guarantees the model returns only a valid JSON object conforming to the schema, with no extra text, for the entity type the user specifies. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior AI integration engineer specialized in structured outputs and API contract validation. ASSUMPTIONS: if the user does not specify the model, assume compatibility with the provider's native JSON mode or structured outputs function (OpenAI/Anthropic); if no fields are indicated, request only the target entity; if no backend language is indicated, assume Python 3.11+. Request clarification only if the target entity is unclear (confidence < 0.85). INPUTS: description of the entity or a sample object pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Identify all needed fields and their data types with examples. 2. Draft the JSON Schema with type, properties, required and additionalProperties: false. 3. Write the system prompt that instructs the model to respond only with the JSON, with no preambles or explanations. 4. Add a validation block in Python using jsonschema or Pydantic that verifies the response before using it. 5. List the most common validation errors and their handling. OUTPUT: (a) complete JSON Schema in a JSON code block; (b) production-ready system prompt; (c) validation snippet in Python; (d) table of common errors and their resolution. EDGE CASES: (1) The model returns text before the JSON — solution: use a regular expression to extract the JSON block or enable native JSON mode. (2) The model omits optional fields — solution: define them in required only if mandatory; use default values in the schema. (3) The schema is too restrictive and the model cannot satisfy it — solution: relax enum or format, document the trade-off. [C · CRITERIA] The JSON Schema must be self-sufficient to validate with jsonschema 4.x. The system prompt must not mention the schema directly but the behavior rules. The snippet must raise a descriptive exception on failed validation. Trade-off: schema exhaustiveness vs. model flexibility — declare the choice explicitly. DoD: valid schema, system prompt tested with at least one example and an executable snippet with no dependencies beyond jsonschema or Pydantic.

Protocolo MetodologIA: validate the resulting JSON Schema with a sample object before closing the task.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-strea:
[S · SITUATION] You are building a user interface or a processing pipeline that needs to display or process a language model's response incrementally, token by token, instead of waiting for the full response to be available. The goal is to reduce perceived latency and enable real-time processing. [P · REQUEST] Produce the complete code and architecture for handling SSE (Server-Sent Events) streaming or the equivalent of the chosen provider, including error management, reconnection and an example of progressive rendering on the client. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior software engineer specialized in real-time AI APIs and low-latency UX. ASSUMPTIONS: if no provider is specified, use the Anthropic API with stream=True in Python; if no frontend is indicated, assume the consumer is an SSE server that forwards to the browser; if no error handling is mentioned, implement retry with exponential backoff by default. Ask only if the backend language is unclear. INPUTS: a snippet of the current model call code (if any) pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Show the basic streaming call with the provider's SDK and the event consumption loop. 2. Implement partial text accumulation and final event detection. 3. Add error handling with automatic retry on timeouts or 529 errors. 4. Show how to forward the chunks to the client via SSE or WebSocket. 5. Add an example of canceling the stream from the client. OUTPUT: (a) complete, self-contained Python module with streaming + error handling; (b) FastAPI or similar endpoint that exposes the stream to the client; (c) JavaScript snippet for browser consumption; (d) stream state flow diagram in text (start → chunk → end / error → retry). EDGE CASES: (1) The stream is interrupted midway — solution: detect premature closure, log the position and emit an error event to the client. (2) The client disconnects — solution: cancel the upstream generator so as not to waste tokens. (3) The model returns an error before streaming — solution: intercept the status code before opening the iterator. [C · CRITERIA] The module must handle all SDK event types without uncaught exceptions. The endpoint must respond with a correct Content-Type: text/event-stream. The client snippet must work with native EventSource. Trade-off: code simplicity vs. retry robustness — document the decision. DoD: code executable without modifications, tested against at least one simulated error case.

Protocolo MetodologIA: trace the flow of a chunk from the model to the browser before closing.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-fallb:
[S · SITUATION] Your application depends on a single language model as the central processing point. When that model is degraded, has high latency or the cost per token exceeds the budget threshold, there is no automatic switching mechanism: requests fail or are queued indefinitely. [P · REQUEST] Design and implement a routing and fallback system between multiple models (at least two providers or model tiers) that switches automatically based on latency, error rate or cost, with state monitoring and logging of each routing decision. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior AI systems architect specialized in resilience, dynamic routing and cost optimization in multi-model pipelines. ASSUMPTIONS: if the models are not specified, use claude-3-5-sonnet as primary and gpt-4o-mini as fallback; if the switching criterion is not indicated, use p95 latency > 3s or error rate > 10% in a 60s window; language Python 3.11 unless otherwise indicated. Ask only if the business criteria for the fallback are unclear. INPUTS: list of available models and their acceptable cost/latency limits, pasted in the chat. STEPS: 1. Define the common client interface that abstracts the provider. 2. Implement the router with a per-model circuit breaker and priority-based selection logic. 3. Add a passive health check that updates each model's state with each response. 4. Implement structured logging of each routing decision (chosen model, reason, latency, estimated cost). 5. Write unit tests that simulate the primary model's failure and verify the switch. OUTPUT: (a) architecture diagram in text/Mermaid; (b) Python module with router, circuit breaker and abstract clients; (c) YAML configuration of the routing system; (d) test suite with at least 3 failure scenarios. EDGE CASES: (1) All models fail simultaneously — solution: return a structured error with an estimated recovery time. (2) The fallback model has different capabilities (no vision, no functions) — solution: validate feature compatibility before routing. (3) The fallback costs more than the primary — solution: log the extra cost and alert if it exceeds the daily threshold. [C · CRITERIA] The circuit breaker must open in fewer than 5 consecutive failed requests. The switch must be transparent to the interface consumer. The logs must include the routing reason in JSON format. Trade-off: router complexity vs. additional response time — document the overhead. DoD: tests pass with a simulated primary model failure, an active fallback and verified logging.

Protocolo MetodologIA: run the primary model's failure scenario and confirm the fallback responds correctly before closing.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-promp:
[S · SITUATION] Your application repeatedly calls a language model with a long, static prefix (system instructions, reference documents, few-shot examples) that is repeated in every request, generating a high input-token cost. The monthly budget is being consumed mainly by repeated tokens rather than by the model's actual work. [P · REQUEST] Design the prompt caching strategy to reduce the input-token cost by at least 60%, producing the implementation code, the cache_control configuration, the expected savings calculation, and the monitoring metrics. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior AI cost-optimization engineer with experience in prompt caching architectures for Anthropic and OpenAI. ASSUMPTIONS: if the provider is not specified, use Anthropic with cache_control: {type: ephemeral}; if the request volume is not indicated, assume 1000 req/day with a 2000-token prefix; if the model is not mentioned, use claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022. Ask only if the percentage of static vs. dynamic prefix is unclear. INPUTS: the complete current prompt (system + user template) pasted into the chat. STEPS: 1. Analyze the prompt and separate the cacheable static part from the dynamic one. 2. Add the cache_control markers in the correct positions of the message. 3. Calculate the expected savings: cached_tokens × (input_price - cache_hit_price) × requests/day. 4. Implement the client with caching enabled and logging of cache_read_input_tokens vs. cache_creation_input_tokens. 5. Define the monitoring metrics: hit rate, tokens saved per day, cost avoided per day. OUTPUT: (a) Refactored prompt with cache_control markers; (b) Python client code with caching; (c) savings calculation table with scenarios (low, medium, high reuse); (d) metrics dashboard in pseudocode or logging script. EDGE CASES: (1) The static prefix changes frequently — solution: measure the effective TTL of the cache and adjust the refresh frequency; document that the first request of each window pays for creation. (2) The cache does not activate because the prefix is too short — solution: verify the minimum number of tokens required by the provider (1024 for Anthropic). (3) Multiple prefix variants — solution: parameterize the template and create a family of caches, measuring the hit rate per variant. [C · CRITERIA] The savings calculation must use the provider's current prices (state the date consulted). The target hit rate must be ≥ 80% for the optimization to be profitable. The code must log cache_read_input_tokens in every response. Trade-off: prefix rigidity vs. savings — document it explicitly. DoD: executable code, savings calculation with real numbers, and monitoring metrics defined.

MetodologIA Protocol: calculate the caching ROI with real numbers before closing the optimization.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-rate-:
[S · SITUATION] Your application makes concurrent calls to a language model's API and frequently receives 429 (Too Many Requests) or 529 (Overloaded) errors, causing cascading failures or lost requests. There is no retry logic or concurrency control, and the errors reach the end user. [P · REQUEST] Implement a complete rate limit management system with exponential backoff and jitter, concurrency control, a request queue, and throttling-event logging, so that no request is lost due to excess load. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Senior site reliability engineer (SRE) specialized in high-availability API integration and flow control. ASSUMPTIONS: if the provider is not specified, use Anthropic; default limit of 50 req/min and 100k tokens/min if the real limits are not indicated; language Python 3.11 with asyncio; maximum 3 retries before returning an error to the caller. Ask only if the target concurrency volume is unclear. INPUTS: a snippet of the current API call code and the 429 error response headers if available. STEPS: 1. Implement a retry decorator or class with exponential backoff (base 2, random jitter) and detection of the Retry-After header. 2. Add an asyncio semaphore to limit maximum concurrency according to the provider's tier. 3. Implement a priority queue for pending requests with a configurable timeout. 4. Add structured logging: each attempt, wait time, error code, and final result. 5. Write tests that simulate bursts of 429 errors and verify the retry behavior. OUTPUT: (a) Complete Python module with retry decorator and concurrency semaphore; (b) RateLimitedClient class ready to use as a wrapper for the provider's client; (c) limit configuration in YAML; (d) examples of a 429 event log in JSON format. EDGE CASES: (1) The Retry-After header comes with a very high value (>60s) — solution: respect the value but log an alert if it exceeds the acceptable SLA threshold. (2) Requests accumulate in the queue faster than they are processed — solution: implement backpressure with early rejection and a 503 code to the caller. (3) Jitter generates collisions between simultaneous workers — solution: use jitter with a seed derived from the request ID to better distribute the retries. [C · CRITERIA] The backoff must cover the interval [base^attempt * 0.5, base^attempt * 1.5] for the jitter. The request loss rate must be zero except for retry exhaustion. The logs must allow calculating the p99 of wait time. Trade-off: retry aggressiveness vs. additional pressure on the provider — document the choice. DoD: tests pass with a burst of 429s, no request lost within the retry limit, and structured logs verified.

MetodologIA Protocol: run the 429 burst test and confirm that all requests within the retry limit complete before closing.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-param:
[S · SITUATION] You are calibrating the behavior of a language model for a specific task (creative generation, data extraction, classification, reasoning) and the responses are too random, too repetitive, or do not converge to the expected format. You need to understand which sampling parameters to adjust and how to do it systematically. [P · REQUEST] Produce a practical guide for tuning temperature, top_p, top_k, and max_tokens for the specific task indicated, with the recommended values, the reasoning behind each one, an experimentation protocol, and the code to run the calibration. [E · EXECUTION] ROLE: Data scientist specialized in language model hyperparameter optimization and output quality evaluation. ASSUMPTIONS: if the task is not specified, assume generation of technical explanatory text; if the model is not indicated, use claude-3-5-sonnet; default temperature 1.0 for creative tasks and 0.0 for deterministic extraction. Ask only if the task has ambiguous quality criteria. INPUTS: description of the task, examples of good and bad outputs, and the current parameters if any. STEPS: 1. Classify the task on the deterministic-creative spectrum and select the appropriate temperature range. 2. Recommend top_p and top_k values compatible with the provider's model. 3. Calculate the appropriate max_tokens based on the expected output plus a 20% safety margin. 4. Design an A/B experiment with 3-5 parameter combinations and a set of test prompts. 5. Provide the Python code to run the experiment and compare outputs with simple metrics. OUTPUT: (a) Table of recommended parameters by task type (5 types minimum); (b) detailed reasoning for the user's specific task; (c) A/B experiment protocol with evaluation metrics; (d) Python code to run the calibration with output comparison. EDGE CASES: (1) Temperature 0.0 produces identical responses but with consistent hallucinations — solution: raise to 0.1-0.2 and add post-generation verification. (2) A very low top_p causes truncation of necessary vocabulary — solution: keep top_p >= 0.9 for tasks with specialized vocabulary. (3) Insufficient max_tokens causes truncated responses — solution: detect finish_reason: max_tokens and alert. [C · CRITERIA] The recommendations must be justified by the expected effect on the token distribution. The experiment must be reproducible with a fixed seed. The table must cover at least: extraction, classification, summarization, creative generation, and step-by-step reasoning. Trade-off: creativity vs. determinism — document the balance point for the specific task. DoD: complete table, executable code, and at least 3 A/B configurations defined with comparison metrics.

MetodologIA Protocol: run at least two configurations of the experiment and compare the outputs before recommending the final values.
spec-ia-automatizacion_integracion-multi:
